“Write like a 38-year-old Israeli woman”: The Kremlin used fake media and fabricated “experts” to spread disinformation in Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:24:02 UTC
01:24:02 KST

As Israel prepares for a key legislative election on Oct. 27, Kremlin-linked disinformation operatives in the country remain active. Their tools include not only media outlets and Telegram channels, but also a newer tactic: specially created “expert centers” that do not possess any actual expertise. Leaked files from Russia’s Social Design Agency (SDA) — described in detail in a recent investigation by The Insider — show which narratives Moscow has sought to promote in Israel and which local media outlets, influencers, rabbis, and even Knesset MPs have been drawn into the effort.
The Kremlin’s agenda in Israel
The Israeli social media space has been polluted by a range of anti-Ukrainian narratives — “NATO weapons supplied to Ukraine are ending up with Hamas!” and “Ukraine is forcibly conscripting Israeli citizens!” — which appear alongside posts from fake Ukrainian personas mocking Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claiming Ukraine had “brought the Israeli prime minister to heel” during a dispute over grain. As it turns out, the Moscow-based Social Design Agency was responsible for their creation and dissemination.
The SDA has been targeting Israel since at least early 2023. The country has a large Russian-speaking immigrant population, but the campaign was clearly intended to reach audiences beyond that community alone. Internal SDA documents connected with the international Doppelgänger campaign outlined four broad lines of messaging:
- “The war is over. The world after the war”
- “Change of government in Ukraine” — #OutgoingZelensky
- “Get America out of Europe!” — #GetAmericaOutofEurope
- “Sanctions against Russia are sanctions against the whole world. The end of the dream”
For obvious reasons, only the first two were deployed in Israel.
The SDA team was given specific performance targets, including the objective that after two months of work from the Russian side, mainstream Israeli media and online platforms would begin discussing possible postwar settlements for Ukraine, along with potential alternatives to Volodymyr Zelensky as president.
In June 2023, suggested SDA-driven article topics included:
- Undermining trust in the United States as a guarantor of Israel’s security.
- Arguing that several people in Zelensky’s circle could become Ukraine’s next president, including Valerii Zaluzhnyi, Kyrylo Budanov, Oleksii Arestovych, and even Olena Zelenska (but that only Zaluzhnyi would serve U.S. interests).
- Forecasts and parallels for Israel in the event that it supplied weapons or other aid to Kyiv.
Fake websites
The campaign did not go unnoticed. By July of 2023, intelligence officials had begun warning about Russian influence operations. Around the same time, cybersecurity company Cybereason determined that Russian propaganda and disinformation in Israel had initially been spread through X (then still known as Twitter) and Telegram.
“We uncovered the Russian government’s fake infrastructure in Israel, aimed at influencing public opinion by impersonating news websites,” Cybereason researcher Ilan Sokol said at the time. “As part of the campaign, well-known Israeli media outlets were forged. For example, the layout and content of the Walla website was copied. This was done to confuse visitors and make them believe they were on the real website.”
Impersonating legitimate media websites became a hallmark of the Doppelgänger campaign in 2022 and 2023, with Cybereason finding that websites imitating N12 and mako.co.il had also been created. Judging by the documents, in June 2023 the project was once again pitched to its client — i.e. the Kremlin — in an effort to secure an extension and increased funding.
By August, campaign planners were considering spreading graffiti and leaflets in Israel, and in September 2023, a report seeking another round of funding proposed highlighting the Israel campaign as an example of the effectiveness of the SDA’s “factory of augmented reality” — its internal term for producing fabricated content.
Then came Oct. 7, and the team developed new ideas and assignments.
How the Kremlin exploited the Oct. 7 attack
As a document dated Oct. 17, 2023 began: “There are currently several emerging trends that can be proactively developed into new and effective lines of attack. The United States is losing the remnants of its influence in the Middle East. The situation around Israel is heating up. And there is no guarantee that U.S. warnings to ‘leave Israel alone’ will be heeded. It is one thing to launch a massive missile strike and impose sanctions on two or three countries. But if the entire Arab and Muslim world is drawn into the war, this will become an extremely serious existential challenge from the Global South to the collective West. At the same time, it is obvious that the United States will leave the EU to deal with the problem on its own while taking shelter on its own continent.”
At an Oct. 20 meeting with Alexander Kharichev — a senior Kremlin official who has been linked in investigations to domestic political management and influence operations — participants proposed exploiting a statement by U.S. President Joe Biden about aid to Ukraine.
“$60 billion for Ukraine, $12 billion for Israel. We have nothing to argue with here. Talk about the shells transferred to Israel! As AXIOS writes! Push it! + they are sending 4,000 troops,” read notes from the meeting reviewed by The Insider.
The propaganda plan targeting Ukraine was adjusted at the same time.
“The U.S. redirected 155 mm shells to Israel instead of Ukraine. ‘Our’ 155 mm shells from the U.S. went to ‘them,’” one set of instructions read.
“Add examples involving aerial bombs and other weapons supplied to Israel. Emphasize the theme: ‘Why them and not us?’ They will get money/we won’t. All world leaders went to Israel, not Ukraine. Israel refused Zelensky entry, while Biden and Scholz entered the country without any problem. Western leaders are already redirecting all aid from us to the Jews, sending another aircraft carrier to Israel with more than 4,000 Marines aboard.”
Prompts intended for the authors of artificial social media comments added that the “first three narratives” should be pushed more heavily in western Ukraine “using traditional antisemitism.” Operatives were also instructed to spread rumors in Ukraine that Muslim units of the Armed Forces of Ukraine would leave to defend Palestine, as well as claims that Jewish troops were being released from the Ukrainian military to defend Israel.
When Readovka founder Alexei Kostylev joined meetings focused on disinformation in Ukraine, he suggested “planting among the Nazis” the idea that they should “go after Ze[lensky] for supporting the Jews.”
Project staff continued posting fake comments on social media.
Examples of AI prompts from April 2024 included:
“Talking points: The country is exhausted by military operations. Burnout and overwork among medical personnel are only one sign that the war has dragged on for too long. If the government had acted more decisively and wisely, and if the United States had really helped us, we would have won by now.
Write a 400-character comment from the perspective of a 38-year-old Israeli woman who believes Israel is overburdened by military spending. Medical workers are now under pressure and stress, as they were during the pandemic. The war is dragging on, and the United States is criticizing the methods used to conduct it. If the government had acted more decisively and wisely, and if the United States had truly helped us, we would have won by now.
Talking points: The government understands that it cannot solve the hostage problem and that the war is gradually reaching a dead end. The minister fled a meeting with evacuated citizens because he had nothing to tell them.
Write a 400-character comment from the perspective of a 45-year-old Israeli woman who thinks the minister is simply a coward. Instead of listening to the problems of people in need and trying to support them, he ran away! The Israeli government understands that it cannot solve the hostage problem and that the war is gradually reaching a dead end. The minister fled the meeting with evacuated citizens because he had nothing to tell them, but rushed to accuse them and call them a ‘loud minority’!”
Kremlin-sponsored content in legitimate media
In late 2023, articles that were also apparently commissioned as part of the project began appearing in genuine news outlets. Starting in November of that year, journalist Nick Kolyohin began putting out interviews in Walla with Israeli politicians, political scientists, and security experts, as well as with former hostage Roni Krivoi, who was said to have been released as a gesture of Hamas’ respect for Vladimir Putin.
Kolyohin presented the series as a joint Walla-Jerusalem Post project titled “The World on Fire,” but in violation of the outlets’ rules, he failed to disclose that the articles themselves had been sponsored by a Russian organization.
As Israeli media watchdog The Seventh Eye noted in its own investigation, the pieces were edited to emphasize themes of interest to the Kremlin, often by taking interviewees’ statements out of context.
For example, an interview with Likud lawmaker Hanoch Milwidsky was headlined: “Israel should focus on domestic affairs and avoid involvement in the Ukraine conflict.” However, in the video version of the interview, Milwidsky criticized Russia’s friendly relationship with Hamas — remarks that were omitted entirely from the published article.
The pieces were edited to emphasize themes of interest to the Kremlin
An interview with Tel Aviv University lecturer Yevgeny Klauber was edited in a similar way. In the video, viewers can hear Klauber criticizing Putin’s “disgusting statements” and even his “antisemitism.” Yet in the written version, only his criticism of the Ukrainian government remained.
The Seventh Eye’s investigation found that Kolyohin was paid for the series by an anonymous organization called the Russia-EU Communication Platform. Its website is now offline, but it previously published poorly formatted articles in Russian and English featuring experts criticizing sanctions, Ukraine, and NATO while praising Russian foreign policy. The Insider found that some of those experts were also part of the Social Design Agency’s pool of commentators.
Kolyohin, also known as Nikita Kulyukhin, was an obvious choice for promoting Russian narratives in Israel. His family moved there from St. Petersburg in 1992, when he was 9, and he speaks Hebrew, Russian, and English fluently.
A decade ago, Kolyohin worked as a special correspondent for Israel’s Channel 10, but his career there later ran into trouble when he produced an investigation into the Israeli Center for Cult Victims, eventually ending up in court after failing to disclose that it had been commissioned by Gilad But, the director of the right-wing organization Ad Kan.
In 2025, Kolyohin and a colleague were ordered to pay 755,000 shekels in damages (nearly 218,000 euros).
Kolyohin is known for more than commissioned articles. Since leaving Channel 10, he has worked mainly as a freelance reporter and regularly appears as a correspondent or “expert” in pro-Kremlin media, including on RT, Channel One, and Channel Five. Channel Five is controlled by National Media Group, whose board is chaired by Alina Kabaeva, widely reported to be Putin’s romantic partner and the mother of two of his children.
Kolyohin’s funding was most likely arranged with the help of the Social Design Agency, which actively involved him in its work. In leaked SDA correspondence, The Insider found a January 2025 proposal to bring “American Gen. Paul Vallely” into the project. As a campaign employee reported to the Kremlin:
“The speech by American Gen. Paul Vallely is ready. Script and screenshot are in the chat. Topic in brief: NATO is losing, Russia is winning. Important: Vallely is close to Trump and is perceived accordingly. Preliminary agreements have been reached with major Israeli media outlets for Vallely to publish ‘his’ experts through them. We are now preparing a letter from Vallely’s organization, the Stand Up U.S. Foundation, to the media and working out the financial arrangements. Probability of success: 90%.”
At the end of February 2025, an interview with Paul Vallely was indeed published by the Israeli radio station Galey Israel. It was summarized by none other than Nick Kolyohin, and the piece was edited much like the earlier interviews with Israeli experts — with an emphasis on narratives favored by the client.
The publication of the Hebrew-language interview then gave Russia’s state news agency TASS an opportunity to republish it less than a week later, saying that “a transcript was obtained by TASS” — without explaining where it had come from. Vallely himself later reposted the TASS text on his foundation’s website.
The main talking points argued that Trump would work with Putin to end the conflict, that “Russia will retain Ukraine’s four eastern regions,” that Zelensky would be replaced by another leader as early as 2025, that NATO would undergo fundamental changes due to the unpopularity of its policies, that the United States would sharply reduce its support for the alliance if Ukraine continued to be pushed toward membership, and that Europe would undergo a “shift to the right” that would see more leaders like Viktor Orbán come to power.
In a later conversation with OCCRP, Vallely said he did not remember giving any interview to Israeli media that he had no ties to Russia. Whether Vallely knew that his remarks would be used for Kolyohin’s Galey Israel publication remains unclear.
In 1980, Vallely, then commander of the U.S. Army’s 7th Psychological Operations Group, co-authored a paper titled “From PSYOP to MindWar: The Psychology of Victory” with his subordinate Michael Aquino, a psychological operations analyst and founder of the Satanist organization Temple of Set. In a preface to a 2003 reissue, Aquino noted that the paper had become a popular subject of conspiracy theories.
In 2005, Vallely founded the conservative organization Stand Up America US. It advocates for a strong national defense, secure borders, state sovereignty, support for the armed forces, limited government, and the protection of Americans’ First and Second Amendment rights. According to the organization’s co-founder, retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Thomas McInerney, its purpose is to defend the United States and explain the dangers of radical Islam and global jihad.
In 2010, Vallely was one of three retired generals who supported U.S. Army Lt. Col. Terrence Lakin, who refused deployment to Afghanistan on the grounds that Barack Obama was not a legitimate commander in chief. Vallely said at the time that many military personnel and civilians doubted Obama had been born in the United States, describing him as “a Muslim by nature” while refusing to rule out the possibility of a “civil uprising” against a president he accused of helping spread radical Islam.
Vallely has also voiced support for the QAnon movement, describing it as a “white hat” operation linked to a group of more than 800 military intelligence specialists advising the president. He has called Q posts a credible source of intelligence.
In 2020, Vallely was among 235 senior military figures who endorsed Donald Trump’s reelection.
Vallely has also visited Russia. He traveled there for Victory Day celebrations in 2014 and was in Moscow again in February and March 2017.
Who was behind the Israeli disinformation campaign
The project was led by Ilya Gambashidze, with Andrei Perla and Alexei Ulyanov serving as ideologues. Both also work for the Tsargrad media group, a Russian ultraconservative, pro-Kremlin media organization.
In the early 2010s, Perla worked as an aide to Igor Kholmanskikh, then the Russian president’s envoy to the Urals Federal District. In 2016, he became head of the Sevastopol government’s public communications department, but he did not remain in the position for long. After dismissing Gambashidze, Sevastopol’s acting governor tasked his successor with “correcting the mistakes accumulated by the department.” Despite that episode, the political consultant still describes himself as “the smart Jew at the governor’s side.”
Perla now works on ideological messaging for fake-content campaigns around the world. In November 2023, the U.S. State Department accused him of involvement in influence operations as far away as South America. Within the Doppelgänger campaign, he produces analysis and sociological material and supervises several staff members.
Alexei Ulyanov is an “advertising and PR specialist” from Tver. He once worked at a creative studio called “The Secret of the Selling Word,” was later declared wanted over unpaid child support, and then began working with the Social Design Agency as head of its writing team. That work led to his inclusion on a British sanctions list in 2025.
Alexander Balakshin handled operational planning and studied social media in Israel and other countries. Anastasia Kazakova served as head of social media operations. And Oleg Perelman translated texts into Hebrew. (Material was also translated into Arabic, but that translator’s identity is unknown.)
For the project, the SDA compiled a list of Israeli media outlets and experts through whom its preferred narratives might be promoted. It is not known with certainty how the list was used or whether any of the outlets or channels received payment for publications. The list is reproduced below:
Russian-language Israeli media targeted for work, including publication placements, comments, and expert opinions
- Novosti Israel — https://nikk.agency/
- Moskovsky Komsomolets — Israel — https://mkisrael.co.il/
- Novosti Izrailya — https://news.israelinfo.co.il/
- Isroil Information Center — https://isroil.info/
- ISRAland — Israeli News — https://isra.land/
Inauthentic comments were posted under messages in Telegram channels such as “Voice of Israel. Israel Now,” “Israel in Russian,” “Israeli Working Days,” and “Intellinews — Israel and the Middle East,” as well as channels run by political analysts Mikhail Pellivert, Mark Kotlyarsky, and David Eidelman.
As in SDA campaigns targeting Ukraine and various EU countries, for reporting purposes operators saved links to each posted comment and stored screenshots in a separate folder on Yandex Disk.
Russian émigrés in Israel as an influence target
The project produced several pitches aimed at shaping opinion among Russian émigrés who had left the country after the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Many of the proposals were likely approved, although perhaps not with full funding.
Particular attention was paid to the Russian diaspora in Israel. One internal proposal read:
“A significant group of émigrés settled in Israel. It is the only country where the number of ‘relocants’ can be reliably estimated on the basis of local official statistics.
Israel has received more than 60,000 Russian citizens since the start of the ‘special military operation.’ All these people now already have dual citizenship because, having Jewish roots, they exercised their right of return.
It is important to note that in Israel, new émigrés immediately found themselves in a specific environment with diverse political views.
The total number of Russian-speaking Israeli citizens is approximately 2 million to 2.5 million people, or more than 20% of the country’s population. This population has its own media, including several Russian-language television channels, radio stations, online media outlets, new media and Telegram channels.
Not all of these media can be considered anti-Russian. On the contrary, pro-Russian sentiment is quite widespread in Israel. According to a recent Pew Research Center poll, at least 16% of respondents in Israel trust Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Clearly, the goals of informational influence on the émigré community should be structured as follows:
1. Shift the attitudes of the majority of émigrés in a pro-Russian direction
- create a pro-Russian diaspora capable of influencing public opinion in host countries;
- increase the number of ‘frightened patriots’ who want and are prepared to return to the Motherland.
2. Discredit active anti-Russian émigrés in the eyes of the broader community of ‘relocated citizens,’ including by
- provoking divisions among the most active anti-Russian figures.
It appears that the best way to achieve these goals would be to create a group of media outlets aimed at émigré audiences.
These media outlets should not be formally connected to Russian state structures. Some of their representatives should themselves live in emigration and participate in events organized by émigré centers, conferences and so on.
Some of these media outlets should target Russian-speaking diasporas as a whole, while others should be geographically focused, above all on Israel, Turkey, Georgia, Armenia and Kazakhstan.”
How the Kremlin created fake “expert centers”
Participants in the Doppelgänger project proposed setting up nonprofit organizations in different countries that would resemble research institutes. The idea was to use them to recruit international experts and promote narratives useful to the campaign.
For example, the SDA requested $80,000 to launch a nonprofit in Israel, plus about 3 million rubles a month ($36,500) “for content creation, work with opinion leaders, and promotion.” It requested even more for an “Institute of Anti-Globalism, writing that “This project costs 5 million rubles a month” — upwards of $61,000.
Nikolai Tupikin also drafted what he called “a justification for strengthening and expanding the project with Israeli colonels from various intelligence services,” presenting the initiative as a form of Russian soft power.
In an apparent effort to justify the project to the Kremlin, the document stated: “Russian information warfare, through interference campaigns, helps Russia preserve its image as a superpower in a cost-effective way. The more Russia participates in active interference campaigns around the world, the stronger its image as a global power.”
An expanded presentation for the proposed Israeli institute said that “our narratives lack a legitimate source of information and a news hook,” but that “in Europe and other Western countries, the narratives we need already exist and enjoy sustained popularity.”
The project appears to have been approved by the Kremlin. In February 2025, someone acquired the domain ibi.institute (which had previously belonged to Instituto Iberoamericano), and used it to create a website for an entity called the International Burke Institute — IBI.
The website listed the United Nations office, UNICEF, UNESCO, the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), and the World Bank as partners. All of them told The Insider in response to inquiries that they were not and had never been partners of IBI.
The website, unsurprisingly, contained no reference to any connection between IBI and Russian experts. Nor did it provide an official address, information about its founders, or details about its financing.
As the disinformation specialists had promised in their pitch to the Kremlin, the site published “economic and political reviews of the country of the month.” In practice, however, reviews were produced for all countries at once in the form of a “sovereignty index.”
Judging by their style and language, the articles were generated using large language models and were almost certainly translated into English from Russian. They contained mistakes characteristic of machine translation or careless Russian-to-English work.
For example, an article about Russia referred to “Lugovoy’s Law (2020),” describing how “he consolidated…” — in English, unlike in Russian, a law would be referred to as “it,” not “he.”
Additionally, an article about the United States used the phrase “guerrilla struggle” where the intended meaning was “partisan struggle” — in the political sense of conflict between parties. The error reflects the fact that the Russian word partizansky can refer both to partisan politics and guerrilla warfare.
The reports also contained signs of AI-generated hallucinations, citing nonexistent UNESCO heritage sites such as “Gerngut” in Germany and “Imbargo” in the United States. Neither exists.
The IBI also claimed that Russia ranked 27th in a 2023 PISA study, even though no such PISA assessment was conducted that year. (The latest study available when the reports were prepared was conducted in 2022, and Russia did not participate.)
In August 2026, OpenAI published the results of an internal investigation showing that IBI content had in fact been produced using the company’s systems and that the operation was run by users in Russia. OpenAI blocked the group of ChatGPT accounts involved.
Although the IBI website was filled with generated content and false claims about institutional partners, the organization itself was indeed registered in Israel in July 2025. Its founders were Igor Kaminnik and Gabriel Mart, and board members with signing authority were Alexei Vilents and Roy Yaakov Yankelovich. The Insider has copies of the organization’s founding documents.
Igor Semyonovich Kaminnik is an Israeli citizen originally from Odesa, Ukraine. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, he was part of a circle of Odesa conceptual artists and belonged to the P. Fomsky collective, along with artist Pavel Fomenko. In the early 2000s, Kaminnik was involved in various civic organizations in Ukraine. In recent years, however, he has adopted a sharply pro-Russian position. “When he talks about Ukraine, it is nothing but Russian propaganda clichés,” a person who knows him personally told The Insider.
Kaminnik is listed as an expert with the Institute of the Newest States, a Russian organization founded by political analysts Modest Kolerov and Alexei Martynov.
Kolerov was the first head of the Kremlin’s Directorate for Interregional and Cultural Relations with Foreign Countries, created in 2005 as part of an effort to counter so-called “velvet revolutions,” the peaceful pro-democracy uprisings that had taken place across parts of the former Soviet bloc.
Martynov has spent about two decades in positions connected with Russian policy toward the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), a grouping of former Soviet republics. During that time, he has been declared persona non grata in Azerbaijan and Moldova.
Kolerov, meanwhile, has been barred for more than a decade from entering Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia, and Georgia.
In 2023, Kaminnik made repeated trips to Russia, including with his wife, Yulia Vasilyeva, and their daughter Tatyana.
Gabriel Mart sits on IBI’s audit committee and also serves with another organization, the Sholem Schwartzbard Memorial Foundation, named in honor of the Jewish writer and anarchist who assassinated Ukrainian political leader Symon Petliura in Paris in May 1926. In 2024, Mart participated in an IBI roundtable titled “The Heuristic Potential of Schizoanalysis,” where he was presented as a researcher at the Catholic University of the West. In one publication listing him as an employee of the university, The Insider found Mart’s other name: Innokenty Martynov.
Notably, Alexei Martynov’s real-life son — Innokenty Martynov — also works with Kaminnik. He travels frequently to Israel and has published several articles on psychoanalysis at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Anthropology and Ethnography under his Russian name.
Kaminnik also sits on the board of Israeli nonprofit Dor Moriah. The organization takes its name from a small street in Haifa near Kaminnik’s home and is registered at his residential address.
Dor Moriah also presents itself as a research center. Even its Russian-language website has a section labeled in English as a “think tank.” It contains articles with titles such as “Turkey is waging cognitive warfare against Israel in a format described in the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry’s communications strategy” and “How the opposition constructs a rejection of election results.”
Dor Moriah also publishes polling and sociological research, including on issues not obviously central to Israeli domestic politics, such as the Putin-Trump meeting in Anchorage.
Dor Moriah was founded in 2017, but it only began receiving substantial income — nearly 200,000 shekels annually ($64,000) — in 2023, the same year the SDA’s campaign in Israel began.
Its annual revenue in 2025 was almost 195,000 shekels, all of it from foreign donations. Israeli law requires disclosure only of donors who contribute at least 50,000 shekels during a reporting period.
In 2023, there were two such donors: Panagiotis Glazko, a Cyprus-based businessman with Greek citizenship, and a U.S. donor named Alan Licht.
In 2024, the only major donor was Israeli citizen Dan Piotkin. In other organizational documents, Piotkin is also listed as a member of Dor Moriah’s supervisory board and a co-author of its research.
Notably, Dor Moriah’s annual budgets vary substantially when measured in shekels. Converted into rubles at the exchange rate for each respective year, however, they come to roughly the same amount: 4.5 million rubles.
The governing party’s leading Russian-speaking rabbi
In April 2024, Dor Moriah announced the creation of a movement called Derech Eretz.
According to the official account, it was co-founded by Dor Moriah, the Sholem Schwartzbard Foundation, and an association called Turei Zahav, which has since been dissolved. Turei Zahav was headed by Rabbi Alexander Hayat, who in April 2024 became head of Derech Eretz.
Around the same time, Hayat posted several photographs with Kaminnik on Facebook.
Among Russian-speaking Israelis, Hayat is known primarily as head of the Russian-speaking branch of United Torah Judaism, one of Israel’s two ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties in the governing coalition. It is in that capacity that he gives interviews and participates in election events.
In Hebrew-language political circles, however, Hayat has been described as “the rabbi for immigrants from Russia in Likud,” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s party. In September 2025, the bar mitzvah of Hayat’s son was attended by Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, Justice Minister Yariv Levin, Environmental Protection Minister Idit Silman, coalition chairman Ofir Katz, Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee chairman Boaz Bismuth, and lawmakers Ariel Kallner and Osher Shkalim. Silman’s presence was not incidental: Hayat also serves as one of her advisers.
Meluhadim News, a Telegram channel close to Likud, regularly reports on Hayat’s work with the Russian-speaking community. In January 2026, he organized the enrollment of 100 Russian-speaking immigrants into the party. In the summer of 2025, he ran a campaign to recruit dozens of Russian speakers to Likud.
By May 2026, Hayat was being described as head of Likud’s Russian-speaking campaign headquarters. He led a meeting between Russian-speaking opinion leaders and Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, along with ministers Yariv Levin, Eli Cohen, Shlomo Karhi, and Zeev Elkin, and coalition chairman Ofir Katz.
Notably, by November 2025, Hayat was no longer attending internal Likud conferences in his personal capacity alone. By then, a group called Derech Eretz — “Russian Mobilization,” headed by Hayat — was participating in at least one such party conference.
Several independent sources confirmed Hayat’s cooperation with Igor Kaminnik to The Insider. One source said Kaminnik had claimed he paid Hayat a salary, an assertion that is indirectly supported by Dor Moriah’s reporting, which lists Derech Eretz activities among the organization’s work.
Dor Moriah’s 2025 annual report lists its areas of activity. In addition to conducting eight sociological studies, writing 15 analytical reports, and publishing 30 media pieces, the organisation also reported that “three open sessions and five working meetings were held in the Knesset devoted to promoting legislation regulating the activities of neighborhood councils in Israeli cities,” and it was also involved in ”development of the Derech Eretz movement, bringing together secular and religious Russian-speaking Israelis: eight working meetings with activists were held and recommendations were prepared for implementing projects at the local community level.”
In other words, work with the movement headed by Likud-linked Rabbi Hayat was listed as one of Dor Moriah’s core activities.
Both Kaminnik and the Burke Institute have also promoted Hayat’s work. Roy Yankelovich, head of the “institute” — and, in his day job, an Israeli sports journalist — wrote an opinion column about Hayat and Derech Eretz for TheJ.ca. Kaminnik, meanwhile, wrote about the movement in the Jerusalem Post, where he described his Dor Moriah nonprofit as Derech Eretz’s research center.
In the summer of 2025, businessman Yossi Prisman, from Samaria, helped Hayat establish a Derech Eretz youth organization. The two later fell out and are now suing each other. Prisman immediately recognized Kaminnik in a photograph.
“Hayat wasn’t paying his coordinators. When one of them asked him about the money, he pointed at Igor [Kaminnik] and said Igor would pay,” Prisman said.
One employee hired for the project has accused Hayat of failing to pay his wages. He told The Insider that the goal of the project was to create a nationwide Israeli political organization for young people with Russian roots. According to the source, Kaminnik attended one of the meetings. Another Dor Moriah representative, Alexei Vilents, a former municipal lawmaker in Moscow, also participated in events.
As part of the youth project, Derech Eretz organized a tour of Samaria for about 50 young people. It also held a wine evening with Russian-speaking businesspeople.
Lobbyists in the Knesset
Dor Moriah also works with sitting members of Israel’s parliament. In March 2025, the organization held a conference titled “Israel as an object of geopolitical confrontation.” Participants included Likud lawmaker Amit Halevi, Shas lawmaker Simon Moshiashvili, and Knesset Deputy Speaker Moshe Solomon of the Religious Zionism party. All three were members of the governing coalition at the time.
Lawmakers and other participants were told that “among world leaders capable of influencing the development of the Abraham Accords, aside from Donald Trump, Israelis primarily named representatives of BRICS countries: 28.9% named Vladimir Putin, 17% Xi Jinping, and 13.9% Narendra Modi.” They were also told that “70% of Israelis see a connection between the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the global confrontation between the West and the South.”
Coalition lawmakers even skipped a Knesset plenary session at which Netanyahu was speaking in order to attend the event. “The fact that these lawmakers left an important plenary meeting attended by the prime minister in order to attend a lobby meeting convincingly demonstrates the importance of the issues under discussion and the relevance of the initiatives being proposed,” Dor Moriah wrote.
The parliamentary lobby was registered by Amit Halevi. It is intended to promote three largely unrelated issues: creating neighborhood councils in Israeli citie, halachic banking (a system of financial services structured to comply with Jewish religious law, broadly analogous in concept to Islamic banking), and the idea of Israel’s future as “a bridge between the collective West and the Global South.”
The three open sessions and five working meetings in the Knesset mentioned in Dor Moriah’s annual report apparently referred to these initiatives.

Municipality of Ferrara launches 'Anti-Maranza Unit'
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:23:01 CEST
01:23:01 KST

In the northern Italian city of Ferrara, the "NAM" (Anti-Maranza Unit) has been established—a task force created by the municipal government of this Emilian city to combat the phenomenon, serving as the first experiment of its kind nationwide, announced Mayor Alan Fabbri of the right-wing League party. 
Maranzas are disaffected youth, often second-generation Italians of North African heritage, who affect wannabe gangsta rapper garb and engage in street crime, most recently in shocking youth riots in Milan last weekend. 
The NAM will see the Municipality of Ferrara take the lead, involving lawyers, psychologists, social workers, local police, and security experts, Fabbri said. 
The announcement comes in light of recent news events that have led to devastation in various Italian cities, such as those seen in Bologna and Milan. 
The unit will focus on prevention, as well as "monitoring and enforcement." Fabbri said he was responding to the concerns of families and business owners. 
The government's new decree in response to the youth street violence also targets maranzas.
"I had already raised the alarm about the 'maranza' some time ago," the mayor explains, "because we recognized it as an issue that could not be downplayed—one that had to be addressed.
And that is exactly what will happen in Ferrara: in the coming weeks, the 'NAM'—the Anti-Maranza Unit—will become operational.
The Municipality of Ferrara will be at the forefront of this initiative, which will also involve lawyers, psychologists, social workers, the local police, and security experts." "This operational unit, which will focus on prevention, monitoring, and enforcement, is also intended to provide a concrete response to the concerns that have emerged recently," he continues.
"With this, Ferrara is responding—through tangible action—to the pleas for help and support from many parents, families, and business owners who are fearful due to the growing sense of insecurity, aggressive behavior, and a blatant disregard for the property and well-being of others."

US to provide up to $389M for semiconductor research, development
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:22:21 UTC
01:22:21 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The US Commerce Department said Thursday it plans to provide up to $389 million in research and development funding to four companies working on power semiconductors and critical materials, including technologies designed to support fusion energy and advanced data centers.
The awards, announced through letters of intent under the CHIPS and Science Act, aim to strengthen domestic production capabilities and reduce reliance on overseas suppliers for components essential to the country's energy infrastructure, it said.
“The Trump Administration is accelerating American semiconductor innovation to enhance our domestic energy and power resources,” said Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. “These investments expand domestic research, secure critical supply chains, and create high-paying American jobs.”
Fusion energy companies Helion and Commonwealth Fusion Systems are among the intended recipients.
Helion could receive up to $175 million to develop high-voltage semiconductors and power modules for fusion generators, while Commonwealth Fusion Systems is set to receive up to $85 million for technologies used in plasma heating, fusion diagnostics and radiation-resistant electronics.
Vertical Semiconductor could receive up to $73 million to advance gallium nitride power semiconductors for advanced computing, including a demonstration project targeting a 2.5-megawatt data center rack.
Materials supplier Sibelco is slated for up to $56 million to develop purification technologies for ultra-high-purity quartz used in semiconductor manufacturing.
The agency said improved power electronics could increase energy efficiency, strengthen grid stability and reduce heat losses, supporting growing electricity demand from data centers and other critical infrastructure.
Bill Frauenhofer, the agency’s executive director of semiconductor investment and innovation, said the awards would help advance technologies for the grid, defense systems and emerging fusion energy.

UN expert urges Indonesia to reconsider involvement in Trump's Gaza board

Breadcrumb
UN expert urges Indonesia to reconsider involvement in Trump's Gaza board
Indonesia should reconsider its involvement in US President Donald Trump's Gaza peace plan because it is being shaped by Israel and the US and lacks a Palestinian voice, the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights in the occupied Palestinian territories told Reuters on Thursday.
The "Board of Peace," of which Indonesia is a key troop-contributing member, was unveiled by Trump in January to address global conflicts typically handled by the United Nations. The world's largest Muslim-majority nation has also pledged troops to be deployed to Gaza as part of an international stabilisation force.
Francesca Albanese, a prominent human rights lawyer known for her vocal criticism of Israel, said in an interview in Jakarta that Indonesia has historically supported the Palestinian cause, but joining the board was dangerous.
Indonesia's Foreign Ministry said on Thursday that Board of Peace discussions remained on hold, reiterating its earlier position.
Albanese has drawn the ire of a number of Western capitals. The US has imposed sanctions on her, and others, including her own native Italy, have called for her resignation.
"I understand (Indonesia's) good intentions. I still think that it's very dangerous, because it risks to normalise a very abnormal mechanism," she said.
Albanese said that, legally, Israel could not have a role in determining the future of Palestinians.
Rights experts have criticised the board for not including a Palestinian representative even though it is meant to supervise the temporary governance of a Palestinian territory.
The Board of Peace did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside US business hours.
Indonesia, which backs a two-state solution and has repeatedly condemned Israeli violence, has drawn criticism from domestic Muslim groups for agreeing to join the board, which also counts Israel as a member.
President Prabowo Subianto has vowed to quit if it does not bring benefits to Palestinians, his office has previously said, adding that joining the board would allow Indonesia to push for cessation of violence.
Albanese said Indonesia risked compromising its close ties with Palestinians. "It's very risky to do so when the rules are set by Israel," she said.
Albanese recommended Jakarta join the Hague Group of countries, which includes South Africa and Indonesia's neighbour Malaysia and seeks to uphold international law and processes, including in the International Criminal Court over Israel's actions.
Trump's Gaza plan has stalled. A 2025 ceasefire secured the release of the remaining captives held by Hamas and hundreds of Palestinian detainees, but efforts to disarm Hamas and secure an Israeli withdrawal have faltered, while Israeli forces continue near-daily attacks in Gaza.

UK rejects Witkoff’s characterization of Putin as “humanitarian”
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's Spokeswoman, Cat Simmons, said this, Bloomberg reports, according to Ukrinform.
“We certainly do not recognize that characterization. Ukraine Destroys Elusive North Korean Koksan Supergun in Operation Vivaldi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:20:20 UTC
01:20:20 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Destroys Elusive North Korean Koksan Supergun in Operation Vivaldi
Ukrainian drone operators from the 3rd Army Corps destroyed a North Korean-made Koksan self-propelled artillery system in the Donetsk region during Operation Vivaldi, according to footage released by Ukraine’s 60th Separate Mechanized Brigade on October 22.
The strike was carried out by operators from the brigade’s Fatum unit, which published a new compilation showing attacks on Russian equipment and personnel.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Hellish autumn notes of ‘Vivaldi.’ Operators of Fatum from the 60th Separate Mechanized Brigade burned a North Korean Koksan self-propelled gun, as well as several vehicles. In addition, quad bikes and buggies were destroyed, along with enemy infantry moving on them. The pilots of the Troika continue to erase the enemy,” the brigade said.
The Koksan is North Korea’s longest-range conventional tube-artillery system and one of the most unusual weapons Pyongyang has supplied to Russia. Western intelligence first identified the system in 1979 near the North Korean city of Koksan, which later gave the artillery piece its commonly used Western name.
The original M1978 Koksan can reportedly strike targets at ranges of up to roughly 40 kilometers with standard ammunition and as far as 60 kilometers with rocket-assisted shells. Its rate of fire is relatively slow at around one to two rounds every five minutes, but its long reach allows it to operate well behind the immediate front line.
The weapon’s gun is mounted in an open configuration, providing little protection for its estimated four-to-six-person crew.
The earlier model also requires a separate vehicle to carry ammunition because of the size of the weapon and its shells, while the later M1989 variant can carry around 12 rounds onboard.
The Koksan has combat history dating back decades. North Korea supplied the system to Iran, where it was used during the Iran-Iraq War and gained a reputation as an effective long-range counter-battery weapon.
Earlier, Ukrainian drone operators destroyed four North Korean–made M1989 Koksan self-propelled artillery systems deployed by Russian forces.
The mission was carried out by the 412th Nemesis Regiment, which used both bomber drones and FPV drones to strike the weapons.

13 far-right militants' convictions upheld for Fascist salutes at Ramelli march
Court of Cassation rejects appeals, four-month sentences confirmed
ROME,
22 October 2026, 18:18
ANSA English Desk
Share
Link copiato
- ALL RIGHTS RESERVED
The supreme Court of Cassation on Thursday rejected the appeals and finalized four-month suspended prison sentences for 13 far-right militants who performed Fascist salutes during an annual march in Milan on April 29, 2018 commemorating Sergio Ramelli, an 18-year-old member of the neofascist youth group Fronte della Gioventù (Youth Front) who was killed by the far-left group Avanguardia Operaia in 1975. Ramelli was brutally attacked with iron bars and wrenches in March 1975 and died 47 days later. His case remains a prominent event from Italy's Anni di Piombo (Years of Lead) of rightist and leftist terrorism. The defendants were charged with engaging in a fascist demonstration, in violation of Article 5 of the Scelba Law banning the reconstitution of Mussolini's Fascist Party.
There have been contradictory rulings on Fascist salutes in Italy in recent years with them often going unpunished if adjudged merely commemorative.

Poland paired with County Donegal for Ireland's EU presidency
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:17:10 CEST
01:17:10 KST

Poland paired with County Donegal for Ireland's EU presidency
As part of the County Pairings Programme, which matched each of Ireland's 26 counties with an EU member state, the north-western County Donegal, a home to just over 161,000 people, was paired with Poland until the end of December.
Thanks to the initiative of the Irish authorities and the efforts of the Polish Embassy in Dublin, the pairing has helped raise awareness in Ireland of Pawel Strzelecki, a largely forgotten Polish hero of the Great Irish Famine. The unveiling of a commemorative plaque at a school in Donegal brought the achievements of the Polish explorer, geographer and philanthropist to the attention of local residents for the first time in 178 years.
In Poland, Strzelecki is best known for naming Australia's highest mountain Mount Kosciuszko in 1840, in honour of the Polish national hero Tadeusz Kosciuszko, whom he admired throughout his life. Strzelecki was the first Pole to undertake a scientific expedition around the world, travelling through both the Americas, the Pacific region, Australia and Tasmania. He also played a remarkable role in Irish history.
During the Great Irish Famine, Strzelecki worked on the island as a volunteer for a British humanitarian organisation. By introducing an innovative food distribution system centred on schools, he helped save the lives of as many as 200,000 children, both Catholic and Protestant.
The Polish explorer and philanthropist visited famine-stricken Ireland twice, working without pay out of a deep sense of compassion and duty. His efforts focused on three counties: Donegal, Mayo and Sligo.
Remembering Strzelecki sheds light on a different chapter in Ireland's history, highlighting the compassion and dedication of a Polish volunteer who devoted himself to helping Irish families through one of the darkest periods in the country's past. His legacy stands as a powerful testament to the solidarity that can transcend national, religious and political divides. (PAP)

The army’s 4th Infantry Division said in a statement that its forces had recaptured the Bakouri and Akleili areas following military operations that inflicted heavy losses in personnel and equipment on opposing forces.

In a separate statement, Sudanese army spokesman Asim Awad said air defenses had shot down a “hostile strategic drone” near Bakouri on Thursday morning.
Awad said the military had tracked the aircraft since it crossed into Sudan from Ethiopia, without identifying the party operating it.

The state has witnessed escalating clashes in recent weeks between the army and the allied forces.
Sudan has been engulfed in fighting between the army and the RSF since April 2023 over disagreements concerning the integration of the paramilitary group into the military. Partner countries (NATO members and other states) make voluntary financial contributions to joint funding packages. With the funds received, the United States will transfer the necessary weapons to Ukraine directly from its own stockpiles

MEPs call for Yemen's Houthis to be added to EU terrorist list
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:16:04 UTC
01:16:04 KST

A non-binding European Parliament resolution urges a freeze on all the Yemeni group's funds, as the EU struggles to counter the threat to civilian maritime traffic in the Red Sea.
The European Parliament on Thursday approved a resolution calling for Yemen's Houthis to be added to the EU’s list of terrorist organisations.
The call follows an escalation in recent weeks of attacks on Saudi Arabia by the Iran-backed group, which prompted the UK to pledge defensive missions to protect Riyadh, while the EU struggles to increase its naval presence in the Red Sea to shield commercial vessels from possible attacks.
The non-binding text, adopted by a large majority of MEPs in a show of hands, urged the freezing of all funds and economic resources belonging to the Houthis and their facilitators.
Inclusion on the EU terrorist list mainly entails financial restrictions — freezing all bank accounts and property held in EU countries, and banning EU individuals and companies from financing the listed group.
The final decision rests with the EU member states, which must approve any new listing unanimously.
The European Parliament justified its request by condemning the Houthi naval blockade of Saudi Arabia and their attacks on energy infrastructure and commercial shipping in the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb strait, which are severely disrupting maritime traffic and driving up energy prices in the region.
The resolution describes the attacks as flagrant violations of international law, stressing that many Yemeni civilians have been killed and displaced, and that the country’s humanitarian crisis has deepened since the latest attacks.
The group formally known as Ansar Allah, which has been at war with the internationally recognised government of Yemen since 2014, launched a blitz offensive along the Red Sea coast in July to take control of the vital waterway crucial to the world's energy and cargo shipping.
A counteroffensive by the Saudi-led coalition saw much of the gains made by the Houthis reversed, but the group still poses a threat to international vessels traversing the strait that links Europe and Asia.
The Houthis have pledged safe passage to all ships bar those linked to Saudi Arabia, while continuing their attacks against energy infrastructure and airports across the neighbouring kingdom.
MEPs also stressed the crucial role of Aspides, the EU naval mission in the Red Sea, and urged member states to provide additional naval and air assets.
The mission currently has three ships from Italy and Greece, with two more pledged by Belgium and the Netherlands. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has said at least 10 are needed.

BRUSSELS, Belgium — Restrictions against Russian refineries and oil export terminals loom large in a new set of EU draft sanctions listings, first presented to EU ambassadors on Oct. 21 and seen by the Kyiv Independent.
The EU's diplomatic arm, the EEAS, "proposed 117 additional listings targeting sectors which raise revenue for Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine, such as the financial sector, energy sector, and the Russian shadow fleet," an Irish Council Presidency spokesperson told journalists.
The draft document lists 12 individuals and 105 entities, which, if adopted, would subject them to a transaction ban with the EU and a freeze on any assets they hold in the bloc. Being a sanctioned entity can also make it hard to do business with companies in third countries, which don't want to risk their own commercial ties with the EU.
A key focus of the latest proposed sanctions listings is Russia's oil processing, refining, and exporting capacity, with 31 listings spanning the breadth of Russia, from St. Petersburg to Sakhalin.
The EEAS' proposal of those listings is especially timely, coming barely two weeks after U.S. President Donald Trump agreed to import diesel — itself a refined oil product — from Russia.
That deal, and the U.S.' wider attitude change to Ukraine, led to widespread condemnation from EU leaders when they met in Brussels on Oct. 15-16.
"We see that we have to pressure the aggressor to stop the war, not the victim to surrender," said the EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas, who oversees the bloc's sanctions.
The other listings included 52 banking and financial institutions, two entities that process Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG), and a steel company operating from Russian-occupied territory in Donetsk Oblast.
The EU has also sanctioned entities in several third countries that have been helping Moscow evade sanctions, 12 in the United Arab Emirates alone, and other listings for companies based in Oman, Singapore, Hong Kong, and the Seychelles.
Also likely to be of interest are some of the 12 individuals sanctioned by the EU, which have ties to e-commerce platforms Ozon and Wildberries, which have been trading in products that help Russia's military effort, as well as Moscow's internet search engine Yandex.
All three companies have been targets of successful Ukrainian military strikes.
Finally, the EU is preparing to apply sanctions to a further 15 companies belonging to Russia's military-industrial complex, and to remove one entity in a third country because "the entity has ceased the activity which led to its inclusion in the list and has committed to refrain from any such activity in the future," reads the EU's draft legal text.
The next step is for the listings to be scrutinized by sanctions experts appointed by the 27 EU countries. After that, the list returns to ambassadors for approval, and then to ministers for a final vote.

Voters prioritise costs, Iran over investigating Trump for next Congress, poll finds
Regardless of the outcome of the 3 November election, a new AP-NORC poll shows voters from both major political parties want the next Congress to focus on making life more affordable and ending the war in Iran, while fewer are looking for an emphasis on President Donald Trump — whether it's investigating him or supporting his agenda.
The results suggest that voters are ready for Congress to tackle core issues, despite Trump’s centrality in the midterm campaign.
About 8 in 10 registered voters, including a large majority of Republicans and Democrats, say lowering the cost of living should be one of the highest priorities for the session coming up, the survey from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds.
Justin Campbell, a 31-year-old Democrat from Brookhaven, Mississippi, said he wants the government to focus on helping people like him rather than wealthy people.
“I’m not a millionaire and probably won’t ever be," he said. "I prefer policy that helps me instead of someone I’ll never be.”
Most voters also want Congress to prioritise ending the war with Iran, with roughly 7 in 10 saying this should be a top focus. Substantially fewer voters, about 4 in 10, want Congress to make investigating the Trump administration a high priority, and only about 2 in 10 want Congress to prioritise supporting the Republican president's agenda.
But the poll also indicates that there are deep divisions within the parties on what to focus on, with moderate Democrats and Republicans differing sharply from voters on the left and right wings of their parties.
Most Democratic voters who identify as supporters of democratic socialism are hoping for a Congress that will investigate the administration, and many want to end military aid to Israel, while MAGA Republicans are interested in Congress supporting Trump’s agenda.
Moderates in both parties, are much more likely to want Democrats and Republicans to find common ground.
Lowering the cost of living and ending the Iran war overshadow a wide range of other issues as voters consider priorities for the next Congress.
While most registered voters say reducing costs and ending the war should be among the highest priorities for Congress, only about half say reducing the budget deficit and finding common ground between the two parties should be high priorities. About 4 in 10 want investigating the administration and passing new laws regulating artificial intelligence to be high priorities.
Fewer, about 3 in 10, prioritise ending military aid to Israel, and only about 2 in 10 want a focus on supporting Trump's agenda.
Though most registered Democrats want Congress to investigate the administration, that falls behind the larger priorities of lowering costs and ending the conflict with Iran. About 6 in 10 registered voters who identify as Democrats call investigations into the administration “one of the highest priorities.”
Arthur Brown, a 71-year-old Democrat in Magee, Mississippi, wants to see the next Congress work on making the economy stronger and prices lower. He feels less urgency about holding Trump accountable, mostly because there will be only two years left in Trump’s term. He thinks it’s more important to try to turn the economy around.
“They should just focus on, you know, trying to tackle these problems,” he said. “Eventually down the road, justice will come.”
For Republican voters, bolstering Trump's goals also falls behind lowering the cost of living, ending the war in Iran and reducing the budget deficit.
In a strikingly tepid show of support for the president, only about 4 in 10 Republican voters say the next Congress should make supporting the administration's agenda one of its highest priorities.
House Democrats have begun planning an ambitious 100-day agenda for what they would do if they win control of Congress in November. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York has said the party's top priorities include making life more affordable and conducting vast oversight of the administration.
But there are potential schisms in the party awaiting Democrats if they win a governing majority. The Democratic Party has reckoned in primary campaigns with a growing wing of democratic socialists. Their progressive stances on some issues have divided the party — including on whether to continue military aid to Israel, whether to compromise with Republicans and how strongly to investigate the administration.
About three-quarters of Democratic voters who identify as supporters of democratic socialism say one of the top priorities should be investigating the administration, compared with slightly less than half of Democrats who say they're not democratic socialists.
Democratic socialists are also more likely to want Congress to end military aid to Israel and less likely to say it’s a top priority to find common ground between the two parties.
Campbell, the Democrat in Mississippi, identifies as a democratic socialist and wants Congress to hold the administration accountable.
“It feels a little cliche to just say roll back the past two years, but honestly, mostly just roll back the stuff he’s done the past two years," Campbell said.
MAGA Republicans
Republicans are broadly aligned on what they want the next Congress to do, regardless of whether they identify with the “Make America Great Again” movement — except when it comes to Trump.
At least half of MAGA and non-MAGA Republicans want leaders to lower costs, end the Iran war and reduce the federal budget deficit.
Richard Longo, a 74-year-old Republican in Lake Forest, California, wants to see the president’s agenda pursued in the next Congress but is especially worried about balancing the budget.
“You’re not going to balance the budget in one year, but you have to have a plan," Longo said.
But while about 6 in 10 MAGA Republicans want Congress to prioritize supporting the administration's agenda, only about 2 in 10 Republicans who are not supporters of MAGA say the same.
Lisa Ostlund, a 46-year-old from Wayland, Massachusetts, who identifies as a MAGA supporter, wants to see the next Congress prioritize Trump's agenda. She doesn't support everything Trump does, but she credits his policies with her recent ability to find housing after struggling with homelessness for several years.
“You got to care about your American people," Ostlund said. "He definitely doesn’t say it right, but you do have to put them first.”

JERUSALEM, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Chinese automaker BYD Auto has launched its new electric bus model in Israel, its local official importer said Thursday.
Dozens of buses of the B12e03 model, capable of carrying up to 105 passengers, are expected to be delivered to public transportation operators across the country by the end of 2026, said a statement from Shlomo Motors.

Besides, electronically controlled shock absorbers adjust to road conditions for better comfort and handling, the statement said.
BYD first supplied Israel's public transportation system with its K9 electric buses back in 2013. ■

Ukraine, Britain and Latvia will track Ukrainian grain stolen by Russia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:10:45 EEST
01:10:45 KST

Ukraine, Britain and Latvia will track Ukrainian grain stolen by Russia
Kyiv • UNN
The three countries will launch a joint grain verification scheme based on isotope and chemical analysis. It will help identify illegally exported produce.
Ukraine, Latvia, and the United Kingdom will introduce a joint mechanism for verifying the origin of grain, which will help identify agricultural products illegally taken by Russia from Ukraine’s temporarily occupied territories. Isotopic and chemical analysis will be used for this purpose. The Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food of Ukraine reports this, UNN writes.
Details
On October 21, the countries signed a trilateral memorandum of understanding on the Grain Verification Scheme (GVS).
The document provides for joint verification of the origin of agricultural products and the creation of an evidence base regarding their possible illegal appropriation and removal from the occupied territories.
Grain samples will be examined using isotopic and chemical analysis, after which they will be compared with a reference database of products whose geographical origin has been confirmed.
The checks will cover wheat, corn, barley, and sunflower seeds. The results obtained will make it possible to identify suspicious batches and may be used as evidence of the illegal removal of Ukrainian agricultural products.
"The Grain Verification Scheme will make it possible to scientifically confirm the origin of grain and create additional opportunities to counter illegal trade. Every attempt to legalize stolen Ukrainian grain must receive an appropriate response," emphasized Taras Vysotskyi, Minister of Agrarian Policy and Food.
The memorandum also provides for authorized bodies of the three countries to access the GVS system, exchange scientific data, and coordinate the work of laboratories.
The parties will appoint responsible representatives, hold technical consultations, and coordinate actions in the event that batches of agricultural products of questionable origin are identified.
The agreement continued the negotiations between Ukraine and Latvia, which took place on September 25, 2026, in Riga.

The US State Department has reportedly asked career diplomats seeking promotions whether they voted for President Donald Trump in the 2016, 2020 and 2024 elections, The Washington Sun reported Thursday.
Senior agency officials indicated that support for Trump could determine eligibility for mid-level and senior Foreign Service positions, according to the report.
Candidates were also reportedly warned that their campaign donation records would be reviewed and contributions to Democratic candidates could cause them to be disqualified.
The report cited six current and former State Department officials, three of whom said they had spoken directly with individuals who faced the questions.
The reported practice has drawn scrutiny from congressional Democrats, who have raised concerns about political loyalty becoming a factor in federal employment decisions.
“The Committee has been following allegations that the Trump Administration is making political affiliation a factor in employment for some time now,” Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, told the newspaper.
“These are critical national security positions and individuals should be chosen for their experience and ability, not their political loyalty,” she said, adding that lawmakers were working with other committees to investigate the allegations.
US federal law prohibits government officials from making personnel decisions based on political affiliation.
The State Department declined to comment directly on the reported questions but defended its staffing and promotion approach.
“Fidelity means upholding the Constitution and the law and executing policy with loyalty to the American people and their interests,” a spokesperson told the newspaper.
The spokesperson said the principle was not about “partisan behavior” but about implementing the president’s foreign policy agenda.
The spokesperson added that Secretary of State Marco Rubio has prioritized merit and “demonstrated performance on behalf of administration priorities” when promoting career employees into leadership roles.

Palestinian youths shield US journalist from Israeli settlers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:10:09 UTC
01:10:09 KST

Breadcrumb
Palestinian youths formed 'protective shield' for US journalist against Israeli settlers
A US photojournalist working for The Washington Post has recounted how Palestinian youths helped save her during a brutal attack by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank that left her seriously injured.
Heidi Levine was attacked by a group of settlers last Friday while covering the olive harvest near Abu Falah, north-east of Ramallah, alongside Palestinian villagers, journalists and activists.
She said local Palestinians formed a “protective shield” to help protect her from the attackers.
“The Palestinian youth put themselves in front and were trying to keep them [the settlers] away, keep a protective shield, which was amazing,” Levine told British newspaper The Guardian on Wednesday.
She described the scene as being “like a biblical battle”.
The Guardian cited witnesses who said Palestinian youths drove the settlers back, allowing US journalist Jasper Nathaniel and other reporters to reach Levine and help her to safety.
Levine said the violence escalated after Israeli forces arrived at the scene.
A group of masked Israeli settlers had appeared on a nearby hilltop, watching the Palestinian villagers, journalists and human rights activists accompanying the harvesters.
“Then all hell broke loose. Some of the farmers started to gather their tarps and bags of olives that they had picked,” she said.
“Then all of a sudden I hear a machine gun, and then saw tear gas in the distance. I started to run … It was just like a lot of commotion and then all of a sudden I see a dozen of them and they started charging at me.”
Levine sustained four fractured vertebrae, two broken ribs and four puncture wounds after being knocked to the ground and repeatedly beaten by the masked settlers.
She said she was kicked and struck with sticks “probably more than a hundred times”, even after attempting to play dead.
The photojournalist also said she feared she could have suffered brain damage or lost an eye had she not managed to keep her face towards the ground during the beating.
Despite her injuries, Levine said she intended to resume reporting from the occupied West Bank once she had recovered.
“My work is important,” she said. “They have bruised me, broken some bones, but they haven’t cracked my spirit.”
Meanwhile, fellow US journalist Jasper Nathaniel, who helped rescue Levine, wrote on his website that the young Palestinians had been instrumental in saving her life, stressing that they were “prepared to defend the community against the invaders”.
Nathaniel added that “had the shabab (young men in Arabic) not stepped up to protect her, she might well be dead”.
“It is no exaggeration to say that young Palestinians armed only with stones risked their lives to save Heidi Levine’s,” he wrote.
Levine also condemned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office for questioning accounts of the assault in a statement posted on the social media platform X, which referred to an “alleged attack”.
The statement further claimed that some footage “appears to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual”.
"That’s such bullshit. They helped me up because they couldn’t get my things off of me. That’s why," Levine told The Guardian.
"They robbed me of everything I have – a pouch with my documents, my American passport, credit card, camera disk and a small camera bag with two other lenses. Everything is gone … That’s why [they stood me up], and then they threw me back down and continued to kick and hit me."
Levine, who is Jewish and has lived in Israel for four decades, said Israeli President Isaac Herzog had personally called her to apologise for the attack. She quoted him as saying the settlers responsible were "not representative of who this country is".
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee also condemned the assault as a “despicable act of terror” and called for those responsible to be prosecuted.
Israeli police have since arrested 10 suspects following the incident in Abu Falah.
However, an Israeli court released four suspects in the assault on Levine on Wednesday and placed them under house arrest, citing insufficient evidence to keep them in custody.
Asked whether she expected her attackers to face justice, Levine rated her confidence at “two out of 10”.
“I am not very hopeful,” she told The Guardian. “Of course, if the government made the decision to do something and crack down on this and get people arrested, they would do it.”
Israeli settlers have intimidated Palestinians harvesting olives in the occupied West Bank for decades.
However, this year has seen a sharp escalation in violence, alongside widespread theft of crops, according to Palestinian witnesses, rights groups and the United Nations.
Israeli rights group Yesh Din reported on Wednesday that it had documented 125 physical attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters during the 24 days since the season began, alongside 168 incidents of crop theft. Israeli military forces were present in at least a quarter of the cases.
Yesh Din warned that settler violence was "part of a campaign of ethnic cleansing, paving the way for the annexation of the West Bank without its Palestinian population".
UN bodies, with support from countries around the world, have repeatedly affirmed that Israeli settlements in territory occupied during war are illegal under international law governing military occupation.
