What Russians are told — and not told — about Ukrainian strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:09:47 UTC
01:09:47 KST

What Russians are told — and not told — about Ukrainian strikes
A woman rides on a bus as smoke rises from the area of Gazprom Neft’s Moscow oil refinery in Moscow, Russia, on Sept. 20, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)
Andrii Sukharyna
Head of analytics at Join Ukraine
On the night of Sept. 12, Ukrainian drones attacked Taganrog. Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) reported hits on an FPV drone production facility, two drone storage sites, a Pantsir air defense system, and a radar.
Local authorities, as usual, listed something else: 16 commercial buildings, five cars, a football club, and a Svetofor store.
Regional social media channels summed it up in a single sentence about "drone debris" that set a store and several non-residential buildings on fire.
Under a post by a Rostov community on VKontakte, one commenter clarified: "One big-box store selling aircraft tires has been burning since 4 a.m. and is still burning."
They were referring to a military airfield where, judging by satellite imagery, fuel tanks caught fire.
Three days later, missiles struck the city.
Ukraine's General Staff reported explosions and a fire at the Atlant Aero plant, which manufactures Molniya strike drones. Russian authorities listed broken windows, a gas pipe, a grocery store, and an Ozon warehouse. The regional communities we monitor published 178 posts about the two strikes on Taganrog. Only one identified the target. Atlant Aero was not mentioned once.
The case of Taganrog offers a clear picture of how Russia's audience is structured. It is divided into segments, each seeing a different war.
Most people get their news from television and local online communities: television remains the main source of information for 61% of Russians.
Those interested in the war also read pro-war bloggers, known in Russia as Z-war bloggers. The smallest group reads independent media run by Russians abroad.
A month ago, using Novorossiysk as an example, we wrote that Russians do not see strikes on military targets. In September, we expanded our monitoring beyond 1,000 regional communities on Telegram and VKontakte to include more than 40 major nationwide channels, giving us a broader picture.
The first group gets the authorities' version.
On Sept. 9, the Ukrainian Navy said a Neptune missile had hit the Admiral Essen frigate in Novorossiysk.
Of 246 regional posts about that night, only one mentioned ships, while nearly 100 posts reported deaths: according to Russian authorities, four people were killed in the city.
Regional Russia knows about the civilian deaths, but not the frigate.
On Sept. 22, Ukraine's General Staff reported a strike on a base near the village of Tsymbulovo in Oryol Oblast, from which Russia launches jet-powered Geran drones.
Over the following month, the village's name did not appear in any of the thousand communities we monitored, including those in Oryol.
The shutdown of the Moscow oil refinery after a Sept. 20 strike, reported by Reuters, appeared in just six of 407 posts. The state-run channels in our sample, Solovyov and Komsomolskaya Pravda, simply repeated official statements in nine out of every 10 posts.
This feed creates the impression that air defenses shoot down hundreds of drones and debris falls on residential buildings.
Readers of Russian military bloggers know much more.
On Sept. 12, the Voyennyy Osvedomitel channel identified a military airfield as the likely target in Taganrog. On Sept. 18, it published a satellite image of damaged Atlant Aero workshops.
Overall, military bloggers identified the target in nine of 16 posts about Taganrog.
On the Moscow oil refinery, Z-blogger Fighterbomber wrote: "Let me remind you, this is the most heavily protected oil refinery in the country. Perhaps even in the world. I predict it will be attacked more than once."
But this knowledge is one-sided. The same channels report Russian strikes on Ukraine far more frequently and in greater detail.
Some 92% of reactions to such posts are positive. And Voyennyy Osvedomitel presented the strike on Tsymbulovo as a story of resilience: the shelters are sturdy, and the launchers are cheap to replace.
Independent media and those run from abroad provide the most comprehensive coverage of the strikes: they identified the target in 14 of 20 posts about Taganrog. Yet they have the smallest audiences.
In our sample, a typical military blogger's post about a strike on Russia receives 73,000 views, compared with 14,000 for a post by an independent media outlet.
Everything changes when a strike hits close to home.
The official account then clashes with what people heard during the night, and they start asking questions.
Under a post about Taganrog, people write: "Your Telegram channels say it wasn't just the store" and "When will they finally learn to tell the truth?"
In Oryol, a woman asked the governor about nighttime explosions during a live broadcast. She heard an explanation about a "piece of a drone" and recounted it in the comments: "Short and clear. Yes, that piece fell with such a bang that almost the whole city heard it."
The same community debunked a deepfake in which the governor supposedly admitted that the region lacked air defenses. The comments under the debunking post read: "This fake is telling the truth" and "I'd vote for the fake."
In Salekhard, the capital of the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, people reasoned this way after a gas plant in Novy Urengoy was hit: "How did it happen that the attack was repelled, the drone was turned into debris, and the facility it attacked is on fire? So the attack wasn't repelled, and this wasn't debris. It hit exactly what it was supposed to hit."
The numbers reflect this pattern, too. In communities based in the region that was hit, 34% of substantive comments question the effectiveness of defenses and the official figures. Another 23% describe what people saw and heard themselves or ask their neighbors about it.
They do not always find the right answers.
Novy Urengoy lies nearly 3,000 kilometers (about 1864 miles) from the Ukrainian border, and drones reached the city for the first time. The neighboring Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug banned the publication of anything about drones that same day.
The most popular comment about the strike in our databases reads: "It's been obvious for a long time that they aren't being launched from Ukraine."
Where the authorities stay silent, Russians find their own answers, and they are not always right.
Ordinary Russians in the regions know little about this war. They are told about downed drones and damaged buildings, and as long as the explosions are far away, that is enough.
Questions emerge when a strike hits their own city. In September, Yamalo-Nenets appeared on our map for the first time, and communities in 24 regions posted about the strike.
Questioning the authorities does not necessarily mean wanting the war to end. In the aftermath of the month's largest attack, the one on Moscow, 59% of substantive comments blamed the authorities and air defenses, while 16% blamed Ukraine and the West. Yet only one in 12 called for the war to end.
To sum up, here is what ordinary Russians were not told in the news in September: a strike drone factory and a military airfield in Taganrog; a frigate carrying Kalibr missiles in Novorossiysk; a launch base for jet-powered Geran drones; the shutdown of the capital's main oil refinery; and a gas plant in Yamalo-Nenets.
Russians in the regions continue to be shielded from learning by accident that the war is not going as victoriously as Putin claims. The results are rather underwhelming.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

====================================================================================================

WATCH: Fueled by a life's mission, Netanyahu asks Israelis for time to 'finish the job' in Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:09:46 UTC
01:09:46 KST

It was 2:14 a.m., and Benjamin Netanyahu wanted to know whether we were tired.
He had just turned 77. Members of his staff were dozing on couches and chairs. Netanyahu was alert, focused, and apparently in no hurry to end the night. We admitted that we were probably more tired than he was.
“You’re not the first to say that.”
A little earlier, his staff had surprised him with a birthday celebration: krembos, the chocolate-covered marshmallow treats; along with chocolates and gummies; and an individual tiramisu for the prime minister. He ate it with evident enjoyment.
Outside, aides had been searching for “the chair,” the one he preferred sitting in. Even at this hour, the small machinery of looking after a prime minister kept turning.
Some of those around him had spent years at his side. They brought drinks, attended to him, and spoke with the conviction that he would win again. They believed Israel needed him. Netanyahu himself would give us a less comfortable assessment of the race.
How did it feel to be 77? “Feels fine. If you know what you’re about, and you have good health and a lot of energy, and a purpose.”
That word, “purpose,” came up repeatedly during the next half-hour. So did Iran, US President Donald Trump, and the danger Netanyahu saw in handing the country to someone else. With the October 27 election approaching, he was asking voters to let him finish work that he regards as the reason for his political life.
His partnership with Trump was central to that request. We wanted to know how his case would hold up when the American president was someone else.
Netanyahu: Iran does not want me elected
Could Iran attack before the election? Could Israel strike first?
Netanyahu said military intelligence and the Mossad had delivered “clear warnings” that Iran and its proxies were considering ways to influence the vote.
“They don’t want me elected.”
He suggested rockets or drones could be used to puncture Israelis’ confidence in the military campaign’s achievements. “If they do, it’ll be a big mistake because we’ll respond with force and might they cannot even imagine.”
People on his team, speaking on background, separately told us that current senior defense officials had contacted Netanyahu to say he needed to win because Israel’s enemies would see his defeat as their success. They also described serious security threats in the near future. That account of private conversations has not been independently verified.
Netanyahu moved quickly through the destruction of enemy capabilities and the killing of their leaders. October 7 was the starting point of his account of Israel’s recovery; the failures that permitted the attack under his government received little attention.
Iran still had capabilities, we pointed out. He acknowledged that it did. For as long as its present leadership survived, he argued, it would try to rebuild its nuclear and ballistic missile programs.
“My purpose is to break Iran’s murderous regime, remove the threat from our heads, and have multiple peace treaties.”
Finishing the job, by that definition, would require an outcome extending far beyond another successful strike.
Netanyahu says he can withstand a post-Trump US, expand Arab ties
Trump’s recent endorsement was quite an item for Netanyahu’s campaign literature: the American president wanted him reelected.
Netanyahu said the decision had surprised him. The motivation had not. He described a president who saw Iran as a danger to American cities and believed he had one reliable partner in confronting it.
We raised Vice President JD Vance’s refusal to offer an endorsement of his own. Vance had also made clear he was not opposing Netanyahu. Still, the question reached beyond this election. What would happen to the relationship when Trump left office?
Netanyahu’s answer began with the remaining opportunity under Trump, then moved to the possibility of a less friendly administration. He disliked that formulation.
“That’s really laundering words,” he said.
“What happens if you have a hostile administration? Who will withstand the pressures? Who will stand up to them? And I think the answer in both cases is the same.”
He meant himself. Experience with Washington, he argued, qualified him to make the most of Trump’s friendship and to resist a successor’s demands. Palestinian statehood was the example he returned to, describing it as the prospect of an Iranian terror base overlooking Israel’s population centers.
“You’re not going to withstand the pressure by succumbing to it, because then you’re finished.”
An Israeli government elected now will have to prepare for an America whose politics are already changing. Netanyahu placed considerable weight on the character of the man sitting across from the American president. He spent more time explaining how he would withstand American pressure than how he would broaden American support.
He did identify three tasks: strengthen the existing American base of support, fight the information war, and widen Israel’s international partnerships. India was one example. In the Middle East, he said, more Arab governments were interested in relations with Israel after seeing it act against Iran.
We tried to get the names. “Since it’s just the three of us, so who are we talking about? Which countries?”
“Well, we’re definitely talking about more than two.”
He gave us a number. Later, it grew to “many more than two.”
He traced the beginnings of the Abraham Accords to his confrontation with former president Barack Obama over the Iran nuclear agreement, recalling calls from Arab officials impressed by his willingness to challenge Washington.
Trump’s presidency had helped turn those contacts into agreements. Further military action against Iran, he argued, had made Israel still more attractive as a partner.
We challenged his suggestion that Arab leaders were untroubled by his coalition partners. Their reservations, we said, were expressed privately too.
“Most of them couldn’t care less.”
He went further: “And they couldn’t care less about the Palestinian issue, and they said, ‘We have to say it, but we don’t mean it.’”
That is his account of their private words. Their public position remains quite different: Saudi Arabia and other Arab governments reaffirmed support for Palestinian statehood in a joint statement on October 16.
Qatar, Qatargate, and Netanyahu’s defense against allegations of influence
Qatar brought the discussion of Israel’s standing abroad uncomfortably close to home.
We asked whether it should again mediate on matters involving Israel. Netanyahu had accused Doha of spreading hatred of the Jewish state; Israel had nevertheless relied on its role in hostage negotiations.
He maintained that Israel used Qatar because the United States did. He then accused it of driving antisemitism and anti-Zionism in American universities and on social media. “Qatar was one of the engines of our vilification, only one.”
This led him to cite his late father, Benzion Netanyahu, the historian of the Inquisition and modern Zionism. He recalled asking him whether America offered Jews an exception to the recurring dangers of European history.
“There are no exceptions if certain things happen,” he remembered his father replying.
Netanyahu described social upheaval and resentment exposing a visible minority to danger. “The Jews are prominent and weak,” he said, “and that’s a very dangerous place to be in a society.”
His father’s warning still shaped his explanation of America. Israel’s strength, he argued, gave Jews the means to prevent the physical destruction that had so often followed their vilification. He saw the current hostility as a historical danger that better public diplomacy alone could not resolve.
Then he returned to Qatar, offering a military action as his answer to suspicions about his own position.
“They accused me of being pro-Qatar; I attacked Qatar.”
Israel’s September 2025 strike in Doha targeted Hamas leaders. It did not answer the question we put to him next: What about the allegations concerning people in his own circle and their connections to Qatar?
“Except that the judge said there was nothing there.”
He continued: “The judge said it’s a witch hunt. Basically that’s what he said.”
He did not identify the judge or ruling. 'Qatargate' remains under investigation. The affair concerns allegations that aides, including Yonatan Urich, promoted Qatari interests while working for Netanyahu. They deny wrongdoing. Netanyahu has given evidence to police but has not been named a suspect.
Netanyahu argued that others who had worked with Qatar were now attacking him over it. “This is one hoax,” he said, before describing a campaign video mocking successive television controversies as manufactured storms.
“The idea is to divert attention and to mask the real issue in this election.”
He did not say whether Israel would use Qatar as a mediator again.
Who gets to join Netanyahu’s next government - and on what terms?
Netanyahu wants to build his next government with his present partners. On one possible appointment, however, he was explicit. Asked about Itamar Ben-Gvir’s ambition to become defense minister, he said: “I think the next defense minister should be from Likud.”
“But it’s going to be our government. We decide what the policy is.”
The conduct of the present government raised a different test of control. We pressed him on extremist settler violence against Palestinians, pointing to criticism from US Ambassador Mike Huckabee, hardly an unfamiliar face among Israel’s friends.
Netanyahu argued that international coverage distorted the scale of the violence compared with terrorism against Israelis. We persisted: “Huckabee knows that, but not everyone does, right?”
“No, I understand that, believe me.”
“We know you do,” we replied.
“You don’t have to explain it to me. I don’t want vigilantism.”
He rejected extremist Jews who have been taking the law into their own hands. The acts were wrong, he said, did “enormous damage to Israel abroad,” and harmed the reputation of the wider settlement community. He spoke about families killed by terrorists and the sons that those communities had lost in military service.
“That’s why I put the Shin Bet onto this and continue to do that.”
When we asked about bringing opponents into a broader government, the conversation turned to the courtroom.
“Why not have a unity government? Would you agree to sit with him?” we asked, referring to Gadi Eisenkot, the former IDF chief of staff.
Netanyahu said his opponents had ruled him out because of his corruption trial. “The trial’s collapsed.”
He spoke about what he and his family had endured, the conduct of investigators, and former attorney-general Avichai Mandelblit’s testimony. We returned to the political question.
“You would offer them a hand?”
“No, first of all, let me finish this because this is important.”
His objection was to proposals barring an indicted politician from serving as prime minister. Such a law, he argued, would hand prosecutors the power to decide who could govern, removing that choice from voters. He termed it “Iranian Bolshevism.”
Then came a demand concerning the trial itself: “It should be ended right now, and we should start an immediate criminal investigation against those who led it.
“You cannot do this to any citizen, and I’m a citizen, but also you cannot try to destroy democracy with the abuse of state power.”
The trial continues. Netanyahu faces fraud and breach-of-trust charges in three cases, and bribery in Case 4000. He denies wrongdoing. The allegations concern gifts from businessmen, discussions with newspaper publisher Arnon Mozes about favorable coverage in return for steps against rival Israel Hayom, and regulatory favors for Bezeq in exchange for intervention in Walla’s coverage.
Mandelblit, testifying for the defense, has acknowledged investigative steps beyond his approvals while defending his authorization of the investigations and the basis for the bribery charge.
Eventually, he answered the coalition question. If he secured a majority of at least 61 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, he would form a government and establish its principles. Others could then accept them and join.
“First principle, no Palestinian state, period.”
He added Israel’s identity as the Jewish nation-state, with minority rights respected; an active security doctrine; a free-market economy; and expanded peace agreements. A broader coalition could follow victory, on terms that he would set.
Explaining his security doctrine, he searched for an English rendering of tachbulot, or stratagems. “My English isn’t that good.” He invoked King James’s translators and the 70 wise men of Alexandria. Biblical translation was one difficulty he was willing to concede.
Victory itself was less certain. We pointed out that polls also showed him struggling to assemble a majority.
“I think right now it’s an even tie. That’s what I see in the big numbers.”
Netanyahu says he wants 'five more terms' as Israel's prime minister
We returned to the birthday. If he won, would this be his last term?
“Oh no, I’m gonna have five more terms.”
He had a proposal for those who described him as worn out or physically inactive. “I invite them to come to the gym with me.” There was a condition: “But they’ll have to do the same thing.”
He recalled a commentator predicting, after his defeat in 1999, that he would not merit a footnote. The commentator was still around, he said; we pointed out that Netanyahu was too. He has had considerable practice reading his political obituaries.
“I don’t need the job. I don’t need the job,” he said. “I’m fueled by a mission.”
He described preventing Iran from acquiring the means to destroy Israel as the work of his adult life. Again came the question he wanted voters to ask: “Who will finish the job?”
It was 2:45 a.m. Netanyahu thanked us for our tenacity. His staff had celebrated another birthday and were expecting another victory; his own assessment still left the election in the balance. After we left, he continued working.
He had turned 77 in the middle of a working night. How much longer he would serve was now a question for the voters.■

What makes Bulgaria attractive to foreign investors?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:08:27 UTC
01:08:27 KST

News
What makes Bulgaria attractive to foreign investors?
A straightforward tax system and the quality of public institutions are among the key considerations for entrepreneurs looking to do business in Bulgaria
Thursday 22 October 2026 17:49
Thursday, 22 October 2026, 17:49
PHOTO AI generated
Font size
Foreign direct investment in Bulgaria more than doubled in the first eight months of 2026, reaching €3.829 billion, according to preliminary figures from the Bulgarian National Bank (BNB). This represents an increase of 100.5% compared with the same period last year, although the figures may still be revised.
Most of the investment came from profits reinvested by foreign-owned companies operating in Bulgaria. These amounted to €3.095 billion, up from €2.816 billion a year earlier.
But what makes Bulgaria an attractive place for foreign investors?
Joining the eurozone is an advantage, although not necessarily the deciding factor, according to Prof. Todor Yalamov, Deputy Dean of the Faculty of Economics and Business Administration at Sofia University St Kliment Ohridski.
"I wouldn't say the eurozone is a factor that will attract investors, but it is a useful addition to the other advantages because it reduces transaction costs and currency risk," he told Radio Bulgaria.
Prof. Todor Yalamov
PHOTO Sofia University St Kliment Ohridski
"A much more important factor is the simplicity of the tax system. You don't need expensive tax consultants to navigate it. In many European countries, you can pay low taxes only if you have good tax advisers. Otherwise, you end up paying high taxes.
Another advantage, according to Yalamov, is Bulgaria's low corporate tax rate of 10%, which is particularly attractive to smaller investors. Even the 15% minimum effective tax rate applicable to qualifying large corporate groups with annual consolidated revenue of at least €750 million is highly competitive.
He believes the flat-rate tax system and the country's social security contribution thresholds offer another competitive advantage.
"The flat tax is a more important factor, along with reasonable social security contribution thresholds compared with the rest of the European market. With the same labour costs for an employer in France or Germany, an employee in Bulgaria would take home more money. This helps companies attract staff and gives Bulgaria an advantage for certain investors."
Not everyone, however, sees rising wages as good news.
"Others who came here solely because labour was cheap have started leaving as wages have risen," he added.
Yalamov points to the growing number of Italian-owned restaurants in Sofia as an example of businesses that can earn more in Bulgaria than they might in their home country. Different investors, he explains, are attracted by different advantages.
PHOTO magnific.com
"Many Greek companies have moved not just their registered offices but also their actual production facilities to Bulgaria. They did so not because labour was cheaper, but because of financial stability. That is another reason Bulgaria is an interesting investment destination."
Yet the discussion about investment tends to overlook another important aspect: Bulgarian companies investing abroad.
Such investments, Yalamov argues, also contribute to Bulgaria's economic growth, employment and competitiveness. Companies cannot continue expanding indefinitely without entering foreign markets.
"Fortunately, many Bulgarian companies are investing abroad. And some of what is recorded as foreign investment in Bulgaria is actually Bulgarian capital. If you look closely at corporate ownership databases, you'll find that some businesses classified as foreign are in fact Bulgarian."
He mentions fintech companies operating worldwide, businesses trading in petroleum products and oils, and pharmaceutical firms. One company from Veliko Tarnovo has even established a textile factory in Florida.
"Learning through investment in foreign markets is extremely useful for the next generation of companies that have taken, or want to take, the same path," Yalamov said.
PHOTO Bulgarian Investment Agency
This raises another question: what prompts Bulgarian companies to invest overseas?
One obvious answer is access to markets.
In the early years after 1990, some foreign investors entered Bulgaria simply to secure a place in the market before their competitors did. This was particularly true in food production, sanitary products and certain services. Today, however, attention is increasingly turning towards foreign entrepreneurs who choose Bulgaria as the place to establish their businesses.
"According to traditional economic theory, investment is the most important thing. Nowadays, however, entrepreneurship seems to matter more than investment, because it is more often driven by innovation and aimed at new markets.
"In other words, attracting entrepreneurs who establish their companies in Bulgaria could prove more valuable than attracting a conventional investor who simply moves here the production of something previously made in Italy."
Yalamov recalls the Italian garment factories that relocated to Bulgaria. Some eventually closed, leaving workers without opportunities to retrain.
Ultimately, attracting investors is only part of the challenge. Keeping them in Bulgaria depends not just on competitive taxes but also on the quality of public institutions and how effectively the state functions. These, Yalamov argues, are among the factors that determine whether foreign businesses choose to stay for the long term.

Pro-Israel lobby AIPAC drops endorsements amid US backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:07:39 UTC
01:07:39 KST

Breadcrumb
Pro-Israel lobby AIPAC drops endorsements amid increasing US unpopularity
The powerful pro-Israel lobby AIPAC has announced it will stop directly funding and endorsing US congressional candidates, marking a major shift in its electoral strategy amid growing public opposition to Israel over its genocidal war in Gaza.
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) announced the decision on Wednesday, saying it would end formal candidate endorsements and direct contributions through its political action committee while continuing to spend heavily on elections through its super PAC, United Democracy Project (UDP).
The move comes as AIPAC faces growing criticism, particularly among Democratic voters, with a leading Palestinian advocacy figure telling The New Arab that the decision amounts to an admission that the lobby's support has become politically toxic.
"They're admitting themselves that their endorsement is a net negative for anyone that they would endorse," Hamid Bendaas, communications director at the Institute for Middle East Understanding (IMEU) Policy Project said.
The decision marks a significant change for one of Washington's most influential lobbying organisations, which established its political action committee and super PAC in 2021, expanding its electoral involvement.
In a letter to members, AIPAC said it would concentrate on mobilising individual donors and developing new fundraising methods, while insisting its objectives remained unchanged.
"Our mission and strategy remain the same," AIPAC spokesperson Deryn Sousa said.
Federal Election Commission filings show that AIPAC contributed nearly $25 million to candidates and political committees through September, while UDP spent more than $53 million on independent electoral expenditures.
Unlike traditional political action committees, super PACs can spend unlimited amounts supporting or opposing candidates, provided they do not coordinate directly with campaigns.
The announcement comes amid sharply deteriorating American attitudes towards Israel following its genocide in Gaza and wider military actions across the Middle East.
An April 2026 Pew Research Center survey found that 60 percent of Americans held an unfavourable view of Israel, including 80 percent of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents.
Polling published by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs in October found that American favourability towards Israel had fallen to its lowest level since the organisation began measuring attitudes towards the country in 1978.
The changing political climate has complicated AIPAC's efforts to support candidates, particularly in Democratic primaries.
In Michigan, AIPAC's super PAC spent heavily attempting to defeat Abdul El-Sayed, a critic of Israel, during the Democratic Senate primary.
El-Sayed nevertheless secured the nomination against Congresswoman Haley Stevens, who received substantial backing from pro-Israel interests.
UDP has subsequently intervened against El-Sayed in the Senate election campaign, where he faces Republican Mike Rogers, departing from AIPAC's traditional emphasis on maintaining bipartisan support.
Bendaas said the intervention was particularly significant given AIPAC's longstanding preference for influencing primaries rather than general elections.
"They usually stick to primaries, and they stay out of general elections because they want to stay bipartisan," he said.
Such interventions risk alienating Democratic voters whose overriding priority is defeating Republican candidates, regardless of their views on Israel.
Nevertheless, AIPAC's withdrawal from endorsements does not mean it is abandoning its ability to influence elections.
Its super PAC will continue operating, while supporters will still be encouraged to contribute to candidates backing its policy objectives.
Bendaas described the decision as a survival strategy intended to preserve AIPAC's financial influence while distancing candidates from an increasingly unpopular association.
"This is a move that's going to ensure that AIPAC stays relevant and continues to have an influence because they're going to continue to spend money through their SuperPAC," he said.
He also argued that AIPAC could increasingly rely on less transparent electoral spending, including committees whose financial backers may not become publicly apparent until after voting.
The restructuring comes as growing numbers of Democratic candidates reject AIPAC's support, challenging an organisation that has historically enjoyed considerable influence over both major parties.
For Bendaas, the most consequential aspect of the decision may be the loss of AIPAC's formerly privileged position in American politics.
"AIPAC is now just kind of one of those lobbies. But they're still a powerful one," he said, comparing the organisation to other wealthy lobbying groups seeking to influence elections.
"That kind of sheen and that feeling of no one should try to challenge us I think is gone probably forever."

Israeli attacks in Gaza kill four, including a young girl
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:06:55 UTC
01:06:55 KST

Israeli attacks kill four as famine risk looms in Gaza
Gaza hospitals report four dead in 24 hours, as the death toll since the October ‘ceasefire’ rises to 1,538.
Israeli attacks across Gaza have killed four Palestinians, including a child, in the past 24 hours as the Israeli military continues to expand its control inside the territory.
This comes amid warnings from a rights group that Gaza could face another famine as Israeli restrictions on incoming goods leave residents struggling to obtain food.
The deaths on Thursday included a young girl who was killed by Israeli gunfire in northern Gaza near the Jabalia refugee camp, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
Al Jazeera’s Hani Mahmoud, reporting from Gaza City, said a strike on a vehicle in Gaza City’s Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood killed one person and seriously injured another.
A separate strike killed a man on a bicycle in the southern city of Khan Younis.
Meanwhile, the Gaza Health Ministry reported that a fourth person had died on Thursday of wounds sustained earlier in an Israeli strike.
Along with the deadly attacks, the Israeli military continues to grab more land inside Gaza. Close to two million people live in what remains of the shrinking territory, which is littered with thousands of tonnes of rubble and debris.
“Israel is expanding their control inside Gaza,” Mahmoud explained, noting that Israeli troops have been “taking more land since the ceasefire” and expanding from northern Gaza inward to the centre and westward.
“People cannot return to their homes, and most buildings in the areas Israel controls have been left in ruins,” the reporter said.
Al Jazeera’s maps have shown that nearly two-thirds of Gaza is under Israeli military control or subject to access restrictions.
At least 1,538 Palestinians have been killed and 5,498 injured since the “ceasefire” took effect in October last year, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
Israel has killed more than 74,400 Palestinians in Gaza since October 2023.
Renewed famine risk
The deadly strikes come as Palestinians across Gaza face an escalating food crisis, which has been renewed by Israeli border closures and severe funding shortfalls targeting international relief operations.
The Geneva-based human rights group, Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor, said on Thursday that its teams observed increasingly empty markets and soaring food prices, warning that Gaza could face another famine.
It accused Israel of “deliberately depriving” Palestinians of adequate nutrition as part of its ongoing genocide.
According to the rights group, after Israeli authorities suspended commercial goods deliveries to Gaza on October 13, it announced on October 19 that some imports would be allowed to resume. However, the group said the decision brought little relief, as shipments remained heavily restricted and fresh fruits and vegetables were still denied entry.
The World Food Programme (WFP) announced this week that severe funding shortages have forced it to slash food assistance to Gaza by one-third, leaving an estimated 500,000 vulnerable residents without essential monthly support as winter approaches.
According to the United Nations, the supply of fresh food and basic staples has rapidly evaporated due to ongoing Israeli restrictions on commercial entry points and aid crossings.
Reporting from Gaza City, Al Jazeera’s Maram Humaid described a sudden and dramatic disappearance of basic sustenance, leaving local markets empty and families increasingly desperate.
“Food disappeared suddenly – no vegetables, no fruit, no meat, no eggs, no bread – prices skyrocketing,” Humaid reported.
“Today, we didn’t have breakfast until noon, after my husband spent hours looking for bread and any kind of fresh vegetables. He came back with just a few loaves. We’re back to canned beans.”
With no electricity or operational refrigeration across the ruined enclave, households are unable to store fresh provisions even when available.
“Stockpiling seems more limited this time,” Humaid noted. “The shortages started with flour and fresh produce, which people can’t store for long, especially with no refrigerators or electricity. Prices of other goods have gone up, but many people can’t afford to stock up. Others are simply exhausted and have lost hope. I’m one of them.”
Beyond physical deprivation, the psychological toll on residents forced to navigate overcrowded shops with dwindling inventory has reached a breaking point.
“It’s the whole experience – the panic and fear that come with shopping to stock up. You find yourself looking at every food item as if it might be the last time you’ll ever see it, saying goodbye to it. Everyone around you is gripped by the same panic, and the shops are unbelievably crowded,” Humaid said, adding that the experience is one many feel they “can’t go through all over again”.

Indian pilots take a spin in upgraded Su-30 jet in Russia (VIDEO)
Indian and Russian air force crews practiced joint drills in Russia’s Chelyabinsk region as part of the wider inter-service Indra-2026 military exercise.
The Russian Aerospace Forces and the Indian Air Force (IAF) teams engaged in joint operations in Su-30SM fighter jets during the drill. The focus of the operations was on actions against small, low-flying targets and destroying carriers of short- and medium-range aerial weaponry.
The personnel also performed air combat maneuvers at medium and low altitudes, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Thursday.
The Su-30SM is a modernized version of the Su-30MKI model, the IAF’s workhorse fighter jet. It has been modified with Russian-specific avionics, radar, and communication systems and has extreme agility.
The IAF is also running its own program to upgrade and make its Su-30MKIs more lethal and survivable, under the ‘Super Sukhoi’ program, at the state-backed Hindustan Aeronautics Limited.
The $7.5 billion modernization program aims to upgrade an initial batch of 84 Su-30MKI fighter jets, with plans to eventually expand to over 200 more aircraft, extending the fleet’s service life through 2055.
Russia’s Rosoboronexport agency earlier highlighted that the modernization program can be performed with significant involvement from the Indian defense industry, while the facilities involved in the manufacturing of the Su-30MKI can be used for co-manufacturing of the Russian fifth-generation Su-57E fighter jet, if India decides to go ahead with Russia’s proposal.
The Indian and Russian crews also conducted exercises with Mi-8 army aviation helicopters.
The exercise’s aim was to build operational capabilities in deploying special forces units and for search-and-rescue operations in hazardous and difficult terrains.
The maritime phase of the drills took place in the Gulf of Peter the Great near Vladivostok over the weekend and involved the Russian Pacific Fleet corvette Aldar Tsydenzhapov and the Indian Navy frigate INS Sahyadri
The land exercises will end on Friday, with troops practicing joint command and control and operations against simulated armed groups.

A collection of rare Pokemon trading cards kept in a British attic for 15 years sold at auction for £1.56 million ($2.09 million), far exceeding its estimated value of £250,000, according to British media reports.
The collection belonged to an anonymous retired decorator from Woking, Surrey, who accumulated 42 sets of Pokemon cards from 1999 to 2009, kept one, and offered the remaining 41 for sale.
The auction, held Wednesday and organized by Ewbank's in Surrey, attracted bidders from around the world.
The most valuable lot was a Legendary Collection master set featuring a rare Charizard card, which fetched £130,000, including buyer's fees.
Another set, Skyridge, which the collector originally purchased for around £300, sold for £97,500, including fees.
The man began collecting Pokemon cards in the late 1990s after his son became interested in trading them at school. He purchased complete sets from a seller in Malaysia on eBay and stored them in his attic after his son lost interest.
He discovered their potential value only after reading a newspaper report about a single Pokemon card selling for more than £6,000.
Ewbank's described the sale as the most valuable trading-card auction in UK history and suggested it could also be a European record.
James Spooner, head of trading cards at Ewbank's, said advance bids had already reached £825,000 the day before the sale.
Andrew Ewbank, who conducted the auction, described the international interest as exceptional.
"The buzz was incredible, especially because the collectors could not believe how good this collection was – extensive, untouched, complete, and with just about every rarity you could hope for," he said.

Italy and Spain lift border controls after months of tension over Ceuta
More than 70,000 people irregularly crossed from Morocco into Ceuta in late July, triggering border security concerns in the EU bloc.
Italy and Spain have agreed to lift border controls on each other’s citizens, ending a three-month standoff triggered after a mass surge of migrants and asylum seekers entered the Spanish enclave of Ceuta.
The Italian Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi and his Spanish counterpart Fernando Grande-Marlaska spoke on the phone and agreed not to extend their suspension of the European Union’s open-border Schengen arrangements, an Italian statement said on Thursday.
“The decision, reached after a careful assessment of the situation, will be accompanied by enhanced information-sharing measures to ensure the full security of the common Schengen area,” the ministry added.
The decision followed a meeting between Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on the sidelines of a European Council meeting.
Italy’s right-wing government first suspended its open-border arrangements with Spain on July 31, saying it wanted to make sure no migrants entering the North African enclave of Ceuta could travel to Italian territory.
Madrid responded by taking similar action against Rome, describing the Italian measures as “unjust, contrary to European Union interests, and discriminatory to the population of Spain”.
Ceuta migrant surge
The tit-for-tat border closures happened after upwards of 70,000 people swam around barricades and entered Ceuta from neighbouring Morocco on July 30 and 31, fuelling tension in the Spanish territory.
Most returned to Morocco within hours, but thousands, including unaccompanied minors, have remained for weeks in often dire conditions.
“We thought our government was going to do something in the short or medium term, but we’ve been here for two months, and these people haven’t been sent back,” Ceuta resident Ruben Gonzalez said.
The Spanish government’s handling of the mass crossing of migrants into Ceuta has complicated Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s bid for re-election in November.
Sanchez was already facing criticism for his government’s decision to open a path to legal status for hundreds of thousands of undocumented foreign residents.
After the Ceuta incident, Far-right Vox and centre-right PP parties accused him of being soft on immigration and put the issue at the centre of their campaigns in the run-up to next month’s elections.

French TV and radio watchdog Arcom urges ‘accurate and balanced’ coverage of protests
Arcom, the French regulator for broadcast media, has urged the country’s TV and radio stations to ensure “accurate and balanced” coverage of the current protests, saying it had received around a dozen complaints in the past few days.

After analysing more than half a million posts across various social media platforms, the group says it was able to track the campaign back to the start of September. Pentagon, Lockheed Agree on 10-Year Framework for Buying F-35s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:02:40 UTC
01:02:40 KST

The Pentagon and Lockheed Martin on Oct. 22 announced a framework agreement to buy F-35 Joint Strike Fighters for the next 10 years.
But the deal, touted by the Pentagon as “landmark” and a first of its kind, depends on Congress granting the military authority to enter into such a multiyear agreement. Details such as pricing and schedules also have yet to be hammered out.
Under the deal, Lockheed will build 156 of the fifth-generation jets per year for both the U.S. and international customers, across lots 21 through 30. The U.S. military will buy at least 850 of those 1,560 aircraft over the decade covering the agreement, as well as procurement of initial spare parts and modification kits, the Pentagon and Lockheed said in statements. The deal also covers sustainment of the global F-35 fleet.
“We have fundamentally changed how we stabilize the American defense industrial base to produce at speed and scale,” Michael Duffey, undersecretary of defense for acquisition and sustainment, said in the Pentagon’s statement. “This agreement with Lockheed Martin proves it. By aligning financial incentives with actual performance, we are ensuring our warfighters are equipped with the lethal capabilities they need to fight and win.”
Lockheed Martin has also agreed to invest at least $7 billion of its own money into projects to support the F-35 program.
“This multiyear framework strengthens the way we can plan and invest in the F-35 enterprise,” Lockheed President and CEO Jim Taiclet said in the company’s statement. “With the greater certainty that comes from the U.S. government’s transformative approach to F-35 production and sustainment, we can make the upfront investments needed to expand capacity, improve efficiency, and build a more resilient supply chain.”
While the Defense Department touted the agreement’s ability to create “a stable, long-term procurement signal to modernize and expand” the F-35, it also noted in its statement that actually executing the agreement “remains subject to congressional authorization and appropriations.”
Congress is currently considering granting the Pentagon the authority to enter into multiyear procurement contracts for the F-35 and F-15EX fighters as part of its work on the 2027 defense policy bill. Lawmakers have also yet to pass a budget for fiscal 2027, leaving the
But that legislation is still pending—meaning the Oct. 22 announcement is only a framework and not finalized.
Lockheed said if Congress does grant the multiyear procurement authority and the necessary appropriations in the next few months, it will work with the F-35 Joint Program Office to finalize the contract terms, pricing, and schedules through a formal award.
Lockheed said having predictable, multiyear procurement plans for the F-35 would save billions of dollars “through long-term pricing and industry volume discounts.” And the agreement will allow the program to combine data from a variety of sources into integrated analytics, that will provide more visibility into parts inventory and readiness metrics and allow “transparent, data-driven decision making.”
The deal will also allow Lockheed to enter into long-term contracts with suppliers to buy raw materials and critical parts in bulk, which the company predicted would improve F-35 mission-capable rates. Currently, those deals are made on an annual basis, which Lockheed said “has historically strained the industrial base.”
In an earnings call with investors Oct. 22, Taiclet said at least 60 percent of an F-35’s content comes from its suppliers, including major suppliers such as Northrop Grumman and BAE Systems, which make the center and aft sections of the jets’ bodies, respectively.
“We want them to have production stability, just as we would like to have it,” Taiclet said.
Taiclet said one of Lockheed’s biggest costs comes from suppliers providing components late, or at poor quality, and he predicted this agreement will help correct those problems.
Taiclet told investors that Lockheed and its suppliers will be under a fixed-price escalation contract, in which set prices increase under certain economic conditions.
“We’ll all collectively—if we do well and perform well, and those investments pay off that we make—we will get to retain those profits under the fixed-price-with-escalator concept,” Taiclet said. “Before, we would have to give back, with price and operating profit, any improvements we invested in internally. So that is going to apply to the production system. Even if it stays at 156, it’ll be a much healthier production system for industry, and a more predictable production system for government.”
And combining aircraft production with the purchase of spare parts and modification kits in the same contract will also yield volume savings and cost predictability, Lockheed said.
“Our new multiyear framework gives suppliers stability to plan for the future and invest with confidence, improving readiness across the F-35 fleet,” Lockheed Martin Aeronautics President OJ Sanchez said in the company’s statement. “This, in addition to the investments Lockheed Martin is making to the global spares pool, will directly translate into higher mission-capable rates and a more resilient supply chain—critical capabilities the warfighter needs to meet today’s mission and prepare for tomorrow’s threats.”
During the earnings call, Taiclet reiterated Lockheed’s desire—first voiced in April 2025, after the company lost the Air Force’s F-47 contract to Boeing—to add sixth-generation technologies into the F-35, which he previously referred to as making a “Ferrari” F-35. Taiclet said this could achieve 80 percent of a bespoke sixth-generation aircraft’s capabilities, at half the cost.
Lockheed’s primary F-35 factory is in Fort Worth, Texas.

Saudi oil boss issues global supply warning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:01:52 UTC
01:01:52 KST

Saudi oil boss issues global supply warning
The US-Israeli war on Iran has caused an “unprecedented” shock to global energy markets, removing some 3 billion barrels of oil supply, Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser has warned.
The war launched in February effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial oil and LNG artery, sending crude prices up roughly 50%. Despite Gulf exports recovering to a reported 80% of pre-war levels, renewed attacks on vessels have kept markets on edge, with Brent hitting a five-month high above $112 this week. Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and shipping have compounded the crisis, threatening another vital trade chokepoint, the Red Sea’s Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
In an interview with Al Arabiya Business aired on Thursday, Nasser said the nearly eight-month crisis had deprived global markets of an estimated 3 billion barrels of oil.
“The impact of this crisis on energy markets is unprecedented,” he said. “We have lost around 3 billion barrels since it began. And bear in mind that the Gulf accounts for roughly 20% of global oil demand.”
The figure is equivalent to nearly a month of global oil consumption and reflects cumulative supply losses caused by disrupted shipping, reduced production and logistical bottlenecks.
With global oil inventories already below their five-year average when the war erupted, prices could have soared past $200 a barrel, Nasser warned. He credited emergency reserve releases, China’s sharp cut in seaborne oil imports and Saudi Aramco’s East-West pipeline, which bypasses Hormuz, with averting an even more severe price shock.
Nasser warned, however, that even an end to the crisis could bring fresh pressure on oil markets, as recovering consumption and a rush to replenish depleted reserves will likely fuel another demand surge.
“Once things return to normal, we expect additional demand of around 3 million barrels per day – about 2 million from consumption growth and another 1 million just to replenish the reserves countries have drawn down during the crisis,” he said, noting that the added demand could keep markets under strain long after shipping routes reopen.
Fresh escalation fears
Meanwhile, fears of another escalation are growing as US-Iran talks remain deadlocked. Reports on Wednesday claimed Washington was quietly pulling troops from bases in Jordan, Qatar and Kuwait, evacuating some diplomats and their families from Saudi Arabia and preparing similar withdrawals elsewhere. Similar precautions were taken ahead of the US-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.
The moves follow US President Donald Trump’s rejection last month of Tehran’s proposal to reopen Hormuz in exchange for lifting the US blockade of Iranian ports, easing oil export restrictions, unfreezing Iranian assets and ending regional hostilities, including Israeli operations in Gaza and Lebanon.
Washington and Israel have since reportedly discussed another major offensive, potentially soon after the November 3 US midterms. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has also openly threatened fresh strikes on Iran, even without US backing.

Shas rabbi warns voters backing rival parties will have 'no place in the afterlife'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:01:09 UTC
01:01:09 KST

A senior rabbi in the ultra-Orthodox Shas party has warned that Jews who vote for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud or another political party will have no place in the afterlife, escalating a fierce battle for religious voters ahead of next week's national election.
Rabbi Moshe Maya, the oldest member of Shas' Council of Torah Sages and a former lawmaker who served in the Knesset in the 1990s, made the declaration as the party sought to prevent supporters from defecting to other parties on the political right.
"Anyone who votes for Likud or another party has no share in the world to come," Maya said, invoking the Jewish religious concept of Olam HaBa, or the world to come, commonly associated with the afterlife and spiritual reward.
The remarks underscored the increasingly heated rhetoric among the ultra-Orthodox parties as they compete for votes with Likud and other right-wing factions.
Shas, which primarily represents Sephardic and Mizrahi ultra-Orthodox Jews, has traditionally relied on the authority of prominent rabbis to mobilize its electorate. Religious endorsements and rulings play a significant role in the party's election campaigns, particularly among voters who regard rabbinical guidance as binding.
Former chief rabbi renews attack on Ben-Gvir
In a separate speech in Jerusalem, former Sephardic Chief Rabbi Yitzhak Yosef, another influential Shas religious leader, warned that a victory by the opposition bloc would bring severe restrictions on the ultra-Orthodox community.
"If the left comes to power, it will create difficulties," Yosef said. "What we have now will be nothing by comparison. It will be many times worse. You cannot imagine the decrees that will come."
Yosef claimed that an opposition leader had proposed expanding compulsory military service to include religious women, in addition to ultra-Orthodox yeshiva students.
"One of the leaders of the left said, 'We are not finished. We will also introduce the conscription of women, not just yeshiva students, but women into the army,'" he said.
"That is something one must die rather than transgress," Yosef added, invoking a principle in Jewish religious law under which certain prohibitions must not be violated even at the cost of one's life.
Military conscription has long been one of the most contentious issues in Israeli politics. Most ultra-Orthodox men have historically received exemptions or deferments while studying in religious seminaries, an arrangement that has faced growing legal and political challenges.
The issue has become especially divisive amid the military's manpower needs and demands for a more equal distribution of the burden of national service.
Yosef also reiterated a religious ruling he issued earlier this week prohibiting his followers from voting for National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, whose far-right political movement competes with Shas for support among religious and nationalist voters.
"It is forbidden to vote for him," Yosef said. "Anyone who votes for him is as though he himself ascended the Temple Mount. A person's agent is considered equivalent to the person himself."
The Temple Mount, known to Muslims as the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, is the holiest site in Judaism and the third-holiest in Islam. While Ben-Gvir has advocated Jewish prayer rights at the site, many leading ultra-Orthodox rabbis prohibit Jews from entering the compound because of religious restrictions concerning ritual purity and the location of the ancient Jewish temples.
Yosef's remarks reflected that longstanding religious disagreement with Ben-Gvir, whose visits to the site have repeatedly generated controversy.
The former chief rabbi also accused Ben-Gvir of failing to intervene against police violence toward ultra-Orthodox demonstrators.
"Look at how the police beat the ultra-Orthodox," Yosef said. "He is the minister responsible for the police. Has he said a word?"
Yosef alleged that Ben-Gvir benefited politically from confrontations between police and ultra-Orthodox protesters because they could weaken support for Shas representatives.
"He is happy about it because people will get angry with our representatives and his support will rise," Yosef said.
He further questioned Ben-Gvir's contributions to ultra-Orthodox religious institutions.
"Has he established a single religious school? A ritual bath? A synagogue?" Yosef asked.
Addressing young religious voters, particularly Sephardic yeshiva students considering supporting Ben-Gvir, he added: "How is that even a consideration?"
Ultra-Orthodox parties devise new voter-tracking system
Meanwhile, United Torah Judaism, the other major ultra-Orthodox party, is preparing an alternative voter-monitoring operation following a Supreme Court ruling barring polling station committee representatives from transmitting real-time information about voter turnout to party campaign headquarters.
The practice has been a central component of ultra-Orthodox election campaigns, particularly in tightly knit religious communities where parties use turnout information to identify supporters who have not yet voted and encourage them to cast ballots.
The court's restrictions prevent party representatives serving on official polling station committees from digitally transmitting such information in real time.
United Torah Judaism is now preparing a separate monitoring operation designed to collect information outside the official election administration system.
Under the plan, a registration booth will be placed at the entrance to each polling station, outside the restricted area reserved for election officials and voters. Workers will record the identities of people entering to vote, with the information subsequently transferred to party headquarters without passing through the official polling station committee.
Agudat Yisrael, a Hasidic faction within United Torah Judaism, is preparing an additional system.
Party officials said they would establish dedicated tents at clusters of polling stations, staffed by married yeshiva students engaged in full-time religious study.
After casting their ballots, voters will be asked to visit the tents and report that they have voted using a designated digital platform.
To encourage participation, the faction has launched a campaign under the slogan, "If you voted but didn't report it, you didn't vote."
The initiative is being led by Jerusalem Deputy Mayor Tzachi Brim.
The arrangements are intended to preserve the parties' ability to monitor turnout and mobilize supporters despite the court-imposed restrictions on information sharing by official polling station representatives.

Are the French police the most violent in the EU?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:01:00 UTC
01:01:00 KST

Are the French police the most violent in the EU?
October 22, 2026
Videos of alleged police violence are going viral on French social media as a wave of protests grips France. One video shows the police beating a man to the floor then dragging him away unconscious. Another shows an officer grabbing a young man from behind, seemingly unprovoked, and dragging him by the neck. Another shows a young woman being hauled off with a twisted arm, screaming in pain. These videos could not be independently verified.
The French police have drawn renewed criticism from rights groups, not only because of their methods but also because of their use of stun grenades and rubber bullets. France has one of the most heavily armed police forces in Europe. During the student protests of the past weeks, several teenagers sustained life-changing injuries as a result: One had a hand blown off, one was blinded in one eye, another had his jaw broken.
France's protests grow
More than half a million people took to the streets in France on Saturday, most of whom protested peacefully, criticizing public sector cuts, the cost-of-living crisis and supporting students' demands for better conditions in classrooms.
Rioters took advantage, burning buildings, looting stores and lobbing projectiles at the police, creating a difficult situation for the officers and other emergency services.
The protests over the weekend followed a series of protests by high-school students, who barricaded school buildings to denounce a shortage of teachers and demand repairs to crumbling infrastructure.
More protests will be happening this weekend, with the French government saying it will even deploy military forces.
Weapons made for war?
The French police have a bigger arsenal than most European countries. For instance, officers use the so-called LBD-40, a type of gun used to fire rubber bullets.
Many countries, like the UK and Germany, mostly do not allow the use of rubber bullets in protests. In some European countries, like Spain, they are sometimes used but cause fewer injuries than in France.
"It is not a French specificity. But there are guidelines. There must be a certain distance," Anastassia Tsoukala, an associate professor of criminology at the University of Paris-Sud, told DW. "Even if you try to respect the guidelines, people may move and then all of a sudden they may lose one eye. So it's extremely dangerous."
Police in France routinely use tear gas, as do police in many other countries in Europe. In warfare, its use is actually forbidden under agreements like the Chemical Weapons Convention.
What makes the French police stand out from other forces is its use of stun grenades.
"These grenades contain a high level of explosive substances. So from this point of view, France is unique," said Tsoukala.
Minister of the Interior Laurent Nunez insists that weapons used by the police are "non-lethal." However, some of the equipment used by the force is classified by France's own internal security code as "war material."
French police: the 'most brutal' in the EU?
The police's use of these weapons has received renewed criticism after it resulted in injuries during the protests. The teenager who lost use of an eye is suspected of being hit at close range with a rubber bullet from an LBD-40.
"When we look at crowd control, it is clear that if we measure police brutality by the number of deaths amongst demonstrators or members of the crowd, and if we also measure it by the number of cases of maiming, the French police are the most brutal in the whole of the European Union," says Roche.
He points to the political context to understand the French police's equipment and how it is used today.
"The political authorities are free to decide on the police's equipment," the police expert says. "When LBDs were introduced into the [French] police force, they were intended for units like anti-organized crime units. This is the same weapon that is today used for crowd control. It gives an idea of how the way in which politicians in France think we can or should deal with political protest has evolved."
Confrontation vs. de-escalation
Another difference between the French police and forces elsewhere is the methods. German police, for example, are supposed to try to avoid escalation.
Roche compares how protestors were moved in Lützerath, Germany, in 2023 to the more aggressive methods in Sainte-Soline, France, in 2023. Both places saw environmental protests.
"In Lützerath, dogs were used, there were some injuries but far fewer seriously injured people on both sides. In Sainte-Soline, the military police was sent in and used LBDs and grenades intensively. There were serious injuries amongst both police officers and demonstrators. Two protestors were left in a coma."
When can police officers use force?
According to international standards set by the United Nations, use of force by officers of the law "should be exceptional," in the case of "prevention of crime" or "lawful arrest." Any use of force should follow a principle of "proportionality," which means no more than necessary to achieve its objective.
French Interior Minister Nunez has insisted in radio interviews that officers have largely respected this principle, which is also enshrined in French law, during the current protests.
However, rights group Amnesty International describes the police response to the current protests as "disproportionate" and calls upon French authorities to "act upon their human rights obligations."
The French branch of the League of Human Rights condemns the "violent repression" of the high school protest movement.
DW contacted two police unions and the French Interior Ministry for comment, but none responded before time of publication.
"It was very complicated to contain all the different groups," Interior Minister Nunez said in Marseille on Tuesday. "The police did a great job and there were a great number of crimes that were prevented thanks to their commitment."
Experts are critical of the police's actions.
"Public order is subordinated to human life and safety," Tsoukala said. "As a jurist I should say that this is a non-negotiable value."
Less oversight than in the UK and Denmark
The French police have no independent watchdog, only an internal division called the IGPN (General Inspectorate of the National Police) that can investigate when problems occur. The IGPN says it has opened at least 40 cases since the beginning of the latest protests.
Countries like the UK and Denmark investigate incidents differently, with independent watchdogs. However, Tsoukala criticizes leniency and a lack of transparency across Europe when incidents with the police occur.
"They are acquitted or they receive extremely light penalties," she said. "And I'm afraid this is the standard method to deal with police brutality cases across Europe."
Edited by: Carla Bleiker

Disney’s multiplatform Super Bowl plan frustrates ABC affiliates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:00:50 UTC
01:00:50 KST

Disney knows that business, like football, is a contact sport. Sometimes the hits come in-house from feuding among executives. Sometimes they come in court, from battling the Federal Communications Commission.
And sometimes, Disney, which owns ABC, takes hits from its own affiliates.
ABC station owners are irritated with Disney's recent decision to air the Super Bowl on many different platforms, including Disney+, ESPN2, NFL Network and ESPNU. The game is already airing on both ABC and ESPN. The aggregate of the different platforms may drop advertising revenue associated with broadcast viewership by up to 35% compared to last year, according to a station group CEO who asked not to be named because the data is private.
Disney has the broadcast rights to this season's Super Bowl. ABC hasn't had the Super Bowl since 2006. Disney got back in the Super Bowl rotation when it struck its most recent media rights deal with the NFL in 2021.
The Super Bowl is a major moneymaker for ABC stations. Some of these are owned by Disney, but the vast majority are part of local station groups owned by companies such as Sinclair, Nexstar and Tegna.
Fox said last year that Super Bowl ads generated more than $800 million in gross revenue across all platforms. The math for the main broadcast network is simple. There are about 85 30-second spots during a standard game. At $8 million a pop on average, that's $680 million.
Most advertising campaigns are national, but some brands buy big markets only. That allows smaller markets to sell advertising locally.
An average primetime audience is around eight million viewers. So, if the Super Bowl gets 15 times the audience, advertising rates increase in lockstep. Super Bowl LX, held in February, had 125.6 million viewers.
About 3% of a typical local affiliate station's annual advertising revenue comes from the Super Bowl when the game is on its air, according to a person familiar with the matter. The number can be much higher for the owned-and-operated big market stations, which typically take in about $10 million in advertising revenue from the Super Bowl, according to a source familiar with the matter.
Local affiliate stations pay the owners of the broadcast networks — Disney for ABC, Comcast for NBC, Fox for Fox and Skydance for CBS — a so-called reverse retransmission fee for the right to carry network programming.
There's a standard process to retransmission fee discussions. Disney pays billions for live sports and then asks its affiliates for money to help pay for them. The affiliates then negotiate with the pay-TV providers and charge them retrans fees.
This is why the broadcast affiliates are steaming. For decades, the Super Bowl was exclusive to broadcast TV. Getting access to the Big Game was a big part of that fee.
For years, media companies have made the Super Bowl available for both broadcast and streaming audiences. Still, this year, Disney has taken a wrecking ball to the broadcast exclusivity of the past.
Disney's different options
Given the game is an ESPN production with ESPN's primary "Monday Night Football" announcing crew — Joe Buck and Troy Aikman — it's reasonable to assume the cable network will get a fair amount of viewership for the game.
Disney is also putting the game on Disney+ — a streaming service that's never been about sports. Airing the Super Bowl on a streaming service isn't new. NBCUniversal's Peacock, Fox's Tubi and Skydance's Paramount+ have streamed the game in the past. But those services allow for geofenced dynamic advertising insertion (DAI), allowing local affiliates to sell commercials to a streaming audience. Disney+, which doesn't typically air live ABC sports programming, doesn't have DAI.
Disney is also airing so-called "alt-casts" of the game on ESPN2 (Eli and Peyton Manning will do their typical "ManningCast"), ESPNU ("Super Bowl LXI Field Pass with The Pat McAfee Show"), and NFL Network ("Super Bowl LXI Playbook with Next Gen Stats").
Disney is even airing a "Star Wars"-themed alt-cast on Disney Channel and Disney XD. The "Star Wars" alternative broadcast will also be on Disney+.
The commercials that run nationally will be the same on all platforms, according to a Disney spokesperson. The "Star Wars" alt-cast will be ad-free.
Disney wants to synergize its platforms to maximize viewership — and collect the ad revenue.
"The Super Bowl is the year's most-watched telecast, and our broad distribution across ESPN, ABC, and Disney+ will give fans everywhere more ways than ever to enjoy the game," according to a statement provided by a Disney spokesperson. "Making marquee live events available via streaming is a well-established industry practice. Fox and NBC have recently offered the Super Bowl on Tubi and Peacock, and we've similarly streamed 'The Oscars' on Hulu and 'Dancing with the Stars' on Disney+, for example. There's nothing unprecedented about this approach as we are meeting the modern consumer where they are."
Still, the totality of it all will certainly lower broadcast viewership. One station group CEO estimated local advertising revenue associated with the game may fall 35%. That executive declined to be named because the analysis is private.
"Any time you fragment distribution, you're destroying value for each of the individual platforms," a station group CEO told me, who asked not to be named for fear of potential retribution. "I don't have a problem with what Disney is doing — I have a problem that there's no acknowledgement that we're losing money."
Affiliate board involvement
This issue of lower broadcast Super Bowl viewership, and associated advertising revenue, is of so much concern that it's currently being discussed at the affiliate board — an elected body of executives across the TV broadcasting industry who act as liaisons between local stations and their parent network (Disney/ABC, in this case).
It's unclear exactly how affiliates may be compensated, if at all.
The decline in traditional TV viewership is pushing Disney to broaden its coverage to new platforms and new audiences that don't watch cable or broadcast TV.
Station executives want Disney to lean in to what continues to be a profitable, albeit declining, business. Several of those executives told me privately they think Disney is doing itself and the broader linear TV ecosystem a disservice by not banding together with affiliates to keep viewers on broadcast platforms.
"Our ABC affiliates are important partners and we always take that into careful consideration when making these decisions," said a Disney spokesperson. "We've successfully navigated similar situations in collaboration with the governing board many times before, and this is no different."
The chairman of the ABC Television Affiliates Association Board of Governors declined to comment.

The region, located in northwestern Ukraine, roughly 87 miles from Kyiv, is far from the current frontline. Vitalii Bunechko, head of the Zhytomyr Regional Military Administration first reported the attack, putting the number of injured at nine and saying two of them had been taken to the regional hospital.

“Russia continues its deliberate terror against the peaceful Zhytomyr region,” Bunechko said.

Psychologists from the Main Directorate in the Zhytomyr region provided support to residents, and the service’s bomb disposal teams were also deployed to the site. Other emergency services and volunteers from the Red Cross rapid response unit worked at the scene alongside rescuers.

Second attack in 2 days

Civilian life under constant fire
Although international humanitarian law prohibits deliberate attacks on civilians and civilian objects, such strikes have become a daily part of life for residents of Ukraine, reaching regions hundreds of miles from the frontline.
Closer to the front, regional authorities are urging civilians, particularly families with children, to leave as soon as possible.

Russian forces have shelled settlements across the Donetsk region 42 times over the past day, prompting regional authorities to evacuate a total of 215 people, including 68 children.
The attack on the community came around the same time Russian forces used an FPV drone to strike an armored evacuation vehicle of the Proliska Humanitarian Mission near Kramatorsk, also located in the Donetsk region.
On Monday, Oct. 19, Russian forces struck a crowded park in Nova Vodolaha, Kharkiv region with a drone, killing six people, including two children. The youngest victim was a little girl just over a year old, who was killed sitting in her stroller. Her mother, Inna, later died in hospital.
Months earlier, on July 30, a Russian missile struck the village of Radushne in the Kryvyi Rih district of Dnipropetrovsk region, killing an entire family of 10 people, including two parents, seven children, and an 18-month-old grandson.

German AfD party asks government about UFOs, aerial phenomena
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:00:30 UTC
01:00:30 KST

Ayhan Simsek
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Germany’s right-wing AfD party has asked the government whether public institutions are reporting incidents of unidentified aerial phenomena, and whether any findings exist on the topic.
The parliamentary question, signed by the party’s co-chairs Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, follows recent US Pentagon reports, congressional hearings involving pilots and officials, and scientific work by NASA.
In the inquiry, lawmakers asked which ministries or offices are responsible for receiving and evaluating reports of unidentified aerial phenomena and since when records have been kept. They also inquired whether specific terms and definitions such as “UAP” or “UFO” are used and whether standardized federal guidelines exist for public officials.
The Defense Ministry replied to the parliamentary question on behalf of the government, and the response was published on the parliament’s website this week. “There is no information available regarding unidentified aerial phenomena,” the ministry said, adding that the government uses no specific terms or definitions such as “UFO,” “UAP” or “unidentifiable contacts.”
The ministry said monitoring of German airspace is handled by the interior, transport and defense ministries, while tracking objects near Earth in space is the job of the research, technology and space and defense ministries. Officials added that there are no special reporting channels for pilots, air traffic controllers and other personnel to report sightings of unidentified objects in the air or space.
