France hands out swift verdicts in fast-track justice after riots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:41:55 UTC
00:41:55 KST

France hands out swift verdicts in fast-track justice after riots
- French courts are using fast-track justice after weekend riots, handing out swift jail terms and suspended sentences to restore order.
- Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said 2,500 were arrested and 917 prosecuted, calling the response a sign of “great firmness”.
- Lawyers say the process is rushed and harsh, with one calling it “state repression” and warning judges face pressure for tougher penalties.
AI generated
PARIS – French courts have swiftly handed out verdicts, including orders to serve jail time, in fast-track justice for defendants accused over the rioting that erupted on the sidelines of protests at the weekend.
The government says the accelerated legal processes are needed to restore order after some of the worst urban violence in recent years on Oct 17.
But courts are also overwhelmed, while some lawyers say the scale of the hearings reeks of state repression.
Mathilde B, a student, 19, and 20-year-old Francois D, who said he wants to be a mountain guide, had come to Paris on Oct 17 from Auxerre, a city south-east of the capital.
But police found a knuckleduster and flick knife in the young man’s bag and discovered the pair had discussed “guerrilla warfare” and “beating up riot police” on social media.
Mathilde B received a five-month suspended prison sentence; but Francois D was sent to jail immediately as part of an eight-month sentence, with two months to be served in custody.
Tristan Lawless, a lawyer at the bar in Melun south of Paris, said he was defending a client for whom prosecutors had demanded a five-month sentence with immediate custody.
He said the trial was taking place “on the basis of a 50-page case file that, in my view, was put together in haste, with reports that are often vague and lacking detail”, and alleged his client had been beaten in custody.
‘Pressure on judges’
Speaking on Oct 21 in the southern city of Marseille, which saw some of the worst violence, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said that out of some 2,500 people arrested nationwide at the weekend, 917 were being prosecuted, a number he hailed as a “truly impressive figure”.
“The holding cells are full,” he said, referring to the units where people are held ahead of trial, adding this was proof of “our great firmness”.
One of the most longstanding and hyperactive members of the government, Darmanin, a former interior minister, is taking a high profile as Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s Cabinet seeks to show it is in control.
Once seen as having presidential ambitions himself, he is a leading supporter of former centre-right premier Edouard Philippe, who is seen as one of the few candidates capable of defeating far-right front runner Marine Le Pen in 2027 elections.
“We’re here to firmly oppose what we see as an attempt by Gerald Darmanin to make the justice system more punitive,” said Paris lawyer Romain Ruiz, a member of the “Colere noire” (Black anger) collective, which is highly critical of the judicial system.
He accused Darmanin of “putting pressure on judges in pursuit of harsher penalties” and “publicly celebrating the imprisonment of young people”.
“We will never accept that the justice system should become an arm of repression.”
‘Perhaps unprecedented’
Manuel, a 21-year-old cook from central France with no prior criminal record, said he had come to Paris “on a whim” to celebrate his birthday with a friend.
But police who stopped him on Oct 17 close to the starting point of a demonstration found several glass bottles, some rags, and a lighter – what the prosecutor described as “the perfect kit” for a Molotov cocktail. He was sentenced to two months in prison and another six suspended.
Souleymane, a 19-year-old from Ivory Coast without valid residency in France, was arrested in northern Paris while allegedly trying to steal a scooter after storming a corner shop. Convicted three times previously, he was sentenced to eight months in prison and taken into custody.
Julien M, 27, a video artist from south-east France, is accused of hurling a traffic cone which just missed a policeman. He vowed that the protest would be his last and the court set him free under judicial control until a trial at the end of November.
In comments on Oct 20 in the northern city of Lille, also badly hit by rioting, Darmanin said 150 people had already been sent to prison, a colossal figure in a country where short sentences are often served outside of prison with electronic tags.
“People with no previous criminal record are being sent to prison. This is extremely unusual, perhaps even unprecedented, for offences involving damage to property,” he added. AFP

Shmyhal provides UAH 400,000 for prize in Teacher-Defender category of Global Teacher Prize
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:41:24 EEST
00:41:24 KST

Denys Shmyhal, First Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Energy of Ukraine, has personally funded a UAH 400,000 cash prize for the winner of the Teacher-Defender category at the Global Teacher Prize Ukraine 2026, the press service for the First Deputy Prime Minister told Interfax-Ukraine.
"Denys Shmyhal has supported the award since its inception; he has participated in voting as a member of the public and attended the ceremonies in his various capacities—as Prime Minister, Minister of Defense, and currently as First Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Energy. This year, in collaboration with the NGO Osvitoria, he initiated a new, special category: Teacher-Defender. This initiative has opened the door for teachers who have defended Ukraine since 2014 to apply for the award. Under the standard rules of the Global Teacher Prize, educators who left to defend the state were previously ineligible, as they were not actively teaching in schools during that period," the press service explained.
Consequently, Shmyhal spearheaded the creation of the entirely new Teacher-Defender category, ensuring that teachers who have defended Ukraine, whether currently serving in the Defense Forces or having returned from the front to the classroom, once again have the opportunity to compete for this award. It is noted that in October of this year, a winner was named for the first time in the Teacher-Defender category: history and law teacher Captain Oleksandr Chuchayev.
"Denys Shmyhal personally presented the award to the winner. As the initiator of this new category, he provided the funding for the UAH 400,000 prize. In his remarks, he noted that 'teacher-defenders' fulfill two vital missions simultaneously: they defend the country today while preparing a better tomorrow for it. He described taking on this dual responsibility and carrying out one's duty with honor as true heroism," the press service stated in response to an inquiry.
As previously reported by Osvitoria, the winner in this category received a cash prize of UAH 500,000.
On October 21, Shmyhal submitted a notification regarding a significant change in his financial status to the Unified State Register of Declarations, disclosing a UAH 400,000 expenditure in the form of a charitable contribution to fund the prize for the Teacher-Defender category winner.
The Global Teacher Prize Ukraine is an annual national award for the country's best teacher, established in 2017 by the non-profit organization Osvitoria. The award is organized with the support of the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine, along with various partners and benefactors.

US Accuses Russia Of 'Deliberately Reckless' Move With Military Satellite Flyby
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:40:45 UTC
00:40:45 KST

US officials publicly accused Russia of threatening a Finnish-operated commercial satellite that provides imagery and intelligence to Ukraine and other nations, calling the move “deliberately reckless.”
In response to the accusations, made during a United Nations debate on October 21, Russia broadly described US claims as "absurd" and accused Washington of its own “aggressive military space ambitions.”
The back-and-forth came days after a Russian military satellite known as Kosmos-2612 moved “dangerously” near to ICEYE-X36, a satellite registered in the United States and operated by a Finnish company called ICEYE.
The Russian satellite came “exceptionally close” -- within 200 meters, by some estimates -- something that space officials and amateur satellite watchers said was extremely unusual.
"This was not a routine conjunction or 'fly by,'" LeoLabs, an aerospace intelligence company, told RFE/RL. "The behavior is consistent with sophisticated rendezvous and proximity operations."
ICEYE-X36 carries a radar technology that can gather detailed terrestrial images, even through cloud cover. The Finnish company in January signed a contract with the Ukrainian Defense Ministry to provide intelligence.
Kosmos-2612 “exhibited threatening behavior by intentionally maneuvering dangerously close to a commercial satellite,” Brian Hardesty, an adviser to the US Delegation to the Conference on Disarmament, said during a meeting in New York of the UN First Committee, a body that debates arms control and disarmament issues. “These behaviors appear consistent with an on-orbit weapons operation."
“The decision to conduct these activities was deliberately reckless,” he said.
Russia’s representative who could not be immediately identified, did not directly address the assertion.
"We call on member states to give the proper response to the aggressive military space ambitions of the United States," he said.
He also referenced comments made last month by the secretary of the US Air Force, the top civilian official for that military branch.
Speaking to a conference outside of Washington, Troy Meink’s comments that Washington has in fact deployed actual weapons in space -- “on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action” -- caused a jolt among policy experts.
Other longtime space watchers, however, said, the announcement merely stated publicly what had already been obvious for some time.
“The United States did not suddenly weaponize space by acknowledging that it possesses these capabilities,” wrote Mallory Stewart, a former top arms control secretary at the US State Department. “An arms race in space has been under way for years.”

Pete Hegseth has reportedly given DHS permission to test ‘heat ray’ for use at US-Mexico border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:40:41 UTC
00:40:41 KST

Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of defense, reportedly signed a memo last month permitting the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to test a non-lethal “heat ray” for potential use at the US southern border.
The “heat ray”, known as the Active Denial System, is a military-grade weapon that shoots an energy beam causing “a sensation of intense heat on the surface of the skin”, according to a 2009 National Defense University case study on the weapon.
The sensation “creates an intolerable sensation and reflexive movement” such as ducking or running.
In a memo, first obtained by CNN, Hegseth authorized a “temporary loan” of the Active Denial System to the DHS for seven months beginning in September. The DHS can request further use of the Pentagon system if needed.
A spokesperson for Customs and Border Protection (CBP) said in a statement it was “continually evaluating new technology, especially technology that can save lives while simultaneously enhancing national security effectiveness”.
When asked for comment, the Pentagon referred the Guardian to the DHS, which shared the CBP statement.
It is unclear what the DHS plans to use the Active Denial System for exactly, but the memo permits the department to use it for potential operations at the US-Mexico border.
The US military initially brought the system to Afghanistan nearly 20 years ago, but it was quickly returned home without ever being used, the Washington Post reported.
Previously, CBP officials reportedly considered using the Active Denial System in areas with a large number of illegal crossings or for crowd dispersal, but it was never deployed.
When used, the Active Denial System can produce an invisible beam of 95 gigahertz that penetrates about 1/64th of an inch into the skin, causing a burning sensation. (The system is technically not a “heat ray” because it uses millimeter waves, not infrared, Forbes reported in 2020.)
Pentagon officials have compared the feeling to a blast of heat when opening a hot oven, according to CNN. The feeling is temporary, lasting between 10 and 15 minutes.
In 2012, the Marine Corps announced that the system was compliant with international legal obligations of the US, and officials said they felt “comfortable” that it was safe.
The new memo, seen by CNN, states that the DHS will be solely responsible for the system’s “employment, use and development of tactics, techniques and procedures”. It also states that no Department of Defense personnel shall operate it.
During the first Trump administration, officials sought to use the Active Denial System, first in 2018 to stop migrants from crossing the border, the New York Times reported. Later, in 2020, the administration also sought it to control protests in Washington DC after the killing of George Floyd, the Washington Post reported.

U.S. orders 60,000 attack drones from nine companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:40:05 UTC
00:40:05 KST

- The U.S. Department of War is preparing orders for 60,000 small attack drones from nine companies after the Drone Dominance Program’s Gauntlet II.
- Perennial Autonomy and Neros topped the Deep Strike and Close Quarters Battle categories, each receiving the maximum initial order of 8,000 drones.
The U.S. Department of War is preparing orders for 60,000 small attack drones from nine companies after the second round of its Drone Dominance Program, with Perennial Autonomy and Neros each set to receive the maximum initial order of 8,000 units.
The Defense Innovation Unit, which runs the program with the Test Resource Management Center, said orders are now in the works following Gauntlet II, a month-long flyoff held in August 2026 at Fort Carson, Colorado. Perennial Autonomy took the top spot in the Deep Strike mission area with 80.1 points, while Neros led the Close Quarters Battle category with 88.1 points, according to the program’s published leaderboard.
“Congratulations to all the winners. Now, it’s time to deliver,” the Defense Innovation Unit wrote in announcing the results.
The orders are split evenly between the two mission areas, with 30,000 drones in each, and scale with each company’s ranking. In Deep Strike, Hyperscale placed second and is in line for 7,000 drones, followed by Neros with 6,000, Skycutter with 5,000 and Swarm Defense Technologies with 4,000. In Close Quarters Battle, ORQA US placed second with 7,000, followed by XTEND with 6,000, Vector with 5,000 and ModalAI with 4,000. Neros is the only company to place in both categories, bringing its combined allocation to 14,000 drones, and final quantities will be set when contracts are awarded.
Gauntlet II tested the drones on a find-fix-finish mission, meaning locating a target, confirming it and striking it. Deep Strike lanes required drones to hit targets from 15 km (9.3 miles) away, while Close Quarters Battle lanes tested performance in confined spaces such as buildings, with part of the testing repeated at night. Additional lanes evaluated controlled strikes and electronic warfare performance, with the drones flown against counter-drone systems designed to jam or defeat them.
Companies were scored on more than flight results. The final rankings combined Gauntlet II performance with evaluations from military operators who flew the systems and an assessment of each company’s ability to produce drones at scale and secure its supply chain.
The second round raised the bar considerably on range. Gauntlet I, held at Fort Benning, Georgia, in February and March 2026, sent 25 companies through testing that included strikes at about 10 km (6.2 miles), and the Defense Innovation Unit said only 24% of drones in that round reached 10 km. That first round produced orders for about 30,000 one-way attack drones worth roughly $150 million, with London-based Skycutter topping the leaderboard and Neros in second place.
The program grew out of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth’s July 2025 memo on military drone dominance, which called for every U.S. Army squad to be armed with small one-way attack drones by the end of fiscal 2026. The Department of War plans to spend about $1.1 billion across four phases of the program, which is designed to build a U.S.-based industrial base for low-cost expendable drones. Officials said in testimony earlier this year that Phase II would exclude systems using motors or batteries from so-called covered countries, a requirement aimed at Chinese components.
Several of the Gauntlet II winners have already shared details of their orders. Vector said it received orders for up to 5,000 drone systems along with its high-voltage electronic safe and arm device, which lets operators arm drones with different munitions, and XTEND said it delivered 120 STRIKER systems for testing, as The Defence Blog reported when the Close Quarters Battle scores were released.
Officials plan to follow Gauntlet II with Gauntlet 2.5, focused on bomber drones that drop munitions, and Gauntlet 3 is scheduled to begin about six months after Gauntlet II.

ChatGPT adds PIN and Face ID chat locks
According to the company’s official guidance, locked conversations disappear from regular chat history, pinned chats and standard conversation searches.
“This can help keep sensitive conversations out of view when you share your screen or use a shared device,” OpenAI said.
Users can access protected conversations through Projects > Locked chats by entering a four-digit account PIN. Supported mobile devices also offer Face ID, Touch ID or device unlock.
To protect an existing conversation, users select “Lock chat” from its options menu and create or enter their PIN.
The feature is rolling out across Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu plans, although some conversation types are ineligible.
Locking a conversation does not add end-to-end encryption or change data retention and model-training settings.
OpenAI also cautions that resetting a forgotten PIN permanently deletes locked conversations and content protected solely by that PIN. Changing a known PIN preserves them.

The facility, operated by German defense manufacturer Rheinmetall in Telford, manufactures barrels and breeches for 120mm and 155mm weapon systems, including the RCH 155 artillery platform.
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting officially opened the facility alongside senior military and company officials on Thursday.

Families of missing Azerbaijanis call for support from European institutions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:37:33 UTC
00:37:33 KST

Families of more than 4,000 Azerbaijanis still missing since the first Karabakh war brought their demand for answers to the EU institutions, hoping that the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan, after decades of suffering on both sides, could finally clarify the fate of their relatives.
Azerbaijani families of missing persons demanded support from EU institutions in Brussels during their demonstrations this week in front of the European Parliament and European Commission headquarters, as they continue to seek the truth about the fate of over 4,000 loved ones still missing since the first Karabakh war.
Organised by the Garabagh Missing Families Public Union, the families asked for help in their quest to establish the fate of their relatives, which include children, women and elderly people, who remain missing since the first war that ended in 1994, urging the EU institutions to pressure Armenia into disclosing archive information and the locations of mass graves.
With 32 mass graves recently discovered in Karabakh, the families have emphasised that their right to know the truth after 30 years requires international attention. They said the group had not received international recognition or aid to help find their relatives.
The families said that Armenia has not disclosed any information about the missing persons, but they hoped that the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan can now shed light on the fate of their loved ones and achieve closure.
The rally participants wore white jackets, each with a picture of their loved one, their date of birth and a question mark, symbolising their unknown fate.
"My husband Azad Jabbarovwent missing in Khojaly and for 34 years we know nothing about him," said Farida Jabbarova, a participant at the rally.
"And here, I represent him and more than 4,000 people who went missing and require justice for them and to receive information."
The demonstration displayed personal items of those missing, including passports, photos and clothes.
According to Konul Behbudova, head of the Garabagh Missing Families Public Union, 328 missing persons were identified with DNA examinations and the remains of 273 victims were handed over to their families, but the fate of thousands is still unknown.
"These territories are contaminated with mines and unexploded ordinance, that's why it's difficult to find them," Behbudova said.
"Our goal is to find the places were these people were buried and find any information about their fate, to get their remains and be able to burry them and to have a place in the cemetery to visit them," Jabbarova said.
The plight of the Azerbaijani families is now part of the wider peace process and reconciliation between Armenia and Azerbaijan after decades of tragic wars over Karabakh which brought immense suffering to both nations, with thousands of casualties and refugees on both sides.
Armenia said that hundreds of Armenians are also missing following the Karabakh wars and has also sought answers about their fate as well.

Top 9 horror films worth watching on Halloween
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:37:15 EEST
00:37:15 KST

Top 9 horror films worth watching on Halloween
Kyiv • UNN
A selection of nine horror films featuring mysticism, psychological tension, and supernatural threats. Among them are "The Witch of Konotop" and classic horror movies.
Scary stories come in many forms: some frighten us with otherworldly creatures, others keep us on edge until the very last minute, while some make us reflect on human fears. Over the decades, horror has evolved from classic monsters to psychological thrillers and unusual experiments with the genre. UNN has compiled a selection of the top 9 films that will create a chilling atmosphere and help set the mood for an evening of horror.
Rosemary’s Baby
In Roman Polanski’s film, an ordinary young woman’s life gradually turns into an unsettling story with mystical overtones. Rosemary begins to suspect that the people around her are hiding something dangerous, and that the events happening to her have a much darker explanation than they initially seem to. The film stands out for its atmosphere of constant anxiety and its skillful use of ambiguity. Rather than immediately revealing the source of the fear, the director leaves viewers room for doubt and speculation. It was this approach that made the film a notable example of supernatural horror.
The Ring
Journalist Rachel Keller begins investigating the mysterious deaths of four teenagers. Shortly before their deaths, they had all watched a strange videotape and then received a phone call warning them that they had only seven days left to live. A fifth girl, who witnessed her friend’s death, lost her mind. Rachel’s niece was among the victims, so the journalist decides to find out what the mysterious recording conceals. She finds the tape and watches it, but soon receives the same call, accompanied by a horrifying prediction of her own death. Together with a friend who works as a video engineer, Rachel tries to uncover the recording’s origins and stop the unknown threat. However, the danger also spreads to her family: the journalist’s son accidentally watches a copy of the video, after which he begins to be haunted by terrifying visions.
The Babadook
Amelia raises her son Sam on her own after the death of her husband, who died on the child’s birthday. The woman tries to cope with everyday difficulties, but the boy’s behavior becomes increasingly strange. Sam is convinced that a terrifying creature named the Babadook has moved into their home. Gradually, fear enters the lives of the entire family. However, the film is not only about a mysterious monster. Through Amelia’s story, the director shows a mother’s exhaustion, her inner tension, and the difficulty of living with constant responsibility for a child. "The Babadook" combines supernatural horror with psychological drama.
The Cabin in the Woods
A group of young people sets out to spend the weekend in a remote cabin in the woods. At first, everything resembles the familiar plot of a classic slasher, in which a group finds itself far from civilization and encounters danger. However, it soon becomes clear that events are unfolding in a completely unexpected way. The film plays with the familiar rules of horror movies and turns well-known genre conventions into part of an unexpected story. It has typical characters, a creepy location, and situations reminiscent of dozens of other horror films, but the creators use these elements to reinterpret the genre.
Paranormal Activity
A young couple moves into a house where unexplained things begin to happen. The woman says that she has felt the presence of an unknown entity since childhood. Her partner decides to set up a camera to record everything that happens at night. The film is shot in the found-footage style: viewers observe events through camera recordings, creating an impression of reality. Oren Peli worked on the film in his own home, and the production budget was approximately $15,000. After its release, the film became a major commercial success and launched an entire franchise.
The Witch
The events unfold in 17th-century New England. A Puritan family is expelled from the community and settles near the forest, hoping to start life anew. But the peace does not last long: the youngest child disappears without a trace, and strange things begin happening in the house. Gradually, distrust and fear grow among the family members. The mother is overcome by despair, the father begins to doubt, and their eldest daughter, Thomasin, is suspected of witchcraft. The film creates tension through its gloomy atmosphere, historical setting, and the conflict between religious beliefs and inexplicable events. It is a slow-burn horror film in which fear gradually builds, while the boundary between superstition and the supernatural remains uncertain.
The Witch of Konotop
The beautiful Olena has left her witching past behind for love and a peaceful life. However, the full-scale invasion destroys her plans: while trying to leave the combat zone, the woman loses her beloved, who is killed by Russian occupiers. What she has endured changes Olena. She returns to her true nature and uses supernatural powers to take revenge on those who took the most precious person in her life from her. The film reimagines the image of the Witch of Konotop in the context of the modern war. The film stars Tetiana Malkova and Taras Tsymbaliuk. For director Andrii Kolesnyk, it was his feature-film debut. Real captured military equipment was also used during filming.
Annabelle
John and Mia are preparing to become parents. To please his wife, the husband gives her a vintage doll to add to her collection. But that very night, their home becomes the site of a brutal attack: members of a Satanic cult break into the house. After this event, the couple encounters inexplicable phenomena connected with the doll. A dark entity is behind them, turning the family home into a place of constant fear. "Annabelle" combines the theme of occultism with a story about a threat to a young family. The doll itself plays a particularly important role in creating the eerie atmosphere, with its stillness only intensifying the sense of danger.
Other
In the mid-1940s, Grace Stewart lives with her two children in an old mansion on the island of Jersey. She is waiting for her husband to return from the war, though there has been no news of him for a long time. Her children cannot tolerate sunlight, so strict rules apply in the house: the windows must be covered with curtains, and the doors must be kept tightly shut. The usual order is disrupted when her daughter Anne tells her about an unfamiliar boy whom she supposedly saw in the house. The girl claims that he lives there with his family. At first, Grace does not believe her, but eventually she begins to notice strange things herself. The film gradually reveals a story in which the secrets of the old mansion intertwine with fear and very unexpected plot twists.
Mama
After the mysterious disappearance of their father, two young sisters, Victoria and Lily, are left alone in an abandoned house in the forest. Several years later, the girls are found and taken in by their uncle Lucas and his girlfriend Annabel. The children gradually adjust to their new life, but they behave strangely and constantly mention a mysterious "Mama" who, according to them, cared for them throughout all the years they were alone. Eventually, the adults begin to notice strange phenomena in the house... It constantly scratches at the walls and makes strange noises. At first, the new parents believe it is either the children’s imagination or emotional trauma, but in the end it becomes clear that it is their dead mother, who has returned from the other world to look after the children.

Greece, Egypt in talks to extend maritime zone further east
Oct 22 - Greece and Egypt are discussing extending their Exclusive Economic Zone eastwards towards Cyprus after eastern Libya's parliament ratified a disputed maritime agreement with Turkey earlier this week, Greece's foreign minister said.
Greece, Egypt and Cyprus have long opposed the Turkey-Libya maritime accord, arguing that it infringes on their own maritime claims in the eastern Mediterranean.
Any extension of the Greece-Egypt agreement would be fully in line with international law and the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis said on X.
Gerapetritis and Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty also reaffirmed their opposition to eastern Libya's ratification of the 2019 maritime memorandum between Turkey and Libya, saying they remained committed to international law and UNCLOS.
Greece and Egypt signed an agreement in 2020 delimiting an Exclusive Economic Zone in the eastern Mediterranean. REUTERS

Hendel: Reservists/Economic Party may not the biggest, but it will be most important - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:35:06 UTC
00:35:06 KST

The Reservists or the New Economic Party will be the most important party in the election even if it is not the largest, its leader Yoaz Hendel told The Jerusalem Post on Thursday.
“We may not be the biggest party, but we will be the most important, because we are in nobody’s pocket,” Hendel said.
The party, he explained, will only join a coalition of Zionist parties, and isn’t ruling any of them out based on whether they are or are not current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
“If a government comprising Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu, and [Naftali] Bennett were formed tomorrow morning, I would be part of it,” he added. “I’m not in the ‘anyone but Bibi’ camp.”
Hendel distinguished between his opposition to Netanyahu’s leadership and his willingness to join a government that includes him. His coalition decisions, he argued, would depend on its partners and policies rather than the prime minister’s presence alone.
“I make no secret of wanting to persuade everyone not to vote for Bibi. I make no secret of believing he bears responsibility for October 7,” he said. “But Netanyahu is not the central issue in my outlook.”
Reservists-Economic chair says his party will decide coalition for 2026 election
His refusal to sit with the haredi (Ultra-Orthodox) parties would also exclude a partnership with Likud if Netanyahu insisted on bringing them into the coalition.
“I won’t sit with the haredi parties. If Likud can’t part ways with them, I won’t sit with Likud,” Hendel said.
Hendel presented his party’s position outside the two rival blocs as the source of its potential influence, arguing that neither camp could form a government without it.
“Without the Reservists/Economic Party, there is a zero percent chance that either bloc will form a government. Zero, not even one percent,” he said.
That prediction underpins his argument for supporting a smaller party: Rather than strengthening an existing bloc, he wants voters to give his party the leverage to demand a different coalition.
“Every vote for our party influences Israel’s future. Every vote for the blocs keeps us stuck,” he said.
Hendel described a constituency spanning voters on the right who support settlement but oppose draft evasion, and voters in the center and on the left who reject cooperation with Arab parties that have not recognized Hamas as a terrorist organization.
“We want to hold the deciding vote,” he said.
Asked whether pressure on parties hovering around the electoral threshold could persuade him to withdraw, Hendel rejected the premise that other political leaders should determine how his supporters vote.
“That’s a quarter of a million Israelis who have the right to choose what they want to do,” he said. “Nobody can tell them what they should do.”
He criticized both Winter’s alignment with Netanyahu and the haredi parties and what he characterized as Eisenkot, Bennett, and Avigdor Liberman’s membership in an opposing bloc dependent on Arab parties.
“The moment you say you will only go with Netanyahu and the haredi parties, you are in the ‘only Bibi’ bloc. That means you won’t address conscription,” he said of Winter.
“There is no chance of recruiting soldiers when you’re with Goldknopf and Goldknopf is your partner.”
Hendel said he had repeatedly urged Winter to break that partnership, describing his own party as Winter’s “natural political home.”
Asked what would make parties such as Ra’am or Shas acceptable partners, Hendel said his objection was not to Arab or haredi citizens.
“I have nothing against haredim or Arabs,” he said. “I hope that one day there will be a haredi party of people who enlist and serve, and that one day there will be an Arab party of people who serve and see themselves as part of Israel.”
He linked that position to demands for core curriculum studies, the teaching of Zionism, and Israeli flags in publicly funded classrooms. Families rejecting that framework should fund their children’s education themselves, he argued.
“Every Israeli citizen will do something for the country, and anyone who doesn’t will receive nothing.”
Hendel backs Zelekha on economic demands
Hendel’s coalition conditions also extend to the economic agenda of his political partner, Yaron Zelekha of the New Economic Party.
“Both issues weigh heavily on reservists,” he said. “It isn’t only conscription. The cost of living hurts them badly, too.”
He also cautioned that easing the burden on existing reservists would take time. Training an infantry soldier takes approximately eight months, he said, while reducing annual reserve service to 30 days under current conditions remained a “pipe dream.”
Asked what he would change about his earlier conduct in politics, Hendel acknowledged making “plenty of mistakes,” pointing to the cycle of elections and dissolving Knessets, arguing that remaining in politics could not be an end in itself.
“Politics brought us to October 7, and politics has to get us out of it,” he said.
Hendel said his experience commanding reservists taught him that leadership depends on persuasion rather than simply issuing orders - an approach he said also shaped his partnership with Zelekha.
“Ultimately, what matters isn’t your rank but your level of commitment,” he said. “The same applies to politics.”

US House committee investigation exposes antisemitism, political indoctrination in public schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:34:26 UTC
00:34:26 KST

A congressional investigation released on Wednesday has detailed widespread antisemitism and political activism within American K-12 public schools and major teachers' unions following the October 7, 2023 attacks against Israel.
The majority staff report, called “Antisemitism in K-12 Schools” and published by the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, stated that antisemitic incidents in US schools increased by 135 percent in 2023, prompting congressional inquiries into several major school districts and labor organizations.
Committee Chairman Tim Walberg said, “Parents send their children to school to learn reading, writing, and math—not to be taught to hate Israel or embrace radical political causes. Yet that’s exactly the kind of material our investigation uncovered. Jewish students deserve to feel safe in their classrooms, and parents deserve to know what their children are being taught. Schools that receive taxpayer dollars must be held accountable when they fail to protect students from antisemitism.”
Investigations opened into California, Pennsylvania, Virginia schools
Under Chairman Walberg’s leadership, the committee opened investigations into Berkeley Unified School District (BUSD) in California, the School District of Philadelphia (SDP) in Pennsylvania, and Fairfax County Public Schools in Virginia.
The committee selected school districts of varying size and geographic location after receiving numerous reports of antisemitic incidents. The committee noted that its inquiry into Fairfax County remains ongoing.
As part of the wider inquiry, the committee conducted a transcribed interview with Philadelphia Superintendent Dr. Tony Watlington on September 18, 2026, and also investigated the nation’s largest teachers union, the National Education Association (NEA), over allegations of antisemitism.
The committee released documents obtained through its investigations into Berkeley, Philadelphia, and the NEA while continuing its inquiry into Fairfax County.
Focusing on the SDP, the report examined the ninth-largest school district in the US, which comprises 330 schools. The district entered into a federal civil rights resolution agreement with the US Department of Education in December 2024 to address the handling of antisemitic harassment following a sharp rise in incidents after October 7, 2023. According to the congressional report, the investigation found that district curricula promoted ideology justifying violent resistance and legitimized radical groups that incite antisemitism.
Curriculum writers portrayed all resistance as righteous
For example, investigators detailed that a world history curriculum unit covering resistance movements directed students to honor a movement of their choice, listing the Gaza Great March of Return as an option, and opened by teaching that the fight to decolonize in India was not always peaceful.
The report noted that teachers were told to examine the works of Frantz Fanon, whose writings argue that decolonization is inherently violent and who is frequently cited by anti-Israel activists to justify the October 7 attacks.
The congressional report stated that the Philadelphia district’s materials also relied on resources from the Racial Justice Organizing Committee, noting that leaders of the group declared that all resistance is righteous and that there are no two sides to ‘apartheid, occupation, and genocide’.
In lessons using these materials, the report found that Philadelphia students were asked to color-code aspects of their identities as dominant or oppressed. These lessons categorized males, white people, and Christians as dominant, and black people, LGBTQ people, immigrants, and non-Christians as oppressed.
Furthermore, investigators outlined that district curricula introduce far-left activism and terms like “intersectionality,” “ally,” and “social justice” as early as the third grade. The report added that curricula recommended children’s books introducing pronouns such as “ey/em” and “ze/zir”.
According to the report, investigators established that district employees responsible for writing curricula fomented antisemitism online and among colleagues. This included the director of social studies curriculum, Ismael Jimenez, who the report noted had repeatedly rationalized violence against Jews.
The report stated that other curriculum writers maintained that all resistance is righteous. Additionally, investigators documented that the district has repeatedly partnered with the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) Philadelphia. The report highlighted that a representative previously suggested that curricular materials be reviewed for bias by qualified Muslim educators, and that Superintendent Watlington’s transition team included the group’s former executive director.
During his September 2026 interview with the committee, Superintendent Watlington stated that the social studies curriculum complied with district policies and did not indoctrinate students. He added that the district would standardize its curriculum by using national experts and that the social studies curriculum director was undergoing termination proceedings.
In Berkeley Unified School District, consisting of 20 schools in California, investigators examined extensive antisemitism complaints lodged by parents and students since October 7, 2023. These complaints occurred alongside the district’s adoption of liberated ethnic studies.
The report found that BUSD collaborated with the Liberated Ethnic Studies Model Curriculum Consortium, paying over $111,000 for curriculum writing and consulting since August 2023. According to the congressional findings, this collaboration resulted in lessons littered with antisemitic resources and activist ideology.
Berkeley’s ninth-grade Arab American Studies unit featured an ancestor acknowledgment of Helen Thomas. The report stated that the unit defended her remarks, which told Jewish people to leave the Middle East and go home to Poland and Germany, by framing the controversial statements as constructive activism, asserting that she was engaged in what is termed “good trouble” and that her comments had been taken out of context.
The congressional report noted that BUSD’s ethnic studies units cover topics like the seven pillars of colonization, including killing cultures and exploiting land, and feature specific lessons arguing that Asian people have been weaponized as pawns to serve a white supremacist agenda.
Leadership rationalized Hamas attacks
Berkeley elementary and high school teachers also collaborated on teaching guides that featured the alphabet book P is for Palestine. The book includes selections such as ‘I is for Intifada’. The guides recommended organizations such as the Middle East Children’s Alliance (MECA) and the Arab Resource and Organizing Center (AROC).
Berkeley high school teachers approved an Israel and Palestine lesson set that the report stated whitewashed terrorism and portrayed the phrase "from the river to the sea" as a call for freedom and peace. The committee noted that teachers warned colleagues that the curriculum could not be shared directly with families.
Furthermore, investigators documented that district staff and students raised money through bake sales and bracelet sales for MECA. The report highlighted that the Network Contagion Research Institute (NCRI) identified this organization as having fiscal and personnel ties to the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), a US-designated foreign terrorist organization.
At the NEA, representing more than three million educators and administrators, investigators found that antisemitism surged following October 7, 2023. This surge culminated in a 2025 delegate vote to ban Anti-Defamation League (ADL) materials.
According to internal NEA documents cited in the report, the union was already not working with the ADL because of the watchdog’s efforts to combat contemporary antisemitism. Internal memos criticized the ADL for denigrating the Black Lives Matter (BLM) movement.
The report also detailed that the NEA’s Center for Racial and Social Justice (CRSJ) advised against implementing a resolution by the union’s Jewish Affairs Caucus (JAC) to combat antisemitism because it utilized the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition.
Union staff wrote in a briefing document that the definition had been used by racist and nationalist actors as cover. Additionally, internal documents showed union leaders were advised to avoid action language regarding historical events in the Middle East because history is hotly contested.
Leadership was also explicitly advised that keffiyehs should be allowed at association gatherings as a sign of support for Palestine. The report confirmed that the union pledged thousands of dollars to Rethinking Schools and the Zinn Education Project.
According to the committee, these organizations published statements after October 7 rationalizing Hamas terrorist attacks by pointing to US and Israeli colonialism.
The committee concluded stating that political activism has increasingly displaced educational neutrality across American public education. This has created an environment where antisemitism is minimized, excused, and permitted to flourish.
The committee stated that “public schools should educate students, not enlist them in political causes.” The report added that “parents should be able to trust that schools will educate their children without subjecting them to radical ideology.”
The report stressed that “Jewish students are entitled to the same protection from discrimination and harassment as every other student, regardless of whether hostility toward them is expressed in overt antisemitic terms or cloaked in political rhetoric.”
The committee vowed that it “will continue to use its oversight authority to examine these issues, consider appropriate legislation, and hold federally funded institutions accountable for compliance with federal civil rights law.”

According to the official, Sunni countries are watching the escalation led by the Houthis against neighboring Saudi Arabia, with encouragement and support from Iran, and understand that they could be next.
Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, is concentrating its efforts on launching powerful attacks against an extensive range of targets in Houthi-controlled areas, seeking to degrade critical military capabilities, including infrastructure.
"Two main points need to be made about this. First, it serves Israel's interests quite well because it wears down the military strength of an Israeli enemy that is preparing and planning to harm us in the future. In addition, we are monitoring and observing methods of operation and tactics, and learning a great deal from what is happening there, including about weapons that are not necessarily manufactured by the Houthis," the official said.
IDF helps Saudi Arabia combat Houthis
The defense official added that the relentless attacks against the Houthis are eroding their capabilities and forcing them to expend considerable effort.
"The Houthis are accustomed to building up their forces, not employing them on this scale. They are a serious enemy, well structured for the long term, but this presents them with a significant challenge. It is no coincidence that they operate sequentially rather than simultaneously against their enemies."
The official further said that the pressure on Saudi Arabia is reshaping alliances and relationships across the Middle East, creating new opportunities.
"The question here is who will intervene on Saudi Arabia's behalf. There is apprehension among countries, but we assess that there will be intervention. Everything remains open, and it is not too late for that to happen."
Meanwhile, the IDF is completing preparations across the sea, air, land, and electromagnetic spectrum domains for a potential Houthi attack as part of a multi-front scenario involving Iran, Hezbollah, and Shi'ite militias operating from Iraq.
The preparations include not only the integration of new technologies and sensors, along with improved connectivity within the IDF and between organizations, but also coordination with the US military.
The US military has a clear interest in protecting Israel's home front because thousands of American troops, aircraft, and US military systems, including air defense systems, are stationed in Israel.

Lockheed lines up deal for 850 U.S. F-35s over 10 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:32:33 UTC
00:32:33 KST

- The U.S. Department of War and Lockheed Martin agreed on a framework for 850 U.S. F-35s over 10 years, covering Lots 21 through 30.
- The deal keeps production at 156 aircraft a year and moves to a formal contract once Congress grants multiyear authority and funding.
The U.S. Department of War and Lockheed Martin have agreed on a framework for a 10-year F-35 production and sustainment deal that covers 850 aircraft for the United States, along with spare parts, modification kits and international orders across production Lots 21 through 30.
The framework keeps F-35 production at 156 aircraft a year and folds three things that have traditionally been bought separately into one long-term plan: new jets with their initial spares, a decade of modification kits, and fleet sustainment. The next step runs through Congress: once multiyear authority and the associated funding are granted, the F-35 Joint Program Office and Lockheed Martin will finalize contract terms, pricing and delivery schedules in a formal contract award.
“This multiyear framework strengthens the way we can plan and invest in the F-35 enterprise,” said Lockheed Martin Chairman, President and CEO Jim Taiclet. “With the greater certainty that comes from the U.S. government’s transformative approach to F-35 production and sustainment, we can make the upfront investments needed to expand capacity, improve efficiency, and build a more resilient supply chain. That’s good for the taxpayer, good for our suppliers and, most importantly, good for the United States and its allies.”
The 850 U.S. aircraft over 10 years work out to an average of 85 jets a year for the U.S. Air Force, U.S. Navy and U.S. Marine Corps, with the remainder of the 156-a-year production rate going to international partners and foreign customers. The United States plans to buy a total of 2,456 F-35s across its three services.
Until now, the F-35 has been bought in lot-by-lot contracts that often took years to negotiate. The most recent deal, covering Lots 18 and 19, was finalized on Sept. 29, 2025, after a handshake agreement the previous December, and covers 296 aircraft worth about $24.3 billion. Long-lead funding for parts for Lot 20 and Lot 21 aircraft has already been awarded, and Lot 21 is now the first lot included in the new framework.
A multiyear arrangement lets Lockheed Martin and its suppliers commit to larger, longer orders for raw materials and parts. The company says that approach will produce volume discounts, lower unit prices and savings for taxpayers estimated in the billions of dollars over the life of the program, while giving the government more predictable costs.
Readiness is a central part of the plan. The framework links aircraft production with purchases of spare and modification parts and adds integrated analytics that tie budget decisions to readiness results and give real-time visibility into parts inventories. Lockheed Martin says replacing the annual contracting cycle with long-term supplier contracts will cut turnaround times for parts and repairs and raise mission capable rates, the share of the fleet ready to fly its assigned missions.
“Our new multiyear framework gives suppliers stability to plan for the future and invest with confidence, improving readiness across the F-35 fleet,” said OJ Sanchez, president of Lockheed Martin Aeronautics.
The company estimates the program will support 317,000 U.S. jobs and generate about $79 billion in annual economic activity over the next decade. International customers would share in the benefits through economies of scale across the global fleet and its shared sustainment network.
More than 1,375 F-35s are now in service around the world, operating from 42 bases, including in 13 countries that fly the jet from home soil, and the fleet has passed 1 million flight hours. Lockheed Martin delivered a record 191 F-35s in 2025.
The F-35 Joint Program Office and Lockheed Martin will move to a formal contract award for Lots 21 through 30 once Congress grants multiyear authority and the associated appropriations, which the companies expect in the coming months.

Save $150 on the Apple Mac Mini M4, but There’s a Catch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:30:31 UTC
00:30:31 KST

Apple’s Mac Mini M4 has become a popular mini-yet-mighty desktop computer for running local agentic AI 24/7—so much so that it’s been out of stock for months. But with the introduction of the new Mac Mini M6, the older M4 is no longer as scarce (there was no M5 Mac Mini), and the base model (256-GB hard drive, 16-GB unified memory) is on sale for $649—$150 off MSRP and $250 cheaper than the M6.
It’s a good deal for a computer that is plenty powerful for most people, and some M4 Mac Mini configurations can even handle AI tasks. But—and it’s a big but—shoppers should be aware that the M4’s original base price was $599 when it launched in 2024. However, with Apple raising prices on hardware across the board this year, driven by chip and memory shortages, the M4 ended up costing $799. In comparison, the new M6 starts at $899.
Depending on how you look at it, it’s either a discount or a hard pill to swallow, knowing that it used to be much cheaper. If you’ve been eyeing a new Mac Mini and don’t need the better performance of the M6, you’re unlikely to get a lower price than this M4.
Older but Still Capable
The M4 Mac Mini may no longer be Apple’s most powerful tiny computer—that title now belongs to the M6 and M5 Pro models—but the M4 is still an incredibly strong and efficient processor. When it was discovered that it could easily run agentic AI locally, people gobbled up the Mac Mini as the affordable computing option.
Of course, for intensive tasks like AI or video editing, you really need more than 16 GB of memory; those who bought it for AI purposes loaded it up with 32 GB of RAM. For most users, however, this base-specs machine is more than capable. While the M6 system on a chip is extra powerful due to having more CPU and GPU cores, Neural Accelerators, and higher memory bandwidth, the M4 Mac Mini isn’t lagging far behind. For things like web browsing and general productivity, you won’t see much of a difference in performance.
If you need the performance, we recommend the newer M6. But for most people, the M4 Mac Mini is more than sufficient for everyday computing, and you're unlikely to find a better deal than this one.

What would make neonatal units safer for babies? | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:27:59 UTC
00:27:59 KST

I support Mark McDonald’s submission that the Thirlwall recommendations will lead to more blame and suspicion in the NHS (17 October). We often hear of hospital scandals where trusts are intent on preserving their reputations, internal inquiries go nowhere, defensive clinical staff deflect blame on to others, non‑disclosure to patients of errors and “lessons learned” rhetoric that is quickly forgotten. There is also an industry of ambulance-chasing lawyers. None of this is conducive to a no-blame, honest, open culture in healthcare. The Thirlwall recommendations of more surveillance will make it worse.
There is an alternative. Most of my professional life as a hospital consultant, clinical director and deputy chief medical officer has been spent in New Zealand, whose publicly funded NHS is the same model as the UK’s – but with a major difference. In the 1970s, New Zealanders lost their right to sue for damages for medical accidents or injury through the public court system with the Accident Compensation Act. This got rid of the grievance culture and ambulance-chasers, and the system provided remedial care for any injury. In the 80s, after a huge scandal regarding medical investigations, the Cartwright inquiry ushered in the creation of the independent Health and Disability Commissioner (HDC) and overriding principles of patient safety, interests and consent.
All complaints – from patients, public and staff – about any health facility, organisation or practitioner go first to the office of the HDC for investigation. If the HDC deems it necessary, it goes to the various professional disciplinary bodies or to the Medical Council of New Zealand. HDC reports on complaints are publicly available.
In 2005, the government passed its “no fault, no blame” legislation. This brought in a duty to report “any risk of harm to the public from authorities responsible for patient safety”. This freed clinicians to engage with any compensation cases with openness. The system has its critics, but overall works well.
 
Dr Pamela S Melding 
 
St Helens, Merseyside
Mark McDonald’s column is a breath of common sense. The Criminal Cases Review Commission is still considering Lucy Letby’s convictions, yet Lady Justice Kathryn Thirlwall has constructed a programme of reform on the assumption that the central conclusion of the case is beyond question. Meanwhile, barely enough time has passed for reflection on what would actually make neonatal units safer.
Thirlwall’s answer appears to be surveillance, suspicion and blame: cameras in cots, encouragement to report colleagues and an explicit retreat from the “no blame” culture developed precisely to make organisations safer.
But what makes a hospital safe? Is it a nurse wondering whether a colleague is about to report them, or a nurse confident enough to admit that they have made a mistake? Is it a doctor practising defensively, or one willing to report a near-miss before it becomes a tragedy?
Destroy candour and you destroy one of the most powerful tools of patient safety. A frightened workforce will hide mistakes, keep quiet about doubts and practise defensively. Patients will pay.
 
Mark Hanson
 
Hitchin, Hertfordshire
In March this year my daughter was born and died in the neonatal intensive care unit seven days later. I believe her death was preventable and one key mistake was made that resulted in her death. But I don’t blame the consultant who made (what I consider to be) the error. She was doing the best she could in a difficult situation.
What I find concerning is the follow-up from the trust’s management. They have bent over backwards to try to hide their tracks rather than discussing it openly and using it as an opportunity to learn and ensure other babies don’t suffer a similar fate. The response has been so heavy-handed that it’s an insight into the fear and blame culture doctors face, which I find so concerning. Mistakes are an opportunity to learn.
 
Name and address supplied
 Mark McDonald makes many good points. But sadly he overlooks the role that patients and families play in their healthcare and safety. The NHS needs staff who can speak up without fear. But it also needs patients who are listened to, informed, supported and involved. Some of the most important safety signals come not from systems, but from the people experiencing care. If there is one lesson from the Lucy Letby case, it is that patients and families must be recognised as partners in identifying risk, seeking answers and driving improvement.
 
Paul Whiteing
 
CEO, Action Against Medical Accidents

Romanian Man From England Jailed 15 Years in Russia After Online Romance Led Him to Abkhazia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:27:04 UTC
00:27:04 KST

- Category
- World
Romanian Man From England Jailed 15 Years in Russia After Online Romance Led Him to Abkhazia
A Romanian citizen raised in England was sentenced to 15 years in prison in Russia on espionage charges, following what Reuters exposed as a staged FSB arrest video filmed months after his actual detention, Reuters reported on October 22.
David Adrian Kercso, now 23, was accused by Russia’s Federal Security Service of passing information about Russian air-defense systems in Sochi to Ukrainian intelligence.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The FSB released footage purporting to show Kercso being arrested in a park in Sochi. However, Reuters analysis of the video and Russian court records showed that he had already been in Russian custody for several months when the footage was recorded.
The first public announcement of Kercso’s detention came from pro-Russian separatist authorities in Abkhazia, a breakaway region of Georgia, after he disappeared on November 28, 2024.
Two weeks later, Abkhazian security authorities released video showing Kercso in custody and confessing that he had been in contact with Ukrainian intelligence and had been instructed to film military sites with a drone.
Kercso later wrote to his family that the confession had been dictated to him by his captors and that he had been told he would be sent home if he memorized and repeated the statement on camera.
Instead, he was transferred to Russia and appeared before a judge in Sochi on December 14, 2024. Court records reviewed by Reuters documented 10 appearances over the following four months as his detention was repeatedly extended.
Kercso wrote that the FSB filmed the staged arrest scene in mid-April 2025, after taking him from jail early in the morning to a park along Sochi’s Matsesta River.
Reuters found that the visible vegetation and location details were consistent with his account and showed the footage could not have been recorded before his documented detention began.
“We have seen this in dozens of cases where individuals detained months earlier are taken to a city street, a forest, or a train station so that a staged arrest video can be filmed,” Russian lawyer Evgeny Smirnov told Reuters.
Kercso also alleged that he was beaten, tortured, and held in isolation after being transferred to Russia. Reuters could not independently verify those claims.
When he was sentenced, the FSB stated that Kercso had transmitted the location of Russian air-defense systems in Sochi to Ukrainian intelligence during the summer of 2024.
Kercso rejected the accusation and stated that his later confession to the FSB had also been coerced.
“None of that happened, they stole my life for no reason and fabricated everything,” he wrote.
Kercso’s family believes he traveled to the Black Sea region after beginning an online relationship with a woman from Abkhazia. His mother stated that she had warned him not to go because of the war.
“Now I know that coming here was a huge mistake,” Kercso wrote from prison. “I was blinded by love and didn’t see the warning signs.”
Kercso’s case is not the only recent example of a Western national facing serious consequences after going to Russia. One such case is Texas resident Derek Huffman, who moved there with his family in 2025 under Moscow’s “shared values” visa program, then joined the Russian military and was reportedly sent near the front line despite initially expecting a non-combat role.

Carers can’t live on 51p an hour | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:26:59 UTC
00:26:59 KST

For 13 years, I have cared for my lovely 101-year-old adoptive mum who requires round-the-clock care. I feel blessed to care for her and have no regrets. But love does not pay the bills.
Carer’s allowance is £86.45 a week for 2026-27. Spread across 168 hours, that is roughly 51p an hour. As a sole carer, I have no downtime. I still work part-time as a self-employed therapist when Mum’s health allows, but when she is poorly, my work stops while the bills continue.
I do not claim carer’s allowance as the frequent paperwork required to report changes in my self-employed earnings is difficult to manage alongside my caring responsibilities.
Last winter, our electricity bill exceeded £400 a month because Mum needs heating round the clock. This is the reality of caring in a cost of living crisis. I worked hard to buy and pay off my own home. But it had no downstairs bedroom or bathroom, and was unsuitable for Mum. I had to rent it out, hoping one day to live there. Eventually, caring and the costs of maintaining the property forced me to sell, and I faced a capital gains tax bill.
I do not blame HMRC for applying the rules. I question whether government policy takes sufficient account of people whose caring responsibilities force them to make difficult decisions about their homes. Unpaid carers save society enormously, often at the expense of their own earnings, pensions and financial security. We need more than praise: we need practical support and a system that recognises the real cost of caring. Loving someone should not mean years of essential care leave you financially vulnerable.
 
Emma Sainsbury
 
Author, Love, Laughter and the Hidden World of Unpaid Carers

Herzog warns political rhetoric can kill, rules out pardon for Rabin assassin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:26:15 UTC
00:26:15 KST

President Isaac Herzog warned Thursday that inflammatory political rhetoric can lead to deadly violence and declared that the assassin of former Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin must never be released from prison, as Israel marked 31 years since the killing of the leader who pursued peace with the Palestinians.
Speaking at a state memorial ceremony at Mount Herzl in Jerusalem, Herzog appealed to politicians, commentators and voters to exercise restraint ahead of national elections scheduled in five days, invoking Rabin's final warning about the dangers of political violence.
"I stand here and warn that words kill," Herzog said. "Candidates, leaders, opinion leaders and commentators — all of you — be careful with your words."
Addressing candidates from across the political spectrum, Herzog urged Israelis to remember Rabin's final public remarks, delivered shortly before his assassination at a peace rally in Tel Aviv on Nov. 4, 1995.
"Violence erodes the foundations of Israeli democracy," Herzog said, quoting Rabin. "Debate must be respected. Violence must be rejected. Elections are not a civil war."
The ceremony commemorated the 31st anniversary of Rabin's assassination and the 26th anniversary of the death of his wife, Leah Rabin.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu did not attend. The government was represented by Minister Gila Gamliel.
Other attendees included Supreme Court President Yitzhak Amit, military chief Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, Shin Bet security agency chief David Zini, former President Reuven Rivlin and political figures Gadi Eisenkot and Yair Golan.
Herzog: Rabin's assassin must die in prison
Earlier Thursday, Herzog delivered an equally forceful message at the annual "Candle for Yitzhak" state memorial ceremony at the President's Residence in Jerusalem, rejecting any possibility of clemency for Yigal Amir, the Jewish extremist convicted of murdering Rabin.
"The despicable murderer aimed his weapon not only at Yitzhak Rabin, but at the heart of the nation," Herzog said. "We lost our leader, and we nearly lost ourselves."
Herzog recounted recently seeing a billboard along Highway 1, the main road connecting Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, calling for Amir's release.
"The very possibility that such a call could appear in public and be met with a shrug should keep us awake at night," Herzog said. "We must not dismiss it as just another provocation."
He warned that calls for Amir's release risk undermining the fundamental principle that political assassination must remain an absolute red line in Israeli society.
"Behind the call to release the murderer lies the horrifying possibility that Israeli society will cease to regard his despicable act as absolutely forbidden, that, God forbid, it will stop treating it as a red line that must never be crossed," Herzog said.
"Thirty-one years are not a cooling-off period for the murder of a prime minister. And the passage of time does not diminish the gravity of the crime."
Herzog said the message passed down to future generations must be unequivocal.
"The murderer must never be released. He must end his life in prison. He must never receive any leniency or pardon whatsoever. There can be no questioning this under any circumstances," the president declared.
Amir, a right-wing Jewish extremist opposed to Rabin's peace efforts with the Palestinians, shot the prime minister after a peace rally in Tel Aviv in 1995. The assassination remains one of the most traumatic events in Israel's political history, exposing deep divisions over the Oslo peace process and the country's democratic institutions.
Rabin's grandson: His legacy belongs to all Israelis
At the Mount Herzl ceremony, Rabin's grandson, Yonatan Ben-Artzi, called for his grandfather's legacy to be remembered beyond partisan divisions.
"The memory of Yitzhak Rabin should not belong to one political camp," Ben-Artzi said. "His diplomatic legacy can be a matter of disagreement, and his actions deserve to be studied, appreciated and also criticized."
Ben-Artzi said the assassination was not merely a personal tragedy but an assault on democratic decision-making.
"The murder was not only a personal loss. It was a successful attempt to settle with bullets a disagreement that should have been resolved among citizens, in the Knesset and at the ballot box," he said.
He described Rabin as a leader defined by responsibility, hard work and difficult decisions rather than political slogans.
"He understood that leadership is measured not only by the ability to lead when everyone agrees, but also by the willingness to make difficult decisions and bear their consequences," Ben-Artzi said.
Rabin, who served as IDF chief of staff during the 1967 Six-Day War before entering politics, understood the human cost of armed conflict, his grandson said.
"He knew war firsthand. He understood its cost, the bereavement, the loss, the moral obligation to secure the release of prisoners of war and the heavy responsibility borne by those who send young people to fight on behalf of the state," Ben-Artzi said.
"He was first and foremost a fighter who struggled for the Jewish state, but he also had the vision and courage to fight for its democratic character."
Ben-Artzi said Rabin was neither naive nor under any illusion that Israel's enemies would necessarily become its friends.
"He understood that courageous decisions could provoke fierce opposition, both in combat and in the diplomatic arena," he said. "He saw and understood that Israeli society was divided over questions concerning its future, but he believed in his path and, above all, in his people."
Recalling remarks Rabin made minutes before his assassination, Ben-Artzi said his grandfather had emphasized that disagreements were legitimate in a democracy, but that political decisions must ultimately be settled through elections.
"It was as though he foresaw his fate and wanted us to remember, for the sake of our own future, that democracy does not require us to agree with one another," Ben-Artzi said.
"It allows us to disagree, argue, protest, criticize the government and try to persuade others. It requires all of us to agree on the fundamental principles of this place: Only free elections are the means by which the public grants its leaders the authority to govern. And once elections have been held, their results must be accepted."
Rabin's daughter: Israel is still struggling with the wounds of war
At the earlier ceremony at the President's Residence, Rabin's daughter, Dalia Rabin, described a country still grappling with the consequences of war and deep political divisions.
"Given what is happening in the State of Israel, this ceremony is not something we can take for granted," she said.
She recalled that the annual memorial had been especially important to her mother, Leah, who died in 2000.
"Thirty-one years, and we are in a difficult, painful and complicated period, on the eve of elections, licking the wounds of a war that has not ended," she said. "A country suffering from post-traumatic stress, with an uncertain future."
Dalia Rabin emphasized that her father's killing was a politically motivated assassination.
"He was murdered in a political assassination. A religious Jew wearing a skullcap emerged from the darkness and fired three shots into his back to stop a diplomatic process," she said.
With elections approaching and divisions in Israeli society at their peak, she said she felt a responsibility to preserve the nonpartisan character of the ceremony.
"The elections are in the air and the divisions in society are at their peak, and I, his daughter, am expected to maintain balance rather than speak candidly," she said. "So I accept the obligation of this house to preserve the dignity of the state and its institutions, as I have always done."
She said the memorial center established in her father's name was dedicated to democracy, tolerance and reducing political violence.
"We have not boycotted or disqualified any person or group," she said. "We have extended a hand to every segment of Israeli society."
Dalia Rabin also reflected on the qualities she hoped younger generations would remember about her father.
She said young visitors, tourists and Israelis frequently ask what she most wants them to take away from his legacy.
"Two elements were always there: an unwavering insistence on details before setting out, and an uncompromising demand for a serious and thorough investigation, because only through that can we learn lessons and do better," she said.
She added that learning from mistakes must go hand in hand with accepting responsibility.
"Yitzhak Rabin knew how to take responsibility for every action he regarded as falling within his authority, without compromise or exceptions," she said.
"That is also how he raised and educated us from an early age: to admit failure, learn lessons and take responsibility."
The ceremonies came as Israel prepared for another national election amid heightened political tensions.
For Herzog, the anniversary served as a warning that the country's democratic institutions depend not only on the outcome of elections, but also on the willingness of political leaders and citizens to reject violence and accept the legitimacy of their opponents.
His message was particularly stark in light of renewed public calls for Amir's release: The passage of three decades, he insisted, must not weaken the country's condemnation of political assassination.

Turkish army gets more Tayfun ballistic missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:24:21 UTC
00:24:21 KST

- Türkiye delivered a new batch of Roketsan Tayfun Block 2 ballistic missiles to its Land Forces Command, following earlier deliveries in May and June 2026.
- The Tayfun Block 2 has a range of more than 500 km and a reported accuracy of under 10 meters.
Türkiye’s Ministry of National Defence has delivered a new batch of Roketsan Tayfun Block 2 ballistic missiles to the Turkish Land Forces Command, adding to a missile force that began entering service only five months ago.
The delivery was reported on Oct. 22, 2026, and in line with previous handovers, the ministry kept the number of missiles classified. The new batch is at least the third known delivery this year: the ministry announced on May 20, 2026, that Tayfun Block 2 missiles had been accepted into the Land Forces inventory for the first time, and a second batch followed on June 25.
Tayfun, Turkish for “typhoon,” is the longest-range ballistic missile Türkiye has developed on its own. Roketsan, the state-owned missile maker, describes the Block 2 as having a range of more than 500 km (310 miles) and designed to strike high-value targets deep behind enemy lines, including air defense systems, command and control centers, aircraft hangars and other critical military facilities.
The missile is about 6.5 meters (21.3 feet) long and 610 mm (24 inches) in diameter, with a launch weight of 2,300 kg (5,070 pounds). It is fired from a wheeled transporter-erector-launcher, a truck that carries, raises and launches the missile and holds two rounds, which allows crews to move quickly between firing positions.
Roketsan says the Tayfun Block 2 lands within 10 meters (33 feet) of its target, measured as circular error probable, the radius within which half of the missiles fired are expected to land. It uses coordinate-based guidance, meaning it flies to a fixed point programmed before launch, and the company says it is highly resistant to GPS jamming and can operate day or night in poor weather. The missile carries a pre-formed fragmentation warhead, which breaks into a pattern of fragments on detonation.
Türkiye first test-fired Tayfun in October 2022 from Rize-Artvin Airport on the Black Sea coast, when the missile flew 561 km (349 miles) in 456 seconds before striking a target area off Sinop. That distance was roughly twice the 280 km (174-mile) range of Roketsan’s earlier Bora missile, previously the longest-range ballistic missile in Turkish service. Further test firings followed in May 2023 and in later years as the program moved toward serial production.
Roketsan has continued to expand the family alongside the Block 2 deliveries. In July 2025, the company unveiled the much larger Tayfun Block 4 at the IDEF defense fair in Istanbul, a missile about 10 meters (33 feet) long and weighing roughly 7,200 kg (15,900 pounds), which Roketsan presents as a hypersonic ballistic missile system. In July 2026, Roketsan released footage of a Tayfun Block 3 striking an unmanned boat at sea, which the company said was the first time a Tayfun had been used against a naval target and the first use of a seeker on the missile.
With three batches delivered since May, the Tayfun Block 2 is now steadily building up inside the Turkish Land Forces, while the Block 3 and Block 4 versions continue through development and testing at Roketsan.
