Chief of the General Staff's speech at the opening of Telford Gun Hall
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:24:03 BST
00:24:03 KST

Chief of the General Staff's speech at the opening of Telford Gun Hall
The Chief of the General Staff, General Sir Roly Walker's speech at the official opening of Telford Gun Hall.
Secretary of State, ladies and gentlemen, it is an absolute privilege to be here at Telford today. This marks the return of large-calibre gun barrel manufacturing to the United Kingdom. This is a capability that sadly has been absent from these shores for decades.
I say sadly because Great Britain has a proud history of producing its own artillery. For centuries the Royal Arsenal at Woolwich was synonymous with excellence in this technology, and it produced artillery that shaped the outcomes of conflicts from the Napoleonic Wars through the World Wars and into the Cold War.
That arc of history reminds us that whilst armies, navies and air forces can win the battles, it takes nations to come together to win wars. The world today has brought that lesson sharply back into focus. Modern warfare consumes equipment and ammunition at extraordinary rates. In Ukraine, we know that both sides fire tens of thousands of rounds of artillery ammunition every day. And that generates a weight of fire and levels of lethality across the battlefield that drones alone cannot replicate.
So, to be ready to defend against attack, we must be prepared to replace and repair those fighting systems at the rate of their consumption. But industrial capacity cannot be conjured in a crisis. It must be built before the conflict.
And this facility represents an important step, a really important step in that direction. It supports the modernisation of our land forces whilst also rebuilding the skills and industrial capacity on which our future fighting power depends. It is also an incredibly strong signal of intent, a commitment to the partnership between governments, industry, and the armed forces to build the national arsenal that underwrites our national security and allows the nation’s soldiers to protect all that we hold dear.
So, in many ways, this is for them, for those soldiers, and on their behalf, today’s and tomorrow’s that I say thank you for doing what you’ve done.

Livestock virus claims first human victim in France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:22:57 UTC
00:22:57 KST

Livestock virus claims first human victim in France
The world’s first documented human infection with the Shamonda virus has been reported in France, where a hospitalized patient later died, according to the health authorities.
The insect-borne disease, which has circulated among livestock for decades, was previously believed to be incapable of infecting humans.
In a joint statement on Thursday, the French Health and Agriculture Ministries confirmed that the patient, who had a severely weakened immune system, died in early October after being hospitalized in Lyon.
“Until now, the Shamonda virus was considered non-transmissible to humans,” the ministries said, according to AFP. They described the infection as the first confirmed detection of the pathogen in a person.
The patient developed severe neurological complications that the authorities believe were linked to the infection. However, investigators have still not established conclusively whether the virus was responsible for the death.
Officials suspect that the patient contracted the virus through the bite of an infected midge in eastern France, where the pathogen has recently been detected in cattle. The circumstances of the infection remain under investigation.
Despite the unprecedented case, the French authorities said there is currently no indication of a wider threat to public health. They stressed that the patient was severely immunocompromised and that no other human infections have been identified.
The Shamonda virus belongs to the orthobunyavirus group and was first identified in Nigeria in the 1960s. It is transmitted by tiny biting insects known as Culicoides midges and has been detected in livestock in Africa and Asia.
The virus has recently emerged among European cattle, triggering concern among the veterinary authorities. In France, infections have been reported across dozens of departments, with affected animals suffering fever, diarrhea, weakness, and falling milk production, according to the French agricultural authorities.
Other viruses that have crossed from animals to humans include HIV, Ebola, and bird flu. The Covid-19 pandemic was caused by a virus widely believed to have originated in bats.
The European Center for Disease Prevention and Control has confirmed the unprecedented human case and is working with the French authorities to assess its implications.
Health officials are continuing epidemiological and laboratory investigations to determine how the patient became infected and whether other cases may have gone undetected.

Türkiye aims to strengthen energy, climate diplomacy through next month's COP31 UN Climage Change Conference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:22:52 UTC
00:22:52 KST

Gulsen Cagatay and Halis Sunnetci
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
As Türkiye prepares to host next month's 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31 or COP31 Türkiye), it aims to strengthen its role in energy and climate diplomacy, help turn global climate targets into concrete action and harness its renewable energy potential through international partnerships.
COP31, scheduled for Nov. 9-20 in Antalya, will provide an opportunity to highlight Türkiye's diplomatic capabilities, position in the energy transition and climate policies on the international stage.
Türkiye will hold the COP31 Presidency and lead the Action Agenda, while Australia will serve as President of Negotiations.
Türkiye's approach to the summit focuses on turning existing climate commitments into achievable and measurable outcomes through dialogue, consensus and action.
Priority areas include electrification, the clean energy transition, green industrialization, the circular economy, climate-resilient cities and climate finance.
The COP31 Presidency has announced initiatives aimed at increasing electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035, reducing energy intensity in buildings by at least 25% and cutting the rate of growth in global waste generation by half.
Turning climate commitments into bankable and investment-ready projects is also a central part of the agenda.
 
Renewable energy potential supports cooperation
Türkiye's solar and wind energy potential provides a foundation for partnerships that could emerge from COP31.
Expanding renewable energy capacity, strengthening electricity grids and accelerating electrification are among the country's energy transition priorities.
Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar has announced that Türkiye aims to increase its installed renewable energy capacity to 120 gigawatts by 2035, with work underway on more ambitious targets for 2040.
COP31 is therefore expected to offer opportunities to advance Türkiye's clean energy investments through international financing, technology transfer and partnerships.
 
Geographic location enables regional energy cooperation
Situated at the crossroads of Europe, the Middle East and Asia, Türkiye is strategically positioned to connect energy sources with consumer markets, creating opportunities for cooperation in climate diplomacy.
Its location along international trade and energy routes allows the country to develop regional partnerships in electricity interconnections, renewable energy investment, energy efficiency and low-carbon industry.
Making better use of this potential to meet climate targets will require increasing the share of renewables in the energy system, upgrading electricity grids and accelerating the transformation of energy infrastructure.
 
International partnerships, green industry gain prominence
Global Energy Association President Murat Dilek told Anadolu that expanding Türkiye's manufacturing capacity for renewable energy equipment, particularly wind turbines and solar panels, offers significant opportunities for green industrialization and for strengthening the country's role in energy and climate diplomacy.
Increasing domestic manufacturing capacity would support renewable energy investment, while Türkiye's strategic position connecting Europe, the Middle East and Asia could help the country play a greater role in regional supply chains, Dilek said.
He added that these developments would improve Türkiye's competitiveness in the global clean energy market.
"Türkiye's diplomatic success in this process will be measured not only by the establishment of dialogue between countries, but also by the transformation of the targets set out in Antalya into concrete partnerships and viable projects," Dilek said.
"To turn this potential into lasting gains, Türkiye needs to implement its national climate targets, accelerate clean energy investments and facilitate access to climate finance," he said, adding: "By boosting domestic manufacturing and technological capabilities, reducing environmental impacts and strengthening international partnerships, Türkiye can demonstrate its potential not only as a diplomatic actor in the COP31 process, but also as a manufacturing and technology hub contributing to the global green transition."

Michael Wynne, Fired as SECAF Alongside CSAF Moseley, Dead at 82
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:21:43 UTC
00:21:43 KST

Michael Wynne, the 21st Secretary of the Air Force died Oct. 17. He was 82 years old.
Wynne was Secretary from 2005 to 2008, a stretch of time when the U.S. military was struggling to quell insurgencies in Iraq and Afghanistan and the Army was struggling to simultaneously man occupation forces in two theaters. Roadside bombs and insurgent attacks were killing U.S. troops, and the Air Force was under intense pressure to support its sister service with increased intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance coverage and manpower and force cuts to ease the Army’s burden.
The Air Force was also fighting to protect its modernization efforts at the time, especially the F-22 Raptor program, which was less than halfway to its objective of 750 planes, new tankers (which would ultimately become the KC-46), and a future bomber (which would eventually yield the B-21).
In 2006, an Air Force B-52 took off from Minot Air Force Base, N.D., and flew to Barksdale Air Force Base, La., its crew unknowingly carrying nuclear weapons on board, a so-called “bent spear” incident. The discovery kicked off an investigation, recriminations, self-examination, and subsequent organizational, procedural, and cultural changes across the nuclear community.
The incident added to the tension between the Air Force and then-Secretary of Defense Robert Gates, who saw the service and particularly then-Chief of Staff Gen. T. Michael “Buzz” Moseley as recalcitrant in their pushback over budget, manning, and modernization. Seeing Wynne and Moseley as a close knit tandem, Gates fired both in June 2008, beheading the service—the first-ever simultaneous removal of a service chief and secretary.
Military Roots
Wynne hailed from a military family and followed his father’s footsteps to attend the U.S. Military Academy at West Point, graduating at the height of the Vietnam War. Among his 578 classmates, 30 died in Vietnam and about 100 others were wounded in fighting in Southeast Asia.
Instead of joining the Army, however, Wynne followed his older brother into the Air Force, reporting for Active Duty in August 1966.
“The day I reported for Active Duty, the report of my brother being shot down was announced,” Wynn recalled in a 2005 interview with the Washington Post. Maj. Patrick Wynne, a 1963 graduate of the U.S. Air Force Academy, had trained as a pilot, and was assigned to the 555th Tactical Fighter Squadron in Thailand. After only four months in country, his F-4C Phantom was shot down over Vietnam on Aug. 8, 1966. He was declared missing in action, and remained so until 1977, when his remains were identified and later returned to the United States. He is buried at the Air Force Academy.
The younger Wynne served seven years in the Air Force, his final tour as an assistant professor of astronautics at the Air Force Academy.
Wynne then went to work for General Dynamics. For the next 26 years, he worked as an executive there, save for a three-year stint with Lockheed Martin after Lockheed acquired GD’s Space Systems Division. His work during in those years spanned General Dynamics’ F-16 and M1A2 tank divisions as well as space systems, including work on the Atlas, Titan, and Centaur launch vehicles.
In 2001, Wynne joined Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld’s Pentagon leadership team. Following the election of President George W. Bush, Wynne was confirmed as Principal Deputy Undersecretary of Defense for Acquisition, Technology, and Logistics, the start of a seven-year run in public service. In 2003, he was made Acting Undersecretary and he remained in that role until June 2005. Among his tasks at the time were leading the Pentagon’s preparations for the 2005 Base Realignment and Closure plan, which sought to “rationalize” the Defense Department’s far-flung bases and increase cross-service cooperation.
The 2005 BRAC results proved disappointing. Projected to save the Pentagon more than $25 billion annually by 2011, the plans failed to deliver due to higher-than anticipated construction costs, inflation, and incorrect assumptions. Instead of savings, the changes yielded a net cost increase, even when spread out over 20 years.
As Air Force Secretary, Wynne opposed efforts to consolidate and adopt joint basing, having come to embrace the Air Force’s explanation that many of its units operate and fight from their home bases rather than deploy to forward theaters.
“The Air Force has a very different concept of operations,” he would tell Air Force Magazine in 2008, weeks after his departure. Putting Air Force bases under the control of other services would undermine combat effectiveness, he said, adding, “I’d probably get fired again over my objection to the way the joint basing is happening.”
During his Air Force tenure, Wynne came under increasing pressure to cut the service’s budget, force structure, and modernization, and increasingly found himself in opposition to Gates, who took over as Secretary about a year after Wynne had been moved to the Air Force.
While he tried to justify force cuts in a 2006 interview, citing emerging technology like cell phones and more capable aircraft as supporting the case for downsizing by a planned 40,000 troops, “trimming in advance of new systems coming on and planning for the future right now,” he acknowledged that the current way the force was being utilized was unsustainable. At the time, 5,000 Airmen were doing Army jobs in Iraq, primarily jobs like convoy duty. “At some point in the future, it doesn’t work in the math—the Army has to pick up combat service support,” he said.
Wynne also butted heads with Gates over the F-22. While Gates suggested the Air Force could give up the “exquisite” F-22 because the then-fledgling F-35 was scheduled to join the fleet in 2014, Wynne disagreed.
“The notion of the F-22 [is] … similar to the F-35—we need to get rid of that,” Wynne said in his 2008 debrief with Air Force Magazine. The F-35, rather, “complements the F-22, but the F-22 is clearly an air superiority and air dominance weapon. The F-35 is a multinational, multirole, [air-to-ground] versatile airplane.”
The Air Force’s pursuit of a new tanker aircraft, a protracted and contentious effort that preceded him and would continue to drag on for years, was another challenge during Wynne’s tenure. As Secretary, he pressed for a single tanker aircraft rather than splitting the order between Boeing and Airbus platforms, as some urged. But after departing the Pentagon, he reconsidered, seeing value in it. He also came to regret not requiring that tankers become network nodes, an extra role for which they might have been well-suited.
And while many in the Pentagon failed to appreciate the Air Force’s contributions to the war in Iraq, Wynne became a strong advocate, noting that the 2007 “surge” of forces in Iraq was not merely an Army ground operation. “We surged 400 percent in the number of sorties and 1,000 percent in the pounds of ordnance dropped,” he said in a press conference on his final day in office. “What happened? I would tell you that what happened was the realization that we could get connectivity between the ground commanders and the air component—that there was true situational awareness available.”
On June 5, 2008, Gates decided he’d had enough. Wynne and Moseley were en route to a Corona meeting of Air Force leaders at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, when Gates demanded their resignations.
The stated reason was the failures of Air Force leadership to safely steward the security of nuclear weapons. But by then it was generally well known that Gates and the Air Force were at odds on a number of issues, from the number of “orbits” flown by surveillance drones over Iraq and Afghanistan to support troops operating on the ground to what Gates termed “next-war-itis” in the Air Force’s conviction that it needed high-end stealth fighter jets to deter a rising China in the Pacific.
Moseley, in an interview, recalled his close working relationship with Wynne as “a privilege and a gift.” The two tried to meet daily and they shared a perspective both in terms of their duty and vision for the service. They also became friends.
“Mike Wynne and I had the best relationship of any that I’ve seen with 13-plus secretaries I worked with,” Moseley said. Wynne was well versed in the workings of the Pentagon hierarchy, the needs of each of the services, and how to get things done, the former chief said. “But he also understood the theater logistics, the technology to address the new world, and he understood the acquisition process better than anybody.”
Together, they worked to lay out and explain their priorities, the need for increased resources—estimated then to be $20 billion annually to modernize, in order:
- tankers
- search and rescue
- satellites that could be protected from cyber and maneuver attack
- F-35s to replace the F-16
- a new bomber
They laid out that plan shortly before the firing in a Pentagon meeting with Gates and other officials. Mosely recalled that afterward Wynne declared the presentation a success.
“I think that meeting went well,” Wynne told him, draping an arm around Moseley’s shoulder as they walked the Pentagon hallway. “But I think we’re both dead.”
Wynne may have been the only one who saw it coming.
When the decision came down to fire them, both were at Scott Air Force Base, en route to Dayton for a planned Corona meeting of Air Force leadership at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio. Moseley was ordered back to Washington, where Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Adm. Mike Mullen delivered the news. In Dayton, Wynne was told to stand by for an unscheduled visit from Deputy Secretary of Defense Gordon England, who was flying in. No reason was given. Was England coming to discuss Moseley’s successor, someone wondered. “No,” Wynne said. “He’s coming for me.”
As the Corona meeting unfolded, Moseley called Wynne from Washington to say he was being relieved. Reporters began to call before England even arrived, adding to Wynne’s convictions. CNN might have been first to report the firings. Defense News Editor Vago Muradian, a rare press gallery guest at the Corona gathering, got his story out online on Defense News and Air Force Times. At the Pentagon, frustrated reporters gathered outside the press secretary’s office looking for answers; inside, staff was still trying to piece together what happened.
Two weeks later, Wynne departed the Pentagon at an official ceremony presided over by Gates, with Moseley at his side. What had been a very public firing was glossed over for public consumption as Gates pinned a medal on Wynne’s chest. Having Gates preside was Wynne’s idea, said retired Maj. Gen. Daryl Burke, Wynne’s military aide at the time. It was a challenge: Gates would either have to refuse or honor Wynne for his public service.
At the ceremony, Wynne expressed love for the service. “But it is the people of the Air Force that make the Air Force,” he added, “so in loving the Air Force, we love the people.”
Burke recalled how Wynne advised him to stand away as they awaited England’s arrival. Burke insisted he would stand with Wynne regardless, but Wynne was trying to ensure that Burke wouldn’t be damaged by association in the future by being seen as too closely associated with a politically unpopular boss. Wynne subsequently worked behind the scenes to find Burke a next assignment that would keep his career on track. In doing so, Wynne demonstrated both caring for his Airman and a savvy hand on the tiller for navigating Pentagon politics.
Lt. Gen. David Deptula, now dean of AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, was on the Air Staff at the time, recalling that Wynne kept working on the issues he believed in up to the very end—in particular, his opposition to joint basing.
“Secretary Wynne was a leader of uncommon integrity, genuine kindness, and extraordinary loyalty,” Deptula said. “He never confused holding a position of authority with the responsibility to do what was right. I witnessed his character firsthand when, even after learning he would be removed as Secretary of the Air Force, he continued working tirelessly to strengthen the service he loved. He put principle above position, loyalty above personal ambition, and the nation’s security above all else. In a famous action, when SECDEF Gates told Secretary Wynne to fire Chief of Staff, Buzz Moseley… Wynne refused. So, Gates fired both. The Air Force and our nation are better for his service, and I am better for having known him. He will be greatly missed.”
Robbin Laird, a military analyst and prolific writer who worked for Wynne during his Pentagon tenure, wrote admiringly of the former secretary in a remembrance, citing what he called the Wynne Doctrine: “If you are ever involved in a fair fight, it is the result of poor planning.”
“It is easy to hear it as swagger. It was the opposite,” Laird wrote. “A fair fight is one whose outcome is in doubt. When the outcome is in doubt, young Americans pay for that doubt with their lives. Mike believed a leader’s first duty was to make sure it never happens. That meant technology, organization, the unglamorous work of logistics and sustainment, and the discipline to think years ahead of the adversary.”
Michael Walter Wynne was born in Clearwater, Fla. He is survived by his wife Barbara and four married daughters.

Just hours after being bombed, we asked people in Kyiv about Witkoff's praise of Putin
Nataliia reacts as she looks at the damage inside her house following an aerial attack in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 22, 2026. (Diego Fedele / Getty Images)
On Oct. 21, U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff gushingly praised Russian President Vladimir Putin for being a "humanitarian."
Just a few hours later, Kyiv once again came under a fresh barrage of devastating Russian missiles, killing at least one person and injuring over 20.
"We thought this was a war and the destruction of Ukraine, but it turns out to be an act of humanity," Nataliia Stativko, a former journalist, told the Kyiv Independent on a street devastated by one of the missiles. .
"Now we will die and bury our children, knowing that this is an act of humanity."
The attack hit the city's central Pecherskyi District, which, throughout Russia's full-scale invasion, had been among the capital's least frequently targeted areas and was considered safe by many residents.
"Now there is no safe place in Kyiv — death is breathing down your neck everywhere," Dasha Bilous, 25, a local resident, told the Kyiv Independent.
"Now we will die and bury our children, knowing that this is an act of humanity."
Kniaziv Ostrozkykh Street is almost entirely covered in shattered glass, and barely a single window in the surrounding buildings remains intact. A crater over a meter in diameter marks the middle of the road, where a fragment of a Russian missile lay just hours ago.
Exhausted after a sleepless night, residents are gathering pieces of plywood and plastic sheeting to cover their broken windows and keep at least some warmth inside their homes, as rain falls outside and a piercing autumn wind cuts through the streets.
While Kyiv residents pick up the pieces and try to resume their lives, they are left grappling with Witkoff's words from his Oct. 21 meeting with Putin in Saint Petersburg, in which the two discussed a "peace settlement" to Russia's war against Ukraine.
During the meeting, Moscow announced the release of 74-year-old American citizen Stephen Hubbard. Russian forces detained Hubbard during the occupation of Ukraine's Kharkiv Oblast in the early months of the full-scale invasion in 2022. In 2024, a Russian court convicted him of serving as a mercenary in the Ukrainian military, an accusation his family and lawyer disputed.
Witkoff described Putin as a "humanitarian" while commenting on Hubbard's release.
The area where Stativko lives was likely targeted overnight not only with conventional cruise and ballistic missiles, but also with cluster munitions, which scatter smaller explosive charges upon detonation, causing more widespread damage across a larger area.
Andrii Saulevych, manager of the local coffee shop Khlibna Kraina, also felt the impact of Russia's missile attack firsthand. The cafe's windows were completely blown out, but by 8 a.m. local time, it was already serving coffee to customers again.
"We put a piece of ourselves into every coffee shop," he said. "It's deeply upsetting to see everything destroyed like this."
"Humanitarians don't act this way. This is something else. This is anti-humanitarian," Saulevych added.
Another resident of the district, teacher Yaroslav Bahai, spent the morning waiting in line for humanitarian aid instead of preparing his lessons. The windows in his apartment had been blown out, and shrapnel had pierced straight through his kitchen refrigerator. His family was fortunate to survive the attack unharmed: they had taken shelter in the hallway with their children when the missiles struck.
Bahai said the war has significantly changed the way he teaches. His school cannot accommodate all its students in the bomb shelter, while the constant air raid alerts that have plagued the capital in recent months have made learning increasingly difficult, even online.
"I used to give children an assignment asking who they see themselves becoming in five years. Now they say it's hard for them to even imagine what tomorrow will look like," he said.
Bahai and his family have no plans to leave Kyiv for now, despite the approaching winter, which could be one of Ukraine's most difficult since 2022 due to continued Russian attacks and damage to the country's energy infrastructure. Bilous, however, is considering leaving the capital. Although reluctant to abandon her home, she said she can no longer cope with the constant sense of danger, which only continues to grow.
A fragment of a Russian missile landed right next to her house, shattering all the windows.
"I thought I was going to die," Bilous said.
"Such a 'gift' arrived in Kyiv after the (Witkoff-Putin) meeting. Who was it from? Putin? Witkoff? Trump?"

Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas, a Trump critic, charged in marijuana racketeering case

15:20:12 UTC
00:20:12 KST

Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas has been charged in a federal indictment with leading an alleged marijuana racketeering conspiracy that included family members of the powerful Democrat, according to court documents made public on Thursday.
The indictment and the FBI said the five-year scheme, which was worth an estimated $4.5 million, obtained and illegally distributed "large quantities of illegal marijuana," and aimed to procure "generational wealth" for members of the enterprise.
Lucas, 82, is a critic of President Donald Trump, and was an architect of ultimately failed efforts in Virginia to redraw the state's congressional map for November to boost chances for Democrats to win certain districts. She also has been a proponent of legalizing marijuana in the state.
The criminal case, which also charges members of Lucas' family, was made public by the Department of Justice less than two weeks before the midterm election. Those contests will determine what political party controls both chambers of Congress.
Lucas, the state Senate's president pro tempore and chairman of the Finance and Appropriations Committee, is not on the ballot this year. The indictment alleges that Lucas, who was first elected to the Senate in 1991, leveraged her position as chairman of the powerful committee to protect her marijuana enterprise.
The indictment says Lucas "was the leader of the enterprise," that she "arranged for the acquisition and distribution of marijuana, supervises the laundering of marijuana proceeds," and "used her political influence to attempt to influence Virginia legislation for the benefit of herself and her family and maintained a premise for the distribution of marijuana." The alleged scheme used two stores, CBD Shopped and The Cannabis Outlet, for its operation.
"On May 6, the FBI executed federal search warrants at The Cannabis Outlet and The CBD Shoppe," the Department of Justice said in a statement. "Agents recovered marijuana and firearms at both locations."
Six other defendants are charged in the alleged scheme, among them Lucas' two daughters and her grandson, Ryan Eichelbeger. One of the daughters, Lisa Lucas-Burke, is running for mayor of Portsmouth.
Lucas is in custody with the other defendants, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced at a press conference Thursday. She is scheduled to appear before a magistrate judge in U.S. District Court in Norfolk, Virginia, at 2:30 p.m. ET Thursday.
In addition to racketeering conspiracy, Lucas is charged with conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute marijuana; conspiracy to launder money; conspiracy to commit honest services fraud; and maintaining a drug involved premises.
"Today, the FBI, the Department of Justice, and the full weight of the federal government have been wielded against an 82-year-old great-grandmother," Lucas said in a statement posted on X.
"I grew up under Jim Crow. I've seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them. I spent my life fighting back, and I'm not stopping now," she said. "I will not be intimidated. I will not be bullied. And I will not back down."
Blanche, when asked at the press conference about criticism from Lucas's attorney that the case is politically motivated, said, "We don't do political paybacks."
The attorney general noted the investigation of Lucas began before the current Trump administration, and that a federal grand jury had determined there was enough evidence to indict her.
"There's decision and processes in place at the department when we're bringing a case against a political official, and the ... first question is: is this investigation proper?" Blanche said. "And the conclusion of that is yes. Is the timing proper? And the conclusion of that is yes."
The indictment was issued by a grand jury on Oct. 14, but was only unsealed Thursday.
The indictment says that after he was hired in 2022, a senior law enforcement officer "warned Louise Lucas that selling marijuana was illegal and was going to get her in trouble one day."
Lucas since 2021 has been a partner in The Cannabis Outlet, a shop that sells selling hemp and CBD, or cannabidiol products.
After a 2024 burglary at the store, two of Lucas' co-defendants claimed to Portsmouth Police that about $3,000 of marijuana products were missing.
One of the overt acts listed in the indictment was an April 2022 meeting between Lucas, her two daughters and an indicted co-conspirator at Lucas' office. At that meeting, the indictment alleges, Lucas asked the unidentified co-conspirator "if they were a member of law enforcement before purchasing between three and five pounds of marijuana" from the co-conspirator with a check for $6,600 from Lisa Lucas-Burke. The check was made out to "Freedom is Dope."
On Feb. 5, 2026, the indictment says, Lucas called an unindicted co-conspirator and discussed the language surrounding the recreational marijuana legislation pending in the Virginia General Assembly, and the possibility of [the co-conspirator] receiving a license and sharing the proceeds with her because 'this is our last chance at generational wealth . . .. I've got too old to not be greedy.'"
The charges come five months after FBI agents executed a search warrant at Lucas' Portsmouth office.
At the time of that May 6 raid, Lucas noted in a statement that it came two weeks after Virginia voters approved the redistricting plan, adding, "Virginians sent a powerful message when they voted to stop Trump's scheme to manipulate the 2026 midterm elections."
"I was proud to help lead that effort and I have never been afraid to stand up to Donald Trump."

EXPLAINER - What are the critical PHP flaws uncovered by AI, and why do they matter?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:20:09 UTC
00:20:09 KST

Two critical security flaws in a programming language used by millions of websites have triggered an urgent cybersecurity response after researchers used artificial intelligence (AI) to identify weaknesses that could let attackers take control of vulnerable web servers.
The flaws affect PHP, a programming language used to build and run websites, including those based on platforms such as WordPress, Drupal and Joomla.
PHP developers released emergency security updates on Oct. 21 and urged users to install them immediately. They warned that the flaws could allow attackers to run malicious code on affected servers without logging in.
Cloudflare, a company that helps protect websites from cyberattacks, reported attack traffic targeting its customers after details of the flaws leaked before their planned public announcement. On Thursday, New Zealand's National Cyber Security Centre said it was aware of reports of active exploitation.
US, British, EU and Australian cybersecurity authorities have issued urgent warnings about the vulnerabilities, while some organizations temporarily took websites offline as a precaution.
The incident is also being seen as a turning point in cyber security: AI helped defenders identify vulnerabilities that had survived years of examination, but experts warn the same technology could help attackers exploit them much faster.
PHP, short for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, is an open-source programming language mainly used to run websites behind the scenes.
When someone visits a website, PHP can retrieve information from databases, process requests and prepare the content that appears on the user's screen.
It is used by platforms including WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and MediaWiki, the software behind Wikipedia.
W3Techs estimates that PHP is used by about 69% of websites whose server-side programming language it can identify.
Because PHP is so widely used, a security flaw in the language itself can affect many different websites, rather than just one application.
The two flaws are identified as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Google Cloud's technical analysis gives each a critical severity score of 9.2 out of 10.
Both involve how PHP handles computer memory when certain errors occur.
One vulnerability involves an out-of-memory condition that can leave internal request data partially initialized; the other involves internal state that can continue referencing memory after it has been freed.
Attackers could send specially designed requests to trigger these problems and potentially run their own code on an affected server without logging in.
If an attack succeeds, criminals could steal information, change website content or use the compromised server to attack other systems.
Because the flaws affect PHP itself, updating WordPress plugins or themes alone will not fix the problem. The underlying PHP software must also be updated.
Cybersecurity company Wiz said the flaws affect PHP versions dating back to version 5.4, released more than a decade ago.
Google Cloud's analysis identifies affected versions ranging from PHP 5.4 through 8.5.11.
Cloudflare also warned that servers using PHP 5.4 or later could be vulnerable.
However, that does not mean every PHP-powered website has been successfully compromised or that every configuration is equally easy to exploit.
PHP's developers said installations serving web requests are at risk and warned that some configurations are especially exposed.
The scale nevertheless prompted governments and major cyber-security agencies to treat the discovery as an emergency.
The US National Security Agency advised organizations to update affected systems and said those unable to do so immediately should consider taking them offline.
Britain's National Cyber Security Centre issued similar advice, while EU cyber-security bodies called for immediate patching, prioritizing internet-facing systems.
The PHP development team released four patched versions Wednesday: PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35.
“All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately,” the project said.
The developers warned there are “no complete mitigations,” meaning organizations cannot safely rely on temporary workarounds instead of installing the update.
Cloudflare said it had already deployed web application firewall protections before public disclosure.
Such measures can help block malicious requests but do not replace patching the underlying software.
Researchers at cybersecurity companies Calif and Wiz used AI tools to examine PHP's code and identify potential security weaknesses.
OpenAI said Calif identified a critical flaw using its GPT-5.6 Sol model as part of a security initiative. Wiz independently discovered the vulnerabilities using several AI tools.
The underlying coding errors had existed for years. However, showing how they could be used in a real attack required detailed technical work and specialist knowledge.
Wiz said AI reduced the time and effort needed for this process. According to the company, one researcher completed work in about a week that could previously have taken a specialized team months.
OpenAI described the PHP discovery as “one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”
The same capabilities that allow AI to search millions of lines of computer code for hidden weaknesses can potentially be used by attackers.
Once information about a vulnerability becomes public, AI systems could help malicious actors understand it, write exploit code and adapt attacks against different targets considerably faster than before.
That could shorten what cyber-security researchers call the defender's window — the period between discovering and fixing a vulnerability and widespread attempts to exploit it.
In this case, researchers and PHP developers coordinated privately for weeks before publicly disclosing the flaws so protective measures could be prepared.
But the details leaked shortly before the planned announcement.
Cloudflare said it subsequently detected attackers changing their techniques in attempts to bypass protections.
For organizations operating PHP systems, the advice from authorities is straightforward: identify PHP installations and update them immediately to a patched version.
Operators should prioritize systems exposed directly to the internet and monitor them for signs that attackers may already have gained access.
Organizations that cannot patch immediately have been advised to consider temporarily taking vulnerable services offline.
For ordinary internet users, there is little that can be done to fix the PHP vulnerability directly because responsibility rests with website operators and hosting providers.
Users should nevertheless watch for security notifications from services they use, change passwords if instructed to do so and be cautious of phishing messages exploiting publicity surrounding the incident.

Was van Gogh’s ‘The Starry Night’ a flight of fancy or a real sky?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:16:10 UTC
00:16:10 KST

Was van Gogh’s ‘The Starry Night’ a flight of fancy or a real sky?
New calculations point to a specific July 1889 constellation, but not everyone agrees
Vincent van Gogh’s “The Starry Night” may have been based on one specific night sky: July 22, 1889, just before dawn over France.
If that’s true, it means the famous painting was based on real observations, not just van Gogh’s imagination, astronomer Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim and colleagues report October 22 in Scientific Reports.
“How could an invented sky fit the sky of a particular date this closely?” the team writes. “Observation and imagination have commonly been treated as an either/or, yet ‘The Starry Night’ shows the two coexisting on one canvas.”
Art historians typically date “The Starry Night” to mid-June 1889, based on one of van Gogh’s letters to his brother Theo.
“At last I have a landscape with olive trees, and also a new study of a starry sky,” van Gogh wrote on or about June 18. About a month earlier, van Gogh had entered a hospital in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, France. “The Starry Night” is thought to represent the view through the window of his room. A short time later, van Gogh experienced an illness during which he didn’t paint for about six weeks, so most historians think “The Starry Night” must have been painted before then.
That letter is taken as strong evidence, says astronomer Donald Olson of Texas State University in San Marcos, who has written about how astronomy shows up in art history. Historians favor the June date because “van Gogh himself said so,” he says.
That assumption has led to some confusion, though. In the 1980s, two astronomers tried to match the painting’s stars to real skies in Saint-Rémy in mid-June. One proposed that the sky was from June 19, 1889, and the collection of swirly stars is the constellation Aries.
But the other concluded it couldn’t have been painted on June 19, based on cloudy weather reports in Aix-en-Provence, France, about 70 kilometers away. That study claimed the painting was “a celestial composite, constructed to make an image of the morning sky.”
Kim, who founded a telescope-building company called SLLAB Inc. in Seoul, South Korea, didn’t know about the June date when he became interested in “The Starry Night.” “Unlike previous astronomical studies, we could start freely,” he says.
Given his job, Kim had an intuition for which stars would be visible when. “People like me, who guide a telescope through its first alignment with the sky, naturally memorize where the stars are,” he says.
He was skeptical of the Aries theory. The stars in that constellation are faint enough that they wouldn’t be all that visible in the predawn sky, “hardly enough to inspire a painter,” he says.
Instead, Kim saw the stars as the Hyades star cluster, which forms a sideways V shape in the constellation Taurus. To test that theory, he and his colleagues applied a statistical technique called Procrustes shape analysis to put a number to how well the stars in the painting matched any particular constellation.
Celestial alignment?
Researchers compared the V-shaped collection of stars in “The Starry Night” (first image) with those in the Hyades star cluster (middle image). The resulting graph (last image) maps the real stars (blue) and the painting’s stars (orange) against each other. They don’t overlap perfectly, but they’re suspiciously close, researchers say. The label Sn stands for “The Starry Night.” while the constellation’s Greek letters represent typical astronomy notation.
The team tested the method on another van Gogh skyscape, “Starry Night Over the Rhône,” which clearly depicts the Big Dipper. “Apart from the Big Dipper, there is no star pattern we can say for certain that Vincent painted,” Kim says. The degree of matching between the art and the sky for both paintings turned out to be similar, a major clue.
Kim also used the position and phase of the moon (a waxing gibbous on June 19, in contrast to the sharp waning crescent in the painting) and Venus to further constrain the painting’s date. He used computer simulations that weren’t available in the ‘80s to calculate the positions of celestial objects on certain dates in 1889 down to the second. He even traveled to France in June and July 2019 to try to find the field of view van Gogh would have seen from his window. Ultimately, July 22, 1889, was the best fit for the team’s data.
“I still cannot forget the moment we finally found the spot, overlaid the drawing on the view and saw it fit perfectly,” Kim says. “I was standing where Vincent had stood 130 years earlier. And the thrill I felt when I confirmed that the moon, the Hyades and Venus of July 22, 1889, fit exactly within the drawing’s field of view is still with me.”
Not to douse Kim’s enthusiasm, but that field of view may not be exactly what van Gogh saw, Olson says.
“The authors’ assumed narrow field of view, essential for their theory that the stars of the Hyades fill most of the canvas, is inconsistent with the much wider field of view required to encompass ‘The Starry Night’s’ round hills and cliffs,” he says. That casts doubt on the paper’s conclusions.
Olson proposes an experiment: Tell an amateur astronomer that “The Starry Night” depicts the Hyades and ask them to point out the star Aldebaran, which is at the bottom left of the V. In real life, this is the brightest star in the Hyades. But the painting has other much more prominent stars.
“If [the authors’] theory is correct, then this should be easy,” Olson says. Kim and colleagues identify Aldebaran as one of the two stars to the left of the cypress tree in “The Starry Night.” But Olson thinks others will see it differently. “A decent guess is that an experienced amateur astronomer, even when prompted to see the Hyades, will not identify Aldebaran as either of the two stars to the left of the cypress tree.”

This Time, the Korean Loudspeaker Standoff Is Different
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:16:00 UTC
00:16:00 KST

On October 21, after inspecting fortification work along North Korea’s southern border, Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, announced that “within October, the loudspeakers for psychological warfare against the ROK will be in operation along the whole border.” (ROK refers to the Republic of Korea, South Korea’s formal name.)
Two days earlier, Kim Yo Jong had said Pyongyang was considering the step, along with deploying more “tactical strike means” near the border. As a rationale, she cited the behavior of South Korean troops near the border, claiming they had issued 2,870 warning broadcasts and fired warning shots on 201 occasions between August 1 and October 17.
South Korea has no large loudspeakers left on the border; it took them down in August 2025 as a sign of goodwill. The Ministry of National Defense said that the warnings Kim referred to were issued by smaller speakers at guard posts as a defensive measure against North Korean soldiers crossing the Military Demarcation Line (MDL).
If the North starts broadcasting, South Korea’s military said it would consider restarting its own loudspeakers on the principle of proportional response.
The loudspeaker broadcasts began in 1963, when North Korea began using the tool and South Korea responded in kind. The first bout lasted over nine years, with broadcasts only switched off in November 1972. North Korea resumed broadcasts in 1980; the loudspeaker contest lasted even longer this time, until 2004.
But since then, loudspeaker use has settled into a pattern: South Korea resumed loudspeaker broadcasts in response to North Korean actions in 2015, 2016, and 2024. The latest round ended in 2025, with the Lee administration’s unilateral decision to dismantle South Korean speakers. This time, North Korea is the one resuming broadcasts, citing a growing dispute over the MDL.
Since 2015, Seoul has used loudspeakers when it wants to respond to North Korean provocations without resorting to force. In August 2015, South Korea’s defense minister called the broadcasts legitimate retaliation after mines that Seoul said the North had planted in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) seriously injured two South Korean soldiers. South Korea also used loudspeaker broadcasts to respond to North Korea’s nuclear test in 2016, and again in 2024 when North Korea sent balloons filled with trash and feces across the border.
There’s a reason South Korean governments turned to loudspeakers. A broadcast is non-lethal and can be switched off at will, yet it targets something Pyongyang guards closely: its control over information. South Korean broadcasts have carried news, weather forecasts, and pop music to North Korea’s front-line soldiers, and officials said in 2015 that the sound could carry 24 kilometers at night. In June 2017, a North Korean soldier who crossed to a South Korean guard post on the central front said the broadcasts had made him decide to defect.
While South Korea considered the broadcasts to be a proportional response, North Korea sees them differently. Pyongyang called the 2015 resumption “a direct provocation of war.” The North turned its own speakers on just days after Seoul did, though South Korean officials said they were so old that their messages were nearly impossible to understand. “It just sounds like a drone,” one official said.
On August 20, 2015, South Korea’s military said North Korean forces had fired toward a loudspeaker site in Yeoncheon, north of Seoul, and South Korean artillery answered with dozens of 155 mm rounds. Pyongyang denied firing, issued an ultimatum to stop the broadcasts and declared a “quasi-state of war.” The standoff closed on August 25, 2015 with a joint statement in which the North expressed regret over the mine blasts and the South agreed to stop broadcasting “unless an abnormal situation occurs.”
That “abnormal situation” came in January 2016, when North Korea conducted an underground nuclear test. Days later, South Korea restarted its loudspeaker broadcasts. This time, the broadcasts went on for over two years. Seoul only switched them off on April 23, 2018, four days before an inter-Korean summit. The resulting Panmunjom Declaration committed both sides to stop all hostile acts along the MDL, including loudspeaker broadcasts, from May 1.
When Seoul turned the speakers back on in June 2024, after suspending the September 2018 inter-Korean military agreement. South Korea held that North Korea had already voided the agreement through its trash balloons and over provocations. South Korea’s broadcasts in 2024 included BTS songs, regional weather, and market prices, along with a message urging North Korean soldiers laying mines to escape what it called a life of slavery.
North Korea answered not with propaganda but with sheer noise: gunshots, screams, eerie laughter, and sounds like howling wolves. Noise levels on Ganghwa Island, about two kilometers from the North, reached 80 decibels late at night. To many, North Korea’s purpose was simply to torment South Koreans.
South Korean law acknowledged the harm being done. A December 2024 amendment to the Framework Act on Civil Defense allows the state to compensate people harmed by enemy actions that fall short of a civil defense emergency. A decree issued in May 2025 included “noise broadcasting” among the “hazardous acts” it covers, alongside balloons, shooting or shelling, and drones. In July 2026, border counties began taking claims, with payments determined by the number of days residents lived with the noise.
Previously, North Korea and South Korea stopped their loudspeaker broadcasts through bilateral agreement, after discussions. But South Korea ended its last round unilaterally. New President Lee Jae-myung ordered the broadcasts stopped on June 11, 2025; the North’s broadcasts ended the next day. In August 2025, the military began dismantling its fixed loudspeakers in what the defense ministry called “a practical measure aimed at helping ease tensions with the North.” Seoul said it had not consulted Pyongyang.
Pyongyang rejected any suggestion of reciprocity. After South Korea’s military reported that the North was removing some of its own speakers, Kim Yo Jong said: “We have never removed loudspeakers installed on the border area and are not willing to remove them.” About a week later, in fact, two new North Korean speakers went up opposite the South Korean border counties of Cheorwon and Hwacheon.
Now North Korea has declared that it will resume broadcasts. If so, the new round of loudspeaker use will be different from recent history. In 2015, 2016, and 2024, Seoul began broadcasting first; this time Pyongyang has declared its intention to do so, in response to alleged South Korean provocations. This is despite repeated efforts on the part of the Lee administration in Seoul to show its goodwill toward the North.
Since Kim Jong Un declared the two Koreas hostile states in December 2023, North Korean troops have fortified the DMZ, laying mines and building roads, fences, and what appear to be anti-tank barriers. In September 2026, two mine explosions along the DMZ injured three South Korean soldiers. Seoul said the mines had been laid during the “so-called border fortification works” since 2023 – and that they were planted south of MDL that separates the two Koreas.
North Korean soldiers working near the line occasionally cross it, as evidenced by the recent mine incident. South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff counted about 50 crossings in August and September 2026; South Korean troops responded with warning broadcasts and warning shots.
Kim Yo Jong, however, insisted that “our soldiers have never crossed the border.” There may be disagreement over where, exactly, the MDL is situated. If so, it will be difficult to resolve; Pyongyang ignored Seoul’s November 2025 offer of military talks to set “a clear reference line for the MDL.”
Kim’s statements framed the loudspeaker broadcasts as about the border rather than propaganda. She also issued a threat, saying that North Korean troops would show “no mercy” if South Korean warning shots ever harmed a North Korean solider. Kim also reiterated her brother’s vision that the MDL is now “a permanent line never to be crossed.”
As long as North Korean troops keep working along – and crossing – the MDL, South Korean warnings are likely to continue. That means North Korea’s responses, including the broadcasts, will as well. Seoul has also reserved the right to carry out a “proportional response” to North Korean broadcasts, although no specific action has been selected yet.
Over the longer term inter-Korean relations are likely to be shaped by interactions along the MDL, which Pyongyang now calls a permanent border and Seoul still treats as a temporary demarcation line set by the armistice. Preventing an accidental clash is now an urgent task.
With inter-Korean hotlines silent since April 2023, South Korea’s Unification Ministry has called for reconciling the two sides’ understandings of the MDL and setting up a communication system to manage it. Thus far, however, Pyongyang has refused to engage. That leaves South Korea with few options for responding to North Korean escalations without raising the risk of conflict.

The measures, released by the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC), China's top economic planner, will take effect on Dec. 1, 2026, replacing the existing rules enacted in 2017.

The revised measures further affirm the principal role of various investors in outbound investment, including domestic enterprises, individual residents, and other organizations.

The revision is part of the country's broader efforts to promote the high-quality development of outbound investment. China's outbound investment has continued to expand in recent years. By the end of 2025, the country's outbound investment stock had reached nearly 3.4 trillion U.S. dollars, keeping China among the world's top three investors for nine consecutive years, according to the Ministry of Commerce.

The vulnerabilities, identified with the assistance of artificial intelligence and disclosed on Wednesday, have prompted governments and businesses worldwide to temporarily suspend websites and online services amid concerns that the flaws could be exploited in cyberattacks.
The PHP development team announced that it had identified two major vulnerabilities by the early hours of Wednesday and released security patches to address them. ■

Interview: China rowing coach hails athletes after eight-medal haul in Qingdao
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
23:15:27 CST
00:15:27 KST

QINGDAO, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- China's Italian head coach Francesco Cattaneo credited teamwork, mutual trust and his athletes' determination for the country's success at the 2026 World Rowing Beach Sprint Finals in Qingdao, where the host nation won four gold, three silver and one bronze medal.
"When a foreign coach arrives in a new country, it is not always easy for everyone to embrace new ideas immediately," Cattaneo told Xinhua. "But in China, the athletes and coaching staff trusted the changes we introduced, and I believe that made a difference."
Known as Franco, Cattaneo is a former elite rower who won several medals at the World Rowing Championships before moving into coaching. He spent 12 years in a senior technical role with Italy's national rowing team and oversaw the country's beach sprint program from 2020 to 2024.
Cattaneo joined China's national team earlier this year, with the squad beginning preparations in late January. Training camps in Italy and Portugal formed part of a nearly 10-month buildup to the Qingdao championships.
Beach sprint rowing, which will make its Olympic debut at Los Angeles 2028, combines running on sand with high-speed rowing in open water. Athletes sprint from the beach, board their boats, navigate around buoys and return to shore before racing across the finish line.
Unlike traditional flat-water rowing, where races typically last around six minutes, beach sprint events demand explosive efforts lasting just two and a half to three minutes.
"Being a good flat-water rower is not enough," Cattaneo said. "Athletes must also learn to run, jump into boats, navigate waves and make turns under pressure."
He said the months of preparation had helped China's athletes develop the physical and technical skills needed to compete at the highest level.
Those preparations were tested in Qingdao, where rough seas and changing weather conditions disrupted the competition schedule and forced organizers to squeeze much of the racing into two days.
"The athletes have followed our advice on how to deal with different situations," Cattaneo said. "I am very pleased with how they responded to the challenges."
Although he acknowledged that competing on familiar waters had given China an advantage, Cattaneo said the team's eight-medal haul had exceeded expectations.
"It confirms that we are on the right path," he said.
However, the Italian warned that success on home waters was no guarantee of Olympic glory, insisting that China still had considerable work to do before the Los Angeles Games.
"We can celebrate these medals for a few days, but then we must put them away and get straight back to work," he said. "The level we have reached will certainly not be enough in Los Angeles."
Cattaneo identified aerobic and anaerobic fitness, explosive power, boat handling and navigation as key areas for improvement, while stressing the importance of adapting to different sea conditions.
He noted that the relatively calm waters expected in Los Angeles could present a different challenge from the rough seas encountered in Qingdao.
"We must be able to make the boat go fast even when there are few waves," he said.
Beyond China's Olympic ambitions, Cattaneo hopes the discipline's inclusion in the Games will inspire more young people to take up the sport.
"It is a beautiful, exciting and very young discipline," he said. "Whether you come from traditional rowing or not, if you have speed, power and the ability to handle the sea, I would encourage you to give it a try." ■

====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: China-Europe freight train trips top 140,000 as land corridor gains ground
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
23:15:08 CST
00:15:08 KST

SHENYANG, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- The China-Europe freight train service passed 140,000 cumulative trips on Thursday, a milestone that underscores its role as a reliable logistics corridor for Eurasian trade, especially as geopolitical tensions and disruptions to traditional shipping routes challenge global supply chains.
The milestone was marked as a train bound for Moscow departed Puhe station in Shenyang, northeast China's Liaoning Province, at around 11:30 a.m. Thursday. The value of goods transported by the China-Europe freight train service has exceeded 560 billion U.S. dollars since 2011.
The figures reflect that Eurasia's overland corridor has shifted from a niche alternative to a mainstay of regional logistics. This shift is seen not merely in the number of trains, but in what they carry, their destinations, and the reliability of their arrivals.
The growth has been steady rather than sudden. Annual trips rose from 1,702 in 2016 to 20,022 in 2025, an average annual increase of more than 30 percent, according to the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC).
As a flagship project and a landmark brand of the Belt and Road Initiative, the China-Europe freight train service, also referred to as the "steel camel caravans," has established a comprehensive logistics network across Eurasia.
The expansion has come as geopolitical tensions, disruptions to maritime routes and high air freight costs pushed more trade firms to look for stable and efficient transport channels. Rail freight costs roughly one-fifth of air transport and takes about one-quarter of the time of sea transport, and it is less exposed to weather and to disruption on traditional maritime routes, according to the NDRC.
The network has broadened in step. Within China, 96 scheduled routes for trains traveling at 120 km per hour link 132 cities along the western, central and eastern corridors, while overseas the network runs on three lines: northern, central and southern.
The overseas routes now reach 237 cities in 26 European countries and more than 100 cities in 12 Asian countries, covering most parts of Eurasia, according to China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway), the national rail operator.
The southern route shows where that demand is going. Operating on a regular basis, it ran 746 trains in the first nine months of 2026, up 125 percent year on year, far faster than the network as a whole. Regular service linking the Chinese city of Xi'an with Baku, capital of Azerbaijan, began in July 2024, and one such service traverses Central Asia and crosses the Caspian Sea before continuing to Europe either via the overland railway network or by crossing the Black Sea.
The reach extends outward as much as inward. Shuai Bin, a professor at the School of Transportation and Logistics at Southwest Jiaotong University, said the service "has drawn global resources and production factors further into inland regions, while fostering a new pattern of opening up featuring highly-coordinated development between coastal ports and inland hubs."
On the European side, Duisburg alone handles about 30 percent of China-Europe rail freight volume, according to Markus Teuber, the German city's China affairs commissioner.
The range of goods that move along those lines has expanded even faster. Goods now span 53 categories and more than 50,000 items. In the first quarter of 2026, mechanical equipment remained the largest category on outbound trips, followed by automobiles and auto parts. Exports of automobiles and auto parts rose 46 percent year on year, while inbound grains, wood pulp and rubber products climbed 87 percent, 64 percent and 24 percent respectively, data released by China Railway in April showed.
According to the operator, the loaded container rate on the return leg had held at 100 percent for 49 consecutive months as of September.
"The rising share of return services shows the China-Europe freight trains are shifting from one-way exports to a healthier, two-way trade corridor, helping make Eurasian trade more balanced and sustainable," Sun Zhang, a professor at Tongji University, was quoted by the Global Times as saying.
Carrying that cargo reliably is harder than finding it, and reliability rather than speed has now become a primary gauge of the service. Trains running on fixed timetables, with designated numbers, routes and crossing times agreed across borders, cut transit time by about a quarter, and the journey from Xi'an to Duisburg takes as little as 11 days, down from 15. Some 22 such services now link nine Chinese and six European cities, and the average value of a single container is 41 percent higher than on regular trains, according to the NDRC.
China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) calls for upgrading the service, and the NDRC has said it will improve transport organization, open more alternative routes and deepen coordination with countries along the corridor.
An official with the logistics center of China Railway said the operator has been advancing infrastructure connectivity and the alignment of standards and rules to build a smooth, efficient, multi-directional network that connects rails with sea routes. ■

From the streets to the ballot box: Serbia’s students hope for election win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:13:34 UTC
00:13:34 KST

From the streets to the ballot box: Serbia’s students hope for election win
Young Serbians have built a system that poses a threat to President Aleksandar Vucic’s grip on power.
It all began on the streets.
A student-led movement has emerged as the most serious challenger to the long rule of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) and its leader, Aleksandar Vucic, ahead of Sunday’s election.
Over the past two years, many citizens, teachers, professors and other experts have joined the students, a protest group that has evolved into a political movement: “Student List–Students Win” (Studentska lista–Studenti pobeđuju).
The catalyst came after the collapse of a concrete canopy at the renovated Novi Sad railway station on November 1, 2024. Sixteen people were killed in the tragedy, which triggered public outrage over alleged corruption and raised questions about construction safety, the quality of renovation work, and government oversight. Students who led protests have sought a fundamental overhaul of a system they deem rotten.
‘Serbia belongs to people, not to criminals’
Kosta Golubovic, a law student at the University of Novi Sad, has been involved since day one.
“Change is clearly necessary. The state must belong to its people, not to the mafia and criminals,” he told Al Jazeera.
“The way they treat the judiciary, the catastrophic conditions at the local level, mayors resorting to violence, dying villages – along with dubious privatisations, money laundering, the erosion of every single institution, police being replaced by thugs, and an education system vanishing before our eyes… these are some of the reasons why change is needed,” said Golubovic.
Demonstrations transformed into the biggest protest movement in Serbia in years, joined by tens of thousands.
The students have not called for the overthrow of Vucic. But their persistence created one of the biggest threats to the president’s long grip on power.
Vucic became prime minister in 2014. In 2017, he was elected president, a traditionally ceremonial role that he has bolstered by maintaining influence over his SNS party.
‘Vucic is afraid of us’
Opposition parties and rights watchdogs accuse Vucic and his SNS party of bribing voters, stifling media freedom, violence against opponents, and ties with organised crime.
Vucic and his allies deny these allegations. But Serbia’s rating on Transparency International’s global corruption index has worsened gradually in recent years.
“Vucic is clearly afraid of us – it’s obvious. He knows that, for the first time in 16 years, the SNS is no longer the most popular political option in the country,” Golubovic said.
The students’ efficiency is down in part to its structure.
The old student parliament at the University of Belgrade has been replaced with plenums – daily assemblies where each group votes on its course of action. Working groups focus on strategy, donations, and security. Universities in different cities coordinate so demands remain broadly aligned.
This is why the students say they do things differently. One rule is to be leaderless, making it harder for authorities to disrupt the protests. Also, demonstrations must be peaceful, and any debris has to be cleaned up. Third, all decisions must be made democratically during hour-long plenary sessions in their university faculties.
“Even though the authorities mobilised criminal groups against the students and citizens participating in the protests, the students have remained focused on their goal: to oust a government they view as authoritarian and deeply corrupt,” said Natasa Kandic, a Serbian peace activist, sociologist, and founder of the Humanitarian Law Center (HLC) in Belgrade.
“For the first time in Serbia, they have managed to lead protests entirely without violence,” she said. “The video clips we see daily represent a new culture – one defined by irony, laughter, and the deliberate disregard for primitivism and political depravity.”
‘Serious and comprehensive plan’
State-affiliated media have maligned the students. Some Serbian authorities claimed that the group has no programme, and Vucic labelled them as “terrorists”. But their leaders, experts from different fields, claim that they have a plan.
The platform is officially titled the “Student Plan” and is divided into three sections. There are 11 points.
Ilija Srdanovic, a cardiologist and the lead candidate and ballot holder for the Student List, explained that the platform deliberately avoids setting fixed, precise deadlines for the proposed changes. He argued that such timelines can only be determined once contributors have gained insight into the “full current state of affairs”.
“[We plan] many things – too many to list – but the goal is to change the system,” said Srdanovic in a brief call to Al Jazeera.
During debates, the establishment of a special prosecutorial police unit, a law on the origin of assets, transitional justice and the renovation of rural medical clinics are some frequent themes.
Could this be implemented in the case of a victory? Kandic is sceptical.
“The student movement doesn’t possess a transformative potential – the capacity to drive social change, break with the past, and alter a political climate where convicted war criminals are celebrated, Kosovo is treated as part of Serbia, and politicians from neighboring countries are branded as enemies,” he said.

If Bulgaria's presidential election had been held in mid-October, 43.4% of voters would have backed incumbent President Iliana Iotova and her running mate Kiril Valchev, according to a nationally representative survey conducted by polling agency Myara for Bulgarian National Radio.

Projected voter turnout stands at 39.4%, slightly higher than in previous surveys.

PHOTO Radio Vidin
Font size
The European Parliament has adopted a resolution calling on the EU to consider a naval operation in the Black Sea following recent drone attacks on commercial shipping. The resolution was approved by 432 votes to 52, with 88 abstentions.
MEPs also criticised the Bulgarian government's response to the Russian threat, expressing concern over Sofia's handling of the situation and its weak diplomatic response to Moscow.
The resolution praises Bulgarian and Romanian maritime rescue services, border police and passing merchant ships for their swift assistance to those affected by the attacks.
It calls on EU member states, working with NATO, to help Bulgaria and Romania detect and track hostile drones threatening shipping in the Black Sea. MEPs also want the EU to press ahead with plans for a maritime security centre and use unspent funds from the SAFE defence financing instrument to support the two countries.
The European Parliament also expressed regret over Bulgaria's delay in joining NATO's counter-drone initiative and called on the government to formally confirm its participation by 30 October.
Eight of Bulgaria's 17 MEPs voted in favour of the resolution, BNR's Brussels correspondent Angelina Piskova reported.

Russian cargo ships have been spotted loading military vehicles and equipment in the port of Baltiysk, in Russia’s Kaliningrad Region. Some of the vessels had previously been observed delivering supplies to Russia’s Africa Corps.
Satellite images confirming the vessels’ locations were published by the open-source intelligence projects GeoInsider and SONARROW_OSINT.
At least three ships were involved in the operation: Ascalon (IMO 9198226), Lady D (IMO 9349289), and Anastasiia (IMO 9349291). The loading took place Oct. 15-16 at the port of Kaliningrad.
The operation could be tracked only through satellite imagery because the vessels’ crews had switched off transmission of their location data, making them impossible to follow through conventional ship-tracking services. Ascalon and Lady D had last transmitted signals from the vicinity of the Kaliningrad Region.
Satellite images show military equipment including infantry fighting vehicles (IFVs), armored personnel carriers (APCs), mine-resistant ambush-protected vehicles (MRAPs), and logistics vehicles.
Analysts said there may have been additional cargo ship rotations in October that could not be tracked because of heavy cloud cover. Some convoys may already be underway, but their destinations are unknown.
All three vessels have previously been linked to Russian military shipments outside Russia.
Last month, the Anastasiia was tracked delivering cargo to the Libyan port of Tobruk. Satellite images taken during unloading also showed large quantities of equipment, including Ural military trucks.
The cargo may have been intended for Russia’s Africa Corps, which operates in the region. The formation, which took over many of the overseas roles previously associated with the Wagner mercenary group, is backed by the Russian Ministry of Defense.
Ascalon was previously used in the so-called “Syrian Express” that supplied Russia’s military contingent in the country before the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in December 2024.
Lady D, for its part, has previously been linked to deliveries of Russian weapons to India.
All three vessels are under U.S. sanctions.
