Musk's clash with Ukraine accelerates demand for Starlink alternatives. Few exist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:08:47 UTC
00:08:47 KST

Elon Musk's latest clash with Ukraine underscores the critical role that his company's Starlink satellite internet service has played in Kyiv's defense against Russia, which invaded unprovoked in 2022.
It's also laid bare the downsides of depending on a single provider for satellite internet communications, though other options are not yet comparable to SpaceX's Starlink and its military-grade Starshield offering.
On Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials accused SpaceX of undermining the country's ability to defend itself.
SpaceX and the U.S., they said, had suddenly and without warning imposed speed limits on Starshield. SpaceX describes Starshield as a "secured satellite network for government entities" that "leverages Starlink technology."
The changes cut wireless internet connectivity in drones and other aircraft moving at speeds over 100 mph that Ukrainian forces were using in the campaign against Russia. A Ukrainian senior commander told The New York Times the Starlink restrictions cost his unit more than $1 million and delayed missions by three days.
Musk and President Donald Trump, both critics of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, have each shirked accountability for the communications disruptions in the war-torn nation.
On Tuesday, The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk individually ordered the service changes, and had discussed them with Trump before putting them in place. Trump insisted on Wednesday that he "was not involved."
Robert Weissman, who is co-president of watchdog group Public Citizen, said the situation is an "extreme danger" that raises antitrust and security concerns around Musk's ability to control a "crucial means of communication."
"People worry about the political, as well as economic, impacts of oligarchy, and this is it," Weissman said in an interview. "It's not just that Musk can drown out other speakers, he can close down communications in a national security context for a country. No person should have that ability or power."
The disruptions have prompted a bipartisan group of lawmakers in the U.S. to call for an investigation into Musk's actions, including calls for him to potentially testify under oath.
Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told CNBC on Wednesday that he doesn't believe Musk would have acted "without at least the acquiescence of the White House," and called attempts to throttle Starlink service in Ukraine "frankly shameful."
"There's a reason why we've had relative peace in Europe since World War II," Cornyn said in a "Squawk on the Street" interview. "And that's because of the alliance between the United States and our European allies. And I think anything we do to undermine that or degrade that is a big mistake."
Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., called for an investigation on the matter and wrote, in a social media post Wednesday, "No billionaire, especially one that gets massive contracts from our government, should have the power to unilaterally decide to shut down communications and weapons during a war of critical importance to the US and Ukraine."
On SpaceX's earnings call this week, executives didn't address the issue and weren't asked about it by analysts.
Starlink dominance
Governments or companies looking for an alternative to Musk, SpaceX and its satellite internet services have few options.
Amazon's Leo, which also delivers internet connectivity via a low Earth orbit satellite constellation, is seven years in the making and has yet to fully come online, with only 390 satellites in orbit.
SpaceX, by comparison, boasts a Starlink constellation of more than 11,000 satellites in orbit, according to data tracked by astronomer Jonathan C. McDowell. Starlink connectivity is live in 174 countries, SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell said on Tuesday's earnings call.
Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos' space company, in January unveiled a service called TeraWave for enterprise and government customers. It's targeting deployment of the first batch of satellites in the fourth quarter of 2027.
France's Eutelsat, also a competitor to Starlink, has more than 600 satellites in orbit. The stock surged 23% on Oct. 14 as reports emerged that Musk had restricted Starlink in Ukraine.
Several countries are looking into sovereign satellite communications systems. The EU is building IRIS², which is expected to span hundreds of satellites, but the first launches aren't expected until 2029.
Most of these planned systems are unlikely to "come anywhere close" in terms of capacity, coverage, resilience or cost compared to Starlink, said Christian Freiherr von der Ropp, an independent satellite consultant. The cost, size, weight and power draw of Eutelsat's terminals make them particularly unsuitable in the battlefield, he added.
While SpaceX's Connectivity business has raced ahead of rivals, the company also has the advantage of overseeing a hugely successful rocket launch business, which has carried satellites to orbit for many of its competitors.
SpaceX is now phasing out commercial rides on its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket, while it tests and develops its massive Starship rocket.
Many new constellations "could therefore face substantial delays and materially higher launch costs," von der Ropp said.
This week, Ukraine and European lawmakers moved to explore alternatives to Starlink, framing the issue as a matter of national security.
Their concern is that access to a critical communications service could potentially be disrupted "as a consequence of Musk's political agenda," said von der Ropp.
"The degree of soft power SpaceX has accumulated over companies, governments and militaries is substantial, and that has now become very visible," von der Ropp said. "Inevitably, this is creating mistrust and accelerating demand for alternatives."
Zelenskyy wrote Wednesday in a post on X that he met with Norwegian officials and Kongsberg, a Norwegian defense company, to discuss air defense systems and "launching work on new satellite communication capabilities for our warriors."
Musk enjoyed accolades for providing Starlink terminals and satellite internet service during the early days of the war, but relations have soured between the world's richest person and Ukrainian officials over the years.
Musk previously ordered SpaceX engineers to shut off Starlink's satellite network over Crimea to thwart a Ukrainian attack on Russian warships, according to a chapter in the 2023 Musk biography written by Walter Isaacson. Musk disputed the report. The revelation drew rebuke from Ukrainian officials, including a top Zelenskyy aide, who said it led to Ukrainian civilians being killed.
"This is the price of a cocktail of ignorance and big ego," Mykhailo Podolyak, a top Zelenskyy advisor, wrote in a post on X, then known as Twitter.
Musk has also repeatedly argued that Ukraine should strike a "truce" with Russia and cede ownership of Crimea, a strategically important territory, to Putin.
Musk's treatment of Ukraine played a part in Canada's decision to cut ties with Starlink. Officials in India and Taiwan have also expressed wariness of Starlink, citing national security concerns and preferring to adopt a mass communications service that's not controlled by SpaceX.
Musk lashed out at Indian "oligarchs" for stalling the Starlink rollout in the country.
He's also targeted some of Starlink's prospective enterprise customers.
Starlink has become the dominant provider for airlines' in-flight satellite Wi-Fi service, signing on dozens of carriers, including United Airlines, Alaska Airlines, American Airlines and Southwest Airlines.
But Delta Air Lines is one of the few carriers to choose Amazon's Leo service.
Earlier this month, Musk posted on X that Delta CEO Ed Bastian would "lose his job" over not choosing Starlink, following unconfirmed comments posted on X that Bastian told employees, "We do not want to be with Elon Musk. Trust me."
Bastian denied making the comment, and told CNBC on Oct. 9 that he's a "big fan" of Starlink and even drives a Tesla.
"All this nonsense about it being personal is not true at all," he said.
-- CNBC's Elsa Ohlen and Leslie Josephs contributed reporting to this story.

Rising costs and tight budgets strain Americans ahead of midterm elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Rising costs and tight budgets strain Americans ahead of midterm elections
Rising costs leave US workers juggling multiple jobs as financial security becomes increasingly elusive.
Stacy Eichel, an empty nester in Florida, spent years balancing two jobs. One was in healthcare; the other was her own venture: a small business making custom-branded merchandise for corporate clients, such as coffee mugs and T-shirts that companies hand out at conferences and holiday parties.
For Eichel, the business was more than a paycheque. It was a side hustle for a woman who couldn’t sit still, who was always hungry for the next opportunity. It was the kind of business that thrived when companies had a little extra to spend on small branded trinkets to make an otherwise mundane corporate conference something memorable.
In September 2025, Eichel lost her job in marketing for a healthcare company after a merger. Suddenly, the business she had run on the side had to shoulder more of the burden of supporting her. Yet just as she needed it to provide more, the market for her products was shrinking.
Faced with uncertainty over trade policy and tariffs, alongside the growing use of artificial intelligence across the economy, companies have been tightening their spending. Custom-branded merchandise was becoming one more expense they could do without.
“The economy is such that fewer people are buying custom-branded swag because it’s more of a luxury item. When they have extra money in the budget, that’s what they’ll use it for, but now their budgets are very tight,” Eichel, who has cut back on her expenses, told Al Jazeera.
Eichel’s experience reflects a broader strain in the US labour market, where a paycheque does not necessarily translate into financial security. The headline unemployment rate captures people actively looking for work, but it does not tell the whole story of people who are working fewer hours than they want or juggling jobs that do not provide enough income.
The Department of Labor documents this through what is called the U-6 rate, a broader measure of unemployment and underemployment. It stands at an elevated 7.6 percent. While that’s down from 8.1 percent a year ago, having a job does not necessarily mean Americans are getting ahead financially.
The U-6 measure includes people who are working part-time because they cannot find full-time jobs, as well as those who want to work but have stopped looking for a job recently.
Wallet strains
Even people who are employed full-time are finding that their earnings do not stretch as far as they once did. An estimated 4.5 million Americans were working part-time because they could not find full-time work. Meanwhile, nine million Americans held multiple jobs, accounting for 5.5 percent of all employed workers, according to the most recent jobs report.
“Underemployment is one of the most misunderstood economic problems in America because it doesn’t always look like unemployment. It looks like a college graduate working retail despite having a degree, a former executive accepting a position paying half their previous salary, or a parent working two jobs because neither provides enough hours, benefits or income to support their family,” Tara Furiani, a workforce strategist based in Richmond, Virginia, told Al Jazeera.
Average hourly wages rose 3 percent over the past year, while consumer prices increased 3.7 percent, according to the latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) report released by the US Labor Department.
That means prices have risen faster than wages, leaving many workers with less purchasing power. Overall, prices rose 0.6 percent from the previous month, while average hourly wages increased by just 0.1 percent, adding to the financial pressure on households like Eichel’s.
Eichel has cut back on expenses and scaled down some of her usual spending, including dining out and takeout, and dropped her cable service.
“I never used to think before ordering in, and now we cook everything,” Eichel said.
With the midterm elections approaching, the cost of living is becoming a greater concern for voters. A Reuters/Ipsos poll found that the cost of living was the most important issue for voters, leading the next-closest issue by a double-digit margin, at 47 percent compared with 22 percent for “democratic norms and values”.
A separate Washington Post–ABC News–Ipsos poll found that voters trust Democrats over Republicans to handle the economy, 40 percent to 33 percent, marking the first time in 12 years that Democrats have held an advantage on the issue.
This comes as 44 percent of Americans said they had struggled to pay for at least one basic necessity over the past year, including transportation, rent or mortgage payments, medical care and food, according to a Pew Research Center poll released earlier this month.
Twenty percent of respondents said they had received food from a food bank or pantry over the past year.
Joshua Teicher, a New York City-based video producer in the advertising industry, said work began drying up after the COVID-19 pandemic, with opportunities dwindling further in recent years as companies tightened their budgets. Even the slow trickle of work has nearly dried up entirely.
Teicher told Al Jazeera that his financial circumstances have changed so significantly that he is now on Medicaid, government-subsidised healthcare for people in lower-income brackets. He said he is struggling to afford prescriptions and food.
“I’m having to go into my savings. Specifically, sometimes I don’t want to get a second cup of coffee because it’s like five bucks for an espresso or something like that. It’s also been harder to eat healthy. Grocery shopping, apples are just ridiculous. I find myself walking a couple of extra blocks to a cheaper store because they have cheaper apples, those sorts of things,” Teicher said.
He told Al Jazeera that his tight budget also prevents him from affording the knee surgery he needs. Cartilage in both knees has worn down. He was able to undergo surgery on his right knee to correct the problem, but cannot afford the same procedure on his left. As a result, one leg is now slightly longer than the other.
Petrol prices are another expense weighing on consumers. The average price for a gallon of gasoline (3.78 litres) on Monday was $4.29, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks fuel prices daily. By comparison, the average price was $2.98 when the US and Israel first struck Iran in late February, leading to ongoing disruptions in the global market.
Market pressures
Even for Americans who have jobs, finding a better-paying position can be difficult. Although some industries have continued to add jobs, uncertainty about economic policy has contributed to what economists call a “low-hire, low-fire” labour market.
Employers are pulling back on hiring even as layoffs remain relatively low. The latest Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) from the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed that job openings and the number of workers quitting their jobs were largely unchanged.
“I have seen highly qualified people who have not been able to find a job for 12-18 months,” Babak Hafezi, a professor of international business at American University, told Al Jazeera.
With fewer opportunities available, workers who already have jobs may be reluctant to leave them, even if they are unhappy or want higher pay. Those looking for work face more competition for available positions, while people who are already employed may have less leverage to negotiate better salaries. That can make it harder for workers to improve their financial situations as everyday expenses continue to rise. This is leading some people who already work full-time to add on part-time jobs.
“We have people come in all the time who are teachers looking for a part-time job, or who are in other fields asking, ‘Do you know anyone hiring part-time? I just need 15–20 hours a week to make ends meet.’ At what point does this end?” Debbie Louis, who owns a coffee shop in Brooklyn, New York, told Al Jazeera.
Although industries such as hospitality and healthcare have added jobs over the last year, Hafezi said that growth could slow or reverse over the next year. He pointed to the potential impact of the Big Beautiful tax legislation, which could reduce funding for programmes that support rural hospitals, as well as immigration policies that have discouraged international travel to the US over the past year, hitting businesses that benefit from those revenues.
At the same time, US consumers are also dealing with the reality of reduced purchasing power.
“Tariffs and economic pressures from high inflation are affecting Americans’ purchasing power. As prices increase, unit consumption decreases [they buy less as] their paycheques don’t go as far,” Hafezi said.
“This ultimately leads Americans to feel poorer and less able to consume. That is the environment that many Americans in the ‘K-shaped’ economy are in.”
In a so-called K-shaped economy, wealthier US consumers continue to prosper while lower- and middle-income households fall behind. The Conference Board’s most recent consumer confidence report found that higher-income households, often supported by investment gains and greater financial reserves, are more optimistic than those in other income brackets.
“Ahead of the midterms, policymakers and employers should be examining not simply how many Americans are working, but whether available employment provides adequate wages, sufficient hours, predictable schedules, benefits and genuine opportunities for advancement. Because a paycheque and economic security are, again, not the same thing,” Furiani, the workforce strategist, added.

Shamonda virus detected in human for first time in France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:07:01 UTC
00:07:01 KST

A man in France has become the first human known to have contracted Shamonda virus, with investigations under way to explore whether it contributed to his death.
Shamonda virus is a type of bunyavirus and is spread by bites from infected midges. According to the Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety, in animals such as cattle, sheep and goats it can cause diarrhoea, lack of appetite and a decline in milk yield, “as well as abortions and congenital abnormalities in newborn calves, lambs and kids”.
“In Switzerland and Germany, the presence of Shav [Shamonda virus] genetic material has also been reported in the brains of horses that died from neurological symptoms,” the agency said.
The virus has previously been found in farm animals outside Europe, but was first detected in livestock on the continent in the summer. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said the patient in France was the first recognised human infection.
It also noted that he had already been seriously ill and had a compromised immune system, meaning it was unclear whether the virus played a role in his death this month.
“Investigations into whether the virus caused or contributed to the patient’s death and how the infection was acquired are ongoing,” the ECDC has said.
Prof Tom Solomon, the director of the pandemic institute at the University of Liverpool, said the risk to the general public appeared to be very low.
“Shamonda virus has been circulating in animals, particularly cattle, but also sheep, goats, horses and alpacas, for many years, yet this is the first recognised human infection,” he said.
“This suggests that transmission to humans is extremely unusual.”
But unknowns remain, he said: “We don’t know whether healthy people can become infected without developing symptoms, what symptoms the virus might normally cause, or how frequently it might cause serious disease.
“French authorities believe the neurological complications in this patient were very likely linked to the infection, although investigations are continuing.
“This is clearly concerning, but one exceptional case does not necessarily mean the virus poses a significant threat to the wider population.”
Dr Ben Brennan from the MRC-University of Glasgow’s centre for virus research, said there was currently no evidence of sustained transmission between humans.
“While this discovery warrants further scientific investigation and continued surveillance, it does not currently suggest a significant new public health threat to the UK,” he said.
“For most people, there is no reason to change their normal activities or take additional precautions.”

Convention on Biological Diversity. What you need to know and why it matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:06:41 UTC
00:06:41 KST

You have probably heard of the UN Convention on Climate Change, which emerged from the Rio Earth Summit in 1992. What is less well known is that two further conventions were also born at the summit: the Convention to Combat Desertification, and the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD). The three were always intended to be implemented together as humankind’s response to the global environmental crisis. The aims of the CBD, which has been ratified by almost every country on the planet, are the conservation of nature, the sustainable use of its products (for example timber from rainforests) and the sharing of benefits fairly by everyone.
Every two years, states that have joined the CBD meet in a “Conference of the Parties” (COP), the global decision-making body that oversees implementation of the convention. This year’s meeting is the 17th – known as COP17. In 2022, in response to challenges including massive-scale deforestation and extinction-level declines in the populations of many species, CBD’s COP15 agreed the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework which sets out 23 targets for nature conservation.
Why is biodiversity important for human rights?
Thriving biodiversity is an essential component of the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment, recognized by the UN in 2022.
Life depends on biodiversity. All living species are interdependent, and the decline or extinction of one species can create a chain reaction resulting in a disastrous crop failure, imbalances favouring a significant predator, or the spread of new and dangerous diseases. A large proportion of medicines which prevent or cure serious diseases are developed following discoveries in the natural world.
Biodiversity is also central to the right to culture. All human cultures are rooted in our relationship with the world around us, including landscapes, rivers, oceans and non-human species; this is evidenced in livelihoods, craft practices, folk tales, songs and spiritual beliefs around the world. Culture is not simply about traditions that people inherit and preserve, but a whole way of life that is continually created and changed through everyday relationships with nature. Biodiversity loss therefore threatens not only existing cultural practices, but people’s ability to develop new knowledge and ways of being in the world.
Threats to ocean biodiversity include deep sea mining, ocean warming and sea level rise and acidification. These can have catastrophic impacts on coastal and fisher communities.
What is the 30×30 target?
The most well-known target of the Kunming-Montreal framework is known as 30 by 30 (or 30×30). This sets a target for states to set aside 30% of land and ocean surface as protected areas for nature conservation by 2030. These can take different forms but in general they involve identifying and delimiting a specific area, usually already home to significant biodiversity, and placing restrictions (in some cases complete bans) on activities such as construction, logging, fishing, hunting and gathering, and extractive industries.
One of the issues with this target is that in many cases it takes nature conservation away from the communities that have been practising it for centuries. Instead, conservation is led by national governments and “Big Green” NGOs, who impose technocratic and often militarized techniques over the local scientific knowledge of the original inhabitants.
Protected areas create income-generating opportunities for those that control them, through tourism revenue as well as carbon and biodiversity credits. This increases the incentives for stronger actors to displace or disenfranchise the original inhabitants. By making these areas empty of humans, they often become easier prey to poachers, illegal loggers, and non-state armed groups.
How are Indigenous Peoples affected by these kinds of targets?
A significant issue with the 30×30 target is that protected areas very often result in human rights violations committed against Indigenous Peoples, racialized communities and other rural and peasant communities. They may be forced out with inadequate or no compensation – a discredited model referred to as “fortress conservation”; or allowed to continue living in the protected area, but with restrictions on livelihoods and movements which are often enforced arbitrarily and violently.
In this way, the very communities that cohabited with non-human species in these areas, often developing sophisticated cultural worldviews and practices built around sustainable interaction with the biodiversity that was intended to be protected, are excluded from participation in nature conservation.
In response, leaders and activists from the affected communities step up to challenge these violations. They are often then criminalized, subjected to sexual abuse, and even killed, in many cases with impunity.
Do civil society and Indigenous Peoples participate in the COP?
Civil society groups and Indigenous Peoples face many barriers to participating and even speaking at COP.
Companies and industry associations have massively stepped up their lobbying to counter and roll back biodiversity protections, which they see as limiting their business opportunities. To do this, they turn up in large numbers at the COPs, and take up space that could be used for the voices of affected communities.
Daria Egereva, an Indigenous leader from the Selkup People in Russia, has participated in many CBD meetings but will not be there this year as she has been imprisoned, labelled a terrorist for her peaceful work defending Indigenous Peoples’ rights.
How will the cost of biodiversity protection be funded?
Lower-income countries have proposed that the majority of funding should come from high-income nations. They argue that not only did they lack these funds but that the crisis itself was largely caused by centuries of unchecked ecological destruction by high-income countries. This principle is enshrined in Article 20.2 of the convention. However, at COP15, there was no concrete commitment to provide such funding from higher income countries, and the Kunming-Montreal framework was only secured by ignoring this call. In the recent context of higher income countries cutting back on development aid and re-routing state finances to defence spending, this funding is still insufficient.
Many activists and leaders from Indigenous Peoples and peasant communities note that the issue of funding should be understood within a context of colonialism; they denounce what is referred to as green colonialism; the continuation of practices of subjugation and expropriation of their resources and territories by governments and companies from former and current colonial powers.
Furthermore, a commitment by states to channel at least 20% of funding for biodiversity protection directly to the communities that live on the areas to be protected, has not been realized. Instead, much of government funding goes to projects which violate the rights of Indigenous Peoples to give their free, prior and informed consent to those projects, and the right to participate in decision-making of racialized and peasant communities.
How are Indigenous Peoples fighting back?
Representatives of Indigenous Peoples as well as racialized and peasant communities put up a strong fight at COP15 to ensure there were robust human rights protections in the Kunming-Montreal framework. This includes for example, “recognizing and respecting the rights of indigenous peoples and local communities, including over their traditional territories” in the 30×30 target.
In protected areas, affected peoples and communities are fighting back to counter human rights violations. These include attacks on community members by national park guards, forced displacement of their communities, denial of access to sites of spiritual importance and herbal medicines, disregard of the right to consultation and free, prior and informed consent, and criminalization of land defenders.
What would be a fair solution that benefits everyone?
In order for both the environment and communities to be protected, Indigenous Peoples as well as racialized and peasant communities’ rights to continue living on their lands should be respected. Their right to continue sustainable practices of care for non-human species, rooted in generations of local scientific knowledge, should be preserved.
Also, the right of communities and peoples that have been forcibly displaced from protected areas to return to their lands should be respected and implemented as a means of reparation. Time and time again, research by academics and international institutions has demonstrated that where these land rights are properly respected and implemented, biodiversity has a better chance of flourishing.
What is Amnesty International doing?
Amnesty International has documented human rights violations connected to fortress conservation in Cambodia, Kenya, Malaysia, Nepal, Tanzania, Uganda and on the Brazil/Paraguay border, and campaigned for justice for the affected communities. A delegate attended COP15 and will be present at COP 17, advocating to improve human rights safeguards, and raising awareness of the stories of Indigenous activists present at the conference.

Russian airstrike damages Ukrainian Red Cross building in Kherson
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:06:11 EEST
00:06:11 KST

A Russian airstrike has damaged the building of the Ukrainian Red Cross Society (URCS) in Kherson.
“Another Russian airstrike on Kherson has damaged the building that houses the Ukrainian Red Cross Kherson Regional Branch,” URCS said on Facebook Thursday.
The strike damaged windows, doors, the ceiling, furniture and office equipment. No Ukrainian Red Cross staff or volunteers were inside the building at the time of the attack, and no team members were injured.
“The Ukrainian Red Cross strongly condemns attacks on civilian infrastructure and facilities used for humanitarian activities, as such attacks constitute violations of international humanitarian law,” URCS stated.
The organization stressed that despite the constant danger and shelling, Ukrainian Red Cross volunteers and staff continue their humanitarian work in Kherson, providing essential assistance and supporting people affected by the war.

Türkiye, Canada to launch free trade talks before year-end: President Erdogan

Gizem Nisa Demir
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said on Thursday that Türkiye and Canada aim to launch talks for a free trade agreement, as well as new projects in energy, trade, transportation and the defense industry to strengthen bilateral relations.
"We hope to increase our trade volume, which currently stands at around $3 billion, to $5 billion initially and then to $10 billion through the steps we will take," Erdogan told a joint news conference with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in Ankara.
Erdogan said the two sides had agreed to begin free trade agreement negotiations before the end of the year to boost trade and investment.
He said elevating Türkiye-Canada relations to the level of a strategic partnership would not be merely a symbolic step on paper.
"We have today overcome the disconnect that had persisted between Türkiye and Canada for many years. Now we are launching a new era between Türkiye and Canada," he said.
"On my first visit to Canada, we will bring our businesspeople together and take steps forward," Erdogan added.
He also welcomed Canada's sanctions targeting illegal Israeli settlements, saying Ankara considers the measures appropriate for deterring violations by Tel Aviv.
On international conflicts, Erdogan said Türkiye hoped diplomatic efforts would pave the way for lasting peace in both Ukraine and the Gulf region.

Pete Hegseth’s staff break priceless historic globe he requested for office
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:04:44 UTC
00:04:44 KST

A priceless pre-second world war globe coveted by the US defence secretary Pete Hegseth for his office in the Pentagon was damaged by his staff in a botched attempt to relocate it, army officials have admitted.
Photographs published by the Washington Post on Thursday show the shattered 30-inch Eisenhower globe, said to have been used by Dwight D Eisenhower, the 34th US president, as he plotted the D-day landings as allied supreme commander.
The fragile item was broken when Hegseth’s aides eschewed the services of specialist movers, then dropped it after deciding they would transport it themselves, the Post said, citing sources familiar with the February incident.
A US army spokesperson, in an email to the newspaper, conceded the damage occurred during “an attempted move”.
“The spherical portion of the globe was detached from the metal mounting that allows it to rotate,” the spokesperson said.
One photograph shows fragments of the globe below its wooden frame on a blue hallway carpet. A second shows an inches-wide gash in the bottom of the globe, with its base punched through.
According to the Post’s sources, Hegseth took a liking to the globe, one of two similar artifacts dating to the 1930s and housed in the Pentagon, and asked for it to be placed in his office.
The defence secretary has a well-documented fascination in the history of war, and has boasted of instilling a “warrior ethos” in the US military since his January 2025 confirmation.
The globe’s historical significance was attractive to him, the Post’s report noted, and aides moved quickly to enact the relocation.
Such was their haste, the sources said, that instead of waiting to engage specialist movers who would have packed the globe with precision and care, they dispatched their own team.
“They lost control of the artifact and dropped it, sending the globe crashing on to its base and impaling the fragile shell near Antarctica,” one of the sources said, blaming an “apparent lack of patience”.
Ultimately, the globe was not relocated, and is now undergoing repair.
An account of a successful 2022 relocation of an Eisenhower globe, between two army facilities in Alabama, appears on the website of specialist moves Craters & Freighters, which highlights the level of expertise and care necessary for such an undertaking.
“Since the globe is considered priceless, we knew its value was much greater than financial, and that our team was heavily relied upon for a safe delivery,” the article said, describing how the company designed and precision-built protective crating.
An spokesperson for the “war department”, as the US Department of Defense has rebranded itself during Donald Trump’s second term, dismissed the significance of the incident in a statement to the Guardian.
“An accident occurred while staff were transporting a replica of the Eisenhower globe as part of its relocation,” the official’s statement said.
“Accidents happen, we are grateful no one was harmed, and the globe is being repaired. It is unsurprising that the Washington Post is once again dedicating time to another inconsequential non-story.”

Iran threatens to strike oil and AI facilities across Gulf if US and Israel renew attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:03:00 UTC
00:03:00 KST

Iran will strike oil facilities, undersea cables, datacentres and AI facilities across as many as seven countries in the Gulf in the event of a fresh US-Israeli attack, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, has said.
Mehdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Mohammad Ghalibaf, the hardliner who led Iran’s negotiations with the US to end the conflict between the two countries, said Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu had agreed in principle on an attack, but could not guarantee a successful outcome. He added: “We see the next conflict as an existential threat. The third war in two years means a threat to existence. Our strategy is ‘zero red lines’.”
Mohammadi said: “We break the temporal and spatial dimensions of the conflict. The war will continue longer and in a wider geographical area than the enemy anticipates.”
Iran’s ability to mount such operations, including any unofficial help it receives from China or Russia, will be a key factor in any American decision to restart the war.
Iranian media reported that Rezaei had declared: “In the event of a war, cables, datacentres and artificial intelligence facilities could also be targeted. If the conflict breaks out again, we will have a broader plan.
“There can be no arrangement in which Iran’s economic lifelines come under attack while the economic architecture enabling those attacks is considered untouched and immune.”
According to recent reports in US media, US military advisers have drawn up a detailed list of targets for a fresh joint US-Israel assault on Iran to be implemented after the US midterm elections on 3 November.
Foreign ministers from three European countries, as well as Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt, will meet in Istanbul on Friday to establish agreed policies on the linked Iranian, Yemini and Palestinian crises. There is an alarm that a further war is now the working assumption in Tehran and Washington.
The naval services of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) claimed to have simultaneously struck four commercial ships seeking to navigate through the strait of Hormuz on Wednesday. The ships were said to be transferring oil from ship to ship.
The IRGC claimed a further three ships had been struck when they hit mines in the strait. There was no independent verification that this number of ships were hit, but Brent crude oil was trading at $113.4 a barrel, a recent high, propelled by US reports of the imminent renewed joint Israeli-Iranian assault on Iran.
Trump has backed away from striking Iran again seven times in the past four months. However, a deadlock in diplomatic negotiations has led US government officials to brief about a potential new military campaign that would target missile sites, oil installations and nuclear sites.
The sabre-rattling by both sides has coincided with extended joint-training manoeuvres by the US and Israel, including practice runs over Iraq. Dozens of Israeli planes also flew close to the Iranian border earlier this week, according to the news site Axios. A big fire at a large aluminium factory in Arak in central Iran suggests sabotage operations may be under way inside the country.
Netanyahu met the US secretary of defence, Pete Hegseth, in Israel on Monday to discuss the timing and purpose of a joint attack, including the possible political implications for Netanyahu’s chances of re-election.
Netanyahu would prefer it if Iran attacked first, he reportedly told Hegseth.
A US military buildup is due to be completed by early November, before a possible newly Democrat-inclined Congress or Senate take their seats in January. Trump intends to have stationed three aircraft carriers, thousands of marines, fighter jets and special operations forces in the Middle East by November.
Reza Nasri, an international lawyer close to the Iranian foreign ministry, said: “A third wave of war would not stay contained. Power grids, desalination plants, refineries and ports across the region would burn. Tens of millions would be left without water or electricity, and a massive wave of refugees would move from Arab countries towards Europe.
“Hormuz would close completely, oil would spike, and the global economy would tip into recession. Israel’s economy, already bled by mobilisation and missile fire, would not survive a prolonged war of attrition. And Trump would be trapped in a crisis that consumes the rest of his presidency and leaves a wreck for his successors,” Nasri said.
Fars news agency, which is close to the IRGC, said Iran had issued directives to its various military and operational units “stipulating that in the event of a new widespread war, involving the assassination of Iranian officials and the killing of civilians, the Iranian response will not be limited to military targets, but will also include political targets”.
Mediators from Iran and Pakistan this week again explored familiar if reconfigured options for a ceasefire, including proposals that Iran receive billions in frozen assets in return for lifting its blockade of the strait, allowing UN weapons inspectors to view its bombed nuclear sites and to export its stockpile of highly enriched uranium to a third country.
Iran has offered to end the Hormuz blockade within seven days and start talks on its nuclear file, but only if preconditions are first met, including lifting US sanctions.

PlayStation 5 sales in US jump 22% ahead of GTA VI release
Unknown

2026-10-22

NEW YORK, October 22. /TASS/. The upcoming release of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI) has boosted demand for PlayStation 5 consoles in the United States, with sales rising 22% in September, Bloomberg reported, citing research firm Circana.
According to the data, sales revenue increased 43%, making Japan’s Sony the leader in revenue among gaming console manufacturers.

Gaza could face another famine as Israeli restrictions on incoming goods leave residents struggling to obtain food, with flour shortages threatening bread production, a Geneva-based human rights group warned Thursday, Anadolu reports.
Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor said its teams observed increasingly empty markets and soaring food prices, accusing Israel of “deliberately depriving” Palestinians of adequate nutrition as part of an ongoing genocide.

Romanian prosecutors send hard-right lawmaker to trial for suspected hate speech
BUCHAREST, Oct 22 - Romanian prosecutors on Thursday sent one of the country's most prominent hard-right politicians, AUR vice-president and lawmaker Dan Tanasa, to trial on charges of inciting hate speech and discrimination against foreign workers.
Tanasa is a senior figure in the opposition hard-right Alliance for Uniting Romanians (AUR), Romania's second-largest party, which currently leads opinion polls.
Prosecutors said Tanasa urged followers in an August 2025 social media post to refuse deliveries made by foreign workers.
"Refuse the order if it is not delivered by a Romanian," Tanasa wrote. "Do not encourage the import of unqualified labourers from Asia and Africa."
He also said he did not want Romania to follow the same path as other Western nations which he said were "drowning under the Islamic wave".
Prosecutors said the statements incited discrimination and could damage relations between citizens by undermining mutual respect. Romanian lawmakers have parliamentary immunity for political views which prosecutors said did not extend to the current case.
Days after the post, a South Asian delivery worker was assaulted in the capital Bucharest and required medical treatment. Tanasa rejected accusations that his comments had encouraged the attack. A second delivery worker was attacked near Bucharest several months later.
Like other countries in central and eastern Europe, European Union member Romania relies on non-EU workers, many from South Asia, to fill labour shortages in sectors including hospitality and construction.
Tanasa was not available for comment. AUR called the prosecution an attack on free speech.
"If simply opposing immigration policy can become a crime then the problem is not Dan Tanasa," it said in a statement.
AUR, which has been critical of the European Union, military aid to Ukraine and defence spending plans, is polling at around 40%, making it Romania's most popular political party. REUTERS

Syria arrests Assad-era brigadier general over civilian attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:00:42 UTC
00:00:42 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria arrests Assad-era brigadier general over attacks on civilians
Syrian authorities have arrested a former brigadier general accused of ordering attacks on civilians under Bashar al-Assad's regime, alongside five other suspects, as the country's new government continues efforts to prosecute those implicated in atrocities during the civil war.
Brigadier General Abdul Hakim Wanous, former chief of staff of the 35th Special Forces Regiment, was detained by military police in the central province of Hama on Wednesday, according to local judicial authorities.
Wanous is accused of ordering artillery attacks, carrying out arbitrary arrests and participating in military raids and operations targeting civilian areas in the Damascus countryside and the Ghab Plain in Hama province.
Ahmed al-Sheikh Khalil, head of the transitional justice prosecution office in Hama, said the former officer was suspected of involvement in serious violations and crimes against humanity committed during the Syrian uprising.
The five other detainees, whose identities have not been disclosed, are also suspected of involvement in abuses against civilians under the former government.
Judicial authorities said preliminary investigations were continuing before the suspects are referred to Hama's specialised transitional justice investigation chamber.
Hama's attorney general, Mohammed Ahmed al-Naasan, stressed the importance of pursuing those implicated in abuses through legal proceedings that ensure accountability, justice for victims and compensation for those affected.
The arrests come amid a broader campaign by Syria's new authorities to locate former military and intelligence personnel accused of atrocities during Assad's rule, which ended in December 2024.
In a separate operation on Wednesday, security forces reportedly detained around 12 former regime officers and personnel in the Masyaf area of Hama province.
A security source told Lebanese newspaper Al-Modon that the operation involved internal security and counterterrorism units, and targeted former regime personnel who had previously undergone security reconciliation procedures after Assad's overthrow.
The detainees are suspected of continuing to gather intelligence on behalf of Assad loyalist networks despite having formally regularised their status with the new authorities.
Al-Modon also reported the arrest of Younes Mohammed, a former prison official accused of involvement in abuses against detainees at the Balouna prison in Homs and the notorious Saydnaya prison near Damascus.
Mohammed was reportedly arrested in Qadmus, in Tartous province, after security forces tracked him to a business he was operating under his wife's name. The allegations against him have not been independently verified.
Earlier this month, Hama authorities referred 30 suspects accused of crimes including murder, kidnapping, sexual violence and extortion to the transitional justice authorities following investigations in the Salamiyah area.
The arrests form part of Syria's attempts to confront the legacy of decades of repression under the Assad family, particularly the widespread detention, torture and killing of civilians during the civil war.
Following Assad's overthrow, the government of President Ahmed al-Sharaa established a National Commission for Transitional Justice in May 2025 to investigate crimes committed by the former regime, support victims and pursue accountability.
Syria began its first public trial of senior Assad-era officials in April 2026, including Atef Najib, a former intelligence chief and cousin of Bashar al-Assad, whose treatment of detained teenagers in Daraa helped ignite the 2011 uprising.
In August, a Damascus court convicted Najib and several other former regime figures, including Bashar al-Assad and his brother Maher, who were tried in absentia, over crimes committed during the uprising.
However, human rights organisations have raised concerns about the capacity of Syria's judicial system to prosecute the vast number of alleged perpetrators while ensuring fair trials and protecting witnesses.
Human Rights Watch has warned that gaps in the country's legal framework, alongside questions over judicial independence and due process, could undermine accountability for crimes committed during the conflict.
The organisation has also called for investigations into abuses committed by all parties to the civil war, rather than limiting prosecutions to former government officials.

Russia intensifies pressure on occupied Ukrainians without Russian passports, military intelligence says
Russian security forces carried out a new round of raids across occupied Ukrainian territories in early October, targeting residents who have refused to obtain Russian passports, Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) said on Oct. 22, as Moscow continues a long-running campaign of forced passportization.
The raids were conducted jointly by Russian police and the Federal Security Service (FSB) during the first 10 days of October as part of an operation dubbed "Illegal-2026," according to HUR.
Ukrainians without Russian passports are classified by occupation authorities as "foreign citizens" and subjected to Russian migration law, HUR said.
According to the agency, residents can face pressure to obtain Russian citizenship, expulsion from occupied territory, dismissal from work, and property seizure.
In occupied Luhansk Oblast, Russian authorities have also checked documents held by minors as part of the campaign, HUR said. Parents whose children do not obtain Russian passports have allegedly been threatened with fines, imprisonment, and the loss of parental rights.
HUR described the operation as another tool in Russia's broader effort to pressure Ukrainians into accepting Russian citizenship and push those who refuse out of occupied territory.
Russia has pressured residents of occupied Ukrainian territories to take Russian passports since 2014, tying access to employment, social services, property rights, and other aspects of daily life to possession of Russian documents.
Russian occupation authorities already carried out earlier phases of the "Illegal-2026" operation. In June, occupation officials said more than 300 administrative cases had been opened and more than 40 people expelled during a 10-day phase of the campaign.

Carney, Erdogan launch ‘strong and resilient’ Canada-Turkiye partnership

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:00:37 UTC

Carney, Erdogan launch ‘strong and resilient’ Canada-Turkiye partnership
On trade, investment and innovation, leaders will work towards conclusion of a Canada-Turkiye Free Trade Agreement.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan have announced the launch of a Canada-Turkiye Strategic Partnership, backed by a three-year action plan.
“In an increasingly complex global security environment, rising geopolitical uncertainties, and evolving humanitarian challenges, a strong and resilient Canada-Turkiye partnership is essential, providing a foundation to mitigate shared threats and capitalise on new opportunities,” said a statement by the two leaders on Thursday.
This comes as Carney is on a two-day visit to Turkiye, seeking to forge a new partnership as Canada looks to reduce its dependence on the United States.
The partnership’s three-year action plan rests on four pillars: trade and investment; defence and security; energy; and ties between people, the statement said.
On trade, investment and innovation, the two leaders agreed to “work toward successful conclusion of a Canada-Turkiye Free Trade Agreement”, it said. They will also expand bilateral trade and investments in priority sectors, including energy supply, defence production, aerospace, and artificial intelligence (AI).
On defence and security, the leaders “underlined their intent to deepen bilateral and multilateral cooperation”. They also agreed to “strengthen cooperation in support of peace and security in the Euro-Atlantic region and beyond including Ukraine, South Caucasus, and the Middle East, in particular Gaza”.
Meanwhile, energy ministers from both countries will work on areas such as liquefied natural gas, nuclear energy and critical minerals.
‘Launching a new era’
Speaking to reporters in Ankara alongside Carney on Thursday, Erdogan said the two countries “hope to increase our trade volume, which currently stands at around $3bn, to $5bn initially and then to $10bn through the steps we will take”.
He said the two sides had agreed to begin free trade agreement negotiations before the end of the year to boost trade and investment, adding that elevating Turkiye-Canada relations to the level of a strategic partnership would not be merely a symbolic step on paper.
Canadian and Turkish leaders will convene next month in Ankara for the first round of trade talks, the joint statement said.
“We have today overcome the disconnect that had persisted between Turkiye and Canada for many years. Now, we are launching a new era between Turkiye and Canada,” Erdogan said.
Relations between the two countries will expand “for generations to come”, Carney said alongside Erdogan.
“Our goal is not self-sufficiency; it is collective resilience, and that’s why Canada is building deeper partnerships with reliable partners that create new opportunities for us both, and in Turkiye, we have an exceptional partner,” he added.
Carney is on the first bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister to Turkiye, although he travelled to Ankara in July to attend the NATO summit.
He was scheduled to meet Erdogan and other officials before travelling to Istanbul for talks with Turkish business groups as the two countries seek to deepen trade ties.
The Canadian prime minister has sought to diversify partnerships and reduce reliance on the US amid an escalating trade war with US President Donald Trump, marked by US tariffs on Canadian goods, followed by retaliatory measures from Canada, as well as Trump’s statements questioning Canadian sovereignty.

Astronomers challenge dating of Van Gogh’s Starry Night
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:00:28 UTC
00:00:28 KST

It was long assumed to be a product of Vincent van Gogh’s rich imagination – but scientific sleuthing now suggests The Starry Night may be based on a real dawn sky.
Researchers say the celestial bodies depicted in the famous painting match the sky the Dutch artist may have seen on about 22 July 1889, a month later than the usual date given for the work.
At that time, Van Gogh was living at an asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, where he had admitted himself after a series of mental health crises.
The June date rests on a letter Van Gogh wrote to his brother Theo on about 18 June, describing “a new study of a starry sky” and on a mental breakdown in July, thought to have left him unable to paint for weeks. However, the authors of the new paper argue that the idea of the sky being imagined also rests on the assumption that the celestial arrangement of the painting did not match what would have been seen in southern France in June.
Moving the date to July, they say, means the moon, Venus and a star cluster called the Hyades that are shown in The Starry Night could have been seen by Van Gogh from his window at the asylum, making the painting an exaggerated reality rather than pure fantasy.
To make their discovery, researchers in South Korea identified a ridge south-west of the asylum and matched an earlier sketch by Van Gogh to the real landscape.
The sketch showed he drew a surprisingly narrow slice of the scene. “I was standing where Vincent had stood 130 years earlier,” said Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, the study’s first author and an astronomer at Kyung Hee University in Yongin, South Korea.
The team used astronomy software to recreate the dawn sky for every day in June and July 1889. In the painting, the moon sits above Venus, so they looked for dawns where this occurred and both fitted inside the narrow frame. Only three dates qualified, and 22 July was the closest match, with a thin crescent moon, Venus and the Hyades arranged as in the painting.
“To bring the question into science, which needs quantitative data we had to measure the degree of resemblance between the star patterns in the painting and the real sky, using shape geometry and statistics,” Kim said.
The study is published in the journal Scientific Reports. However, the researchers acknowledged the results were not conclusive, with Kim noting that Van Gogh may have combined the skies of several days.
The Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam, which was not involved in the research, said its experts had established that Van Gogh painted The Starry Night in June 1889. It said the painting was made on a roll of canvas he received in early June, and on 2 July Van Gogh sent his brother Theo a drawing based on it. The museum also said the artist had a severe breakdown on about 22 July that left him unable to paint for more than a month.
“Van Gogh was not concerned with exact likenesses,” a museum spokesperson said. “The positions of the celestial bodies depicted can therefore not form a reliable basis for dating the work.”
Donald Olson, professor emeritus of physics and astronomy at Texas State University, was also not convinced by the study because the positions of Venus and the Hyades cluster in the painting do not match their calculated position.
He added: “The authors’ assumed narrow field of view, essential for their theory that the stars of the Hyades fill most of the canvas, is inconsistent with the much wider field of view required to encompass Starry Night’s round hills and cliffs.”

Dreadnought reactor still on schedule, minister says
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:00:11 BST
00:00:11 KST

Ministers have confirmed that good progress is being made in developing and manufacturing the Rolls-Royce PWR3 reactor for the Dreadnought class submarines, and that reactor components remain on course to support the first boat entering service in the early 2030s as planned, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked the Secretary of State for Defence what progress he had made on delivering the Rolls Royce PWR3 reactor for Dreadnought.
Luke Pollard replied: “Good progress is being made in developing and manufacturing the PWR3 reactor for the Dreadnought Class submarines. The Ministry of Defence continues to work closely with Rolls-Royce Submarines to ensure delivery of the reactor components in time to support Dreadnought entering service in the early 2030s as planned.”
PWR3 is the first wholly new British submarine reactor design since PWR2 entered service in the Vanguard class in the 1990s, developed by Rolls-Royce Submarines at Derby with design input drawn from American practice under the Mutual Defence Agreement. The plant is intended to run for the life of the boat without refuelling, which removes the mid-life refuelling docking that Vanguard required and changes the availability arithmetic across a four boat force.
Rolls-Royce has doubled its Derby site under a contract worth around nine billion pounds covering reactors for both Dreadnought and SSN-AUKUS, and has been recruiting at a rate the company has not managed since the Cold War. Reactor components are among the longest lead items on any submarine, so they drive the build schedule at Barrow.
Dreadnought replaces the Vanguard class on continuous at-sea deterrent patrol, four boats carrying Trident D5 missiles, with the first entering service in the early 2030s after a programme the National Audit Office has repeatedly flagged for schedule and cost pressure. The Vanguards are already serving well beyond their design lives, and patrol lengths have stretched past six months as a result.

Farage plays down his Trump friendship in Britain — and talks it up to MAGA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Busts of Donald Trump and Reform Nigel Farage sit alongside a "Make Britain Great Again" hat on a stall during a Reform UK rally. | Leon Neal/Getty Images
LONDON — Nigel Farage has been careful to downplay his closeness to Donald Trump to a MAGA-loathing British public. But to U.S. conservatives, it’s a different story.
“There are very few human beings I know with whom I agree on so much as I do with Donald Trump,” the Reform UK leader told an American podcast. “And I admire his guts and I admire his courage.”
During an interview with Trump-aligned commentator Benny Johnson on Sept 30., the veteran Brexiteer struck a markedly warmer tone toward the U.S. president than in any of his recent remarks for a British audience.
Advertisement
“Donald’s been a friend for many, many years. I’m a regular at Mar-a-Lago,” Farage boasted on the Benny Show. “I get on with many of his family. We have a laugh together — I mean, he’s a proper bloke.”
In Britain, Farage has publicly dampened his closeness to Trump as he tries to position himself as a contender for U.K. prime minister, particularly since the war with Iran.
“I haven’t really been in touch with Trump for many months,” Farage said in an interview with Times Radio in April, as the U.S. and Israel got bogged down in a price-spiking conflict with Tehran.
A spokesperson for Farage told POLITICO: “Nigel has never hidden his relationship with the President. However, he has been a critical friend over Canada, Greenland, Ukraine and various other issues.”
Farage, whose right-wing Reform insurgency has been a disruptive force to traditional British politics, had to correct his initial support for the war, which has been perceived negatively in U.K. from the off.
Initially Farage said that Britain should “do all we can” to support the U.S.-Israeli action in the Middle East. He’d later go on to say “let’s not get ourselves involved in another foreign war.”
But Farage clearly sees his links with the U.S. right as deeply important, too. As he told Johnson, there have been numerous trips to D.C. and Mar-a-Lago — even if allies have also noted their relationship has cooled since 2024 and not all his Palm Beach visits have yielded meetings with Trump.
Farage noted on the show that there are things they don’t see eye-to-eye on, but was keen to stress they are “friends and allies” who “agree on quite a lot.”

The National Police has found 74 migrants crammed into a house in Ceuta's Príncipe district, including 10 unaccompanied minors, and arrested a man on suspicion of labour exploitation, assault and facilitating irregular immigration.
Spanish National Police reported on Thursday that the located 74 irregular migrants last Tuesday, living in overcrowded, precarious conditions, including ten unaccompanied minors, at a property in the El Príncipe neighbourhood of Ceuta.
The operation led to the arrest of a local resident, who is allegedly the leader of a criminal organisation involved in facilitating irregular migration and other criminal activities.
The intervention forms part of an investigation into suspected offences related to facilitating irregular immigration, violations of workers' rights, bodily harm and the labour exploitation of minors.
Police enquiries have uncovered indications that some of the minors housed in the property may have suffered physical assaults, including injuries caused by dog bites. Investigators are also seeking to determine whether both minors and adults were subjected to labour exploitation and forced to carry out various tasks, with their vulnerability being exploited.
Large police deployment in the El Príncipe neighbourhood
The operation required a significant police deployment because of the complexity of the area where the property was located and the potential danger posed by the organisation under investigation. According to the National Police, several of its members have extensive criminal records.
Inside the property, officers found 54 men, ten women and ten unaccompanied foreign minors. The detainee is suspected of offences involving the facilitation of irregular immigration, violations of workers' rights, causing injury to a minor and the labour exploitation of minors.
Police step up operations after migrant camps cleared in Ceuta
The operation comes against a backdrop of increased police activity in Ceuta, following the clearance of the settlements on Benítez beach and El Trampolín. The dismantling of these camps is thought to have led some of the migrants who had been living there to move to other parts of the city, including the El Príncipe neighbourhood.
In response to this situation, the National Police are maintaining surveillance and operational deployments both around and inside the neighbourhood.
The operation also targets the logistical infrastructure of the organisation under investigation, which allegedly housed large numbers of people while preparing to arrange their irregular transfer to mainland Spain.
The investigation was conducted in coordination with various police units along the Andalusian coast and central services, in collaboration with the public prosecutor's office to combat migrant smuggling.

Britain must outproduce its adversaries, says Streeting
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:57:16 BST
23:57:16 KST

Britain must be able to manufacture critical defence components at home in sufficient quantities, increase production and replenish stockpiles when threats increase, and sustain its armed forces through a prolonged conflict, according to the Defence Secretary.
Wes Streeting was speaking at the official opening of the UK Gun Hall at Telford, the Rheinmetall facility that returns large-calibre weapon production to Britain.
He said: “But those armaments do not get produced by waving a magic wand. Nor in the event that this country finds itself in a war fighting state, can that capability and capacity in industry be conjured up.”
He said: “To make sure we can deter and, if necessary, defeat, our adversaries, Britain must have the capacity to manufacture critical defence components at home and in sufficient quantities. We must have the capacity to increase production and replenish stockpiles when threats increase. We must have robust supply chains to back them up, and we must have the wider industrial resilience to sustain our armed forces through prolonged conflict.”
On the balance between technology and mass, Streeting said: “Despite the advent of drones and data of AI and autonomy, it is not enough to simply out-innovate those who would wish us harm, though we must. We must also outproduce them too, because advantage increasingly belongs to those who can manufacture at scale and field capability fastest.”
He referred to remarks made at the event by the Chief of the General Staff, saying: “As the Chief of the General Staff just said, we are making daily discoveries about the changing nature of the conflict in Ukraine. Yet, as was also pointed out, for all of the technological advances we’re seeing on the battlefield, what you might call more traditional weaponry still has its place in modern warfare.”
On the facility itself, Streeting said: “And so what we’re opening the doors to here is more than a manufacturing plant. We’re opening the doors to something much greater and much more ambitious. And that is readiness and resilience. For the first time in decades, artillery gun barrels will be produced in Britain. They will be made using British steel from Forgemasters. As we’ve heard, their production will create one hundred jobs here and hundreds more across the supply chain right across the country.”
He added: “Gun Hall will also support the next generation of equipment for the British Army, helping to deliver the firepower that will make us warfighting ready by 2030.”
The Telford facility will manufacture 120mm and 155mm weapon systems, including those supporting Challenger 3 and future artillery platforms, with a peak capacity of up to 245 barrels a year across both calibres and more than fifty breeches annually. Rheinmetall turned an empty building into an operational manufacturing capability in eight months, with breech production beginning in May and barrel production in June.
Streeting also set out the case for combining domestic production with allied integration, saying: “And this factory is a reminder that stronger domestic industries and deeper allied integration are not contradictory. Done right, each strengthens the other.”
He said: “The defining test is not where every single component of a piece of kit or equipment was made. It is whether our combined industrial base can give our armed forces what they need, when they need it, because an alliance that can mobilise its armies must also be able to mobilise its industries.”
The Defence Committee reported this week that general munition stocks are among the capabilities European NATO members lack in sufficient numbers, and that the unglamorous enablers of warfighting capacity including logistics networks and ammunition stockpiles have withered through decades of underinvestment across the alliance.
Ministers confirmed in Parliament this month that there is no current requirement to procure new 105mm barrels for the L118 Light Gun, and consequently no plans to restore domestic production of that calibre. This publication has reported on the wider effort to rebuild Britain’s ability to manufacture large calibre guns.

Netanyahu promises Iran regime change: Can Israel topple Tehran government?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:55:59 UTC
23:55:59 KST

Netanyahu promises Iran regime change: Can Israel topple Tehran government?
Israel can inflict devastating damage on Iran, but analysts question its ability to overthrow Tehran’s government.
Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said that overthrowing Iran’s government remains Israel’s “primary objective”, as he faces declining support in the polls before national elections next week.
His remarks came after conversations with United States President Donald Trump on Sunday and a visit to Israel by Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth. But Netanyahu offered no indication that Washington had agreed to join another offensive against Iran, let alone a campaign to bring down Iran’s leadership.
While Israel has the firepower to inflict serious damage on Iran, analysts told Al Jazeera, it lacks a clear strategy for translating military gains into the overthrow of Iran’s government. Air strikes alone are unlikely to achieve that objective, while a ground invasion would demand a far greater military commitment, they said.
A renewed offensive would also mean confronting a state that has already survived two rounds of attacks and retains the means to retaliate – both against Israel and its Gulf neighbours who are hosting US military assets. US backing, meanwhile, remains uncertain, with experts questioning Washington’s appetite for renewed fighting as it is yet to find a credible prospect of forcing Iran’s government to surrender to its demands.
Does Israel have the firepower?
Israel’s ability to attack Iran is not in doubt, experts say. Urban Coningham, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told Al Jazeera that its offensive weapons stockpiles, and “aerial refuelling” capabilities give it a substantial advantage. “Israel could again establish air superiority and strike Iranian targets,” he said.
But while Israel can inflict serious damage, analysts are sceptical that it can accomplish regime change.
Netanyahu has portrayed Iran’s leaders as a major threat since his first term as prime minister in 1996. Addressing the US Congress that July, he said, “The most dangerous of these regimes is Iran, that has wed a cruel despotism to a fanatic militancy.”
Nearly 30 years later, US participation in the June 2025 war, and again in the campaign launched on February 28 this year, delivered the military intervention Netanyahu had long sought. The overthrow of Iran’s government, however, did not follow. Netanyahu himself acknowledged the limits of airpower in March, saying, “You can’t do it only from the air.”
“There has to be a ground component, as well,” he added, without explaining what that would involve.
Caglar Kurc, an assistant professor at Abdullah Gul University in Kayseri, Turkiye, said bombing could weaken Iran’s military but not necessarily eliminate its ability to fight back. “Airpower can degrade military capabilities but cannot fully destroy offensive capabilities,” he told Al Jazeera. “Well-hidden systems would survive.”
Overthrowing the government, Kurc said, would require a willingness to deploy troops and remain on the ground for years. Israel can also no longer assume that covert methods used in earlier attacks would prove equally effective again.
Coningham described intelligence assets as “use and burn” because deploying these methods risks exposing networks that Iranian security services will investigate and disrupt.
Israel still has “human intelligence assets on the ground”, he said, while “cyberattacks” could also form part of another campaign. But using those capabilities risks revealing and sacrificing them, making the prospect of a tangible military gain an important consideration.
Covert operations and cyberattacks, in his assessment, do not offer a clear route to overthrowing Iran’s government. Coningham was similarly sceptical that Kurdish or Baloch armed groups could provide the ground force needed to challenge the state. In March, the Trump administration was said to be actively discussing providing arms to opposition Kurdish groups, according to CNN, which cited Kurdish and US officials. But this never progressed.
“Kurdish groups lacked the military capabilities to take on the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC),” he said.
Iran can still retaliate
Iran also does not need to match Israel aircraft-for-aircraft to make another offensive very costly, experts say.
Sidharth Kaushal, a senior research fellow at RUSI, told Al Jazeera that the “Iranians likely retain sizeable stocks of missiles,” even if damage to their targeting systems may constrain their effectiveness.
“The actual antiship missile stockpiles likely remain large, both because they are comparatively easy to make, and Iran has in-housed much of the production of older Chinese ASCMs, and Iran’s southern mountains provide natural shelters against air attack,” Kaushal said.
Coningham said that, for Israel, sustaining its defences would be more difficult, with previous exchanges having drawn down interceptor stocks.
Repeated attacks also impose a financial burden, as Israel will be intercepting relatively inexpensive Iranian drones with far more costly defensive weapons. Over a prolonged exchange, that imbalance could place further pressure on Israel’s interceptor supplies, while Iran retains the capacity to mass-produce more cheap weapons for a lot longer.
Would Washington join another attack?
Analysts consider this unlikely, pointing to diverging political interests between Tel Aviv and Washington, with Trump facing pressure to avoid renewed escalation before the US midterm elections.
The Financial Times reported this week that an Israeli proposal for renewed strikes had failed to secure Trump’s approval, although it suggested disagreement about immediate action rather than Washington ruling out future attacks altogether.
Without Trump’s participation, Coningham said, Israel would lack US capabilities for striking deeply buried facilities. These include the 30,000-pound GBU-57 bunker-busting bombs that US B-2 bombers dropped on Iran’s Fordow and Natanz nuclear facilities in June 2025. Designed to penetrate deeply buried targets, the weapons gave Washington an offensive capability Israel could not match on its own.
Coningham also suggested that, if Israel were to attack without US support, Iran might concentrate its retaliation on Israeli territory while avoiding US targets and disruption to the Strait of Hormuz.
Such an approach would seek to punish Israel without drawing Washington directly into the fighting, potentially further isolating a country already widely ostracised by the international community amid its genocide in Gaza.
But analysts say the central obstacle that could ultimately prevent Israel from attacking Iran is the gap between its ability to destroy military targets and its capacity to force political change within Iran.
“You cannot change a regime unless you are prepared to deploy troops and stay in the country for some years. Israel cannot control Iran. The United States would not engage in another regime change, which could take decades,” Kurc added.

Staff sought in Antarctica to count penguins — what the job entails and how much it pays
Kyiv • UNN
The UK Antarctic Heritage Trust is offering a six-month position at Port Lockroy station with a salary of up to £2,096 per month. Physical fitness, residence in the UK, and the right to work are required.
The British UK Antarctic Heritage Trust is looking for staff to work at the former Port Lockroy research station in Antarctica. They will be responsible for monitoring a penguin colony, running a museum and gift shop, and working at the southernmost post office in the world. The salary is up to £2,096 — approximately €2,400 per month, UNN reports, citing Bild.
Details
The job lasts six months and requires serious physical fitness. Staff will have to carry 20-liter water containers, lift boxes weighing up to 15 kg, clear snow, and unload boats near slippery cliffs. The station has no running water, mobile phone service, or medical assistance. Showers are usually taken once a week, and staff have to live in a shared dormitory.
Duties include counting nests, eggs, and chicks. This data helps researchers track changes in the colony's population and assess the impact of tourism. In addition, staff welcome visitors from cruise ships, run the museum, and process mail by hand.
Port Lockroy is a former British research base founded in 1944. Today, it is a popular stop for Antarctic cruises: in summer, up to two ships carrying tourists may arrive there every day. The team itself lives in historic buildings that are preserved in their original form.
There is an important restriction for applicants: candidates must be at least 18 years old, reside in the United Kingdom, and have the right to work there.
