Saudi Aramco evacuates HQ for first time since Yemen war resumed
Saudi Aramco reportedly ordered employees to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran and work remotely on Thursday, amid escalating Houthi attacks on oil facilities across Saudi Arabia.
Reuters, citing six sources familiar with the matter, reported that it was the first time since the resumption of the war in Yemen in September 2026 that the Saudi oil giant had instructed staff to leave its main headquarters.
Aramco did not respond to the news agency's request for comment.
Bloomberg separately reported that the evacuation followed an alarm at the company's headquarters, citing people familiar with the situation.
The cause of the alarm was not immediately known, while neither Aramco nor the Saudi Energy Ministry responded to Bloomberg's requests for comment.
The evacuation comes just over a week after Aramco's headquarters was targeted in an attack on 13 October, which reportedly caused damage to several floors of the complex.
Reuters, citing three people familiar with the incident, reported at the time that the strike caused extensive damage and sparked a fire that spread across multiple floors.
Bloomberg reported that the attack struck a tower within the office complex, damaging approximately three floors.
However, the Saudi Energy Ministry said in a statement on Tuesday that the attack had caused only a limited fire and resulted in no injuries or deaths.
Strategic oil operations centre
Aramco's Dhahran headquarters houses a major operations centre responsible for monitoring and coordinating the company's vast oil and gas infrastructure.
The facility helps oversee onshore and offshore oilfields, refineries, export terminals and thousands of kilometres of pipelines.
Its operations coordination centre plays a central role in monitoring production and distribution networks, coordinating activities and responding to disruptions.
According to Aramco's 2017 annual report, the Dhahran operations centre monitors the company's distribution network to ensure continuity and respond to operational problems.
Dhahran, located between Dammam and Khobar in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province, is home to Aramco's main administrative, operational and research facilities.
The company also established a research and development centre in the city in 2000.
The surrounding Eastern Province is the heart of Saudi Arabia's oil industry, containing some of the kingdom's most important energy facilities.
These include the giant onshore Ghawar oilfield and the offshore Safaniya field, as well as major crude processing and export infrastructure.
At Abqaiq, Aramco operates its largest crude oil processing and stabilisation facilities, while Ras Tanura is home to a major oil export port and terminals.
An extensive pipeline network connects the oilfields to processing, refining and export facilities, while the East-West Pipeline transports crude from the Eastern Province to Yanbu on the Red Sea coast.
Houthi attacks target oilfield and airport
Thursday's evacuation followed Houthi attacks on Saudi energy and transport infrastructure the previous day.
On Wednesday, Houthi forces targeted the Shaybah oilfield and King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, in the latest escalation of attacks against the kingdom.
Saudi authorities said the airport attack killed two people and injured eight others.
Airport operations subsequently resumed, with air traffic returning to normal.
Bloomberg, citing the Saudi Energy Ministry, reported that the attack on the Shaybah oilfield had not affected production.
The latest incidents have raised concerns over the security of Saudi Arabia's critical energy infrastructure as the conflict with the Houthis intensifies.
Aramco, one of the world's largest oil producers, operates an extensive network of facilities that are central to Saudi Arabia's economy and global oil supplies.
The evacuation of its main headquarters marks a significant precautionary measure amid the continuing attacks, although there was no immediate indication that Thursday's evacuation had disrupted oil production or exports.

Wreckage of Soviet World War II fighter plane, pilot's personal items found buried underground in Hungary
The wreckage of a World War II-era Soviet jet was discovered in rural Hungary, along with some of its pilot's personal items, according to the Hungarian Museum of Military History and local media.
Excavators unearthed the Soviet Yakovlev Yak-1 fighter aircraft from about 17 feet underground in the central Hungarian village of Törtel, which is located about 50 miles southeast of Budapest, museum officials said. István Kocsis, a member of the research association who led the investigation into the wreck, said excavations in the area began in September.
Several portions of the plane were relatively intact when archaeologists recovered them from the crash site. The relics included what officials identified as a piece of the red star insignia printed on all Soviet military properties at the time, which they said was "in relatively good condition."
Part of the aircraft's fuselage was also recovered, displaying the jet's side number, in addition to the pilot's personal belongings. Among them was a book containing the pilot's signature, which experts at the museum are currently working to restore, the museum said.
Some of the best-preserved pieces of the wreck will be exhibited by the military museum, once its archaeology department has finished carrying out restoration procedures and logged records of their obervations.
Although scientists and archaeologists alike are still working to learn more about the decades-old debris, they were able to trace the wreckage back to a particular wartime crash that took place in November 1944, Hungarian local media reported. While opposing each other over Törtel, German Lt. Peter Düttmann and Soviet Lt. Alexander Semyonovich Andrianov's aerial duel ended with Düttmann shooting down the Soviet aircraft. Although Andrianov escaped by parachute, he later became a prisoner of war, according to the news site Hungary Today.

American Airlines forecast deeper losses this year and said it will slow its capacity growth next year as record revenue failed to help the airline recover from a spike in fuel costs.
American said Thursday that it expects to lose between $1 and $1.60 a share, on an adjusted basis in 2026. In July, it forecast adjusted full-year earnings per share between a loss of 65 cents and a profit of 65 cents.
The Fort Worth, Texas-based airline is the fourth major U.S. carrier to cut its forecast for 2026 due to a jump in jet fuel following the start of the Iran war. Rising jet fuel prices have driven up airfare more than 20% from last year, according to airline reports and federal data. Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Southwest Airlines also slashed their outlooks this month.
Jet fuel is airlines' biggest expense after labor, and the spike has added billions to costs this year. American's fuel bill was up 67.5% in the third quarter alone, from last year to $4.64 billion.
"American delivered record third-quarter revenue and the strongest year-over-year revenue growth in my career, with premium performance leading the way," American CEO Robert Isom said in a news release.
Confidence in 2027 profitability
Despite the lower expectations for deeper losses in 2026, Isom said on an earnings call Thursday that he has "great confidence" that the company will return to profitability next year.
The CEO has been under pressure to boost profits at the carrier, which has dramatically trailed profitable rivals Delta and United. American has been investing in new lounges and revamped cabins with more premium seats and said this year that it plans to add seat-back screens again to its narrow-body fleet.
Earlier this month, the airline named a new network chief. It was the latest move in a management shake-up that has included new hires in its operations department and its commercial team. Last year, American brought in a new commercial chief, industry veteran Nat Pieper.
International and premium-travel demand has remained especially robust, executives said. Late last month, American said it would deepen its partnership with Alaska Airlines as the Seattle-based carrier would join American's trans-Atlantic and trans-Pacific joint businesses.
The airline is also closing in on an order for new wide-body airplanes, executives said. CFO Devon May told CNBC on Thursday that the airline has considered the Boeing 787 Dreamliner, Airbus A330 and Airbus A350.
American forecast it will lose between 50 cents and $1.10 a share, adjusted, in the fourth quarter, with revenue expected to be up as much as 22.5% from a year earlier and capacity up between 5.5% and 6.5%.
Here is what American reported in the third quarter compared with Wall Street estimates compiled by LSEG:
- Loss per share: 28 cents adjusted vs. 35 cents expected
- Revenue: $16.34 billion vs. $16.22 billion expected
For the third quarter, American had a net loss of $269 million or 41 cents a share, compared with $114 million, or 17 cents a share, a year earlier. Adjusting for one-time items, American reported a loss of 28 cents a share. Revenue jumped 19.3% from a year earlier to $16.34 billion.

EU and Canada draw closer in Trump’s unpredictable world – with Britain looking on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:51:58 UTC
23:51:58 KST

The EU and Canada are hoping to deepen ties at their upcoming Montreal summit, in areas like trade, energy, defence and critical minerals. Meanwhile, the UK is seeking its own reset with Brussels.
The European Union has offered Canada something it has never offered another country: associate membership. Quite what that means remains unclear, but Brussels and Ottawa are determined to turn their shared values and increasingly close relationship into a new kind of partnership in a world shaken by Donald Trump's unpredictable foreign policy.
The experiment is being watched closely in London, where Prime Minister Andy Burnham is seeking to rebuild Britain's post-Brexit relationship with the EU, raising the question of whether a similar arrangement might eventually be available to the UK.
The offer, made by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen last month, has raised questions about whether associate membership is a meaningful new status, an honorary title or something in between.
At a summit in Montreal next week, the two sides will begin putting substance behind the idea, seeking closer cooperation on trade, defence, technology and energy without Canada formally joining the bloc.
But while Canada is searching for a new framework, Britain is attempting to improve an existing one, with EU and UK leaders set to meet next month to seek a much-needed reset in their relationship.
"This is a moment to act with clarity and ambition. By aligning more closely - economically, technologically, and strategically - Canada and the EU are building an Alliance for the Future based on trust and shared values," reads the latest draft of the EU-Canada joint statement, discussed by ambassadors on Wednesday.
A blank sheet
Since European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen invited Canada last month to become the EU’s first “associate member,” Brussels and Ottawa have been exploring what this privileged partnership could look like.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney prefers to talk about an “Alliance for the Future.” He has sidestepped questions on whether he is comfortable with the “associate membership” label, stressing that substance matters more.
The summit in Montreal on 29-30 October is the first real chance to define the partnership in more detail. The latest draft uses “associate membership” interchangeably with “Alliance for the Future.”
Crucially, the proposal envisages giving Canada a more regular place at the EU's table, with participation in summits, ministerial meetings and technical discussions.
It calls for "early consultations on major policy and regulatory initiatives, with Canada’s participation in these processes as an associate member of the Union."
Whether the term survives in the final text is an open question. In any case, “the full scope of this associate membership will be defined by the 2027 Canada-EU Summit,” the conclusions read.
From trade to defence
The document nonetheless tries to put more meat on the bone. It builds on the 2016 Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), which 10 EU countries have yet to ratify, to remove remaining trade barriers and ensure reciprocal market access.
“We will ensure mutually favourable treatment in our respective economic security measures, based on the principle of reciprocity in industrial sectors where both sides have agreed to align their external measures to ensure the same outcome,” the draft statement reads.
On energy, the conclusions open the door to “the development of liquefied natural gas exchanges,” notably through a joint long-term feasibility study on LNG exports to Europe.
On technology, Canada will join the EU’s supercomputer initiative, a new digital partnership will tackle issues like AI and digital identity, and an agreement to facilitate cross-border data flows is in the making.
Critical raw materials, one of Canada’s key assets for the EU, are also on the table. The two sides have agreed that the European Investment Bank will play a role in critical mineral projects, from extraction and processing to manufacturing and recycling.
In defence, Canada is already part of several EU projects, including the Permanent Structured Cooperation and the Capability Coalition, and both sides intend to deepen that cooperation on maritime security, crisis management and industrial cooperation.
The partners also envisage a cooperation framework to safeguard the information space and protect electoral integrity, with an early warning mechanism and a dialogue dedicated to foreign interference.
Other areas under discussion include border security cooperation with EU agency Frontex, criminal justice, climate security, transport and the Arctic.
Taken together, the proposals suggest a partnership extending far beyond conventional trade agreements, even if its institutional form remains uncertain.
Searching for a reset
The EU's growing closeness to Canada comes as Britain searches for a new relationship with the bloc, a decade after the Brexit referendum.
The contrast is striking. While Ottawa is being offered an undefined but potentially far-reaching new status, London is still negotiating improvements to its relationship with Brussels, largely one sector at a time.
The next EU-UK summit, postponed from the summer following Keir Starmer's resignation and Burnham's arrival in Downing Street, offers an opportunity to make progress.
While the UK government was already searching for amending ties with the bloc, Canada's approach to the EU definitively shattered one of the Brexiteers' key hopes to turn the so-called Anglosphere into a free trade area encompassing the UK, US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.
"It is hardly surprising that Brexit has not delivered on that promise, and UK opinion polls have slowly started to shift in favour of rejoining," Charles Tannock, a former Conservative MEP who campaigned for Remain, told Euronews.
Since becoming Prime Minister, Burnham has repeatedly signalled that he wants to take the UK closer to the EU. He considers the status quo “not good enough” and has vowed to consider options ranging from following Canada’s example to re-entering the bloc.
While Burnham has restarted the domestic debate about rejoining the EU, the post-Brexit relationship between Brussels and London has not always been easy, with some UK officials asking why "associate membership" should not also be available for them.
“In an ideal world, with the UK we have even closer ties to the extent that the UK is a European country and if it wishes so, the ambition should not be an associate membership, but full membership,” Tobias Cremer (Germany/S&D), a leading lawmaker on EU-Canada relations, told Euronews.
Moving forward
Speaking during a European Parliament debate on Wednesday, Bernd Lange, the German Socialist who chairs the Trade Committee, welcomed a “new mood” in EU-UK relations.
He suggested that Britain could pursue an arrangement resembling Switzerland's relationship with the bloc, alongside closer political and security cooperation and a customs union.
But Brussels rejected the Swiss model as a template for Britain during the Brexit negotiations.
Switzerland's complex network of bilateral agreements has long frustrated EU officials, who argue that such arrangements are difficult to oversee and enforce, particularly when they provide access to parts of the single market without all the accompanying obligations.
Instead, British and EU negotiators are focusing on specific agreements covering agricultural trade, emissions trading and youth mobility.
A recent Franco-German proposal to include the UK in the 'Made in Europe' rules removed one sore point, but London is hoping to extend it to other sectors where it sees EU industrial policy becoming increasingly protectionist.
In defence, the EU needs the UK as part of a broader European security architecture, but the two sides failed to agree to include Britain in the planned Security Action for Europe (SAFE) for defence procurement.
Brussels offered Canada much better terms for SAFE, with a token upfront payment of around €10m. It asked the UK for a whopping €6.5bn, with no guarantee its industry would win any contracts, leading to a breakdown in the negotiations.
“Burnham is on a learning curve, to be honest," Tannock said. "He needs to. He’s been the mayor of Manchester for some years. He hasn’t been focused on this issue. He will be trying to get fully up to speed with what’s available."
Peggy Corlin contributed to the reporting.

Latvia to verify grain to ensure it was not stolen by Russia from occupied territories

Latvia to verify grain to ensure it was not stolen by Russia from occupied territories
Latvia will use isotopic and chemical analysis to determine the geographical origin of agricultural products, which will help detect grain illegally exported from the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.
Source: Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food of Ukraine
Details: Ukraine, the UK and Latvia are strengthening cooperation to counter the illegal export of Ukrainian grain from the temporarily occupied territories.
On 21 October 2026, the countries signed a trilateral Memorandum of Understanding on the Grain Verification Scheme (GVS).
The document defines mechanisms for the joint verification of the origin of agricultural products using scientific methods. This will allow the identification of suspicious batches of grain and the formation of an evidence base regarding its possible illegal appropriation and export.
The memorandum was signed by Taras Vysotskyi, Ukraine's Minister of Agrarian Policy and Food; Baroness Hayman of Ullock, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State at the UK Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs; and Uldis Augulis, Latvia's Minister of Agriculture.
"The signing of the document is a continuation of the agreements reached during a working meeting between Ukraine and Latvia in Riga on 25 September 2026, where the parties agreed on practical steps to implement the GVS and prepare a trilateral memorandum involving the UK," the ministry said.
A key tool for cooperation will be the Grain Verification Scheme, which makes it possible to determine the geographical origin of agricultural products using isotopic and chemical analysis.
To do this, samples will be compared with a reference database containing information on products with a confirmed origin.
The verification process will cover wheat, maize, barley and sunflower seeds.
This approach will help detect batches of products of dubious origin and obtain scientifically sound data that can serve as evidence of their possible illegal export from the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.
Quote from Vysotskyi: "The Grain Verification Scheme will make it possible to scientifically confirm its origin and create additional opportunities to counter illegal trade. Every attempt to legalise stolen Ukrainian grain must be met with an appropriate response."
Details: The signed memorandum defines cooperation mechanisms between the three countries. In particular, it provides for access to the GVS system by authorised bodies, the exchange of scientific data and the coordination of specialised laboratories' work.
To ensure effective interaction, the parties will appoint responsible representatives, hold regular technical consultations and coordinate joint actions in the event that suspicious batches of agricultural products are detected.
Background:
- Estonia has introduced a ban on the transit of Russian and Belarusian grain through its territory in response to Russia's blockade of grain exports from Ukraine.
- The Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) uncovered a scheme to legalise Ukrainian grain worth over UAH 60 million (about US$1.4 million) that the Russians had illegally exported from temporarily occupied Mariupol. The heads of an Odesa-based company who helped sell the stolen grain were detained.
- A Swedish court ruled that the seizure of the merchant vessel Caffa in the Baltic Sea was lawful and permitted its transfer to Ukraine as part of an investigation into the export of grain from Russian-occupied territories.

French police to sue state over riots

French police to sue state over riots
France’s leading police union has announced that it is set to sue the state, accusing it of leaving officers “betrayed and abandoned” during a wave of violent nationwide protests.
The union’s planned legal action comes in the wake of unrest last week, when around 550,000 people took to the streets over rising prices and deteriorating school conditions. Demonstrations descended into rioting across Paris, Lyon, Marseille, and Bordeaux, with businesses looted and buildings set on fire. According to Le Monde, 997 police officers and gendarmes were injured, including seven seriously.
Speaking on Thursday, union representative Stanislas Gaudon criticized successive governments over what he described as a “20-year lack of political courage” in security policy.
Alliance Police Nationale accused the government of creating the conditions for the violence that has swept across the country, as well as abandoning officers on the front lines while issuing contradictory orders and failing to provide adequate training and equipment for riot-control operations.
“Police officers will not be shields for political spin, nor scapegoats for an administration that refuses to take responsibility for its decisions,” the union stated last week.
Alliance also directly challenged Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez over conflicting instructions from the police hierarchy.
“Mr. Minister, is your administration lying to you? Or are the police deliberately being sacrificed on the altar of political communication?” it asked, demanding an investigation into the chain of command.
The protests first erupted in September over staff shortages and deteriorating conditions at a high school near Paris before spreading nationwide. Thousands of students have demanded better education funding and an end to public spending cuts, accusing the government of prioritizing weapons over schools. The unrest has triggered massive arrests and accusations of excessive police force.
Around 2,500 people have been taken into custody, with more than 900 referred for immediate prosecution and 174 jailed, Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said on Wednesday. Authorities have also imposed localized curfews.
Police tactics have meanwhile come under scrutiny after a 17-year-old protester lost a hand in a grenade explosion in Saint-Étienne. His lawyer has filed a complaint against Nuñez over the use of controversial riot-control weapons. The government has defended the police response.
The unrest comes as President Emmanuel Macron’s government cuts public spending while increasing military expenditure and weapons supplies to Kiev. France has raised its 2026 defense budget by €6.7 billion despite mounting public debt.
Further protests are expected this weekend, while the General Confederation of Labour (CGT) and other unions have called for a nationwide strike beginning November 5.

Russia used an Iskander ballistic missile carrying a cluster warhead against Kyiv’s historic center during its overnight attack on Thursday, Oct. 22, Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to him, the warhead operates above the ground and contains 58 explosive elements intended to strike people and equipment across an area measuring approximately 400 by 400 meters (437 by 437 yards).
He reported civilian injuries and destruction, accusing Russia of deliberately attacking the historic part of the capital.
“The aim was to destroy part of the old city and injure as many people as possible,” Beskrestnov said.
Beskrestnov identified the K5 warhead and assessed the attack’s intended target. He did not provide a separate casualty count attributable specifically to that missile.
Homes, monastery and emergency vehicles damaged
The statement followed successive waves of Russian missile and drone strikes across Kyiv, which killed one person and injured at least 24 others, according to morning updates from Ukrainian authorities.
The Kyiv City Military Administration said at 9:21 a.m. that 16 of those injured had been hospitalized.

Sloviansk Expands Forced Evacuation Zone for Families With Children to Entire Community
In the central Pecherskyi district, buildings and a monastery sustained damage. Eight people were injured there, including three children, according to the State Emergency Service’s district-by-district account.

In the Dniprovskyi district, one person was killed, homes and vehicles were damaged, and fires broke out in residential and non-residential buildings. Six people were injured in the Holosiivskyi district, while two others were hurt in the Obolonskyi district.
A restaurant complex and another non-residential building caught fire in the Sviatoshynskyi district. Transport infrastructure was damaged in the Darnytskyi district.
Zelensky reports 3 waves of ballistic strikes
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia launched 21 ballistic missiles toward Kyiv in three waves during the overnight attack.
He reported damage to residential buildings, energy facilities, railway and metro infrastructure, shopping centers and industrial enterprises.
Zelensky said 12 regions across Ukraine came under attack. His morning statement reported two deaths and 34 people wounded nationwide, including five children.
The bombardment came after Russian President Vladimir Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday for discussions about ending the war.
Zelensky argued that the strikes demonstrated no genuine change in Moscow’s approach despite the diplomatic contacts. He called for greater pressure on Russia, stronger air defenses and faster deliveries of interceptor missiles.
Ukraine’s Air Force said Russia also launched 210 drones during the broader overnight assault. By 9 a.m., Ukrainian defenses had shot down or suppressed 181, while Russian weapons struck 32 locations and intercepted-drone debris fell at eight others.
Missile attacks leave further hazards
The latest barrage follows earlier ballistic missile strikes that left unexploded warheads near homes in the capital.
On Oct. 8, the National Police reported disposing of two unexploded Iskander-M warheads from an attack the previous day.
The warheads, each weighing approximately half a metric ton (1,102 pounds), had fallen near residential buildings in the Shevchenkivskyi and Darnytskyi districts.
Police bomb technicians and emergency service specialists used specialized equipment to remove the fragments to a temporary demolition site for destruction. That earlier operation involved separate missiles from the cluster-warhead strike Beskrestnov described on Thursday.

Helsinki confirmed as host of 2030 European athletics championships
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:46:46 EEST
23:46:46 KST

The European Athletics Championships will be held in Helsinki in 2030.
The week-long event will take place in August, and the programme includes seven evening sessions and five morning sessions.
The Finnish capital was awarded the hosting rights at a meeting of the board of European Athletics (EA) in Lausanne, Switzerland on Thursday.
Riikka Pakarinen, chair of the Finnish Athletics Federation, noted in a press release that the decision was a reward for three years of hard work and close cooperation.
"A big thank you to the City of Helsinki, the Finnish government, and dozens of other partners and supporters of the project. Hopefully this will also encourage other Finnish sports to bid for major international events to come to Finland," Pakarinen said.
Helsinki's only competitor in the race to host the championships was the Belgian capital, Brussels.
The Swiss city of Zurich was also supposed to be in the running, but it ultimately withdrew from the bidding process.
The decision means that Helsinki will host the biennial championships for a record-breaking fourth time, having previously hosted in 1971, 1994 and 2012.
The World Athletics Championships have meanwhile been held in Helsinki twice, in 1983 and 2005.
As is customary, the 2030 championships will be held at Helsinki's Olympic Stadium, which recently underwent an extensive renovation, completed in 2020.
"We are absolutely certain that Helsinki will once again offer magnificent facilities for Europe's best athletes. The recently renovated Helsinki Olympic Stadium is one of the most historic athletics stadiums in the world," EA President Dobromir Karamarinov wrote in a press release.

Kazakhstan, Germany hold political consultations on multilateral cooperation

Germany was invited to join the Coalition.
The delegations also discussed strengthening international humanitarian law, including through the Global Initiative to Galvanize Political Commitment to International Humanitarian Law, where Kazakhstan is a founding member.

Fake pollsters fool US media with made-up election surveys
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:46:08 UTC
23:46:08 KST

Fake pollsters fool US media with made-up election surveys
Major US news outlets amplified fabricated election polls showing gains by Democrats, giving a bogus months-old polling operation national credibility before investigators exposed its invented data.
Wedgewood Polls, which appeared in June, secured coverage from publications including Newsweek, the Daily Beast, and The Hill. Its surveys also entered polling databases maintained by the New York Times, election analyst Nate Silver, and other prominent aggregators.
On Tuesday, however, after researchers at election analysis website FiftyPlusOne confronted it, Wedgewood admitted that almost all its surveys were fake. It described the deception as an experiment testing how easily a fictitious firm could gain recognition.
“We wanted to test a simple hypothesis: how easy is it for an entirely fabricated polling firm to gain traction, be taken seriously, and expose how little scrutinization exists in media and public commentary? The short answer: Far too easy,” the group said in a press statement.
Wedgewood noted that despite having no history, formal credentials or real data, it was added to multiple major polling aggregators, was treated as a legitimate data source, and was being cited on air by mainstream outlets like MS NOW.
The group added that “out of curiosity and for our own internal baseline,” it actually carried one genuine crowdfunded poll in Nebraska during its run.
The admission prompted a mass cleanup across mainstream media. The Times removed 15 Wedgewood surveys, election tracker Decision Desk HQ removed 17, and Newsweek retracted three articles and corrected others.
Before the retractions, Wedgewood’s numbers had helped fuel stories that Democrats were gaining ground ahead of the midterms. Its surveys purported to show Democratic Senate candidates leading in Republican strongholds including Texas, Ohio and Kansas.
The figures also reached campaign publicity. A Democratic Senate campaign in Mississippi cited a fabricated result as evidence of “massive momentum.”
Other invented results damaged candidates. Michigan state senator Mallory McMorrow said a bogus survey showing her support collapsing helped dry up donations and demoralize volunteers before she withdrew from the Democratic Senate primary in July.
Questions about Wedgewood had circulated for months, but its surveys continued entering news coverage and polling databases. FiftyPlusOne eventually exposed the fabrication by examining underlying survey records and checking inconsistencies with the platform the firm claimed to use.
The revelations come less than two weeks before the November 3 midterms, which will determine control of Congress. Republicans are defending narrow majorities in both chambers as President Donald Trump campaigns amid dissatisfaction over living costs and the US-Israeli war on Iran.

iris van herpen translates invisible rhythms of nature into sculptural forms for perrier-jouët
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:44:53 UTC
23:44:53 KST

iris van herpen translates invisible rhythms of nature into sculptural forms for perrier-jouët
the dutch couturier draws on vineyard soundscapes and art nouveau to explore how nature can be translated into material form.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
iris van herpen explores nature through cymatics
For her collaboration with the champagne house Maison Perrier-Jouët, Iris van Herpen looks to the vineyards of Champagne, where she records sounds and explores their visual patterns through cymatics, a technique that makes sound visible by showing how vibrations create patterns in materials such as water, sand, or powder. The Dutch fashion designer uses these patterns to create a sculpture made from silk and recycled gold, as well as designs for champagne bottles, drawing on her interest in the forms and rhythms found in nature. The project also draws on the Art Nouveau tradition, which has long informed the visual identity of Maison Perrier-Jouët, bringing van Herpen’s interest in natural forms into dialogue with its artistic heritage.‘The world is not only visual but vibrational – woven together by invisible forces that connect all living things,’ says van Herpen.
ART NOUVEAU INFLUENCES PERRIER-JOUËT BELLE ÉPOQUE 1988 SCULPTURE
The collaboration between Maison Perrier-Jouët and Iris van Herpen began in December 2025, when the fashion designer became the first recipient of the Perrier-Jouët Design for Nature Award. Both the designer and the champagne house draw inspiration from nature, a connection that reflects Perrier-Jouët’s association with Art Nouveau and its use of organic forms. For this project, van Herpen recorded sounds in the house’s vineyards in Ambonnay and Cramant, then explored them through cymatics, a technique that makes sound vibrations visible as patterns, which became a starting point for the forms developed throughout the collection.
Van Herpen is interested in how vibrations can create patterns that are invisible to the naked eye. This idea runs through much of her work, where she brings science and nature together to explore forms that might otherwise go unnoticed. For Symphonic Bloom, she translates these studies into a sculptural piece that surrounds a rare jeroboam of Perrier-Jouët Belle Époque 1988. Made from silk and recycled 22-carat gold, the sculpture rises from the neck of the bottle, with organic forms inspired by her cymatics research. The design draws on conversations with the cellar master of the house, Séverine Frerson, about how the flavors of champagne develop over time. The upward movement of the sculpture recalls dancer Loïe Fuller’s flowing costumes, as well as an Art Nouveau lamp by Raoul Larche from the collection of the champagne house at Maison Belle Époque in Épernay.
SYMPHONIC LIFE AND THE BELLE ÉPOQUE 2018 CHAMPAGNE EDITION
Van Herpen continues the project with Symphonic Life, a limited edition of ten pieces, each featuring a magnum of Perrier-Jouët Belle Époque 1999. Made from recycled 22-carat gold, the designs build on the organic shapes of Symphonic Bloom, wrapping around the bottles. She has worked with cellar master Séverine Frerson on a special edition of Perrier-Jouët Belle Époque 2018, with a redesigned bottle and gift box. The design takes cues from the textures of metal, wood, silk, and velvet. Working with van Herpen, Frerson adjusted the dosage to bring out the cuvée’s floral notes and texture in the champange. ‘The floral signature of Perrier-Jouët is born from a deep connection with nature and a continual search for elegance and nuance. Through our dialogue with Iris van Herpen, we explored texture as a shared language, from the tactile qualities of her work to the layered sensations that define an exceptional champagne,’ notes Frerson.
The works were revealed at Tokyo Gendai in September 2026 and presented during Perrier-Jouët’s Banquet of Nature at The Peninsula Paris on October 21st, before continuing to Design Miami in December 2026.

Defense forces, under the command of the 2nd Corps of the National Guard of Ukraine (NGU) Khartia, have broken the positional stalemate in Kupiansk sector, marking a new phase in the liberation of Kharkiv region through an underground operation dubbed Veles.
According to the NGU Khartia press service, the unit has pioneered a new domain of modern warfare—the underground—by traversing over 15 kilometers of subterranean infrastructure to reach the enemy's rear.
The Corps noted that while tunnels have been used in conflicts ranging from Vietnam to Gaza, they were previously employed solely for defense, shelter, or localized acts of sabotage. Meanwhile, near Avdiyivka, the Russian army utilized underground conduits for "meat-grinder" style infantry infiltrations.
Veles stands as the first full-scale, underground counter-offensive maneuver in world history.
Khartia integrated these underground passages into a unified technological framework, incorporating navigation, specialized communications, silent logistics, and synchronized aerial strikes carried out by drones from the Achilles Brigade. "This represents a victory of Ukrainian military planning over the enemy's numerical superiority," the message reads.
The Corps' fighters covered more than 15 kilometers underground—a distance that, on the surface, would often be the site of months-long, grueling combat in this war.
"The Russians believed that underground infrastructure was their exclusive tool for bypassing our defenses. We studied their experience, outplayed them on their own turf, and turned this threat into an advantage for our own counteroffensive," emphasized Brigadier General Ihor Obolensky, commander of the 2nd Corps of the National Guard of Ukraine (NGU), known as the Khartia (Charter) unit.
The Khartia unit is convinced that Operation Veles proves there is no such thing as a positional stalemate for those who hold the initiative and possess the right technology.
"Underground, there is neither GPS, nor stable radio communication, and nor daylight; every emergence onto the surface leads to combat in the most challenging conditions. In synchronization with the underground advance, the corps' units pushed forward on the surface, leaving the enemy under attack from two dimensions simultaneously," the corps reported.
Key figures from the operation: Underground advance: over 15 km. Enemy personnel captured: more than 30. Enemy casualties: over 100. The corps notes that, in doing so, the Khartia fighters have opened a new front in the war: the underground front.
To carry out Operation Veles, the Khartia corps prepared its fighters, both physically and psychologically, for operations in confined spaces. They deployed sappers, engineers, and a support battalion to establish the route, utilized proprietary technological solutions for underground communication, navigation, and life support, and coordinated the subterranean advance with surface operations and drone strikes facilitated, in part, by a joint coordination center with the Achilles strike drone battalion.
"Operation Veles served as another stage in the liberation of Kharkiv region. Through this underground maneuver, Ukrainian service members prevented the occupiers from infiltrating the rear of Kupiansk sector. Khartiya is clearing its native land of occupiers, meter by meter—both above ground and below it," the corps stated.
The operation was carried out by a task force under the command of the headquarters of the 2nd Corps of the National Guard of Ukraine (NGU), Khartia. It included the 13th NGU Brigade Khartia; units of the Main Intelligence Agency (GUR), specifically the Freedom of Russia Legion and the Russian Volunteer Corps (RDK); the 23rd Assault Regiment R.U.G.; the 21st Unmanned Systems Regiment Lava; the 429th Unmanned Systems Brigade Achilles; and other units of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to Khartia, the operation was named after Veles—the god of the underworld in Slavic mythology. In traditional cultural belief, the world was composed of three levels: the celestial Prav (the realm of truth/divine law), the earthly Yav (the physical world), and the subterranean Nav (the underworld). Veles ruled over Nav—a realm beneath the earth, hidden from sight. He was also revered as the god of wisdom, cunning, and wealth.

SAT Hospital authorities have maintained that the medicine distributed was the approved generic formulation
NEW DELHI: Days after a controversy erupted in Kerala over Natco Pharma’s generic drug for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), regulatory clarifications suggest the row stemmed from labels on bottles supplied free of cost. The words “Physician Sample/Clinical Trial” raised fears among parents that their children were being given medicines meant for clinical trials rather than an authorised drug for routine treatment.In response to queries from TOI, Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) officials said Natco’s risdiplam powder for oral solution (0.75 mg/ml) had been approved by the Telangana State Food and Drug Administration under the applicable regulations. The bulk drug had received CDSCO approval on April 7, 2025.The officials said bioequivalence studies were not required for the oral solution under the regulator’s draft guidance and that additional clinical trials were not necessary before patients could be switched to the generic formulation.Natco said it emerged as the lowest bidder in Kerala’s tender and supplies one free bottle for every three purchased under its Patient Assistance Programme, bringing the effective cost to around ₹8,500 per bottle against ₹1.5 lakh earlier for Roche’s drug.
The company acknowledged that the free bottles carry the label “Physician Sample/Clinical trials only”, but said they were supplied as samples under the rate contract and not for clinical trials. It said its generic risdiplam, priced at an MRP of ₹15,900 against ₹6 lakh for Roche’s product, had met regulatory requirements.The issue became a political controversy after Leader of the Opposition Pinarayi Vijayan said parents of children with SMA had flagged the labels on medicines distributed through SAT Hospital in Thiruvananthapuram. He alleged violations of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules and procurement norms and demanded an inquiry.SAT Hospital authorities have maintained that the medicine distributed was the approved generic formulation, not an experimental drug.Risdiplam is used to treat SMA, a rare genetic disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness. Kerala had been supplying Roche’s branded medicine free to eligible children at a negotiated price. The shift to Natco’s generic version could substantially reduce treatment costs and potentially allow the state to extend support to more patients.The controversy comes amid opposition from parents and the Cure SMA Foundation of India to Kerala’s decision to replace Roche’s medicine with Natco’s generic version. Parents have sought assurances about the safety and efficacy of switching children who have improved on the existing treatment.
While the regulatory clarification addresses the generic drug’s approval status, the episode raises a separate question: whether labelling that combines “Physician Sample” and “Clinical Trial” can cause confusion when medicines are supplied for patient use.

Israel Aerospace Industries initial share offering will happen within a year, board chairman says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22

23:44:17 KST

Israel Aerospace Industries will hold a public offering of a minority stake within the coming year, incoming board chairman Boaz Levy said Thursday at ManpowerGroup Israel’s annual customer conference at the Peres Center for Peace and Innovation in Jaffa.
“There is no choice,” Levy said. “I am certain, 100% convinced, that it will happen in the coming year. I am very optimistic.”
Speaking at the conference “The Exchange: Human First, Digital Always,” Levy addressed the planned offering, his transition from CEO to chairman, and the challenges of developing artificial intelligence tools for military systems.
Levy argued that IAI’s growth, uncertainty in Israel, and recurring budget constraints had made the offering necessary.
“It is good for the state, good for the company, good for the employees, and good for our customers abroad,” he said. “I do not think there is anyone today who thinks otherwise.”
IAI will always be a national company
He pointed to a November 2020 government decision to pursue a minority offering, stressing that the state would retain control.
“Israel Aerospace Industries will always be managed by the State of Israel. It will always be a national company; it will always be a government company,” Levy said, adding that approximately half its shares could be held by the public.
Levy said the company operates under several layers of oversight, including the Defense Ministry, the Israel Securities Authority, and the Government Companies Authority, along with salary control by the Finance Ministry.
He argued those constraints limit how far the company can improve its performance, even after achieving growth.
He said preparations were advancing on the regulatory front, including a court process involving the attorney-general that is required because some of the company’s products are classified.
Levy described his move from CEO to chairman as the first such transition at an Israeli government company, acknowledging that it raised questions about conflicts of interest.
He said clear arrangements were in place to address situations in which the audit committee examines decisions made during his tenure as CEO.
He also rejected the suggestion that the absence of a permanent chairman had prevented the board from functioning properly. The board met monthly and selected a chairman for each meeting and the corresponding month, he said.
Levy stressed the importance of professional leadership at a company whose performance, he argued, affects both Israel’s security and its economy.
“Our national resilience depends on the performance of Israel Aerospace Industries, not only for security but also for Israel’s economy,” he said.
His familiarity with the company and his involvement in selecting its new CEO through a search committee would help the leadership work together during a period of uncertainty, he added.
AI a tool, human judgement central to IAI
Turning to artificial intelligence, Levy said human judgment would remain central to the company’s work.
“Ultimately, AI is a tool,” he said. “AI may be more efficient in certain areas, but the human element must always be there.”
He argued that employees also have a responsibility to develop their skills and adapt to market demands, rather than relying entirely on their employer to provide training.
Levy said IAI’s products, including satellites, radar, the Arrow missile defense system, and land systems, generate vast quantities of information that AI tools can help process and analyze.
However, the company’s security requirements restrict its ability to introduce externally available tools into military products.
“I cannot go online, download a tool, and then put it into a military product that someone could take control of at some point,” he said.
IAI therefore develops its AI tools internally, Levy said, to maintain control over those capabilities throughout their operational use, whether by Israel’s defense establishment or customers abroad.
He added that a major challenge is the underlying physical infrastructure that supports AI tools and lets users define the parameters needed to produce useful analysis.

Beyond the horizon: The evolution of the Houthi autonomous naval fleet- opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:44:14 UTC
23:44:14 KST

The Houthi terror organization in Yemen recently launched another barrage of ballistic missiles into Saudi Arabia, targeting Riyadh International Airport. The attack claimed 12 lives, including a US citizen, wounded hundreds, and inflicted severe destruction upon the airport’s terminals.
The strike illustrates that the Houthi threat in the region is as lethal as ever, and its most alarming strategic shift is unfolding simultaneously at sea. The Houthis have effectively transposed their asymmetric warfare doctrine from the mountains of Yemen to the maritime domain.
The organization’s ability to impose an effective blockade on global trade routes across the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean marks the emergence of an entirely new terror equation for the Houthis, one that threatens the economic and security stability of the entire free world.
The Yemeni mountains and the great Western mistake
For years, numerous intelligence agencies in the West and the Middle East have tended to depict Houthi aggression as the relatively marginal activities of an isolated mountain militia. They have been viewed as a terrestrial guerrilla force equipped with sandals, khat, and light weaponry — culturally and operationally very far removed from naval warfare.
But for the international seafaring community and modern naval warfare planners, this has proven to be one of the most severe geopolitical errors of the past decade.
The geographic history of Yemen has been intertwined for centuries with control over the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Surprisingly, the Houthis, who belong to the Zaidi-Shia branch and control northwestern Yemen, decided to extend their mountainous warfare to the maritime arena and operate as a well-trained proxy vanguard of Iran.
The Houthis transformed into a lethal, asymmetric navy, executing, for the first time in the 21st century, an effective, violent, and paralyzing naval blockade on a critical maritime trade route.
This succeeded in wearing down the fleets of major global superpowers, creating an active threat to international trade routes, and generating a direct, multi-theater challenge to global shipping insurance, as well as to Israel’s maritime resilience, with the Eilat Port nearly paralyzed for the past three years.
Thus, the Houthis led the way for other terrorist organizations and states that have understood that threatening a shipping lane and extorting protection or « transit » fees from the free world is no less significant than a nuclear threat.
Currently, we are witnessing the daily struggle between Iran and the United States for control over the shipping lanes in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran is completely ignoring international maritime regulations and encouraging terrorist organizations, including the Houthis, to ignore the maritime convention.
Violent attacks and protection fees
The Houthi army comprises an estimated 400,000 fighters, with some 20,000 belonging to the organization's core and many of them specializing in naval warfare, from the coast and at sea.
The Houthis’ naval warfare in the Red Sea from 2023 represents a reshaping of the asymmetric naval warfare doctrine, combining the deployment of traditional assets: ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, anti-ship missiles, and helicopters) alongside autonomous, AI-based assets, including Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) and Unmanned Surface Vessels (USVs) across multiple theaters such as the Red Sea, the Gulf of Eilat, the Mediterranean Sea, and the Indian Ocean.
Despite powerful counterstrikes by the US, the Western coalition, and Israel against the Houthis, which inflicted severe damage on their leadership as well as on energy and port infrastructures in Yemen, the Houthis continue striking vessels and instilling terror.
The collection of protection fees by the Houthis has become a significant source of livelihood for the terror group at a time when Yemen is economically at rock bottom.
All of this is enabled by the influx of funds and combat material from Iran. This ensures that the Houthi arena remains alive, serving as a sort of "weapons testing laboratory" and source of inspiration.
In 2024, there was talk of clandestine protection fees paid through shell companies and Hawala networks. According to the United Nations Panel of Experts on Yemen, the Houthi rebels generated approximately $180 million per month from extortion and the collection of illegal "transit fees" from shipping companies.
On an annual basis, this amounts to a staggering $2.2 billion per year.
Reports from international maritime security and intelligence firms (such as the British firm Ambrey) and published in the media (Lloyd's List) in April 2026 revealed that the Houthis held discussions at the highest levels to institutionalize a formal mechanism for transit tolls in the Red Sea.
Recent reports on the Turkiye Today news website quoted Iranian parliament member Ali Khezrian as saying that proposals were even raised by regional actors to establish official Houthi transit tolls of up to $5 million per ship.
The evolution of the Houthi threat from 2023-2026
Though in the past, Iran trained the Houthis and provided them with weaponry and funding, the group operated within Yemen and its immediate surroundings. During the Israel-Hamas War, the Houthis significantly expanded their reach, striking the State of Israel at a distance of approximately 2,000 kilometers.
It seems there is no Israeli who has not heard of them after October 7, 2023. They acted progressively until they became an additional, independent, and surprisingly hot theater for Israel and the entire world.
In October 2023, they entered into an active campaign against Israel, utilizing ballistic fire and UAVs toward Tel Aviv, Haifa, and Eilat.
By November, the Houthis transited to direct warfare, executing a heliborne commando raid on the Galaxy Leader. They attacked ships with commercial ties or ownership links to Israel and Western nations, as well as those unwilling to pay the transit tolls in the Red Sea.
Over the following years of the blockade, the Houthis attacked over 100 ships, and Operation Prosperity Guardian was launched against them by a US-led coalition of the UK, Canada, France, and Italy. It aimed to protect the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which constitute a vital maritime traffic artery for roughly 12% of global trade.
Israel struck the Houthis in Yemen for the first time on July 20, 2024, in Operation Long Arm, in response to a Houthi UAV strike in Tel Aviv that targeted energy infrastructure and the Port of Hodeidah. Since then, Israel has struck the Houthis in Yemen dozens of times.
Expansion of Houthi strike radius to Indian Ocean
The ship MSC Orion was attacked by Houthi rebels on April 26, 2024, utilizing a UAV, reportedly an Iranian model from the Shahed series. The ship was targeted deep within the Indian Ocean, at a distance of approximately 300 to 400 nautical miles from the Horn of Africa (about 600 km. from the Yemeni coast). The damage was relatively light, and the Orion continued its voyage, but the attack served as proof of the Houthis' capability to operate far from the Red Sea region.
In this sense, the Houthis rely on a forward intelligence network with several key aspects.
Iranian spy ships disguised as cargo vessels, notably the MV Behshad, operating as a floating intelligence command center.
In 2025, Iran also began using the Zagros, a modern, official signals intelligence (SIGINT) and reconnaissance Iranian Navy ship designed to expand their electronic espionage capabilities across maritime expanses. This type of ship is equipped with radars and eavesdropping systems, providing positioning data to the Houthis.
The Houthis have also begun establishing intelligence and observation networks in Somalia (in cooperation with the Al-Shabaab terror organization), Djibouti, and Eritrea.
Deploying operatives or collaborators in ports and lookout points across the Horn of Africa enables them to gather visual and electronic data on ships departing toward the Indian Ocean.
Electronic warfare and cyber systems, utilizing Automatic Identification System (AIS) data from ships and cross-referencing it with Iranian intelligence data to identify the ownership and affiliation of the ship (whether linked to Israel, the US, or the UK) before a missile is launched.
During Operation Roaring Lion, the Houthis continued to stage attacks using autonomous USVs and artificial intelligence.
According to a Congressional report from May 2026, the Houthis halted direct attacks at sea. The report claimed the cessation of attacks stemmed from US operations against them, the imposition of sanctions, and understandings. Additionally, the Houthis likely stopped attacking because Israel struck back, and they likely received directives from Iran to preserve their strength.
However, in light of the struggle in the Strait of Hormuz, it is expected that the economic importance of vessel transit through Bab el-Mandeb will rise again, and the Houthis may attack again.
Driven by deep religious perceptions and funding ties with Iran, the Houthis continue to declare their support for Iran and Gaza.
Currently, the Houthis are also occupied with a reignited war on Yemeni soil against the Saudis.
Despite various similarities, the Houthis are still not identical to other Iranian proxies like Hezbollah or Hamas. Although loyal to Iran and the Islamic Ummah, they primarily prioritize their own interests.
They continue to train, refine forces, smuggle weapons, and even deepen their underground infrastructure in Yemen. They will return to action the moment such a move serves their interests.
Turning the Bab el-Mandeb Strait into a killing zone
The Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which at its narrowest point is only about 26 kilometers wide, was transformed from a bustling global shipping lane into a lethal asymmetric fire trap. The congested geography of the strait forced massive commercial ships to move along narrow fixed routes, rendering them targets for the Houthi coastal missile array.
The Houthis refined their combat methods in the strait through three integrated axes of operation.
They used kamikaze UAVs and anti-ship cruise missiles flying at a very low altitude above the water surface (sea skimming), such as the El-Mandeb 2, a Houthi development of an Iranian missile, to actively evade ship radars.They employed flooding and saturation tactics, simultaneously launching swarms of low-cost assets, forcing Western warships to deplete their inventories of expensive air defense missiles.
They also undertook Smart Maritime Mining by dispersing floating naval mines within the narrow water corridors, resulting in a complete halt and paralysis of the exposed traffic routes.
The success of the Houthi blockade in Bab el-Mandeb led to global economic turmoil. Container and tanker traffic through the strait and the Suez Canal plummeted by over 70%. International shipping giants (such as Maersk and MSC) chose to bypass the African continent via the Cape of Good Hope — a move that has extended the voyage to Israel by approximately 12 sailing days and inflated shipping and insurance costs by roughly 30%.
The crisis exposed that American and British warships were forced to use advanced air defense missiles (at a cost of $2-4 million per missile) to intercept cheap UAVs costing only a few thousand dollars. This war has created an urgent need for the production of new interceptors.
The Houthi arsenal of assets
The Houthi naval power does not rely on conventional warships, such as frigates or corvettes, but rather on a mix of asymmetric threats, notably anti-ship ballistic missiles (ASBM) such as Asef, Tankil, and Faleq; anti-ship cruise missiles (Al-Mandab); USVs and maritime kamikaze UAVs; and smart maritime mining that can paralyze ports and commercial ships, creating the need for lengthy and complex minesweeping operations.
In the near future, the Houthi maritime arm will likely complete its transformation into a hybrid fleet possessing advanced technological capabilities that pose significant challenges to naval combatants.
The Houthis may be fighting in sandals, but they are organized, armed with advanced weaponry, trained by Iran and Hezbollah, and above all, they learn rapidly to implement advanced and creative naval combat tactics with the objective of controlling international trade routes.
The writer is a Defense and Maritime Strategy senior analyst and a member of the Institute for Maritime Policy and Strategy, as well as the Dvora Forum.

Tension along Korean border fuels concern as Kim Jong Un's sister issues "not a threat, but a clear warning"

It follows hostile back-to-back statements from Kim Yo Jung – the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un – who said loudspeakers broadcasting anti-South Korea propaganda would be activated within days along the entire 160-mile border.
She also warned Seoul of "the most horrible and distressing situation" if South Korea continues what Pyongyang called interference in North Korean internal affairs.
"This is not a threat," she said, "but a clear warning."
On Wednesday, Kim Yo Jung joined senior military officials to visit fortification sites along the border, where she said North Korean tactical units had taken up positions. She accused South Korean forces of broadcasting warning messages and firing warning shots at multiple locations near the border.
South Korea acknowledged that its forces had fired warning shots, calling them "legitimate and defensive measures."
North Korea expert Bob Carlin, a former U.S. State Department analyst who took part in negotiations with Pyongyang and has followed the country closely for four decades, told CBS News that Kim's statements about "tactical units" are a cause for concern.

"Kim Yo Jung also spoke of the possibility of 'deploying more tactical strike means.' This sounds more like artillery and battlefield missile units, and if the decision has been made to move these up, it will be an even more serious change along the front lines."
Swirling in the background of the rising tension this week were online rumors that North Korea's leader, Kim Jong Un, had died after suffering a brain hemorrhage. The regime discredited the uncorroborated claims by having state media release photos of the 42-year-old dictator touring a clothing and footwear exhibition in Pyongyang with his wife and teenage daughter Kim Ju Ae.
Kim's father, Kim Jong Il, died in 2011 at the age of 69 from a heart attack. His death was only announced to the public two days later. There has been much speculation over who would succeed Kim Jong Un if he were to die suddenly.
Within the South Korean intelligence community, Kim Ju Ae, who has been a constant figure by her father's side in public in recent years, has been labeled the likely heir apparent. She would be the fourth generation for the Kim dynasty.

Yang Moo-jin, chair professor at the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, said Kim Yo Jong's frequent public appearances "serve two purposes: demonstrating to Kim Jong Un that she is working diligently, while also asserting her own profile and influence toward both South Korea and the United States."
Yang said the focus for both governments now should be on resolving the current tension along the demilitarized zone that separates North and South Korea — where some 28,500 U.S. forces are still based more than 70 years after the Korean War.
"The issue of North Korean troops moving southward takes precedence," he told CBS News. "The realistic and rational way to resolve the problem is not through further border fortification, but by sitting down together and finding a mutually acceptable solution through dialogue."
The demilitarized border zone, or DMZ, was established as part of the 1953 armistice agreement between the U.S.-backed South and the China- and Soviet-backed North that ended hostilities in the Korean War.
Since 2024, North Korea has reinforced its side of the DMZ with mines, barriers and more fencing to establish what it calls a permanent border with South Korea.
Last month, two South Korean soldiers were seriously wounded by what Seoul says were North Korean mines planted as part of those fortifications.
South Korea announced Thursday that it would inform the United Nations Security Council that the mine blasts, in its view, represent a violation of the armistice. Seoul has demanded an apology and the initiation of dialogue with Pyongyang to prevent further escalation.

On Borrowed Time: Ukraine's Economy in the War's Fifth Winter – KI Insights monthly briefing
Ukraine is heading into 2027 with a rising fiscal gap. Growth forecasts have been cut, inflation is rising, and the need for external financing seems to just keep going up. The economy is being squeezed by a labor market drained by mobilization and emigration, energy infrastructure has been decimated, and the IMF is pressing to increase revenues. How these pressures are managed over the coming months will shape not only Ukraine's fiscal stability but also its ability to keep financing the war.
Our upcoming briefing will focus on the following issues:
- The 2027 budget: how large the gap really is, who is expected to fill it, and what happens if partner money arrives late.
- Growth and inflation: why the 2026 recovery stalled and what to expect from prices, the hryvnia, and the National Bank.
- The labor shortage: how mobilization and emigration are reshaping the workforce and which sectors are hit hardest.

Explainer: What is Shamonda virus and what are the risks to humans and animals?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:41:38 UTC
23:41:38 KST

Explainer: What is Shamonda virus and what are the risks to humans and animals?
- France reported the first known human case of Shamonda virus, and the patient died. The case was in Lyon and involved a severely weakened immune system.
- Shamonda is a livestock virus spread by biting midges. It mainly affects cattle, but also sheep, goats, horses and alpacas, and can cause fever, diarrhoea and lower milk output.
- The virus has spread across more than a dozen European countries. WHO says the human case is isolated, but the long-term impact in animals is still uncertain and reporting is incomplete.
AI generated
PARIS - France has reported the first known human case of Shamonda virus in a patient who died, raising questions about the risks posed by a livestock virus that has reached Europe this year decades after first being detected in Nigeria.
What is Shamonda virus?
Shamonda is transmitted by biting midges and mainly affects cattle, though infections have also been identified in sheep, goats, horses and alpacas.
It belongs to the same group as Schmallenberg virus, which causes reproductive disorders in livestock.
Where has it spread?
First detected in cattle in Nigeria in 1965, it has since been found in parts of Africa and Asia.
First identified in Europe in late July, by October 20 cases had been reported in more than a dozen European countries including in top cattle breeders France, Germany, Spain and Ireland.
France said the virus had been likely been circulating in the country since the spring.
How dangerous is it for animals?
Symptoms include fever, diarrhoea and reduced milk production.
More serious complications include abortions and severe foetal malformations. Neurological disorders have also been reported in some horses.
The World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) says the long-term impact of the European variants remains uncertain.
What is the risk to humans?
The first documented patient was being treated for a serious illness at a hospital in Lyon and had a severely weakened immune system.
The UN's World Health Organisation said that based on current information and knowledge of the transmission of closely related viruses, this was an isolated human case and unlikely to lead to wider spread at this time.
French authorities suspect infection occurred through a midge bite in eastern France, where the virus circulated among livestock earlier this year.
They said the patient’s brain complications were very likely linked to Shamonda, although investigations into the infection and death are continuing.
What is its current status?
Shamonda is not a disease listed by the WOAH and countries are therefore not required to notify WOAH of cases under its disease-specific reporting obligations.
Nor is it listed under the European Union's Animal Health Law framework, meaning it is not subject to EU disease-specific mandatory surveillance.
Because of this, available data may not provide a complete picture of its spread. REUTERS
