Russia kept sneaking troops through gas pipes behind Ukrainian lines. Now Ukraine has gone more than 15 km underground to do the same to Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:38:50 UTC
22:38:50 KST

Ukraine's Defense Forces advanced more than 15 km through underground utility tunnels into Russia's rear on the Kupiansk axis in Kharkiv Oblast, the Khartiia Corps of Ukraine's National Guard reported on 22 October. The corps called it Operation Veles. The underground advance was paired with attacks on the surface and drone strikes, hitting Russian forces from two directions, the corps told Militarnyi.
Russian troops have repeatedly crawled through gas pipelines around Kupiansk to get behind Ukrainian lines, even after Ukraine reported confident control of the city in February. This time, Ukraine went underground itself. The operation took away Russia's chance to get into Kupiansk's rear, the corps said.
The corps reported more than 30 Russian soldiers captured and Russian losses of more than 100. Militarnyi, citing the unit, put the number of Russian troops killed at over 100.
Khartiia studied how Russian troops moved through pipes before going underground itself, the corps commander, Brigadier General Ihor Obolenskyi, said.
"We watched how the enemy works underground and studied how they do it. The Russians intended to use gas pipelines to get into the rear of our troops. So we went underground ourselves. We anticipated the enemy's actions and mastered the tactics of underground combat," he said.
For the operation, troops trained physically and psychologically to fight in confined spaces, sappers and engineers prepared the underground route, and special communications, navigation, silent logistics, and life-support systems were put in place, Khartiia told Militarnyi. The operation was named after Veles, the Slavic pagan god of the underworld.
Khartiia's brigade, the R.U.H. assault regiment, the Lava drone regiment, the Achilles drone brigade, and units of Ukraine's military intelligence, including the Freedom of Russia Legion and the Russian Volunteer Corps, took part, the corps said.
Russia has used pipelines to infiltrate before
By September 2025, Russian forces had used pipelines to move troops behind Ukrainian lines three times, Ukrainian monitoring project DeepState reported on 12 September 2025. The first was in Avdiivka, the second near Sudzha, and the third near Kupiansk, where groups crossed the Oskil River through a gas pipe.
Near Sudzha in March 2025, Russian special forces walked through a pipeline that until recently had carried Russian gas to Europe, the Associated Press reported. A pro-Kremlin blogger claimed they covered about 15 km and that some spent several days inside.
Russian troops kept using the pipeline near Kupiansk this year. On 27 September, Khartiia's reconnaissance drones recorded Russian forces leading nine civilians, including children, elderly people, and a person on crutches, through the gas pipeline out of the Kupiansk community. Men of military age in civilian clothes walked alongside them, and the corps believes they were Russian soldiers using the group as cover to withdraw. Ukrainian troops held fire because of the civilians, the corps said, adding that the case has been documented for a war crimes investigation.
Why the war is moving underground
Drones, constant surveillance, and AI-assisted targeting have made the battlefield surface transparent and deadly, argue John Spencer, chair of urban warfare studies at West Point's Modern War Institute, and Col. Drew Craig, principal military engineering staff officer at NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. In an August analysis, they write that soldiers in Ukraine describe a "death zone" of some 30 km, where moving above ground can draw an attack within minutes. When firepower makes the surface too dangerous, armies have historically gone underground, as they did in World War I and Vietnam, and more recently in Gaza and Lebanon.
"Armies that cannot survive above ground must adapt below it," the authors write.
Fighting in tunnels brings its own requirements, the authors write: detecting the enemy by sound and vibration, and specialized unmanned systems that cannot rely on GPS or stable radio links. Long stretches underground also take a severe psychological and physical toll on soldiers.
Western militaries are not ready for this, Spencer and Craig write. No NATO partner maintains even general capabilities for large-scale underground warfare, and US and British efforts focused mainly on detecting and clearing tunnels rather than occupying and operating in them.

UK must prepare for infrastructure attacks by hostile states, says Streeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:38:22 UTC
22:38:22 KST

The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, has said Britain should prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” by hostile powers targeting everyday infrastructure as part of a national conversation about resilience in the face of emergencies.
He said on Thursday the public should consider how to respond to hybrid warfare risks, such as cyber-attacks that could knock out payment systems used by businesses or cause supply chains to collapse. He also said the public should consider natural risks, such as flooding or wildfires.
European states have become increasingly vocal about the threat of sabotage efforts by enemies, particularly Russia, which can cause disruption or even directly threaten safety. These efforts have included an explosives-laden drone found next to a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport in August, and a series of unexplained explosions and fires at defence facilities.
Streeting was speaking at a new tank gun barrel factory in Telford in the West Midlands. The factory, owned by the German manufacturer Rheinmetall, is part of efforts to accelerate rearmament in the face of Russian military threats, but Streeting also emphasised that the public should be prepared for hybrid warfare, or sabotage actions that stop short of outright war.
“Terms like hybrid warfare and grey zone threats do not accurately capture or convey to the general public what I prefer to describe as state-sponsored terrorism,” he said. “So in the face of those threats, which are not hypothetical but real, and not somewhere else but increasingly here, we have to step up and take seriously our national resilience as well as our national defence.
“It’s really important that we ask households and businesses, are they prepared? Are they ready? Do they know how they would respond in the event of everyday challenges that might manifest themselves?”
The government indicated in August that UK citizens will be told to stock up on tinned food and take other steps to prepare for national emergencies.
Streeting’s comments came less than a week before the first budget under Andy Burnham and his chancellor, John Healey. The defence secretary said Healey would set out plans to increase military spending to 3.5% of GDP in next year’s spending review.
He said: “I suspect at this stage of the budget cycle I am the only member of the cabinet who can confidently say both at this budget coming up and next year’s spending review that not only have we been spending more on defence, but we will continue to invest even more in defence, and it’s vital that we win.”

Finns Party unveils €8b cuts list, spares small pensions
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:37:51 EEST
22:37:51 KST

The Finns Party on Thursday presented its cuts list for the next parliamentary term, amounting to eight billion euros in cuts, plus a further one billion in other measures, including taxes.
The package is the party's plan for meeting the 'debt brake' that the majority of parliamentary parties agreed upon earlier this year. The next government will decide the actual savings in coalition talks after next April's parliamentary elections.
The savings would hit areas such as immigration, social security, the wellbeing services counties and development aid, while small pensions would be spared.
Taxes and pensions
The new levies include a higher tax on data centres as well as a sugar tax. The party would also impose an index brake on pensions above 2,000 euros a month in 2028-2031, with pensions below this threshold spared.
Immigration
"We will address immigration significantly, especially by reforming social security," Finns Party leader Riikka Purra said, adding that the party still wants to make the entire social security system citizenship-based at some point in the future.
The party would also raise income thresholds, restrict social security, end humanitarian immigration, and abolish the refugee quota and municipal integration compensation.
Government and agencies
The party would eradicate Sitra, the Finnish Innovation Fund, which would free up some one billion euros. Purra said this is a capital transfer, not a saving, and the money would go to growth measures and reforming basic education.
"In the spirit of Sitra, the sum would be used for the future of Finns. In other words, for growth measures and especially for reforming basic education," Purra said.
The Ministry of the Environment and the Natural Resources Institute Finland (Luke) would be merged into other state administration, and the National Agency for Education abolished, saving 10 million euros.
Public broadcaster Yle would lose 200 million, and its index linkage would be removed.
Development aid
Parliamentary group leader Jani Mäkelä said development cooperation would end entirely.
"New commitments will be ended and existing commitments will be terminated as far as is possible, however, within the coming parliamentary term."
Support for Ukraine, crisis aid and disaster relief would be unaffected.

Western partners view Ukraine’s defense industry as collection of individual manufacturers due to lack of state strategy – Zaluzhny
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:37:44 EEST
22:37:44 KST

Western partners perceive Ukraine’s defense industry not as a cohesive system, but as a collection of separate manufacturers, because the state lacks a unified policy, a national strategy, and long-term funding for the sector. This was stated by Valeriy Zaluzhny, Ukraine’s Ambassador to the United Kingdom and former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (2021–2024), during the fourth annual export forum hosted by Ekonomichna Pravda in Kyiv on Wednesday.
According to him, any defense sector rests on three core pillars: research and personnel training, production, and controlled operation—all of which must be supported by a unified state approach. Currently, Ukraine has around 500 manufacturers, each independently pursuing development within its own narrow niche.
"Is this really how we should describe the perception of the Ukrainian defense industry? Let’s be honest: we are viewed merely as a group of manufacturers trying to push their own specific products under various guises. I can tell you, as a citizen of Ukraine, that this no longer resembles what one would typically call an 'industry,'" Zaluzhny remarked.
He emphasized that, given the lack of independent resource backing and technological capabilities, Ukraine’s defense sector will likely follow a "niche" model. Under this approach, the country would focus on meeting specific, targeted needs essential for achieving victory—in part through cooperation with foreign partners.
"Clearly, given that we have certain achievements but lack the necessary technological capabilities and resources, we will likely adopt a 'niche' model, filling specific niches essential for achieving our political objective: ultimately, Ukraine’s victory in the Russia-Ukraine War. For instance, the British could supply the Ukrainian defense industry with missile engines, while another nation might provide space-related capabilities, and so on," he said.
As previously reported, Zaluzhny expressed skepticism regarding the possibility of a rapid breakthrough for Ukraine’s defense-industrial complex into foreign markets. He noted that the large-scale export of domestic weaponry and technology is complicated by the absence of relevant military doctrines among NATO member states, as well as the fact that many new technologies are still in the developmental stage.

One in 10 adults in England and Wales experienced domestic abuse in last year, ONS finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:36:45 UTC
22:36:45 KST

Almost one in 10 adults in England and Wales have experienced domestic abuse in the last year, a survey from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) has found.
The Crime Survey for England and Wales (CSEW) found that 9.6% of people aged 16 and over had experienced domestic abuse in the last year – which equates to about 4.7 million people.
This marked an increase compared with the year to September 2025, when the same survey found that 7.8% of adults – about 3.8 million people – had experienced domestic abuse.
Domestic abuse charities said the figures were concerning, as they indicated the government was “not on track to fulfil its pledge” to halve violence against women and girls in a decade.
The increase was driven by a significant rise in intimate partner abuse, which had increased by almost 2% compared with the previous year; there was no significant difference in family abuse, which had only grown by 0.1%.
The survey also found that 2.1% of people, equating to about 1 million, had experienced sexual victimisation, and 3.9%, or about 1.9 million, had experienced stalking. These figures were based on new questions, so are not comparable with previous estimates.
The ONS estimates that in total, 10.9% of people aged 16 years and over, or about 5.3 million adults, have experienced at least one of the three crimes of domestic abuse, sexual victimisation, and stalking.
Prevalence was higher among female victims, at 12.8%, or about 3.2 million women. But 8.9% of men – about 2.1 million – were also affected.
Meghan Elkin, head of crime statistics at the ONS, said: “While minor survey changes and the usual uncertainty around gathering data on this sensitive topic are likely to have affected these estimates, our assessment is that the rise in domestic abuse includes real change. More data points are needed to further understand the uncertainty and what this tells us about trends in domestic abuse.”
The statistics will be used as the main measure for monitoring the government’s ambition to halve violence against women and girls.
The CSEW is a face-to-face household survey based on more than 30,000 adult interviews annually. The data is released by financial year, with this year’s statistics relating to the year ending March 2026.
Alice Russell-Harris, the public affairs lead at Refuge, said: “The government has pledged to halve violence against women and girls … by 2034, but latest domestic abuse data from the ONS tells a troubling story.” She added: “This figure reflects what we sadly know to be true at Refuge: domestic abuse is devastating an unacceptable number of lives.
“Domestic abuse often goes unseen and unreported, so these figures likely represent the tip of the iceberg. While ONS has highlighted that changes in data collection, such as the introduction and implementation of new survey questions, may have contributed to this increase, what remains steadfast is our concern that the government is not on track to fulfil its pledge.”
She called for “vital investment” before next week’s autumn budget, urging the government “to provide the vital investment required to meet rising demand”.
“Refuge has been clear that this ambitious goal is simply not achievable without sustainable, long-term funding for specialist domestic abuse services,” she said, “but we have yet to see a financial commitment that matches the scale needed for every survivor to access timely support.
“Specialist support services, and the survivors which depend on them, cannot afford to bear the brunt of underfunding any longer.”
Farah Nazeer, CEO of Women’s Aid said the statistics represented “a staggering number of people affected in the last year” and were “a reminder that if domestic abuse doesn’t affect us directly it will be affecting someone we know”.
She said the charity was particularly concerned about the rise of online harassment “and how new forms of abuse are being perpetrated in line with digital trends”.
As government considered how to respond to these statistics, ministers should ensure their approach included investment in specialist responses, including in support services by and for the women that used them, and in the public services on the frontline of responding to domestic abuse, from policing and probation to health and education. “We hope that as the chancellor prepares the budget for next week, these shocking prevalence figures are at the top of his mind,” she added.
Sam Smethers, the CEO of Surviving Economic Abuse, said the statistics were “shocking, but sadly not surprising”.
“This rise highlights the urgent need to challenge the harmful attitudes that normalise men’s control over women’s money and tackle the rising living costs that give abusive partners further opportunities to tighten their control,” she said.
She added that research by SEA found that “young women and girls are twice as likely to experience economic abuse as any other age group, with abuse often beginning in the very first month of a relationship”.
She called on the government to act on its commitment to halve violence against women and girls “by transforming systems to stop abusers from taking economic control and ensuring victim-survivors have the support they need to escape and rebuild their lives”.
- In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid. In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org.

Around 100 Lithuanian websites vulnerable to critical PHP flaw, cybersecurity chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:36:00 UTC
22:36:00 KST

Around 100 websites in Lithuania have been identified as vulnerable to a critical flaw in PHP, a programming language used by an estimated 80% to 90% of websites in the country, the head of the National Cyber Security Centre said Thursday.
Antanas Aleknavičius told M1 radio that the affected sites included those operated by private businesses and state institutions. The centre is conducting further scans to determine the full extent of the vulnerability.
Authorities rated the severity of the threat at 9.5 out of 10 and notified institutions in advance, he said.
The National Cyber Security Centre issued a warning Wednesday following international reports of a global vulnerability in PHP code. In response, the Centre of Registers temporarily suspended some services, announcing Thursday that they were being restored.
Aleknavičius warned that failure to address the flaw could leave websites and their servers exposed to attacks, potentially disrupting information systems. The extent of the damage would depend on existing security measures and the data stored on affected sites.
Some websites might need only software updates, while others could require more extensive reconstruction, he said.
Tools to exploit the vulnerability are being developed, but there is currently no evidence they have been used, Aleknavičius added.
Antanas Raguotis, IT director at the Centre of Registers, said exploiting the flaw could enable unauthorised access to systems, allowing attackers to alter or steal data and take control of affected systems. An investigation into the incident will be conducted.
Raguotis also warned of a critical vulnerability in Java, another widely used programming language, announced by Oracle. The Centre of Registers is assessing the potential impact on its systems and is awaiting international recommendations before deciding whether further precautions, including suspending services, are necessary.
He said advances in artificial intelligence were making it possible to identify and exploit software vulnerabilities much faster, potentially increasing the scale of cyberattacks.
When new technologies emerge, tools to exploit them are often developed before effective defensive measures become available, Raguotis said.

How Sudan’s shift to drone warfare is fuelling a civilian crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:35:31 UTC
22:35:31 KST

How Sudan’s shift to drone warfare is fuelling a civilian crisis
As Sudan’s warring factions escalate deadly unmanned aerial strikes, hundreds of civilians are caught in the crossfire.
In the Imtidad Nasser neighbourhood east of Sudan’s capital Khartoum, residents are grappling with a terrifying new reality of skies filled with drones.
“We heard the buzz of drones in the sky, but did not pay attention to it at first,” Ahmed Abdel Hamid, a resident of the area, told Al Jazeera about a recent drone attack by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
Then, anti-aircraft fire and two huge explosions shook the area, killing three children from a family in the community.
A devastating wave of drone attacks across Sudan has killed more than 160 people in recent days, marking a lethal evolution in the conflict between competing military forces which began in April 2023.
A rise in the use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) by the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary RSF has pushed the war deep into residential neighbourhoods, driven by shifting battlefield motives and a mutual desire to exhaust the opponent.
Shifting military tactics
The use of drones is a relatively new development in the brutal civil war, which is now in its fourth year and has killed at least 59,000 people, according to conflict monitor ACLED. Some 14 million people have been displaced from their homes, with 4.5 million fleeing the country.
In the meantime, the SAF and the RSF have continued to vie for control of different parts of the country, mostly through ground invasions and fighting – and often at the cost of civilians. The massacre in el-Fasher in the west of the country last year – described by Amnesty International as “ethnic cleansing” – propelled the crisis to international headlines. RSF fighters murdered tens of thousands of inhabitants of the city after holding it under siege for 18 months and then capturing it – at the time the last SAF stronghold in the Darfur region.
Now, the intensified reliance on drones by both sides reflects a deliberate shift towards long-range, preemptive operations. For the SAF, drones offer a crucial tool to navigate complex geography and neutralise RSF advantages.
Military expert Abu Bakr Abdel Rahim said the army’s main motive for escalating drone strikes deep inside the Darfur and Kordofan regions is “targeting command and control centres, fuel and ammunition depots, and main supply routes, especially those linked to the borders with Libya, Chad and South Sudan”.
Geography plays a pivotal role in this strategy. “The Darfur region is vast, separated from the army’s current concentration areas in Kordofan by desert distances and long, militarily exposed roads, making ground advance highly complex without massive engineering, aerial, and logistical cover,” Abdel Rahim explained.
Through these targeted strikes, Abdel Rahim noted, army leadership seeks to weaken the RSF’s “ability to assemble its forces and launch counterattacks, or reclaim the strategic areas it lost”. Furthermore, by striking cities like Nyala, the army aims to “strike their morale, make them feel insecure even in their rear control areas, and disrupt any efforts to establish parallel administrative entities”.
Competing battlefield narratives
Military officials say there are specific tactical goals behind the recent escalation. Mohamed Didan, spokesperson for the SAF’s Special Action Forces in Kordofan, stated in a Facebook post that the army launched “75 air strikes targeting fixed and moving targets, along with infantry forces, vehicles, commanders and individuals from the Rapid Support Forces” across Kordofan, West Darfur and South Darfur.
Didan directly linked the RSF’s recent drone attacks on Khartoum to their battlefield losses, attributing the escalation to “the killing of about 80 mobilised personnel for the forces in strikes that targeted them in the Al-Dabbab area in West Kordofan”.
He added that the RSF is deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, “as happened at Khartoum airport, fuel stations in Damazin, and the electrical transformer station in Tendelti city in North Kordofan state last Tuesday, which led to the blackout of cities in the state and the neighbouring North Kordofan state”.
In response, the RSF issued a statement on Monday accusing the military of using drones to carry out “massacres in the livestock market in Nyala and al-Na’am market in Abyei, and at a truck station in the al-Dabbab area in West Kordofan“.
A Sudanese government official, speaking to Al Jazeera on condition of anonymity, said the military’s use of drones is strictly tactical. “The army does not target civilians, but it considers all military and logistical sites and supply lines of the Rapid Support Forces as legitimate targets,” the official stated.
Mounting civilian death toll
Civilians are paying the highest price for all this. The deadliest recent attack occurred near a market in al-Dabba town in West Kordofan, where a drone struck a transport hub, killing 80 people.
Early on Monday, an army drone attack hit the RSF stronghold of Nyala, killing 17 people, while a strike by the paramilitary group on a gathering of displaced people in the Blue Nile province killed 41 individuals.
The United Nations has condemned the strikes. “We are alarmed by the continued deadly drone strikes across the country that are killing civilians, including children, and that are disrupting central services,” Stephane Dujarric, spokesperson for the UN secretary-general, told reporters.
An investigative report by the Centre for Information Resilience (CIR) revealed that 21 different drone models have been used since the war erupted.
A diverse international supply chain is behind their procurement of these weapons, which have been found to originate mainly from six countries: Belarus, Iran, China, Russia, Sudan and Turkiye.
According to the CIR investigation, the RSF has deployed 10 different types of drones, while the SAF has used five different models. The overall result is a terrifying and rapidly mechanising conflict where the skies offer no sanctuary to the civilians below.

The US is letting a convicted Bolsonaro spy chief stay in Florida. Brazil wants answers.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:34:44 UTC
22:34:44 KST

LATIN AMERICA
The US is letting a convicted Bolsonaro spy chief stay in Florida. Brazil wants answers.
Former intelligence director Alexandre Ramagem fled after his conviction for trying to overturn Brazil’s 2022 election. Authorities there are investigating whether he had help.
It was an unusual request. On Nov. 21, 2025, the owner of an apartment in a luxury complex north of Miami drafted a message asking the building’s management to remove his houseguest immediately, the same man his family had vouched for in writing two months earlier.
The guest was Alexandre Ramagem, a Brazilian congressman and spy chief under former President Jair Bolsonaro. In September, Ramagem had fled Brazil days before being sentenced to 16 years in prison for his role in Bolsonaro’s plot to overturn the 2022 election. The message was drafted the same day the country’s Supreme Court ordered Ramagem’s arrest and two days after a Brazilian news site published photos of him and his wife strolling through the Miami complex in workout clothes, causing outrage back home.
The message was written in the name of Rodrigo Martins de Mello, who was convicted of running an illegal mining operation on protected indigenous land in the Amazon. De Mello claimed he had only just learned from the press that his guest was barred from leaving Brazil. “In order to avoid any issues for the condominium or for myself, I hereby request that the condominium IMMEDIATELY notify him of my directive for him to leave my property,” De Mello wrote.
But Brazilian investigators say De Mello and his family knew all along that Ramagem was on the run. Messages, notes and photos from confidential records reviewed by ICIJ and Agência Pública show that they housed Ramagem for months, vouched for him to building management and sought paperwork needed to obtain a Florida driver’s license for him, including a lease drafted to make it look as if he was renting a room.
The records, obtained by Agência Pública and shared with ICIJ, are part of a sealed investigation by Brazil’s Federal Police into Ramagem’s escape, conducted within the Supreme Court’s sprawling investigation into the plot to overturn the 2022 election.
The Federal Police had an officer in Miami working alongside the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. With the officer’s help, the confidential records say, ICE found Ramagem, who Brazil wants to extradite, and arrested him in Orlando in April for overstaying his visa.
Then the case took an unexpected turn. After two days, ICE released Ramagem while he pursues asylum. Days after that, the State Department told the Brazilian officer who had helped locate Ramagem to leave the country, accusing him of trying to extend “political witch hunts” to U.S. soil.
There’s a lot of favoritism and discrimination and double standards in the immigration system now. — Tessa Petit, Florida Immigrant Coalition
Six months later, Ramagem remains free in Florida. Officials in Brazil declined to say whether the U.S. has responded to its extradition request.
Ramagem’s treatment stands in sharp contrast with that of thousands of asylum seekers who have been deported since Trump returned to office.
“There’s a lot of favoritism and discrimination and double standards in the immigration system now,” said Tessa Petit, executive director of the advocacy group Florida Immigrant Coalition.
Most immigrants don’t get the break Ramagem got, said Petit, who fled Haiti in 2001 and was initially denied asylum before winning her case in immigration court. “The reality for the majority of people is: Be vigilant, be careful, and hopefully be lucky enough to not get picked up.”
Neither Ramagem nor the De Mellos responded to requests for comment for this story.
In Brazil and in the U.S., supporters of Jair Bolsonaro, a close ally of President Donald Trump, praised the White House for Ramagem’s release.
On Oct. 25, Brazilians will vote in a presidential runoff in which the narrow front-runner, Flavio Bolsonaro, a son of the former leader, has promised pardons for everyone convicted in the coup plot.
‘An illegal alien from Brazil’
Ramagem’s only known run-in with U.S. authorities came after months of living in plain sight in Florida and publicly accusing the Brazilian government of persecution.
Ramagem entered the country legally on Sept. 11, 2025, with permission to stay six months, the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, told ICIJ. But he “chose to illegally overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” the agency said, calling him, “an illegal alien from Brazil.”
Brazil filed a formal extradition request with the State Department on Dec. 30, 2025, according to Brazil’s Justice Ministry.
On April 13, police detained Ramagem in Orlando during a traffic stop and handed him over to ICE. Two days later, ICE let him go, pending the outcome of his removal proceedings, the agency said. He paid no bail, according to Paulo Figueiredo, a U.S.-based Brazilian commentator and Bolsonaro ally who said his immigration consulting firm has assisted Ramagem. Detained immigrants usually must go before a judge to seek release, but ICIJ found no record of Ramagem petitioning the court for his freedom. ICE told Brazilian police at the time that the release was an administrative decision and that Ramagem could remain free while his asylum claim was reviewed, according to Brazilian media reports citing police sources.
Ramagem’s allies credited Washington for his release. “Thank you, President Trump and everyone in the administration,” Figueiredo wrote on X. Eduardo Bolsonaro, another son of the former president, thanked Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Sóstenes Cavalcante, a leader of Bolsonaro’s party in Brazil’s Congress, said Rubio had helped speed up the release, which he said would otherwise have taken at least two weeks.
RAMAGEM IS FREE AND BACK HOME!
My deepest thanks go to Donald Trump @realDonaldTrump and @SecRubio for their sensitivity and attention in addressing the case of this true national hero, who, even under persecution, has never wavered.
Alexandre Ramagem deserves asylum in the land of freedom, alongside his courageous wife – tireless in fighting for his liberty – and their beautiful daughters.
— Eduardo Bolsonaro🇧🇷 (@BolsonaroSP) April 15, 2026
Ramagem himself suggested he had U.S. government support. In November, after the publication of photos showing him in Miami, Brazil’s Supreme Court had ordered his arrest. The next day, in a livestreamed interview, Ramagem said he was safe in the United States “with the consent and knowledge of the American government.”
On April 20, five days after Ramagem’s release from immigration custody, the State Department asked Marcelo Ivo de Carvalho, the Brazilian Federal Police liaison officer posted in Miami to work with ICE, to leave the country. “No foreigner gets to game our immigration system to both circumvent formal extradition requests and extend political witch hunts into U.S. territory,” the department’s Bureau of Western Hemisphere Affairs wrote on X.
The government in Brasília retaliated and suspended the duties of a U.S. immigration agent posted there, who then left the country on April 22. In a statement, the Foreign Ministry said the U.S. had failed to consult Brazil first, as the two countries’ agreement on police liaisons requires, and ignored “good diplomatic practice of dialogue between friendly nations, such as Brazil and the United States, over more than 200 years of relations.”
Neither the State Department nor the White House responded to multiple requests for comment. In its statement, DHS did not explain why Ramagem was released, saying only that he was freed “pending the outcome of his removal proceedings” and “will receive due process.” It added that a pending application “does NOT confer any type of legal status in the United States” and that “illegal aliens are not welcome in our country.”
The handling of Ramagem’s case stands out among those of hundreds of thousands of asylum seekers in the United States.
Since Trump returned to office, immigration judges have ordered more than 440,000 asylum seekers removed, more than in the previous eight years combined, according to a recent Washington Post analysis. Release from ICE detention has also become the exception. By late 2025, ICE was deporting more than 14 people directly from detention for every one it released to await a hearing, according to the American Immigration Council, an advocacy group that analyzed ICE data. In December, the administration paused decisions on all asylum applications pending with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.
Ramagem’s release was not just an immigration matter. A career federal police officer, he headed Bolsonaro’s security when Bolsonaro was president-elect. He was then appointed head of Brazil’s intelligence agency, becoming part of the inner circle of a president whose prosecution the Trump administration has criticized. In July 2025, Trump imposed 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, calling Bolsonaro’s trial a “witch hunt,” and his administration sanctioned Alexandre de Moraes, the Supreme Court justice who oversees the coup case against Bolsonaro and Ramagem. A White House executive order that month accused Brazilian officials of politically persecuting the former president.
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a leftist who defeated Bolsonaro in the 2022 election, has accused Washington of meddling in Brazil’s affairs. Last month, Lula used his speech at the United Nations General Assembly to warn against foreign interference in the upcoming election there.
Investigation in Brazil
According to the confidential records, Federal Police investigators in Brazil believe De Mello’s November plea for his condo to expel Ramagem was drafted as a “precaution,” after the press linked the family’s apartment to Ramagem’s escape.
But the note didn’t spare the De Mello family. In December, on orders from Brazil’s Supreme Court, the Federal Police arrested Rodrigo’s son Celso, on suspicion of helping Ramagem flee. In a statement, the family said Celso is innocent. Moraes also ordered Rodrigo’s arrest, and Rodrigo remains a fugitive. (This week, another Supreme Court justice rejected Rodrigo’s request to overturn the order, the Brazilian news site Amado Mundo reported.)
Ramagem has denied that Celso helped him. In an Instagram post after the ICE arrest, he said he didn’t know “a certain” Priscila or Celso. “They arrested a young man, a kid, who only met me when I was already in the U.S.,” he said. “In fact, this young man is American.”
Celso now wears an ankle monitor while the investigation, which is under seal, continues.
The confidential records show the De Mello family’s alleged involvement began early. Since June 2025, Ramagem, then a member of Brazil’s Congress, had been barred by court order from leaving Brazil and was required to surrender all his passports while on trial. He was charged with using the country’s intelligence agency to help Bolsonaro discredit its voting system. (Ramagem’s defense told the Supreme Court that the evidence against him was “extremely timid.”)
On Sept. 9, while on medical leave from Congress, he crossed from the northern town of Bonfim into Lethem, Guyana. A photo found on the phone of Priscila Freitas de Mello, then Rodrigo’s wife, shows him there the next day, smiling, at what appears to be an immigration post in Guyana. Brazilian Federal Police investigators say Rodrigo took the picture, according to the records.
On Sept. 11, as Brazil’s Supreme Court convicted him, Ramagem flew to the United States on a diplomatic passport that he had kept.
On Sept. 15, Celso messaged Priscila asking for a utility bill in his father’s name so Ramagem could apply for a Florida driver’s license, the confidential records show.
“Hi Pri, good evening,” Celso wrote to his stepmother. “Can you send me a bill for your apartment in my dad’s name? Water, electricity, phone, internet… We’re going to try to get Alexandre’s driver’s license tomorrow at the DMV.” He had drafted a lease, Celso wrote, to make it look as if Ramagem “had rented the room.”
“Let me see,” Priscila replied.
Two days later, Priscila wrote to the condominium’s management asking for a new gate access card. “Since we are traveling, we won’t be able to pick it up,” she said. “Therefore, we authorize a friend of ours, Alexandre Rodrigues Ramagem, to collect the new card on our behalf.” Celso also contested parking fines Ramagem had run up at the complex, the records show.
On Nov. 17, Ramagem’s spouse and daughters joined him in the apartment, according to the wife’s social media posts.
Investigators in Brazil allege in the confidential records that the De Mello family played a key role in keeping Ramagem hidden, both by housing him and by helping him deceive U.S. authorities with false documents. It is unclear whether a driver’s license was ultimately issued.
Rodrigo, the De Mello patriarch, has denied helping Ramagem escape. In November, he called the escape story a “fallacious narrative” meant to persecute the right, and said that when Ramagem was with him, he faced no conviction or legal impediment to leaving Brazil. The two men appeared together publicly in March 2025, when Rodrigo posted a photo of Ramagem’s visit to Boa Vista, De Mello’s longtime base in the state of Roraima, near the Guyana border, calling him “a great ally” of Bolsonaro.
Gold and politics
The De Mellos’ ties to Florida go back decades.
Rodrigo de Mello registered to vote in Florida in 1997, according to voter records from the Miami-Dade Department of Elections obtained by ICIJ, an action that requires attesting to U.S. citizenship. Celso is a U.S. citizen and a registered Florida voter.
Public records link Rodrigo, Celso and Celso’s mother to several companies registered in Florida, including a yacht-charter business and a freight company tied to the Sole Mia apartment where the family hosted Ramagem. Rodrigo and Celso’s mother also owned a home in Boca Raton.
Known in Brazil as Rodrigo Cataratas, De Mello ran what Brazilian federal prosecutors describe as a criminal organization mining illegally in the Yanomami Indigenous territory, a vast stretch of rainforest along the Venezuelan border. In January 2023, Brazil’s government declared a public health emergency in the territory, citing malnutrition and disease among the Yanomami and mercury contamination linked to illegal mining.
In February, a federal court in Roraima sentenced Rodrigo to 16 years and 7 months in prison for leading the enterprise, which prosecutors say extracted gold and cassiterite, a tin ore used in electronics, from the territory with the support of a fleet of helicopters. Celso was sentenced to eight years for managing the operation’s finances and logistics. Both remain free pending appeal.
Rodrigo has made no secret of his politics. His Instagram profile picture shows him alongside Jair Bolsonaro, with the words “anistia já,” or “amnesty now.” In 2020, the Bolsonaro government sent Congress a bill to allow mining on Indigenous lands. His administration also reportedly had a poor track record of acting on complaints about deforestation tied to illegal mining.
Rodrigo has also sought public office himself. He ran unsuccessfully for Congress in 2022 with Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party, and, before his conviction, he announced a run for the Senate with the right-wing Democratic Renewal Party. In October 2023, weeks after a federal court made him a defendant for the fifth time in cases tied to the Yanomami territory, he announced he was relocating to Guyana, where he opened a gold-mining company, according to Brazilian media.
Pardon promises
From Florida, the Bolsonaro camp has kept fighting for power in Brazil. Eduardo Bolsonaro, who moved to the United States in 2025, lobbied the Trump administration to pressure Brazilian authorities over his father’s prosecution. Washington later sanctioned Moraes, the Supreme Court judge in charge of the criminal trial against Bolsonaro, and imposed tariffs on Brazilian goods, both measures Eduardo had publicly sought.
Brazilian prosecutors argued that Eduardo’s campaign amounted to coercion, saying he had used his political position to pressure the justices and officials handling his father’s case. This month, the Supreme Court ordered his arrest to serve a sentence of four years and two months, which is unlikely to happen as long as he remains in the United States.
Earlier this month, Ramagem’s wife, Rebeca, ran for Congress in Rio de Janeiro, the state her husband represented as a lawmaker, saying she was running in his place. She campaigned without leaving Florida. Her campaign workers carried life-size cardboard cutouts of her and her husband through the streets of Rio, according to newspaper Metrópoles. The cutouts popped up at the launch of Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidential campaign on Copacabana beach, where Flavio’s wife, Fernanda Bolsonaro, posed with them. At the event, Flávio displayed a T-shirt that read “Bring the Ramagem family back, do justice!”
Rebeca Ramagem received 1.5 million reais, about $275,000, in public party funds for her campaign, Agência Pública found. She lost the election on Oct. 4.
On Oct. 25, Brazilians will choose between Flávio Bolsonaro and Lula. Flávio, who won the first round and holds a narrow lead in the polls, has promised a “broad, general and unrestricted” amnesty for his father and others convicted in the coup plot.
While Brazil’s extradition request awaits a response from the U.S., Ramagem lives in a lakefront house in Orlando, about half an hour from Disney World, and co-hosts a YouTube show with a pro-Bolsonaro blogger who is also wanted in Brazil.
“Of course, I wasn’t going to stay in Brazil,” Ramagem said in a livestream, adding that he didn’t want his daughters to see him arrested. “I don’t know how long it will take,” he said, “but we’re going to turn Brazil around.”
Natalia Viana and Ethel Rudnitzki from Agência Pública, and Gerardo Reyes from N+ Univision Investiga contributed to this report.

Combatting online scams in the age of AI

One in four Europeans has fallen victim to an online scam, from identity fraud to fake romances. The rise of artificial intelligence is ushering in new risks. Minh Nguyen, Chief Product Officer at security solutions provider Entrust, says both online platforms and governments can play a role in protecting consumers and businesses.
"The last couple of years have been fascinating in terms of seeing the evolution of the fraud landscape, and it ultimately boils down to how we create trust," Nguyen says. "We've seen the rise of deepfakes and AI, and it's much easier now for fraudsters to take your voice, to take images that are publicly available on social media, and try and recreate your identity, to impersonate you, in an attempt to access, for example, your bank account."
He believes the introduction of an EU digital wallet is a first step towards protecting data. "The EU have been one of the leaders globally in both protecting consumer and citizens' data, but also ensuring that we can access services and products online in a secure way."
Nguyen says that despite its risks, artificial intelligence can also help build countermeasures to new types of fraud. "We are also developing solutions that are better at combatting AI and deepfakes, that are able to bring multiple layers of fraud detection together, in detecting things like organised crime, so spotting patterns in fraud rings when they tend to use similar types of devices, or IP or time zones."
"I always check the type of links that are being sent to me – so if they redirect you out of the platform, it's usually not a good sign (...) If there's any doubt, it's better to err on the side of caution. You can always contact a platform's support service."

Denmark to purchase long-range missiles amid growing Russian threat - media
Kyiv • UNN
Denmark will acquire Joint Strike and Anthem long-range missiles to strengthen offensive capabilities and deter Russia. The deal includes weapons for F-35s.
Denmark plans to spend billions of kroner on high-precision, long-range missiles for its armed forces, including weapons for its F-35 fighter jets, fulfilling a promise to add offensive capabilities as the Scandinavian country strengthens its defenses against Russia. UNN writes about this, citing Bloomberg.
Details
The government in Copenhagen will purchase missiles from two suppliers, according to sources familiar with the deal. The package includes Joint Strike missiles manufactured by Norway's Kongsberg Gruppen ASA, as well as Anthem missiles from Covenant, which are produced in Germany, the sources said.
The German government is also negotiating the details of a procurement contract with Covenant, according to the sources.
TV2 reported on the deal earlier and said that Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus would brief the press later on Thursday. His ministry declined to comment. Spokespeople for Covenant and Kongsberg also declined to comment.
Denmark's acquisition comes after last year's decision to add longer-range missiles and drones to the country's arsenal, a move that Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called at the time a "paradigm shift" for a country that had focused on defensive weapons.
The country's government said at the time that the new systems would enable Denmark not only to counter air threats but also to strike threats far from its territory. Frederiksen said the goal was to strengthen deterrence and avoid war, as Russia has adopted an increasingly aggressive stance toward Europe.
Denmark sharply increased military spending after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine changed Europe's security environment, investing in everything from air defenses and fighter jets to drones and ammunition.

Outposts, violence, impunity: The anatomy of Israeli settler land grabs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:33:27 UTC
22:33:27 KST

Outposts, violence, impunity: The anatomy of Israeli settler land grabs
With government backing and little accountability, an ominous pattern casts a shadow over the Palestinian olive harvest.
Beita, occupied West Bank – Olive harvest season is traditionally a time when Palestinian families gather in their groves, pick olives and cook over open fires.
But when Musa Bani Shamsa and his 17-year-old son, who requested anonymity, arrived at his land in Beita, southeast of Nablus, the groves were empty.
On the morning of October 14 after they arrived, a group of masked Israeli men surrounded them. They carried pistols, knives, pipes, sticks and a hammer, Shamsa told Al Jazeera. Only their eyes were visible.
“At one point, I would take the beating for my son, and at another, my son would take the beating for me,” he said. “I was afraid they would kill him, kill him dead, because this has happened a lot.”
He lifted his shirt to show his bruises and stab wounds that were still healing. The beating lasted at least 20 minutes until he and his son were left lying on the ground. Shamsa was bleeding and lost consciousness.
“They thought we were dead, so they left us,” he said.
Shamsa said his attackers came from an Israeli outpost on the adjacent hill. Three days after the assault, his son was still unable to speak from the shock.
Settler violence across the occupied West Bank is rising sharply.
Since September 1, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs recorded more than 200 attacks on Palestinian farmers, more than the total number of similar assaults for the entire season last year.
With more beatings, arson attacks and livestock theft, “people are afraid,” Shamsa said, “in every sense of the word.”
He shares that fear but refuses to abandon his land.
Farmers have adapted their routines.
Harvesting begins earlier, at 5am. People block roads with stones to slow approaching settlers and take turns picking olives and keeping watch from rooftops with binoculars.
When settlers approach, families flee. Some return at night to harvest by phone light.
But these precautions offer little protection. In nearby villages, Shamsa said, settlers wait until farmers have finished picking before stealing their harvest and equipment.
“They come and take their olives and beat them, and they also take the mats they place under the olive trees,” he said. “Every time we give up a little, they take a little more. They do not want to give us safety.”
How an outpost takes root
At the centre of Israeli settlement expansion are outposts, which often begin with little more than a flag, a tent or a livestock pen on Palestinian land. Established near Palestinian villages, they can expand to control surrounding fields and grazing areas.
From his porch, Khalil Tafakji, a cartographer and an expert on borders and settlements, pointed to a hill where Israeli flags flew above Palestinian homes.
He described outposts as “the offspring of the mother settlements”.
Positioned between existing Israeli settlements, they help link them and extend Israeli control “over the largest possible area of land with the smallest number of residents”, Tafakji told Al Jazeera.
Under international law, all Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal. Outposts are also illegal under Israeli law until approved by the government, yet many receive state support even before formal recognition.
“The state is behind the settlers, supporting them financially, morally, politically, militarily and in every detail,” Tafakji said.
In 2024, settlers established 62 new outposts, backed by 75 million shekels ($20m) in government funding. In total, the government has channelled at least 100 million shekels ($30m) to outposts and farms for security equipment and infrastructure, including roads, vehicles, drones, cameras and electric gates, according to Peace Now, an Israeli NGO. The government also retroactively legalises outposts.
In March, Israel’s security cabinet approved 34 new settlements, including 10 existing outposts. Israeli media reported that the decision provides for water and electricity infrastructure before final planning approval.
In Beita, a similar pattern is unfolding. Israel authorised the Evyatar outpost, first established in 2013, as a settlement in 2024. Since then, residents said, three smaller outposts have emerged around it.
Rabee al-Sharafa, a Beita resident living on the edge of the village, said settlers at first draw power from lines near the village before infrastructure is formally extended to them.
“If there is a power line close to the village, they may simply steal from it, no problem,” he said. “If it is cut off from them, they have no problem. The electricity company comes and extends it to them.”
As the number of outposts rises, so too do the threats of violence and force to remove Palestinian families from their land.
“The policy they follow is a policy of slow surrender,” al-Sharafa said of the settlers.
In March, 10 masked men armed with sticks, machetes and axes attacked a family and threatened to kill its members if they did not leave, he said. The family fled. Another home was emptied in June, and since early October, settlers have targeted a third, cutting off its electricity and water.
“We compare it to a string of prayer beads that comes apart,” al-Sharafa said.
No protection, no recourse
Palestinians said they have nowhere to turn.
The Israeli army protects the settlers, and Palestinians are rarely able to get recourse through the legal system .
When residents try to defend their homes, settlers “immediately bring the army against you”, al-Sharafa said. “Sometimes the army knows there is an attack but does not want to intervene until the attack is over.”
Al Jazeera has reached out to the Israeli military for comment but has yet to receive a response.
The law is also used to take the land itself.
Israel draws on a patchwork of Ottoman, British and Jordanian laws alongside its own military orders to seize Palestinian territory. Under an Ottoman-era law, land left uncultivated for several years can be claimed by the state. Israel uses this provision to declare areas “state land”, where Tafakji said many settlements have been established.
Other land is seized through military orders or expropriated for “public purposes”.
“They are confiscating our lands in order to establish another state and expel us. This is a process of uprooting and replacement,” Tafakji said.
Palestinians with formal title deeds have occasionally won in Israeli courts. But even then, “the military governor comes and turns it into a military zone,” Tafakji said.
In Beita, Shamsa fears that if violence forces farmers to abandon their olive groves, Israel could eventually claim them as state property.
He kept a tent on his land for about six years to enjoy time with friends and family, but settlers demolished it.
“If I abandon [the land] for a few years, they could cut down the trees and use that to say the land belongs to the state,” he said.
Meanwhile, criminal complaints rarely lead anywhere. Of the police investigations into settler violence monitored by the Israeli rights group Yesh Din from 2005 to 2023, 94 percent were closed without an indictment.
“Who are we supposed to complain to? Complain to the one oppressing you?” Shamsa asked.

Normalization of Russia-US ties underpins European development — senior diplomat

ISTANBUL, October 22. /TASS/. Normal relations between Moscow and Washington are, contrary to what the West’s current ruling elites believe, a fundamental prerequisite for Europe’s peaceful development, as only with security and predictability between Russia and the US can Europeans become an independent pole of power, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko said, addressing the Verona Eurasian Economic Forum.
"Strange as it may seem, the West’s current ruling elite views the prospect of better or healthier Russia-US ties as one of the key threats to its own security," the senior diplomat noted. "Even from the standpoint of formal logic and the history of the continent’s development, normal relations between the US and the USSR, between the US and Russia are a fundamental condition for Europe’s peaceful development and, I would like to add, for its prosperity in the multipolar world."
If Europe continues to live amid geopolitical tensions between the two great powers, its political, economic, military and other weight will decrease exponentially, Grushko said. "And only under conditions of security and predictability can Europeans fulfil their potential as an independent pole of power," he noted.

OPINION - Palestinian political prisoners in the shadow of a collapsing international human rights system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:31:47 UTC
22:31:47 KST

- Raed Mohammed Mahmood Amer is president of the Palestinian Prisoners Association.
Palestinian political prisoners held in Israeli occupation prisons continue to face a grave human rights crisis. Their suffering reflects not only the brutality of Israel’s prison system but also the devastating failure of the international community to protect fundamental human rights, uphold international law, and hold those responsible for violations accountable. Reports and testimonies detail a reality of severe abuse, torture, denial of medical care, and other forms of degrading and inhumane treatment. Over 100 Palestinian political prisoners have lost their lives due to these horrific policies since the onset of the genocide in the occupied Gaza Strip. These practices demand urgent international intervention, independent investigation, and concrete measures to end the suffering of Palestinian prisoners.
The treatment of Palestinian prisoners cannot be separated from the broader system of occupation, repression, and collective suffering imposed on the Palestinian people. Within this context, prisons have become a central concern in the struggle for dignity, freedom, and basic human rights. Accounts of rubber-coated bullets fired directly at prisoners inside their cells at point-blank range, the refusal to provide medical care, and delays or refusals in transferring seriously ill or injured prisoners to hospitals raise urgent questions about the protection of life and the responsibilities of the occupation authorities.
Particular concern surrounds the policies and public positions associated with Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, whose portfolio includes responsibility for the Israel Prison Service. Political leadership cannot be separated from the conditions under which prisoners are held. Authorities responsible for prison policy must be held accountable for the consequences of their decisions, directives, and practices. Any policy that facilitates abuse, strips prisoners of basic protections, obstructs access to essential medical care, or encourages degrading treatment must be challenged and brought under independent scrutiny.
The international legal framework is unequivocal in its rejection of torture and cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. The prohibition of torture is absolute. It cannot be justified by political considerations, security arguments, national interests, or the identity of the person subjected to abuse. International humanitarian law and international human rights law establish protections for people deprived of their liberty, including obligations concerning humane treatment, medical care, and the prevention of violence. These protections are not privileges granted at the discretion of occupying authorities; they are legal obligations that must be respected and enforced.
Yet the international response has failed to demonstrate the urgency, consistency, and determination that this crisis demands. Palestinian prisoners and their families, alongside Palestinian human rights organizations and civil society institutions, have repeatedly called for international intervention, effective monitoring, and meaningful pressure to end violations. Their demands are not requests for political favors. They are calls for the enforcement of fundamental rights and the protection of human lives.
The continued gap between international declarations and practical action exposes a profound crisis of credibility. Governments and international institutions frequently invoke human rights, the protection of women and children, the rule of law, and the dignity of every human being. These principles become meaningless when they are applied selectively, abandoned when politically inconvenient, or denied to Palestinians because of their national identity. The prohibition of torture cannot be defended in one part of the world while the suffering of prisoners elsewhere is met with silence, delay, or diplomatic indifference.
Silence in the face of credible reports of grave abuse is not an acceptable substitute for responsibility. Nor can statements of concern, without sustained action and measurable outcomes, constitute an adequate response. Where institutions possess the authority to act, they must use it. Where governments have the capacity to exert diplomatic or other lawful pressure, they must explain why that capacity is not being used effectively.
The failure to act also raises fundamental questions about the independence, consistency, and effectiveness of international human rights organizations and mechanisms. Double standards undermine the legitimacy of the international human rights system and weaken the principles it claims to defend. Selective concern encourages impunity, deepens the suffering of victims, and sends a dangerous message that violations can continue when the victims belong to a politically marginalized or occupied population. No credible human rights system can tolerate such a distinction.
The international community must therefore take immediate, concrete, and verifiable action. It must demand independent access to detention facilities, effective monitoring of prison conditions, protection against torture and prompt, and adequate medical care for every injured or ill prisoner. It must insist on transparent investigations into deaths, serious injuries, and other grave violations. Evidence must be preserved, witnesses protected, and investigations conducted independently of those who may bear responsibility. Where sufficient evidence establishes individual criminal responsibility, the appropriate legal mechanisms must be pursued in accordance with international law.
International organizations, governments, human rights bodies, and humanitarian institutions must also intensify their efforts to protect Palestinian women and men in detention, secure access to legal representation and family contact as provided by applicable law, and challenge practices that violate international standards. Accountability must extend beyond individual perpetrators to include, where the evidence and law warrant it, those who ordered, enabled, facilitated, or knowingly failed to prevent serious violations.
The demand is clear: Palestinian prisoners must not be abandoned to a system in which their suffering is ignored and their rights are treated as expendable. Their lives are not bargaining chips. Their dignity is not conditional. Their protection is not a matter of political convenience. The protection of Palestinian prisoners is an urgent legal, moral, and humanitarian responsibility. Every day of inaction leads to more deaths of Palestinian prisoners and further erodes confidence in the international institutions entrusted with defending human dignity.
Justice cannot be selective. Human rights cannot depend on nationality. Palestinian prisoners must never be treated as though their lives matter less than those of any other human being. The international community must act decisively to protect them, end abuses, and ensure that no authority is permitted to stand above the law.
*Opinions expressed in this article are the author's own and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Anadolu.

Two Tel Aviv luxury hotels rank among Middle East's best in international travelers' poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:31:42 UTC
22:31:42 KST

The David Kempinski Hotel in central Tel Aviv ranked 11th on Condé Nast Traveler’s recently published list of the 20 best hotels in the Middle East, first among Israeli hotels.
Condé Nast Traveler magazine published the results of its 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards on Oct. 6, ranking the David Kempinski 11th among Middle Eastern hotels with a score of 95.02.
The rise comes from reviews by approximately 800,000 travelers from around the world, placing the hotel four spots higher than last year.
That ranking comes as foreign tourism to Israel remains down from last year. Israel recorded 788,500 international tourist arrivals from January through September 2026, a 15% drop from 927,800 in the same period of 2025, according to the Central Bureau of Statistics.
Condé Nast Traveler’s Readers’ Choice Awards are highly respected and influential in the travel industry. They are based on the opinions of about 800,000 travelers worldwide, who rated hotels on service, location, design, amenities, food, and overall hospitality experience.
“The fact that the hotel has moved up four spots compared to last year – just five years after its opening – attests to the team’s ongoing commitment to providing a hospitality experience of the highest caliber,” said Guy Kelman, general manager of the David Kempinski.
Two Tel Aviv hotels sit back to back in regional top 12
The Norman Hotel in Tel Aviv now sits just behind the David Kempinski Hotel in the regional top 12, ranking 12th with a score of 94.48.
“We are proud to once again be recognized in the Condé Nast Traveler Readers’ Choice Awards, which reflect our guests’ satisfaction and the trust they place in us,” said Kelman.
“This recognition also inspires us to continue creating personalized experiences for our guests that reflect Tel Aviv’s unique character.”
Gulf hotels dominate the top of the list
Most of the hotels on the list are located in the Gulf states, primarily Dubai, Abu Dhabi, and Qatar. First place went to Dorchester Collection’s Lana Hotel in Dubai, scoring 99.68, and second place to the Rosewood Abu Dhabi with a score of 99.19.
“David Kempinski’s design is meticulous down to the smallest details—from the guest rooms to the Horizon Lounge—making even seasoned travelers feel as though they’ve never experienced hospitality like this before,” one Condé Nast Traveler magazine reader wrote.
‘Award-winning’ amenities
The 250-room-and-suite hotel occupies 34 stories in a seaside skyscraper built by Feigin Architects, with interior design by Ara Design. It is located on Yarkon Street along the Mediterranean Sea promenade, adjacent to Tel Aviv Beach and Trumpeldor Beach.
The hotel’s culinary offerings include ‘Katzir’, a kosher chef’s restaurant led by chef Daniel Raymond, and an ‘award-winning’ breakfast. It also offers the OKOA Spa, two infinity pools, and wellness and fitness facilities.
Cloud, a seasonal rooftop bar, sits on the hotel's rooftop and offers panoramic views of Tel Aviv and the sea, along with DJ sets and an Asian-inspired menu. The hotel’s main suite, the David Penthouse, spans three floors and includes a private pool and a gym.
Since its opening in early 2022, the hotel has won a string of international awards, including the title of “Best New Hotel in the World” from Luxury Travel Advisor and inclusion in that magazine’s list of the 14 best breakfasts in the world.
“A luxurious, impeccable, and service-oriented experience unlike any other in Tel Aviv. The views from the rooms are breathtaking, the service is unobtrusive, and the food is top-notch,” a review said in Condé Nast Traveler magazine.
Established 125 years ago, Kempinski Hotels is Europe’s oldest luxury hotel group, with 80 locations around the world. Its Tel Aviv property is the first in Israel.
Zev Stub contributed to this report.

Saudi Aramco tells staff to evacuate Dhahran as clashes with Yemen's Houthis continue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:31:37 UTC
22:31:37 KST

Saudi state oil company Aramco 2223.SE has told staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran on the Gulf, six people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters on Thursday, as fighting between the world's largest crude exporter and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis intensifies.
Clashes between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognized government have raged since the group pushed towards Bab el-Mandeb, a shipping chokepoint at the Red Sea's mouth.
The instruction to staff to evacuate the building and work remotely follows a wave of Houthi attacks on the kingdom, targeting the company and Saudi airports. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment on what would be the first evacuation since the start of the Iran war.
It was unclear what the reason for the evacuation was.
The kingdom's benchmark index.TASI dropped 2.5% on Thursday following the Aramco news, according to LSEG data. Oil prices rose to their highest since May on Thursday on concern over an escalation of the Middle East conflict and its impact on crude oil supplies from the world's key exporting region.
Houthis target Aramco facility in Yanbu
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a televised speech that the group had launched attacks on Aramco facilities in the Red Sea city of Yanbu and the Saudi defense ministry in the capital Riyadh. Saudi authorities did not confirm the attack.
The Saudi-led coalition said on Thursday it had intercepted drones over Riyadh and Islam's holy city of Medina, which is near Yanbu.
The renewed fighting between Saudi Arabia and Houthi militias in recent weeks ended a 2022 UN-brokered truce, which had largely halted cross-border attacks, and opened another front in the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The Houthis caused extensive damage to Aramco's headquarters earlier this month when they struck the building, with fire spreading across several floors.
Saudi Arabia has responded to Houthi attacks with a wave of strikes on missile launcher sites, vowing to protect the kingdom, and says it has intercepted many ballistic missiles fired by the group.
Saree said that Saudi attacks on Yemen have killed and wounded 562 people since mid July, when the Houthis imposed a naval blockade on the kingdom, which then drew a warning from the Saudi-led coalition that it would respond "firmly."
Separately, he said earlier on Thursday that the group is rescuing a boat carrying 14 Indians that was attacked off Jabal Zuqar island near the strait, one of the territories the group seized in an advance in September.
Saree blamed the attack on Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.
Houthis strike King Fahd airport
A Houthi attack on King Fahd International Airport in Saudi Arabia's eastern oil hub of Dammam near Dhahran on Wednesday evening killed two people, a Saudi citizen and an Indian national, and wounded eight others.
Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation said on Thursday that operations at the airport had resumed and air traffic had returned to normal.
The Houthis had warned airlines this month against using Saudi airspace as they have repeatedly targeted Saudi airports, including Riyadh's international airport and the southern airport of Abha.
Brent crude futures LCOc1 climbed $3.06, or 2.81%, to $111.88 a barrel by 1104 GMT on Thursday. They hit $112.55 a barrel earlier in the session, the highest since May 18.

Kfar Saba mayor, wife suspected of fraud released to house arrest, forbidden to communicate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:31:30 UTC
22:31:30 KST

A court in central Israel ordered the release of Kfar Saba Mayor Rafi Saar and his wife, Meital, from police custody to house arrest on Thursday as police continue investigating their alleged involvement in a bribery scheme.
Under the ruling by the Rishon Lezion Magistrate's Court, the couple is prohibited from speaking to each other until November 1, while Saar is barred from entering municipal facilities until November 15.
Police had sought stricter restrictions, arguing that contact between the couple could interfere with the ongoing investigation. Investigators requested that the two be prohibited from meeting for 60 days, that Saar be barred from municipal facilities for the same period, and that Meital remain under house arrest for 14 days. Judge Yuval Keidar granted only part of the request.
Meital Saar will remain under full house arrest until November 1 and is prohibited from contacting anyone involved in the case during that period. Her release is conditional on a NIS 50,000 cash deposit, plus a personal guarantee and a NIS 50,000 guarantee from a third party. Similar conditions were imposed on Rafi Saar, along with the additional restrictions on entering municipal facilities.
Police suspect mayor's wife managed bribery scheme
The police request to keep the couple apart stems from investigators' suspicions about their respective roles in the alleged bribery scheme.
Police suspect that Meital managed the operation, using her position to advance the interests of businesspeople in exchange for money. Investigators allege that Saar knew about the payments and used his authority as mayor to act on his wife's demands.
During the hearing, Chief Inspector Ilan Yanko, representing the police, argued that concerns about obstruction of the investigation were supported by concrete evidence presented to the court.
The defense, however, sought to ease the restrictions. Saar's attorney, Micha Fetman, opposed the police request to keep the mayor away from municipal facilities for two months, challenging investigators: "If in 12 days you haven't found any evidence that he received money, then what is this about now?"
Meital's attorney, Haya Zion Zakai, objected to the police demand for a NIS 100,000 cash deposit, arguing that the amount was unreasonable. She also sought to shorten the house arrest period. The court ultimately set the cash deposit at NIS 50,000, half of the amount the police requested.
Investigation focuses on municipal contracts and development projects
The investigation centers on suspected corruption involving several areas of municipal activity, including permits for mobile food kiosks, urban renewal projects in the Yoseftal neighborhood, and school construction and renovation work during summer vacations.
Investigators are examining whether bribes were paid to advance business interests and influence municipal bidding processes, including those handled through the city's economic development company. Police suspect that the payments were made in cash to conceal evidence of the alleged scheme.
Saar is suspected of accepting bribes, fraud and breach of trust, conspiracy to commit a felony, money laundering, and tax offenses. His wife is suspected of bribery offenses, receiving improper benefits, conspiracy to commit a felony, and related offenses.
The National Fraud Investigation Unit of Lahav 433, a division of the Israel Police responsible for investigating serious fraud and corruption, is conducting the investigation.
Meanwhile, attorneys representing other suspects in the case have accused police of seeking to keep their clients in custody to pressure them into becoming state witnesses.

UK government reports disruption to 32 services amid cybersecurity issue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:30:49 UTC
22:30:49 KST

Aysu Bicer
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Thirty-two UK government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable amid an ongoing cybersecurity issue involving the PHP programming language, a minister told the House of Lords on Thursday.
Baroness Lloyd of Effra, parliamentary under-secretary of state for the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, said the disruption "largely resulted" from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while updates and security mitigations are applied.
She said the government was working closely with agencies to "restore the services safely and securely."
"The government acted proactively ahead of public disclosure," said Lloyd, adding that agencies had been alerted to the vulnerability and advised to identify potentially affected systems, assess their exposure and prepare to implement security updates and mitigations.
Lloyd said the National Cyber Security Centre had made "50,000 proactive notifications to the wider economy to advise business and other organizations on what actions they should take."
"The government continues to monitor the situation closely and work with departments to maintain the security resilience and availability of public services," she added.
Downing Street said that "no large public-facing critical services are being affected" while acknowledging that some "limited services may temporarily be offline" as security work continues.
"This does not mean they were hacked," it added.
The vulnerability in PHP, a programming language widely used to develop websites, has prompted organizations around the world to take action to secure potentially affected systems.
Internet infrastructure platform Cloudflare said on US social media company X that it had observed "millions" of hacking attempts on its network. There was no evidence, however, that the attempts had been successful.
