A superconducting ‘brain’ chip races to keep up with fusion’s unruly plasma
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:57:47 UTC
20:57:47 KST

Artificial intelligence has crept into nearly every industry, and the companies building its hardware keep hunting for harder domains to flex in. The latest area runs particularly hot: the plasma inside a fusion reactor.
On Monday Brookhaven National Laboratory debuted a superconducting chip designed to help monitor fusion plasma in real time. The lab developed it with other U.S. Department of Energy facilities and the AI hardware start-up Great Sky.
Before fusion powers anything, its machines must be able to control misbehaving plasma. The chip’s makers hope their hardware can operate quickly enough to keep pace with changes in the plasma and help control them.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Such chips are destined for tokamaks, the large, doughnut-shaped machines that use magnets to hold the fusion plasma in place and that sit at the heart of many proposed fusion power plants. The extremely hot plasma fuel inside is temperamental. When it acts unexpectedly, it can cause a disruption, a sudden collapse that sheds its energy and can harm the device. “Disruptions are something that are kind of existential for tokamaks,” says Michael Churchill, a research scientist at the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, who worked on the project. “If we can’t figure out how to control disruptions, then we won’t have an operating tokamak.”
Trouble can come on fast, but analyzing the plasma live takes lots of data, and processing these can easily bog down typical computers. Neuromorphic AI systems, which mimic the structure of the human brain to crunch huge amounts of data in parallel, could keep up. Great Sky builds its version out of superconducting circuits—a cousin of the hardware used inside some quantum computers—which is meant to let the company run its specialized AI right on the chip at the speed the job demands.
The chip hasn’t been wired to a working tokamak yet. Instead the team replayed data recorded at the DIII-D tokamak in San Diego, Calif., at its original clip of a million samples per second, and the chip kept up while running algorithms meant to flag anomalies and predict disruptions. The AI model on the chip is much smaller than, say, today’s large language models, and the team is still writing up its results for publication. “All of this is very demonstration-stage right now,” Churchill admits.
It’s unclear whether this will make nuclear fusion more reliable and safe or remain a show of chip power. Tokamaks already run without chips like this one, and their control mechanisms can’t react to problems with the plasma as fast as the new chip is meant to detect them. “I’m personally more excited about the use of AI in the area of materials discovery,” says Carlos Paz-Soldan, an associate professor of applied physics at Columbia University.
Shinjae Yoo, who chairs Brookhaven’s AI department and led the project, isn’t pinning the chip’s future on fusion alone, either. He wants to test it out in places where a traditional data center won’t fit. “I see immediate benefit in edge computing because it’s operating at the gigahertz” speed, Yoo says. “It has a memory already integrated.”
First, though, the team intends to build a successor chip with a neural network that will be 10 times larger. and it plans to debut that chip at Brookhaven early next year and install at DIII-D sometime after. It’s then that Great Sky’s hardware could finally face a fusion plasma with no hard drive in between.

Thieving Israeli settlers hit Palestinian olive harvest hard in W. Bank
Unknown

2026-10-22

Spike in violence and widespread theft by terrorist settlers have plagued the West Bank olive harvest this year, a trend Palestinian residents, Israeli human rights groups and the U.N. say follows decades of intimidation.
Brought to tears as he recalled Israeli settlers hitting his cherished olive trees with sticks and taking off with the olives, Palestinian Ahmed Salem said he feared being attacked if he tried to intervene.
The Jewish settlers dumped Salem's olives into sacks and then drove them to a nearby Israeli settler outpost to be pressed into olive oil, the 50-year-old Palestinian told Reuters of the incident around two weeks ago near his village Lubban al-Gharbi.
"How would you feel if something that belonged to you was being violated and you could do nothing about it?" he asked.
The couple living in the outpost, whose olive press settlers have urged Israelis to use for West Bank olives, declined multiple Reuters requests for comment, while the Yesha Council, which oversees Israeli settlements in the West Bank, did not immediately respond.
The attacks have accelerated ahead of an Israeli election next week that opinion polls show Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his pro-settler coalition could lose to opponents who have taken a more critical stance against settler violence.
The olive harvest starts with the onset of cooler weather, allowing Palestinian families to gather in the lush, terraced groves that they have groomed for generations.
"My 6-year-old son remembers going there with me, eating there, making tea there," Salem said.
With the establishment of hundreds of small settler outposts under Netanyahu's government since 2022, the military has increasingly restricted Palestinian access to areas nearby, including many olive groves.
"This creates a situation where Palestinians, in many of the cases, many of the lands, especially in proximity to settlements and outposts, cannot enter the land and harvest the trees," said Ziv Stahl, executive director of Israeli rights group Yesh Din.
"But settlers can come and go freely and that's what they do."
Even when Palestinians can access their trees, it is not without risk. Yesh Din on Wednesday reported 125 physical attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters over the 24 days since the season began and 168 incidents of crop theft, with Israeli military forces present in at least a quarter of cases.
An Israeli military official said it takes acts of violence, criminal activity and attempts to undermine security very seriously. The official did not refer to settlers or comment on the reports of olive theft in the presence of the Israeli military, which has separately uprooted trees with excavators, citing what it said was a need to prevent Palestinian attacks.
The removal of Palestinians' olives has met with widely differing responses from Israeli rabbis.
"I call it theft. From my perspective, I define it as theft or robbery and it is forbidden," said Zev Weitman, the rabbi for the Alon Shvut settlement south of Bethlehem.
Prominent Orthodox rabbi Dov Lior said settlers should harvest across the West Bank, asserting in an open letter that Palestinians had no ownership rights to the land and that harvesting olives fulfilled "the commandment of conquering the land."
Hundreds of acres of the land around Salem's village, Lubban al-Gharbi, including olive groves, were fenced off and seized between 2023 and 2026 by Avichai Farm, an Israeli settler outpost built on a nearby hill.
Salem said villagers have seen settlers harvest olives from the seized land and take them to the outpost's olive press.
At the start of the olive harvest, settlers posted on social media calling on Israelis to harvest occupied West Bank olives and bring them to Avichai Farm's press.
"Both fine oil and strengthening the Jewish hold on the vast expanses of our land!," read a message on a settler Telegram group. "It's either us or our enemy!"
The press at Avichai Farm advertises "premium products produced by Avichai Farm" with olive oil at about $20 a bottle via a website run by the Farms Association, a settler group that Reuters has reported receives significant financial support from the Israeli government, which says the aim is to promote peace.
The Farms Association did not immediately respond to a request for comment and the couple who live on the farm with their children declined to be interviewed by a Reuters reporter who approached the area Sunday.
On a road leading to Avichai Farm, Reuters spoke to a man who declined to be identified and said he had driven from a settlement around 90 minutes away to press 14 bags of olives from trees he said he grew himself.
Lubban al-Gharbi villagers and other Palestinians who have lost land to settler expansion say the harvesting of olives from trees in groves seized from Palestinian land constitutes theft.
U.N. bodies and most countries deem Israel's settlements on land occupied in war illegal under international law regarding military occupations. Israel rejects this, viewing the territory as disputed rather than occupied.
During this year's olive harvest, Palestinian authorities say three Palestinians have been killed in daily settler terrorist attacks, which have also injured several journalists, European diplomats and a French mayor.
Stahl from the Yesh Din Israeli rights group said the violence was "part of a campaign of ethnic cleansing, paving the way for the annexation of the West Bank without its Palestinian population."
Israel, which has considered the idea of annexation, said it is investigating some of the incidents.
An Israeli government spokesperson said olives "picked by a Jew in the ancestral homeland of the Jewish people" did not constitute theft and that Jews owned and cultivated "millions of olive trees" in the area. No one should take the law into their own hands, the spokesperson added.
Palestinian farmer Samer Ben Shamsi said masked settlers attacked him on Oct. 9 in the Palestinian village of Beita near Nablus, then sped away in a pickup truck with his harvest of olives after he and other farmers fled.
"This year, they steal without fear because they have a state and a powerful force backing them," Ben Shamsi said, referring to the security forces.
Within the past year alone, settlers had shot him in the leg, beaten him and smashed his possessions, he said.
"We pay in blood for the olives."

What's behind Hamas's threat, and can it strike Israel? ‘The capabilities are there’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:56:02 UTC
20:56:02 KST

What is behind Hamas's latest threat to carry out another October 7-style attack against Israel, and does the terrorist organization still have the military capabilities to follow through? According to senior Israeli officials, the capabilities exist, although Hamas is no longer believed to be capable of launching an assault on the scale of the 2023 massacre. It could, however, attack military outposts, abduct soldiers or attempt to infiltrate Israeli communities.
The assessment follows ynet's revelation earlier Thursday that senior Hamas officials had delivered an unusually direct warning to Israel through U.N. humanitarian coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov, threatening renewed attacks inside Israel, in the West Bank and abroad. The warning has intensified concerns within Israel's security establishment that Hamas is preparing for another confrontation rather than merely seeking to exert political pressure.
According to assessments recently presented to the security cabinet, Hamas has stepped up preparations for renewed fighting, accumulating weapons and personnel and transferring military equipment into civilian areas. Israeli officials believe the organization assumes that Israel's ability to undertake major military operations is constrained by the October 27 Israeli election and the November 3 U.S. midterms, giving Hamas an opportunity to strengthen its position.
At a cabinet meeting earlier this month, Military Intelligence chief Maj. Gen. Shlomi Binder addressed the thousands of attackers who crossed into Israel on October 7, 2023. "Of the 6,000 who crossed the fence on October 7, 4,000 have been eliminated. Two thousand remain. We will get every last one of them," he said, according to the account of the meeting.
Senior officials say Hamas is deliberately buying time to manufacture additional weapons and recruit new fighters, while recognizing that its opportunity to do so may be narrowing. Against that backdrop, Israeli intelligence has identified several significant changes in the organization's behavior.
Weapons, visible gunmen and arms distributed to civilians
One of the most noticeable developments is Hamas's increasingly open presence above ground. Whereas its members previously tended to remain concealed or move around in civilian clothing, they are now more frequently seen wearing uniforms and openly exercising authority over Gaza's population.
Israeli officials also report that Hamas is transferring weapons from underground tunnels into civilian facilities, including hospitals and schools. According to the military, similar practices were identified during earlier stages of the war, when Israeli troops regularly discovered weapons in civilian buildings and populated areas.
Another change concerns Hamas's public statements. Since the Gaza agreement was announced, the organization had at times suggested that it would surrender its weapons and respect its obligations. That language has increasingly been replaced by more confrontational rhetoric, culminating in the threat reported Thursday.
Israeli officials say they have not encountered a warning of comparable force, boldness and directness from Hamas since the October 7 massacre.
There are also reports that Hamas has begun distributing weapons to civilians. Israeli officials suspect the move is intended to preserve part of the organization's arsenal ahead of any disarmament process, allowing it to hide weapons while claiming to have surrendered those in its possession.
The developments have reinforced an Israeli assessment that Hamas no longer believes the current agreement has a realistic chance of succeeding and is preparing for a possible return to fighting.
Officials also believe Hamas may not wait for Israel to initiate hostilities. Instead, once it concludes that Israel is about to receive a green light for renewed military operations, the organization could attempt to strike first.
Hamas stops playing along
Israeli officials also point to a widening gap between the international perception of Hamas and the picture emerging from Israeli intelligence assessments.
Since the Gaza agreement was announced, Hamas has benefited from the impression that it is prepared to relinquish its weapons and surrender political control of the territory. Israel, meanwhile, has increasingly been portrayed as the party obstructing implementation of President Donald Trump's Gaza plan.
Israeli officials believe Hamas has exploited its apparent willingness to cooperate with the American initiative to buy time and preserve its remaining military and political power.
The significance of the latest threat, they argue, is that Hamas may now be signaling that it is no longer prepared to maintain that appearance.
According to assessments by the IDF and Shin Bet, the central condition for advancing the Gaza plan, Hamas's disarmament, is not being fulfilled. Israeli officials say the organization continues to violate the understandings and has shown no genuine willingness to surrender its weapons.
Officials familiar with the intelligence acknowledge that there is no known date for renewed hostilities and no information about a finalized operational plan for an attack. However, they describe the assessment that Hamas will not voluntarily disarm as unequivocal.
That assessment has also been presented to Israel's political leadership. The military's position is that Israeli ground forces will eventually have to return to areas deep inside Gaza to dismantle Hamas's remaining military infrastructure, a task officials believe cannot be accomplished by an international force.
Israeli officials also anticipate that Hamas would attempt to manipulate any disarmament process. They believe the organization could surrender weapons that are defective or already known to Israeli intelligence, claim to have fulfilled its obligations and conceal a substantial portion of its remaining arsenal and personnel.
What Hamas has lost, and what it can still do
Despite the extensive damage inflicted on its military infrastructure, Hamas retains considerable manpower. Israeli estimates place the organization's armed wing at tens of thousands of members, with some assessments suggesting approximately 30,000, not dramatically different from its estimated strength before October 7.
An additional estimated 50,000 employees work in government ministries controlled by Hamas. The organization continues to dominate civilian administration in Gaza and has prevented the proposed technocratic government from beginning its work.
Recruitment also remains relatively easy. Israeli officials attribute this partly to years of indoctrination among young Gazans and partly to Hamas's ability to offer salaries higher than those available through most other employment opportunities in the territory.
The organization also retains members of its elite Nukhba force, which played a central role in the October 7 attack.
Nevertheless, cabinet ministers say Hamas's current fighters are generally less skilled and less thoroughly trained than their predecessors, while the weapons available to them are often of lower quality.
Much of their training is now theoretical because conducting practical exercises in open areas would expose them to Israeli strikes.
Hamas's command-and-control capabilities have suffered particularly severe damage. According to senior Israeli officials, some key positions have changed hands six or seven times since October 7, with each replacement generally possessing less experience and training than the person who preceded him.
Targeted Israeli strikes against Hamas commanders and fighters have continued during the ceasefire, further disrupting the organization's leadership structure.
Its rocket arsenal has also been severely degraded. Israeli assessments indicate that hundreds of rockets remain in Gaza, although many are not capable of reaching distant targets.
Officials believe Hamas has almost no ability to rebuild this capability and that its capacity to cause significant damage inside Israel through rocket fire is now extremely limited, if it exists at all.
There are, however, gaps in Israeli intelligence. The IDF has not identified every rocket-launching shaft or position remaining in the territory.
Another concern involves areas of Gaza where Israeli ground forces have not operated extensively. These include the humanitarian zone in Al-Mawasi, the central Gaza refugee camps of Al-Bureij, Al-Maghazi and Nuseirat, and parts of Gaza City.
Israeli officials believe Hamas retains weapons depots, manufacturing workshops and underground tunnels in those areas. The IDF also assesses that the organization has restored a substantial portion of its tunnel network in territory outside Israeli control.
Targeting these facilities presents additional difficulties because they are situated in densely populated areas where military operations could result in extensive civilian casualties.
In the West Bank, Hamas retains the capability to attempt terrorist attacks, although Israeli officials assess that the security situation is more tightly controlled because of intensive IDF and Shin Bet operations and continued security coordination with the Palestinian Authority.
Nevertheless, attempts to organize attacks cannot be ruled out.
The organization has also threatened to operate abroad, partly because carrying out attacks inside Gaza has become more difficult.
Israeli officials believe that, with no Israeli hostages remaining in Gaza, Hamas has lost a major bargaining chip. This may help explain the organization's renewed references to abducting soldiers.
According to the Israeli assessment, any Hamas attack, whether inside Israel or overseas, would also provide Israel with considerably greater freedom to launch military operations against the organization.
Beyond its military capabilities, Hamas's financial position is another important factor in assessing whether it can sustain a renewed confrontation.
Israeli security officials believe the organization's finances have improved in recent months through money transferred from outside Gaza and its control over humanitarian aid entering the territory.
Security sources identify Iran and Turkey as Hamas's principal sources of funding. According to those officials, much of the money arrives through digital currencies, which Hamas subsequently converts into cash to pay members of its military wing and civilian administrative structures.
Hamas also remains the dominant governing force in Gaza, according to Israeli assessments, with no significant local rival currently capable of challenging its authority.
That assessment persists despite the presence of armed clans and militias supported by Israel as potential alternatives to Hamas rule.
Israeli officials believe those groups have lost much of their influence as larger quantities of aid have entered areas controlled by Hamas, reinforcing doubts about whether a viable alternative government can be established through local Palestinian factions.
Meanwhile, meaningful reconstruction of Gaza has yet to begin because of insufficient funding. Neither the proposed technocratic administrative committee nor the international stabilization force is operating inside the territory.
COGAT's dilemma: Supplying Gaza without financing Hamas
As winter approaches, Israel is preparing to gradually restore coordination for commercial goods entering Gaza, following reports from Palestinian merchants that Hamas has canceled substantial payment demands previously imposed on traders.
The development prompted requests from merchants to resume the import coordination process, but Israeli officials remain concerned that Hamas could continue exploiting commercial activity to generate revenue and preserve its grip on the territory.
According to Israel's Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT), merchants reported that Hamas had withdrawn demands for approximately 10,000 shekels per truck entering Gaza, alongside requirements that goods be sold for cash and that the organization receive 30% of each truck's cargo value.
At a rate of approximately 600 trucks entering Gaza each day, a charge of 10,000 shekels per truck would theoretically generate 180 million shekels a month. That calculation illustrates the potential value of the mechanism rather than establishing how much Hamas actually collected.
COGAT has stressed that the merchants' reports do not independently confirm that Hamas has stopped collecting taxes or demanding payments.
The Israeli authority therefore intends to restore coordination gradually, giving priority to essential supplies ahead of winter while increasing oversight of the traders involved.
Under the arrangements, merchants will be required to make and receive payments exclusively through documented bank transfers. Any trader found to have transferred money to Hamas will lose authorization to operate under the import mechanism.
COGAT says the purpose is to prevent the organization from using commercial imports to strengthen its military and economic capabilities.
The financial stakes are substantial. Previous ynet reporting, based on Israeli security assessments, estimated that approximately 30,000 Hamas personnel across a range of military and administrative roles receive salaries averaging 3,000 shekels a month, creating an estimated monthly payroll of 90 million shekels.
Israeli officials believe Hamas imposed substantial taxes on Gaza merchants, including those receiving goods from outside the territory, partly to finance these payments and prevent the organization from disintegrating.
The question now is whether the reported cancellation of the organization's tax demands is genuine or whether Hamas has simply changed how it collects money from commercial activity.
The dispute over truck payments and cash transactions reflects a broader Israeli concern that Hamas can continue operating extensive financial and administrative networks even as Israel seeks to weaken its military and political control over Gaza.
As winter approaches, Israeli authorities face a dual challenge: allowing essential supplies to reach Gaza's civilian population while preventing Hamas from using the same commercial channels to generate revenue and rebuild its capabilities.
COGAT has emphasized that restoring coordination does not constitute confirmation that Hamas has stopped collecting payments. Officials say the tighter banking requirements and transaction monitoring are intended to reduce the possibility of the organization benefiting financially from incoming goods.
Another component of the Gaza reconstruction effort is also stalled. A company expected to begin clearing areas as part of a pilot project in Rafah has so far completed only a survey and mapping of the territory, with no further progress reported.
The unresolved question is how Israel can ensure that goods and resources entering Gaza reach their intended civilian recipients rather than reinforcing Hamas's control over the territory.
For Israeli security officials, that economic challenge is inseparable from the military threat. Their assessment is that Hamas has lost much of its conventional strength but retains substantial manpower, underground infrastructure, financial resources and the ability to organize smaller attacks.
The central concern is therefore not that Hamas can reproduce the October 7 massacre on the same scale. Israeli officials believe it cannot. It is that the organization, convinced the diplomatic process is approaching failure, may attempt to use the capabilities it still possesses before Israel moves to dismantle them.

France has recorded its first case of infection with the Shamonda virus.
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:55:49 EEST
20:55:49 KST

France has recorded its first case of infection with the Shamonda virus.
Kyiv • UNN
France has recorded the first human infection with the Shamonda virus; the patient died. Authorities said there is no threat to the population.
France has recorded its first case of a person infected with the Shamonda virus — the patient died, although medical officials assure that there is no threat to the population. BBC reports this, UNN writes.
The patient died, but the authorities stress that this was an exceptional case and that, in general, the virus does not pose a threat to people
The Shamonda virus is usually transmitted among animals through the bites of small blood-sucking insects. It has been circulating in Africa and Asia for several decades, and was first detected in Europe this summer.
A joint statement by France's ministries of health and agriculture said that the deceased patient had serious problems with their immune system, making this case exceptional.
Background information
The Shamonda virus is an orthobunyavirus spread through the bites of small blood-sucking insects, mainly biting midges. The virus's main hosts are livestock, in which it causes fever.
The virus circulated in Africa and Asia for decades, and was first detected in animals in Europe in the summer of 2026. It does not pose a mass threat to humans. The case in France was the first recorded instance of a human infection, and the fatal outcome was caused by the patient having severe immunodeficiency.

Czech KBP International Unveils Shahed-Like Drones: Piston TARON and Jet SABRE

Czech company KBP International unveiled the Shahed-like TARON and SABRE drones at the FUTURE FORCES FORUM military exhibition in Prague.
A Militarnyi correspondent reported this.
The company has been specializing in the development, production, and export of advanced solutions for the defence, aerospace, and security sectors for more than 30 years.
TARON is a piston-powered target drone with an endurance of up to 30 minutes and a range of 70 km. Its maximum flight altitude is 1,500 meters (5,000 feet).
Similar drones are used to train various air defence crews, including those operating surface-to-air missile systems, anti-aircraft artillery systems, and interceptor drones.
The SABRE is a multirole drone capable of carrying a payload of up to 30 kg over a range of up to 400 km at a speed of 400 km/h.
It is launched using the mobile SATA ground launcher developed by THREOD.

Europe gripped by protests, cost-of-living pressures spark fresh unrest in France and Italy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:53:27 UTC
20:53:27 KST

France and Italy are facing renewed unrest over living costs and fuel prices, with planned demonstrations in France prompting heightened security measures and truck drivers in southern Italy staging road blockades.
France’s minister delegate to the Interior Ministry, Jean-Didier Berger, said on Thursday that authorities were maintaining a “maximum level of vigilance” ahead of nationwide demonstrations planned for October 24.
“We are at a maximum level of vigilance,” Berger told broadcaster BFMTV, adding that the government “absolutely rules nothing out” in the coming days and weeks, including bans on gatherings and cultural or sporting events if deemed necessary.
Security force deployments on Saturday will be 20 percent higher than on October 17, Berger said.
Authorities have cancelled leave and recalled personnel, while Sentinelle forces and specialist units, including GIGN and RAID, will also be deployed.
The announcement follows protests on October 17 over the cost of living and fuel prices, involving Yellow Vest demonstrators and students.
Authorities reported damage to businesses and public buildings, leading to localised curfews in several cities.
French President Emmanuel Macron summoned intelligence services to the Elysee Palace for a security meeting following criticism over their failure to anticipate the October 17 mobilisation. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu and relevant ministers also attended.
Further demonstrations are planned for October 24, while unions have called for a nationwide strike and protest day on November 5.
As of noon on Tuesday, 149 people had been jailed, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said. Authorities had previously reported that 2,513 people had been taken into custody and around 50 judicial investigations had been opened.
Italy truckers block roads over diesel prices
In Italy, protests by truck drivers against high diesel prices spread across the south on Thursday, raising concerns about potential disruptions to the supply of goods, according to ANSA news agency.
Some drivers have suspended their protests, but truckers in Gela, in Sicily’s Caltanissetta province, have maintained their blockade. Dozens of heavy vehicles remained stationary at a roundabout on the SS 117 bis Gela-Catania road at the town’s entrance.
“We will continue until there are concrete results. Announcements are of no use to us,” the truck drivers said, describing their parked vehicles as representing their livelihoods and work.
The mayors of Naples and Bari have reportedly warned that their cities could face paralysis if the protests continue.
Interior minister Matteo Piantedosi has urged prefects and police chiefs to monitor possible “criminal infiltration” of the protests, according to reports.
The interior ministry is also expected to safeguard supplies of essential goods, while police are prepared to escort truck drivers who request assistance.
The government is preparing a decree combining support for the road transport sector with funding for agriculture. The measure was scheduled to be examined by the Council of Ministers on Thursday.
In Italy, more than 100,000 people have taken part in demonstrations across Rome, Milan, Bologna and other cities since October 17. Italian police have arrested 28 people, including 12 minors, as protests turned violent, while 141 law enforcement officers were injured.

The third Italian-Estonian Space Cooperation Conference, organized by the Italian Embassy in collaboration with the ICE office in Stockholm, will be held on October 26 at the Estonian Business School in Tallinn. The event is part of the “Software Defined Space Conference 2026” and is dedicated to the theme “Italy and Estonia After Artemis II: Driving the Next Lunar Renaissance.”

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Philippines wants to work more closely with Taiwan on protecting undersea cables, according to a Philippine diplomat, Reuters reported.
Felipe F. Carino III, the Philippines’ deputy chief of mission to the US, said a “pragmatic and practical approach” to work with Taiwan would protect shared interests in the Bashi Channel, adding that such collaboration could help address “gray-zone issues in our part of the world.”
Speaking at the Center for a New American Security in Washington, Carino said Manila would work with Taipei “notwithstanding our one China policy.” Undersea cables carry nearly all intercontinental data traffic, and 60-67% of cyber incidents occur in this region, he explained.
Carino gave no specifics on how the two sides would cooperate, but when asked during the seminar, he said joint patrols or holding vessels that disrupt communication accountable could be the options.
Earlier this month, the Philippine coast guard said it sent its largest ship and an aircraft to confront a Chinese research vessel operating off Batanes province near undersea cable corridors.
Taiwan, for its part, faces frequent disruptions to its submarine cable network. The Ministry of Digital Affairs says its coastal waters have seen an average of seven to eight cable incidents a year over the past four years.
At the seminar, Andrea Yang, Taiwan’s deputy representative in Washington, referred to the jailing of a Chinese captain for damaging an undersea cable off southwestern Taiwan and said Taipei would devote more resources to strengthening maritime surveillance by developing unmanned systems.

Iran's Balochistan border region sees growing unrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:48:00 UTC
20:48:00 KST

Iran's Balochistan border region sees growing unrest
October 22, 2026
Recent weeks have seen renewed attacks, assassinations and armed clashes in the southeastern province bordering Pakistan and Afghanistan. The incidents occurred in the provincial capital of Zahedan, as well as smaller border towns.
The border region of Iran, Pakistan and Afghanistan is home to the Baloch ethnic minority. The region on either side of the Iran-Pakistan border is among the most economically disadvantaged of the wider area.
The Pakistani province of Balochistan is economically underdeveloped, despite having large reserves of natural gas, gold and copper.
The situation is similarly dire in the Iranian province of Sistan and Baluchistan, which is predominantly inhabited by Sunni Baluchis. It is one of the poorest regions in the country and marked by underdeveloped infrastructure, limited educational opportunities and water supply shortages.
Significantly less information is available about the situation of the Baloch in Afghanistan.
Armed groups sense security gaps
Various Baloch groups are active in Iran and Pakistan, some of whom seek Balochistan independence. Yet to date, there is no evidence of coordinated cross-border cooperation among these organizations.
In December 2025, several Baloch opposition groups in Iran united under the umbrella of the Popular Fighters Front. Observers see this as an attempt to more closely integrate their political and military activities.
This coalition, which formed before the outbreak of the Iran war, could try to exploit security gaps created by the current situation, Iranian journalist Mehdi Nakhl Ahmadi told DW.
Ahmadi, who lives in Italy, has been covering the situation of the Baloch people for years. He said the new security situation could allow armed groups to expand their operations.
Struggling with poverty, suffering marginalization
Ahmadi said there are structural reasons for Baloch dissatisfaction. "The Islamic Republic's security policy toward ethnic and religious regions has widened the gap in economic development between these regions and other parts of the country in recent decades," he said.
He added that the rising number of attacks points to a shift in dynamics, as do increased coordination and changes in the way recent operations have been carried out.
Among the victims of recent clashes were members of Iran's Revolutionary Guards, the Basij militia, armed individuals, and a Sunni cleric.
A source within Iran, who is familiar with the situation of the Baloch people, yet whose identity we cannot disclose security for reasons, attributed some of the armed violence to political, economic and religious discontent.
Discrimination in employment, education, regional development and religious matters contribute to the tension, the source said.
That's why the armed conflict should not be viewed in isolation, the Iranian source explained. Clergy, academics and other social leaders had been trying for years to peacefully voice their demands for better social policies and greater investment in the region, the source said.
The fact that these efforts were largely unsuccessful had led to a growing willingness among some to resort to more radical measures.
"The high number of executions in recent decades is another factor that fuels discontent," said the source. Most documented executions in the province, meanwhile, are related to drug offenses.
Although Baluchis make only up an estimated 2–6% of the Iranian population, they are significantly overrepresented among those put to death. Iran Human Rights reports that Baluchis accounted for 9% of all recorded executions in 2025. In previous years, that figure was 11% (2024) and 20% (2023), respectively.
For many people who live in this economically disadvantaged region, smuggling opium into Iran, and fuel out of the country, are one of the few ways to earn a living. This, in turn, has contributed to a continued military and security presence at the border.
It is not, meanwhile, known whether armed groups in southeastern Iran are being supported from abroad.
Violence has also escalated in the Pakistani province of Balochistan. According to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies, 131 armed attacks were recorded there in September, up from 89 in August.
In addition to the separatist movement, which has been active for years, the Pakistani Taliban (TTP) are also expanding their operations. This had led to strategically important transportation links between Iran and Pakistan coming under growing pressure.
Still, it cannot be said with certainty whether the recent uptick in violence in Iran's Sistan and Baluchistan province stems from security gaps resulting from the Iran war.
The growing number of attacks does, however, suggests that the security situation in the already fragile border region continues to deteriorate.
Additional reporting by Morad Rahmati.
This article was originally written in German.

Will deposit rates rise - NBU has issued a forecast
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

14:43:32 EEST
20:43:32 KST

Will deposit rates rise - NBU has issued a forecast
Kyiv • UNN
Customer funds in banks increased, primarily due to households. Financial institutions expect an increase in deposit rates and the cost of funding.
Banks are attracting more funds from clients, primarily households, and expect deposit rates for businesses and households to rise. This is evidenced by the results of the NBU survey on bank funding for the third quarter of 2026, UNN reports.
Details
The volume of client funds in banks increased, primarily those of households, while the cost of attracting them rose mainly due to the increased cost of business funds
The regulator briefly outlined the results of the survey for the third quarter of 2026:
-  the volume of banks’ liabilities increased overall, mainly due to growth in household funds; 
-  the volume of wholesale funding has been growing since mid-2025, primarily due to loans attracted from international financial organizations and development banks; 
-  going forward, banks expect an increase in the volume of household and corporate funds, as well as wholesale funding; 
-  the average cost of borrowing rose due to the increased cost of corporate funds and, to some extent, household funds, while the cost of wholesale funds remained almost unchanged; 
-  banks forecast an increase in the cost of funding and higher deposit rates for businesses and households, as well as an increase in the cost of wholesale funding; 
-  the share of liabilities in foreign currency increased slightly, but it is expected to remain unchanged going forward; 
-  the maturity of funding increased, and financial institutions expect it to continue increasing; 
-  the majority of banks reported an increase in total capital over the past 12 months and expect this trend to continue; 
-  banks once again identified profitability as the key factor behind the increase in capital; 
-  for the first time since the first quarter of 2025, respondents expect the cost of capital to rise. 
For reference
The survey on bank funding was conducted from September 16 to October 7, 2026, among bank managers responsible for liability management. Responses were provided by 25 financial institutions accounting for 95% of the banking system’s total assets. The survey results reflect the respondents’ views and are not NBU estimates or forecasts.

Germany arrests Ukrainian man suspected of spying for Russia
October 22, 2026
Police in the German state of Brandenburg have arrested a Ukrainian man on suspicion of spying for Russia, the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office in Karlsruhe said Thursday.
The man, identified only as Vadym Y. by prosecutors, is suspected of having used his connections to European defense firms to gather information that he then allegedly passed on to a Russian spy agency.
What do we know about the alleged espionage in Germany?
Prosecutors said he had been in touch with a middleman since July 2025. They said he had been gathering intelligence in connection with the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine from Germany.
This information reportedly included "details regarding the production of armored vehicles, ammunition and explosives, as well as information on personnel and military facilities at locations intended to secure NATO's eastern flank."
Germany has been on high alert for acts of sabotage in recent months, especially since an explosive-laden drone was discovered near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig airport. Berlin said Moscow was behind the attempted attack.
Why is Germany worried about Russia's 'hybrid' war?
Germany is one of the biggest military and political supporters of Ukraine, especially following an increasingly friendly US stance toward Russia under President Donald Trump.
This seems to have put Germany in Russia's crosshairs as part of what has been called a "hybrid" campaign of espionage, sabotage and other disruptions.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he was not surprised by the arrest, adding that there would be more such cases in the future.
Besides the incident at Leipzig airport, there have been numerous cases of people being arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia. Moscow has denied all allegations.
This has led Germany to give increased powers to its own spying agency, the BND.
The agency's chief, Martin Jaeger, told German lawmakers earlier in October that the Russian "shadow war" is escalating and has "taken on a new, more dangerous character."
"Germany is at risk of being drawn into a violent conflict with Russia," he told a hearing of parliament's intelligence oversight committee in Berlin.

Large calibre gun production returns to Britain
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:42:19 BST
20:42:19 KST

Rheinmetall has officially opened its UK Gun Hall at Telford in the presence of Wes Streeting, the Secretary of State for Defence, marking the return of independent production of large-calibre weapons to Britain, according to the company.
The facility will manufacture 120mm and 155mm weapon systems, including those supporting Challenger 3 and future artillery platforms. It offers 11,500 square metres of production space and at peak capacity can produce up to 245 barrels a year across both calibres, along with more than fifty breeches annually.
Wes Streeting said: “Britain is back in the business of making the weapons that our Armed Forces need to defend the nation against our adversaries. From an empty site to full production in eight months, this is rapid reindustrialisation in action. One hundred skilled jobs in world-class manufacturing and the return of large-calibre weapon production to UK soil for the first time in twenty years – this is what defence as an engine for growth looks like.”
Rheinmetall turned an empty facility into an operational manufacturing capability in eight months, installing and commissioning advanced manufacturing equipment and transferring specialist expertise to the British workforce. Production of breeches and breech blocks began in May and barrel production followed in June.
Armin Papperger, chief executive of Rheinmetall AG, who hosted the opening ceremony alongside Streeting, said: “Today’s opening is an important milestone for Rheinmetall and for the United Kingdom. In a remarkably short period of time, we have turned our commitment into a sovereign manufacturing capability that will strengthen Britain’s defence industrial base for decades to come. The UK has been a long-standing and valued partner for Rheinmetall, and today we are building on an already strong relationship. We are committed to investing in the UK for the long term, expanding our industrial footprint and working together to deliver the capabilities needed for the future. By combining Rheinmetall’s expertise with British skills, innovation and manufacturing, we are strengthening the UK’s sovereign industrial capacity, supporting the Armed Forces and contributing to the security of NATO and Europe.”
Rebecca Richards, managing director of Rheinmetall UK, said: “The official opening of our UK Gun Hall is a landmark moment for Rheinmetall UK and for Britain’s defence industrial base. In just eight months, we transformed an empty facility into an operational manufacturing capability by investing in British people, British skills and British industry. From the outset, we have listened to what the UK needs and focused on delivering sovereign capability at pace. By transferring specialist knowledge from Germany and developing a highly skilled British workforce here in Telford, we are creating skilled jobs, supporting British businesses and building the industrial capacity needed to equip our Armed Forces while investing in the long-term prosperity of the UK.”
The Gun Hall is expected to support more than a hundred highly skilled people as production develops. Rheinmetall currently employs around 685 people in Telford, thirty-five of them at the Gun Hall, and the facility forms part of more than £200 million the company has invested across its British operations over the past five years.
British employees undertook training and knowledge transfer at Rheinmetall’s production facility at Unterlüß in Germany, gaining expertise in precision manufacturing, quality assurance and specialist weapon production before bringing it back to Telford. The company has also recruited specialist skills from across the Telford region.
Rheinmetall said it intends to introduce British steel from Sheffield Forgemasters into production. This publication has reported on the wider work to rebuild Britain’s ability to manufacture large calibre guns and on the point at which the first British-made artillery barrels headed to Ukraine.
The company described the Gun Hall as a concrete example of the industrial partnership between the United Kingdom and Germany established under the Trinity House Agreement. The investment complements Rheinmetall UK’s work on the Boxer Mechanised Infantry Vehicle and the Challenger 3 programme, both of which are built at Telford by Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land.
Ministers confirmed in Parliament this month that there is no current requirement to procure new 105mm barrels for the L118 Light Gun, and consequently no plans to restore domestic production of that calibre.

EAEU

A non-preferential trade agreement is being implemented. Negotiations are underway on the parameters of trade liberalization with India. A decision was made to launch corresponding negotiations with Tunisia. The feasibility of such a step in relations with Pakistan and Jordan is being studied."

Oxford scientists discover how viruses build themselves without a blueprint
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:42:05 UTC
20:42:05 KST

Oxford scientists discover how viruses build themselves without a blueprint
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- Scientists have captured virus-like particles assembling themselves step by step, revealing how a surprisingly simple process of trial and error produces complex structures with remarkable precision. The discovery uncovers a crucial molecular turning point that speeds up assembly and could lead to new ways to disrupt viruses and develop vaccines.
- Share:
Researchers at the University of Oxford have observed virus-like particles assembling themselves one molecule at a time, uncovering the surprisingly simple rules that allow complex biological structures to form with remarkable reliability. The findings, published in Nature, offer a detailed look at a process that scientists have struggled to observe directly for decades.
Understanding how viruses construct their protective protein shells, and how that construction might be interrupted, could lead to new antiviral drugs, improved vaccines, and other medical treatments. The discovery helps explain how individual proteins consistently organize themselves into the correct structures despite having thousands of possible ways to connect.
The researchers found that viral assembly resembles navigating a complicated maze, where only certain paths lead to lasting progress. At first, protein components form weak connections that can easily break apart if the arrangement is unsuccessful. This flexibility allows the molecules to keep trying different combinations until they form particular closed structures. Once multiple connections hold these structures together, they become far more stable.
These stable arrangements serve as molecular checkpoints, narrowing the enormous number of possible assembly routes into a much smaller set of successful pathways. One especially important milestone occurs when five larger protein building blocks connect to form a closed pentagonal ring. This is the first highly stable structure in the assembly process. Once it forms, each subsequent stable stage requires fewer additional building blocks, allowing the particle to grow more quickly.
Co-lead author Dr. Roi Asor (Department of Chemistry and Kavli Institute for Nanoscience Discovery, University of Oxford) explained: "A virus has to solve an extraordinary construction problem. Its components somehow have to find the right arrangement among a huge number of possibilities, without a blueprint or machinery directing the process. We can now watch what happens molecule by molecule and see the physical rules that make it possible."
Watching Virus Particles Assemble Molecule by Molecule
Viruses store and protect their genetic material within organized protein shells known as capsids. Depending on the virus, these shells may consist of tens or even thousands of individual protein components. Remarkably, in many cases, the proteins can arrange themselves into the correct structure without any external machinery directing their assembly.
Although scientists have investigated viral self-assembly for decades, capturing the process as it unfolds has been a major challenge. Many of the intermediate structures exist only briefly and appear in very small quantities. As a result, traditional methods have generally allowed researchers to examine the starting materials and finished particles without clearly showing how one transforms into the other.
To overcome this limitation, the Oxford researchers studied an engineered virus-like particle composed of 60 protein units. They used mass photometry, a technique developed at Oxford that determines the mass of individual molecules by measuring the light they scatter. By combining this technology with a new approach for keeping individual molecules confined and continuously observable, the team could repeatedly measure the mass of a growing particle as additional proteins attached.
This approach allowed the scientists to follow the construction process as it happened, effectively tracking the addition of individual molecular building blocks over time.
Co-first author PhD student Dan Loewenthal (Department of Chemistry and Kavli Institute for Nanoscience Discovery, University of Oxford) said: "This method lets us study the assembly process directly, we just take a video!"
Co-lead author Professor Philipp Kukura (Department of Chemistry and Kavli Institute for Nanoscience Discovery, Oxford University) said: "Until now, much of our understanding of how these structures assemble has had to be reconstructed from snapshots or theoretical models. Being able to both quantify the underlying interactions and follow one particle as it grows changes that. We can see the important intermediate structures appear and deduce a detailed model of the construction process."
The Surprising Trick That Makes Viral Assembly Work
The results help explain how a process involving an overwhelming number of possible molecular arrangements can consistently produce the correct structure. Rather than exploring every possible route, the proteins progress through a relatively small number of stable intermediate stages that guide assembly toward completion.
The findings also clarify why the earliest stage of construction, called nucleation, is particularly difficult and why growth becomes substantially faster after the first stable structure appears.
A key part of this efficiency comes from the ability of protein building blocks to make mistakes without permanently disrupting the process. Weak initial connections allow incorrect combinations to separate, giving the proteins another opportunity to find a better arrangement. When enough components eventually connect in the correct closed configuration, the resulting structure becomes stable enough to support further growth.
Dr. Asor added: "The weak interactions give the system room to make mistakes. Most encounters don't have to be successful: the components can separate and try again. But once enough of them come together in the right closed arrangement, the structure becomes stable, and assembly can move forward. That combination of trial and error followed by locking in successful structures is what makes the process so reliable."
New Possibilities for Antiviral Drugs and Vaccines
By identifying the molecular interactions that control viral assembly, scientists may eventually be able to develop treatments that interfere with the construction of viral protein shells. The same insights could also support efforts to engineer virus-like particles for vaccines and other therapeutic applications.
Co-author Dr. Jack Tan (MRC Weatherall Institute of Molecular Medicine and CAMS-Oxford Institute) noted: "The ability to understand these processes at the molecular level could have important applications in vaccine development and antivirals that disrupt viral assembly."
The implications may extend far beyond viruses. Self-assembly is essential throughout biology, helping create everything from the internal skeletons of cells to specialized molecular compartments and large protein complexes.
By making it possible to observe these intricate construction processes one molecule at a time, the Oxford team's approach offers researchers a powerful new way to investigate how complex biological structures emerge from relatively simple interactions.
Story Source:

Researchers in Australia identify cause of premature avocado fruit drop
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:40:48 CST
20:40:48 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have identified hormonal changes in avocado seeds as the trigger for premature fruit drop, a longstanding problem that can significantly reduce growers' yields.
A five-year project found that hormonal changes in the fruit's seed coat trigger immature fruit abscission when a tree sheds most fruitlets in response to reduced carbohydrate availability, according to a statement released Thursday by the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organization (CSIRO), Australia's national science agency.
The project, led by the CSIRO, with support from Hort Innovation, Australia's horticulture research and development corporation, has published the findings in the Journal of Experimental Botany, with the next stage of research focusing on developing ways to reduce fruit loss.
The team had also identified plant growth regulators with the potential to reduce immature fruit drop.
Avocados Australia CEO John Tyas said growers had reported fruit drop of up to 80 percent, adding that the industry had been trying to understand the cause since the late 1970s and would welcome measures to increase and stabilize yields.
The Australian avocado industry produces more than 130,000 tonnes of fruit annually and is worth about 800 million Australian dollars (about 561 million U.S. dollars) to the country's economy, according to CSIRO. ■

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:40:43 CST

BEIJING, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- China has released a set of guidelines on promoting the deep integration of scientific and technological innovation and industrial innovation.
Issued by the General Office of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the General Office of the State Council, this document provides a comprehensive blueprint for advancing the deep integration of sci-tech and industrial innovations.
It requires efforts to deepen the implementation of the innovation-driven development strategy, with the goals of developing new quality productive forces and building a modern industrial system, and with a focus on establishing an enterprise-led, multi-stakeholder collaborative system for integrated industry-academia-research innovation, so as to form a new pattern in which sci-tech innovation and industrial innovation promote each other.
This document is of great significance for accelerating high-level sci-tech self-reliance and strength, cultivating and developing new quality productive forces, building China into a competitive sci-tech country, and realizing Chinese modernization, said an official with the Ministry of Science and Technology.
It highlights the necessity to stimulate vitality via reform, requiring that sci-tech innovation should be strengthened with an application-oriented approach while industrial development should clearly define its sci-tech innovation tasks.
The document specifies concrete measures in six areas, namely seamlessly connecting the innovation chain with the industrial chain, supporting the building of a modern industrial system with the supply of high-quality sci-tech achievements, strengthening enterprise-led industry-academia-research collaborative innovation, improving the efficiency of coordinated allocation of innovation resources, fostering a sound ecosystem, and expanding the space for deep integration.
The official noted that the translation of sci-tech achievements into practical productive forces is manifested in spawning new industries and driving industrial transformation. Therefore, it is necessary to promptly apply innovation achievements to industries and industrial chains.
The document puts forward three measures in this regard: enhancing the self-reliance and controllability of industrial chains through breakthroughs in key technologies, cultivating and expanding emerging industries and future industries via original and disruptive sci-tech innovation, and transforming and upgrading traditional industries through the application of advanced technologies.
The official underlined the significance of strengthening enterprises' principal role in innovation. The document outlines three measures regarding this aim, which are enhancing corporate innovation capabilities, accelerating the development of sci-tech enterprises, and promoting greater synergy among innovators.
To improve the allocation of innovation resources, it stipulates measures to foster a virtuous cycle among science, industry and finance, enhance coordinated talent development and utilization, and build integrated innovation platforms. ■

Researchers in Australia develop controllable cell therapy platform
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:40:38 CST
20:40:38 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have developed a gene-editing platform that could give doctors more control over cell therapies, making them more practical for patients with complex immune conditions.
The new approach using prime editing could allow clinicians to use existing immune-suppressing drugs as a "control dial" for cell therapies and help corrected cells survive in the body, according to a recent statement released by Australia's Walter and Eliza Hall Institute of Medical Research (WEHI).
Cell and gene therapies involve modifying a patient's immune cells in the lab and returning them to the body, but clinicians have limited ways to control them afterward. This is particularly challenging for patients who need ongoing immunosuppression, as drugs used to control disease or protect transplanted organs can also suppress the therapeutic cells, researchers said.
The WEHI-led research aims to make cell and gene therapies more feasible for people who need ongoing immunosuppression, including those with rare immune disorders, organ or stem cell transplant recipients and patients receiving cell therapies for cancer, the statement said.
The researchers have turned existing medicines into a potential control system for future cell therapies. Because it uses common drugs, the platform may be more practical to translate into the clinic than strategies requiring entirely new medicines, according to the study published in Blood. ■

World Insights: Growing practical cooperation boosts China-Russia ties
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:40:29 CST
20:40:29 KST

MOSCOW, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- China-Russia trade has topped 200 billion U.S. dollars for three consecutive years, with China remaining Russia's largest trading partner for 16 years -- a sign of the economic momentum underpinning their deepening ties.
From Russian agricultural products reaching the dining tables of Chinese households to Chinese-made automobiles traveling on streets in Russia, practical cooperation between the two countries continues to deepen, injecting vitality into the growth of bilateral ties.
VIBRANT COOPERATION
Today, China-Russia comprehensive strategic partnership of coordination is at the highest level in history, setting an example for relations between countries. Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said on Wednesday that despite mounting external pressure, Russia-China trade and economic cooperation is gaining strong momentum: mutual trade has increased more than 30-fold over 25 years.
Cooperation in investment, energy, cultural and humanitarian fields is developing steadily. Interregional ties are being consistently strengthened and, most importantly, people-to-people contacts are expanding, Mishustin added.
According to Chinese Ambassador to Russia Zhang Hanhui, two-way trade from January to August this year reached 185 billion dollars, up by 28.4 percent year-on-year, and a full-year figure is expected to hit a new all-time high.
"The share of local currency settlement in China-Russia trade has exceeded 99 percent. Cross-border e-commerce volume has surpassed 40 billion dollars, and the platform economy boasts enormous potential. Energy cooperation is advancing steadily. Russia remains a major crude oil supplier to China, with a marked rise in supplies of liquefied natural gas. Dividends from the mutual visa-free policy keep unlocking. Russia has become the second-largest source of foreign tourists to China," Zhang said.
Moreover, high-tech manufacturing sectors have become highlights of bilateral cooperation, with expanded areas in artificial intelligence, logistics, finance, energy, science and technology, agriculture and healthcare.
Aisen Nikolayev, head of Russia's Republic of Sakha, told Xinhua that the republic is a key implementer of Russia's "Pivot to the East" strategy and an active participant in Russia-China regional cooperation.
Its cooperation with Chinese provinces and municipalities spans trade, energy, logistics, science and technology, innovation and other areas, with bilateral trade with China surging 52 percent year-on-year in the first five months of 2026.
Dmitry Bakanov, head of Russia's state space corporation Roscosmos, said the cooperation agenda between the two countries covers several topics, including joint work on the lunar mission and the Mars mission.
HEART-TO-HEART BONDS
Beyond growing economic ties, China and Russia are also deepening their friendship through cultural exchanges to foster greater mutual understanding.
China was the Guest of Honor at the 39th Moscow International Book Fair held in September. Under the theme of "Reading China," more than 2,000 titles and nearly 5,000 books were displayed. During the Guest of Honor program, the Chinese side hosted over 40 cultural events, including a China-Russia civilization exchange forum, copyright negotiations, new book launches, and dialogues between writers and scholars.
"Many Russians have begun reading Chinese novels. In particular, numerous online novels have gained great popularity after being translated into Russian. This serves as a direct reflection of the steadily warming relations between China and Russia," said Xie Xiaocheng, director of the International Exhibition Center at China National Publications Import and Export Group.
"Chinese literature delivers a wealth of emotions and adventures all at once," Maria Rudneva, editor-in-chief of Freedom, an imprint of Russia's leading publishing house Eksmo, told Xinhua.
In the eyes of publishers and readers, Chinese works offer more than entertainment; they open a window to Chinese culture and classical Chinese literature for Russian readers, who have shown demand for new Chinese stories.
This summer, Moscow hosted its first-ever Wushu Festival, drawing more than 30,000 spectators and roughly 830 athletes from multiple Russian cities.
"Wushu (martial arts) is deeply loved in Russia. I am confident that this festival will serve to further popularize it, drawing more and more people, young and old, into this beautiful art and sport," said Sergey Sanakoev, deputy chairman of the Russian-Chinese Friendship Society.
Close people-to-people exchanges are also reflected in education. At present, Chinese language courses are available at 360 schools across Russia, with more than 100,000 Chinese learners.
Maria Zvereva, a student at the Russian State University for the Humanities, has visited many places across China. In her view, China has achieved outstanding accomplishments in medicine, robotics, rocket manufacturing and other fields.
"While preserving its traditions and history, China has also made tremendous strides in high and new technologies," said Zvereva. ■

Sri Lanka maintains landslide alerts as prolonged rainfall threatens over 30,000 locations

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:40:26 CST
20:40:26 KST

COLOMBO, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Landslide warnings remain in effect across parts of Sri Lanka despite variations in rainfall intensity, as prolonged wet weather has left rocks and soil layers vulnerable to collapse, a senior geologist said Thursday.
Wasantha Senadheera, senior geologist at the National Building Research Institute, said rainfall accumulated over several days could trigger landslides even when an affected area receives only light rain.
Speaking at a media briefing, Senadheera said more than 30,000 locations nationwide had been identified as facing high landslide risks under the prevailing weather conditions.
Level 2 alerts were updated Wednesday for eight areas across three districts, including Udapalatha, Medadumbara and Kundasale in Kandy District, Ambagamuwa and Norwood in Nuwara Eliya District, and Ratnapura, Elapatha and Kuruwita in Ratnapura District.
Senadheera said the impact of Cyclone Ditwah last year had contributed to early signs of slope instability in numerous areas, where rocks and soil deposits remained temporarily lodged but could be dislodged by further rainfall.
Sri Lankan authorities have issued 25 updates to landslide early warnings since Oct. 3, reflecting changing weather conditions and the continuing threat to vulnerable communities. ■

Feature: China's Li adds Asian Para Games gold to Paralympic triumph
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:40:06 CST
20:40:06 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- China's Li Yujie added another title to her growing collection on Tuesday, rallying from a round down to defeat Iran's Zahra Rahimi 2-1 in the women's K44 57kg para taekwondo final at the 2026 Asian Para Games.
The victory capped a memorable Games for the 25-year-old, who had earlier carried China's national flag at the opening ceremony.
Li lost the opening round 4-0 but responded emphatically, winning the next two rounds 4-0 and 8-0 to secure the gold medal.
After the final, Li and her coach, Yu Jie, celebrated by carrying the Chinese flag around the arena before embracing.
"I'm proud to be Chinese and grateful to my country for this opportunity and recognition," Li said, reflecting on her role as flagbearer. "This year's Games have been especially fulfilling for me."
The victory marked another milestone in a career that has taken Li from a childhood accident to the top of international para taekwondo.
Born in 2001 in Zibo, Shandong Province, Li lost her right hand in a fireworks accident at the age of 10. She initially took up sprinting at school before being encouraged to switch to taekwondo after a talent scout noticed her explosive power at a provincial athletics competition in 2016.
The transition proved difficult. The loss of her hand affected her balance and coordination, and she frequently fell while attempting kicks. Determined to improve, Li supplemented her eight-hour daily training sessions with additional practice.
Her persistence paid off in 2019 when she won gold at the World Para Taekwondo Championships in Türkiye. She followed that with bronze at the Tokyo Paralympics, becoming China's first Paralympic medalist in the sport.
Three years later, Li made history again at Paris 2024, winning the women's K44 57kg title to secure China's first Paralympic taekwondo gold medal.
However, her rise was complicated by persistent leg injuries following Tokyo, which at one stage threatened to require surgery.
Working with Yu, Li adjusted her training program to reduce the physical strain while improving her technique and tactical awareness.
"I used to rely on charging forward with my kicks. Now I have a wider range of techniques and pay more attention to tactics," she said. "I've also become calmer and more open to others' advice."
Li credited her coach, national team support and able-bodied sparring partners for helping her develop into a more complete fighter.
With another gold medal secured, Li has already turned her attention to next month's World Para Taekwondo Championships in South Korea, although she is reluctant to look too far ahead.
"One step at a time, one day at a time," she said. ■

KYIV – Ukraine has received the bodies of 252 people in an exchange of war dead with Russia, the Ukrainian authorities said on Oct 22.
Russia received 25 bodies in return, Russian lawmaker Shamsail Saraliev was quoted as saying by the RBC news outlet.
The exchange of prisoners of war and fallen soldiers is one of the few areas of cooperation between the warring sides.
“As a result of repatriation measures, the bodies of 252 deceased have been returned to Ukraine,” said Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War.
The police and other officials would “carry out all the necessary procedures to identify the repatriated deceased”, it said.
It thanked the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) for help facilitating the exchange, posting pictures on social media of several large white trailer trucks parked back to back, as workers in white, hooded jumpsuits emblazoned with the ICRC logo stood nearby.
The I Want to Live foundation, which is affiliated with Ukraine’s Intelligence Directorate and involved in managing Russia’s prisoners of war, meanwhile said “the remains of Russian servicemen were repatriated”.
Among them was the body of a Sri Lankan citizen, the organisation said, adding that he was sent to Russia since he was considered under international law as a combatant in the Russian army.
The exchanges of remains between the two sides take place regularly.
Earlier in October, Ukraine’s military intelligence chief Kyrylo Budanov estimated that more than 26,000 bodies and human remains had been repatriated to Ukraine through exchange operations.
Most of them are still awaiting identification.
According to official announcements from the two sides, Ukraine has received the remains of 5,300 people since the start of 2026 alone, while Russia has received fewer than 300.
The war, Europe’s worst conflict since World War II, has claimed tens of thousands of lives since Russia’s invasion in February 2022. AFP

Over 50% of Americans believe Trump deserves impeachment, Politico says
A new public opinion poll has found that 54% of Americans believe US President Donald Trump has committed offences warranting impeachment.
Source: a poll conducted by Politico between 16 and 19 October, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The results show that 81% of voters planning to support Democrats in the midterm congressional elections and a quarter of Republican voters intending to vote believe Trump has committed offences that should trigger impeachment proceedings.
More than 41% of respondents said he had used his office as president for financial gain for himself or his family.
A third of those surveyed believe Democrats should prioritise investigating how Trump enriched himself, while another third think they should focus on investigating his tough measures against immigrants.
Meanwhile, most respondents from both political camps said Trump's first two impeachments had no impact on the president or his political course. More Americans believe another impeachment would make Trump more popular (24%) than less popular (18%).
Democratic voters are also divided over whether their candidates should raise the issue of impeachment during campaigns for the midterm elections. Some 43% of respondents believe candidates should announce plans to pursue impeachment even if this costs Democrats votes, while 41% favour avoiding the issue if doing so would help them win the election.
It is worth noting that the US House of Representatives impeached Trump twice during his first term: in 2019 for abuse of power and obstruction of Congress and again in 2021 for inciting an insurrection during the storming of the Capitol. Just one presidential election cycle later, he returned to the White House with 312 electoral votes.
To impeach a US president, the decision must be approved by both chambers of Congress: a majority in the House of Representatives (218 votes) and two-thirds of the Senate (67 votes). No US president has ever been removed from office through this procedure.
Background:
- Trump's approval rating recently fell to a record low ahead of the midterm congressional elections scheduled for 3 November. It currently stands at 31%.
- The US midterm elections will take place on 3 November. Trump previously said he would pay every adult American a US$5,000 "Trump dividend" if Republicans retain control of Congress in the November midterms.

Commission criticises University of Zurich senior leaders
The Zurich Cantonal Council’s Supervisory Commission for Education and Health (ABG) has criticised the university, or rather its management. It claims that there are people in management positions who are not suited to the role.
Normally, the approval of an annual report in the Cantonal Council is a mere formality. The relevant committee, which prepares the matter, recommends that Parliament approve the annual report. In the vast majority of cases, this is then carried out without a hitch.
Not so this year. In its statement on Thursday, the ABG criticised the University of Zurich quite sharply. The criticism goes so far that it intends to withhold its approval of the annual report.
The reason, according to the ABG, is the university’s “outdated approach to leadership”. Greater attention must be paid to leadership skills when selecting and training senior staff. The ABG, in particular, sees major shortcomings among the university’s senior management.
‘Concerned’ about ongoing problems
The Commission has also criticised the collaboration between the University and the University Hospital. The Commission is “concerned” about the ongoing problems. While the exchange of information between the two institutions has improved significantly, according to the ABG, when it comes to dual appointments – that is, people who work at both the university and the university hospital – it is difficult to find joint solutions when problems arise.
+ Tribunal rules Zurich university unfairly dismissed professor
The Commission is also dissatisfied with the exchange of information between itself and the university. The members of the Cantonal Council are calling for this to become more transparent. This is necessary for the ABG to effectively exercise its supervisory role and verify whether the university is actually implementing its recommendations.
The Cantonal Council will debate the University of Zurich’s annual report at one of its forthcoming meetings. These issues will also be raised during the debate.

Who are the Americans detained in Russia?
