====================================================================================================

Beneath psilocybin’s apparent brain chaos, scientists find signs of a hidden order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:00:28 UTC
20:00:28 KST

A new neuroimaging study suggests that the psychedelic compound psilocybin does not simply scramble brain communication into random disorder, but instead reorganizes neural activity to align with a person’s immediate environment. Using brain scans and advanced computational modeling, researchers found that under the drug, brain activity formed structured patterns that tracked what participants were doing and experiencing, especially in those who reported a dissolving sense of self. The findings were published in Nature.
Psilocybin is a psychoactive chemical compound found naturally in certain species of mushrooms. After ingestion, the body converts it into psilocin, which binds mainly to serotonin 2A receptors on brain cells, changing how distinct neural networks interact and altering perception, emotion, and self-awareness. Earlier neuroimaging work characterized psychedelic states as predominantly chaotic, marked by a breakdown of coordinated brain rhythms. An influential 2013 study recorded brain signals after psilocybin administration and found widespread drops in coordinated electrical oscillations, suggesting that the drug plunged neural circuits into an uncoordinated state.
Building on these observations, the authors of a 2018 review led by Robin Carhart-Harris, who is also a co-author of the new study, updated what is known as the entropic brain hypothesis, arguing that psychedelics make brain activity more varied and unpredictable, a property known as entropy, and that this makes the brain unusually sensitive to a person’s mindset and physical setting. Later work began to test this idea directly: a study first posted as a preprint in 2020 and later published in a peer-reviewed journal indicated that sensory inputs like music and video alter the diversity of brain signals under psychedelics, showing that external context helps determine neural activity.
Brain imaging has also shown that psychedelics modify how higher regions of the brain communicate with sensory systems. In a study covered by PsyPost in 2024, psilocybin was found to strengthen signals traveling from higher-order thinking regions down to visual areas, providing a biological basis for vivid closed-eye mental imagery. Despite these insights, scientists still lacked an understanding of whether the brain under psychedelics is truly disorganized or if it follows hidden patterns that track real-world experiences as they unfold over time.
The project was led by Devon Stoliker, a Turner Impact research fellow in the Computational Neuroscience Laboratory at Monash University‘s Turner Institute for Brain and Mental Health, and Adeel Razi, a professor of computational neuroscience and director of the laboratory. Stoliker told PsyPost that the project was motivated by a desire to understand how mindset and setting interact with brain function.
“Psychedelic experiences vary considerably with mindset and setting, but how these differences are reflected in brain activity remains unclear,” Stoliker explained. “Brain-imaging studies often describe disrupted networks or increased disorder, leaving a gap in explaining experiences that people find coherent and deeply meaningful. We wanted to understand how brain activity becomes reorganized during psychedelic experiences, how that reorganization is modulated by what a person is doing and experiencing, and how it relates to subsequent psychological change.”
To carry out the project, the research team recruited 65 healthy adults between the ages of 18 and 55 who had no meaningful prior experience with psychedelic substances. Three participants reported minor or remote exposure without noticeable effects, while the remaining participants had never taken a serotonergic psychedelic. Two individuals left the study before drug administration due to protocol exclusions, leaving 63 participants who received a standardized oral dose of 19 milligrams of psilocybin.
Each volunteer took part in two separate testing visits spaced roughly one week apart: a baseline visit with no drug and an active dosing visit. During each visit, participants completed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which measures changes in blood oxygenation across the brain, followed by electroencephalography (EEG), which records electrical brain waves through sensors on the scalp. The imaging sessions began about 80 minutes after taking the capsule, while electrical recordings started roughly 150 minutes post-dose, during the drug’s acute effects.
In both the brain scanner and the EEG session, participants moved through four distinct conditions designed to present varying levels of sensory engagement. These conditions included resting quietly with eyes closed, following a guided audio meditation, listening to an emotionally evocative music playlist with eyes closed, and watching a silent video of drifting clouds with eyes open.
The sequence progressed from low-stimulus to high-stimulus contexts in the scanner, while the movie was presented first in the EEG session. Half of the participants had also completed an eight-week mindfulness meditation course before their scans, but differences between meditators and non-meditators were not statistically significant, leading the authors to combine both groups for the primary analyses.
After applying quality checks to exclude scans affected by excessive head movement, the final analyzed functional imaging dataset included 60 participants during rest, 59 during meditation, 56 during music listening, and 57 during movie watching. A balanced group of 54 participants with complete data across all four conditions was used for machine learning models. The final electrical recording dataset included 58 participants per condition during the psilocybin session.
When the authors analyzed overall communication across the brain, they discovered that psilocybin redistributed functional connections depending on whether participants had their eyes open or closed. During eyes-closed conditions, overall connectivity decreased in sensory regions by up to 39 percent while increasing in associative thinking areas by up to 72 percent. During the eyes-open movie condition, by comparison, connectivity increased across both sensory and associative areas. Overall, the differences in brain connectivity between having eyes open and having eyes closed shrank by 85 percent in the visual system after psilocybin, indicating that eyes-closed states began to resemble eyes-open processing.
The traditional measure of brain modularity, which quantifies how cleanly the brain divides itself into separate functional communities, dropped under psilocybin across all four conditions. Modularity decreased during rest with an effect size of minus 0.63, during meditation at minus 0.60, during music at minus 0.70, and during video viewing at minus 0.91. However, these static, time-averaged modularity scores failed to predict how participants actually felt during the session, and correlations with subjective reports were not statistically significant.
“The striking finding was that reduced separation between the usual brain networks, a common finding known as reduced modularity, coexisted with the organization detectable using machine learning,” Stoliker observed. “Only the machine learning methods, which preserve each individual’s brain activity over time, identified an association with subjective effects.”
To look beyond static averages, the researchers used machine learning to map moment-by-moment brain activity into smooth, lower-dimensional geometric trajectories. An automated classifier could identify which condition a participant was engaged in based on their brain trajectories, and its accuracy rose with the intensity of the experience. In a closer analysis of six participants with strong subjective effects, accuracy climbed from roughly 62 percent at baseline to about 98 percent under psilocybin.
“Uniquely, this method measured each individual separately, rather than an average across the group of participants,” Stoliker remarked. “We think the development of similar measures that preserve each individual’s brain activity over time is an important next step, but whether the current methods can help predict or improve treatment outcomes remains to be tested.”
To capture different facets of this neural reorganization, the scientists used a second machine-learning tool, called TAVRNN, that tracks how connections between brain regions shift over time. “The main analysis captured context-aligned patterns in each person’s brain activity over time, while a complementary machine learning analysis, TAVRNN—developed in-house by co-author Moein Khajehnejad—showed greater cohesion in the connectivity within and across networks,” the researchers pointed out. “Both analyses showed that organization varied with the strength of subjective effects and both showed that the apparent disorder of the psychedelic state contained structure that became visible when we examined brain activity differently.”
This organizational structure tracked the emotional and psychological quality of each participant’s experience. Higher classification accuracy correlated strongly with overall scores on a questionnaire measuring mystical-type experiences (r = 0.64), while correlations with anxiety or impaired thinking were low and not statistically significant. Among specific kinds of experience, accuracy tracked most closely with positively felt ones, such as bliss, unity, and spiritual feelings. Participants who experienced strong feelings of unity showed tightly packed neural patterns aligned with each condition, a pattern the authors call context alignment; they reserve a separate term, embeddedness, for the felt experience that accompanied it.
“Psychedelics may provide a window into how the brain ordinarily maintains the experience of being a separate self within the world,” Stoliker elaborated. “We use the term embeddedness to describe the felt continuity with a broader physical and psychological context that some participants reported. Embeddedness is the phenomenological correlate of context alignment, thus our findings suggest that this change in experience has a measurable counterpart in how brain activity is organized.”
A perturbation analysis indicated that this context-aligned organization depended most heavily on two major brain networks: the default mode network, which typically supports internal self-reflection, and the visual network, which processes external visual inputs. In those six participants, when researchers mathematically replaced the psilocybin-altered signals in either network with that person’s drug-free data, classification accuracy dropped noticeably, with each network contributing roughly 23 percent to the total accuracy gain.
Subjective questionnaires confirmed the profound psychological impact of the session. More than half of the participants rated the experience among the most meaningful of their lives, with 24 placing it in their top five, and most rated the overall intensity at nine or ten out of ten. Participants also completed follow-up assessments one day later, showing positive mindset improvements related to inner peace, patience, and feelings of connection to nature and other people. Mindset change was most strongly associated with feelings of insightfulness during the session (r = 0.65), followed by mystical, blissful, and spiritual experiences.
“The authors acquired neuroimaging data from individuals at baseline and after a dose of psilocybin, the serotonergic psychedelic contained in ‘magic mushrooms’ of the Psilocybe genus,” said Enzo Tagliazucchi, a researcher at the University of Buenos Aires who was not involved in the study. “Instead of obtaining neuroimaging data just during rest, as is most frequent in this type of study, they acquired the data under different conditions, including music and movie viewing, and meditation. There are multiple results included in this paper, but in my opinion the most salient result is the psilocybin-induced enhancement of context sensitivity.”
“In other words, under psilocybin the neuroimaging data allowed for a much clearer distinction between the different experimental conditions, relative to the baseline,” Tagliazucchi told PsyPost. “Moreover, the authors linked this sensitivity to the occurrence of mystical-type experiences under the drug. This experience is interesting from the perspective of basic and clinical neuroscience, as it can predict symptom improvement after psychedelic therapy.”
The findings are in line with a 2024 study covered by PsyPost, which found that psilocybin causes brain networks to shift into temporary states of heightened communication that predict feelings of ego dissolution. The results also align with an international brain imaging analysis covered by PsyPost in 2026, which found that psychedelics consistently bridge the gap between sensory and associative systems, though that study found weak evidence for within-network breakdown while the current work observed drops in within-network connectivity.
In addition, the findings offer a different emphasis from research covered by PsyPost in May 2026, which linked increased brain entropy under psilocybin to later insight and well-being. The new study also found signs of higher entropy, but argues that this apparent disorder contains structured organization aligned with context.
Tagliazucchi also highlighted how the results fit with longstanding concepts in psychedelic science. “The findings in this study align with the context-dependent effects of psychedelics,” he noted. “Today, we are familiar with terms such as ‘set’ and ‘setting,’ coined decades ago to represent the mental and environmental aspects that can influence a psychedelic trip, respectively. From this perspective, the authors found a neural signature of this sensitivity to context; that is, a much easier distinction between the ‘settings’ explored in the study during the psychedelic state compared to the baseline.”
The authors note that earlier psychedelic imaging studies often relied on small samples of experienced users. A second outside expert highlighted the size of the new dataset.
“Psilocybin can produce a rich range of subjective experiences, such as changes in perception to shifts in mood and sense of self,” said Alex Kwan, a professor in the Meinig School of Biomedical Engineering at Cornell University and head of the Kwan Lab, who was not involved in the study. “What makes this study exciting is that it begins to connect these different aspects of the psychedelic experience to distinct patterns of brain activity. One strength of this study is its relatively large sample size, drawing on brain imaging data from more than 60 people. That is a substantial dataset for this type of psychedelic research.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. All participants knew they were receiving psilocybin, as the study used an open-label design without an active placebo group. Although an active placebo that convincingly mimics a psychedelic trip is difficult to implement, expectations could have influenced participants’ subjective reports and emotional responses. The four conditions were also presented in a fixed order during imaging to prioritize safety and comfort for first-time participants.
“I think the authors did an excellent job in several aspects, including data collection, participant number, and computational analyses,” Tagliazucchi evaluated. “The latter, especially, are a ‘tour de force’ in neuroimaging data analysis.”
“My only concern relates to the experimental design,” he added. “This study did not include a placebo condition, and the order of the conditions was fixed across all participants. Therefore, the authors’ analysis might be capturing the differential temporal effects of psilocybin on factors such as vigilance, arousal, attention, or even the temporal evolution of the subjective intensity of the effects, which spans several hours.”
For their part, the authors note that context-aligned organization was already strong during rest, the very first condition scanned, before order effects or fatigue could accumulate. In addition, the types of stimuli presented during the scan sessions represent an important consideration for understanding what context meant in this experiment.
“It would be important to distinguish ‘context’ in a broad sense from a more fine grained definition of ‘context’ which implicates the specific contents of consciousness present at any given time,” Tagliazucchi explained. “The authors used visual stimuli composed by slowly drifting clouds, this stimulus is interesting for inducing a certain global ‘setting,’ but it lacks semantic content. The same applies to the auditory stimulation, which comprised slow, ambient music but lacked strong temporal dynamics. A new study would be required to test whether the context-sensitivity also extends to different forms of conscious content, such as faces, objects, or complex situations like those seen in movies.”
Kwan told PsyPost that the physical environment of brain imaging introduces its own unique influences. “Context is indeed important,” Kwan pointed out. “For this study, we should keep in mind that the participants are lying inside a large and loud brain scanner while they are under the influence of a psychedelic drug. That itself is an unusual context that can affect the results and the qualities of the subjective experience.”
In addition, the participants were healthy volunteers who were generally curious and willing to experience an altered state in an imaging scanner, meaning the findings might not generalize directly to clinical populations undergoing psychedelic-assisted therapy for specific psychiatric disorders. Future investigations will need to examine whether similar patterns of brain reorganization occur in individuals being treated for depression, anxiety, or addiction.
The authors also highlighted important caveats regarding how brain scans are interpreted. “‘Organization’ here is inferred from the structure of patterns observed in the machine learning results derived from the fMRI signal. fMRI measures changes in blood oxygenation associated with neural activity, rather than recording neuronal activity directly,” Stoliker cautioned. “Under psilocybin, this context-aligned structure became more detectable, particularly in participants reporting stronger positive subjective effects, but not in those reporting negative subjective effects or just visual effects—the profound changes to self and boundary, a reduced sense of separation, or continuity with the internal and externally oriented environment, seemed to occur with the emergence of the organization we observed.”
“We want to identify the conditions that make this organization more likely, and whether changing those conditions improves outcomes,” Stoliker said. “This means studying individual characteristics, expectations and preparation before dosing, psychological state around administration, and context and support during the session. Behavioral and brain measurements prior to dosing could help establish which factors are modifiable and whether preparation should differ between people. The clinical goal is to determine whether tailoring these conditions can support more reliable and sustained benefit.”
The study, “Psychedelics align brain activity with context,” was authored by Devon Stoliker, Leonardo Novelli, Moein Khajehnejad, Mana Biabani, Matthew D. Greaves, Tamrin Barta, Martin Williams, Sidhant Chopra, Olivier Bazin, Otto Simonsson, Richard Chambers, Frederick S. Barrett, Gustavo Deco, Katrin H. Preller, Robin L. Carhart-Harris, Anil K. Seth, Suresh Sundram, Gary F. Egan, and Adeel Razi.

Britain still plans new nuclear sub every eighteen months
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:00:24 BST
20:00:24 KST

Ministers have confirmed that the intention remains to procure up to twelve SSN-AUKUS submarines, and that the investments needed to establish industrial capacity for a submarine every eighteen months from the mid-2030s have been made, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Andrew Rosindell, the Reform UK member for Romford, asked the Secretary of State for Defence whether he would make it his department’s policy to increase total hull numbers in the submarine service.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “As set out in the Defence Investment Plan (DIP), the Ministry of Defence intends to procure up to 12 SSN AUKUS submarines.
“The programme is currently midway through the Detailed Design and Long Lead (D2L2) phase and we anticipate that the number of submarines will be confirmed before the end of this phase in 2028.
“Through the DIP, the Government has made the investments necessary to establish the industrial capacity required to ultimately deliver a submarine every 18 months from the mid-2030s to ensure we can deliver an expanded SSN force.”
Britain currently operates seven Astute class attack submarines, and this publication reported the government’s commitment to build twelve new nuclear attack submarines when the plan appeared. A drumbeat of one boat every eighteen months would be the fastest sustained British submarine production rate since the Cold War, and the figure follows from the capacity being built at Barrow.
Barrow has been expanding through the Barrow Infrastructure Programme, with new build halls, a reconfigured yard and a recruitment effort that has taken the BAE Systems workforce there past twelve thousand. Rolls-Royce Submarines in Derby has doubled its site to produce reactors for both Dreadnought and SSN-AUKUS, and the Sheffield Forgemasters work on large forgings feeds the same chain.
Confirmation of the final number before the end of the detailed design phase in 2028 ties the fleet size to what the yard can actually sustain. Senior officials told the Commons Defence Committee earlier this year that submarine fleet size was conditional on Barrow output, and a decision due in 2028 falls inside this Parliament.
Australia will build its own SSN-AUKUS boats at Osborne in South Australia to a common design, and the two production lines are intended to share a supply chain, which is part of the case for the industrial investment on the British side. Dreadnought holds priority at Barrow through the late 2020s, so attack submarine production builds up behind the ballistic missile boats.
Pollard confirmed in a separate answer the same day that steel will be cut on the first British SSN-AUKUS next year, and that the Preliminary Design Review for the class concluded on the first of July. Twelve boats remains an upper bound until the design phase closes.

Snowy 2.0 to cost 12 times more than initial budget with further delays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:00:08 UTC
20:00:08 KST

Review finds Snowy 2.0 hydropower project could cost up to $25b with delays to late 2029
In short:
A major review into Australia's biggest renewable energy project has found it could cost up to $25 billion, which is about 12 times the original price.
Snowy 2.0 was initially set to cost $2b and come online in 2021.
What's next?
The project is now expected to be delivered in 2029.
The cost of delivering Australia's biggest renewable energy project has doubled since the last estimate and is now set to become fully operational a year later than expected, according to a major review.
Snowy Hydro has released its much-anticipated cost reassessment for the Snowy 2.0 hydropower project, revealing it could cost up to $25 billion, with first power expected in early 2029 and the project to be fully operational later that year.
While the Commonwealth-owned company has set a target cost of $22 billion, it is allowing for an additional $3 billion to be spent on the project if required.
Snowy 2.0, which started being built seven years ago, had an initial budget of $2 billion and was originally expected to start operating in 2021.
Those figures were revised as part of a "project reset" three years ago, which projected first power would be delivered in late 2027 and Snowy 2.0 would be fully operational a year later, at a cost of $12 billion.
Late last year it was announced that the project's contractor Future Generation Joint Venture (FGJV) would conduct a "line-by-line reassessment", which has now been released three months later than initially expected.
Snowy Hydro CEO Dennis Barnes said he was "incredibly disappointed" with the update.
"We had a project that was stalled and had billions of dollars of claims on the table in 2023," he said.
"I'm pleased we've got progress, progress doubled in the first year after the reset.
"What I'm disappointed about is obviously the resultant costs of the progress we're making."
Mr Barnes said the "design immaturity" that was faced before the 2023 reset had contributed to the latest cost blowouts.
"We've understood that we're going to need a lot more people for a lot longer to deliver this job," he said.
"This job is 80 per cent people costs, we've got 5,000 people on the job now working across multiple work fronts and that's obviously a lot more than we thought in 2023."
The review found 65 per cent of machine tunnelling and 90 per cent of cavern excavation had now been completed and work to build the underground power station was underway.
While Mr Barnes said the project was in its "strongest position yet", he could not rule out further cost blowouts beyond the most recent targets.
"There's never any guarantees with mega projects, we're doing a world first thing in many respects in really complex conditions," he said.
"But the project is hitting its milestones of late, we have a lot of the risks behind us."
How did Snowy 2.0 get here?
Snowy 2.0 is designed to underpin Australia's electricity security and affordability over coming decades, as the country transitions away from fossil fuels.
Based in the New South Wales Snowy Mountains, it will link two dams through about 27 kilometres of tunnels and include an underground pumped hydro station the size of the Sydney Opera House.
The project will act like a giant battery, pumping water upstream when electricity is cheap and releasing it back downstream to generate power when demand is high.
It has a total capacity of 2,200 MW and is expected to power three million homes for a week, the equivalent of about 26 million household batteries.
Unlike batteries, pumped hydro offers long-duration storage, meaning it is designed to be a renewable energy insurance policy during days when there is limited sun or wind.
But Snowy 2.0 has been embroiled in controversy since it was announced by former Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull in 2017, including cost blowouts, missed deadlines, scrutiny over safety issues and contractor disputes.
A major setback came after one of the initial three tunnel boring machines, Florence, got stuck in early 2023 for 11 months after hitting soft ground and creating a sinkhole.
The National Audit Office gave Snowy 2.0 a glowing review in 2022 but the most recent audit, released earlier this year, found "significant deficiencies" in the management of the hydropower project.
In a submission to a parliamentary inquiry examining the project's delivery, Snowy Hydro said initial "design immaturity" and the project's "inherent complexity" had been the primary drivers of additional costs.
"Productivity underperformance and cost escalation have also been significant factors," the submission read.
"Others have related to project-specific complexities that have developed during delivery.
"Snowy Hydro has learned and taken action in response to these challenges."
A submission from Future Generation Joint Venture (FGJV), the group responsible for the project's construction, said "unprecedented geotechnical uncertainty" and "significant geopolitical upheaval" had contributed to cost escalations.
"Unlike metropolitan tunnelling projects, where initial ground investigations are typically well-developed, ground investigations within a national park are necessarily limited," the submission said.
"As a result, conditions only become fully apparent as excavation progresses."
Project benefits report released
Along with the cost reassessment, Snowy Hydro has also released an economic study conducted by engineering consultant GHD.
It found the project will contribute $18 billion to Australia's economy during the delivery phase and reduce wholesale electricity costs by more than $7b by 2075.
Mr Barnes said all technologies were needed for the energy transition, including batteries, pumped hydro and gas for firming.
"We issued a report earlier in the year to show what the grid looked like with and without Snowy 2.0 and on those periods, which are pretty common, where we get no wind and we get no sun for days on end, batteries run out of juice, they don't get recharged," he said.
"We actually saw that in January in South Australia, there was a period where the batteries run out of juice and prices went very high.
"So with Snowy 2.0 in the grid, we see that the prices in those periods were $7,000 a MWh lower."
A joint statement from Energy Minister Chris Bowen and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said abandoning the hydropower project would "undermine grid reliability", scrap 5,000 jobs and lead to higher electricity bills.
"Once completed, Snowy 2.0 will be an incredible national asset, supporting Australia's energy security, price stability and the transition to renewable energy," the statement said.
"The pumped hydro expansion of the Snowy Scheme will provide more than half of the total energy storage the grid needs by 2050, strengthening energy security and putting downwards pressure on energy prices."

Exclusive: Ben-Gvir’s Plan to Push Netanyahu Right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:00:04 UTC
20:00:04 KST

In a small office in the industrial district of Lod, a city outside Tel Aviv where Israeli forces expelled thousands of Palestinians during the 1948 war, sits the campaign headquarters of Otzma Yehudit, or “Jewish Power.” The ultra-nationalist party is led by Itamar Ben-Gvir, a far-right firebrand once deemed too extreme to serve in Israel’s military. He now sits in Benjamin Netanyahu’s cabinet as national security minister, overseeing the country’s police and prison services.
If Ben-Gvir has his way, the Oct. 27 election will give his party more seats in parliament and himself greater leverage over another right-wing government led by Netanyahu. His ambition is not to replace the prime minister but to make him even more dependent on the hardline parties pushing for Palestinians to leave Gaza and the West Bank—and for Israel to extend sovereignty over the territories.
“I want Netanyahu to be prime minister. He’s a leader. I prefer him a million times over Eisenkot,” Ben-Gvir tells me in a rare interview on Oct. 19, referring to Netanyahu’s chief rival, the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. Pounding his chest, he adds: “What will really help Netanyahu be right wing is if I, Ben-Gvir, will be a senior minister and it’s a full right-wing government.”
The post he covets is defense minister, which would give him command over Israel’s armed forces and greater authority to pursue his vision for Gaza and the West Bank: fewer constraints on military operations, the “voluntary emigration” of Palestinians from both territories, and the expansion of Israeli control over lands he believes belong to the Jewish people. Netanyahu has resisted giving Ben-Gvir the portfolio. But Ben-Gvir and his allies hope to win enough seats to force Netanyahu to accommodate their demands or risk losing power. He may benefit from the rightward shift of Israeli politics, particularly among younger voters drawn to his confrontational style and uncompromising vision of Jewish sovereignty. In a Channel 12 survey of first-time Jewish voters, nearly three-quarters identified as right-wing or center-right.
Polls suggest a tight contest, with Eisenkot’s centrist Yashar party edging ahead of Netanyahu’s Likud in several recent surveys, but neither the prime minister’s right-wing bloc nor the opposition appears close to the 61 Knesset seats needed to govern. An average of four recent polls puts the two camps at roughly 50 and 53 seats, respectively, leaving Arab parties and smaller factions potentially pivotal. The result could be another fragile coalition; an unlikely unity government between Netanyahu and Eisenkot; or a prolonged deadlock that sends Israelis back to the polls.
Ben-Gvir, dressed in a white shirt and white kippah, speaks halting English. Under his leadership, Israel’s prison service has drawn allegations of abuse for its treatment of Palestinian detainees. But he wants a more direct role in determining Israel’s future in Gaza and the West Bank.
“If Israel wants to continue to live and not be destroyed, we have to capture all of Gaza,” he says. “We have to promote voluntary emigration. Gaza could be a Riviera. It’s a beautiful place. But we can’t have one Hamas member there.” His proposal would have Palestinians leave Gaza for countries willing to receive them, and then allow Israelis to establish settlements in the coastal enclave. It would reverse a defining decision of an earlier right-wing prime minister, Ariel Sharon, who in 2005 withdrew Israeli forces and evacuated more than 8,000 Jewish settlers from Gaza.
Ben-Gvir offers no clear explanation of which countries would accept large numbers of Palestinians, or how their departure could be considered voluntary under the conditions he proposes. “Gaza was always ours,” he says. “Israel is a tiny country. We have to be wider, broader. Hamas are terrorists who don’t just want to destroy Israel. They want to destroy the whole world.”
When I suggest that removing Palestinians from Gaza and resettling it would deepen Israel’s international isolation, he dismisses the concern. “I think that the stronger we are, we won’t be isolated,” he says. “Israel is isolated when it’s weak. If we help the population leave Gaza, we can be very strong.”
Ben-Gvir’s rhetoric and policy designs have drawn widespread condemnation at home and abroad, with critics across the political spectrum accusing him of inciting war crimes and eroding the foundations of Israeli democracy. “He’s a source of immense trouble,” Efraim Halevy, a former head of the Mossad, tells me.
His ambitions in the West Bank are no less sweeping. Ben-Gvir wants Israel to annex the territory, which he, like most Israelis, calls by its biblical names, Judea and Samaria. It is home to 3.3 million Palestinians and partially governed by the Palestinian Authority (PA), created by the 1993 Oslo Accords that envisioned a Palestinian state. Controlled by the Fatah party, the PA has a lightly armed security force that is trained by the U.S. military and historically works with Israel to suppress terror attacks. But Ben-Gvir wants Israeli security control over the area Palestinians envisage as the heartland of a future state. “We need to take away the weapons for the Palestinian Authority,” he says. “As of now, they are training in Jericho. They’re not training to direct traffic, are they? They want to do another Oct. 7.” A spokesperson for the PA did not respond to a request for comment.
The vision goes beyond annexation. Ben-Gvir says he would encourage millions of Palestinians who have lived in the West Bank for generations to pack up and go. “We want sovereignty in Judea and Samaria, where we also want voluntary emigration,” he says. “Just so we understand, we want voluntary emigration—not kicking anyone out. People will choose the option to leave.”
Whether Ben-Gvir can translate those ambitions into official Israeli policy will depend in part on the leverage his party wins on Oct. 27. He is counting on voters to strengthen his hand. “I hope the nation sends its message,” he says.
Ben-Gvir, 50, was born into a relatively secular Jewish family of Iraqi and Kurdish descent in Mevaseret Zion, a suburb of Jerusalem. His mother had belonged to the Irgun, the Jewish underground that fought British rule before Israel’s founding, but his parents were, by all accounts, not ideological zealots. Ben-Gvir took a different path. He became religious at 12 and, amid the violence of the first Palestinian intifada, gravitated toward the teachings of Meir Kahane, the American-born rabbi who advocated expelling Arabs from Israel and the occupied territories. By his teens, he was an activist in Kahane’s movement, which Israel eventually outlawed as a terrorist organization. Ben-Gvir was considered so extreme that the Israeli military barred him from compulsory service.
Today, Ben-Gvir continues to revere Kahane, even as he disavows some of his mentor’s most fanatical positions. “I went to his yeshiva. He did a lot of good things. He protected Jews. He was murdered sanctifying God’s name,” he tells me. “Not everything that he did do I fully agree with. In the past, I thought we should kick out all the Arabs from the land of Israel. Now I think there can be some. I accept that there are some Arabs who live here. And I have no problem with part of them. Those who recognize the State of Israel as the Jewish state. Those who are loyal to the Jewish State.”
As a young adult, Ben-Gvir moved to Kiryat Arba, a Jewish settlement overlooking the Palestinian city of Hebron, where Kahane’s legacy runs particularly deep. According to published accounts, he and his future wife, Ayala, visited the grave of Baruch Goldstein on their first date. Goldstein, an American-born physician and Kahane admirer, had massacred 29 Palestinian Muslims at prayer in Hebron in 1994 before being beaten to death by survivors. For years, Ben-Gvir displayed Goldstein’s portrait in his living room. He became an attorney for Jewish settlers and activists accused of extremist violence. He also acquired a criminal record, including convictions for incitement to racism and supporting a terrorist organization.
For years, Ben-Gvir remained on the fringes of Israeli politics, a familiar presence at settler demonstrations but an unlikely candidate for national office. Over time, he softened some of his rhetoric, publicly distanced himself from Kahane’s demand to remove all Arabs, and cultivated a more approachable persona without abandoning his annexationist aspirations.
His political breakthrough came under Netanyahu. Ahead of the 2022 election, the prime minister helped broker an alliance between Ben-Gvir’s party and Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism, giving Netanyahu enough seats to assemble a government. Netanyahu’s decision to bring two Jewish supremacists into government became emblematic of Israel’s rightward turn—and one of the factors in its growing international isolation.
As national security minister, Ben-Gvir has pursued a hardline agenda: expanding civilian gun ownership, imposing an increasingly draconian regime on Palestinian prisoners, and pressing for tougher policing of anti-government protests. He wore a noose-shaped pin as he championed legislation imposing the death penalty on Palestinians convicted of deadly terrorist attacks, and released an AI-generated video depicting Palestinian prisoners emerging from Israeli jails emaciated and weeping, a grotesque statement about the conditions of their confinement.
Ben-Gvir also encouraged Jewish prayer at the Jerusalem holy site known to Jews as the Temple Mount and to Muslims as Haram al-Sharif, challenging a decades-old arrangement governing the disputed religious site, which has traditionally permitted non-Muslims to visit but reserved the right to worship there for Muslims. Under Ben-Gvir, Israeli police have increasingly allowed Jews to pray at the site, a deliberate provocation to the Arab world, drawing condemnation from Palestinian and Jordanian authorities. “It used to be an apartheid up there and Jews could not pray,” he tells me. “That could not happen in any normal country. I returned justice to the Temple Mount.”
Ben-Gvir has also become one of the leading voices on the Israeli right seeking to shift responsibility for Oct. 7 away from Netanyahu and onto Israel’s military and intelligence establishment. Among the claims he repeats is that security officials failed to wake the prime minister as the attack unfolded—which is disputed by former security officials.
“Even if he’s not perfect, and even if he made mistakes, and he indeed made mistakes, what screwed him up on Oct. 7 was our intelligence,” Ben-Gvir says of Netanyahu. “The army, the intelligence, the Shin Bet. They are all to blame,” he adds. “Netanyahu is not clear of blame, but there are many people who are more at fault than him.”
Ben-Gvir’s relationship with the prime minister is not exactly warm. “I’m not backing him; I’m not his crony on everything. I think he’s much better than Eisenkot,” Ben-Gvir says. “I want to be next to him. I want him to be very strong. I want to pull him to the right.”
He tells me he would not join a unity government between Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a possibility if neither can assemble a governing coalition. “Governments like that are never good,” he says. “It's dancing in two weddings.” Besides, he adds, “It won’t fulfill my dreams.”
What Ben-Gvir wants from another Netanyahu government would place him at odds with the diplomatic framework advanced by the Trump Administration and its partners in Europe and the Arab world. The American-led Board of Peace envisions Gaza’s reconstruction under Palestinian leadership, the withdrawal of Israeli forces, and a possible path toward Palestinian statehood.
Ben-Gvir, on the other hand, wants Israeli sovereignty and the departure of much of Gaza’s Palestinian population. He cites polling that he says shows 52% of Gazans want to leave the territory, devastated by years of war and Hamas rule. If Israel helps that majority leave, he reasons, those who remain will eventually want to follow. “They will see it is successful for them, they’ll see there’s a future, there’s a life,” he says. “There’s good places in the world. Pretty places.” He offers no evidence that the remaining population would choose to relocate, or how such a migration could be arranged without coercion.
For Ben-Gvir and his allies, the coming election offers a chance to advance a far-reaching transformation of Israeli politics and society—to move the country toward a maximalist vision of a Jewish state, one with expanded territorial ambitions, fewer judicial constraints, and a government less inclined to heed international objections. Ben-Gvir dismisses concerns that such policies would cement Israel’s status as a pariah state. In his telling, the military campaigns against Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran demonstrate the value of uncompromising power. “We made Israel stronger,” he says. “When Israel is stronger, the world respects that.”
– With reporting by Liam Forberg

Trump budget cuts threaten late Redondo Beach couple's soccer refugee program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- A soccer program iACT founded by late Redondo Beach activists Katie-Jay Scott and Gabriel Stauring helped refugees in Chad find hope.
- The program helped former refugees Mohammed Annour and Moubarak Abdallah thrive in Sweden, where they raise families and coach.
- Trump administration cuts to foreign aid and tighter refugee policies threaten the program as humanitarian needs grow.
Mohammed Annour spent much of his youth living in a flimsy shelter in a dusty, overcrowded refugee camp in east Africa, where the days were long, the food was poor and the future nonexistent.
“Go to the army and fight. That’s one option,” said Annour, who fled war in Sudan for the refugee camp in Chad when he was 9. “The other one is you stay there. But you don’t have a future.”
If he had stayed, Annour, now 33, has little doubt how his story would have ended.
“Probably,” he said, “I’m dead.”
Instead, he’s in Sweden, raising two boys, working as a quality control inspector for a textile company and playing amateur soccer for a team in the country’s fifth division. And the only thing that separates his experience from the tens of thousands of desperate people he left behind in the camp is the fact someone believed in him enough to give him a chance.
“Everybody needs a chance,” Annour said. “Don’t throw people out. People just need a chance in life.”
“And we got that chance,” he continued, “because of Katie-Jay and Gabriel.”
That would be Katie-Jay Scott and Gabriel Stauring, a pair of South Bay activists who showed up at Annour’s camp on a blazing hot day in 2011, rolled a battered soccer ball across a barren field and transformed an untold number of lives.
Scott and Stauring founded the humanitarian group iACT largely to respond to the crisis in Darfur, a semi-desert plateau in western Sudan that has known nothing but war this century. But unlike many of the dozens of other similarly minded people and groups working in Africa, Scott and Stauring came not to preach, but to listen. They came with questions, not answers.
And what they were told was that the children in the camps needed more than food and shelter. They needed a routine, they needed recreation, they needed joy and they needed hope.
In other words, they needed soccer.
“Many organizations came into the camps. They just came around and took some pictures and then they leave,” said Annour, a slight man with a serious countenance. “I think [Scott and Stauring] understood us as humans, not just these kids or these people who need food or shelter.
“They saw another side. They saw these people that can make something in life.”
Stauring and Scott were killed in a car accident in Manhattan Beach five years ago, but their legacy lives on in the unique advocacy and aid program they created, one that uses soccer to teach skills and provide structure to refugees stranded in camps, shelters and intolerable poverty in four countries on two continents.
“They were so kind, careful,” Annour said. “Listening to everyone. It didn’t matter where you came from, which color you are. They were open and gave time to everyone they met.”
“Honestly, I didn’t know they were going to change my life or anything,” added Moubarak Abdallah, another refugee introduced to soccer by Scott and Stauring. “I saw them as other people who just come and go. But they were quite special people.
“They wanted to help our ideas shine, to [give] other people hope. They were listening to what I needed.”
Today, there are more than 5,000 children participating in iACT soccer academies in Chad, the Central African Republic, Cameroon and Mexico. Another 1,800 children are enrolled in the group’s Little Ripples preschool program, which also served 475,000 meals to students and staff last year.
But the organization, like many similarly focused humanitarian groups, is fighting for its survival amid a global backlash against refugees and migrants.
The hostility has been especially strong in the U.S., where the second Trump administration has sharply restricted immigration and asylum access and drastically cut congressionally approved spending for life-sustaining programs previously funded through USAID. Many European countries have followed that lead, adopting a stauncher approach to border enforcement and deportations and slashing support for development assistance by 13.8% in 2025, the largest cut in a decade.
This summer, violent anti-immigrant protests in South Africa forced more than 178,000 people to flee to Zimbabwe, Malawi, Nigeria and other countries, reversing a trend that has seen the region’s richest country welcome migrants to work on farms, in construction and other low-paid jobs. Public sentiment toward refugees and migrants has also hardened elsewhere, creating a crisis for nonprofit aid groups.
The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, or UNHCR, this month warned the gap between humanitarian needs and donor contributions is widening, leading to deep cuts and forcing aid groups to fight one another for the shrinking dollars that remain — all at a time when conflicts in Syria, Gaza and Ukraine have swelled the number of refugees worldwide to nearly 42 million; another 69 million people are displaced.
A couple killed nearly a year ago in a Manhattan Beach car crash ran soccer clinics at refugee camps around the world. This is how work has continued after their death.
That’s more than 1 out of every 70 people on Earth, according to the UNHCR.
Annour and his family were once part of that wave, fleeing their home in Sudan in 2003, stepping around dead bodies and witnessing unimaginable horror, to escape one in a series of continuing civil wars that have given way to genocide. More than 15 million people have been displaced in the 23 years of fighting, with more than 1.3 million still stranded in teeming refugee camps in eastern Chad.
Annour said he would have perished there if not for Stauring and Scott, who introduced soccer to their camp. Three years after the pair arrived, an international tournament for stateless players, the CONIFA World Football Cup, was held and iACT entered a 20-man team comprised of players from 12 camps. Annour, a left back, made the cut as did Abdallah, a physical midfielder with a perpetual smile who would become the team captain.
“No one is thinking this [is] going to be life-changing,” Abdallah remembers thinking. “You know, there was like a small chance but it became big dreams for us.”
The team, Darfur United, was outscored 39-0 in its two games in Ostersund, Sweden, but most of the players chose to stay in Ostersund rather than return to their camps and were welcomed by the Swedish government. They received asylum and eventually formed an integration team, the Mighty Cosmos, that advanced as high as the fifth division of Swedish soccer.
Abdallah is a natural leader, said Alan Barker, chairman of the Mighty Cosmos, and the kind of person who receives total respect from the other players.
“He is a sort of guy you can rely on 100%,” Barker said. “Personally, I would trust him with my life. He is a doer, not a talker. A problem solver not a problem creator. And he always wants the best for everybody.”
Annour, he added, has been troubled by knee injuries on the field but remains “a strong and quiet yet forceful personality of the group.”
“He is a passionate believer in fair play and honesty and has no room for dishonesty or deception in any aspect of life,” Barker continued. “Maybe that’s a reflection of his childhood in the refugee camps and Chad, where there was no time for such things. He’s a sort of guy whose name would be first on the team sheet. The team sheet of football and life.”
More important is the fact that the players, teenagers or young adults when they arrived in Sweden, have married, had children of their own, become citizens and integrated into the local community, where their civic work was this year recognized with one of Sweden’s most prestigious awards.
“I never dreamed to be in this position when I was a kid. I was trying to survive, to live day by day,” said Annour, who is working three jobs to support his sons, aged 1 ½ and 4.
“I’m here. I can provide for my family. Moubarak provides for his family. It’s like saving a generation, not just me and Moubarak.”
A Redondo Beach couple who offered Darfur refugees hope and a way out via soccer are killed in a four-car traffic accident in Manhattan Beach.
“It’s about the chances,” agreed Abdallah, 35, who also lives in Sweden where he coaches the Mighty Cosmos while raising a 5-year-old son.
“The door has to open. That’s all.”
iACT offered a way to open those doors when it first rolled that battered soccer ball onto a dirt lot. Without that, “these guys wouldn’t be here, wouldn‘t have the lives they have,” said Darren Hamlin, a British filmmaker who has started a Kickstarter campaign to fund a documentary on the refugee players.
By focusing on single players and their game and not the vastness of the sprawling global refugee crisis, Hamlin says the film has the power to redefine these former refugees not as obscure numbers but as flesh-and-blood people with dreams and talents and aspirations. That was what inspired Scott and Stauring when they founded iACT.
“Football has this power to transcend sports. It becomes an emotional thing,” said Hamlin, who is behind on his goal of raising $66,000 by the end of the month to expand work on the documentary. “It doesn’t matter how many stats or things we put in front of people; they don’t really pay attention.
“But football kind of goes deeper sometimes. Football is kind of the vehicle that delivers the message.”
Redondo Beach’s Gabriel Stauring and Katie-Jay Scott are determined to grow the Refugees United Soccer Academy, which teaches soccer and life skills to displaced Darfuri people and other refugees.
Getting that message out, however, is becoming increasingly difficult. As government funding for refugee programs around the world has dried up, groups like iACT have found themselves fighting for the same slice of a much smaller funding pie.
“Fundraising at all levels has become more difficult with the gutting of USAID, especially with the increase in larger NGOs [non-government organizations] applying for foundation grants,” said Merri Weir, a retired teacher and iACT board member since 2016. “It is becoming harder and harder because we’re competing with larger NGOs. The funding stream has become tighter.”
At the same time, the need has swelled.
“The refugee camps in Chad are still very unstable,” said Weir, who has visited the camps multiple times. “The current war has not ended and shows no sign of ending. Refugees are still coming across the border, which has more than doubled the number of Sudanese refugees.
“It is critical that we are able to sustain our current refugee-led programs.”
In response, Weir’s group, which will hold its annual fundraising event in Manhattan Beach next month, has considered everything short of a corner lemonade stand and selling chocolate door to door to make up for the lost financial backing it needs to continue what Scott and Stauring started.
“In the past, it is our uniqueness and our innovation and our refugee-led action [that] set us apart,” said Weir. “It was very appealing.”
The Trump administration complicated things even further in June 2025 when it instituted a travel ban and entry restriction list on Chad, leading the Chadian government to retaliate by revoking visas for American citizens, including aid workers. That means fewer children playing soccer and attending preschool, fewer meals being served — and fewer success stories like the ones told by Abdallah and Annour.
Players representing 29 countries took part in the Homeless World Cup, a tournament that aims to raise awareness about people who are homeless or refugees.
“I spent 12 years in a refugee camp,” Abdallah said. “People just hope to get a meal for the day. [iACT] brought the footballs and then just brought the idea. A chance to change our lives. Opportunity.
“There’s a lot of people in the refugee camps [that] could be pilots, doctors, better football players. Maybe there is the next Lionel Messi, Cristiano [Ronaldo], Lamine Yamal in the camp. But they don’t have any opportunity to get out.”
“The world is crazy. It’s just war everywhere,” added Annour, who is about to begin a college course on sports science. “Those people who don’t like refugees, who don’t want the United Nations to bring more refugees, they need to put themselves in our shoes.
“People are so naive to think they can just ignore what’s going on. It’s getting bigger every day.“
Abdallah and Annour may have left the camps, but the camps have not left them. The work they have done in Sweden includes the construction of a community sports and culture center, addressing crime prevention and mental health, refugee resettlement, and fundraising efforts that support the work of iACT and other groups working with the people they left behind.
“My mom is still in the same camp, so I’ve been back three times now with a lot of footballs, football boots and football equipment,” Abdallah said.
Scott and Stauring, who lived in Redondo Beach before the fatal car crash, thought they were bringing soccer to the camps in Africa, but what they really brought was hope and proof that if someone just opens the door, you might be surprised what you find on the other side.

Taipei rejects Lee Chen-hsiu's bid to run for Zhubei mayor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:52:37 UTC
19:52:37 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Taipei High Administrative Court on Thursday rejected former TPP Legislator Lee Chen-hsiu's (李貞秀) bid to run for Zhubei mayor after she challenged her disqualification.
CNA reported that the court said the Hsinchu County Election Commission had legal grounds to reject Lee's candidacy. It also warned that letting her run could spark election disputes and harm the public interest.
Lee registered to run for Zhubei mayor on Aug. 31. Still, the commission rejected her application on Oct. 8. Officials said she had not met the 10-year residency requirement because she submitted proof of canceling her Chinese household registration in March 2025.
Lee was born in China and moved to Taiwan after marrying a Taiwanese citizen. She established her household registration in the country in December 1999 but did not submit proof of canceling her Chinese registration until more than 25 years later, per CTS News.
Under an April 16 interpretation by the Mainland Affairs Council, the 10-year residency requirement begins when a person submits proof of canceling their Chinese household registration. The commission therefore ruled Lee was ineligible under cross-strait relations law, per UDN.
Lee challenged the decision and sought temporary permission to run while her case proceeded. However, the court found no clear evidence that the commission's decision was unlawful.
The court said further investigation would be needed to determine whether the government's interpretation imposed restrictions beyond those set by law. It added that Lee had not shown she was likely to win her legal challenge.
Judges warned that allowing Lee to run could create legal problems if she won the election but later lost her case. Such an outcome could lead to a challenge to her election victory or a new election.
The court ruled that the potential harm to the public interest outweighed the harm Lee would face from being barred from the election. It therefore rejected her request for temporary permission to run, although she can appeal the ruling.

China Focus: Farming by data: how smart agriculture is reshaping China's fields
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:51:54 CST
19:51:54 KST

HARBIN, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- As autumn winds ripple through fields of fragrant rice at a Beidahuang farm in northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, grower Wei Guodong rubs a freshly plucked panicle between his palms, revealing plump, gleaming grains.
"This year's harvest looks solid," he says with a smile.
The farm belongs to Heilongjiang Agriculture Company Limited, the A-share-listed arm of Beidahuang Group, a major state-owned agribusiness in the province.
Wei's confidence had been boosted months earlier, during the seedling stage, when the greenhouses at the farm underwent a full-chain smart upgrade that is now reshaping rice production in one of China's major grain-producing regions.
Liu Dong, a manager at the 852 Farm branch, said the company invested this year to retrofit its seedling greenhouses with sensors, automated film rollers, smart irrigation valves and panoramic cameras. The system monitors soil pH, temperature, humidity and light around the clock, allowing a single skilled technician to manage up to three greenhouses and cutting labor costs by about 60 percent.
That same data-driven approach runs through the summer growing season, when crops are most vulnerable to weeds, pests and weather. At the farm, an AI laser-weeding robot uses industrial cameras to distinguish crops from weeds in milliseconds. With millimeter-level positioning and a weed-removal rate above 95 percent, the machine can cover 80 to 100 mu (about 5.3 to 6.7 hectares) a day, easing labor shortages while reducing herbicide use.
By harvest season, multispectral drones and ground instruments at Heshan Farm measure chlorophyll levels and crop maturity in soybean fields. The readings are cross-checked with satellite remote sensing to produce high-precision maturity maps that show which plots are ready, which need more time and when the optimal harvest window opens.
"In the past, we relied on experience. Now we rely on data," said Liu Zhaokai, deputy head of the farm's agricultural development department.
Beidahuang's changes reflect a wider push in Heilongjiang Province to deepen the integration of technology and modern farming. The province's overall agricultural mechanization rate has reached 99.34 percent, the highest in China, with smart-agriculture demonstration zones being built to shift production from "watching the sky" to "watching the screen" -- a microcosm of the thousands of farms across China embracing smart agriculture.
Nationally, the shift has been made a priority in recent policy documents. The Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs has launched an action plan that calls for demonstration zones, agricultural big-data platforms and wider adoption of smart equipment.
Zhang Xingwang, Vice Minister of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, said that in 2025, the contribution rate of agricultural scientific and technological progress in China exceeded 64 percent. Smart agriculture applications now span the entire industrial chain, with more than 300,000 agricultural drones in use and annual drone operation area exceeding 460 million mu.
For farmers in the fields, the shift is already tangible. The rice in Wei's hands may still smell the same, but the way it was grown has been transformed from instinct and tradition to sensors, algorithms and screens. ■

Letter from Lhasa: A window into 20 years of change along the world's highest railway
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:51:21 CST
19:51:21 KST

by Xinhua writer Liu Zhoupeng
LHASA, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- As a Lhasa-based journalist, I used to see trains simply as transport between assignments. But as the Qinghai-Xizang Railway marked 20 years of operation, the journey itself became my story.
In 2006, the Qinghai-Xizang Railway opened to traffic, linking Lhasa, capital of southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, with the rest of the country by rail for the first time. With its highest point at 5,072 meters, it was -- and remains -- the world's highest railway.
This time, I bought a ticket to Xining, capital of northwest China's Qinghai Province and the other end of the line, and chose a window seat to see what had changed over 20 years.
In the morning, the train pulled out of Lhasa Railway Station. Out the window, glass facades of office buildings caught the sun, and wide boulevards formed a grid across land that had been open fields when the first train departed in 2006.
The station is in Liuwu, which became Liuwu New Area a year after the railway opened and is now the Lhasa High-tech Zone, a national-level high-tech zone whose core industries include new energy, the digital economy and financial services.
Better access has brought capital, talent and businesses, and local residents have benefited directly.
Dawa Sangpo, Party chief of the Liuwu community, whom I met at the ticket gate, said the community operates rental housing, hostels and street shops, and its collective income has increased fivefold.
"Six households once received subsistence allowances. Now none do," he told me, adding that per capita annual income has risen from 7,800 yuan (about 1,164 U.S. dollars) to more than 30,000 yuan over the past two decades.
The freight has changed too. Train attendant Wang Jiajia, a veteran on this line, told me that early trains carried mostly steel, fuel and daily necessities. Today, freight cars carry household appliances, pet carriers and furniture to the plateau, along with new energy vehicles for export via Xizang.
Figures from the railway authorities show that in 2025, freight between the region and the rest of the country increased 22 times over the 2006 level, with outbound shipments such as yak meat and highland barley climbing every year. The railway has become a corridor linking the national market with the plateau's specialty resources, moving more people and goods every year.
I was thinking about how the railway had reshaped the plateau when something outside the window caught my eye. As the train rumbled across a modern bridge, the majestic Potala Palace, a UNESCO World Heritage site dating back some 1,300 years, came into view on the hillside, its white walls and gold roofs glowing in the sun. It felt as if history and the present met in a single frame, and for a moment I could hardly look away.
The view caused a stir in the carriage. Passengers nudged each other toward the windows, raising phones and cameras to capture the moment.
Wang explained that many first-time visitors, both domestic and international, choose to travel to Xizang by train rather than by air. The plateau scenery outside the window is one attraction, and the onboard oxygen supply is another, allowing passengers to adjust gradually to the thin air rather than adapt suddenly after a flight.
With its pristine landscapes and rich Tibetan culture, Xizang received over 70.73 million tourist visits in 2025, up 10.71 percent year on year, with total tourism revenue up 9.51 percent to 81.68 billion yuan.
Several hours later, the train crested the Tanggula Pass -- the line's highest point at 5,072 meters above sea level -- and pulled into Yanshiping station at 4,721 meters for a four-minute stop. The stop, which opened to passenger service at the end of 2025, serves herders from four townships in Amdo County.
I struck up a conversation with Champa, a local herder who boarded at the station. We compared the trip: a bus ride to the county seat could be expensive and took more than four hours. The train now covers the distance in two hours for 30 yuan.
As the train rolled north, the view outside shifted from modern buildings to open grassland, where yaks and sheep grazed in the sun. Further on, the vegetation grew sparser, and kiangs and yaks appeared occasionally on the vast plain.
The railway has made room for wild animals, with 33 wildlife crossings totaling nearly 60 km located under bridges, on gentle embankment slopes and above tunnels. The 11.7-km Qingshuihe (Clear Water River) Bridge, which also serves as a wildlife corridor across permafrost, and other bridges were raised on stilts, leaving nearly 3,000 openings below.
"Trains are not allowed to sound their horns when passing these crossings," Wang told me.
Thanks to conservation efforts in recent decades, the number of Tibetan antelopes has increased from over 70,000 in the 1990s to over 300,000, and the International Union for Conservation of Nature has adjusted the species' status from endangered to near threatened, reflecting its population recovery.
On the human side, the numbers are no less striking. Since it began operation, the Qinghai-Xizang Railway has handled more than 100 million passenger trips, with more than 12.25 million passenger trips in and out of Xizang between 2021 and 2025.
Over the years, the rail network in Xizang has grown from a single line into a Y-shaped network, with the Lhasa-Xigaze line opening in 2014 and the Lhasa-Nyingchi line in 2021 joining the original spine.
According to a white paper released in March last year, Xizang's operational railway length grew from 701 km in 2012 to 1,359 km in 2024.
Inside the carriage, some passengers rested while using supplemental oxygen, some chatted and others looked at their phones.
Twenty years ago, boarding a train was an event on the plateau; today it is so ordinary that few people comment on it. I realized the railway has been woven into daily life here, turning the extraordinary into the ordinary. ■

Asia-Pacific Community: Traditional Chinese medicine finds wider audience in multicultural Malaysia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:51:20 CST
19:51:20 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- When Shyamala, an Indian Malaysian woman with a spinal condition, first considered acupuncture on a friend's recommendation, she had already tried various treatments and had been advised by doctors to consider surgery. An avid hiker, she was reluctant to take that route and decided to try acupuncture instead.
After several sessions, her back pain gradually eased, and her physical condition improved beyond her expectations. She later traveled to Peru for a hiking trip and has recently returned to Malaysia. She now turns to acupuncture as needed and shares her experience with friends, hoping more people will become familiar with the treatment.
Her story illustrates how traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), long associated with Malaysia's Chinese community, is finding a wider audience among people from different cultural backgrounds.
At Tung Shin Hospital in Kuala Lumpur, patients from outside the Chinese community are making up a growing share of those seeking TCM treatment.
Angeline Liew Ai Ying, deputy superintendent of the hospital's Chinese Medical Division (CMD), said such patients accounted for 17 percent of the division's patients so far this year, with the proportion increasing in recent years.
Acupuncture is particularly popular among them, Liew said. Common reasons for seeking treatment include health problems following a stroke, sleep disorders and pain.
Founded in 1881, Tung Shin Hospital is one of Kuala Lumpur's oldest medical institutions, offering both traditional Chinese and Western medical services. Its CMD provides acupuncture, internal medicine, gynecology, bone and joint treatment, and tuina massage. The hospital also conducts charitable consultations and community outreach clinics, extending its services beyond its premises.
Beyond hospitals, traditional Chinese medicine shops are also adapting to the needs of a changing customer base.
Kien Fatt Medical Store, a family-run business along Petaling Street with a history of more than 80 years, has witnessed changes in how people access traditional remedies. Ng Chee Yat, the third-generation custodian of the business, said the shop initially focused on the wholesale of Chinese herbal medicines while also providing traditional remedies to neighbors.
Today, the shop serves customers from different backgrounds. While many Malaysians outside the Chinese community are already familiar with acupuncture, Chinese herbal medicine can be less familiar to them and often requires more explanation, Ng said.
One challenge is convenience. Traditional herbal decoctions take time to prepare, which may not suit the routines of people with busy lifestyles. In response to changing needs, ready-made herbal preparations in pill form offer an alternative to decoctions, making traditional remedies easier to take and more accessible to customers, including those from the Malay community.
The exchange of clinical expertise between Chinese and Malaysian practitioners is another part of TCM's development in the country.
Yu Dongdong, an associate professor at Henan University of Chinese Medicine, returned to China in September after spending about a year working in Malaysia. During his stay, he treated local patients, took part in community health consultations and shared clinical techniques with Malaysian practitioners.
One of his early Malay patients was a man in his 60s who suffered from neck pain and numbness in both hands. After hearing from others that acupuncture might help, the man sought treatment from Yu.
Yu examined the man's pulse, and the patient felt that his assessment closely matched his condition. After about three acupuncture sessions, the man reported feeling much better and recommended Yu to a neighbor suffering from back pain.
The referrals continued. The man's daughter and other members of his community also sought treatment, Yu said. Some patients came to him already knowing they wanted acupuncture because friends or relatives had recommended it.
Yu also trained several local Malaysian Chinese medicine practitioners in acupuncture. One of them, who runs his own clinic, later told Yu that his patient numbers had doubled after the training. The practitioner also reported receiving more positive reviews on Google Maps, with patients praising his acupuncture skills, Yu said.
Yu said exchanges between Chinese and Malaysian practitioners offered opportunities to share clinical experience and techniques, helping local practitioners further develop their skills and enabling more people to understand and benefit from TCM.
"Taking traditional Chinese medicine overseas is a long-term effort to help more people understand and use it," Yu said. "Through exchanges and the sharing of clinical experience between Chinese and Malaysian practitioners, we can help bring the benefits of traditional Chinese medicine to more people." ■

France reports world's first documented case of human infection with Shamonda virus
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:51:17 CST
19:51:17 KST

PARIS, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- French health authorities announced Thursday the world's first documented case of human infection with the Shamonda virus. The patient died in early October. No health risk to the general population has been identified to date.
The Shamonda virus is transmitted to animals by biting midges of the genus Culicoides. First detected in Nigeria in the mid-1960s, the virus has been sporadically reported in cattle in West, East and Southern Africa, as well as in Japan. Despite circulating in Africa and Asia for several decades, no human infection had been officially documented until now.
According to the statement, the patient, who was severely immunocompromised, was receiving treatment in Lyon, France, for a serious illness. Preliminary investigations indicated that the brain complications observed in the patient before death were very likely linked to the Shamonda virus infection. At this stage, health authorities consider infection through the bite of a virus-carrying midge of the genus Culicoides in eastern France to be the most likely explanation.
The health authorities stressed that this was an exceptional case involving a severely immunocompromised patient. They have also notified the World Health Organization (WHO) and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) of the case. ■

Two weeks later, the girl took her own life. Her mother later discovered messages between the girl and her friend in which the victim revealed she had been sexually assaulted.

Twenty-three members of the U.S. House of Representatives have urged President Donald Trump to allow Ukraine to use the Starlink satellite network for military operations inside Russia.
According to The Hill, the lawmakers believe that such authorization would help Ukraine detect Russian missile launchers in a timely manner and strike them on Russian territory.
The initiative was led by Republican Joe Wilson. The letter was signed by 16 Democrats and seven Republicans, who urged Trump to personally contact SpaceX founder Elon Musk to secure the lifting of the relevant restrictions.
“We urge you to ask Elon Musk to allow Ukraine to use the Starlink satellite internet system to locate missile launchers on Russian territory. One phone call could save lives and increase Vladimir Putin’s incentives to negotiate,” the lawmakers wrote.
According to lawmakers, if Ukrainian forces cannot reliably intercept Russian missiles, they should be able to strike the launchers from which those missiles are fired.
The letter also noted that Ukraine had already approached Elon Musk with a request for an exemption from the restrictions preventing the use of Starlink for such operations inside Russia.
The lawmakers believe that Donald Trump could help secure the decision.
In July 2026, during closed-door talks at the White House, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reportedly asked the U.S. President Donald Trump to authorize the use of Starlink to guide long-range drones toward ballistic missile launchers on Russian territory.
In August 2026, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk held talks with former Ukrainian Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov.
According to reports, the talks proved ‘extremely unsuccessful,’ after which Musk reportedly became firmly inclined to deny Ukraine permission to use Starlink for such operations.
Following his departure from office on August 7, Fedorov said he was continuing negotiations with Musk but did not specify their subject or outcome.
