Across China: Wild apricots bring new life to north China mountain city
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:24:54 CST
16:24:54 KST

Farmers harvest wild apricots in Caifenggou Village of Chengde City, north China's Hebei Province, Aug. 10, 2026. (Xinhua)
SHIJIAZHUANG, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- In autumn in the city of Chengde, north China's Hebei Province, the wild apricot trees had shed their leaves, leaving only sturdy trunks and bare branches. Meanwhile, an apricot kernel trading market in Pingquan, a county-level city under Chengde, was still bustling.
"This truckload is eight tonnes. Good quality! Take a look!" Broker Wang Dawei exclaimed as he patted sacks and called out to the inspector. Plump apricot kernels were piled across the trading floor as farmers lined up to have their goods weighed.
Dozens of kilometers away, in the workshop of Chengde Huajing Activated Carbon Co., Ltd., gasification furnaces were running. In the raw material yard, piles of wild apricot shells rose like small mountains. Those shells, once used by farmers as firewood, are now being turned into a resource that "gives off light and heat."
"In the past, people burned them for cooking, and the smoke was choking. Now these apricot shells have turned into activated carbon, and their value has increased dozens of times over," said Wei Shujun with the company.
"The waste heat we generate can also supply heating to nearby residents. Nothing goes to waste. The company uses about 50,000 tonnes of various fruit shells annually, produces more than 10,000 tonnes of activated carbon, and provides heating to an area of 300,000 square meters," Wei added.
"Burning coal in winter used to be a hassle. Now the plant's waste heat reaches our homes, keeping us warm and clean," said Ma Guoqing, a local worker.
At a specialty store on the lane outside Chengde Mountain Resort, an imperial garden and temple complex in Hebei, apricot kernel products, hot tea and pastries made of apricot kernels have become popular choices for tourists.
Shop owner Cao Yang was serving freshly made apricot kernel tofu in a small aluminum bowl decorated with auspicious patterns and topped with a layer of golden osmanthus honey. Its sweet fragrance filled the air.
Li Fenglan runs a homestay in Guchengchuan Village, Luanping County, Chengde. In spring, wild apricot blossoms stretched across 100,000 mu (around 6,667 hectares) of hills, drawing visitors to the area.
"During those days, guest rooms were booked up half a month in advance, and we received dozens of tourists a day on average," she said. "Local specialties like apricot kernel drinks and honey were in short supply. Some guests even asked us to mail products to them after returning home."
Chengde lies in the heart of the Yanshan Mountains and is an important part of the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei water conservation area. Wild apricot trees are resistant to cold and drought with well-developed root systems, making them suitable for reforesting barren hills in this region.
According to an official with the Chengde forestry and grassland bureau, the city's wild apricot base now covers 4.27 million mu, with an annual output of 11,000 tonnes of apricot kernels.
"In the past, these mountains were bare. When it rained, gullies formed, and nothing would grow," said Guo Qiang, Party secretary of Caifenggou Village in Taitoushan Township, Pingquan. Currently, more than 20,000 mu of the village's rocky barren hills have been planted with wild apricot trees.
"The roots now hold the soil in place, the mountains are green, and everyone's wallets are fuller," Guo said. ■
A staff member makes apricot kernel tofu in Chengde City, north China's Hebei Province, Sept. 23, 2026. (Photo by Yan Ming/Xinhua)

Heating season formally kicks off in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
07:23:54 UTC
16:23:54 KST

MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. Net withdrawals (the net difference between withdrawal and injection volumes) of natural gas from Europe's underground storage facilities (UGS) turned positive for the first time this fall, according to TASS calculations based on data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).
This marks the official start of the heating season in the region. To date, Europe has managed to inject only 75% of the target gas volumes required for the upcoming winter.
As of October 20, Europe's UGS facilities are filled to 74.58% (14.58 percentage points lower than the five-year average for this date), compared to 82.8% a year earlier. This remains the lowest level recorded for this date since observations began in 2011. EU storage facilities currently hold about 81.7 billion cubic meters (bcm) of gas, which is 9.7 bcm less than last year's accumulation and the lowest level since 2013.

Digital AI worms can threaten business networks — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
07:22:05 UTC
16:22:05 KST

YEKATERINBURG, October 22. /TASS/. The potential spread of digital AI worms to Internet of Things (IoT) devices could threaten not only their owners but also corporations as infected cameras, TVs, and videoconferencing systems could serve as entry points for intranet attacks, Daniil Borislavsky, Product Director at Staffcop, told TASS.
"This problem doesn't just affect home users. Smart cameras, televisions, videoconferencing systems, and other similar equipment are actively deployed in corporate environments. If such devices are insufficiently secured and have access to the company's internal network, their compromise could potentially become a launchpad for further attacks on corporate infrastructure," the expert said.
IoT devices have long been considered a major vulnerability in network infrastructure, Borislavsky said. Manufacturers do not always prioritize their security, while users often fail to recognize this technology as a viable target for a cyberattack. To mitigate these threats, companies must strictly monitor all devices connected to corporate infrastructure, segment their networks, and track any suspicious activity, the expert added.

State by state, some SIR hurdles are falling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
07:19:16 UTC
16:19:16 KST

For booth-level officers in Goa, enrolling a voter no longer involves one particularly tedious search: tracing the elector or a parent in the electoral rolls of 2002. That requirement has gone from the current registration process. The papers needed to establish eligibility have not.In Dehradun, Vibhanshu Bhatt, the BLO for Ajabpur, says a wider choice of supporting documents has made it easier to answer voters’ questions. A retired govt employee, for instance, can now offer documents other than a pension letter to establish their status.“With voters now having more options, it has become easier for us to deal with public queries and concerns,” he said.Across several states, BLOs are returning to households, collecting documents to resolve notices issued during the special intensive revision (SIR), and helping eligible voters left out of the rolls apply for re-inclusion. Some are working with a wider range of evidence. Others are helping applicants through the regular registration process, without the additional declarations or links to old rolls required during SIR.
The states are at different stages, with officers handling pending verification, fresh enrolment or preparations for special summary revision (SSR). Nor has every state relaxed its documentary requirements. What connects much of the fieldwork is a more active effort to reach voters and help them complete the process.
From queues to doorsteps
In Delhi, voters served notices because their details contained discrepancies or could not be linked to the 2002 roll no longer have to routinely queue for physical hearings at electoral offices. BLOs visit their homes and collect supporting papers. Assistant electoral registration officers can dispose of cases without formal hearings where the verification is sufficient.For daily-wage earners, the earlier visits to election offices meant losing work. Minor spelling differences, such as Narendra and Narender, are now being corrected without extensive documentation, officials said.“Officials have been directed to facilitate eligible voters rather than reject cases over procedural difficulties. However, prescribed eligibility requirements and documents remain applicable and BLOs do see documents such as birth certificate, passport wherever applicable before submitting declaration forms recommending disposal of cases,” an official said.By October 16, around 25 lakh of Delhi’s 33 lakh SIR notices had been resolved, against around 4 lakh by September 29.In Maharashtra, the BLO mobile application now has an “Other/Equivalent” option. Added after a proposal from chief electoral officer S Chockalingam, it allows supporting evidence beyond the 13 categories originally prescribed to be submitted for scrutiny.
Then vs now
The provision is intended to help, among others, homeless people, particularly vulnerable tribal groups and sex workers who may lack the specified papers. Electoral registration officers (EROs) and assistant EROs assess the relevance and validity of the evidence.The numbers are substantial. Maharashtra issued notices to about 1.22 crore electors: roughly 59.76 lakh whose records could not be mapped to the previous roll and 62.48 lakh over logical discrepancies.BLOs can collect documents during home visits and upload them on ECINET for scrutiny. Where the evidence resolves the discrepancy, a routine personal hearing is no longer necessary. Further hearings can still be held when verification requires them.
Less searching through old rolls
In Ahmedabad, engineering student Krisha Patel found that enrolling as a new voter required fewer papers than some of her friends had been asked to produce.“Unlike some of my friends who were asked to submit proof that their father or grandfather was a voter, I was asked to submit basic documents like Aadhaar card, birth certificate and photos.”Gujarat chief electoral officer Sandip Sagale said BLOs had been instructed to follow revised EC guidelines issued on Oct 15.“The documents establishing the relation of applicants to parents and grandparents are no longer mandatory according to the revised ECI guidelines. Registrations by first-time voters are very encouraging.”In Uttar Pradesh, chief electoral officer Navdeep Rinwa says current enrolment uses the regular statutory Form 6. Applicants no longer have to establish links with the 2003 rolls through their own names or those of parents or relatives.This is a return to the standard registration procedure after SIR, rather than a new nationwide concession. Rinwa said the original statutory Form 6 is being used during continuous updating of the rolls and will continue during SSR beginning Nov 12.Madhya Pradesh has also instructed district election officials not to seek a separate declaration with Form 6. Applicants must still provide the prescribed identity and address documents and make the form’s standard declaration that their information is true to the best of their knowledge.In Bengal’s current special enrolment drive, an official from the chief electoral officer’s office said applicants need not submit Annexure IV, the declaration used to establish family links with existing or previous rolls. BLOs continue to accept documents from the EC’s prescribed list.For Goa’s BLOs, removing the search through the 2002 roll eliminates a difficult step. But they say the documents for enrolment under Form 6 remain the same, whether someone is applying for the first time or seeking inclusion after deletion during SIR.
Chhattisgarh SIR drive
Finding the voters left out
For another set of BLOs, the immediate task is to return to names that did not make it onto the rolls.In Keralam, a drive that began on Oct 15 involves comparing pre- and post-SIR rolls to identify eligible voters omitted during revision. In Thiruvananthapuram’s Fort ward, BLO N Sajankumar is helping such voters seek inclusion. The exercise also involves checking information on deceased electors against local body databases maintained by the Information Keralam Mission.Chhattisgarh has supplied BLOs with booth-wise lists for a month-long drive to locate eligible omitted voters. They are making household visits, holding polling-station camps twice a week and organising separate camps at educational institutions for young voters.“BLOs are going door to door and, if a person earlier marked absent or shifted is now found, the Form 6 process is facilitated immediately,” a state govt official said. “But the documentary requirements have not been relaxed. The same standard documents applicable to an eligible voter continue to apply.”Completed applications and field-verification reports go to EROs for scrutiny. Finding a person at home does not, by itself, settle the application.In Ahmedabad’s Amraiwadi, special evening camps are scheduled from Oct 21 for night-shelter residents, labourers and homeless citizens, ahead of publication of the draft roll on Nov 12.Bihar is deploying 90,172 BLOs for a drive to enrol left-out voters and first-time applicants, with house-to-house searches and verification of records. The exercise is scheduled to finish by Nov 8.Odisha offers a measure of the additions already made. Since SIR, around 35,000 voters have been added to its rolls. Nearly 1,200 were eligible voters left out during revision; the remainder were newly enrolled voters. BLOs conducted door-to-door visits during a three-day drive from Oct 7 to 9, and registration continues till Oct 31.Delhi’s BLOs, meanwhile, have begun re-verifying 47.6 lakh people categorised as absent, shifted, dead or duplicate after they did not submit enumeration forms and were excluded from the draft rolls. Eligible voters found to have been wrongly excluded will need to apply through Form 6, with assistance from BLOs.
When the usual apers are missing
In Jharkhand’s Khunti district, two tribal residents who lacked Aadhaar cards and conventional identity and address documents were enrolled after their eligibility was verified through land records, khatian documents and Gram Sabha testimony. Such evidence is subject to scrutiny by electoral registration officers, who decide applications on the basis of records available in each case.
Chief electoral officer K Ravi Kumar has directed registration officers not to demand special or additional documents at SIR hearings and to consider available records where conventional proof is unavailable. Alternative verification has also been reported for vulnerable groups, including orphans, destitute women, residents of old-age homes and transgender persons.“Depending on the category, declarations, institutional certificates and field verification may be used,” Kumar said.
BLOs can receive the evidence. EROs must examine it before deciding whether an applicant is eligible.In Dehradun’s Gandhigram, BLO Sarthak Srivastava said officers were finishing door-to-door checks of voters left off the roll, who now had more documentary options.In Goa, BLOs say residence proof remains a problem for tenants whose landlords refuse to give NOCs. Applicants must still furnish proof of residence, along with a birth certificate or school-leaving certificate.With inputs from Arvind Chauhan, Kaushik Pradhan, Nisha Nambiar, Alok K N Mishra, Abhay Singh, Saptarshi Banerjee, Ashok Pradhan, Kautilya Singh, Lisa Monteiro, Amarjeet Singh, Rashmi Drolia, Navjeeven Gopal, Manvir Saini, Sreerag P S, K Krishnachand, Jignesh Parmar and Kapil Dave

Ukraine and Norway Collaborate on Air Defense and Satellite Communications Projects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
07:17:59 UTC
16:17:59 KST

Ukraine and Norway are working on three joint defense projects.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced this during a press briefing with journalists, according to Ukrinform.
The first project aims to protect Ukrainian cities and infrastructure from Russian Geran-type strike drones.
According to the president, Ukraine expects to see concrete results in this area within the next six to eight weeks.
Zelensky decided not to disclose details of the second joint project until it has been fully implemented.
“Let everything arrive – everything we have been working on. The second project is FREYJA,” Volodymyr Zelensky noted.
The third joint defense project between the two countries is related to strengthening air defense and ensuring satellite communications.
As previously reported, Norwegian company Kongsberg has developed an anti-aircraft combat module for Ukrainian Inguar-3 armored vehicles.
The system is based on the CROWS platform, a mobile solution designed to detect and engage enemy drones, including Geran-type drones and, in some cases, cruise missiles.
According to sources familiar with the project, the platform is being developed specifically for Ukraine using donor funding. Once the first phase of testing is complete, it is expected to be handed over to the Ukrainian side.
The Norwegian government, together with Kongsberg and Ukraine, will also fund and develop missiles for the NASAMS surface-to-air missile system.
As part of the European FREYJA air and missile defense program, Norway could supply Kongsberg Fire Distribution Center (FDC) command posts featuring an open architecture, as well as Network Access Nodes.

Swiss and Austrian hostages freed in Niger
Unknown

Swiss and Austrian hostages freed in Niger
Two European nationals, a Swiss woman and an Austrian woman, who were kidnapped in Niger over a year ago, have been released. They have arrived in Benghazi, in eastern Libya, a local television channel announced during the night between Wednesday and Thursday.
“Two hostages, a Swiss woman and an Austrian woman, have been released after a year and a half in captivity in Niger and have arrived in Benghazi thanks to the intervention of the Deputy Commander-in-Chief,” Saddam Haftar, deputy commander-in-chief of Libya’s armed forces, said Libyan television Al-Masar announced.
+ Hostage in the desert: situation of kidnapped Swiss woman remains dire
In a video broadcast by al-Masar, the two women appeared tired and were sitting beneath a portrait of Field Marshal Haftar. They thanked their rescuers, speaking in French.
“I was taken hostage a year and six months ago. Now I am happy to be free and thank Marshal Khalifa Haftar and his son, General Saddam Haftar, for everything they have done for my release,” the 69-year-old Swiss woman said in the video.
The Austrian expressed a similar opinion. She had been a hostage for one year and nine months.
Libyan officials said the women would be handed over to
authorities in their respective countries after the necessary
procedures were completed.
Niger is battling a jihadist insurgency linked to al Qaeda and the Islamic State that spun out of a Tuareg rebellion in northern Mali in 2012. The fighting has led to many deaths and displaced millions across the central Sahel region over the past decade.
Kidnappings have also intensified in Niger over the last year.

Taiwan warns China plans cheap flights to influence elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
07:16:23 UTC
16:16:23 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — China plans to offer discounted flights to Taiwanese living in China to return home to vote in the Nov. 28 local elections, National Security Bureau Director-General Tsai Ming-yen (蔡明彥) said Thursday.
Tsai outlined several tactics China was using to influence the elections, per Liberty Times. One involved inviting supporters and campaign workers for selected candidates to travel to China.
Discounted tickets for Taiwanese living and working in China to return home to vote were expected to become available about three weeks before the election, he said. The bureau was also using AI tools to trace disinformation from China.
Other tactics included illegally funding candidates or political groups and organizing underground election betting. Tsai said hackers were also likely to target campaigns to obtain confidential information.
The bureau was monitoring nearly 100 suspected interference cases, Liberty Times reported. Tsai said he hoped it could complete its inquiries and refer cases to prosecutors if needed.
Separately, Tsai said the bureau was coordinating with the Coast Guard Administration to monitor Chinese coast guard activity east of Taiwan. The bureau planned to share relevant intelligence and analysis with Taiwan’s allies.

Expert urges Taiwan to attract young talent as power sector goes high-tech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
07:16:07 UTC
16:16:07 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan should attract more young professionals to the power sector as AI and semiconductor advances transform electricity systems, said Liu Wen-hsiung (劉文雄), chair of the Taiwan Power and Energy Engineering Association.
Liu said power had evolved into a high-tech industry, according to Business Today. Reliable electricity supports semiconductor manufacturing, while power systems themselves increasingly use AI, semiconductor technology, and new hardware and software to improve efficiency and reliability.
Electricity demand would grow alongside AI adoption and digitalization, creating long-term opportunities for engineers, he said.
Liu said Taiwan’s engineering education had traditionally emphasized technical training, with less attention to the humanities and social sciences. Engineers also need to understand economics, market mechanisms, law, and environmental issues.
These skills are particularly important for the energy transition, he said. Renewable energy projects depend on economic and social considerations, public policy, and land-use planning, as well as technical feasibility.
Liu said this was one reason he promoted interdisciplinary education during his tenure as president of the Industrial Technology Research Institute. He worked with several universities to establish programs encouraging electrical and mechanical engineering students to take courses in economics, management, and communication.
As the power sector expands into areas such as AI and smart grids, it increasingly draws on expertise from different fields, Liu said. He added that the sector underpins Taiwan’s industrial competitiveness and its cities’ international development.
“It’s a journey,” Liu said of the energy transition, emphasizing that the process cannot be completed overnight. Sustained progress requires continued technological innovation, stable institutional frameworks, and a new generation of professionals willing to commit to the sector over the long term.

Love affair to staged arrest: how a Romanian from England was jailed in Russia as a spy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
07:11:35 UTC
16:11:35 KST

Love affair to staged arrest: how a Romanian from England was jailed in Russia as a spy
LONDON, Oct 22 - Springtime in a park. Grey sky. A young man in a blue knitted hat and Adidas backpack walks down a path. Two burly security agents spring from a van and pin him to the pavement.
"What is your name?" asks a voice in English as a gloved hand holds the man's face towards the camera.
"David Adrian Kercso," he swiftly responds. Where is he from? "Romania. Romania."
The video, released by Russia's FSB security service and published by state media, purports to show the arrest of Kercso, now 23, a Romanian citizen who grew up in England and was sentenced earlier this year to 15 years for spying for Ukraine.
Reuters has not been able to verify all of the evidence in Kercso's case. But what is clear is that the arrest video is not what it purports to be: Reuters analysis of the video and of court records of his detention shows that at the time it was made he had already been in Russian custody for months.
It was filmed in a park inside Russia, in the southern city of Sochi. But Kercso's arrest was first announced elsewhere, by pro-Russian separatists across the border in Abkhazia, a breakaway region of neighbouring Georgia, who released their own video of him in their custody the day before he first turned up in a Russian court.
The FSB did not respond to requests for comment for this story, including why it would release a video depicting the purported arrest of a suspect who was already in custody.
Requests for comment were also sent to the Abkhazian separatists' SGB security agency, the Russian embassy in London, the Romanian and Ukrainian foreign ministries. None replied.
To Kercso's family, who say he was lured to the Black Sea coast to pursue a romance with a woman he had met online, the FSB video of a staged arrest is just another bizarre turn in a story that alarmed them from the outset. He hopes to lodge an appeal against his conviction.
"I told him to not go there because it's very dangerous, because it's a war," his mother Julia Kercso told Reuters. "And he never listened to me yet."
MOTHER WARNED HIM NOT TO GO
In late 2023, Kercso was living in the English city of Reading, west of London, working for a company that recycles electronics, when he first connected online with a woman called Valeria.
She was from Abkhazia, a picturesque sliver of Georgia's mountainous Black Sea coast that has been in the hands of separatists since the early 1990s.
An online romance blossomed, and his family says he travelled via Turkey in August 2024 to meet her.
Reuters obtained contact information for Valeria from the family but did not receive a reply to requests sent to her for comment.
According to Kercso's accounts to his family, the couple met up in Sochi, and after a few days crossed the border into Abkhazia, where Kercso stayed through the autumn. But his mother said the relationship deteriorated as he began to run short of money, and he told his family he would return home.
His trip back was planned for November 28, 2024, but he never arrived. That day, he stopped answering phone calls and messages. In subsequent letters from prison, Kercso said that was the day he was arrested in Abkhazia.
The first announcement of Kercso's arrest came two weeks later from the Abkhazian separatist authorities, who released a video on December 13 depicting their own SGB security service leading the young man from a car into a building.
He was shown confessing that he had been in contact with Ukrainian intelligence and had been told to film Abkhazian military sites with a drone.
In his letters, Kercso says that initial confession videotaped in Abkhazia had consisted of a text he had been ordered to memorise by his captors. The separatists told him that if he recited it on camera he would be sent home. But instead, he wrote, he was brought to the border and transferred into the custody of the Russian FSB.
The day after the Abkhazians released their video, Kercso was indeed in Russian custody, appearing before a judge at Sochi's Khostinsky District Court on December 14, according to court records available online.
It was the first of 10 court appearances that would be registered over the next four months, at which his detention in Russia would be extended roughly every two weeks.
TAKEN FROM JAIL TO FILM 'ARREST'
In his letters, Kercso says that the staged Russian video of his "arrest" was filmed in mid-April in Sochi, after he had already been captured in Abkhazia, transferred to Russia and held there for four months. He was awakened in jail around dawn by FSB officers who took him to a nearby location to film it.
Reuters analysis of the video is consistent with this account. Though the exact date cannot be established, ample green foliage is clearly visible, showing it was filmed after the start of spring, and could not have been filmed before he began the four months of detention documented in his 10 Sochi court appearances since December.
The location - a strip of parkland along Sochi's Matsesta River - can be established from visible features. These include the pathway layout, a bridge pillar, lamp posts, trees, a grassy strip and a wall, all of which match archive and satellite imagery of the area.
Evgeny Smirnov, a Russian lawyer familiar with the case, said it was common for the FSB to compel suspects to film dramatic arrest scenes long after they are detained.
"We have seen this in dozens of cases where individuals detained months earlier are taken to a city street, a forest, or a train station so that a staged arrest video can be filmed," he said.
Kercso says in his letters that in the months following his transfer to Russia he was beaten, held in isolation and tortured. Reuters could not independently verify those allegations.
When he was sentenced, the FSB said he had transmitted the location of Russian air-defence systems in Sochi to a Ukrainian intelligence agency in the summer of 2024. Video released by the agency showed him confessing to that charge.
Kercso says that confession was also coerced.
"None of that happened, they stole my life for no reason and fabricated everything," he wrote. He has learned Russian in prison, misses his family deeply and dreams of returning home.
"Now I know that coming here was a huge mistake," he said. "I was blinded by love and didn't see the warning signs." REUTERS

Beatings, cyberattacks and threats darken Vucic's Serbia ahead of elections

Beatings, cyberattacks and threats darken Vucic's Serbia ahead of elections
BELGRADE, Oct 22 - Serbian activist Marko Marjanovic was on his way back from the supermarket in Belgrade when masked officers bundled him into a car and took him to a police station basement where he was held in solitary confinement for two days under bright lights.
Marjanovic, a popular social media commentator and vocal opponent of Serbia's long-time leader Aleksandar Vucic, said he was terrified, and it wasn't the first time. Days before that, in August 2025, police had beaten up Marjanovic during anti-government protests, part of what he and his lawyer describe as a campaign to silence him.
As former President Vucic seeks to extend his 12-year hold on power by running for prime minister in an October 25 election, interviews with activists, student protesters and opposition politicians paint an increasingly authoritarian picture of the Balkan country where critics are routinely threatened, press freedoms are waning and corruption is on the rise.
"How much corruption...how much destruction of everything that should and must be of value here. Someone has to be held accountable," said Marjanovic, who has experienced lengthy social media bans for his posts, one of which included the phone number of acting President Ana Brnabic, who was speaker of parliament at the time.
Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) have repeatedly denied accusations of repression and corruption. His office and the Interior Ministry did not respond to requests for comment on this story.
PRESS FREEDOM AT NEW LOW AS PROTESTS GROW
Vucic is facing his biggest political challenge since coming to power: the student-led protest movement, which blossomed in the wake of the Novi Sad train station canopy collapse that killed 16 people in 2024, is now fielding 250 of its own candidates in Sunday's election. A poll this week put the students neck and neck with the SNS.
"For as long as the SNS have been in power, there has never been such good organisation on that pro-democratic side of society," said Dragan Popovic, who heads the Center for Practical Politics. "The more (Vucic) is threatened, the more the pressure increases."
After serving as information minister in the late 1990s when then-President Slobodan Milosevic sought to silence critics of Serbia's war in Kosovo and subsequent clashes with NATO, Vucic broke with the ultra-nationalist Serbian Radical Party in 2008 and now says that he wants the country to join the European Union.
But Serbia's credentials have slipped.
The 2026 World Press Freedom Index compiled by Reporters Without Borders (RSF) ranked Serbia 104th out of 180 countries, the lowest ever, and also the worst in the EU-Balkan region. In Transparency International's 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, Serbia's score was the lowest in two decades.
According to RSF, six Serbian journalists - including four who fled this year - are in exile because of threats to their security motivated by political attacks. Data from the Slavko Curuvija Foundation, a non-governmental media organisation, says that Vucic verbally attacked journalists and media outlets at least 182 times in the first nine months of this year.
Vucic has denied intimidating the media and says he has not shut down any news organisations.
But veteran reporters say things are getting worse. Veran Matic runs a commission for the safety of journalists. In June, a young man attacked him and took his phone when he filmed a protest, and he was insulted on the streets. He blames the violence on Vucic, who has publicly singled out Matic for criticism. Reuters could not verify the assertion and Vucic's office did not respond to a question on the matter.
"There is almost no day, almost no week, without attacks occurring, not only against me, but against many journalists," Matic told Reuters.
CYBERATTACKS AND SPYWARE
Members of the student movement and other high-profile Vucic adversaries have also been the victims of cyberattacks, watchdogs say. Digital rights group SHARE Foundation said in September that 14 people had been targeted with advanced spyware.
Jelena Kontic, who has been part of the nationwide protest movement to oust Vucic, said she received a message from Apple in March saying that the Pegasus spyware tool may have been installed on her phone. Later forensic tests, including by Canadian cyber watchdog group Citizen Lab, confirmed this, she added.
"They had access to your entire life," Kontic said. "They knew when I have a workout, when I sleep, when I eat, when I drink water, how much water I drink, what I eat."
Serbia's Security Information Agency called claims of state involvement "trivial sensationalism" and Brnabic said at the time that the students had "absolutely not" been spied on. Interior Ministry officials have also dismissed allegations of cyberespionage.
Kontic is not alone, though. Two Serbian opposition figures were recently targeted with powerful cyberespionage tools, according to one of the men and a report issued on Monday by Citizen Lab.
Reuters could not determine who was responsible for the alleged infections. Israel's NSO Group, the maker of Pegasus, has said it only sells to governments.
VIDEO CAPTURES BRUTAL BEATING
Nowhere is the threat to safety more apparent than on the streets, where protesters say police have often used force against peaceful demonstrations.
Dusan Radovic, a 26-year-old architect, was helping someone who had fallen over as police rushed a crowd of protesters in the town of Valjevo in August last year when officers in riot gear began striking him with batons.
"Ten of them surrounded me, they kicked me, spit on me, at one point one stepped on my head. They put me up and then continued hitting so I fell down," Radovic told Reuters.
A video verified by Reuters captures the beating. It was two months before he could walk without limping.
Radovic was among 25 people, some of them minors, who were badly beaten that night, according to an independent report by forensic specialist Dr. Djordje Alempijevic.
"Injuries are not the result of isolated incidents or necessary police self-defence, but demonstrate a clear, organised and systemic pattern of punitive police brutality and torture," the report said.
The Interior Ministry did not respond to a question on the Valjevo protest and the report.
"My first reaction was anger, anger at those people capable of such cruelty," Radovic told Reuters. "But then I realised I cannot withdraw after this. I have to fight for justice and truth." REUTERS

Israeli settlers steal Palestinians' olives as attacks on harvest grow more violent
LUBBAN AL-GHARBI, West Bank, Oct 22 - Brought to tears as he recalled Israeli settlers hitting his cherished olive trees with sticks and taking off with the olives, Palestinian Ahmed Salem said he feared being attacked if he tried to intervene.
Settlers have intimidated Palestinians harvesting their olives in the occupied West Bank for decades, but this year, not only has violence increased sharply, theft has been widespread, according to Palestinians, Israeli rights groups and the UN.
The settlers dumped Salem's olives into sacks and then drove them to a nearby Israeli settler outpost to be pressed into olive oil, the 50-year-old Palestinian told Reuters of the incident around two weeks ago near his village Lubban al-Gharbi.
"How would you feel if something that belonged to you was being violated, and you could do nothing about it?" he asked.
The couple living in the outpost, whose olive press settlers have urged Israelis to use for West Bank olives, declined multiple Reuters requests for comment, while the Yesha Council, which oversees Israeli settlements in the West Bank, did not immediately respond.
The attacks have accelerated ahead of an Israeli election next week that opinion polls show Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his pro-settler coalition could lose to opponents who have taken a more critical stance against settler violence.
'SETTLERS CAN COME AND GO FREELY'
The olive harvest starts with the onset of cooler weather, allowing Palestinian families to gather in the lush, terraced groves that they have groomed for generations.
"My six-year-old son remembers going there with me, eating there, making tea there," Salem said.
With the establishment of hundreds of small settler outposts under Netanyahu's government since 2022, the military has increasingly restricted Palestinian access to areas nearby, including many olive groves.
"This creates a situation where Palestinians, in many of the cases, many of the lands, especially in proximity to settlements and outposts, cannot enter the land and harvest the trees," said Ziv Stahl, executive director of Israeli rights group Yesh Din.
"But settlers can come and go freely, and that's what they do."
Even when Palestinians can access their trees, it is not without risk. Yesh Din on Wednesday reported 125 physical attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters over the 24 days since the season began and 168 incidents of crop theft, with Israeli military forces present in at least a quarter of cases.
An Israeli military official said it takes acts of violence, criminal activity and attempts to undermine security very seriously. The official did not refer to settlers or comment on the reports of olive theft in the presence of the Israeli military, which has separately uprooted trees with excavators, citing what it said was a need to prevent Palestinian attacks.
The removal of Palestinians' olives has met with widely differing responses from Israeli rabbis.
"I call it theft. From my perspective, I define it as theft or robbery, and it is forbidden," said Zev Weitman, the rabbi for the Alon Shvut settlement south of Bethlehem.
Prominent Orthodox rabbi Dov Lior said settlers should harvest across the West Bank, asserting in an open letter that Palestinians had no ownership rights to the land and that harvesting olives fulfilled "the commandment of conquering the land."
'IT'S EITHER US OR OUR ENEMY', SETTLERS SAY ON SOCIAL MEDIA
Hundreds of acres of the land around Salem's village, Lubban al-Gharbi, including olive groves, were fenced off and seized between 2023 and 2026 by Avichai Farm, an Israeli settler outpost built on a nearby hill.
Salem said villagers have seen settlers harvest olives from the seized land and take them to the outpost's olive press.
At the start of the olive harvest, settlers posted on social media calling on Israelis to harvest West Bank olives and bring them to Avichai Farm's press.
"Both fine oil and strengthening the Jewish hold on the vast expanses of our land!," read a message on a settler Telegram group. "It's either us or our enemy!"
The press at Avichai Farm advertises "premium products produced by Avichai Farm" with olive oil at about $20 a bottle via a website run by the Farms Association, a settler group that Reuters has reported receives significant financial support from the Israeli government, which says the aim is to promote peace.
The Farms Association did not immediately respond to a request for comment and the couple who live on the farm with their children declined to be interviewed by a Reuters reporter who approached the area on Sunday.
On a road leading to Avichai Farm, Reuters spoke to a man who declined to be identified and said he had driven from a settlement around 90 minutes away to press 14 bags of olives from trees he said he grew himself.
Lubban al-Gharbi villagers and other Palestinians who have lost land to settler expansion say the harvesting of olives from trees in groves seized from Palestinian land constitutes theft.
UN bodies and most countries deem Israel's settlements on land occupied in war illegal under international law regarding military occupations. Israel rejects this, viewing the territory as disputed rather than occupied.
'WE PAY IN BLOOD FOR THE OLIVES'
During this year's olive harvest, Palestinian authorities say three Palestinians have been killed in daily militant settler attacks, which have also injured several journalists, European diplomats and a French mayor.
Stahl from the Yesh Din Israeli rights group said the violence was "part of a campaign of ethnic cleansing, paving the way for the annexation of the West Bank without its Palestinian population."
Israel, which has considered the idea of annexation, said it is investigating some of the incidents.
An Israeli government spokesperson said olives "picked by a Jew in the ancestral homeland of the Jewish people" did not constitute theft and that Jews owned and cultivated "millions of olive trees" in the area. No one should take the law into their own hands, the spokesperson added.
Palestinian farmer Samer Ben Shamsi said masked settlers attacked him on October 9 in the Palestinian village of Beita near Nablus, then sped away in a pickup truck with his harvest of olives after he and other farmers fled.
"This year, they steal without fear because they have a state and a powerful force backing them," Ben Shamsi said, referring to the security forces.
Within the past year alone, settlers had shot him in the leg, beaten him and smashed his possessions, he said.
"We pay in blood for the olives." REUTERS

Geopolitical shocks are reconfiguring the Swiss industry’s coffee supply chains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22

16:00:00 KST

Geopolitical shocks are reconfiguring the Swiss industry’s coffee supply chains
War is a top concern for Swiss coffee traders and alternative routes a top priority. But adapting supply chains in an era of constant disruption is no easy task.
Next time you sip a cup of coffee you can thank the Swiss Coffee Trade Association (SCTA). SCTA members – such as Nestlé, Starbucks, Sucafina, Olam, COFCO and LDC – represent over half of the coffee volume traded globally. Switzerland is a globally important coffee trading hub but threats to shipping routes and rising oil prices are pressuring supply chains. Participants polled at this year’s SCTA annual forum on October 1 listed “war” as their main cause for concern and “flexibility and alternative routes” as their top priority.
Shipping woes
Coffee beans are grown and harvested in South America, Asia and Africa. The beans called “green coffee” must then be transported across oceans to Europe and North America where most coffee roasters are based. According to the International Coffee Organization (ICO), of the 183.6 million 60kg bags of coffee harvested in 2025, 77% was exported via 246 different routes. The most popular routes by volume are exports out of Brazil, Colombia and Vietnam to Europe or the United States. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz since February has not had a major impact on coffee trade but has forced carriers to reroute vessels and add fuel surcharges which have had a knock-on effect on coffee traders. The shortest shipping route between Asia and Europe have effectively been closed. Shipments of coffee beans from Vietnam must take the longer route via the Cape of Good Hope.
“We operate as a network. If one route is affected it has a knock-on effect on our entire shipping fleet,” a senior executive at a European shipping company told coffee traders at the SCTA forum. The executive wished to remain anonymous because the comments were made as part of a panel discussion meant for coffee traders.
The European shipping firm manages 700 vessels that transport 25,000 containers from Asia to Europe. According to the executive, rerouting coffee through the Cape of Good Hope increased transit time for their shipments by 20 days from Asia to Europe.
The new norm
It remains to be seen if such route diversions become the norm. Maritime research firm Drewery estimates that Suez Canal transits will return to 80% of their pre-diversion levels by February 2027. However, cost savings from shorter shipping time compared to the Cape of Good Hope will not be as significant as before because from now on insurers are likely to charge a war-risk premium which the shipping companies will pass on to coffee traders as surcharges.
“Coffee traders must get used to fast and bold decision-making with incomplete information because this ‘never normal’ situation will continue and exception management will be critical,” the shipping company executive said.
More
How Switzerland became a land of coffee
The Hormuz crisis thus served as a kind of litmus test for the resilience of coffee traders’ supply chains.
“Companies doing well now are the ones that were well-prepared. The companies that waited longer to adapt to longer shipping times did not do so well,” says Dany Barkha, global head of logistics at Geneva-based coffee trader Sucafina.
The company chose to act fast and commit to the longer transit time rather than wait to see how the situation would evolve.
“Putting the coffee on water with delayed transit time is better than waiting for the unknown. And the unknown is still not known till date after months of conflict,” says Barkha.
According to Barkha, resilience will not be an option but a compulsory core skill in supply chain management. He says in the future, coffee traders should invest in diversification of routes, smart inventory planning and strengthening relationships with shipping companies. Sucafina invested in a combination of all three to ensure a resilient supply chain.
“Diversification of routes gave us flexibility. Smart inventory planning bought us time and the carrier relationship gave us solutions when we hit severe disruptions,” says Barkha.
Rethinking supply chain planning
“In most cases, coffee supply chain is ‘just-in-time’. Roasters know they can buy spot coffee and survive a couple of weeks during a crisis,” says José Luis Pérez, head of commodities at Commodity Supplies AG. The canton Schwyz-based ocean freight broker has around 200 coffee customers.
According to Pérez, this “just-in-time” strategy is no longer as attractive as before because unexpected conflicts and changing government policies occur more often. The more time the coffee shipment is at sea, the more money a roaster loses as they have to make up for any shortfall by sourcing beans from warehouses more expensively. To avoid running out of beans, coffee roasters are now obliged to have larger inventories even if it means tying up more working capital and increases in financing and insurance costs.
“Five to 10 years ago the focus was on efficient supply chains, now it is resilient supply chains and in the future it will be adaptable supply chains,” Pérez concludes.
More
Better latte than never: Swiss coffee industry joins forces to improve conditions of coffee growers
Being adaptable means letting go of the old ways that no longer serve their purpose. Some of the supply chain planning in the coffee industry is no longer fit for purpose after the Hormuz crisis, according to Aleks Sidorecs, global head of supply chain at Swiss coffee trading firm Volcafe.
Instead of focusing on reports from the last month, he says the industry will have to keep track of leading shipping indicators that signal where disruptions are likely to happen, such as pre-shipment sample approval status, shipping instructions status and booking placed and accepted.
“These indicators give coffee industry players advance signals of potential disruptions and help them plan accordingly,” says Sidorecs.
The price of a cup of coffee
Reduced supply and increased demand have pushed green coffee prices to record highs over the last two years. ICO reported the first surplus in five years for 2025/2026 but consumers are still paying more because beans bought expensively are still circulating in supply chains. For example, price increases accounted for 4.7% of Nestlé’s coffee sales growth in the first half of the year. The Swiss multinational with brands like Nespresso and Nescafe expects lower green coffee prices in the second half of the year but cautioned investors that this will be “offset by some higher transportation and energy costs arising from the Middle East conflict”.
Weather conditions in top coffee producing countries like Brazil or Vietnam play a much bigger role in determining coffee prices than logistics costs. However, shipping bottlenecks can compound existing price pressure, especially when supply is already tight. Burkha reiterates that the cost of coffee isn’t only shaped at its origin and when logistics becomes more expensive, coffee becomes more expensive to move, store, and deliver.
“Not every increase reaches the consumer directly, but the pressure builds across the value chain. And that is why efficient logistics matters more than ever,” he says.

Swiss drone defence: ‘We’re flying partly blind’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Swiss drone defence: ‘We’re flying partly blind’
A drone suddenly appears over an airfield or nuclear power plant. Is it the mistake of a hobbyist or an act of espionage? According to security expert Ivo Capaul, Switzerland lacks a clear picture of the threat.
Swiss public broadcaster SRF: Is the danger posed by drones in Switzerland being underestimated?
Ivo Capaul: Generally speaking, yes. In Switzerland, we have lost some sense of the current threat situation. We certainly need to take this issue seriously and address it.
SRF: How serious is the problem? How often do potentially dangerous drones fly over critical infrastructure, for example?
I.C.: In a sense, we’re flying blind. There is no national, centralised record of drone sightings. Although the army records incidents, it is not always clear what is behind the figures.
More
What does the future hold for Swiss neutrality?
According to the army, around 80% of cases involve misidentifications or drones operated by harmless hobbyists. In 20% of cases, it could be a hybrid attack by a state.
Ivo Capaul is a researcher in the Defence Policy and Armaments Team at the Centre for Security Studies (CSS) at the federal technology institute ETH Zurich.
SRF: How difficult is it to distinguish between a harmless drone and a hostile one?
I.C.: It’s not that simple. These days a commercial drone effectively has a virtual number plate and is registered. A sensor can identify it. But a malicious actor can assemble a drone themselves using off-the-shelf parts or tamper with the control system. This makes identification difficult and requires sophisticated radar sensors.
More
Our newsletter on geopolitics
SRF: What would be the most important steps to take to get out of this “blind flight” situation?
I.C.: It is important to install sensors at critical infrastructure sites so that we can detect what is happening in the sky. Furthermore, there needs to be a reporting obligation for operators of critical infrastructure, similar to that for cyber-attacks.
They must report any drones they spot. This is the only way we can obtain a picture of the national situation on which we can take action.
SRF: What are the main aims of state actors that carry out drone flights over critical infrastructure?
I.C.: Often people think it’s all about sabotage: a drone loaded with explosives that flies into a target. But in the context of hybrid operations a drone can pursue a wide variety of objectives: espionage, testing a facility’s security measures, delegitimising the security authorities or sowing uncertainty among the public. The spectrum is very broad.
SRF: Who is operating these drones?
I.C.: Attribution is very difficult and time-consuming. The case at Leipzig Airport, where Germany clearly identified Russia as the perpetrator, is an exception. In most cases, it cannot be conclusively proven whether a state actor is behind it, or which one.
SRF: The war in Ukraine shows just how rapidly drone technology is developing. Is it possible to protect yourself effectively?
I.C.: There is no such thing as absolute security, nor will there ever be. It would be illusory to believe that every sensitive site in Switzerland could be protected by a defence system. That is why we must prioritise. Where is the threat greatest?
We must also strengthen our own defences, for example through structural measures. A protective net can shield critical infrastructure from espionage or sabotage. Resilience is also important, such as the ability to resume normal operations quickly following an attack.
More

Kongsberg to arm Polish K2 tanks with remote weapon stations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:46:20 UTC
15:46:20 KST

- Kongsberg signed a contract worth about NOK 700 million ($75 million) with Hyundai Rotem to supply PROTECTOR RS4 remote weapon stations for Poland’s K2 program.
- The stations will equip K2 tanks, armored recovery vehicles and combat engineering vehicles, with first deliveries for integration starting in spring 2027.
Norway’s Kongsberg will arm Poland’s new K2 tanks and their support vehicles with its PROTECTOR RS4 remote weapon stations. The contract, worth about NOK 700 million ($75 million), was signed with South Korean tank maker Hyundai Rotem.
The stations will go on three versions of the K2 built for the Polish Armed Forces: the main battle tank itself, the K2 armored recovery vehicle and the K2 combat engineering vehicle.
Kongsberg will begin shipping the first stations to Hyundai Rotem for vehicle integration in spring 2027. The deal also includes a support package covering initial spare parts, training for Polish crews and other services needed to keep the systems running once the vehicles enter service.
A remote weapon station lets a crew fire a roof-mounted machine gun or automatic grenade launcher from inside the armor, using a joystick and a screen fed by day and thermal cameras, so no one has to stand exposed in an open hatch to engage a target. The RS4 can carry a 12.7 mm (.50-caliber) heavy machine gun, a 7.62 mm or 5.56 mm machine gun, or a 40 mm grenade launcher. Its stabilized mount lets the gunner shoot accurately while the vehicle is moving. Kongsberg has delivered more than 20,000 PROTECTOR stations to armies around the world, and the U.S. Army’s Common Remotely Operated Weapon Station, known as CROWS, belongs to the same family.
“This contract further strengthens the long-standing cooperation between KONGSBERG and Hyundai Rotem Company and confirms KONGSBERG’s position as a leading supplier of advanced remote weapon systems for international defence programmes,” said Kjetil Reiten Myhra, president of Kongsberg’s Defence Systems division.
The order is tied to the second executive contract Poland signed with Hyundai Rotem in August 2025, a deal worth about $6.5 billion that covers 180 more K2 tanks and 81 support vehicles built on the K2 chassis. Under that agreement, 116 tanks in the K2GF configuration are being delivered in 2026 and 2027, and the first 28 of them reached Poland in August for the 16th Mechanized Division. The remaining 64 tanks will be built to the upgraded K2PL standard, which adds an active protection system and an anti-drone system. Sixty-one of them will be assembled at the Bumar-Łabędy plant in Gliwice between 2028 and 2030.
The 81 support vehicles, due between 2029 and 2031, are 31 armored recovery vehicles, 25 combat engineering vehicles and 25 armored bridge layers. Kongsberg’s contract names the recovery and engineering versions but not the bridge layer. The recovery vehicles tow damaged tanks off the battlefield, and the engineering vehicles clear obstacles and minefields under fire. The RS4 stations will let their crews defend themselves without leaving the protection of the hull.
Kongsberg and Hyundai Rotem first agreed to work together on remote weapon stations and unmanned turrets in September 2022. That was shortly after Poland placed its first order for 180 K2GF tanks, which was completed in November 2025. Poland already buys heavily from both companies, fielding hundreds of South Korean K2 tanks alongside Kongsberg’s Naval Strike Missile in its coastal missile units.
The first RS4 stations are due at Hyundai Rotem in spring 2027. K2PL tank deliveries begin in 2028, and support vehicle deliveries start in 2029.

How Türkiye is helping Baltic states meet steel demand amid dwindling supplies from Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:45:30 UTC
15:45:30 KST

The three Baltic countries – Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania – are facing a sharp reduction in steel supplies from Russia following its years-long conflict with Ukraine and the resulting EU trade restrictions against Moscow.
This evolving geopolitical development has given Türkiye, already Europe’s largest steelmaker, an opportunity to emerge as a viable alternative supplier to these three EU members.
With no significant domestic steel production, these countries traditionally relied on imports. Russia accounted for a dominant share of regional supply before the EU stopped its members from importing steel from Moscow.
But the restructuring of trade relations after the Russia-Ukraine war has created space for established exporters, such as Türkiye, to fill the vacuum left by traditional trade partners of the Baltic states.
Lithuania imported approximately 1.45 million tonnes of steel in 2025. Türkiye supplied about 10.2 percent of the total, trailing only Poland.
A trade delegation to Latvia and Lithuania early this month, consisting of 19 Turkish steel producers and exporters, held more than 300 bilateral meetings with regional importers.
Media reports suggested they laid the groundwork for roughly $100 million in potential business deals.
Demand from the Baltic nations consists of reinforcing bars or ‘rebar’, which are embedded inside concrete to add tensile strength and prevent cracking.
Other items in demand are welded pipes, and hot-rolled flat products, such as steel sheets, coils, or plates that can be reshaped and used in heavy industrial equipment.
Last year, Türkiye surpassed Germany as Europe’s biggest steel producer. China leads global crude steel output by a wide margin, followed by India, Japan, the US, and Russia. This makes Ankara the world’s seventh-largest steel maker.
Experts say the competitiveness of Turkish steel should be judged on total delivered cost rather than headline mill prices.
“Turkish producers can be competitive in several product categories, particularly reinforcing bars, welded pipes and certain flat-steel products,” Baris Alpaslan, an economist and chief adviser at IC Holding, a Turkish conglomerate with energy interests, tells TRT World.
Türkiye benefits from an established steelmaking industry, a broad export network, and geographic proximity to European markets, which support competitive pricing and flexible delivery, he adds.
However, he cautions against blanket claims that Turkish steel is always cheaper.
Competitiveness varies by product, grade, production route, energy and raw-material costs, order size, freight, insurance, financing, and delivery reliability, he notes.
Regulatory factors matter too: the EU’s steel import regime, effective July 1, provides tariff-free quotas totalling 18.3 million tonnes a year across 26 steel product categories. There will be a 50 percent duty on out-of-quota imports of steel.
The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), the EU’s environmental policy tool that places a carbon price on carbon-intensive goods imported into the bloc, further elevates the importance of emissions data and verification, Alpaslan says.
Mian Waqar Badshah, assistant professor in the Faculty of Economics at Istanbul University, tells TRT World that Turkish steel is “well-positioned to compete in the Baltic market” in rebar, welded steel pipes, and hot-rolled flat steel categories.
Even though Turkish producers can offer an “attractive alternative” to European suppliers, EU producers still retain advantages in proximity, distribution networks, shorter lead times and, in some cases, lower regulatory or administrative friction, he insists.
The new EU quota regime and 50 percent out-of-quota duty can “materially affect” the economics of Turkish steel exports, depending on the product category and applicable quota conditions, Badshah says.
Can Turkish steel mills meet EU standards?
Solidifying its position in the global steel supply chain as a dominant player, Türkiye’s crude steel production increased 6.8 percent year-on-year to 26.6 million tonnes in the first eight months of 2026.
Exports of Turkish steel grew 3.1 percent to 10.3 million tonnes over the same period. The EU remained the largest export destination for Turkish steel.
On technical suitability, both experts say Turkish mills can supply the grades, specifications, and quality levels Baltic construction, infrastructure, and manufacturing need.
However, Alpaslan notes that compliance must be assessed at the product and producer levels.
“It would be inaccurate to assume that every mill produces every grade or meets every technical specification required by a particular customer,” he says.
Buyers need to verify the relevant European product standards, mechanical properties, chemical composition, and certification requirements, he says.
EU construction-product rules and CE-marking – a mandatory legal certification showing a product meets EU safety, health, and environmental protection standards – may apply depending on the product and use, he notes.
“Turkish origin is not, in itself, a barrier to meeting European technical requirements,” Alpaslan says.
“What matters is whether the particular product has been manufactured, tested and documented in accordance with the applicable standards,” he says.
Badshah is similarly optimistic about the capability of Turkish steel mills to meet grades, specifications and quality levels required by Baltic buyers.
“Yes. Türkiye has a mature steel industry capable of producing a broad range of construction and industrial steel products,” he says.
Potential to double market share?
Recent reporting shows that Ankara aims to double its market share in the Baltic region.
Alpaslan says the target is “achievable in principle” but conditional rather than guaranteed.
His optimism stems from the restructuring of trade and EU restrictions on Russian steel, which have encouraged Baltic buyers to diversify.
Another supporting factor is Türkiye’s established export industry and commercial links in the Baltic nations.
Recent trade-delegation activity that is developing relationships with importers and distributors is another positive sign, he notes.
The existing market in Lithuania for Turkish steel – roughly 10.2 percent of total steel imports – provides a foundation for market share expansion, he says.
He notes that doubling share depends on total demand evolution, the speed with which buyers establish new relationships, and competitors’ responses on price, delivery, and availability.
EU quotas, safeguard measures, and CBAM remain major constraints, as does competition from EU and other international suppliers.
“My assessment is that doubling market share over the medium term is a credible commercial ambition, particularly if Turkish producers focus on product categories where they have a clear cost or delivery advantage,” Alpaslan says.
Achieving it will require sustained competitiveness, dependable logistics, product compliance, and long-term relationships, rather than merely filling a temporary gap left by Russian suppliers.
“Ultimately, the opportunity is not simply to replace Russian steel, but to establish Türkiye as a reliable and competitive long-term supplier to the Baltic region,” he says.
For Badshah, doubling Turkish steel exports and market presence is a “realistic ambition” if treated as a medium-term commercial target rather than an automatic outcome.
He says Ankara is in an “encouraging” starting position in Lithuania and that there is “room to expand”, especially in Latvia.
Constraints include competition from Poland and other European suppliers, freight costs, price volatility, trade restrictions, and carbon-border requirements.
Success depends on securing sustained customer contracts, maintaining consistent quality, building dependable distribution, and remaining competitive after logistics and regulatory costs, he says.

+ Nestlé running its Russian business as normal despite forced administration

With these figures, Nestlé significantly exceeded the expectations of analysts surveyed by the AWP news agency. On average, they had expected organic growth of just 3.5% and volume growth of 1.7% for the third quarter.
+ New Nestlé boss plots strategic overhaul to reignite growth
The momentum was driven primarily by a recovery in the pet food business, strong performance in food and snacks such as Maggi seasoning and KitKat, and the water business, which benefited from the hot summer. Volume growth was broadly based: sales volumes increased across all regions of the world and in all globally managed business segments.
Operational recovery
The trend in sales volumes is regarded as a key indicator of the Group’s operational recovery. Following several years of weak growth, driven primarily by price increases, Group CEO Philipp Navratil – who has been in post for just over a year – has made sustainable volume growth his top priority.
To this end, Navratil intends to invest more heavily in successful brands, advertising and innovation. At the same time, the Group aims to become leaner and more effective, focusing on high-growth, high-margin businesses.
As expected, management confirmed its 2026 annual targets. The Group continues to expect organic growth of 3-4% and an improvement in the adjusted operating margin compared with the previous year’s figure of 16.1%.

Israel’s IWI arms Thai soldiers with anti-drone rifles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:33:11 UTC
15:33:11 KST

- Israel Weapon Industries has delivered its ARBEL anti-drone fire-control system to Thailand, installing it in existing Thai rifles by replacing their lower receivers.
- The system is operational day and night, and Thai military officials are discussing an additional ARBEL order with IWI.
Israel Weapon Industries has delivered its ARBEL anti-drone system to Thailand’s Ministry of Defence, where the computerized fire-control kit is now fitted into rifles already in Thai service and is in operational use by day and by night.
Thai military officials are already discussing a follow-on order with the company, after IWI finished the integration work and trained Thai soldiers on site.
IWI sells ARBEL either built into a complete IWI rifle or installed in a customer’s existing weapon, and Thailand chose the second option, with the company’s team carrying out the conversion in the country by replacing each rifle’s lower receiver with the ARBEL unit. Thai troops therefore keep the rifles, ammunition and optics they already know, while gaining the ability to engage small drones with them.
ARBEL does not detect drones or point the rifle for the soldier, but instead controls the exact moment each shot is released. The first round fires mechanically, as with any standard rifle, and while the soldier keeps the trigger pulled, the system releases follow-up rounds at the cadence that gives the best chance of a hit, leaving the shooter free to concentrate on tracking a small drone that flies fast and erratically at a distance. The rifle still fires normally if the battery runs flat, and the kit uses standard 5.56 mm ammunition and works with any optic, from red dots and low-power variable scopes to thermal and night vision sights.
“Small tactical drones have become a direct and growing threat to soldiers on the battlefield. We developed the ARBEL ADS to give soldiers an effective means of defending themselves against this evolving threat, while providing armed forces with a critical tactical advantage in an increasingly complex battlespace,” said Ronen Hamudot, vice chairman of SK Group, IWI’s parent company.
The system weighs about 400 grams (14 ounces), and IWI quotes an engagement range against aerial targets of up to 450 m (490 yards) in daylight and about 250 m (270 yards) at night. The current generation was unveiled in February 2025, when IWI introduced ARBEL versions for its ARAD rifle, any 5.56 mm AR-15-pattern rifle and the NEGEV light machine gun ahead of the IDEX exhibition in Abu Dhabi.
Speaking to The Defence Blog in July, IWI chief product manager Adam Fraser described ARBEL as a soldier’s last line of defense against small tactical drones, mainly first-person-view (FPV) attack drones, and said it is meant to work as one layer alongside detection systems and electronic warfare. IWI said its demonstrations had shown attacking drones brought down within 10 seconds with only a few rounds, against targets flying at up to 60 km/h (37 mph) at ranges beyond 100 m (330 feet), and the company estimated at the time that the system was fielded or in procurement in 10 to 15 European countries.
Thailand gives ARBEL its first announced operational customer in Asia, and IWI said several other Southeast Asian countries are at different stages of buying the system, with more deployments in the region expected within months.
“As Southeast Asian militaries place greater emphasis on counter-drone capabilities, Thailand’s adoption of ARBEL ADS reflects this growing operational priority. We see rising demand across the region for solutions that can help soldiers meet this challenge,” said Doron Korol, SK Group vice president for the Asia-Pacific region.
IWI, based in Kiryat Gat and best known for the Uzi submachine gun, the Tavor bullpup rifle and the Negev light machine gun, is the main small arms supplier to the Israel Defense Forces and Israel Police, and its weapons serve with military, police and special forces units in more than 60 countries.

Russians may face complete blocking in ChatGPT, Claude after IPO — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:32:53 UTC
15:32:53 KST

MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. AI developers Anthropic and OpenAI could potentially block all users of ChatGPT and Claude from Russia and other countries after going public, Russian company MWS AI told TASS.
This could happen because the companies will need to "reduce operational costs," Tech Lead at MWS AI's Applied Solutions Center Ivan Kopylov said. "Companies are already banning access to ChatGPT and Claude from Russia, China, and several other nations, but they are not always strictly enforcing these restrictions yet," he noted.
Mass bans of corporate Claude users are already visible in certain countries where users access the AI via alternative platforms, the expert said. Individual users are less affected so far, he noted. "Before going public, platforms find it beneficial to showcase maximum reach in terms of paid subscriptions," Kopylov said.
Both Anthropic and OpenAI have been actively preparing for their IPOs for a long time. Anthropic, the developer of Claude, spends billions of dollars on infrastructure and AI training, and submitted a draft registration application for an IPO to the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in June. The financial community expects the company to rake up to $100 bln at a $2 trillion valuation.
OpenAI also filed a preliminary application with the SEC in early summer, but its IPO could be pushed back to 2027. The company is competing with Anthropic at the same time and aims to secure investor commitments before its rival goes public - Anthropic could launch its IPO as early as November 2026.
"After an IPO, investors look not only at user growth but also at expenses, cash flow, and profit margins. If a user generates less revenue than the company spends on serving them, expanding that user base only increases losses. This is particularly evident in AI: every single query requires computational power, so even a free user generates ongoing operational costs," Kopylov added.

California's largest state-worker union stages first strike
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:31:30 CST
15:31:30 KST

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Thousands of California state employees staged a one-day statewide strike on Wednesday over pay, healthcare and remote work, marking the first such walkout for California's largest public employees union in its 44-year history.
The Service Employees International Union (SEIU) Local 1000, which represents more than 100,000 working people employed by the State of California, is seeking salary increases totaling 20 percent over three years, higher state healthcare contributions and department-level remote-work policies based on operational needs.
Workers rallied in Sacramento, San Francisco, Oakland and Los Angeles, nonprofit California news outlet CalMatters reported.
"We're making noise on the picket line and sending a clear message to the State: we won't be silenced because state workers deserve fair bargaining NOW!" said the union in a post on Facebook.
Union President Anica Walls said workers needed a contract that would allow them to afford groceries, childcare, rent and other necessities, according to a statement reported by San Francisco public broadcaster KQED.
About 95,000 employees were eligible to strike, while fewer than 5,000 designated essential employees were required to continue working under staffing requirements determined by the labor board, according to the union.
Some motor vehicle offices and state parks had modified or limited operations ahead of the strike, CalMatters reported. The Department of Motor Vehicles had warned that offices could face delays or close early, the outlet reported, citing a department spokesperson.
The union has accused the California state government of negotiating in bad faith, as workers' collective bargaining agreement with the government expired on June 30, according to local media.
The state had sought to stop the walkout, arguing that it put pressure on negotiations and threatened public health and safety, KQED said. ■

Feature: Vietnamese diners develop growing appetite for Chinese cuisine
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:30:59 CST
15:30:59 KST

People enjoy hotpot at Chinese hotpot chain Haidilao in Hanoi, Vietnam, Oct. 20, 2026.(Xinhua/Liu Ying)
HANOI, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- The spicy aroma of mala hotpot drifted from the Chinese booth at the second Cultures of the World Festival in Hanoi earlier this month, drawing a long queue of Vietnamese visitors curious to sample its fiery flavors.
The scene was one sign of a growing curiosity about Chinese food in Vietnam, where diners are discovering not only familiar hotpot and dim sum but also the cooking traditions of different Chinese regions.
For some young Vietnamese, the attraction begins with the heat.
Pham Linh Dan, a 19-year-old university student in Hanoi, said she eats at Chinese hotpot chain Haidilao two to three times a week and has also tried several other Chinese-style hotpot restaurants.
Dan, who describes herself as a fan of spicy food, said what draws her to Chinese cuisine is not simply the level of heat, but the way different spices build the flavor.
"Chinese food is not just spicy in an ordinary way. It combines spices such as cinnamon and star anise, which create a kind of spiciness that is different from what we have in Vietnam," she said.
The distinctive taste has also made her curious about the culture behind the food.
"It makes me like Chinese food even more and want to explore more of Chinese culture and cuisine," Dan said, adding that Sichuan would be her first choice if she had the chance to travel to China for food.
That enthusiasm is also reflected in the performance of larger Chinese restaurant brands in Vietnam.
According to data released by Super Hi International, Haidilao generated about 57 million U.S. dollars in revenue in Vietnam in the first half of 2026, up 31 percent year on year and accounting for more than 10 percent of its global revenue.
But the appetite for Chinese flavors is no longer confined to Vietnam's major cities.
In central Vietnam's Nghe An province, a newly opened restaurant specializing in Jiangxi cuisine has also been drawing local diners as well as visitors from neighboring areas curious about Chinese food.
Nguyen Thu Hien traveled about an hour from neighboring Ha Tinh province to Nghe An and took the opportunity to try Chinese food for a change.
"Before trying it, I thought Chinese food was quite spicy and a little oily," Hien said.
After tasting the dishes, however, she said they were less oily than she had expected and thought the flavors had been adjusted for local diners.
Pham Thi Nhu Quynh, who had previously traveled to southwest China's Yunnan Province and eaten Chinese food there, offered a different perspective.
"I think the food is quite authentic, still oily and spicy," Quynh said, adding that it was neither too sweet nor too spicy for her taste.
For Quynh, seeing more Chinese regional cuisines appear in Vietnam also carries meaning beyond the meal itself.
"I think it is also a way to convey culture, especially food culture, and gives Vietnamese people more diverse choices," she said.
For Wang Shixiang from the Jiangxi Chamber of Commerce in Vietnam, the spread of regional Chinese cuisines to more parts of the country carries a broader cultural meaning.
"We hope to use food as a bridge to preserve and promote Chinese culinary culture, bring Chinese cuisine to the world, and help more people learn about China and fall in love with Chinese flavors," Wang said. ■
