Gold medalists team China (C), silver medalists team USA and bronze medalists team Japan celebrate during the awarding ceremony for the women's team final at Artistic Gymnastics World Championships 2026 in Rotterdam, the Netherlands, Oct. 21, 2026. (Xinhua/Weng Xinyang)
ROTTERDAM, the Netherlands, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- China edged the United States by 0.233 points to claim its first women's team title in 20 years at the World Artistic Gymnastics Championships here on Wednesday.
China topped the standings with 165.764 points, ahead of the United States with 165.531 and Japan with 164.063.
The victory gave China its second women's world team title after its breakthrough triumph in 2006 and ended the United States' run of seven consecutive titles. All three medal-winning teams secured qualification for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games.
China, which led qualification, turned the contest around on balance beam after trailing the United States through the opening two rotations.
The United States posted the highest team totals on vault and uneven bars, scoring 42.633 and 42.766 respectively, while China recorded 40.966 and 42.466 on the same apparatus. Those scores left China 1.967 points behind at the halfway stage.
The balance beam changed the complexion of the contest. Zhang Qingying delivered 15.066 points, the highest beam score of the final, while Ke Qinqin contributed 14.400 and Qiu Qiyuan added 13.900. China's combined 43.366, compared with the United States' 39.199, turned the deficit into a 2.200-point advantage heading into the final rotation.
The United States fought back on floor exercise, where Claire Pease scored 13.933, Dulcy Caylor 13.600 and Reese Esponda 13.400 for a team total of 40.933.
China responded with 13.033 from Zhang and 13.100 from Ke before Qiu closed the competition with 12.833, enough to preserve a narrow winning margin.
Japan's bronze ended a 60-year wait for a women's team medal at the World Championships, with its previous podium finish coming in 1966. Aiko Sugihara contributed 14.200 on vault and 13.900 on floor to help Japan finish comfortably ahead of fourth-placed France.
France scored 161.130, followed by Brazil with 159.730, Russia with 159.394, Italy with 158.129 and Canada with 158.096.
The championships continue with the men's all-around final on Thursday and the women's all-around final on Friday, followed by the apparatus finals over the weekend. ■

What a Russian Satellite Stalking a Commercial Spacecraft Means for the Space Force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
01:14:39 UTC
10:14:39 KST

Over a two-week period beginning in late September and culminating in mid-October, a Russian satellite maneuvered dangerously close to a commercial Finnish satellite currently providing intelligence to the Ukrainian military.
The apparent provocation has experts wondering why Russia made the move—testing new capabilities, collecting intelligence, or trying to intimidate the Finnish company—and what, if anything, the U.S. Space Force could or should do about these types of events in the future.
While the incident did not involve a U.S. asset, the Russian action highlights the growing importance of commercial space assets to military operations and how those relatively defenseless assets could be vulnerable in or before a conflict.
Between Oct. 15-19, a Russian satellite dubbed COSMOS 2612 performed deliberate, fuel-intensive maneuvers to close in on the Finnish ICEYE-X36 satellite, according to a report by LeoLabs, which the company shared with Air & Space Forces Magazine.
Instead of a somewhat standard flyby, COSMOS matched, shadowed, and orbited around the ICEYE satellite, coming as close as 500 meters to it, according to the report.
The Russian satellite spent months adjusting its orbit, then rapidly closed the distance with the ICEYE satellite, continuously maneuvering around it before COSMOS abruptly ended its movements and distanced itself Oct. 18-19.
The LeoLabs report characterizes the event as a “red” on “blue” engagement in orbit and calls it a planned, highly coordinated rendezvous and proximity operation, which required precise navigation and onboard sensing.
An ICEYE spokesperson declined to provide a detailed response to a query from Air & Space Forces Magazine about the incident.
“We are aware of the situation and tracking it closely. Our constellation architecture is designed for continuity and resilience,” the spokesperson said in an email.
The Center for Strategic and International Studies held an online event Oct. 21 to discuss the incident and its implications for the U.S..
Neither of the two experts at the CSIS event claimed to understand Russia’s goals with the stunt, but Greg Gillinger, senior vice president of strategy and development at Integrity ISR, called it unusual and said it indicated Russia’s intent to send a message to the Finnish company.
“I still scratch my head about what the Russian endgame is with this,” Gillinger said.
Clayton Swope, deputy director of the CSIS Aerospace Security Project, said the event certainly was not “benign.”
“I don’t think we have enough information right now to know whether or not Russia achieved the objectives it wanted to achieve here,” Swope said.
The COSMOS/ICEYE incident comes about a month after Space Force leadership publicly announced that the force has on-orbit offensive space weapons at its disposal and under Guardians’ control.
“Today, we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenge of evolving threats wherever they exist,” Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink said during the opening keynote at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference on Sept. 14. “This is why the Space Force now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action.”
The timing of the satellite maneuvers, following Meink’s comments, could be a Russian signal, threat, or influence campaign meant to deter outside, commercial support for Ukraine—or even a bluff, retired Air Force Col. Jennifer Reeves, the senior resident fellow for Space Studies at the Mitchell Institute, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
What USSF Can Do
In 2025, USSF’s Rapid Capabilities Office kicked off a project to field threat-awareness sensors that communicate close hazards to space asset operators. Such sensors would presumably alert operators if a Russian satellite came as close as it did to the ICEYE bird.
Beyond sensing and communicating, though, an April report from the Secure World Foundation noted that more nations are starting to fund “bodyguard” capabilities for their space assets, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported at the time. Germany, India, France, and Japan are all either building or planning to acquire such space-based bodyguards, which could protect and counterattack any space-based incursions.
Swope, speaking on the COSMOS/ICEYE incident, said spacefaring nations need clearer expectations for behavior in space, and predicted events like the recent incident would likely happen again.
“I just feel like it’s not a question of if; it is a question of when we see these satellites do something that we’re going to say is hostile again,” Swope said.
He also said any use of bodyguard satellites needed to include a clearer explanation of what they will accomplish in orbit.
Reeves likewise said the Space Force needs to be prepared to both understand and respond to future incidents like this one. While the service has been building its space domain awareness capabilities in recent years, that’s only one piece of the larger puzzle, she said.
“There’s a big difference between knowing where something is and understanding what it’s doing,” she said.
The force has made “tremendous progress” in tracking orbits and objects with a sophisticated sensor network and other tools, she said. But the Pentagon must put more “rigor” into protecting both military and commercial assets in space, Reeves said.
“The Space Force needs to be running through these scenarios on the regular, and hopefully they are,” Reeves said. “I’m going to trust that they are in their wargames and exercises.”
Those exercises need to include both allies and commercial partners, Reeves added.
“We’ve got to determine how quickly we can determine what happened,” she said. “Can we distinguish an accident from something deliberate? How confident are we in attribution?”
Both Reeves and Swope separately noted that any counterattacks or deterrence to space-based provocations don’t have to involve space-based retaliation or actions.
Reeves pointed to the U.S. ability to strike ground-based facilities to sever links to satellites. Swope noted increased pressure on Russia’s oil “shadow fleet,” a network of an estimated hundreds of old tankers used to export oil while evading sanctions, could be a lever to nudge Russia away from space tomfoolery.
Necessary Guidance
Ultimately, while the Space Force will be the entity dealing with satellite harassment or attacks, the force’s role needs clearer definitions on what constitutes aggression and merits a response, especially given the long-term consequences of space debris and other factors involved in kinetic actions in orbit, Reeves said.
“I don’t think it’s necessarily the Space Force itself that should be determining that,” Reeves said. “I think it should be our national leadership that’s coming up with that. … Because at this point in time, we don’t have that coming from the national-level leadership.”
That lack of guidance has placed the burden on military leadership to decide what the U.S. believes hostile actions in space look like and how the military should respond.
“We don’t want to be doing this thought work when we’re living it in real time,” Reeves said. “There are dire consequences in space if the wrong action is taken or a hostile action is taken.”

Two OpenAI agents disabled security monitoring systems during testing, with one later denying it had done so, the company has revealed.
The disclosure follows a string of similar incidents in recent months involving autonomous AI agents, which can independently plan and carry out tasks using external tools.
In a blog post on Tuesday, OpenAI said that the incidents occurred on October 3 and 6, involving its GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra agents, respectively.
In the first case, the coding agent tasked with creating evaluation tasks using employee feedback collected via Slack disabled automatic alerts to the company’s security team. According to OpenAI, the agent reasoned that the user’s prior instruction not to send messages on the team communication platform during the process applied to all notifications, including security alerts.
Three days later, the GPT-6 Astra agent removed the monitoring integration of a program it was migrating, taking its cue from a reference it had been fed that did not have the security feature. When asked later by the human user, the agent denied removing the monitoring system.
OpenAI said that it was investigating why the agents disabled the safeguards and working to prevent similar incidents. While the behavior may have resulted from “benign overpersistence” by the agents to complete the task, the company said that it was also “developing evaluations to test whether models might have a propensity to evade misalignment monitoring in particular.”
Last month, the Wall Street Journal, citing Saachi Jain, OpenAI’s head of safety systems, reported that the company had scrapped the release of its GPT-6.1 Astra model. The decision reportedly came after internal testing had found the model to be more deceptive than its predecessors and apt to employ potentially unsafe external tools without first seeking the user’s permission.
Also in September, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said that an OpenAI agent had hacked his country’s Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal, with the company failing to report the breach for nearly three months.
Earlier, in July, OpenAI disclosed that its models had escaped their sandbox during cybersecurity testing, accessed the internet, and hacked into the servers of the Hugging Face online repository for AI models and datasets.
Other developers have reported similarly troubling behavior in tests.
Earlier this month, Anthropic released a report detailing instances of “unintended” actions by its AI models, including Claude Haiku 4.5 providing a bogus tip to Philadelphia police regarding an ongoing homicide investigation.
Calls to halt AI development or impose tighter regulations on the industry have grown louder.
Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton has warned that increasingly powerful AI could eventually escape human control, with potentially catastrophic consequences. Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has also urged governments to adopt a more active role in imposing safety standards on the industry.
However, US President Donald Trump has brushed off such concerns, saying that restrictions on AI development could allow China to overtake the US in the technological race.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, too, has argued that the world must absorb some “bad things” resulting from AI development, including hacks and scams, as the benefits afforded by the technology far outweigh the drawbacks.

Stealthy F-117 Nighthawk Goes on Display at Smithsonian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
00:52:02 UTC
09:52:02 KST

A historic Lockheed F-117 Nighthawk is now on permanent display at the National Air and Space Museum’s Stephen F. Udvar-Hazy Center. The exhibit debuted Oct. 21, showcasing the first operational stealth aircraft at one of the most visited aircraft museums in the world.
The F-117 joining the collection at Udvar-Hazy Center in Chantilly, Va., is unique: Dubbed “Overachiever,” tail number 85-0818 is the only F-117 to have flown combat missions in all four of the major conflicts from when the F-117 was active: 1989’s Operation Just Cause in Panama; 1991’s Operation Desert Storm in Iraq; 1999’s Operation Allied Force in Kosovo; and 2003’s Operation Iraqi Freedom in Iraq.
The F-117 Nighthawk was the first operational aircraft designed to evade radar with its unique shape and materials and was a triumph of technical ingenuity and skill at a time before computer-aided design. The aircraft proved how reducing an aircraft’s radar cross-section could provide a decisive advantage in combat.
Michael Hankins, the museum’s curator of modern military aviation, said today’s F-35 stealth fighter builds on the foundation set by the F-117. Beyond the “jaw drop moment” he expects visitors to experience when they see its sharp, angular features, he hopes the display teaches them to appreciate the visionary designers and groundbreaking pilots and maintainers who took the F-117 into battle and kept the jets running.
Jeff Corbets, a program manager at Lockheed Martin’s Skunk Works, oversaw the Overachiever’s restoration, which included removing parts of the plane that remain classified secrets to this day. He said he hopes the jet will connect future generations to the story of stealth.
“This was the aircraft that ushered in the era of [stealth],” he said, noting that the F-22, F-35, B-2, and B-21 followed. “All of them now are kind of based on the legacy of this airplane.”
Skunk Works engineers developed the sharply faceted jets’ shape to minimize its appearance on radar screens. Subsequent stealth aircraft have used curves to achieve the same effect, but in the 1970s when the F-117 was developed, the computer power to calculate those curves was not yet available. Air Force tests calculated the radar signature as being on par with a marble.
The Nighthawk went into service in the early 1980s and wasn’t officially acknowledged until 1988. Although it debuted operationally in Panama in 1989, that operation was not deemed a success. Rather, it was the role the Nighthawk played in 1991’s Operation Desert Storm that demonstrated its value: an ability to fly undetected, without jammers or other escorts, into contested enemy territory and deliver ordnance at will.
“The F-117 was the centerpiece of the success that we experienced during the Desert Storm air campaign,” said Lt. Gen. David A. Deptula, USAF (Ret.), dean of the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies and principal attack planner for the campaign. “It was the linchpin of our success.”
Deptula said the combination of stealth jets and precision munitions enabled planners to strike more targets in the first 24 hours than would have been possible with standard force packages of conventional aircraft.
“We’re pretty sure that this one [the Overachiever], on the first night of Desert Storm, took out a main communication center in Baghdad,” Hankins said. He cautioned that details are hard to come by because much of the jet’s history remains classified. It will likely take years for information to be cleared for public release.
F-117s remain in rare but limited use in training and other activities. The Overachiever is among several F-117s to become museum pieces, but the first to join the Smithsonian collection. The Air Force, working with Lockheed and Smithsonian officials, spent years orchestrating the transfer, which was officially announced at AFA’s 2026 Air, Space & Cyber Conference in September.
Lockheed donated the hours to restore and demilitarize classified elements of the aircraft, including removing its original stealth coatings. The work was completed over about eight months, after which the jet’s wings were removed so that it could be loaded onto a C-5M Super Galaxy cargo aircraft for the flight to Washington.
Now, hundreds of thousands of people will get to see the “Overachiever” and learn about the origins of stealth. The Udvar-Hazy Center is open every day except Christmas from 10 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. Admission is free, but parking costs $15.

Son of Stephen Hubbard, American freed from Russian jail, speaks out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
00:51:57 UTC
09:51:57 KST

Son says Stephen Hubbard was experiencing "extreme tiredness with life" before release from Russian jail
Washington — Fr. Joseph Coleman feared he would never again see his father, Stephen Hubbard, when they had a brief phone conversation last year while Hubbard was in a Russian prison.
"He was expressing a very extreme tiredness with life, the life that he was experiencing at that time. I don't want to say suicidal thoughts, but the conversation hinted it leaned in that direction," Coleman, a Greek Orthodox priest, told CBS News on Wednesday in his first television interview since his father's release.
Hubbard's release was announced earlier Wednesday during a meeting between U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Hubbard, a U.S. citizen, was imprisoned in Russia for more than four years after being accused of fighting for Ukraine. The U.S. government had deemed Hubbard wrongfully detained.
Hubbard touched down back in the U.S. Wednesday night, President Trump said while returning from a rally in South Carolina. He said Hubbard would visit the White House "in the next day or so."
Mr. Trump said Putin had agreed to release Hubbard at his request, with "no 'swap' necessary," though he also said that his decision to waive new sanctions against Russia played a role in Hubbard's release.
In a one-minute phone call with his father before Hubbard took off from St. Petersburg, Coleman said he sounded better than he had during their last conversation in May 2025. Witkoff was also present, leaving little opportunity for a private exchange.
"I want to embrace him as a son embraces his father. I want to personally assess his health to make sure he's well," Coleman said. He said he would also give his dad space to adjust to freedom and expected to see Hubbard later that evening.
Coleman, who lives in Cyprus, did not grow up in the same home as Hubbard, who was divorced from Coleman's mother. He said the family had lost track of Hubbard entirely for roughly three years after his detention.
Martin De Luca, Hubbard's U.S.-based attorney, told CBS News that when his legal team took on the case in February 2025, neither the family nor the U.S. Embassy knew precisely where Hubbard was being held.
Lawyers in Russia eventually located him and arranged for legal visits, money for food and basic necessities, and the brief phone call with his son.
De Luca said the isolation had taken an enormous toll.
"It's just being isolated from everybody you've ever known and just from the outside world," he said.
After Putin granted Hubbard's release, Witkoff praised the Russian president as a "humanitarian," prompting swift backlash from Republican and Democratic lawmakers. Putin is wanted by the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes involving the deportation of Ukrainian children, and Russian forces have been accused of widespread abuses during the war.
Asked about Witkoff's description of Putin, Coleman called his father's release "a small step toward peace in this greater conflict" and thanked Putin for signing off on the deal.
He described the decision as an act of "compassion and even mercy."
Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired schoolteacher, was captured in Ukraine shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022 and accused of manning a checkpoint for mercenaries. He was later sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony following a closed-door trial.
His family has consistently disputed the charges.
De Luca said his legal team conducted its own investigation, interviewing people who knew Hubbard and examining his circumstances before the invasion. He said they found no evidence that Hubbard had served in the Ukrainian military or was physically capable of doing so at roughly 70 years old.
"We have not seen any evidence to support those allegations," De Luca said. He added that the Russian case file was largely sealed and that his team had repeatedly sought evidence substantiating the charges.
De Luca and Coleman both credited the Trump administration's diplomatic engagement with Moscow for securing Hubbard's freedom.
Asked whether recent U.S. decisions benefiting Russia — including sanctions relief and purchases of Russian diesel — were connected to Hubbard's release, De Luca said he did not believe there was a direct link, though he acknowledged that bilateral relationships involve multiple overlapping interests.
Mr. Trump, however, has explicitly said that allowing new sanctions to take effect would have prevented Hubbard's release.
And despite Hubbard's release, as many as 20 Americans remain imprisoned in Russia, including some whose families dispute the charges against them. The State Department continues to warn Americans against traveling to Russia because of the risk of wrongful detention.
De Luca said he was not concerned that the administration's engagement with Moscow would encourage further detentions, arguing that diplomatic dialogue had helped secure several Americans' freedom.
But Russia has not been designated a state sponsor of wrongful detention under a new Trump administration policy, despite its history of imprisoning Americans on questionable charges. Iran and Afghanistan have both received the designation.
Coleman stopped short of blaming his father for his circumstances but acknowledged he might have made a mistake by remaining in Ukraine as Russian forces advanced.
"The Russian forces told foreign nationals to leave and he did not," Coleman said. "I do not like what happened to my father. I am ecstatic that he is free. But he was living in an area that was a war zone."
"I'm not saying his detainment was justifiable. I'm not saying that," he said. "But these things happen in war."

US and Israel draw up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after American elections: Sources
Julian E. Barnes, Eric Schmitt, Farnaz Fassihi, Natan Odenheimer and Ronen Bergman
- US and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the American elections, with targets likely to include energy sites, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone weapons.
- The two militaries are already training for a short, intense operation, while US diplomats use the threat of war to push Iran on its nuclear programme and Strait of Hormuz demands.
- The plan faces major risks: Iran has vowed wider retaliation, the earlier strikes raised global prices and strained defences, and Israeli politics could block or delay any attack.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The US and Israeli militaries have developed specific plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the American midterm elections, according to US officials and other people briefed on the deliberations.
As planning for a short but intensive operation progresses, the US and Israeli militaries have stepped up exercises, flying planes over Iraq to practise strike manoeuvres.
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel earlier in October to discuss new strikes, US officials said. The targets would likely include Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal.
Some officials say one more big round of attacks could push Iran’s economy over the brink and force it to make diplomatic concessions after nearly eight months of conflict.
Still, there are reasons to be sceptical that a renewed war would be any more successful than the first phase of intense US-Israeli strikes between February and April.
Those rounds of fighting drove up energy prices and inflation around the world, eroded security in the Middle East and severely strained the Pentagon’s supply of missile interceptors.
It is also far from certain US President Donald Trump will approve fresh strikes. He has repeatedly vetoed plans in 2026 for a return to major combat operations.
All of the officials interviewed for this story spoke on condition of anonymity.
Iranian officials have promised to retaliate this time by expanding their targets beyond commercial ships and energy infrastructure in the region to data centres and underwater internet cables.
They say the fighting will be neither quick nor limited.
While the United States is assembling a massive arsenal that will be fully in place by early November, diplomatic efforts have continued, as US negotiators use the potential return to war as leverage with Iran to make progress on their demands on its nuclear programme and control over the Strait of Hormuz.
So far, however, Iran’s negotiators have been unwilling to make concessions on the nuclear programme, insisting on deferring that issue until later in the talks.
Israel’s election on Oct 27 could complicate the plans. If Netanyahu loses, he will become a caretaker prime minister, and it will be difficult for him to launch a war, experts say. But some analysts believe that Netanyahu could leverage the prospect of an imminent joint US-Israel strike to pressure his rivals into joining a unity government to manage the war, which would extend his hold on power. Australians facing spike in data breaches after 'critical' flaw uncovered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
00:48:22 UTC
09:48:22 KST

Australians face spike in data breaches after AI helps uncover 'critical' website flaw
In short:
Australian website operators are choosing to take their services offline or to limit access after researchers using AI discovered critical infrastructure flaws.
PHP is a common programming language powering seven in 10 websites, including popular platforms such as Wordpress and Wikipedia.
What's next?
Security fixes have been released and experts are urging operators to patch affected services immediately.
Australians should expect an increase in future data breaches as a result of critical software flaws that have forced major government websites, education platforms and web hosts to go offline.
The AI-assisted discovery of a vulnerability in a crucial piece of web architecture used by most websites, known as PHP, has set off a global scramble to patch millions of devices as major tech companies warn that bad actors have begun seizing on it.
The flaws, dubbed "PHP2shell", have been present for more than a decade, but are so serious that cybersecurity experts have urged widespread action to avoid major breaches.
"You have to patch it very, very quickly, or the suggestion is to take it offline," Australian web security expert Troy Hunt told ABC News Breakfast.
What you can do to protect yourself
Read more
There is not much an individual can do about a server they do not control, so the practical advice is the same hygiene that always pays off:
- Use unique passwords or even better, use passkeys and a password manager so a breach at one site doesn't unlock your other accounts
- Keep an eye on card statements over the coming weeks
- Be extra wary of unexpected prompts to log in or download something, even on sites you trust
What happened?
Yesterday, the organisation behind PHP issued a security alert about the discovery of two "critical" vulnerabilities.
PHP is used in the back end of an estimated seven in 10 websites and applications, including Wordpress and Wikipedia.
These vulnerabilities would allow attackers to run their own code on affected servers without logging in, a major cybersecurity flaw that would allow unauthorised control to do anything from extracting user data to implanting other malware.
PHP works on the server behind a website, producing content for a visitor's browser. The flaws can let attackers run their own code on affected servers without logging in, according to PHP's security advisory.
The risk varies with the way a server is set up, but PHP's developers urged all users serving web pages to update immediately.
The PHP Foundation, a non-profit organisation maintaining and developing the PHP ecosystem, released a fix early this morning and urged all operators to update immediately.
Amazon Web Services, a subsidiary of the US tech giant offering cloud computing platforms, said it had already seen evidence of attempts to exploit the vulnerability as early as October 17.
"The targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure," it said in a blog post.
Major organisations go dark
Australia's own cybersecurity agency, the Australian Signals Directorate, put out a rare critical alert about the flaw directed at everyone from government and critical infrastructure to individuals and families.
Major Australian organisations took drastic steps to avoid falling victim until they were able to ensure that they had patched their own devices.
GovCMS, which hosts many major Australian government websites, blocked direct access to its servers while keeping cached copies of public pages available.
Moodle, an Australian education technology company whose software powers hundreds of thousands of university and schools' online learning platforms, also took its website offline as a precaution, before beginning to restore them after applying security fixes.
Australian hosting provider VentraIP restricted some of its file uploads on customer hosting, warning that forms accepting attachments could fail.
Even smaller website operators such as those running Australian forum for customising computer hardware went down as a precaution.
Mr Hunt said there was little Australians needed to do, but the worst-case scenario was a breach of websites holding their personal information.
"We just need to expect that we may have some elevated instances of the data breaches that we're already seeing every day," he said.
AI helped discover 'critical' flaw
US-based security firm Calif said it had identified a critical flaw using OpenAI's AI models as part of a cybersecurity program it was running.
While the bug appears to have been present in versions of PHP released as far back as 2012, Calif said it took existing research that theorised about a possible attack vector and used AI to confirm the existence of a legitimate vulnerability.
The PHP Foundation said a developer had found the first signs of the underlying problem behind one of the flaws in 2024, but its work repeatedly stalled amid difficult technical choices and limited resources.
AI helped assess reports, the foundation said, while humans remained responsible for decisions and fixes.
"A person makes every call and works on every patch," it said.
OpenAI warned that the same capabilities helping defenders find vulnerabilities could help attackers rapidly develop tools to exploit them.
Additional reporting by national technology reporter Ange Lavoipierre

The Impending Impeachment Conviction of Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
00:06:00 UTC
09:06:00 KST

Recent political realignments in the Philippines suggest that a guilty verdict has already been secured in the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
The House of Representatives twice impeached Duterte, but it was only in July that a trial was convened by the Senate, which needs to deliver a verdict on the allegations that the vice president committed high crimes and betrayed public trust.
In several articles, I wrote about the slim prospect of a conviction given the dominance of Duterte supporters in the Senate. Even President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. publicly rejected a “divisive” trial, which eventually led to the archiving of the initial impeachment complaint in 2025.
The push to remove the vice president from office became clearer in the second half of the year when the Senate convened an impeachment court, and when the president allowed Duterte’s tax and bank records to be used as evidence. The prosecution panel’s first presentation was about the alleged grave threats made by Duterte against the First Family, which was intended to consolidate the ranks of the president’s supporters.
The start of the trial coincided with the filing of non-bailable plunder charges against two pro-Duterte senators, which prevented them from attending the impeachment sessions. Another pro-Duterte senator, who was a former police chief, went into hiding after an arrest warrant was issued against him by the International Criminal Court for his role in the bloody “war on drugs” during the previous administration of Rodrigo Duterte, the vice president’s father.
During the course of the trial, one member of the Senate Duterte bloc decided to join the majority. Another member went abroad to seek medical treatment, but it became an indefinite leave after a plunder complaint was filed against her. The absence of pro-Duterte senators has made it easier for the majority to lower the number of votes needed to convict the vice president. The Senate decision to lower the voting threshold was questioned by pro-Duterte lawyers at the Supreme Court, but the latter dismissed their petition on procedural grounds.
The prosecution’s presentation of evidence on the alleged unexplained wealth of Duterte and her husband provided the public with new information about the vice president’s undeclared assets and business dealings. Some of the suspicious financial transactions were traced to China, which prompted some Marcos officials to comment that it should be further investigated as a potential national security threat.
Duterte has denied ownership of the bank accounts and properties mentioned during her trial. She also insisted that doing business in China is legitimate. Nevertheless, she still needs to explain the mismatch and omissions in her statement of assets as a government official, and the large amount of earnings from her husband’s vague business operations in China.
The prosecution is confident that they can get a guilty verdict on the issue of Duterte’s unexplained wealth, and they made a bold move by dropping other charges in their presentation, including the grave threats against the First Family, misuse of confidential funds, and bribery.
This could also signal that there is now enough number of votes in the Senate to convict Duterte. The impeachment trial may last until the end of the year unless the defense panel decides to present additional witnesses to extend the sessions until early 2027.
The decision to limit the impeachment case to the issue of unexplained wealth has drawn mixed reactions. On one hand, it has been welcomed for expediting the trial and allowing the prosecution to focus on an issue with strong evidence. But it has also been criticized for its potential to undermine the public clamor for accountability, especially since the allegation about the anomalous spending of confidential funds was dropped from the charges. Critics said it could set a precedent by reducing the impeachment process to a transactional matter involving legislators and the presidential office, instead of upholding its role in exacting full accountability against erring officials.
Duterte’s political future will soon be decided by the Senate. Whatever happens, she can take comfort that she still leads in presidential election surveys. If she is convicted, her younger brother could run for president. So far, Marcos has no clear successor, which still makes the Dutertes the formidable team to beat at the 2028 presidential election.
In the meantime, the public awaits the counterarguments and evidence to be presented by Duterte’s legal team in the second half of the impeachment trial.

Russia warns against distorting Dayton principles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
00:04:12 UTC
09:04:12 KST

VIENNA, October 22. /TASS/. Yulia Zhdanova, head of Russia’s delegation to the Vienna talks on military security and arms control, has warned that attempts at distorting the principles of the Dayton Agreement will have catastrophic consequences for both Bosnia and Herzegovina and the entire Western Balkans region.
"We would like to warn that any attempts to distort the Dayton principles will have catastrophic consequences for Bosnia and Herzegovina and the entire Western Balkans region. We insist that the UN Security Council must prevent events from unfolding in this way," Zhdanova said at the 25th meeting of the commission established under the Dayton Agreement.
According to the Russian diplomat, Western countries are seeking to dismantle the state architecture of Bosnia and Herzegovina enshrined in the Dayton Agreement. She emphasized that Russia considers the Dayton Agreement to be the only possible basis for a settlement in the region.
Under the constitution envisaged by the General Framework Agreement for Peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina (Dayton Agreement) of 1995, Bosnia and Herzegovina is comprised of two entities, namely the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (around 51% of the territory) and the Republic of Srpska (around 49%), as well as the Brcko District. The three key ethno-religious groups, i.e. Bosniaks (Slavs professing Islam), Serbs (Orthodox Christians), and Croats (Catholics), are proportionally represented in the state governance system.
In fact, the country is governed via the High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina, whose office was set up under the Dayton Agreement and who is appointed by the Steering Board of the Peace Implementation Council (PIC) upon the UN Security Council’s consent. However, in 2021, the Board members appointed Hans Christian Schmidt of Germany to the post without agreeing his candidature with the UN Security Council.
On May 10, Schmidt announced his resignation. Former US Consul General in Vladivostok Louis Crischock will serve as acting high representative until a new high representative is elected.
Meanwhile, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova stated that the West’s attempts to endorse Crischock "as acting high representative" for Bosnia and Herzegovina have no legal grounds.

Meta fined $25 billion in privacy scandal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

00:03:02 UTC
09:03:02 KST

Meta to pay billions over ‘Cambridge Analytica’ privacy abuse
A US judge has ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in civil penalties for deceiving Facebook users about the privacy of their personal data, in a landmark ruling stemming from the Cambridge Analytica scandal, which exposed the harvesting of personal information from millions of Americans for political campaigns.
New Mexico District Judge Francis Mathew issued the ruling on Wednesday, following a jury verdict in September finding Facebook’s parent company responsible for nearly 44 million violations of the state’s consumer protection laws.
The judge concluded that Meta’s misconduct warranted a penalty exceeding $219 billion under state law, but reduced the amount to $25 billion, making it one of the largest financial penalties ever imposed on an American corporation.
“Facebook’s wrongdoing – over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public – goes to the heart of Facebook’s core business practices,” Mathew wrote in his order.
The case arose from the 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal, when it emerged that the British political consulting firm obtained personal information from as many as 87 million Facebook users without their consent.
woah, it gets worse. In the Meta securities lawsuit for Cambridge Analytica cover-up, plaintiffs just posted deposition list. If they have the courage to 'go to the mat' (as Zuckerberg says) like New Mexico AG has done for over $25B, this could be very, very bad for Team Zuck. 1/3
— Jason Kint (@jason_kint) October 22, 2026
The information was collected through a third-party personality quiz application that exploited Facebook’s system for accessing users’ friends’ data. Cambridge Analytica used the information to develop psychological profiles of voters and deliver targeted political advertising, including during the 2016 US presidential election.
The company was established in 2013 as the American political-data arm of the British SCL Group, a private contractor specializing in behavioral influence, psychological profiling, and strategic communications. SCL also marketed influence and research services to defense clients, including the UK Defense Ministry.
The scandal also exposed connections to Palantir Technologies, a Silicon Valley data-analysis company with extensive contracts involving US intelligence agencies and the Pentagon. A 2018 New York Times investigation revealed that at least one Palantir employee advised Cambridge Analytica’s researchers during the company’s 2014 efforts to harvest Facebook information.
Palantir denied having a formal business relationship with Cambridge Analytica, maintaining that the employee acted in a personal capacity.
Cambridge Analytica collapsed in 2018 amid worldwide scrutiny of its operations, while Facebook faced regulatory investigations, lawsuits, and billions of dollars in penalties.
Attorney General Raul Torrez hailed Wednesday’s judgment as a warning to Silicon Valley that even the largest technology companies could be held accountable for violating consumer protection laws.
Meta has denied misleading users and plans to appeal the ruling, arguing that the unprecedented penalty is unconstitutional. Responding to the jury’s verdict last month, the company also invoked freedom of speech, insisting that Facebook is a forum for free expression.

China, Djibouti say all countries should enjoy freedom of navigation in Red Sea
- China and Djibouti said all countries should have freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait, as security there worsens.
- They urged respect for Red Sea coastal states, international law, and merchant ship rights, and warned against raising regional security risks.
- The statement came as Yemen fighting spread and the US told some diplomats and families to leave missions in Saudi Arabia.
AI generated
BEIJING – All countries should enjoy freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, China and Djibouti said in a joint statement following a meeting of their foreign ministers in Beijing, expressing concern about the deteriorating security situation.
Djibouti sits on the other side of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait from Yemen, where Iran-backed Houthis have been battling Saudi-backed government forces and seeking to control the whole Yemeni Red Sea coast, disrupting some shipping.
In 2017, China formally opened its first overseas military base in Djibouti. The barren former French colony, which is about the size of Wales, is sandwiched between Ethiopia, Eritrea and Somalia, and also hosts US, Japanese and French bases.
The joint statement, released early on Oct 22, said both China and Djibouti stressed the importance of maintaining freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and the strait, and “emphasised that the right of merchant ships of all countries to exercise navigation rights in accordance with international law should be respected”.
“Both sides believe that in governing and securing the Red Sea, the sovereignty, territorial integrity and wishes of the Red Sea littoral states should be genuinely respected, avoiding any increase in the overall security risks of the region.”
China supports the littoral states of the Red Sea in “constructively maintaining” the safety and smooth flow of international shipping lanes, said the statement, carried by China’s official Xinhua news agency.
Neither country wants regional tensions to spill further into the Red Sea, and “major powers outside the region” should respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of regional countries, and avoid resorting to force and unilateral sanctions, it added.
The statement came as the US State Department ordered some diplomats and family members to depart from its missions in Saudi Arabia following the escalation of the fighting in Yemen, which has opened another front in the regional conflict triggered by the US-Israeli war on Iran. REUTERS

Britain near bottom of NATO rearmament table
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
01:00:10 BST
09:00:10 KST

Britain stands thirty-first out of thirty-two NATO countries on an internal alliance measure of how effectively members are meeting their rearmament promises, with only Iceland lower, according to a report by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, sets the figure against the government’s Defence Investment Plan and the warning that Russia could attack NATO as soon as 2030.
Dhesi said: “And if the UK government means what it says – that Russia could attack NATO as soon as 2030 – then work to rectify these vulnerabilities cannot start soon enough.”
The report states: “However, the current reality could hardly be bleaker. According to an internal document apparently drawn up by NATO to measure how effectively members are meeting their rearmament promises, the UK is number 31 out of 32 Alliance countries. Only Iceland, a country with no military capability, is lower on the table.”
Ed Arnold, senior research fellow for European security at the Royal United Services Institute, told the committee: “[s]o that’s a pretty poor position to be in… [a]nd the only way that you can increase that really is through cash because it’s all about fleet availability, it’s all about readiness to be out of the door as soon as possible and as soon as needed.”
The Defence Investment Plan published in June splits funding into two parts, investing £298 billion in the four years to 2029-30 to reach 2.7 per cent of national income spent on defence, and a period running to 2035 by which all NATO allies including Britain have committed to spending 3.5 per cent of national income on defence.
Sir Keir Starmer, then Prime Minister, said in June this year that it was the British intelligence assessment, and the assessment of other NATO countries, that there could be an attack by Russia on NATO as soon as 2030.
The committee concludes that the near £300 billion investment over the next four years represents the bedrock on which any British contribution to deterring or defeating Russian hostility against NATO from 2030 rests, and that the Ministry of Defence needs to enhance the readiness of existing military assets as well as investing in new capabilities.
A separate conclusion states: “Government is already investing in the Hybrid Navy and Atlantic Bastion concepts to deter and, if necessary, defeat those threats in the High North. However, Royal Navy equipment readiness and platform numbers in particular are currently far worse than the government’s stated requirements. With 2030 identified as a key date by which to be ready to deter or defeat any Russian threat, dramatic progress is required before the end of the decade to improve the availability and capabilities of the UK’s Armed Forces for operations in the High North.”
In evidence to the inquiry the Ministry of Defence said capabilities are held at varying levels of readiness, that every platform goes through a cycle of deployment, maintenance, training and preparation, and that equipment is held at different readiness depending on the capability it is required to meet for NATO.

Staff say jobs are moving offshore as NAB sheds workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:59:52 UTC
08:59:52 KST

NAB staff speak out after mass job cut announcement
In short:
Entire teams of National Australia Bank workers are having to reapply for their jobs and compete among themselves as part of a major restructure.
Staff say the writing was on the wall as they witnessed the bank pushing to offshore workers and take up AI.
What's next?
The major bank revealed plans to slash 2,500 roles by June next year, with 1,500 expected to be out the door before Christmas.
National Australia Bank (NAB) workers have accused the banking giant of a "spill and fill" redundancy strategy, forcing entire teams to reapply for their positions as part of a sweeping restructure.
Earlier this week the major bank revealed plans to slash 2,500 roles by June, including 1,500 before Christmas.
This is about 6 per cent of its total workforce, with corporate roles bearing the brunt.
Several workers who spoke to the ABC on condition of anonymity said the writing was on the wall as the bank pushed the uptake of AI and moved work offshore.
"Until today, it's been a lovely place to work," said Dylan*, who has worked in NAB's technology team for a decade but learnt he could be unemployed by the end of the year.
His team will have to reapply for their jobs in what is known as a "spill and fill" type of workforce restructure, where existing roles are made vacant and current employees have to fight for a smaller number of positions.
There is a two-week consultation period for Dylan's team and, for those being shown the door, their last day will be December 2 or 17.
NAB chief executive Andrew Irvine said in a note to staff he encouraged colleagues to be "thoughtful" and check in on one another, and indicated support would be offered to those "impacted personally".
The bank said in an ASX announcement that the mass redundancies, which are estimated to cost the bank about $300 million in restructuring costs, were part of "actions to simplify its operating model and better align its workforce to prioritise growth and technology initiatives for customers".
The bank declined to comment to the ABC on staff members' claims.
Jobs offshored
The looming redundancies have sparked serious concerns about offshoring among staff, as the banking heavyweight bolsters its Indian and Vietnamese headcount while it cuts staff based in Australia.
A leaked workforce plan seen by the ABC shows Dylan's team in technology, which consists of just under 500 people, is currently 53 per cent Australian-based.
The rest are based in NAB's offices in India (14 per cent), Vietnam (13 per cent), or are external contractors.
But, under the plan, the number of staff would be reduced to 400 by the 2027 financial year while the percentage of offshore workers would increase.
The Australian-based workforce would be cut to 40 per cent, with the Indian and Vietnamese offices upping their numbers to 30 and 20 per cent respectively.
James* resigned last Friday, just days before NAB announced it was going to slash staff, because of fears about the longevity of his business banking role.
He shared an email NAB sent in March, which stated the bank would be "expanding out teams in NAB India" to help in its goal of "focusing on digitising and simplifying processes, including increasing automation to speed up turnaround time" and "investing in our global teams".
James said the messaging in NAB had changed so drastically in the past six months that he no longer felt safe in his job and had left the banking industry.
"People are feeling the anxiety," he said, adding that he had moved to a service-based industry because, "I can't be replaced realistically for the next five to 10 years."
AI concerns
AI is also an issue on everyone's lips.
While there was no direct reference to AI, NAB did refer to "rapid technological change" in its announcement to the market and experts say its impact is clear.
MST Financial analyst Brian Johnson said that for a long time it was politically unacceptable to essentially replace people with AI.
"We're probably approaching the point where it becomes more politically palatable to actually shed staff than perhaps it was even six months ago,"
he said.
"Technology will supplant a lot of functions at jobs. You can just do things better and faster."
Recruiter Clinton Marks from Robert Half said bank redundancies in 2026 appeared to be driven more by cost-cutting and organisational restructuring than direct AI replacement, despite growing pressure on executives to find productivity gains through technology.
Mr Marks said C-level managers were "under great pressure to reduce cost" and that "AI [is] an answer to those questions".
However, he said most organisations were not ready for large-scale AI deployment and he was not yet seeing workers replaced by the technology.
Instead, Mr Marks said, recent redundancy rounds were largely about reducing costs and streamlining operations, while demand remained strongest for workers with skills in cyber security, governance, risk, compliance and AI adoption.
'Wrecking ball'
The union representing bank employees said it was appalled by NAB's redundancy plans and dubbed it a "wrecking ball" to hit staff with the news so close to Christmas.
"Cutting 6 per cent of a workforce will not simplify NAB's operating model or better align its workforce to prioritise growth," Finance Sector Union (FSU) national assistant secretary Nicole McPherson said.
"It will wreak chaos and entrench a culture of anxiety at a bank that seems hell-bent on self-destruction.
"To take a wrecking ball to 6 per cent of one of Australia's largest workforces this close to Christmas is disgraceful and shows that NAB's leadership is completely detached from the lived experience of their workers."
Australian banks, large and small, have been cutting their workforces, with a major restructure at ANZ leading to thousands of job losses in the past year.
Last month, Bendigo and Adelaide Bank proposed cutting 137 jobs as part of an ongoing restructure.
The FSU has also said it had already seen 1,000 jobs cut so far this year at the Commonwealth Bank.
At the Commonwealth Bank's annual general meeting last week, the FSU asked if it could receive assurances workers' jobs were safe, prompting the bank to say there was "no ability to give a blanket commitment", adding that "AI is changing and complementing the way we work".
* Names have been changed to protect workers from potential negative repercussions.

To Import or Build? Southeast Asia’s Rolling Stock Dilemma
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:58:00 UTC
08:58:00 KST

Urban rail systems are growing fast across Southeast Asia. This is fueling demand for rolling stock – the train cars that actually carry millions of riders around town every day. The most common option is to import trainsets from established industry leaders in China, Japan, South Korea, or Europe. But some countries in Southeast are turning to domestic firms to meet their orders. This raises an obvious question: is this wise?
The trade-offs are clear enough. Importing trains from an established global brand like China’s CRRC means you are buying a proven product, with after-sales service and support that makes it easier to maintain the trains. Sometimes foreign firms also provide electronic systems like signalling, which makes system integration easier. For many rail providers, this is a fine deal. Metro and commuter rail systems in Bangkok and Manila rely mainly on imported rolling stock.
But some countries want more. They want to manufacture the rolling stock domestically because they believe it will generate local jobs, create long-term value, and develop important skills and technical expertise. If done well, it will allow domestic firms to grow and export their products. Indonesia is a prominent example of this strategy, with state-owned INKA producing rolling stock for the local market and for export.
INKA’s main customer is the state-owned railway company, KAI, with which it is currently in the process of merging. If you have ever traveled on an intercity train in Java it most likely was made by INKA. More recently, INKA supplied the rolling stock for the Greater Jakarta LRT and has been delivering new trainsets for Jakarta’s large, aging and very busy commuter rail system, the KRL.
INKA is a classic case of industrial policy. Rather than relying on foreign firms, the government requires KAI to procure some of its rolling stock from INKA and places restrictions on imports. This guarantees INKA a minimum level of orders while also protecting it from foreign competition, providing the train-maker some breathing room to develop industrial capabilities it might not otherwise be able to.
But here’s the catch. For such industrial policy to be effective, INKA needs to deliver the goods. It must deliver rolling stock on time and that meets basic quality standards. It must show evidence that it is making progress toward mastery of more complex technologies, skills and production capabilities. The government can bend the market to give a state-owned firm a leg up, but the firm needs to prove this intervention is worth it. Industrial policy fails when firms don’t make good use of the strategic advantage they have been given.
At the moment, INKA is struggling to deliver the goods. The train cars built for the LRT in 2023 were plagued with problems, including electrical and mechanical issues. Almost as soon as they went into service, many had to be pulled out and modified. The LRT project was run mainly by Indonesian SOEs, so the fact that it experienced growing pains was not necessarily evidence of policy failure. The key was that domestic firms, including INKA, learned from these mistakes and used them to improve.
In recent weeks, rolling stock made by INKA for Jakarta’s commuter rail system has been malfunctioning, throwing commutes into chaos. Doors are getting stuck open, forcing trains out of service. Seven cars were recalled after KAI raised concerns about structural weakness in the undercarriage. KAI is seeking special permission from the government to import used rolling stock from Japan to meet immediate operational needs while these issues are worked out. Public anger and scrutiny are rising.
Similar attempts by other home-grown firms in the region also have spotty records. In 2011, Malaysia’s Scomi won a nearly 500 million ringgit contract to supply trainsets for the Kuala Lumpur monorail. The rolling stock was delivered late, and faced performance and safety issues. The procurement became embroiled in legal disputes, and Scomi was eventually dissolved. So INKA is not alone in facing hurdles as it tries to expand its footprint. But if the government is to continue aiding such efforts, INKA needs to start delivering the goods.
This is especially true now that intra-ASEAN competition is intensifying. Vietnamese conglomerate Vingroup just announced it was launching a joint venture with France’s Alstom to co-produce 200 trainsets for the Hanoi metro under a technology licensing agreement. This is a very large and ambitious project, which would represent a major step-up in capabilities for Vingroup and Vietnam’s domestic railway industry. Of course, Vingroup has a history of taking huge swings that don’t always pan out. So we will have to see.
Most urban rail systems in Southeast Asia simply import their trains, working with established manufacturers who can deliver a proven product and after-sales service and support. For some countries, domestic manufacturing is a more important goal and the state will intervene to give local firms a head-start. Ultimately, no amount of state support or industrial policy can cover up for production failings that leave commuters stranded with unreliable products. The trains must run, and local firms like INKA must deliver the goods. Otherwise, the whole logic of industrial policy comes flying off the rails.

Airbnb scraps check-out chores for guests under new rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21

Airbnb scraps check-out chores for guests under new rules
In short:
Airbnb will ban hosts from requiring guests to complete check-out chores such as stripping beds, washing dishes or taking out rubbish, under new rules.
The changes announced on its website apply to bookings made on or from November 20.
What's next?
Some Airbnb hosts have reacted angrily to the changes, with several threatening to move to other booking platforms or change their prices.
Airbnb guests will no longer have to strip beds, wash dishes or remove rubbish when checking out, under new rules to be introduced next month.
The changes have sparked anger among hosts, with some warning the crackdown could drive up costs and push smaller operators off the platform.
The short-term rental platform announced the changes on its website. They apply to reservations booked on or after November 20.
The changes come amid complaints from some travellers about being charged cleaning fees, which can cost hundreds of dollars, while also being expected to complete a list of chores before leaving a property.
The company said while cleaning fees would not be abolished completely, hosts could not require guests to perform tasks that took "significant time and effort or would normally be done by a cleaner".
"House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage," Airbnb said in a statement.
"So we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises."
Hosts can still ask guests to complete simpler tasks, such as placing used dishes in the sink and gathering used towels.
They will also continue to set their own cleaning fees.
Changes spark anger from hosts
Hundreds of hosts have criticised the new rules on Airbnb's online community forum.
Townsville Airbnb host Nadia Di Martino, who operates three listings from her Kirwin home, said the changes were "infuriating".
"I think that many hosts will either have to increase their prices and then pay someone else to do the whole cleaning," Ms Di Martino said.
She said she did the cleaning herself and did not charge guests a cleaning fee, but asked them to wash their dishes before checking out.
"I don't think it's unreasonable,"
she said.
She said she understood why Airbnb had acted, because some hosts had imposed excessive check-out chores.
But she said she was now considering leaving the platform and renting her rooms to students instead, or would ban the use of cooking facilities.
"I think that I would rather probably just … have permanent flatmates. I think it will be more comfortable for me," she said.
Kendra, a host from South Carolina in the US, warned the policy could drive smaller hosts away from the platform and increase costs for guests.
"It's going to incentivise soulless, basic rentals and raise cleaning and liability costs that guests will ultimately bear the burden of," she said.
Mindy, from New Mexico, accused Airbnb management of being "so out of touch with the people cleaning vacation rentals", while Becky, from Canada, said she had "never been so upset by a policy change".
What does it mean for Australian travellers?
The changes apply to Airbnb reservations covered by the platform's global policy, including bookings in Australia.
Hosts will still be able to set house rules, including check-in and check-out times, limits on the number of guests, smoking restrictions, pet rules and quiet hours.
Airbnb said guests were still expected to leave properties in a reasonable condition and may be held responsible for damage or excessive cleaning caused by their stay.

Prabowo Accuses MSCI of Attempting to ‘Intimidate’ Indonesia After Downgrade Threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:49:00 UTC
08:49:00 KST

Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has accused MSCI of attempting to “intimidate” Indonesia, after the global index provider threatened to downgrade the country due to serious stock market transparency issues.
In a statement on October 16, MSCI announced that it had launched “a consultation on a proposal to reclassify the MSCI Indonesia Indexes from Emerging Market to Standalone Market status.” Among its concerns are coordinated trading practices, the high concentration of ownership in certain companies, and the limited “free float” of shares – i.e., those openly available for public trading.
Speaking to his cabinet yesterday, Prabowo said that MSCI “intended to intimidate us,” Reuters reported. “I simply say to the MSCI: the Indonesian nation fears no one and will not be cowed… We possess strength, we have courage, we are willing to make sacrifices, and we refuse to surrender.”
MSCI’s proposal was more serious than its threat in January to downgrade Indonesia to “frontier market” status due to the transparency concerns in its stock market. The “standalone market” category, which includes the likes of Argentina, Lebanon, Palestine, Ukraine, and Zimbabwe, is a rung below “frontier market.”
MSCI said last week that it decided on a more serious downgrade because the long list of reforms announced by Indonesian policymakers to address its concerns had not achieved “sufficient progress.”
“Despite the announced reforms, significant concerns remain around market dysfunction, including continued suspected coordinated trading behavior and lack of evidence of meaningful enforcement,” it stated. “Feedback from market participants suggests that a reclassification to Frontier Markets would not properly recognize the depth of the market problems.” MSCI said that it “expects to proceed with the proposed reclassification” barring clear evidence of “material improvements in market governance and functioning.”
The announcement prompted a bloodbath on the Jakarta Composite Index, which plunged by around 15 percent over two days of trading. The Indonesian stock market has been among the worst performing in the world in 2026, losing around 40 percent of its value, while the rupiah has fallen to levels not seen since the Asian financial crisis of 1997-1998.
The prospect of a further outflow of capital – a likely result of a downgrade to “standalone” status – has heaped pressure on Prabowo’s administration, which since coming to office in late 2024, has rattled markets with its centralized and free-spending approach to economic management. This has included both a multibillion-dollar free meal program and an increase in the state’s involvement in the Indonesian economy.
Perhaps less important than specific policies is Prabowo’s volatile, unpredictable and highly personalized style of economic governance, which represents a significant change from the conservative stewardship of the past few administrations. In March, both Moody’s and Fitch announced ratings outlook downgrades for Indonesia, with the latter citing the “increasing policy uncertainty and erosion of Indonesia’s policy mix consistency and credibility” and the “growing centralization of policymaking authority.” George Xu, a Director in Fitch Ratings’ Sovereigns team, said in a statement on Tuesday that MSCI’s announcement and the subsequent market sell-off only “reinforce the risks” identified by Fitch during its downgrade in March.
Prabowo’s defiant remarks about the MSCI threat, which have also been echoed by other Indonesian politicians in recent days, are characteristic of his political style and nationalist leanings. They are also unlikely to do much to address the growing concerns about Indonesia’s investability, making it likely that Indonesia will face more economic turbulence during the remainder of his term.

Tesla beats on earnings and sales even as auto revenue declines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:32:04 UTC
08:32:04 KST

Tesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday, even as automotive revenue dropped. The stock slid more than 3% in extended trading.
Here's how the company did, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG:
- Earnings per share: 48 cents adjusted vs. 43 cents estimated
- Revenue: $28.05 billion vs. $27.9 billion estimated
Tesla's earnings report lands a day after CEO Elon Musk told investors on SpaceX's quarterly call that it would be a "good idea" for his two companies to merge, and said the boards at both have formed special committees to discuss a possible tie-up.
"I feel like I'm tap dancing through a minefield," Musk said on the call, responding to a question about a potential merger.
Musk addressed the matter in his opening comments on the Tesla call, but didn't provide any additional information.
"I think I said everything that should be said yesterday," he said.
Tesla's revenue was down slightly flat from a year earlier, when the company generated sales of $28.24 billion, according to the earnings deck. In Tesla's core automotive business, revenue declined 3% from a year earlier to $20.56 billion in the quarter. Energy revenue fell 16% to $2.88 billion.
Balancing out the declines were gains in Tesla's services and other revenue. Sales there climbed 33% from a year ago to $4.61 billion.
Tesla blamed its lackluster automotive revenue and profits on lower average sales prices for its cars during the quarter, and trouble securing battery supplies to make enough vehicles to fulfill a backlog of orders.
Net income attributable to common share holders plummeted 29% to $787 million, or 22 cents a share, from $1.11 billion, or 32 cents a share, a year earlier, Tesla said.
The drop in profitability reflects a surge in spending on Optimus humanoid robots and other artificial intelligence initiatives. Capital expenditures more than doubled from a year earlier to $3.73 billion. Free cash flow plunged by 62% year over year to $1.53 billion, after Tesla turned free cash flow negative in the second quarter.
Tesla said uptake of its FSD (Supervised), a partially automated driving system the company sells for $99 per month in the U.S., grew by 20 percentage points from the second quarter. Active FSD subscriptions increased 67% from a year earlier to 1.74 million.
"We believe that FSD is driving demand in markets where it is available, and we continue to work with regulators to get it approved in other markets," the company said in its investor deck.
Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla's vice president of Autopilot, said on the earnings call that the company plans to give some customer cars access to its forthcoming FSD (Unsupervised) systems around the second quarter of next year.
Tesla is testing its Cybercab, a bronze two-seater designed for use as a robotaxi, but it's not yet sold to individuals. Musk said on the call that "the vast majority of the Cybercab stuff will be essentially Tesla-owned and transport-as-a-service."
The company plans to bring Cybercab to cities beyond Austin, Texas, this year, Taneja said, paying attention to operating costs like maintenance, charging and cleaning.
Musk said the company's driverless Robotaxi fleet will start to contribute to the company's financials in 2027. That fleet now includes 362 Model Y Robotaxi, and 449 Cybercab vehicles authorized for driverless operations in Texas, according to the state's Department of Motor Vehicles,
"It's not like going to move the needle this quarter," Musk said, "I think it starts to become noticeable in Q2 and then probably a big deal by Q3 or Q4 of next year."
Barring regulatory intervention and protectionism, Musk predicted that Tesla "will end up doing a majority of all passenger miles on Earth in any country where it is allowed to operate freely."
Tesla said its auto sales in Canada, Japan, Taiwan and Australia hit new records during the quarter. However, the company has gotten meager growth out of its core market of late as Chinese EV makers such as BYD and Xiaomi gained popularity in Asia and Europe with affordable and innovative EVs. Tesla was also hit last year by the end of a federal EV tax credit.
Earlier this month, Tesla reported vehicle deliveries for the third quarter of 486,532, about 2% below the year-ago number. Deliveries are the closest approximation of sales reported by Tesla but are not precisely defined in its shareholder communications.
One of Tesla's big investments is in a semiconductor factory that it's building with SpaceX and Intel in Grimes County, Texas. That partnership with SpaceX along with other areas of overlap, including work on Tesla's recently announced Roadster refresh, fueled intensifying speculation that Musk's companies were on the verge of combining in what would be a historic transaction.
On Optimus, Musk said Tesla is "making good progress" on the AI systems that control the robots in development. He said there's "still quite a lot of work to do with regard to the AI and the robot for it to be truly useful for open-ended tasks."
Musk said he expects current issues around electromechanical design, reliability, usage duration, and AI to be "solved around the end of next year."

Chinese-linked hackers compromise ConnectWise, target hundreds in global attack: Microsoft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:25:00 UTC
08:25:00 KST

Chinese-linked hackers compromise ConnectWise, target hundreds in global attack: Microsoft
- Microsoft said a Chinese-linked group, Storm-0940, used the AI tool ARTEX to breach ConnectWise and target hundreds of organisations worldwide.
- ConnectWise said a China state-aligned group likely attacked its Cloud Backup service and that it has contained affected connections and is restoring services in phases.
- The campaign hit many sectors, including defence, finance and government, and Microsoft warned the hackers gained privileged cloud persistence at many firms despite most attacks failing.
AI generated
A Chinese-linked hacking group used an AI-driven penetration testing tool to compromise IT services firm ConnectWise as part of a campaign that targeted hundreds of organisations globally, Microsoft said on Oct 21.
Based on Microsoft’s analysis and evidence available to ConnectWise, “it appears that a China state-aligned group was responsible for the attack on ConnectWise Cloud Backup”, ConnectWise chief executive officer Manny Rivelo said in a separate statement.
Rivelo said ConnectWise “contained the affected application connections and is restoring services in controlled phases”. He added that “those actions do not remove unauthorised access that may have already been established within individual customer tenants, which require separate review”.
A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington said China “opposes and fights hacking activities in accordance with the law. At the same time, we oppose smears and attacks against China under the excuse of cybersecurity issues”.
The hackers, which Microsoft tracks as Storm-0940, used an open-source penetration testing framework called ARTEX to carry out the campaign, the company said. There are multiple tools used to conduct penetration testing, a form of legitimate testing of the security of networks or services.
ARTEX allows users to use any AI model to automate a variety of penetration testing tasks and can be configured to run autonomous tasks including reconnaissance and data exfiltration, Microsoft said.
The attack targeted organisations across a wide variety of sectors, including aerospace, defence, automotive, chemicals, energy, financial services, government, legal, manufacturing, media, military, semiconductor, software, technology, think-tanks and non-profit organisations, Microsoft said.
While the majority of the targeting was not successful, Microsoft said, Storm-0940 achieved privileged cloud persistence – or high-level access that could continue even after clean-up efforts – at many organisations in a brief time. REUTERS
