Anthropic, music publishers square off on ‘fair use’ defence in AI copyright case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:18:00 UTC
08:18:00 KST

Anthropic, music publishers square off on ‘fair use’ defence in AI copyright case
- Anthropic asked a California judge to rule that using millions of song lyrics to train Claude is “fair use” under US copyright law.
- Music publishers UMG, Concord and ABKCO say Anthropic’s AI makes competing lyrics and harms songwriters, citing nearly 120,000 “synthetic” lyric requests in six months.
- The case could affect many AI copyright lawsuits, after earlier Northern California rulings split on whether AI training is fair use.
AI generated
SAN JOSE, California – Anthropic urged a judge in California on Oct 21 to rule that the AI company’s use of millions of song lyrics to train its chatbot Claude is protected as “fair use” under US copyright law, as it seeks to scuttle a lawsuit brought by Universal Music Group and other music publishers.
US District Judge Eumi Lee did not rule at a hearing in San Jose but pressed both sides on the fair use question, which could be key to dozens of other high-stakes copyright infringement cases in the AI era.
Lee also questioned the publishers’ assertion that Claude’s ability to compose lyrics threatens the market for the publishers’ lyrics.
Anthropic lawyer Sonal Mehta of WilmerHale argued that its AI training leads to the creation of transformative new content, putting it squarely under the fair use doctrine.
The publishers’ attorney Matt Oppenheim of Oppenheim + Zebrak responded that Anthropic misuses its lyrics to generate competing content that harms human songwriters.
Oppenheim said Claude received nearly 120,000 requests to generate “synthetic” lyrics over a six-month period. He said large language models like Claude “could overwhelm the market with AI-generated content very easily”.
Mehta countered that AI has not reduced demand for the lyrics, and that the publishers could not identify any specific instances of market harm from Claude or other large language models.
Mehta also said that UMG itself has said that AI is “overwhelmingly a net positive” for the music industry.
Early fair use rulings
Fair use could determine the fate of pending lawsuits brought by authors, news outlets, visual artists and others against tech giants including Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta Platforms over their AI training.
Two other Northern California judges who have already weighed in on the closely watched issue have split on whether generative AI training generally makes fair use of copyrighted material, which would shield tech companies from liability for using millions of copyrighted works to train their systems without content owners’ permission.
Now-retired US District Judge William Alsup sided with Anthropic in 2025 on its argument that its AI training made fair use of books. Two days later, US District Judge Vince Chhabria ruled for Meta in a similar lawsuit but warned that AI training “in many circumstances” would not be fair use.
In the case being heard by Lee, music publishers UMG, Concord and ABKCO sued Anthropic in 2023, alleging its use of their lyrics to train Claude to respond to human prompts infringed their copyrights in hundreds of songs by artists including Beyonce, the Rolling Stones and the Beach Boys.
Anthropic has argued that its AI training makes transformative use of song lyrics to “help Claude understand human language and enable progress and productivity in science, business and education”. REUTERS

Britain's MI5 spied on NHS founder Bevan, secret documents show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:11:26 UTC
08:11:26 KST

Britain's MI5 spied on NHS founder Bevan, secret documents show
LONDON, Oct 22 - British spies monitored Nye Bevan, the much lauded architect of the National Health Service, for three decades because of his links to the Communist Party and criticism of Britain's government in World War Two, newly released papers show.
Declassified secret documents from MI5 made public by the National Archives on Thursday reveal that Bevan's activities in parliament, and his movements and meetings outside, were closely watched by MI5 from 1933 until his death in 1960.
MI5 had suspected that Bevan, a committed socialist and one of the most prominent parliamentary critics of Winston Churchill and his wartime coalition, was a communist sympathiser.
However, the agency's investigations seem to have determined that there was nothing to worry about.
"What information we have on Bevan's relations with the Communist Party since 1943 show that from time to time both the Communist Party and the Trotskyists have made attempts to get him to work with them without success," a 1955 note said.
Bevan, who died in 1960, became health minister after the war and is credited with founding the state-funded NHS in 1948.
While the one-time Welsh coal miner was heralded for his oratory skills, he was also seen as a highly divisive figure, not just within the Labour Party but the country as whole.
Two years after his death, a review of his MI5 case file stated: "Considering what a controversial character Nye Bevan was, the file is remarkably tame."
The other newly material released also included MI5 files about Wolfgang zu Putlitz, a German diplomat who leaked information about Hitler's plans to Britain, and Soviet agents and suspected operatives such as Frank Bossard who was jailed for 21 years for passing defence material to Russian spies. X Community Notes ‘failed’ to flag US election falsehoods, study says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:10:00 UTC
08:10:00 KST

X Community Notes ‘failed’ to flag US election falsehoods, study says
- X’s Community Notes missed most false US election claims, with NewsGuard saying it failed to flag 93.1% of them before the Nov 3 midterm elections.
- Only 13 of dozens of false posts were corrected, including claims about voter ID laws and several false posts shared by Musk.
- The study raises doubts about community fact-checking, as researchers say it works best on clear topics and can be shaped by partisan bias.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – A crowdsourced verification system used by Elon Musk’s X failed to flag a vast majority of false claims related to the US midterm elections – including those promoted by the billionaire – a study said on Oct 21.
Community Notes, which allows users to contribute notes that add context or corrections to posts, was introduced by X in late 2022 and the same model is increasingly being adopted by other tech platforms.
But researchers have repeatedly questioned its effectiveness in combating misinformation.
NewsGuard, a US watchdog that rates the credibility of news and information sites, identified dozens of posts on X that advanced false claims related to the elections, including bogus allegations of election fraud.
Only 13 of those posts were tagged with Community Notes.
“X’s crowdsourced fact-checking programme failed to flag 93.1% of false claims related to the US midterm elections,” NewsGuard said.
“The uncorrected X posts have drawn millions of interactions ahead of the Nov 3 midterm elections.”
The falsehoods included a post by a conservative commentator claiming that New York and California had made it illegal for voters to show – and officials to ask for – their voter ID. No such rule exists in either Democratic stronghold.
Musk has often promoted Community Notes, calling it “awesome” and asserting that all users, including himself, were subject to being corrected by the crowdsourced model.
NewsGuard, however, said that Musk, who has 241.5 million followers on X, has advanced at least four false claims related to the midterm elections, none of which carried Community Notes.
X did not respond to AFP’s request for comment.
Studies have shown Community Notes can work to dispel some falsehoods, like vaccine misinformation, but researchers have long cautioned that it works best for topics where there is broad consensus.
Some researchers have also cautioned that Community Notes users can be motivated to target political opponents by partisan beliefs.
Tech platforms increasingly view the community-driven model as an alternative to professional fact-checking.
In 2025, Meta ended its third-party fact-checking programme in the United States, with CEO Mark Zuckerberg saying it had led to “too much censorship”. Professional fact-checkers vehemently reject the claim.
In September, Meta said it had begun testing its own version of Community Notes in 16 Spanish-speaking countries in Latin America, in a step toward replacing its fact-checking programme.
Meta gave no timeline for when the change will become official.
Meta’s Oversight Board, a quasi-independent body the company funds to review its moderation decisions, said Community Notes was not an adequate replacement for fact-checking.
AFP currently works in 26 languages with Meta’s global fact-checking programme, including in Latin America. AFP

Britain lacks what it needs in the High North, says report
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
00:01:29 BST
08:01:29 KST

Britain must address serious military capability gaps in the High North, and should consider whether the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force ought to focus more on threats in the region, particularly if it has to plan for uncertainty over American support for NATO, according to a report by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, published its findings after an inquiry that took evidence between March and July this year and included visits to Norway, Denmark and Greenland.
Dhesi said: “The High North poses a major strategic challenge for the UK’s security. This is a demanding, hostile environment, and one that our greatest adversary, Russia, is seeking to dominate for military advantage.”
He said: “The UK needs to be willing to address a hard truth: it does not currently have all the capabilities to operate successfully in the High North. Russian submarine and sabotage forces in the High North pose direct risks to the North Atlantic and the UK, including the nuclear deterrent. Despite this, the Ministry of Defence has accepted a serious anti-submarine warfare gap. Publicly available evidence of low availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines calls into question whether the UK can meet its commitments in the High North.”
He added: “And if the UK government means what it says – that Russia could attack NATO as soon as 2030 – then work to rectify these vulnerabilities cannot start soon enough.”
The report warns of serious consequences if the region is left inadequately defended. Failure to deter Russia there, particularly from underwater threats, would put subsea data cables and energy pipelines in and around British waters at particular risk during peacetime. In the event of hostilities, failure to counter Russia in the High North would threaten the British population, military and civilian critical national infrastructure including the nuclear deterrent, and Atlantic resupply routes from the United States.
On the capability gaps themselves, the committee sets out that the Royal Navy has a requirement for eight of its thirteen frigates to carry the Sonar 2087 towed array for anti-submarine work and currently holds five, all of them Type 23s. It records eleven frigates and destroyers in service against a requirement for nineteen, and calls for no further towed array-equipped Type 23 to leave service until replaced one-for-one by a Type 26.
It also finds that Britain has allowed its submarine under-ice capability to lapse just as the region has become strategically more important, leaving it less able to contest Russian freedom of action and at risk of being forced into a more defensive posture.
On the Joint Expeditionary Force, the ten-nation grouping Britain leads alongside the Netherlands and the Baltic and Nordic states, Dhesi said: “Our Defence in the High North inquiry found that the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force has not yet realised its full potential. Although it was originally conceived as capable of operating across the full spectrum of conflict, and of covering both the High North and Baltic regions, its role has become increasingly focused on countering sub-threshold and hybrid threats.”
He said: “Our report calls for the government to reassess the JEF’s role and consider whether it should focus more on countering threats in the High North, particularly if the UK has to plan for uncertainty over US support for NATO. The UK’s presence in the Baltics, particularly in Estonia, may need to be bolstered to offset the effects of any greater JEF focus on the High North.”
Building the British Army force in Estonia up to brigade strength would match what Germany is already undertaking in Lithuania. The committee also asks the government, within a year of assuming leadership of NATO’s Joint Force Command Norfolk, to reassess the added value the force brings to European security, and either strengthen it and align it more closely with NATO or focus its finite resources on NATO instead.
Sir Keir Starmer, then Prime Minister, said in June this year that it was the British intelligence assessment, and that of other NATO countries, that there could be an attack by Russia on NATO as soon as 2030. The Defence Investment Plan published the same month committed £298 billion over four years to 2029-30.
In evidence to the inquiry the Ministry of Defence described anti-submarine warfare as a core strength of Britain’s armed forces, and said capabilities are held at varying levels of readiness, with every platform going through a cycle of deployment, maintenance, training and preparation, and equipment held at different readiness depending on the capability it is required to meet for NATO.
The government is expected to respond to the report within two months.

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- U.S. technology giant Meta Platforms reported a 26 percent year-on-year increase in third-quarter revenue on Wednesday, while operating profit fell 37 percent largely due to a multi-billion-dollar charge related to a legal settlement over teen mental health and social media.
According to the company's latest financial report, revenue rose to 64.60 billion U.S. dollars in the quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with 51.24 billion dollars a year earlier, exceeding analysts' expectations of 63.37 billion dollars.
Net income reached 9.86 billion dollars, up 264 percent from 2.71 billion dollars a year earlier, while diluted earnings per share increased to 3.83 dollars from 1.05 dollars. The year-earlier net income was affected by a one-time, non-cash tax charge of 15.93 billion dollars.
Operating income declined 37 percent to 12.99 billion dollars from 20.54 billion dollars a year earlier, with the operating margin narrowing to 20 percent from 40 percent.
Meta said its third-quarter expenses included a 9.89-billion-dollar charge related to an August agreement with U.S. state attorneys general to settle litigation concerning teen mental health and social media. Excluding the charge, operating income would have reached approximately 22.88 billion dollars.
Advertising revenue, which accounts for the overwhelming majority of Meta's business, increased to 63.06 billion dollars from 50.08 billion dollars a year earlier.
The company's family of apps, including Facebook, Instagram, Messenger and WhatsApp, recorded an average of 3.64 billion daily active users in September, up 3 percent from 3.54 billion a year earlier, representing an increase of approximately 100 million people. The figure also rose by about 40 million from June 2026.
Meta continued to expand its investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure. Capital expenditures, including principal payments on finance leases, totaled 34.91 billion dollars during the quarter.
Free cash flow turned negative at 2.12 billion dollars, compared with positive free cash flow of 10.63 billion dollars a year earlier.
Looking ahead, Meta forecast fourth-quarter revenue of between 73 billion and 76 billion dollars. It also narrowed its full-year capital expenditure forecast to between 135 billion and 145 billion dollars, raising the lower end from its previous projection of 130 billion dollars.
Separately, Meta announced plans to establish a new class of publicly listed, non-voting Class C common stock in January 2027. The move is intended to support future investment, acquisitions and employee compensation while preserving the company's existing voting structure. ■

Why Kazakhstan Joined Both the American and Chinese AI Initiatives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

Why Kazakhstan Joined Both the American and Chinese AI Initiatives
Kazakhstan did not choose between Washington’s Pax Silica and Beijing’s WAICO: it joined both. It needs technology from both superpowers, and a say in the rules.
‘No country should remain only a consumer of artificial intelligence,’ Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev told the opening ceremony of the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai on 17 July. Every state, he said, should have the opportunity to build its own digital infrastructure and institutional capacity.
He stood at Xi Jinping’s right for the group photograph, sat beside him through the session and spoke second, ahead of two prime ministers and the UN Secretary-General. He opened in Mandarin. Such arrangements are settled in advance.
The day before, 29 governments had signed the founding agreement of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), to be headquartered in Shanghai. Kazakhstan was among them.
Three weeks earlier, the country’s AI minister, Zhaslan Madiyev, had been in Washington signing the Pax Silica declaration, the State Department’s initiative on AI and supply chain security. Of the 25 signatories, Kazakhstan is so far the only one that also belongs to WAICO.
Kazakhstan does not produce the core technology it is trying to acquire for its AI agenda. What a country in that position can build, and what it has to trade to do it, is a question most of the world will face. Yet the reporting concentrates on the AI race between Washington and Beijing, and much less on what everyone else is doing.
A National Project
Since mid-2025, AI has become a central focus of the state. A presidential council on AI development, chaired by Tokayev, was established in May 2025. His annual address to the nation that September was devoted to the subject, and ten days later the country had a ministry for it headed by a deputy prime minister. This year was declared the year of digitalisation and artificial intelligence, and on 18 January an AI law came into force. In June, the government adopted Digital Qazaqstan, a national strategy for digital transformation and AI development running to 2029. The Digital Code took effect on 12 July, five days before Tokayev spoke in Shanghai.
AI is being asked to do two jobs: improve how the state and the wider economy run, and become an export industry in its own right
The drive has two sources. The first is systemic. Competition between the frontier laboratories has produced rapid and visible gains in what the leading models can do, and with them a widening expectation that this technology will transform economies and societies faster than earlier industrial transitions did. Most states are moving because they do not want to arrive late.
The second is country-level. Kazakhstan’s economy depends on natural resources, above all oil, which is about half of what it sells abroad. Diversifying away from that has been declared policy for decades. Broadly, AI is being asked to do two jobs: improve how the state and the wider economy run, and become an export industry in its own right.
Who Supplies What
Meeting any of those targets requires technology and infrastructure Kazakhstan cannot supply on its own. Several suppliers provide it.
The US supplies the chips, the model foundations and, in time, the cloud. The chips matter most. Both national supercomputers run on Nvidia H200s, and the first was delayed while Kazakhstan waited for an American export licence. In June 2026, the AI ministry and Kazakhtelecom signed framework agreements with Firebird – an American data centre developer partnered with Nvidia – for the Data Center Valley at Ekibastuz, a coal-mining and power-generating city. The minister says it will run 100,000 GPUs (graphics processing units), including Nvidia’s GB300 and Vera Rubin, on a planned $10 billion investment. The site is under construction. On 2 October, Kazakhtelecom, KT-Telecom and Firebird AI KZ signed an initial agreement to build a data centre, and the minister plans to commission 186 megawatts of capacity in 2027. KazLLM and Sherkala, the two flagship Kazakh-language models, are built on weights published by Meta.Google Cloud has agreed to run a node in Astana.
China supplies pieces of several layers, and the full extent is harder to establish. AlemLLM, the largest Kazakh model, was developed with technical support from 01.AI. At Ekibastuz, where Firebird is installing the compute, Kazakhtelecom has agreed guiding principles with Hengtong, one of China’s largest optical fibre manufacturers, for the same project. Huawei signed agreements with both the AI ministry and the sovereign wealth fund. Chinese firms have taken connectivity and cloud roles at the Akashi data centre in Astana, which is also under construction. Several of these were signed during Tokayev’s July visit to Shanghai, among more than 70 agreements worth over $15 billion whose full list has yet to be published.
Russia supplies the routes for Kazakhstan’s international internet traffic. It is by far the country’s main source of bandwidth to the outside world, and most local providers send their traffic through Russian networks, over an estimated 17 cross-border fibre connections. A new cable across the Caspian, launched on 15 October, opens a route to Europe through Azerbaijan and Georgia that could reduce overreliance on Russia, but its effects have yet to show. Electricity is another critical layer. In September, Russia’s state nuclear corporation, Rosatom, signed a contract to build Kazakhstan’s first nuclear plant. The country’s Atomic Energy Agency says demand for reliable power will keep rising with digitalisation and AI, and that nuclear energy will provide stable baseload generation for decades. The Rosatom contract, however, still needs government approval, and no completion date has been announced.
The UAE is the recurring partner. In 2024, Presight, part of G42, signed an agreement with Kazakhstan’s digital ministry and the sovereign wealth fund to develop a national AI supercomputer, the first project of its joint venture with the fund. Sherkala was co-developed by G42’s Inception and Abu Dhabi’s AI university and trained on Condor Galaxy, the G42–Cerebras supercomputer. On 1 October, Tokayev discussed G42’s possible participation in the Data Center Valley.
The legal architecture borrows from Europe, selectively. The AI law that came into force this January takes five of the eight practices the EU AI Act prohibits, leaving out the three that restrict policing and surveillance. It takes its rule on training data from the EU’s copyright opt-out rather than from American fair use.
How the Choices are Made
Kazakhstan’s moves in AI, whether procuring hardware and models or joining institutional arrangements, broadly rest on two grounds. The first is pragmatism, exercised within external constraints and on the strength of what the country holds. Bloc-building is not pragmatic. The US and China hold the leading positions in the technology, so going to both is going where the capability is.
What Kazakhstan holds sits on the other side of that exchange. It is the world’s largest producer of uranium, at a time when AI is driving demand for nuclear power. It is, the UK government says, ‘a globally significant producer of 18 minerals’ on Britain’s priority list. That is why minerals have moved to the centre of its external engagement, and why it is increasingly described as an alternative to Chinese supply. Yet selling to a country seeking to reduce its dependence on China is not, from Astana’s perspective, taking a side.
Kazakhstan is the world’s largest producer of uranium, at a time when AI is driving demand for nuclear power
Tungsten shows it plainly. Boguty in the Almaty region, developed by a subsidiary of Hong Kong-listed Jiaxin International Resources, reached commercial production in April 2025 and made Kazakhstan the world’s third-largest producer that year. The country’s first exports of the metal went entirely to China. While that mine was coming onstream, Samruk-Kazyna, the sovereign wealth fund, was taking bids for the larger Karaganda deposits. Bloomberg reported in October 2025 that the American firm Cove Capital faced competition from at least one state-backed Chinese firm prepared to pay above market price, and that it needed US government backing to raise the financing at all. Kazakhstan signed in November with Cove, which holds 70% of the venture and markets all of the output.
The second ground is a view of international politics. Kazakhstan, just like most states, prefers a world that is predictable because it runs on clear rules. It also works to build the institutions that make them. The memberships deliver practical benefits as well as a seat at the table where rules are written.
On that reading it is unsurprising that Kazakhstan joined both Pax Silica and WAICO, and others are likely to follow. Since its launch, WAICO has enlarged once, adding eight members, taking it to 37. Uzbekistan, also a WAICO founder, has asked to join Pax Silica and Indonesia, another founder, sees room for both. Washington, however, may press for a choice: in August, Reuters reported on an undated draft State Department letter to the 35 signatories of a US AI statement, which warns that ‘to be part of everything is to be part of nothing’. It is unclear whether the letter has been sent. In Samarkand on 19 October, though, Marco Rubio said that US engagement in Central Asia was not about telling countries to stop working with others, but he was speaking of economic ties generally. For now, the mixed signals leave room for Kazakhstan to keep both memberships.
Yet what neither initiative supplies is what Tokayev himself named in Shanghai: AI capabilities ‘are advancing faster than our collective ability to understand, evaluate and govern them’. That ability sits almost entirely inside the companies building the systems, and the weeks after Shanghai showed its limits there. OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta each disclosed that their models had reached outside their test environments. OpenAI established that its models were behind an intrusion Hugging Face had detected. Anthropic found its own cases only after OpenAI’s disclosure prompted it to check its test records, and Meta attributed its case to a misconfiguration by the outside firm it uses to run tests.
Kazakhstan runs models built on weights it did not produce, on chips it cannot make, and has no means of inspecting either. Nor does almost any state outside the frontier. Tokayev’s two proposals – common standards for testing and certifying AI systems and a permanent expert platform on regulation and ethics – describe a capability that exists nowhere.
This is a technology without precedent and it is moving quickly, so the machinery for governing it is needed now. That falls at a moment when existing rules are being disregarded, including by the power that wrote most of them. Whatever WAICO and Pax Silica are eventually asked to do matters more to Kazakhstan than to the US or China, because rules, however imperfectly, constrain the strong in a way that bilateral bargains do not.

07:59:59 KST

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- U.S. electric vehicle maker Tesla reported a 43 percent year-on-year decline in third-quarter net profit on Wednesday, while revenue remained largely unchanged amid falling vehicle deliveries and higher operating expenses.
According to the company's latest financial report, revenue totaled 28.05 billion U.S. dollars in the quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with 28.1 billion dollars a year earlier, representing a slight decline of 0.2 percent.
Net income attributable to common stockholders fell to 787 million dollars from 1.37 billion dollars in the same period last year, while diluted earnings per share declined to 22 cents from 39 cents.
Operating income dropped 56 percent year on year to 718 million dollars from 1.62 billion dollars, with the operating margin narrowing to 2.6 percent from 5.8 percent.
Tesla said the decline in operating profit was primarily driven by higher operating expenses related to artificial intelligence and research and development projects, increased stock-based compensation and lower regulatory credit revenue.
Despite the decline in operating income, the company's overall gross margin improved to 19.6 percent from 18 percent a year earlier.
The company reported third-quarter capital expenditures of 4.73 billion dollars, more than double the 2.25 billion dollars recorded a year earlier, as it continued to invest in manufacturing capacity, artificial intelligence and other projects.
During the quarter, Tesla's automotive revenue fell 3 percent year on year to 20.56 billion dollars, compared with 21.21 billion dollars a year earlier. The company delivered 486,532 vehicles worldwide, down approximately 2 percent from a year earlier. Vehicle production, meanwhile, rose 4 percent to 464,391 units.
Tesla also reported a 67 percent year-on-year increase in active subscriptions to its Full Self-Driving system, to 1.74 million, and progress in its autonomous driving and robotics businesses, including the launch of rides using its purpose-built Cybercab vehicles in Austin, Texas, on Sept. 3.
Looking ahead, Tesla said it would focus on maximizing factory capacity utilization while continuing to invest in autonomous driving, robotics, artificial intelligence infrastructure and energy storage. ■

Hundreds of authors, actors, and musicians have signed an open letter backing Irish novelist Sally Rooney and her publisher, Faber, demanding an immediate amendment to legislation that has halted the distribution and sale of her books in the United Kingdom.
Published in the New Statesman, the open letter warns that the withdrawal of Rooney's works from British shelves raises profound concerns regarding freedom of expression following the UK government’s official designation of Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation.
"Sally Rooney is a writer, not a terrorist. Her books must be available to the public," the letter stated.
High-profile signatories include authors Zadie Smith, Patrick Ness, Damian Barr, and Juno Dawson; actors Paul Mescal, Daisy Edgar-Jones, and Tilda Swinton; musician Kate Nash; filmmaker Jonathan Glazer; and Irish rap group Kneecap.
Censorship claims
The signatories characterised the removal of Rooney’s titles from bookshops as an "affront to basic principles of free speech and expression so long taken for granted in this country," directly attributing the crisis to "ill-conceived and draconian anti-terror legislation."
"We categorically reject censorship – whether direct or indirect – and urge the government to change course, amending the legislation which has led us to this point of repressive absurdity," the letter added.
Under current UK counter-terrorism laws, expressing public support or providing financial assistance to Palestine Action constitutes a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment.
Rooney previously declared she would continue donating proceeds from her book sales to the activist group, arguing that the government's proscription conflates demonstrations, civil disobedience, and vandalism at military facilities with terrorism.
Earlier this month, Rooney confirmed that Faber had determined it could "no longer supply my work within the UK," noting that the decision was reached with her full concurrence.
"I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions," she said.
"And I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences."

Iran has warned that US political assets and infrastructure belonging to countries joining a new war against it would become “legitimate targets” if Iranian officials were assassinated or civilians killed, according to a senior Iranian security official quoted by the semi-official Fars News Agency.
The Tehran-based official said Iran assumes that the US and Israel will launch another attack and considers Washington’s diplomatic gestures “unreliable.”
The official said this perception had intensified following remarks by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Athens, which Tehran interpreted as giving a historical and civilisational justification for Washington’s war against Iran.
According to the official, Iranian political and intellectual leaders have increasingly concluded that US Middle East policy is directed by Israel, which they believe is preventing Washington from pursuing a diplomatic solution.
He added that growing pressure from different segments of Iranian society was pushing authorities towards “decisive action” to break the blockade under what Tehran considers its right to self-defence.
Provoking Iranian response
According to the official, Iran has instructed various operational units that, in the event of another large-scale conflict involving the assassination of Iranian officials and the killing of civilians, it would consider US political assets and the infrastructure of countries participating in the war as “legitimate targets.”
The warning comes amid heightened tensions between Tehran and Washington over the US naval blockade and restrictions on maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
The US and Israel launched military strikes against Iran on February 28, triggering a wider regional conflict.
Despite subsequent diplomatic efforts, disagreements over the blockade and security arrangements in the strategic waterway have continued.
The warning also follows an Israeli media report on Wednesday that dozens of Israeli fighter jets flew close to Iran’s border earlier this week, with US sources suggesting the operation may have been intended to provoke an Iranian response.

Walmart launches tools for AI agents to shop for customers as Anthropic launches its own
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:47:00 UTC
07:47:00 KST

Walmart launches tools for AI agents to shop for customers as Anthropic launches its own
- Walmart will let AI agents shop for customers through new “Agent Profiles”, with approval or spending limits, while keeping agent purchases separate from personal orders.
- The move follows growing investment in AI agents from OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and Meta, as firms see them as the next phase after ChatGPT.
- Amazon is taking the opposite path by blocking third-party shopping agents, including Meta’s Muse, while pushing its own AI tools such as Alexa for Shopping and Buy for Me.
AI generated
US shopping giant Walmart on Oct 21 unveiled tools allowing artificial intelligence agents such as Meta’s Muse to shop on behalf of its customers, taking the opposite approach to rival Amazon, which bars outside AI agents from its platform.
AI agents are programmes that can carry out multi-step tasks on a user’s behalf – such as searching for products, comparing prices and completing a purchase – rather than only answering questions as chatbots do.
Tech companies including OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and Meta are investing heavily in agents, which much of the industry sees as the next phase of the AI boom that followed the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022.
Anthropic on Oct 21 released a preview of Claude Duet, an agent that works in the background across users’ connected apps and can make online purchases with their approval.
Its archrival OpenAI launched its own always-on agents, called Dots, in September.
Muse, which Meta launched in September and has made available only in the United States and Canada, has been downloaded more than 10 million times, according to an analysis of third-party data by Sensor Tower.
Walmart said it would launch “Agent Profiles” within the next month, letting customers register each AI assistant they use as a separate profile within their Walmart account so that purchases made by the agent appear apart from their own.
Customers will be able to require approval for every purchase or let an agent buy on its own up to a spending limit they set, such as US$50, US$100 or US$200, and delete a profile at any time.
Walmart compared the arrangement to adding an authorised user to a credit card.
Amazon, the largest US online retailer, has taken a harder line, blocking third-party shopping agents while promoting its own AI tools such as Alexa for Shopping and its Buy for Me feature.
In September, Amazon blocked Muse from its site, with users shown a notice saying unauthorized AI agents violate Amazon’s conditions of use.
Amazon sued Perplexity in November 2025, accusing the startup of using its Comet browser agent to covertly make purchases on its marketplace, and has also moved to restrict agents from Google and OpenAI. AFP

Government websites down amid global security flaw scare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:46:37 UTC
07:46:37 KST

Global government websites go dark after security flaw revealed
Numerous websites worldwide, including government-run pages, temporarily went dark after the AI-assisted discovery of critical vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language, which powers around 70% of the web globally.
On Wednesday, the developers of the popular open-source programming language, which helps websites run and display content, issued an urgent security alert over “critical remote code execution vulnerabilities.”
The flaws could allow hackers to take control of affected websites, prompting the release of urgent fixes, with all PHP users “strongly encouraged to update immediately.”
Cybersecurity agencies worldwide, including the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity, the UK’s National Cyber Security Center, the Australian Signals Directorate, and the Canadian Center for Cyber Security, issued their own alerts, advising users to apply the patches immediately and prioritize internet-facing systems.
Organizations that were unable to update immediately or that relied on outdated, unsupported PHP versions were advised to take their systems offline until the fixes could be applied.
The announcement prompted France’s Interior Ministry to temporarily shut down prefecture websites, with local government pages also unavailable. In neighboring Belgium, the Foreign Ministry similarly took its websites offline on Wednesday. In the Netherlands, the National Cyber Security Center, the websites of all major political parties, and at least one port took similar precautionary measures.
In Denmark, the national school communication platform was temporarily shut down; in Finland, the government’s public web services went dark.
Disruptions also affected services operated by the Wikimedia Foundation, which runs the online encyclopedia Wikipedia.
The flaws in PHP were identified by two cybersecurity companies, Calif and Wiz, in August. PHP developers have since worked on fixes, while keeping the discovery under wraps to prevent malicious actors from exploiting the vulnerabilities.
The cybersecurity companies said they made extensive use of AI models in the process, including Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol.
Wiz stated that the “underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve.”
OpenAI described the case as “one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory,” and predicted that more flaws would be discovered in the coming months with the help of AI.

Victorian public schools to be fully funded — but only by 2034
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:44:55 UTC
07:44:55 KST

Victoria strikes deal with Commonwealth to fully fund state schools by 2034
In short:
Victoria currently only pays 70 per cent of the agreed School Resource Standard, recommended by the Gonski review in 2012.
Premier Ben Carroll announced yesterday that the state's contribution would lift to 75 per cent, enabling more federal funds to flow to Victorian public schools.
What's next?
Victorian public schools will not receive 100 per cent of the Schooling Resource Standard until 2034.
The basketball court at Pembroke Primary School has not seen a game in two years.
The court is full of potholes, and parent James Dunn said the school in Melbourne's outer east cannot afford to fix them.
"When you've got 90 kids running around and you've got half your playground fenced off, it's pretty frustrating," said Mr Dunn, who has been treasurer on the school council for three years.
Pembroke students were missing out altogether on school camps and extracurricular activities because the school was "running on a shoestring", Mr Dunn said.
Yesterday Victorian Premier Ben Carroll announced his government had finally signed off on a promised deal with the federal government on school funding.
Victoria currently only pays 70 per cent of the agreed School Resource Standard, recommended by the Gonski review in 2012, while the federal government contributes 20 per cent.
Mr Carroll confirmed Victoria will lift its contribution to 75 per cent after a move signed off by state cabinet this week, calling it the "biggest investment in schools ever" by the Victorian government.
However, state schools will not receive 100 per cent of the school resourcing standard until 2034.
Mr Dunn said that the deal had only been made a month out from the state election, after Labor had run Victoria for 12 years, was disappointing.
"It feels like the kids are now a political football," he said, expressing frustration over the prolonged timeline for full funding.
"Things have got to be done now."
Principals, union cautiously welcome deal
The Australian Principals Federation welcomed the deal but said the proposed timeline meant full funding remained years away.
"The challenges facing our schools are immediate," said Victorian branch president Andrew Cock.
"It is essential that meaningful funding increases are delivered progressively, rather than schools having to wait until the end of this period to see the benefits," he said.
"Our message continues to be simple — if we expect Victorian government schools to deliver a world-class education, we must fund them to do so."
Australian Education Union Victorian Branch president Justin Mullaly said while the announcement was welcome and provided greater certainty, there was devil in the detail.
"Victorian public schools will not receive some of the additional funding as soon as other states and territories," he said.
"The delay in signing and the decision to back-end the deal, will short change Victorian public schools by hundreds of millions of dollars over the next few years.
"Funding delays have real consequences, and this needs to be addressed."
Mr Carroll said: "If we can bring forward the timeline and meet the 75 per cent earlier, we will."
Voluntary contributions policy remains a sore point
Prior to yesterday's announcement, tensions had already been growing over parent contributions to keep state schools functioning adequately.
Last month, Victoria's Department of Education instructed schools to tell parents that all curriculum-based instruction and resources, including textbooks, are free and that there was no obligation to pay for school contributions.
Schools can ask for contributions for extra-curricular activities like camps and excursions or learning materials to keep.
Education Minister Gabrielle Williams defended the guidance, telling the ABC it was "updated to make it absolutely clear that school contributions are voluntary".
Kim, a librarian at a Melbourne public high school not given permission to speak publicly, said her school would cover items for lower income students, but could not afford "extras" like school camps.
"Our school is 'free' but it's falling apart, any couches are from hard rubbish and the roof is leaking," she said.
"School is free, but with 12-year-old science textbooks … free with old humanities textbooks with no covers.
"It's not a recipe for a winning education offering."
Australian Catholic University researcher Sarah Langman has analysed how voluntary parent payments were characterised in annual reports from 1500 Victorian public schools in 2024.
She said parent contributions were important for "a wide range of things, everything from school libraries to first aid offices to general programs, excursions and camps".
"The concern is then: what are schools going to be left with if they aren't able to provide these opportunities to their students?"
Ms Langman predicted the new Education Department advice would make budgets tighter.
"We would expect that this problem is probably going to become a lot more widespread as these policy restrictions come into place," she said.
"The real question we want people to consider is whether access to educational opportunities should depend on schools' ability to attract voluntary contributions."
Parents Victoria chief executive Gail McHardy said payments should not feel like a "moral obligation or source of pressure" for families struggling with the cost of living.
"School leaders and school councils should not be made to feel responsible for passing government funding shortfalls on to parents," Ms McHardy said.
Back at Pembroke primary, Mr Dunn was lukewarm on the Gonski funding announcement and whether it would be enough to repair his school's aging facilities.
"We'll see. Politicians aren't at the top of my trust list," he said.

Mark Zuckerberg Agrees to Stay in California Despite Billionaires’ Tax Ballot Measure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:39:50 UTC
07:39:50 KST

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has agreed to keep living in Silicon Valley for eight years, potentially exposing himself to billions of dollars in one-time taxes if California voters approve a contentious ballot measure next month, according to a company regulatory filing released Wednesday.
During a dinner with Meta board members on September 9, Zuckerberg informed them that he was considering leaving California because of the measure, known as Proposition 40, and that he planned to list his Palo Alto, California, home for sale four days later, the 109-page filing stated. The ballot proposal, which could be subject to lawsuits even if voters approve it, calls for a one-time 5 percent tax on stock and other assets held by billionaires in the state as of January 2026.
Many wealthy individuals, including Zuckerberg, currently avoid significant tax payments by borrowing against their shares and taking low salaries—$1 annually in the Meta CEO’s case. Zuckerberg purchased a home in Florida this past February, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time.
His potential cross-country move concerned a special committee of the board, whose members included attorney Robert Kimmitt, venture capitalist Charlie Songhurst, and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu. “The special committee was mindful about the difficulties the company faced during the COVID-19 pandemic when Zuckerberg could not be physically present with the company’s management team and did not want the company to face similar challenges going forward,” according to Wednesday’s filing.
Within days of the Meta board dinner, the special committee and Zuckerberg reached an agreement that links his ability to sell special company shares to his continued residence in California. It was finalized a week ago, and on Wednesday, Meta announced the details. It plans to create a new class of shares that hold no voting power. Selling these shares could potentially help raise funds for Meta’s expensive investments in AI data centers, without diluting Zuckerberg’s existing voting control.
All existing shareholders will receive the new nonvoting shares automatically in proportion to their existing holdings. Under what Meta called a “Founder Alignment Agreement” with Zuckerberg, he can sell 20 percent of those new shares to help pay any taxes he may owe. The remaining 80 percent would be available for sale in chunks over the next eight years as long as he remains in California. Any attempt to sell them early would require offloading some of his voting shares “unless there are material unforeseen circumstances that would render it prudent or advisable for Zuckerberg to reside elsewhere.”
Notably, the agreement specifies that Zuckerberg merely has to remain wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, so it’s possible that both he and the company could move together to another state. A number of California companies have left for Texas, Nevada, and other states in recent years. Google cofounders Sergey Brin and Larry Page are among the handful of billionaires widely believed to have exited California over the potential tax.
But with much of the most pioneering AI development happening in Silicon Valley, leaving the city of Menlo Park could be a difficult proposition for the Meta board to stomach. “The goal is to keep Zuckerberg continuing to lead the company from California and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs,” the filing stated, referring to the company unit behind its recent Muse AI models.
In the end, the exercise may have been for naught. Recent polling in California suggests that with about $129 million spent campaigning against Prop 40, it will fail to muster enough votes.

Man United captain branded 'disgrace' for comments following latest loss
Unknown

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes labelled 'disgrace' after questioning Michael Carrick's tactics
In short:
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes has been labelled a "disgrace" after questioning the tactics of under-fire manager Michael Carrick following another loss.
United were thumped 4-1 by Como in the UEFA Champions League, increasing the pressure on Carrick just months into the new season.
Former Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher said Fernandes's attitude was "awful" and "not what a Manchester United captain should be".
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes has been labelled a "disgrace" after questioning manager Michael Carrick's tactics following a Champions League defeat to Como.
Fernandes said his side failed to apply enough pressure and adopted a "mood of defeat" after conceding early in Thursday morning's 4-1 loss, a result that increased scrutiny on Carrick.
Como opened the scoring in the second minute and United collapsed, with only a stoppage‑time consolation goal from Joshua Zirkzee making the scoreline slightly less severe.
"We started on the wrong foot and they scored very early," Fernandes told TNT Sports. "There was not enough pressure on the ball and not many good movements off the ball. There were many things not going our way.
"It's a decision from the [coaching] staff not to press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence.
Asked if his comments amounted to criticism of Carrick's tactics, Fernandes said: "That's on the manager and staff to see, not me.
"Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable."
The Manchester United captain was heavily criticised by former Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher for his comments.
"For Bruno Fernandes to do that, it's a disgrace really," he said on CBS Sports Golazo.
"Last season he got Player of the Year, that was on the back of Michael Carrick becoming the manager, he wouldn't have got that award without Michael Carrick.
"When you think of him as a footballer, he's a talent, but in terms of attitude and the way he goes about things, it's not right at all.
"He's reacted like that because he's been brought off and he's embarrassed tonight by the manager.
"When he talks about pressing … for years, Bruno Fernandes has meant Manchester United can't press because he does things for the crowd.
"I commentate on games watching Man United, and he runs all over the place like a kid in the schoolyard, for the supporters.
"They all think he's working hard, he's not, he's killing the rest of the team.
"Watching him play every week, throwing his arms up at the other players constantly in the game is an absolute disgrace what he's done there, considering how he's performed this season.
"Awful attitude and not what a Manchester United captain should be."
Carrick's position has come under increasing pressure with United now winless in seven matches, and he responded by questioning the players' lack of willingness to run.
"There's a little bit on whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don't run and you don't run forward and you don't run back, you ain't gonna win," he said in his press conference when notified of Fernandes's criticism.
"It was more than disappointing," the 45-year-old manager said in a separate interview for TNT Sports. "I think everybody's got to take responsibility for that. I'll take responsibility for the overall team and performance, it stops with me and I'm fine with that.
"But as a supporter of this football club, to see a performance like that is unacceptable, I have to say."
Carrick said his side had failed to show the required intensity.
"It's the motivation and the purpose and the intensity of a game of football that you have to bring. We didn't bring that today," he said. "I've got to apologise for the performance."
Fernandes also questioned United's mentality after the early setback.
"Conceding early makes us go into the game with a mood of defeat," he said.
United have three points from their opening three Champions League matches and host AS Roma in their next fixture in the competition.

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Oct 22, 2026
Global diesel prices seen staying high despite Russia deal
US President Donald Trump’s deal with Russia to supply diesel to US and global markets is unlikely to meaningfully lower diesel prices, market watchers and analysts said, noting that the promised volumes are too small to ease a global supply squeeze.
Diesel prices have shot to record highs during the US-Israeli war on Iran, creating a political liability for Trump and his Republican party as they campaign to maintain thin majorities in the US Congress in the Nov 3 midterm elections.
Critics of Trump’s move said lifting sanctions on Russian diesel could help Moscow fund further attacks on Ukraine, undermining years of efforts to curb Russian energy revenues and raising the risk the Kremlin could profit while consumers get little relief from high fuel prices.
Trump said Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tons, or 2.25 million barrels, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter”.
Russia frees retired US schoolteacher in goodwill gesture
Russia freed Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired US schoolteacher in custody since 2022, from prison on Oct 21 and took him to St Petersburg to fly back to the United States, after talks that Washington said were a step towards ending the war in Ukraine.
Russian President Vladimir Putin made the announcement at a meeting in St Petersburg with US envoy Steve Witkoff, who later said the talks will continue towards planned technical-level discussions involving the US, Russia and Ukraine.
Witkoff thanked Putin for Hubbard’s release and called the Russian leader a “humanitarian”, in footage of the exchange, a remark that drew sharp rebuke from Republican and Democratic lawmakers given Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Pope Leo will not need further cancer treatment
Pope Leo will not need any further therapy after undergoing lung cancer surgery last week, his doctors said on Oct 21, indicating that his tumour had not spread.
The announcement came as it was still unclear whether the US-born pope would proceed with a planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, scheduled for Nov 6-17.
The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung removed in surgery on Oct 13 and was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
PHP developers issue updates fixing vulnerabilities
Developers of the PHP programming language said a set of new updates fixing two previously identified critical vulnerabilities was now live, and acknowledged a delay in addressing a previously identified flaw.
Government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline on Oct 21 after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in PHP sent website operators around the world scrambling to protect their systems.
PHP underpins large parts of the internet and the vulnerabilities had raised concerns that a significant number of websites could be vulnerable to attack. The developers issued four patches to address two “critical” vulnerabilities that could allow hackers to execute code on vulnerable systems.
‘Mood of defeat’: Como hammer Manchester United
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes said his side failed to apply enough pressure and adopted a “mood of defeat” after conceding early in their 4-1 Champions League loss at Como on Oct 21, a result that increased scrutiny on manager Michael Carrick.
Como opened the scoring in the second minute and United collapsed, with only a stoppage‑time consolation goal from Joshua Zirkzee making the scoreline slightly less severe.
“We started on the wrong foot, and they scored very early,” Fernandes told TNT Sports. “There was not enough pressure on the ball and not many good movements off the ball. There were many things not going our way.”

Meta ordered to pay US$25b to New Mexico after jury finds company misled consumers about data privacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:18:00 UTC
07:18:00 KST

Meta ordered to pay historic US$25b penalty to New Mexico for misleading consumers on data privacy
- A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay US$25 billion after a jury said it misled users about data privacy and Facebook data access linked to Cambridge Analytica.
- The state said Meta lied about who could access user data and how it handled hate speech and misinformation. It called the ruling a major win for consumer protection.
- Meta said it will appeal and called the case a “tax on speech”. Experts expect a long legal fight, and the money will go to New Mexico schools.
AI generated
NEW MEXICO – A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms on Oct 21 to pay the state US$25 billion (S$32 billion) after a jury found the company had misled consumers about the privacy of their data, hitting the company with one of the largest financial penalties in US history.
The ruling came in a case stemming from allegations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign, obtained data from millions of Facebook users without their consent. New Mexico had sued Meta, accusing it of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data.
“Facebook’s wrongdoing – over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public – goes to the heart of Facebook’s core business practices,” Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order, which came more than three weeks after the verdict.
He found that a penalty of more than US$219 billion was warranted based on state law, but reduced the figure to US$25 billion.
In a statement, C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal. “This ruling, and the Attorney-General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” he said.
“At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.”
New Mexico Attorney-General Raul Torrez said in a statement after the ruling the penalty was one of the largest financial penalties against a corporation in US history.
Meta previously faced a US$5 billion penalty from the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 over the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
Six other states settled their lawsuits against Meta related to Cambridge Analytica for US$459.2 million as part of a US$17.1 billion multistate settlement the company reached in August to resolve states’ claims that the company’s platforms had harmed teen mental health.
Lawsuit filed five years ago
New Mexico’s attorney-general had sued Meta in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app.
The state accused Meta of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data, how the company handles hate speech and misinformation posted on the platform and other internal policies.
The company knew that third parties had broad access to users’ personal data, and it tolerated hate speech or other harmful content when it benefited the company’s bottom line, the state said.
Cambridge Analytica, now defunct, worked for Trump’s successful presidential campaign in 2016, and gained access to the personal information from millions of Facebook accounts for the purposes of voter profiling and targeting.
It obtained that information without users’ consent from a researcher who had been allowed by Facebook to deploy an app on its social media network.
“It has been a long time coming holding Big Tech accountable,” Torrez told a press conference in Albuquerque after Wednesday’s ruling.
“I think today’s judgment is a clear break with that past and a very clear warning to those in this space and beyond that we intend to protect our people and protect our consumers.”
Analyst Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson & Co, called the ruling costly but unlikely to impact the company’s value.
“Meta is worth nearly two trillion dollars, and will likely continue to appeal these cases and drag them out,” Luria said.
Experts expect long appeal fight
Legal experts and financial analysts said the penalty was likely to face a lengthy battle on appeal.
Jurors on Sept 25 found that 26 of 29 statements made by the company and its leadership on those issues were misleading. They said the company had committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws, based on the number of Facebook users or New Mexico residents who were the audience for each misleading statement.
State law allows a penalty of up to US$5,000 per violation, and directs that all of the money go to New Mexico’s school system, Torrez told reporters after the verdict.
At a hearing on Oct 1, Randi McGinn, a lawyer for New Mexico, had asked Mathew to award the state between US$35 billion and US$40 billion, saying that would be supported by the US Constitution’s protections on due process and the jury’s verdict.
“This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money, and the value of its stock price,” McGinn said.
In court filings, Meta urged Mathew to cap the penalties at US$3.45 billion, saying a higher penalty ran the risk of scaring businesses out of the state. The evidence showed that Meta does not sell user data and New Mexico did not prove that any consumer had actually been misled, the company said in court filings.
Daryl Lim, an associate dean at Penn State Dickinson Law, said that while the US Constitution generally protects against excessive fines, because of the way New Mexico law is written, the large size of the penalty does not automatically mean it could be overturned.
Two juries sided with state
The verdict was the second in six months by a Santa Fe jury in a lawsuit brought by the state of New Mexico against Meta Platforms.
In the first trial, which ended in March, a Santa Fe jury found Meta misled users about young users’ safety on its Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp platforms and ordered the company to pay US$375 million in civil penalties.
After a second phase of that trial, a judge directed the company to pay US$567 million into a New Mexico fund for teen mental health and ordered Meta to implement measures to protect teen Facebook and Instagram users in New Mexico. REUTERS

Türkiye plans $2B investment in aviation, space industries over three years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:12:28 UTC
07:12:28 KST

Ankara has planned to allocate nearly $2 billion to its aviation and space industries over the next three years, according to the 2027 central government budget draft and budget justification.
The budget dedicated to the national space and aviation programme stood at $176 million this year and is set to surge by 181.7 percent to $495.7 million in 2027 to strengthen Türkiye's global competitiveness in the sector.
Financial commitments are projected to rise further to $616.9 million in 2028 and $745 million in 2029.
Under the spending framework, approximately $377.3 million will be directed towards the construction, operation, and servicing of air transport facilities, with total aviation infrastructure investments projected to reach $581.1 million in 2028 and $596.2 million in 2029 to meet rising domestic travel demand.
Ankara aims to accommodate 272 million airport passengers next year, including direct transit travellers, rising to 282 million in 2028 and 291 million by 2029.
Orbital infrastructure
The expanded space budget will support Türkiye's National Space Programme, dedicated research, testing infrastructure, and the commercialisation of high-value-added domestic technologies.
The push follows notable sector milestones in recent years, including the deployment of the country's first indigenous communications satellite, Turksat 6A, and the sub-metre Earth observation satellite, Imece.
Türkiye also completed its first crewed scientific space missions in 2024, when astronauts Alper Gezeravci and Tuva Cihangir Atasever conducted experiments in orbit.
The southwestern city of Antalya hosted the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) on October 5–9, ahead of preparations for Türkiye's maiden deep-space lunar mission scheduled for next year.
The lunar venture relies on a homegrown spacecraft featuring more than 80 percent domestic content and a hybrid propulsion system; the craft has completed assembly and is undergoing final testing.
Concurrently, the Turkish Space Agency is advancing efforts to establish a spaceport in Somalia to secure sovereign, independent access to orbit.

Government agencies and companies around the world shut down websites as they raced Thursday to protect themselves from hacks after artificial intelligence uncovered critical flaws in a widely used programming language called PHP.
Wiz, one of the cybersecurity firms that found the two flaws, estimated that PHP code helps run about 70 per cent of the world’s websites – from online stores and news outlets to government services.

PHP programmers released a fix on Wednesday, and the US National Security Agency told organisations to patch their sites immediately or pull vulnerable systems offline.

Poland fumes as Ukrainian city celebrates ‘architect of genocide’

Unknown Publisher

Poland fumes as Ukrainian city celebrates ‘architect of genocide’
Poland has accused Kiev of making unacceptable “suicidal” moves after the Ukrainian city of Lviv dedicated 2027 to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and its leader, Nazi collaborator Roman Shukhevich.
To celebrate the 120th anniversary of Shukhevich’s birth and mark 85 years since the creation of the militant group that perpetrated mass killings of ethnic Poles, Jews, and Russians, the Lviv Regional Council decided on Tuesday to organize “cultural, memorial, scientific, and mass media events,” as well as exhibitions and national-patriotic rallies.
The announcement was met with widespread condemnation in Poland, which regards the UPA as perpetrators of genocide against Poles in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia and its leader, Shukhevich, as a key ‘architect’ of the massacres. From 1943 to 1945, Ukrainian nationalist militants murdered an estimated 100,000 ethnic Poles in the regions, which are now largely part of modern Ukraine.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the move a “suicidal tactic,” and Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz called it “unacceptable.” Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski condemned the announcement, calling for the resolution’s key sponsor, Lviv regional lawmaker Svyatoslav Sheremet, to be placed on Poland’s travel ban list.
The Ukrainian Foreign Ministry attempted to downplay the incident, blaming the Lviv regional authorities for making the “harmful decision.” The ministry also said the regional council did not consult any central authorities regarding “the consequences of their actions for bilateral relations with Poland.”
The resolution ultimately vanished from the Lviv council’s website without any explanation. Speaking to Polish media on Wednesday, Deputy Foreign Minister Marcin Bosacki said Warsaw received assurances from Kiev that the resolution would not be implemented.
“We take on faith the words of the administration of Vladimir Zelensky that this catastrophic decision will not be implemented,” Bosacki stated, calling the disappearance of the resolution from the council’s website a “good sign,” but cautioning against interpreting it as an official cancellation of the celebrations.
Ukraine’s increasingly open honoring of WWII-era nationalists and Nazi collaborators has drawn criticism from Warsaw, which remains one of Ukraine’s key backers in the conflict with Russia.
Poland regards the UPA and the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN), which collaborated with Nazi Germany during the early stages of its 1941 invasion of the Soviet Union, as perpetrators of genocide, while modern Ukraine cherishes them as freedom fighters and national heroes.
Earlier this year, Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky named a military unit after the ‘Heroes of the UPA’ and established a ‘pantheon of outstanding Ukrainians’ at Kiev’s main military cemetery, where OUN leader and Nazi collaborator Andrey Melnik was reinterred with state honors in May.

Hegseth Directs Air Force to Establish New Guard Special Tactics Squadron
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:06:39 UTC
07:06:39 KST

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has directed the Air Force to establish a new Special Tactics Squadron under the Florida Air National Guard, growing a small but elite group of special operators.
The Pentagon announced Hegseth’s order Oct. 21, releasing a brief Sept. 23 memo from Hegseth to Air Force Secretary Troy Meink, directing him to create the new squadron at Hurlburt Field “with an associated new organization at MacDill Air Force Base,” both in Florida.
Pentagon and Air Force spokespersons offered no further details. The Air National Guard did not immediately respond to a query.
Hurlburt is the headquarters of Air Force Special Operations Command, and MacDill is home to U.S. Special Operations Command. Connecting the new unit to both “creates an unparalleled ecosystem of combat-ready training and mission execution,” the Pentagon’s announcement states. “This move maximizes joint-force synergy, ensures seamless operational readiness, and provides the President with highly responsive, lethal options to counter pacing threats.”
Special tactics squadrons are some of the Air Force’s premier ground forces, consisting of combat controllers, pararescuemen, special reconnaissance, and Tactical Air Control Party specialists. They conduct a wide range of missions in covert, remote, or hostile areas, including combat search and rescue, airfield seizure, emergency air traffic controller, and coordination of close air support.
There are just a handful of special tactics squadrons across the Air Force, and only two in the Guard—the 123rd Special Tactics Squadron in Kentucky and the 125th Special Tactics Squadron in Oregon. The Florida Air National Guard has one special ops unit, the 249th Special Operations Squadron, which flies the CV-22 Osprey.
It is unclear how quickly the new unit will be established and be fully manned. Hegseth’s memo states that “any further resourcing for this direction, to include military construction, equipment, and manpower authorizations will be developed in the President’s Budget 2028 budget cycle.”
The memo also directs the National Guard Bureau and the Air Force to follow Air Force policy for establishing the new unit, “consistent with applicable DAF Strategic Basing process and environmental legal requirements.”
It is highly unusual—if not unprecedented—for the Secretary of Defense to direct the establishment of a squadron-level unit in any component.
Hegseth, a former Army officer, has praised special operations forces, seeing them as a model for innovation and acquisition reform, and they have played key roles in operations during his tenure, including Operation Absolute Resolve to seize Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January, Operation Rough Rider in Yemen in 2025, and the ongoing strikes against alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific.

Trump asks US Supreme Court to allow Big Bend border wall construction

Trump asks US Supreme Court to allow Big Bend border wall construction
Oct 21 - President Donald Trump's administration asked the US Supreme Court on Wednesday to let it proceed with a plan to build a US-Mexico border barrier in a remote region in West Texas that includes Big Bend National Park.
The Justice Department filed an emergency request for the court to lift a federal judge's order halting wall construction in the region while a lawsuit against the project brought by an environmental group and other challengers plays out.
The Republican president has long touted building or reinforcing barriers along the US-Mexico border as a signature part of his anti-immigration policies. But his administration's push to extend border infrastructure into the national park, around 250 miles (400 km) southeast of El Paso, has faced opposition from local officials, conservationists and some Texas Republicans.
The lawsuit was brought by the Center for Biological Diversity, a Big Bend-area river guide and a group seeking to preserve a historic church in Ruidosa, Texas, that says its fragile adobe structure is threatened by the border construction.
The plaintiffs challenged a series of waivers issued by the US Department of Homeland Security to expedite construction of roads and barriers in the Big Bend region, avoiding the application of a variety of environmental and conservation laws.
Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and the current Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who issued the waivers between February and July, found the region to be an "area of high illegal entry," requiring additional barriers to control the border.
US District Judge Kathleen Cardone in El Paso issued an injunction on October 2 halting the construction. In an opinion issued later, the judge found that the waivers exceeded the authority of Noem and Mullin.
The Justice Department in its request urged the Supreme Court to pause or overturn Cardone's injunction.
"Even assuming that the secretary's waiver authority implicates a question of 'vast economic and political significance,' Congress did clearly authorize the secretary both to build border barriers and to waive legal requirements in order to facilitate their expeditious construction," the Justice Department wrote.
In August, the administration paused construction in Big Bend after the project drew bipartisan criticism over its potential impact on the park's landscape and wildlife. Crews had begun clearing land in the park for roads and border security infrastructure, prompting protests and lawsuits seeking to halt the work. REUTERS

IBM shares slipped in extended trading on Wednesday after the technology vendor reported better-than-predicted third-quarter results.
Here's how the company performed relative to LSEG consensus:
- Earnings: $2.95 adjusted vs. $2.86 expected
- Revenue: $17.10 billion vs. $16.82 billion expected
IBM's revenue grew about 5% from a year ago, according to a statement. Net income, at $2.19 billion, or $2.30 per share, increased from $1.74 billion, or $1.84 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude acquisition-related adjustments.
"Our clients are now deploying 'Super Intelligence' in ways that transform entire operating models, instead of simply addressing narrow or novel problems," IBM CEO Arvind Krishna was quoted as saying in a statement.
With respect to guidance, IBM called for full-year free cash flow to increase by more than $1 billion. The forecast as of July was a bump of approximately $1 billion. IBM still sees 2026 constant-currency revenue growth between 4% and 5%.
In the third quarter, IBM generated $7.80 billion in software revenue, growing 8% and topping the $7.66 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount.
Consulting revenue, at $5.34 billion, was flat and just below StreetAccount's $5.37 billion consensus.
"AI is increasingly embedded in broader transformations our clients are undertaking, representing about 30% of our consulting revenue in the quarter and 35% of our backlog," Jim Kavanaugh, IBM's finance chief, said on a conference call with analysts.
The consulting unit's 27.4% gross margin narrowed from 28.9% in the second quarter.
"We reinvested productivity gains into digital assets, accelerating our transition towards a services as software model to capture the growing AI opportunity," Kavanaugh said.
Infrastructure revenue came to $3.70 billion. That was up 4% and higher than the $3.57 billion consensus from StreetAccount.
The company's adjusted gross margin, at 58.5%, was narrower than the StreetAccount consensus of 59.1%.
During the quarter, IBM said it agreed to buy Boeing and General Motors' HRL Laboratories, formerly known as Hughes Aircraft's research division, for an undisclosed sum.
As of Wednesday's close, IBM stock has come down 15%, while the S&P 500 index has gained 13%.
"I think the current street estimates for the year are about $32 billion of revenue," Kavanaugh said. "We feel comfortable with that $32 billion of revenue."
