UNDP Asia-Pacific Director Kanni Wignaraja on the Necessity of Redefining Security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:18:00 UTC
05:18:00 KST

In an age of intersectional crises, of threats that bleed across borders and between sectors, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) believes what’s needed is a redefinition of security. In a new report, the UNDP argues that development ought to have a larger role in addressing insecurity – not as it is traditionally understood, but as it actually affects people across Asia and the Pacific.
It’s not about making a binary choice between defense and development, Kanni Wignaraja, UNDP regional director for Asia and the Pacific, told The Diplomat’s Managing Editor Catherine Putz. Instead, what’s critical is getting the balance right, investing in development and prevention, and leveraging development to enhance security.
In pursuit of this, the UNDP proposes in its report a framework of “development circuit breakers” addressing economic insecurity, weak institutions, digital disruption and climate-health pressures that interact and reinforce each other.
“Trust is the one switch that allows all four circuit breakers to work. Each switch depends on trust: between people and institutions, and among the institutions responsible for different parts of the system,” Wignaraja said.
In the following interview, Wignaraja expands on the structural vulnerabilities that define the modern security landscape, puts defense spending trends in context, and urges regional governments to shift their mindset from managing individual crises to managing shared risks.
What structural vulnerabilities define the modern security landscape across Asia and the Pacific? How is the current reality different from previous periods, what’s changed?
A lot has changed in the way we see and feel vulnerability and insecurity today across the region and the world.
Previously, maybe there were more episodic periods of intense pain, wars, for example, but more contained. Now I feel it’s almost like having chronic pain. It’s all of the time and in so many more places. And that is a very different scenario of insecurity and feeling unsafe.
Countries face overlapping shocks, often before they have recovered from the last. The old crisis-recovery-rebuilding cycle is breaking down, putting hard-won development gains repeatedly at risk.
The nature of the threats has changed too: many are not contained within borders. Climate shocks, pandemics, cybercrime, disinformation, supply-chain disruptions and water insecurity move across countries and systems. The scale is enormous. Online criminal economies are estimated at $1.03 trillion annually, with $114.1 billion in losses to cybercrime victims in 2025.
There is also an exponential factor, as these risks now travel faster, connect more quickly and spread like wildfires. Economic insecurity can erode trust; climate shocks destroy livelihoods and strain public finances; weak institutions create space for illicit economies. Sri Lanka illustrates the connections, amid its economic crisis, poverty rose from 11 percent in 2019 to more than 25 percent in 2023, alongside wider social and political unrest. Myanmar shows what can happen when several pressures converge and collide. Conflict, economic decline, poverty, weak governance and criminal economies increasingly reinforce one another. These cannot be neatly separated into security problems on the one hand and development problems on the other.
Our response systems were built for episodic emergencies. They now have to manage chronic, connected insecurity.
Defense spending is soaring across the world, including in Asia, while development budgets have been trimmed down, in some cases dramatically. Do these trends reflect – or do they ignore – the actual threats communities across Asia and the Pacific face?
Today recorded military budgets are close to US$3 trillion. At the same time official development assistance (ODA) has fallen to $175 billion. This is just 6 cents to the dollar if we compare the ratio between the two.
We are not arguing to choose between defense and development but getting the balance of investment right. And to optimize security spending that aligns with development outcomes. The questions is how to use both military and development budgets to invest in common outcomes. That’s the win-win. And how do you leverage one to get more of the other?
Military, police and intelligence institutions remain essential. And their budgets can also be a frontline to ensure dual outcomes that ensure national and people’s safety and well-being.
Investments in technology that enhances wellbeing with protection, early warning and preparedness systems, vaccine production and access, AI integrity and strong rule of law and justice institutions prevent risks from becoming crises.
Wherever the money comes from, we need to invest much more deliberately in prevention, and for the longer term. Each dollar invested in prevention can mean up to $103 in avoided conflict and crisis costs. For example, in the Philippines anticipatory systems can reach 125,000 vulnerable people three days before a Category 4 or 5 typhoon, before assets and savings are lost.
Some of the new risks also require us to work differently. Cyber scams are a good example: they combine cybercrime, human trafficking, illicit finance and organized crime, and in many case promote cross border conflict. No single institution can make a dent in this.
Ultimately, it is about getting a better security return from the investments we make. And where together, one-plus-one can be way beyond two. The opportunity is to find these investments that strengthen both.
What is meant by “the securitization of development” and why is it important to avoid securitizing development as you encourage governments to rethink the connections between development and security?
The risk is that development could come to be seen primarily through a security lens. Development through the lens of human wellbeing must remain an objective in its own right. That is reducing poverty, eliminating major diseases, a full education and decent jobs, affordable energy, water and food for all, protecting rights and enabling people to live with dignity.
The report argues that sustaining security – which is about a safer present and future for all not just a few – cannot be achieved without development defined as improved human wellbeing for all. Investing in people, institutions and resilience is not separate from security but is one of the most effective ways to achieve it. That is different from turning development into a security instrument. Development and security are mutually reinforcing.
Incentives matter. Development should be about enabling people to live free from fear, free from want and in dignity, expanding people’s capabilities, strengthening rights, improving access to services and creating opportunities.
This is why the report places such emphasis on people-centered security. Individuals and communities should be at the heart of both development policy and security decisions. These are not alternative or conflicting choices. Security seen through this lens is about whether people can feel safe in their homes, protect their livelihoods, access justice and basic services, and live without fear. That is very much the human security tradition that UNDP has championed since the early 1990s.
The central message is that if governments are serious about security in the fullest sense, investment in development is non-negotiable. Effective governance, economic opportunity, social protection, digital resilience, climate adaptation and access to justice are not substitutes for security; they are among its most important foundations.
One section of the report states that “Current responses generate the crises they were meant to prevent,” in reference to what’s termed “the response and reactive trap.” Why is it so difficult for regional governments to invest in prevention? How can governments break out of this particular trap?
The fundamental problem with prevention is that when it works, it is often invisible. Political and budget cycles reward visible results, while the return on prevention is often a crisis that did not occur. This makes it easier to finance response and reconstruction than investments that could have reduced the losses in the first place.
We have to make prevention politically meaningful, economically visible and financially viable. That means translating risks into investments with clearer costs, returns and avoided losses. We need to move from paying for disasters to investing in resilience before they happen.
The shift is from managing each emergency to managing compounding risks over time. Countries need the capacity to anticipate and absorb shocks, protect development gains and recover faster, rather than rebuilding over the same vulnerabilities after every crisis.
The public budget leads the way. Finance ministries, local governments and financing institutions increasingly shape resilience through decisions on public finance, regulation and development planning. Prevention needs to become a criterion for allocating public resources, as we are already beginning to see across the region.
A better integrated financing architecture is central to breaking the reactive cycle. UNDP’s Integrated National Financing Frameworks (INFFs) which are being implemented in over 90 countries show how countries can align public and private finance around interconnected risks, making prevention economically visible and investable. Mongolia’s green energy transition where UNDP is supporting implementation of the INFF, illustrates this: a single integrated financing pathway strengthened climate resilience, energy security and economic stability at once.
We need to change the economics and politics of prevention. Making risks, avoided losses and returns more visible makes prevention easier to justify politically and more investable financially. Security is not only about our capacity to respond when something goes wrong, but our capacity to stop disruption from becoming an explosive crisis. Bangladesh and Nepal are recent examples of doing so.
One of the report’s key messages frames governance and institutional legitimacy, digital system integrity, economic security, and climate-health resilience as integrated “circuit breakers.” Can you briefly describe how these are intertwined and why they can’t necessarily be separated?
For too long, I think we’ve run responses, even analytically, looking at some of the big issues, the big disruptors of our times as separate systems. Think of it as a building. If an electrical fire starts in one place, you need to stop it from spreading and burning down the whole house. That is the purpose of the circuit breakers.
The four circuit breakers presented in the report are distinct, but the risks they address do not operate separately. The Big Four address economic insecurity, weak institutions, digital disruption and climate-health pressures that increasingly interact and reinforce each other. The most volatile risks that can set the place on fire often lie in the connections between them.
A shock in one area can quickly travel through the whole system. Climate shocks can undermine economic security; economic insecurity can erode trust; weak governance can enable criminal networks and disinformation; digital harms can deepen social divisions. That is how one vulnerability can become a much wider crisis.
Trust is the one switch that allows all four circuit breakers to work. Each switch depends on trust: between people and institutions, and among the institutions responsible for different parts of the system.
Trusted institutions can avoid or reduce the tensions through which risks escalate. In Pakistan, virtual courts and community access points have improved perceptions of police and justice institutions, while in Bangladesh, village courts help resolve everyday disputes before they grow. These examples show how strengthening trust at the community level reinforces all four circuit breakers.
The same on the digital and this AI spurt. How do we make sure that something like AI does not undermine trust that has been built over time, but it is used as an extender or accelerator on the positive side.
It is about managing these four circuit breakers, but in one system.
The report’s central message is that new approaches to “anticipating, preventing and managing both internal and transboundary challenges” are needed. Can you summarize some of those new approaches?
We need to move from managing individual crises to managing shared risks. Cybercrime does not recognize borders. Neither do climate risks, human trafficking, illicit financial flows or many of the other pressures we face today. No country or institution can address these challenges alone.
It requires a level of multi-country, regional and global cooperation that we have not seen before. And that, I think, is where institutions like the United Nations are so key.
That means cooperation itself becomes a form of prevention. But cooperation works when countries see it in their own interest. Shared interest and self-interest are not contradictory. They can be mutually reinforcing. That requires trust, particularly when countries are being asked to share information, coordinate responses or make decisions whose benefits extend across borders. Subregional cooperation mechanisms, such as ASEAN and the Mekong River Commission, show how countries can move beyond purely national responses and ask: how can we collectively address shared risks?
Institutions of development and security need to work differently together, starting with where outcomes align. The goal is not to expand everyone’s mandate, but to build a shared understanding of risk and clearer responsibilities for managing it in the collective interest.
Ultimately, we need to move to strengthen these connected systems. Success is not only how well we will respond to the next crisis, but how well we prevent a shock from becoming one.

====================================================================================================

Space Force Needs Third Launch Range by 2030, Acquisition Leader Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:16:02 UTC
05:16:02 KST

The head of the Space Force’s largest acquisition organization said the service needs a third spaceport to support medium and heavy launch by 2030—a goal he called “aspirational” even as he stressed the importance of building out the U.S. military’s launch infrastructure.
“We need this capability by 2030, but I’m also a pragmatist,” Space Systems Command boss Lt. Gen. Philip Garrant said Oct. 21. “That is not an inconsequential demand to build a spaceport when you factor in orbital regimes, safety, access to commodities … There are a lot of considerations.”
The Space Force operates ranges at Cape Canaveral Space Force Base, Fla., and Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif., but those expect to run out of space in the coming years as demand for government and commercial launch surges. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed in May that the service expects to need a third site.
“We probably need another site that’s capable of heavy and super-heavy launch capability, both from a resiliency perspective and just, even at the Cape, limitations on how much space we’ve got,” Meink said at the time.
The White House signed out an update to its National Space Transportation Policy in August, predicting the U.S. could see its annual launch cadence grow to 1,000 launches by 2030—a fivefold increase over 2025. The document calls on the Defense Department to work with the Department of Homeland Security and NASA to explore options to build additional spaceport infrastructure on federal property.
Garrant, who spoke to reporters during AFCEA’s annual Space Industry Days event, said the Space Force recently formed an operational planning team to “take a hard look” at what building a third spaceport would require.
“That work is pretty nascent, but we’re going to take some ideas to leadership at NASA, the National Reconnaissance Office, and the Space Force, and get some suggestions on how we might actually pursue a third spaceport,” he said. “That’s a recognition that the demand is there, and that we want to make sure that we meet those needs and support our launch service providers.”
The team right now is looking at a range of options for buying or leasing land for the third site, Garrant said—from a public-private partnership to using commercial land to building a new federal installation.
“All have pros and cons,” he said. “We haven’t made that decision yet, but we’re not discounting any of those.”
In the meantime, the Space Force is deepening its partnerships with commercial spaceports like the Mid-Atlantic Regional Spaceport on Wallops Island, Va., and the Pacific Spaceport Complex in Alaska.
The service is also investing heavily in its existing coastal spaceports and has plans to expand capacity at both ranges over the next five to 10 years. Congress allocated $1.3 billion in 2024 for “Spaceport of the Future” upgrades through 2028, and the Space Force plans to request more funding in the fiscal 2028 budget request to add more pads and launch support facilities, improve roads and bridges, and give launch companies better access to commodities like propellant and water. Both ranges are also looking to expand their harbors to support more providers.

Bose Is Buying Skullcandy. It’s Not as Weird as It Sounds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:15:00 UTC
05:15:00 KST

Longtime audio giant Bose announced on Wednesday that it's acquiring Skullcandy, the lifestyle brand known for its bass-heavy headphones. Skullcandy will remain a separate company within Bose's Premium Consumer Audio business and will still be based in Park City, Utah.
The acquisition isn't out of left field. Bose has lent its audio expertise to Skullcandy over the past year under its Sound by Bose licensing program. Skullcandy designs the headphones and then works with Bose on the audio front. The relationship began with the Skullcandy Method 360 ANC earbuds in 2025 and more recently, with the Crusher 1080 ANC headphones in July.
When WIRED spoke with Skullcandy CEO Brian Garofalow in July about the partnership, Garofalow highlighted the 23-year-old company's ability to build community and culture, specifically around the board sports community (the first Skullcandy product was designed on a ski chairlift). But he admitted the company wasn't “the greatest at the engineering part of innovation with products.”
This is hardly Bose's first audio acquisition (though it may be the most mainstream). Bose acquired McIntosh Group, owners of luxury audio brands McIntosh Laboratory and Sonus Faber, back in 2024. But Bose seems to be after Skullcandy's connection to its community.
“What does the brand stand for? Does it have meaning for consumers? Is it relevant to a group of consumers that, frankly, we otherwise aren’t reaching?" Bose CEO Lila Snyder tells WIRED. "If you think about McIntosh, Sonus Faber, and Skullcandy, they all fit into that realm. Skullcandy gives us access to a customer base that we think we’re largely missing with the Bose brand.”
That's why Bose has no plans to relocate Skullcandy from Park City, Utah, which Snyder says is the epicenter of board sports culture. “We want to make sure we’re right at the heart of it, as they always have been,” she says. Skullcandy products are also affordable, especially compared to other Bose products and Bose-owned brands, which lets Bose compete at both ends of the market.
As WIRED's headphone reviewer, I find Bose and Skullcandy an odd pairing. In consumer audio, Bose pioneered active noise-cancelation (ANC) in headphones, and maintains that legacy with ANC-leading products like the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen) and Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (2nd Gen). Skullcandy, on the other hand, has often been viewed as the butt of the joke when it comes to audio quality. It has had a reputation for middling sound, bass-over-everything headphones, and a loud, bold aesthetic.
Recent collaborations have started to change those perceptions—WIRED rated the Method 360 ANC earbuds an 8/10, noting good sound quality and ANC for the money. Snyder says those buds and the recent Crusher collab are just the tip of the iceberg. “It’s the beginning of what we think we can do together,” she says.
I’m very curious about what comes next from Skullcandy, headphones or otherwise. Either way, we’ll see if Bose's acoustic muscle can give the lifestyle brand the permanent glow-up it’s been chasing.

GM aims to develop vehicles in as little as two years with AI, software push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:14:36 UTC
05:14:36 KST

NEW YORK — General Motors plans to lean into artificial intelligence and vehicle software for future growth and development amid increasing competition abroad from Chinese automakers and a tougher U.S. market.
The Detroit automaker on Wednesday shared new details about a proprietary AI agent it's releasing under its OnStar brand, plans for a fourth generation of more efficient all-electric vehicles and a target to cut its vehicle development time in half.
GM also reconfirmed that by 2028, it wants to have eyes-off highway driving, or "personal autonomy," that will let drivers take their attention off the road. The automaker said that technology would start with the Cadillac Escalade IQ EV before rolling out to other, more high-volume models.
"All of these developments are building us the car of the future," CEO Mary Barra said Wednesday during an event laying out the plans, called "GM Forward," in downtown Manhattan.
The initiatives, which Barra, Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson and other executives discussed at the event, are designed to streamline the automaker's operations, while also improving the capabilities of its vehicles for customers.
"Over the last 12 months, we've evolved how we design, engineer and build our vehicles," said Anderson, who led the event and who has been tasked with overseeing GM's latest technology transformation.
GM said it is now targeting a vehicle development time of roughly two years from concept to production versus a traditional four- to five-year cycle. However, the company did not detail a timeline for reaching that goal.
The event comes as Chinese automakers are growing outside of the U.S. with rapid development times of new technologies and vehicles. Consulting firm AlixPartners said it believes China is currently bringing vehicles to market twice as fast as traditional automakers, with 40% to 50% less investment and a 30% cost advantage.
GM also continues to play catch-up to U.S. EV leader Tesla when it comes to delivering technology advancements through over-the-air updates and automated driving capabilities.
Anderson, a former Tesla executive, declined to speak specifically about how GM's technologies will compare to the EV maker, but said GM's systems will be able to visualize, or see, more things through the use of multiple types of sensors than a strictly camera-based system, which Tesla uses.
He also said the rapid development and new software architecture will help the company better compete against Chinese automakers abroad.
"There's inherent virtue to speed," Anderson told CNBC during an interview after the event. "Not just in being able to get a car out faster, it's being able to develop a system that's far more performant that you could have otherwise."
Next-generation vehicles
GM said Wednesday it has major plans for its next generation of EVs and traditional vehicles with internal combustion engines.
The company said those coming vehicles — regardless of type — will have 40 times the computing power and up to 50% faster cellular connectivity than prior systems.
That computing power is expected to help the automaker with over-the-air updates, onboard diagnostics and AI, as well as other technologies such as automated driving features.
The new brain of the vehicle will launch on the $130,000 Cadillac Escalade IQ EV in 2028 before rolling out to other models, including its next generation of EVs.
GM said the forthcoming EVs are expected to be 25% more aerodynamic and 15% lighter and feature electric motors and battery packs that are more compact.
GM President Mark Reuss said despite lackluster consumer adoption and the automaker pulling back billions of dollars in investments in EVs, it remains committed to producing them.
"We continue to develop our future EVs and work to reduce battery costs," Reuss said during the event. "And when the U.S. market is ready for EVs in large numbers, we will be there for them."
AI development
GM expects to achieve such targets through the use of AI in research and development.
The company said it is developing a "new operating approach for vehicle development" that leans into enterprise AI and virtualization to increase speed.
"This concurrent engineering model allows us to innovate faster, improve continuously, and scale new technologies across our lineup with incredible agility," the company said in a release.
GM used the development of its next-generation vehicles, including a new battery chemistry, as an example of how the new technologies are reshaping its vehicle development.
The company said it virtually tested more than 300,000 battery designs using its recently announced lithium manganese rich battery chemistry, or LMR, before building a single physical prototype.
Anderson said Wednesday that LMR will be the exclusive battery tech for its fourth-generation EVs. GM had previously said it wanted to use those batteries in full-size electric vehicles such as its Chevrolet Silverado and Escalade IQ beginning in 2028.
Anderson said GM is uniquely positioned to use AI compared to other automotive companies because of its more than 100 years in the industry as well as 30 years of OnStar.
"In the age of AI, data is currency," Anderson said. "For decades, GM's engineering, manufacturing and product teams have generated unparalleled body of data that we're now using to build industry-leading AI tools."
In-vehicle AI
The company is building on its internal use of AI to better shape its experiences for customers.
GM on Wednesday reconfirmed that it plans to launch a proprietary in-vehicle AI assistant through its OnStar technology brand.
The OnStar AI assistant is expected to launch in the coming months on the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq EV through an over-the-air update before expanding to other models.
GM currently uses Google's Gemini for its in-vehicle AI assistant. The company told CNBC earlier this year that the GM-developed AI will be more integrated with the vehicle.
The goal for OnStar AI, which will be available through a subscription, is to help customers be productive while in the car, especially if the vehicle has self-driving capabilities that don't require the driver or passengers to monitor the system.
GM on Wednesday also reiterated its plans to launch eyes-off highway driving in 2028. The automaker said a year ago that it wanted to launch that technology. It's been five years since Barra said she expected the automaker to offer personal autonomous vehicles this decade.
"Our vision is that eventually every vehicle should drive itself or its occupants anywhere, and we're investing across the self-driving stack to make that real," Anderson said.

In brief
- Cathy McGowan says one update brought her “enormous relief”.
- Helen Haines’ supporters are rallying around her recovery.
The first-ever federal independent member for Indi, and predecessor of Helen Haines, says she felt "enormous relief" after hearing her friend is alive, while also pleading with the local community to disengage in "negative political argument".
When former independent MP Cathy McGowan found out what happened to her close friend Helen Haines, first came shock and disbelief.
She was holding a workshop on preferential voting ahead of Victoria's upcoming state election when the news reached her.
"I couldn’t believe it. What happened?" she recalled herself asking.
As the days followed, a complex layer of emotions set in, which she says the electorate of Indi is now forced to grapple with.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The violence inflicted on Haines, struck by a four-wheel drive on Monday outside her Wangaratta electorate office in an alleged targeted attack, could happen to anyone, McGowan says.
"We can no longer think in rural Australia with our strong communities that we’re immune," she told SBS News.
"It was one of us in our community, by one of us, and saved by us as well. So, I think there's a sense of ownership but also shame that we've got to manage as well."
Haines has had both her legs amputated, her husband Phil confirmed on Wednesday, in an event that has stunned the nation.
Forty-three-year-old Brendan Nugent did not make a bail application when he fronted Wangaratta Magistrates' Court on Wednesday for the first time after being charged over the incident.
McGowan says hearing Phil’s update brought her "enormous relief".
"Her head's going to be okay. She'll come back. She'll bring her brilliant intellect, her humour, her love, and her laughter. We haven't lost it," she said.
McGowan won the seat of Indi in 2013 as the electorate’s first-ever independent MP, triggering the country’s first independent regional push before retiring in 2019. Haines has successfully continued the movement in the region.
At a council-run vigil in nearby Wodonga, where hundreds attended to show their support for Haines, McGowan addressed the crowd in a moving speech.
"We cannot change what has happened, but we can choose how we respond with the same compassion, the same kindness, and the same unity that Helen has always led with," she said.
She had one request.
"Could we commit to ourselves, [those] that are here, to not get involved in negative political argument?"
McGowan encouraged attendees to "be more like Helen" by listening “courageously, to respectful engagement, and being the change we want to see".
"It feels like there's been an attack on Helen … and in attacking her, there's a sense that there's an attack on our political system, on our democracy."
Orange cockatoos flock to vigil as symbol of democracy
In northeast Victoria, that democracy, and the independent regional movement, is represented by the symbol of an orange cockatoo.
Some were plastered on Haines’ electorate office. At the vigil, people wore printed shirts and carried posters with the bird’s illustration. McGowan even wore cockatoo-shaped earrings.
The symbol emerged in 2016, Haines explained in an Instagram post eight years later, when it was endearingly observed that McGowan’s campaign volunteers "were like a flock of cockatoos".
"The association and symbolism has grown from there, representing a community flocking together to build a vibrant democracy," she wrote.
When vigil attendee Wolfgang Huber told SBS News about an old orange cardboard cockatoo sitting in his home for a decade, he held back tears.
Its crest is frayed, and its edges are tattered. But for the retired engineer from Wodonga, the bird now carries greater weight than ever.
Huber has worked for the Voices of Indi campaign since its inception in 2012. He kept his first cardboard cockatoo, a symbol that emerged in 2016, as a memento.
"When Helen Haines retires from federal politics, I want to frame it and gift it to her," an emotional Huber said.
“I consider her a friend, and she is just such an integral … and an honest part of Australian politics. What happened to her is just unbelievable," he said.
Susan Gordon-Brown has never met Helen Haines, and yet she feels like she knows her. She moved to Wodonga just a year-and-a-half ago, and voted for her in the 2025 federal election.
"She has this huge constituency, yet she seems to be everywhere," she told SBS News
She said the gravity of what happened this week only set in for her at the vigil, which she attended to support Haines.
"You go to work one day. This shouldn't happen to you."

As midterms near, bipartisan furor grows over Trump targeting Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

As midterms near, bipartisan furor grows over Trump targeting Ukraine
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- President Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, described Russian President Vladimir Putin as a ‘humanitarian.’
- The prospect of an unchecked Trump has stoked fears on Capitol Hill that the White House could abandon Ukraine altogether in the war.
WASHINGTON — President Trump’s latest embrace of Russian President Vladimir Putin is deepening alarm in Washington and among America’s allies that the White House pressure campaign could leave Ukraine vulnerable as Moscow advances.
Trump’s push to end the war, which has raged since 2022, comes on the cusp of a midterm election that could give Democrats partial or full control of Congress, expanding their oversight powers, and as polls show more than two-thirds of Americans disapprove of the president’s handling of foreign policy and support Kyiv’s fight against Russian aggression.
On Monday, Trump dismissed Russia’s ongoing assault on its neighbor, telling reporters that “they haven’t been doing much,” even as Russian forces bombed a park in Kharkiv that day, killing a mother and her 14-month-old child in her stroller.
Two days later, in St. Petersburg, Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, described Putin as a “humanitarian,” despite his invasion unleashing Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II.
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir,” Witkoff said after securing the release of a detained U.S. citizen from the Kremlin. At least two other Americans, both from Los Angeles, remain wrongfully detained by Russia. “I salute you, and I commend you,” he added.
Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) described Witkoff’s remarks as “another embarrassment” after a steady stream of entreaties to Moscow from the Trump administration.
The diplomatic push follows Trump’s decision two weeks ago to import Russian diesel, a move that could bolster Moscow’s war effort and violate U.S. law. Days later, after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky publicly condemned the move, Trump ally Elon Musk reportedly throttled the speed of Starshield, a military-grade satellite internet service from Starlink that Kyiv relies on to defend itself against Russian attacks.
Trump posted online that he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin last week to free Stephen Hubbard, and that the U.S. was not required to reciprocate.
The Trump administration failed to provide Kyiv with intelligence warnings of incoming ballistic missile strikes, blaming the weather. The president waived sanctions on Russia that were passed just months earlier with overwhelming bipartisan support in the aftermath of the death of Sen. Lindsey Graham, a Trump ally and Ukraine supporter. And Trump declined to approve the transfer of interceptor missiles to Ukraine — more defensive weaponry used to protect the country from Russian strikes that have increasingly targeted civilian areas.
The developments have raised fresh questions over whether Trump has exceeded his legal authority in reshaping U.S. policy on Ukraine.
Russian diesel imports could violate a 2022 federal ban, the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act, and throttling Starshield, withholding intelligence and delaying missile transfers could breach contractual or statutory obligations set forth by Congress — all potential subjects of investigation for a willing Congress.
And Trump’s push comes at a moment of political peril, as he faces the prospect of a Democratic-led legislature and a Republican Party ready to move beyond his lame-duck presidency.
But freedom from political obligation could also allow Trump to pursue his agenda without the needs for coalitions or popular support.
The prospect of an unchecked Trump has stoked fears on Capitol Hill that the White House could abandon Kyiv altogether.
Nine senators from both parties have asked the Pentagon’s inspector general to investigate the Starlink episode, while lawmakers across the aisle have condemned the speed restrictions. And should they take power after the midterms, Democrats are also weighing whether to make Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s resignation a condition of further defense funding, citing his criticism of Ukraine, according to a report in the newspaper the Hill.
“Congress will unequivocally reaffirm that Ukraine is an indispensable ally to the United States, that Russia is a self-declared enemy of the United States, and that the United States will 100% support and defend the people of Ukraine in their fight for their own freedom against this brutal, illegal, and unprovoked Russian invasion,” said Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.).
“The United States must provide any and all defensive equipment that Ukraine needs to defend itself,” Fitzpatrick added. “Anyone who attempts to limit the use of Starshield for Ukraine will be fully investigated and will be held fully accountable, to include public congressional oversight hearings.”
Marco Rubio, the president’s secretary of State and national security advisor, was initially silent on Trump’s moves. But he ultimately defended them when confronted by reporters on a recent visit to Central Asia.
“We’re no longer going to be defensive about this topic,” Rubio said. “If it were not for the assistance of the United States, including under the Trump administration, there would be no Ukraine right now. Ukraine, as a sovereign state, would not exist.”
Still, Rep. Michael R. Turner (R-Ohio), a former chair of the House Intelligence Committee, said Sunday that Rubio’s explanation of Ukraine’s loss of Starlink access was “absolutely not” sufficient.
“This is something where there needs to be an investigation, there needs to be a congressional investigation,” Turner told CBS. “Lives are at risk, and lives are lost over these things.”
Trump has told reporters in recent days that his goal remains to secure a peace deal that ends the world’s deadliest conflict since World War II. But Mitt Romney, a former GOP senator from Utah and the Republican presidential nominee in 2012, dismissed Trump’s arguments as a break from U.S. values.
“Churchill could have shortened WW2 by years if he had just ‘done a deal’ with Hitler,” Romney wrote on social media. “George Washington could have done a deal to end the American Revolution.”
Zelensky “is in good company,” he added.
Europe, too, is preparing for a new confrontation with the Trump administration over the defense of Ukraine.
Germany’s chancellor rejected Trump’s approach, saying of Europe, “We are the firewall.” And the European diplomatic service responded with derision to Trump’s waiver of sanctions.
“When Russia escalates aggression against Ukraine,” the European Union’s diplomatic service said in a statement, “Europe responds with more pressure on the aggressor.”
Depending on which Republican is speaking, Americans are getting a different perspective on how bad things are with the economy. Trump says “the golden age of America is upon us.” Vance walks a tightrope to show that he knows voters are feeling an economic pinch.
Trump has floated a trilateral summit with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, next month, fueling European fears that he could strike a deal on Ukraine without Kyiv at the table.
The Russians and Ukrainians agreed this week in principle to begin peace talks at a technical level moderated by the United States. No timeline or framework has been set for the talks.
In an interview on Fox News, Zelensky said that he was prepared to agree to a peace deal that froze the existing battle lines, ceding nearly a quarter of Ukrainian land to Russian control. Over the last year, Russia has demanded that Kyiv also relinquish land in the Donbas region that it has failed to conquer through military means.
“Right now, we have to freeze. And I think this is a real way to end this war. We call this ceasefire,” Zelensky said. “This is minimum what we need from Russia today.”
“The most important is peace, and secure peace,” he added, “not to be afraid that occupation will come back, aggression will come back, killing will come back.”

Meta ordered to pay $25 billion penalty in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:04:07 UTC
05:04:07 KST

Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago.
The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services.
Although the jury concluded that Meta had more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion.
"The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing.
The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full.
"For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement.
He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences."
Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the penalty, saying in a statement that the company is "confident" that it will "prevail on appeal."
"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said in the statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."
Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September.
In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg-led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users, raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices.
Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations.
"Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said.
Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Torrez oversaw the related trial.
Torrez also led his state's child safety-related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act. A New Mexico judge would later order Meta to pay $567 million into an abatement fund as part of a second phase of the case that determined the social media firm's actions created a public nuisance.
Meta said it disagreed with that New Mexico ruling and planned to appeal.

Putin, Xi and Trump could hold ‘historic summit’ – Kremlin
Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump could hold a “historic” three-way meeting at the APEC summit in China, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov has said.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit is scheduled to take place in Shenzhen, China, on November 18-19.
Speaking to the Russian outlet Vesti on Wednesday, Ushakov said Beijing had already begun preparations for the potential talks. 
“Everyone is ready for this, but much, if not everything, depends on the Chinese hosts of the summit,” he said.
The possibility of three-way talks was also discussed during Putin’s meeting with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday, according to the Kremlin.
Ushakov described the proposed gathering as potentially “historic,” noting that it would be the first meeting of the three leaders in this format.
Putin and Trump last met in person at a summit in Anchorage, Alaska, in August 2025, and have remained in contact by phone, most recently on October 9.
Putin and Xi have also held regular talks, including on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek in August. The two previously met in Beijing in May during Putin’s state visit.
Trump and Xi have met twice so far this year, first in Beijing in May and then at the White House last month.
Trump has previously expressed openness to three-way talks, suggesting that nuclear disarmament could be among the issues discussed.
Asked whether the talks could also contribute to peace efforts in the Ukraine conflict, Ushakov said a single meeting would not be enough. “Even if the meeting lasts one, two or five hours, it still won’t be possible to resolve all the problems,” he said.
Commenting on whether the summit could amount to a “new Yalta,” Ushakov said: “I think that if the meeting takes place, there will be a storm of comments and assessments.”
The 1945 Yalta Conference brought together Soviet leader Joseph Stalin, US President Franklin D. Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill to discuss the final stages of World War II and the postwar international order.

Türkiye seeks parliament approval for joint defence agreement with Pakistan, Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:00:57 UTC
05:00:57 KST

A bill seeking parliamentary approval of a joint defence agreement between Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia has been submitted to the Turkish parliament.
The three-article bill, submitted on Wednesday under the signature of Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus, seeks approval of the Mecca Agreement on Joint Defence, signed by the three countries in Mecca on August 7, 2026.
According to the bill's explanatory memorandum, the agreement aims to strengthen strategic dialogue and cooperation based on mutual trust among regional countries.
It also seeks to establish a security framework based on cooperation and collective deterrence in the Middle East and beyond, while developing regional solutions to security challenges.
The memorandum said deterring aggression and establishing lasting regional stability would have positive socioeconomic effects in the medium and long term.
Under the agreement, the three countries undertake to cooperate to protect one another's independence, territorial integrity and sovereignty.
They also pledge mutual support in exercising their right to self-defence under the UN Charter.
Such measures would be subject to each country's constitutional obligations, national legislation and decisions by competent authorities, according to the memorandum.
The memorandum clarified that the collective defence provision would not be triggered automatically.
Instead, any response would depend on decisions reached by mutual agreement following consultations among the parties.
The agreement aims to strengthen collective deterrence against threats and attacks that the three countries jointly assess as affecting their security, including terrorism.
It also seeks to improve interoperability, cooperation and coordination among their armed forces and deepen defence industry cooperation.
Agreement does not affect NATO obligations
The memorandum stressed that the agreement is exclusively defensive and does not target any country.
It said the framework is based on regional ownership, cooperative security and inclusivity.
The agreement is open to regional countries seeking to contribute to peace, stability and security while respecting international law, territorial integrity, sovereign equality and non-interference in internal affairs, according to the memorandum.
It emphasised that the agreement would neither cancel nor replace Türkiye's existing bilateral or multilateral obligations.
It said the regional security and stability objectives of the agreement were compatible with NATO's Euro-Atlantic security objectives.
Türkiye's rights and obligations within NATO would remain unaffected, according to the memorandum.
The agreement is expected to deepen Türkiye's bilateral defence and security relations with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia while supporting an inclusive regional security mechanism.
The bill will be considered by parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee, which has been designated as the lead committee.
If approved by the committee, it will be placed on the agenda of parliament's General Assembly.

Children who later develop psychosis tend to have slightly smaller heads, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:00:49 UTC
05:00:49 KST

A longitudinal study tracking thousands of children from birth to mid-adolescence suggests that young people who develop psychotic disorders tend to have smaller heads throughout their early lives. Published in Psychological Medicine, the research indicates that these head size differences are largely tied to overall body height, pointing toward a broader pattern of altered physical growth rather than an isolated issue with brain expansion. The findings also point to distinct trajectories between males and females who experience milder psychotic symptoms.
Psychosis is a psychiatric condition in which a person loses some contact with reality. It often involves hallucinations, which are sensory experiences of things that are not present, and delusions, which are firmly held false beliefs. Psychosis exists on a spectrum, with clinical psychotic disorders like schizophrenia at the severe end, which disrupt daily life and typically emerge in late adolescence or early adulthood. A much larger segment of the population reports isolated psychotic experiences, such as occasionally hearing a voice or feeling unusually suspicious, without meeting the threshold for a clinical illness.
Even though psychotic disorders usually appear in young adulthood, the neurodevelopmental model of schizophrenia proposes that the underlying biological roots of these conditions begin during fetal development and early childhood. Adults diagnosed with schizophrenia tend to have slightly smaller total brain volumes than peers without the condition, even before they ever take psychiatric medications. Because performing brain scans on thousands of infants and children is costly and impractical, scientists often rely on head circumference, a simple tape-measure reading around the widest part of the skull that is routinely recorded by pediatricians, as an indirect indicator of early brain size.
“The study was motivated by the need to identify inexpensive and accessible biomarkers of psychosis risk,” study co-author Kate Merritt, a lecturer in human neuroscience in the Division of Psychiatry at University College London, told PsyPost. “If we can identify people who are more likely to develop psychosis, this could eventually help us target preventative interventions toward those at greatest risk.”
“Much of our work focuses on using MRI to identify biological markers that predict outcomes in psychosis, but MRI is expensive and not widely accessible,” Merritt explained. “We therefore wondered whether a much simpler measure, head circumference, might provide useful information. Head circumference is correlated with brain volume, so we looked at whether differences in head growth might be associated with psychosis risk.”
Prior research examining infant head size and later mental health has produced mixed results. Some studies, including a 2005 study of Swedish twins, found that babies born with smaller head circumferences and lower birth weights were more likely to develop schizophrenia as adults. Other studies found larger head sizes, no link at all, or differences that only appeared in females or vanished by early childhood. Most of this earlier work only looked at measurements taken at birth or during the first few months of life, leaving it unknown how head growth unfolds through later childhood and adolescence.
Scientists have also questioned whether a smaller head reflects a biological process restricted to the brain or a whole-body growth pattern. For example, a 2007 study of over 1.3 million Swedish men indicated that shorter adult height and lower body mass index were associated with a higher risk of schizophrenia. Similarly, a 2007 birth cohort study found that women who developed schizophrenia-spectrum disorders grew in height about one centimeter per year slower during early childhood than women without these conditions.
To determine whether head growth trajectories differ across the psychosis spectrum and whether those differences are independent of overall body size, Merritt, lead author Sarah A. Ashley of University College London, and their colleagues examined data from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children. This population-based project tracked children born to pregnant women in the Southwest of England between April 1991 and December 1992.
The researchers analyzed an overall sample of 3,866 participants, including 2,177 females and 1,689 males, who had complete background records and at least one head circumference measurement between birth and age 15. Head measurements were collected across up to 22 time points, with major assessments occurring during the first year of life, at age 7, and at age 15. On average, participants had about eight head circumference measurements recorded over their childhood.
When the participants reached age 17 or 18, trained psychologists interviewed them using a semi-structured assessment to evaluate whether they had experienced hallucinations, delusions, or thought interference since age 12. Thought interference refers to the belief that one’s private thoughts are being broadcast out loud, inserted into one’s mind, or taken away by an outside force. Based on these interviews, 339 participants (8.8 percent of the sample, comprising 218 females and 121 males) were classified as having definite psychotic experiences.
Within that group, 62 individuals (1.6 percent of the sample, comprising 49 females and 13 males) met the operational criteria for a psychotic disorder. This meant their experiences occurred at least once a month over the preceding six months and caused severe distress, impaired their social or work functioning, or prompted them to seek professional help. The remaining 3,527 participants served as the comparison control group.
To confirm that external head measurements accurately reflected internal brain size in their sample, the researchers also analyzed structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain scans from a subset of 347 participants at age 20. From these scans, they calculated total intracranial volume, which is the total space inside the skull cavity occupied by the brain and surrounding fluids.
In their statistical models, the authors controlled for several maternal and birth factors that can influence physical growth. These included the mother’s highest level of education, her pre-pregnancy body mass index, the length of the pregnancy, and the baby’s weight at birth. In a secondary step, the researchers added the child’s height across development to see if head size differences persisted when accounting for overall physical stature.
The neuroimaging analysis confirmed that childhood head circumference was a reliable proxy for young adult brain size. Head size at birth showed a moderate positive correlation with total intracranial volume at age 20, while head measurements taken at ages 7 and 15 showed strong correlations with adult intracranial volume across both males and females.
When looking at growth trajectories over time, the researchers found that young people who met criteria for a psychotic disorder at age 18 had consistently smaller head circumferences than the control group from birth right through to age 15. Across the developmental span, the psychotic disorder group had an average head circumference about 0.26 centimeters smaller than controls in the statistical model, a small fraction of overall head size. The gap did not widen or narrow as the children aged, indicating that the modeled gap was similar in size from birth through adolescence.
The difference remained after accounting for maternal education and maternal body mass index, and shrank only slightly, to about 0.20 centimeters, when length of pregnancy and birth weight were added, though at that point it fell just short of statistical significance. Sensitivity checks looking strictly at birth, age 7, and age 15 also found smaller head sizes in the psychotic disorder group at each milestone, with the differences reaching statistical significance at ages 7 and 15.
When the team examined the larger group of 339 young people who reported broader psychotic experiences, they discovered contrasting patterns between males and females. Females with psychotic experiences had consistently smaller head circumferences across childhood and adolescence compared to female controls, averaging about 0.27 centimeters smaller in the unadjusted trajectory model.
In contrast, males with psychotic experiences had larger head circumferences than male controls across the overall trajectory model, averaging about 0.35 centimeters larger. In the age-by-age checks, however, males with psychotic experiences had smaller heads at birth and larger heads at ages 7 and 15. Both of the overall sex-specific patterns remained intact after adjusting for maternal and birth characteristics.
The smaller head sizes seen in the psychotic disorder group and among females with psychotic experiences stand in contrast to findings in autism spectrum disorder, a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by differences in social communication and restricted or repetitive behaviors. “For me, one of the most interesting aspects of this finding is what it tells us when considered alongside our work in autism spectrum disorder,” Merritt noted. “In a separate paper, we found the opposite pattern, with larger head circumference associated with autism. This suggests that patterns of brain growth may differ across different forms of neurodevelopmental risk, rather than there being a single pattern of atypical brain development.”
The picture shifted when the researchers factored in the children’s height over time. After controlling for height across development, the head circumference differences between the psychotic disorder group and the control group shrank and were no longer statistically significant. The same thing happened among females with psychotic experiences: once height was taken into account, their smaller head size was no longer statistically significant. The raw height differences between groups at age 15.5 were small and not statistically tested: females in the psychotic disorder group averaged about 1.6 centimeters shorter than female controls, while the 13 males in that group averaged slightly taller than male controls.
In males with psychotic experiences, however, controlling for height did not change the outcome, and their head circumferences remained larger than those of male controls. Together, these results suggest that for individuals with psychotic disorders and females with psychotic experiences, a smaller head circumference may reflect a broader, whole-body growth restriction rather than an issue confined to brain growth.
The authors noted that hormones regulating early physical development might help explain why general growth restriction and sex differences appear across the psychosis spectrum. One candidate they pointed to is insulin-like growth factor-I, a hormone that manages both fetal and childhood physical growth and naturally circulates at different levels in males and females. Early environmental stressors, such as maternal infections during pregnancy or nutritional deficiencies, could also influence both overall physical stature and future mental health risk.
“The key takeaway is that head circumference is a potentially useful, inexpensive measure for understanding developmental differences associated with psychosis risk,” Merritt said. “However, these findings reflect differences between groups and cannot currently be used to predict psychosis in an individual. We would not want people to interpret a smaller head circumference as meaning that someone will develop psychosis. There are many factors that contribute to psychosis risk, and head circumference would need to be considered alongside other measures.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these findings. Because the study followed participants over nearly two decades, not every child had their head measured at every possible age, and the researchers had to rely on statistical modeling to chart continuous trajectories across gaps in time. In addition, the classification of psychotic disorder at age 18 was based on structured research interviews rather than formal clinical diagnoses from a medical doctor.
The total number of participants who met the criteria for a psychotic disorder was relatively small at 62 people, and only 13 of them were male. Because of this small male sample size in the disorder group, the researchers may not have had enough statistical power to detect sex differences among those with full psychotic disorders, and findings involving males in that group should be viewed cautiously. Future studies using larger, independent birth cohorts will be needed to verify these sex-specific growth patterns and examine the biological mechanisms that link early physical growth to adult mental health.
“In the longer term, we are interested in whether head circumference could be combined with other developmental, genetic and environmental risk measures to improve our ability to identify individuals who might benefit from early intervention,” Merritt added.
The study, “Course of head growth from birth to adolescence across the psychosis spectrum,” was authored by Sarah A. Ashley, Kate Merritt, Francesca Solmi, Pedro Luque Laguna, Yanakan Logeswaran, Derek K. Jones, David Linden, Anthony S. David, and Abraham Reichenberg.

How do we actually turn down the temperature in political debate?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:47:44 UTC
04:47:44 KST

analysis
After alleged attack on Helen Haines, how do we actually turn down the temperature?
Only two months ago, a group called Compassion in Politics Australia gained the first signatory to its "Civility Pledge".
Helen Haines.
The organisation, based on a similar foundation in the United Kingdom, aims to turn the tide of toxic debate and build a better politics.
As a start, it's asking elected officials to sign a simple pledge. "In my political life, I pledge to act with honesty, respect, and compassion," is all it states.
This week the independent MP was the victim of an attack widely described as shocking but unsurprising. Sadly predictable was the common reaction amongst MPs who have been at the receiving end of increasing threats and harassment.
Yesterday, security agencies briefed MPs on the risks to their safety. Security will no doubt be improved as much as practicable, without sacrificing MPs' ability to interact in their communities.
The more difficult question is what, if anything, can be done about the increasingly hostile political environment. What can be done to restore the "civility" that Haines, at least, pledged to pursue?
Civility was the word emphasised by the Governor-General late yesterday, who stood alongside the husband of Helen Haines in an effort to calm a worried nation.
"We don't have to all agree, but we can wrestle with the issue not the person," Sam Mostyn said from Melbourne's Alfred Hospital. Her message echoed the call to turn the temperature down.
"Words matter, whether spoken or in written form or increasingly in the virtual world."
This call for civility is something ASIO boss Mike Burgess has been going on about now for years.
"I genuinely believe the temperature of our security environment would be several degrees lower if we recommitted to conversing with civility, debating with respect and disagreeing with restraint," he said after the attack on Haines.
Burgess draws a line between words and actions: "ASIO has seen direct correlations between inflamed language, inflamed tensions and acts of violence."
The intelligence chief must feel at times he's talking to a brick wall. He warned against "inflamed language" and called for a return to civility after the October 7 Hamas attack on Israel in 2023, again after lifting the terrorism threat level to "probable" in 2024, and again after the Bondi terrorist attack in 2025.
Will anyone listen this time? Will an attack on one of their own force politicians to re-think their part in setting the tone of political discourse?
For some, the answer is clearly yes. There is a degree of self-reflection this week.
"We should all, every single one of us, me included, find ways to minimise the temperature of these debates," said shadow minister Jono Duniam, who will soon depart the Senate.
"We could all do better. I don't exclude myself or any political party," acknowledged the prime minister who, like Burgess, has repeatedly called for a more civil debate.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, by contrast, is worried about limiting robust argument. While condemning anything that intimidates or incites violence, he defended the role of vigorous debate.
"We have, like so few other countries in the world, avoided political violence. This is part of the great Australian achievement, and we've done that by having vigorous and rigorous debate and choice at the ballot box," he said.
"This is what's worked for us. We need to make sure it stays there."
It's certainly true — Australia has long enjoyed robust political debate while largely avoiding political violence.
But this misses the point being made by the ASIO boss. Times have changed.
We're now in an environment, according to Burgess, where "politically motivated violence is more likely than previous years".
Angus Taylor's own colleagues can recognise the deterioration, too.
"It's clear that the political environment has become more heated in recent years," said shadow minister James Paterson.
"In the last few years things have gotten much worse," said independent MP Monique Ryan, adding that "the 2025 election was completely different to 2022", with more aggression and anger. It's a common view, particularly among female politicians.
MPs are worried. For themselves, for their families, and for the fate of Australia's democracy.
So, what does it take to turn the temperature down?
"Gosh, if only I could say what the answer to that is," One Nation's Barnaby Joyce admitted on Radio National yesterday. "I don't know," he said.
It's rare to hear Barnaby Joyce stumped for an answer on anything. He's certainly not accepting any blame on the part of One Nation for raising the temperature.
Many might agree with Joyce that there are no easy solutions to counter the powerful domestic and global forces driving voter frustration, political polarisation, toxic online discourse and hate.
Politicians are certainly limited in what they can control. But they're not entirely powerless.
As Burgess says, language matters: "By all means, disagree. But consider how you disagree."
Signing a "Civility Pledge" might seem like a mere symbolic gesture, but it's something. If it's good enough for Helen Haines, why not others?
Compassion in Politics Australia issued a statement after the horrific attack on Monday, calling it "a stark reminder that compassion and civility in public life are not abstract ideals. They matter profoundly".
The attack on Helen Haines may prove to be just another brief interruption before regular political mud-slinging resumes. Or it could see all sides of politics try to course correct.
David Speers is national political lead and host of Insiders, which airs on ABC TV at 9am on Sunday or can be streamed anytime on ABC iview.

AI generated
VATICAN CITY - Pope Leo will not need any further therapy after undergoing lung cancer surgery last week, his doctors said on Oct 21, indicating that his tumour had not spread.
The announcement came as it was still unclear whether the US-born pope would proceed with a planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, scheduled for Nov 6-17.
The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung removed in surgery on Oct 13 and was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
Final histological examinations and molecular biology analyses of the tissue removed confirmed the diagnosis, with the disease remaining localised, the doctors said in a statement released by the Vatican.
“A subsequent oncological evaluation has confirmed that no further therapy is required,” the pope’s lead surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, and his personal physician, Luigi Carbone, said.
Leo was discharged from hospital on Oct 17 and is gradually resuming his normal duties.
On Oct 21, he returned to St Peter’s Square for his weekly audience with pilgrims.
Margaritora said last week there were “no clinical reasons” preventing the pope from travelling to South America, but the Vatican’s secretary of state has indicated the pontiff may need to adjust the pace of his schedule to aid his recovery. REUTERS

Five Facts You Need To Know From The U.N.'s Major Emissions Gap Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:44:08 UTC
04:44:08 KST

The goal of limiting global warming to below 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels is largely out of reach. That’s according to the United Nations Environmental Program’s (UNEP) 2026 Emissions Gap report released on Wednesday, considered the definitive assessment of global climate action.
“We’ve spent decades postponing cuts to emissions and now we’re facing the consequences,” Anne Olhoff, director of the UNEP-Copenhagen Climate Centre, and one of the report’s authors, said after the report’s publication. “The world can still attain the goals of the Paris Agreement but we must work hard to not only meet but surpass our most ambitious climate targets. The longer we wait, the larger the risk that we jeopardize the temperature goal.”
While the report’s warning is stark, that doesn’t mean that all hope is lost. Coordinated efforts to reduce emissions can still have a meaningful impact on climate change, it says—but action must be taken quickly.
Here are the biggest takeaways from the Emissions Gap report.
The 1.5°C target is mostly out of reach
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, the world agreed to halt planetary warming at 2°C above pre-industrial temperatures and to pursue efforts to limit warming by 1.5°C. Doing so would provide a greater chance at avoiding the worst impacts of climate change. The window to avoid overshooting the 1.5°C goal, however, is now closed, the report finds.
But that doesn’t mean that there’s no hope for climate action. It is still possible to limit the overshoot and bring temperatures back below 1.5 degrees by the end of the century. Every fraction of a degree of warming above 1.5°C increases climate impacts, making the goal to limit as much warming beyond 1.5°C all the more important.
The world is on track to reach 2.8°C of warming by 2100
Under the terms of the Paris Agreement, countries must submit updated climate pledges, known as Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), which outline specific goals to reduce national emissions. Based on the policies currently in place under the NDCs submitted by over 150 nations, the planet is on track to reach 2.8°C of warming by the end of the century.
Based on this, today’s report concludes that global climate pledges are falling short. If countries meet their new NDCs, which set upgraded targets for 2035 and were due last year, global warming is still projected to reach 2.6°C by the end of the century.
Both scenarios would have devastating consequences—dramatically transforming sea levels and ecosystems, and triggering compounding climate extremes such as higher temperatures and drought, increasing the likelihood of wildfires.
We need to cut carbon emissions by 18% in the next four years
The report notes that it is still possible to peak warming at 1.7°C or 1.8°C. Doing so would require major changes. We would need to cut emissions by 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035, and 69% by 2040, relative to 2025 levels. This would require sustained emissions cuts along with carbon dioxide removal.
“Every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5°C increases climate impacts and risks, such as the deadly floods, heat waves, and wildfires that have plagued many nations this year,” said UNEP executive director Inger Andersen. “So, we must pull out all the stops to minimize peak warming and return to 1.5°C by the end of the century.”
The U.S. is a major outlier for emissions
While emissions growth has slowed down in most G20 countries, emissions in the United States “far exceeded that of all other countries," the report says. That’s due to the increased electricity demand, in part due to data centers, and new policies that encouraged the use of fossil fuels like coal over clean energy sources.
The report includes a statement from the State Department, noting that the U.S. "does not endorse or agree with its analysis or conclusions, and has not provided comments to this report."
The Trump Administration’s decision to withdraw from the Paris Agreement also worsened the climate projections, as estimates no longer include climate action that would have been taken under the United States’s NDC targets.
The U.S. is the second largest emitter of climate-warming greenhouse gases, behind China, which has quickly become a world leader in renewable energy (while also ramping up coal production.)
Climate policies are reducing emissions
Since the adoption of the Paris Agreement just over a decade ago, global renewable electricity capacity has grown three times faster than anticipated, while solar PV build-out has increased seven times faster. If these trends were to continue, and coupled with more policies to support clean energy, the world would be on track to reach its renewable energy goals.
The report examined more than 200 climate policies and found that they target emission reductions across a wide range of sectors and countries. That’s an encouraging sign the report notes. All that’s left is for these solutions to be scaled faster.
“We have a wealth of success stories showing that emissions can be cut quickly,” said Andersen. “It is now up to nations to urgently put in place policies that spark fast, deep and sustained emissions reductions, and put the world on track for a more stable climate and more stable economies and societies.”
