03:00:52 KST

A judge in New Mexico has ordered Meta Platforms to pay $25 billion after a jury found the company had misled consumers in a case arising from allegations that a political consulting firm obtained data from millions of Facebook users without their consent.
"Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the heart of Facebook's core business practices," Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order following the verdict on Wednesday.
Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219 billion was warranted, based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25 billion.
A spokesperson for Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The state's attorney general had sued Meta in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm, had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app.
The state accused Meta of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data, how the company handles hate speech and misinformation posted on the platform and other internal policies.
The company knew that third parties had broad access to users' personal data, and it tolerated hate speech or other harmful content when it benefited the company's bottom line, the state said.
$5,000 per violation
Jurors on September 25 found that 26 of 29 statements made by the company and its leadership on those issues were misleading.
They said the company had committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws, based on the number of Facebook users or New Mexico residents who were the audience for each misleading statement.
State law allows a penalty of up to $5,000 per violation, and directs that all of the money go to New Mexico's school system, New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez told reporters after the verdict.
In court filings, Meta urged Mathew to cap the penalties at $3.45 billion, saying a higher penalty ran the risk of scaring businesses out of the state.
The evidence showed that Meta does not sell user data and New Mexico did not prove that any consumer had actually been misled, the company said in court filings.
The verdict was the second in six months by a Santa Fe jury in a lawsuit brought by the state of New Mexico against Meta Platforms.
In the first trial, which ended in March, a Santa Fe jury found Meta misled users about young users’ safety on its Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp platforms and ordered the company to pay $375 million in civil penalties.
After a second phase of that trial, a judge directed the company to pay $567 million into a New Mexico fund for teen mental health and ordered Meta to implement measures to protect teen Facebook and Instagram users in New Mexico.

====================================================================================================

Intelligence predicts charitable giving and voting in massive Swedish study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:00:47 UTC
03:00:47 KST

People with higher cognitive abilities are more likely to engage in actions that benefit society, such as donating to charity, voting in elections, and buying environmentally friendly vehicles. These findings suggest that general intelligence plays a direct role in driving cooperative, socially minded actions. The research was published in The Economic Journal.
Humans are uniquely inclined to cooperate with strangers and contribute to public goods. Evolutionary biologists and economists often categorize these actions as prosocial behaviors. Finding a rational explanation for why humans evolved into such cooperative animals has long challenged researchers across multiple disciplines.
One proposed explanation centers on human intelligence. Some theorists suggest that cognitive ability improves logical reasoning and the capacity to understand the perspectives of others. These mental skills naturally foster ethical reasoning, which can ultimately lead to a sense of altruism.
Other researchers propose that intelligent individuals often achieve higher incomes and better social standing. This wealth could lower the personal financial cost of giving away money or time. Up until now, evidence linking intelligence to prosocial behavior has mostly come from brief laboratory games or surveys where people report their own habits.
To find concrete answers, economists Mikael Elinder and Oscar Erixson analyzed a massive set of Swedish administrative records. They wanted to see if objective measures of intelligence predicted documented, real world prosocial behaviors. The researchers focused on three specific actions: charitable giving, voting, and the ownership of environmentally friendly cars.
The researchers first analyzed data from over 1.2 million Swedish men and about 3,000 Swedish women. All of these individuals took a standardized cognitive test during their military enlistment process between 1969 and 1997. This exam evaluated logical, verbal, spatial, and technical abilities on a nine point scale.
The researchers then matched these historical test scores with modern government records. They looked at tax registries from 2012 to 2015 to track charitable donations. Because Swedish charities automatically report donations to the government for tax purposes, the data minimizes biases related to a person’s financial literacy or their willingness to fill out tax forms.
To measure political participation, the researchers examined electoral rolls for the 2009 European Parliament election. By using validated voter turnout data, the team avoided the common problem of people lying about their voting habits in surveys. Finally, they consulted a national vehicle database to identify households that owned cars powered by electricity, ethanol, or natural gas.
Individuals with higher cognitive scores were much more likely to engage in all three prosocial behaviors. Men with the highest cognitive scores were more than five times as likely to donate to charity compared to men with the lowest scores. A one standard deviation increase in intelligence matched a 40 percent relative increase in the likelihood of charitable giving.
The same bump in test scores corresponded to a 31 percent increase in voting. It also matched a 14 percent increase in eco-friendly car ownership. The data from the female participants revealed very similar positive trends for voting and charity, showing that the effect was not limited to men.
When looking at specific types of intelligence, the researchers noticed that logical and verbal reasoning were the strongest predictors of prosocial action. These two traits are widely considered the best indicators of general fluid intelligence. Fluid intelligence is the ability to think abstractly and solve novel problems.
Observing a link in the general population does not prove that intelligence directly causes prosocial behavior. People with high cognitive scores often grow up in wealthy families or specific neighborhoods that might actively encourage civic duties. To account for these shared background variables, Elinder and Erixson conducted a second analysis using a large sample of 5,786 twin pairs.
Because twins typically share the same upbringing, home environment, and a large portion of their genetics, comparing siblings helps account for many confounding factors and better isolate the effect of intelligence. The researchers looked at twin pairs where one sibling scored higher on the enlistment cognitive test than the other. They also controlled for general personality traits evaluated during the military interviews, such as emotional stability and sociality.
The researchers found that the smarter twin was consistently more likely to vote and donate to charity. The associations decreased in size by about half compared to the massive population sample. A one standard deviation increase in cognitive ability among twins matched a 26 percent increase in charitable giving and a 13 percent increase in voting.
The link to eco-friendly car ownership also dropped to a 13 percent increase. This twin based approach indicates that unobserved family factors account for some of the population wide trend. However, those family factors do not entirely explain the connection between cognitive ability and prosocial habits.
Elinder and Erixson then ran a third analysis to test specific lifestyle variables that might bridge the gap between intelligence and behavior. A person’s intelligence influences their life trajectory, which could in turn dictate their civic engagement. The researchers factored in differences in education, total income, marriage status, the presence of children, and the municipality of residence.
Education explained a noticeable portion of the link between cognitive scores and civic habits. This aligns with the idea that schools help transmit prosocial values or develop a person’s ethical awareness. Individuals who spend more years in the educational system often learn to prioritize community well being.
Income did not act as a major mediator. Smarter individuals were not simply donating or buying eco-friendly cars just because they had more money to spare. When accounting for all these lifestyle variables, the direct mathematical link between intelligence and owning an eco-friendly car was not statistically significant.
However, the direct connection to voting and charitable giving held firm even after adjusting for education and income. The researchers interpreted this as evidence of a profound, direct tie between intelligence and certain types of cooperation. General intelligence appears to influence these behaviors independently of a person’s life circumstances.
Finally, the researchers looked at survey responses from a separate sample of about 600 men. These men had previously reported their own feelings of altruism on a numerical scale, along with their patience and risk preferences. The researchers matched these survey answers to the men’s military enlistment cognitive scores.
Individuals with higher cognitive abilities expressed a higher degree of personal altruism, with a one standard deviation increase in cognitive ability associated with a 0.16 standard deviation increase in self-reported altruism. This self reported data is in line with the behavioral records found in the national registries. While the survey results cannot firmly distinguish between different mechanisms, they are consistent with the theory that cognitive ability influences prosocial behavior through ethical reasoning and altruism.
While the twin analysis helps control for many background factors, the findings do not guarantee a strict cause and effect relationship in every scenario. The study relies heavily on data from Swedish men born between 1951 and 1979. The exact percentages might vary across different cultures, age groups, or time periods.
Additionally, the research defines prosocial behavior through three specific financial and political actions. People with lower cognitive scores might be equally cooperative in ways that do not show up in tax or vehicle registries, such as volunteering or helping neighbors physically. Future research will need to explore how other cognitive functions, like empathy and the ability to read emotions, interact with general intelligence to shape human cooperation.
The study, “An inquiry into the relationship between intelligence and prosocial behaviour: Evidence from Swedish population registers,” was authored by Mikael Elinder and Oscar Erixson.

GM Wants Your Car to Do Your Chores
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Americans spent about 95 billion hours behind the wheel last year, traveling something like 2.76 trillion miles. On Wednesday, General Motors executives are outlining the future of automotive at the company’s annual GM Forward event in New York City, and they say their goal isn’t to reduce that number. After all, it’s a car company.
But GM does want to make car time better. Or, as Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson put it in an interview with WIRED, “make it more productive, make it more relaxing, make it more engaging. We’d like to make your vehicle a more central, more useful part of your life than it has been historically.” Your future car is sort of a personal assistant, and sort of a spouse, and sort of a tool, and sort of a best friend.
It’s a tall order. But in a raft of announcements this week, GM hopes to demonstrate that, armed with AI-enabled capabilities, the automaker is inching closer to that future.
GM says it will roll out a new in-car AI assistant, called OnStar AI, starting with 2027 Cadillac Lyriqs. (The name borrows from the 30-year-old roadside assistance and security service, which has 12 million subscribers.) Paired with a new app, the system will start by letting drivers, for example, turn on their air conditioning with a voice command without navigating through a menu. Eventually, though, it might coordinate kid pickups and drop-offs depending on which spouse’s car is closer, Anderson says.
GM also says it will use AI to speed up new-vehicle development, eventually cutting its four- to five-year development time in half—the speed at which Chinese carmakers create new vehicles today.
The automaker plans to expand its “eyes-off” highway driving technology to its most popular cars, inching closer to its years-old promise of making a personal self-driving car. It previously said the system was coming to the Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028. Today, the company’s Super Cruise feature lets drivers take their hands off their steering wheels on hundreds of thousands of miles of pre-mapped highways. Reaching true autonomy will take time, but GM isn’t ready to talk about that publicly. “This industry is rife with promises that were not fulfilled. I am not keen on making them,” Anderson says.
But GM is taking a different approach from, say, Tesla. The electric carmaker sells a driver-assistance feature called “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” that can navigate many highways and local roads but requires drivers to stay alert and ready to take over at any moment. That kind of system “presents the illusion of autonomy without its benefits,” Anderson says, who for a time led Tesla’s Autopilot program. If drivers can’t do other things while their car is doing most of the driving, it’s less useful and “comes with the direct expense of the safety of your vehicle and the people around you,” he says. “That would not be a responsible way to operate.”
GM’s method, by contrast, is to slowly expand “eyes-off” capabilities to more sorts of roads, letting drivers text or eat or watch YouTube first on some highways, and then on more highways, and then on local roads, and then maybe everywhere.
That’s when the automaker's vision gets bigger and blurrier. The cabin, the company says in a blog post, can become a space to “relax, work, and unwind. … In time, this will pave the way for a future where your car can take on everyday errands,” the company says. The personal self-driving car will pick up groceries, drop off children, and then maybe even find a parking spot at the end.
Urban planners and infrastructure experts have worried about this vision. If you lower the price of a car trip, in money and time spent driving, won’t everyone send their cars out for every task? Won’t the roads be crowded with pods full of people sleeping, emailing, and YouTubing while their vehicles slowly pilot them onward—or worse, cars with no one in them? Won’t cities become sprawlier?
Anderson says yes. If you have cheap, personal driving robots, “you will very likely incur more of those robots on the roads. And so there's a lot of societal and infrastructural considerations to make here,” he says. But he argues we have time, and that cities take time to sprawl. “I wouldn't call this an imminent thing, but it certainly is something we should be thinking about.”

Supercharged fire seasons now threaten half Australia's homes: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Supercharged fire seasons cost Australia $6b annually as El Niño summer looms
In short:
New modelling reveals bushfires will cost Australia $6 billion a year, with a single major event costing almost $30 billion.
Fire seasons are now 21 per cent longer, with 5.6 million households exposed to bushfire risk.
What's next?
Large parts of Australia are bracing for a hotter and drier summer due to El Niño.
As Australians prepare for a summer influenced by what is likely to become the strongest El Niño on record, a new report reveals billions of dollars are being spent tackling bushfire seasons supercharged by climate change.
The modelling, commissioned by Emergency Leaders for Climate Action (ELCA), found the country's fire seasons have lengthened by 21 per cent since 1979 due to warming global temperatures.
The longer seasons will cost the Australian economy $6 billion each year over the next 30 years, with a majority being spent on harm to health and wellbeing, ahead of damaged businesses and lost homes.
ELCA's Greg Mullins, a former Fire and Rescue NSW commissioner, said the high costs come as climate change, driven by the burning of fossil fuels, squeezes fire seasons closer together.
"The fire seasons are longer, they're overlapping between states and we're getting catastrophic fire weather," he said.
"Previous studies only looked at insured costs, which were far less, but costs across the economy are huge; in 30 years that's $180 billion."
Black Summer highlights cost of extreme fires
The ELCA report found half of Australian households are exposed to some bushfire risk, at 5.6 million, while major events, such as the Black Summer fires, cost almost $30 billion. And between 2003 and 2020 more than a million Australians had lived in a home within one kilometre of an active fire front.
The 2019/20 bushfires tore through about 45 per cent of the Snowy Valleys Council (SVC) local government area (LGA), killing one person and destroying almost 200 homes.
There were almost 9,000 livestock fatalities within the LGA and 400,000 hectares of land burnt.
The local council spent more than $50 million on direct recovery, which included road repairs and managing damaged and fallen trees.
SVC's manager of technical services, Glen McGrath, said the region was still recovering from the event more than six years later.
"You look at the softwood industry, they had a very large impact and it takes 20-plus years for softwood or pine tree to grow and be harvested and processed through the local industry processes, so they won't be coming back online until 2040 or thereabouts," he said.
"There's still a number of houses that weren't rebuilt after the fire, so there's widespread impacts and recovery efforts still."
Research has found the Black Summer bushfires cost Australia's tourism industry almost $3b, while the Insurance Council has found the event accounts for about $2b of the $2.58b in bushfire claims since 2019.
Preparation key ahead of high-risk summers
While no two events are the same, El Niño often brings hotter and drier conditions to southern and eastern parts of Australia.
Despite 2026 shaping up to become Australia's wettest El Niño year on record, drier than average conditions are starting to persist across parts of the country's east.
"In the last three months since El Niño has been active, we've seen drier-than-average conditions along much of the eastern seaboard," senior climatologist at the Bureau of Meteorology Felicity Gamble said.
"Extending from central Queensland through to south-east Queensland, down the New South Wales eastern seaboard and across southern Victoria and Tasmania."
There are concerns that unusually hot temperatures, combined with an increase in baseline warming due to climate change, could increase the risk of "flash droughts" this summer.
"When we get heatwaves, vegetation gives up its moisture very quickly … so things can very quickly turn into drought-like conditions and that drives fires," Mr Mullins said.
"All you need then is wind and you can have catastrophic fires."
Given the typical "lag effect" seen during an El Niño, there is speculation next year could become the hottest on record globally, leading to a particularly bad fire season in 2027/28.
But the ELCA report also found that better protecting infrastructure and homes could avoid $600m in bushfire losses and protect more than 5,600 jobs each year.
"The federal government has a Disaster Ready Fund, it's invested hundreds of millions over the last few years, which is great, but it needs to be targeted to help households," Mr Mullins said.
"For example, bringing their homes up to bushfire standards so that they'll withstand fire, making sure that communities still have the electricity on and have communications after a fire."

Politicians urged to report threats and vary daily habits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Violent threats, intimidation and harassment 'new reality' of Australian politics
In short:
Politicians have revealed harrowing experiences of threats and harassment, including intimidation targeting their children.
The alleged attack on Indi MP Helen Haines has fuelled concerns about how to keep parliamentarians safe while remaining accessible to the public.
What's next?
The Australian Federal Police has urged MPs to report threats more and advised them to vary their daily routines as a safety precaution.
When a Sydney woman faced court accused of sending death threats to multiple Australian politicians, some of her alleged targets had no idea they were on the list.
They only became aware through media reports on the case, a scenario described by one of the MPs as "surreal".
It was just one example of the increasingly routine nature of threats against elected representatives from across the political spectrum, with police now laying charges almost weekly.
In the wake of the alleged attack on Indi MP Helen Haines, for which the motive remains unknown, parliamentarians have detailed harrowing accounts of rape threats, intimidation, stalking and harassment.
One senior Labor MP told the ABC the "worst" threat they had received was from a man who sent an "itemised list" of times and places where he had seen the politician's children in public.
One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce has revealed a man previously made a U-Turn and tried to drive at him, while Labor MP Jerome Laxale has told The Guardian he once received a bomb threat.
Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek said someone slipped a note under the door of her home, telling her they hoped her children "die of painful cancers".
Ms Plibersek also said she could not "count" the number of death and rape threats she has received over the years.
Politicians told to vary daily routines
On Wednesday, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) offered safety briefings to parliamentarians who have expressed their horror, but not their surprise, at the alleged attack on Ms Haines.
MPs were encouraged to report more of the threats they received and urged to share their diaries with the AFP to help police keep track of scheduled public events.
They were also advised to frequently change their daily habits, such as the route they took to work or other common destinations.
Parliamentarians have previously been told not to advertise public appearances in advance, and in the briefing were advised to maintain situational awareness of their surroundings, particularly when around their electorate offices.
Police did not advise of any specific or immediate threats but reiterated the importance of vigilance at all times.
Several MPs said they felt the meetings offered an opportunity for them to voice their concerns, which the AFP agreed to take on board.
But others were underwhelmed and told the ABC they did not get the answers they were seeking about baseline security for their homes and electorate offices.
Chalmers says Australia not 'immune' to political violence
The AFP charged 41 people with offences relating to threats against parliamentarians in the past year, while reports of harassing, nuisance, offensive and threatening behaviour have quadrupled since 2020.
In August, a 47-year-old Perth man faced court accused of threatening One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, including in one Facebook post in which he said he would "hunt her down and kill her".
A 19-year-old Western Australian man in March admitted to threatening to kill Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and NSW Premier Chris Minns, though told the court he "didn't mean for it to be a threat".
The man's lawyer told the court her client had made an "error in judgement", adding he had been "reading a lot of political stuff online".
Records show alleged perpetrators often later argued they did not intend to follow through with their threats.
But that excuse was recently rejected by a Queensland magistrate hearing a case in September about a man who left voicemails with violent threats against Mr Albanese and Treasurer Jim Chalmers.
"That's not relevant to the threat … the people on the receiving end have got no idea what your intentions are," Magistrate Pamela Dowse told the man.
Mr Chalmers told the ABC what had happened to Ms Haines was "shocking, but unfortunately not surprising".
"Helen is the closest thing to a perfect temperament in an imperfect workplace, and it shows even the parliament's most rational person is not safe from random acts of irrational violence," he said.
Mr Chalmers said, more broadly, Australia was not "immune" from the political violence that could be seen around the world.
"Random acts of irrational violence are just as possible in the centre of Paris as the main drag of Wangaratta," he said.
Australia faces 'new reality' amid surge in threats
Labor MP Josh Burns was one of 15 high-profile figures allegedly sent death threats by a 36-year-old woman who in August fronted a Sydney court facing 62 charges, including stalking and intimidation.
He only learned of the incident when the case reached court and said it stood in contrast to the majority of his interactions in the community, which were "overwhelmingly really kind".
Senator Hanson, independent MP Allegra Spender, Labor MP Andrew Charlton and NSW Labor MP Jihad Dib were also allegedly threatened by the accused over a five-year period.
Mr Burns said managing abusive online comments was the "worst bit" of daily life as an MP and he praised how the AFP had responded to serious threats.
"But I do think there is, especially for women online and for what's happened this week, there is a new reality that we have to meet," he said.
"We need to ensure that politics and people who put their hands up for public office can do so safely and good people who have something to contribute to our country are not deterred."
Calls to lift support at state level
In Victoria, Animal Justice Party MP Georgie Purcell has long been a target of abuse and said state politicians were offered considerably less support than federal ones.
"I spent the first few years of my political career reporting voicemails, emails, comments, graffiti on the office and it goes nowhere," she said.
Ms Purcell said having Mr Burns as a partner had given her a "unique" insight into how the AFP tackled threats, and she would like a similar "continuity model" deployed at a state level.
Recently, someone has been "consistently" writing antisemitic graffiti on her office, but Ms Purcell said she has been told to "wipe it off with metho" as it did not meet the threshold of "property damage".
"But it's not the property damage that was my concern, it was the views of the person participating in the behaviour," she said.
Victorian Premier Ben Carroll announced on Wednesday there would be additional resources and arrangements in place for the upcoming state election.
'Don't attack character' in political debate
Speaking at the National Press Club on Tuesday, ACT Senator David Pocock said whatever measures were put in place to protect politicians must be balanced against remaining accessible to voters.
"We have to ensure that we have a democracy where your local politician lives in the community, goes to the local coffee shop, does the groceries," he said.
"That's something Australians love about Australia."
Senator Pocock said the tenor of online discussion was something "we have to grapple with as a society".
"People are saying things online that they would not say to your face," he said.
Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie said he had been targeted online and subsequently identified by the AFP for "additional security".
"That's just the nature of our politics at the moment," he said.
Mr Hastie said the Westminster system of government was "adversarial", but there had to be a "line" where opponents were not demonised.
"We don't attack their character, their standing, so that someone might feel justified in using violence against them," he said.

The 7 Key Governor Races to Watch in the Midterm Elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:58:30 UTC
02:58:30 KST

As Election Day looms, much of the national focus is on whether Democrats will win control of Congress. But in several states, the race for governor is among the tightest, and most consequential, races on the ballot.
The party in control of the White House typically fares poorly in midterm elections. While that usually translates most clearly into losing congressional seats, true “wave” elections often lead to similar shifts in state governments as well.
Multiple states could see the party in the governor’s seat flip. Voters in Ohio, Alaska, and Texas might end up electing their first Democratic governors in decades. In Oregon, the reverse could pan out, with a Republican in contention to upend a Democrat’s hold on the office for the first time since 1982.
Here are seven races for governor to watch on Election Day.
Ohio
Ohio's governor's race was thrust into the national spotlight this week after Republican Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign released an ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democrat opponent Amy Acton. Acton’s mother lost custody of Acton and her brother after their stepfather was arrested and indicted on a charge of raping Acton when she was a child.
The ad immediately drew widespread outrage, the latest twist in a race that Republicans had thought they were well positioned to win after Trump won the state by 11 points in 2024. Many Republicans had been expected to vie to replace Gov. Mike DeWine, who couldn’t run again because of term limits. But Trump’s endorsement of Ramaswamy essentially cleared the field for him.
Now Ramaswamy is in a very tight race against Acton, who previously led the Ohio Department of Health during the Covid-19 pandemic. While the Cook Political Report previously marked the Ohio gubernatorial race as “Lean Republican,” it later shifted its rating slightly in favor of Democrats, to “Toss Up.”
Many polls show Acton with a narrow lead, but a few suggest that Ramaswamy has a razor-thin lead.
If Acton ultimately wins, it would be the first time in 20 years that Ohio voters had elected a Democrat as governor.
Alaska
The Cook Political Report recently changed its rating for the race in Alaska from a “Toss Up” to “Lean Democrat.” Alaska’s current governor, Republican Mike Dunleavy, is prohibited from running again because of term limits. The open race to replace him includes one Democrat, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, and three Republicans: Bernadette Wilson, a business owner who has received the backing of President Trump; Dave Bronson, the previous mayor of Anchorage; and Treg Taylor, a former state attorney general.
Kreiss-Tomkins, who was previously a state legislator, finished the state’s open primary race in August in the top spot, with another Democratic candidate, Tom Begich, in second place. In Alaska, the top four candidates in the open primary move on to the general election. But Begich later announced that he was dropping out of the race and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins, allowing Taylor to land a spot in the general election ballot.
“The data we’ve seen makes clear that the strongest path to winning in November is not two Democratic candidates competing for the same donors and resources—it’s bringing those people together behind one ticket,” Begich said in a video announcing the suspension of his campaign in August.
Many recent polls show Kreiss-Tomkins leading his three opponents. This month, Trump expressed frustration with all the Republicans still in the race, noting on Truth Social that he had urged Bronson to drop out.
“All Bronson and Taylor will do is take away Votes from the Candidate that has, by far, the best chance of winning,” Trump said in his post. “Now is the time for all Republicans to unite behind Bernadette to ensure she has a tremendous Victory in November!”
Texas
The last time Texas Gov. Greg Abbott ran for re-election in 2022, he won by double digits. He now may be facing his most competitive re-election fight yet; some polls show him holding a slim lead over Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, while others show Hinojosa ahead by a small margin.
“This is an unusual situation in Texas politics,” Joshua Blank, the research director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin, previously told TIME. “It’s rather uncommon to see any Democratic candidate leading in anything other than a single outlying poll leading up to the election.”
If Hinojosa were to win, it would be the first time voters chose to put a Democrat in the state’s governor’s mansion in more than three decades. The tightness of the race mirrors that of the state’s Senate race, where Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton are locked in an expensive fight.
Still, the Cook Political Report suggests that the odds are in Abbott’s favor, rating the race as “Lean Republican.”
Oregon
Amid talk of a national blue wave, the race for governor in Oregon may prove to be a bright spot for Republicans. Gov. Tina Kotek, a Democrat, is trying to fend off a challenge by Republican Christine Drazan, a state senator. Some polls show Kotek ahead by a narrow margin, while others show Drazan in the lead by a similarly small measure. The Cook Political Report previously rated the race as “Likely Democrat,” but has since shifted it slightly in Republicans’ favor, to “Lean Democrat.”
The Cook Political Report says the battle “is one of the rare races moving in Republicans’ direction.” If Drazan were to defeat Kotek, it would mark the first time since 1982 that Oregonians have elected a Republican to the governorship.
Georgia
Georgia is shaping up to be one of the tightest gubernatorial races in the country. It’s one of four that the Cook Political Report has marked as a “Toss Up.” Republican Gov. Brian Kemp couldn’t run for re-election because of term limits, leaving the field open for another member of his party, billionaire Rick Jackson, and Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, the previous mayor of Atlanta. Polls suggest the race is essentially tied, with some indicating Jackson has a razor-thin lead.
A win by Bottoms would mark a significant shift in the southern state’s politics. While both of Georgia’s current Senators are Democrats, it has been led by a Republican governor since 2003. It would also mean the breaking of a national barrier: Georgia would be the first state in the country to have elected a Black woman as governor.
Nevada
A perennial swing state, Republicans are vying to hold on to its leadership of Nevada’s government. Gov. Joe Lombardo is fending off a challenge from Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford. Polls are split over who’s in the lead—some showing Lombardo while others showing Ford, both by slim margins. The Cook Political Report rates the race as a “Toss Up.”.
Wisconsin
The race to lead this swing state became a wide open free-for-all last year, when Democratic Gov. Tony Evers announced he wasn't running for another term. The race was on the verge of becoming a marquee one for democratic socialists, with progressive Francesca Hong leading in the polls ahead of the Democratic primary, before she ultimately lost the nomination to Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, a moderate.
Crowley is now vying for the job against Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany in a race where campaign funding has become a prominent issue, as Tiffany’s bid has been largely bankrolled by three billionaires.
While the Cook Political Report rates this a “Toss Up," multiple recent polls show Crowley with a small lead over Tiffany.

Congress pulls up SBI over data breach, seeks accountability; experts call leak 'no ordinary incident'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:57:59 UTC
02:57:59 KST

SBI data leak: Personal details of 3,897 customers were identified on the dark web. Congress's media and publicity department head, Pawan Khera, questioned the bank's ability to detect the breach and its response towards affected customers.
NEW DELHI: The Congress on Wednesday pulled up the State Bank of India (SBI) over the suspected exposure of 3,897 customer records on the dark web, demanding answers from the country's largest bank and accountability for those responsible. Cybersecurity law expert Pawan Duggal called the incident "no ordinary incident", warning that the exposure could have implications for India's national security.The criticism came after SBI said a preliminary analysis of around 3.75 lakh records available on the dark web had identified 3,897 customer records containing personally identifiable information. The bank said it was investigating the suspected exposure after receiving alerts on October 16 from its threat intelligence service provider, the Defence Cyber Agency, and the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In).
Congress's media and publicity department head, Pawan Khera, questioned the bank's ability to detect the breach and its response towards affected customers."It is bad enough that the State Bank of India @TheOfficialSBI, the country's largest public sector bank, has suffered a data breach involving 3.75 lakh rows of data, with 3,897 records containing personally identifiable customer information -- including mobile numbers, dates of birth, names, email addresses, residential addresses, branch and CIF identifiers, lead IDs, and loan-related details."
"What makes this even more alarming is that SBI did not even detect the breach itself. An external agency had to alert the bank that its customers' data had already been published on the dark web," he said on X.Khera alleged that the bank had yet to inform customers whose personal information was exposed." A bank entrusted with the financial security of millions cannot afford such a catastrophic failure of data security, breach detection and customer accountability. SBI owes its customers answers. Those responsible must be held accountable," he asserted.
Pawan Duggal, chairman of the International Commission on Cyber Security Law, said the suspected leak was particularly serious given SBI's size and the volume of sensitive information it holds."The SBI data leak is no ordinary incident. India is the world’s most populous nation. The SBI is the country’s largest bank, holding a volume of accounts unmatched by any other financial institution. A leak here involves far more than just names; it includes numerous government accounts, such as those of public sector employees, meaning a vast amount of sensitive government information is exposed. The intent behind such a leak is clear: state and non-state actors could exploit this data to negatively impact India’s sovereignty, integrity, and security... Section 79 of the IT Act mandates that intermediaries must exercise "due diligence" in the discharge of their functions. The central government has established specific rules, such as the IT Rules, 2021, and the IT Directions, 2022, that define what constitutes due diligence; it remains to be seen whether these requirements were met... It is high time for India to wake up; the country still lacks a dedicated national law on cybersecurity, and the existing Information Technology Act of 2000 does not adequately address these critical aspects..."
The suspected exposure reportedly includes customers' registered mobile numbers, dates of birth, names, gender, email addresses and residential addresses. The records also contain branch and Customer Information File (CIF) identifiers, lead IDs, and metadata associated with loan and lead records and other related files.
SBI says customer balances are safe
Responding to the incident, SBI said the suspected exposure had affected a very small number of customers and had not materially affected its core business operations, financial performance or business continuity."Customer balances are completely safe, and we are taking all possible steps to protect the interest of our valued customers," the bank said in a post on X.
SBI said it had activated its cyber incident response and containment protocols and engaged an independent cybersecurity agency empanelled by CERT-In to investigate the alleged compromise.The bank said a detailed investigation was needed to establish the authenticity and completeness of the exposed data, determine the potential source and extent of the exposure, and assess the risks to customers and the bank."We reiterate that safety of our customers' financial assets, data and their trust in us remain our highest priorities," it said, adding that remedial and preventive measures were being implemented.
The suspected data exposure comes days after CERT-In issued a 'critical' advisory warning that autonomous artificial intelligence agents had accessed live systems and confidential data belonging to Indian organisations without authorisation.In its advisory, titled 'AI Agents as Attack Vectors', the agency said some AI models and agents undergoing research and evaluation had exceeded the authorised scope of their tasks and accessed live systems. The agents reportedly used credentials and connection settings exposed in application configurations, public code repositories and overly permissive cloud service roles.CERT-In also reported a compromise involving private keys linked to eight intermediate certification authority certificates belonging to India-based certification authority eMudhra Ltd. The affected certificates included six Transport Layer Security certificates and two code-signing certificates.The agency warned that the compromised keys could be used to issue fraudulent certificates, impersonate legitimate websites and potentially intercept or modify encrypted communications.

Inaccessible by Design: AIIB’s Complaint Mechanism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:51:00 UTC
02:51:00 KST

On September 28, the first day of the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB)’s annual meeting in Doha, 108 Indigenous people from Lombok, Indonesia, filed a complaint with the bank’s grievance body, the Project-affected People’s Mechanism (PPM). They said the AIIB-financed Mandalika Urban and Tourism Infrastructure Project forced them from their homes, took their farming land, cost them their livelihoods, and ignored their right to be consulted. Many now struggle to make ends meet and fear future evictions.
Headquartered in Beijing, with China its largest shareholder, the AIIB began operations in 2016. In a decade, it has grown to 111 members and invested almost $70 billion in more than 350 projects across 40 economies. At the Doha meeting, AIIB President Zou Jiayi announced plans to double its annual financing to about $20 billion by 2030. A growing footprint in Asia and beyond demands an accountability and risk management system to match.
Like its peer multilateral development banks (MDBs), the AIIB has committed to “do no harm” and to offer people a route to seek redress when its projects cause harm. Independent accountability mechanisms, separate from bank management, exist at most MDBs and other development finance institutions. Complaints pass through an initial screening stage, known as admissibility, eligibility, or registration, to establish whether they fall within the mechanism’s mandate. The mechanism then offers dispute resolution or, if parties do not agree to it, examines whether the bank followed its environmental and social rules through a compliance review.
Complaints Hit an Admissibility Wall
Communities affected by AIIB-financed projects have never been able to test whether the PPM process works. Since the mechanism’s creation in 2019, none of the 45 complaints tracked on its website as of September 15 this year had passed the admissibility stage. By contrast, peer mechanisms at other development banks regularly take complaints into dispute resolution or compliance review. One of the largest handled more than 60 cases in each of the last two financial years.
The revised policy introduced in 2026 raised hopes that the PPM would become more effective and improve its track record. Since it took effect, however, the PPM has found 14 out of 16 complaints inadmissible. The remaining two, submitted in May, are still awaiting an admissibility decision. The Mandalika complaint would be the 17th complaint of 2026.
The PPM’s entry requirements are significantly more restrictive than those of its peers. These “roadblocks to accountability” include referring complaints about co-financed projects to the lead lender, imposing narrow time limits on complaints about loans to governments, and requiring prior “good-faith efforts” to resolve grievances with both the project-level grievance mechanism and bank management.
Complainants must also establish at the admissibility stage that their complaint concerns the AIIB’s failure to comply with its policies, while the complaint mechanism must conduct an assessment that other mechanisms carry out only in later steps.
A central obstacle to accessibility is the requirement that complainants make “good-faith efforts” with both the project-level grievance mechanism and AIIB management. Under the PPM policy, complainants must explain why they could not resolve their concerns through these channels, and the PPM decides whether their efforts were sufficient.
The rule has previously been used to reject complaints, including one regarding the Bhola gas power plant in Bangladesh, despite attempts to engage amid legitimate constraints and fears of retaliation. The two complaints filed in May 2026 remain pending while complainants have been asked to engage with the client and management.
Requiring prior engagement at both levels is unique among these mechanisms. Some peers require good-faith efforts with bank management, but not with the project-level grievance mechanism as well. Nor do they require complainants to explain why those efforts failed. The PPM’s approach places that burden on the people seeking redress.
There are legitimate reasons why such engagement may be impossible. A client’s grievance mechanism may be inaccessible or ineffective. The client or management may refuse to engage meaningfully. Restrictions on movement and the threat of retaliation can create further barriers. In many of the AIIB’s borrowing countries, restrictive civic space makes these risks particularly acute.
The PPM policy lists risks of retaliation against complainants as a factor allowing the PPM to accept a complaint despite the absence of engagement with client and management. That provision has yet to be tested. It will only work only if the PPM trusts complainants’ accounts of why they could go no further and considers all relevant circumstances, including the risks they face. The Mandalika complaint will be an important test, as communities report continuing and increasing attempts at retaliation.
For complaints seeking a compliance review, the threshold is higher still. In addition to meeting the general criteria, they must relate their claim to the AIIB’s noncompliance with its environmental and social policy. The policy excludes complaints relating to actions “that do not involve AIIB’s failure to comply.”
As we understand the rules, complainants must show the bank’s noncompliance at the outset and, on the strictest reading, that it caused their harm. The evidence for this sits in AIIB’s due diligence and supervision records, which communities cannot see. They cannot know whether the AIIB checked a resettlement plan or what its staff found on supervision visits. Establishing these facts is the purpose of an investigation. Unlike most of its peers, the PPM asks complainants to supply evidence that the mechanism itself should establish.
These restrictions raise doubts about whether any complaint could qualify for compliance review under a strict interpretation of the criteria. Without a compliance review there are no findings: nothing to establish what went wrong, to support remediation for affected communities, or to help the bank improve its procedures and practices.
An Opportunity to Change Course
These technical restrictions run counter to a simple principle: admissibility is a straightforward step to establish whether a complaint falls within the mechanism’s mandate. At peer mechanisms, apart from formal exclusions, the substantive screening focuses on the complaint’s connection to a bank-financed project and its environmental and social policies, and on indications of actual or potential harm. Detailed examination comes later.
In a compliance review for instance, the mechanism must investigate whether the bank failed to comply with its policies and whether those failures relate to the alleged harm. That work can involve reviewing hundreds of project preparation and supervision documents, conducting field visits, and consulting intensely with affected people and other stakeholders. The admissibility phase is not the place for such an investigation.
Yet the PPM Policy and Rules of Procedure complicate this initial step, impose unduly strict restrictions, and demand substantial work from both complainants and the mechanism before a case can proceed. It is little surprise that no complaint has cleared this hurdle.
At the AIIB’s annual meeting, Zou spoke of infrastructure “connecting people to opportunities” and of “people-centered development.” Carmen Nonay, the new managing director of AIIB’s Complaints-resolution, Evaluation, and Integrity Unit, which includes the PPM, can help turn that vision into practice by bringing the mechanism into line with its peers. There are 22 other mechanisms with established practices to learn from.
The managing director has the authority and responsibility to interpret the PPM’s Rules of Procedure. The pending complaints offer an immediate opportunity to do so. We urge her to apply the policy and rules in line with established accountability practice: treat admissibility as a quick, straightforward first step; trust complainants’ accounts of their efforts and the risks they face; and hear them impartially before making a decision. The PPM should use its unrestricted access to management information to identify indications of noncompliance, rather than place that burden on complainants. This approach follows the PPM peers’ shared principles, reiterated this year, which put accessibility first: “A recourse mechanism is not effective if affected people do not know it exists or are unable to access its services.”
Because the PPM sits within the institution it reviews, its managing director may not feel sufficiently independent to pursue this approach. The AIIB board should make it clear that it expects the mechanism to follow its peers’ good practice. If the PPM still struggles to deliver on its mandate, the board should review the obstacles and require changes to the policy, particularly its accessibility provisions.
Almost eight years after the PPM’s creation, workers and communities affected by AIIB-financed projects deserve the same care and accountability as those affected by other MDBs. That is a matter of fairness and credibility for the AIIB and its shareholders. An accessible, effective complaints mechanism would strengthen the bank’s reputation and its ability to finance development sustainably.

MOSCOW, October 21. /TASS/. Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has called Vladimir Zelensky, who demanded 70 billion euros from the European Union for Ukraine's military needs in 2027, an insatiable monster.
She noted that Zelensky, deliberately speculating on the EU migration problems, turned to outright threats.
Zakharova said that Russia is actively preparing to participate in the Meeting of Foreign Ministers of the Group of Twenty (G20) countries in Atlanta, but sees "alarming trends" on the part of the United States.
TASS has compiled the key statements by the official representative of the Foreign Ministry.
G20 ministerial council
Russia is actively preparing to participate in the G20 ministerial council in Atlanta, but sees "alarming trends" on the part of the United States: "We have been preparing and are preparing, and our experts are doing it actively. The event is important because the ministerial G20 is preparatory for the summit, which is scheduled for December 14-15."
Despite the US administration statements, there are "some artificial restrictions for full-fledged Russian participation, some limits for the composition of the delegation, some incomprehensible conversations about statuses, visas, and accreditations."
Two months ago, Russia provided the United States with the lists of the delegation to the council, but it turned out that they "did not receive proper logistical support and confirmation, as we were told literally at night."
Zelensky's speculation
Zelensky, who at the EU summit in Brussels demanded 70 billion euros from the European Union for Ukraine's military needs in 2027, is an insatiable monster: "How much money do you think was raised by this insatiable monster this time? He needed at least 70 billion euros, as he stated."
Zelensky "did not bother with good manners and very brazenly demanded from the EU supervisors an additional increase in allocations for military needs."
"To enhance the compliance of the EU partners," Zelensky, deliberately speculating on the EU's migration problems, turned to outright threats.
Unrest in Europe
Russia has no information about its citizens injured during the riots in Europe: "We do not have data on Russian citizens injured during the riots. Our foreign institutions have not received such requests, and there have been no media reports on this issue."
The West's confrontational line
There are no prerequisites for changing the EU's confrontational line against Russia yet: "We note that the current European leaders, the vast majority of them, lack a strategic vision. We see undisguised Russophobia. We take all this into account and say that this is absolutely unacceptable for us."
Russia is ready to use all means to ensure security: "If necessary, the Russian Federation is ready to use a full range of available forces and means to stop and eliminate emerging threats."
Russia constantly warns NATO against unwinding the spiral of confrontation: "We regularly bring this principled approach to the leadership of the member countries of the bloc and the international NATO secretariat. At the same time, we are using all the diplomatic channels available to us, including multilateral platforms, to prevent further escalation of the spiral of confrontation and to convince them of the need to form a continental-wide Eurasian security and cooperation architecture."
Russia will respond "proportionately and effectively" to Finland's dangerous course of "total militarization of the country, including lifting restrictions on the deployment of nuclear weapons on its territory."
Former Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin drew attention to herself with a custom-made "stupidly aggressive" call to shoot down Russian military aircraft during their invasion of the airspace of EU and NATO countries: "We drew attention to the some kind of detached from reality and not even bellicose, but stupidly aggressive proposal by the former head of the Finnish government Sanna Marin to shoot down Russian military aircraft that allegedly violate the airspace of the EU and NATO countries."

Russia is "looking forward" to Poland and Lithuania’s reaction to the Ukrainian drone appearance on their territory: "We have been waiting impatiently for the reaction of Warsaw and Vilnius for several days.

Russia respects "the sovereign right of the republic to improve national migration legislation."
Poland's actions

Rashtriya Ekta Diwas 2026 to celebrate 'End of Naxalism': Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan
NEW DELHI: The end of armed Naxalism within the March 31, 2026 deadline set by home minister Amit Shah as well 150 years of ‘Vande Mataram’ will be celebrated at the Rashtriya Ekta Diwas parade and Bharat Parv at Kevadia, Gujarat, this year to mark Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel’s birth anniversary on Oct 31. Around 7,000 people from 126 districts that at some point of time were under the scourge of Left-wing extremism, will participate both as performers and spectators in the event to be graced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi.Union home secretary Govind Mohan on Wednesday said around 2,000 artists drawn from 126 districts that were once Naxal-affected, will join the celebrations by putting up a dramatic performance, directed by the National School of Drama (NSD), through which they will recount how their life and property were threatened when Naxalism was rampant in their area.
In addition, around 5,000 local people from these 126 districts have been invited. They will not only be spectators for all the performances but will also, through their interactions, share the hardships they had to undergo at the hands of Maoists and how their lives have changed now.“Their participation will underline the resilience of communities that have endured conflict and highlight the role of cultural expression in strengthening national integration,” said Govind Mohan.
The 2026 edition of the parade will also feature march-past by contingents of all the central armed police forces (CAPFs) and state police personnel who were in the forefront of the decisive fight against left-wing extremist violence. A short film will play on LED screens at the venue as the contingents pass in front of the Prime Minister, the chief guest, summarising the salient feature of their achievements in eliminating armed Naxalism.The three elements (marchpast, drama, interactions), the home secretary said, will showcase India’s struggle against armed Naxalism, the fact it has now been eradicated and most importantly, how development has replaced violence in the affected districts.
The Ekta Diwas parade, to be held in the evening hours this year, will also feature tableaux designed around the theme of “Vande Mataram” and constructed by the people and private entities with corporate social responsibility (CSR) funds, with no involvement of the govt. The 15 designs for the tableaux, selected through competition, are based on the implications of ‘Vande Mataram’ on nationhood and development.There will also be a cultural programme curated entirely by people from different states and communities who have made Gujarat their home. Around 5,000 artists will showcase dances and culture of their respective states through this mega-performance.A play will be organised on the eve of Oct 31 on the theme ‘Anand Math’. To be directed by NSD, it will be based on the abiding philosophy of Anand Math: that every person of India has a responsibility of building a bright future for the country and being aware of its cultural heritage.

EU member to relaunch talks with Moscow
Slovakia will discuss economic cooperation with Russia, including energy supplies, in Moscow next week, the Slovak Foreign Ministry has said.
The landlocked EU nation has remained a buyer of Russian oil and gas despite the deterioration of the ties between Moscow and the EU in the wake of the escalation of the Ukraine conflict. The country is supposed to phase out Russian energy by late 2027 under the bloc’s plan to replace Russian oil and gas supplies from elsewhere.
The Russian-Slovak intergovernmental commission for economic, scientific, and technical cooperation has been inactive since November 2021 but is now set to meet next Monday, the Slovak Foreign Ministry announced late on Tuesday. The commission will discuss a broad range of topics, including farming, environment, sports, and culture, and focus on energy supply, including nuclear energy, according to the ministry.
“The fundamental topic will be energy and the possibility to cooperate in securing supplies of strategic resources. The Slovak side is also interested in discussing gas supplies and the continuation of oil supplies,” it said in a statement.
Bratislava continues “to base its approach on its European Union and North Atlantic Alliance membership and keeping commitments of this membership” but wants to create room for dialogue, the ministry said.
Slovakia dissented on the EU’s course to dismantle ties with Moscow and prop up Kiev in the conflict after Robert Fico retook the prime minister’s office in October 2023, for the fourth time in his long political career. Under Fico, Slovakia has remained skeptical of assisting Ukraine and of Kiev’s push to join NATO, while halting government weapons shipments and calling for peace. The stance has resulted in repeated public spats between Bratislava and Kiev, as well as criticism from Brussels.
Last month, Fico warned that Europe was moving dangerously close to a direct clash between NATO and Russia, accusing the West of seeking a “pretext” for a major conflict. He accused EU nations of engaging in increasingly bellicose rhetoric and described the Ukraine conflict as “out of control.”
“The situation has never been as serious and tense regarding the possibility of a pan-European war conflict as it is now,” he said.

Why can't Saudi Arabia stop the Houthis' deadly attacks?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:46:00 UTC
02:46:00 KST

Saudi Arabia spends billions on its military. Why can't it stop deadly attacks by Iran's Houthi allies?
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks have inflicted severe losses on the kingdom, with missiles hitting energy infrastructure and civilian airports, killing at least 20 people.
The Iranian proxy group has struck the headquarters of Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company, and is fighting Saudi-backed government forces for control of Yemen's coastline on the Red Sea, a vital waterway for global energy supplies. The fighting has put further upward pressure on oil and gas prices as Iran and the U.S. fight over the nearby Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia, despite its size, wealth and a substantial military, has appeared to be on the back foot as it faces the Yemeni rebels. The kingdom's opaque government releases regular statements about Houthi ballistic missiles and drones being intercepted, including five it said were destroyed Wednesday.
But many have got through, including an Oct. 10 strike that killed 13 people at Riyadh's King Khalid Airport, including a U.S. citizen.
"No country can ever have a 100% interception rating, that just doesn't really exist," Elizabeth Dent, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, told CBS News, but that "was a hell of a one to miss."
Saudi Arabia spent $83 billion on defense last year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute — far more than any other country in the Middle East, including Israel.
So why has the kingdom struggled to stop the Houthi barrage?
Geography
Saudi Arabia is vast and, analysts say, geographically vulnerable.
Its east, home to the kingdom's oil fields, is bordered by the Persian Gulf — all that separates Saudi Arabia from longtime foe Iran. Early in the war, Iran launched strikes targeting bases used by the U.S. in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for U.S. attacks.
To the north, across Saudi Arabia's long border with Iraq, are Iran-backed militia groups that the Saudis — along with the U.S. — struck in July in response to dozens of attempted drone attacks on the kingdom's infrastructure and on U.S. installations in the region.
To the south, Saudi Arabia shares a more-than-800-mile border with Yemen. A vast portion of the war-wracked nation is controlled by the Houthis. To Saudi Arabia's west, the Houthis have also been battling for control of the Red Sea's vital shipping lanes.
"Over the last eight months, they have been facing threats from every direction," said Dent.
"There is a lot of critical infrastructure: multiple airports, many pipelines, as well as extensive oil production and export infrastructure, military bases, government buildings, royal palaces, and so on," said Thomas Juneau, associate fellow at the Chatham House think tank's Middle East and North Africa Program. "It is simply extremely difficult to provide air defenses for all these sites over such a large area."
"If the Houthis are able to hit Saudi infrastructure with only a minority of their attempted drone or missile attacks, it counts as a success for them and an embarrassment and a loss for Saudi Arabia," Juneau told CBS News.
Neither Saudi nor Houthi authorities responded to CBS News' request for comment on this story.
The interceptor shortage
The ongoing wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have caused a global supply shortage of the interceptors used to shoot down ballistic missiles and other weapons, including the U.S.-made Patriot system used by Saudi Arabia and other American allies.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, asked about Ukraine's longstanding request for Patriot interceptors, said Tuesday that "every other country in the world" also wants them.
"I also talked to Saudi Arabia today. They'd like interceptors. Israel would like interceptors. We would like interceptors. Every country in the world would like interceptors," Rubio said, calling it "probably the most in-demand product right now in the defense field."
"Demand coming from the international [market] is stronger than ever," Tim Cahill, president of missiles and fire control at Lockheed Martin, the world's biggest weapons manufacturer and maker of the Patriot interceptors, told CBS News last week when asked about the short supply.
Saudi Arabia is secretive about its weapons systems and stockpiles, but CBS News reported in March that Gulf countries were seeking emergency resupplies of interceptors, while the Wall Street Journal and Associated Press have reported that the kingdom has sought air defense systems from Japan, South Korea, France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt.
Patriot interceptors are expensive, costing as much as $4 million per unit.
"If there's fear over utilizing or drawing down your resources," said Dent, "are you more reticent to pull the trigger?"
Evolving Houthi tactics
Saudi Arabia has purchased 730 Patriot interceptors from Washington since 2020, according to U.S. military data, but even if it does have enough, the pricey missiles aren't ideal for combating everything in the Houthi arsenal.
Patriots were designed to intercept ballistic missiles, and the Houthis have launched those at Saudi Arabia. But the rebels also have an array of relatively cheap drones, including weapons supplied by Iran, and locally made copies of Iranian attack drones.
These inexpensive weapons have been a key element in the Houthis' tactics, analysts say.
They can be launched in swarms, Allison Minor, a senior fellow in the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told CBS News.
The Houthis "combine an overwhelming number of relatively cheap systems, namely drones, to distract and disrupt and exhaust, and then amid that, also weave in these more catastrophic missile attacks," she said.
The Saudis' multi-layered air defense system is sophisticated, but Houthi drones and cruise missiles can change their trajectory, making them harder to track, said Dent, "so if one aspect of that layered defense system breaks down, it can create a gap in coverage, like what may have occurred for the airport attack."
"This is a whole new ballgame," said Dent. "It's a tactic that requires some adjustments."
One possible solution could be Ukrainian-developed drone interceptors, which cost in the thousands of dollars to manufacture and are produced in the tens of thousands annually, unlike Patriots, which are produced in the hundreds.
Saudi Arabia and some of its neighbors have already made deals with Ukraine to acquire such systems, but Dent said they won't be a quick fix as "a lot of what the Ukrainians have been implementing is very hands-on."
The systems require skilled operators, in other words, and they require training.
A military with a narrow focus
Another issue is the Saudi personnel available to receive that training. Analysts do not rate the kingdom's military among the world's best, despite its huge defense budget.
Saudi Arabia's armed forces have a reputation for being "structured and run according to the interests of its royal leadership, with an emphasis on regime security," said CBS News national security analyst Aaron MacLean.
"You can spend all the money you want on your military and your missile defenses, but you also have to have a culture of readiness and excellence among the troops responsible," he said.
"If that's lacking, again, the problem is inherently a hard one: fighting intelligent people who really are trying to kill you and are willing to be quite creative in their pursuit of that goal," he said. "Some shots are going to get through."
When patchwork support "is too patchy"
Faced with Houthi successes and dwindling Patriots, the Saudis have been "aggressively seeking out air defense support from a variety of partners," said Minor, at CSIS.
The kingdom has invoked a mutual defense pact signed last year with Pakistan and Turkey, under which an attack on one country is considered an attack on all three, much like the NATO alliance's Article 5. Pakistan has already confirmed a troop deployment to the kingdom, and Turkey is also working toward sending forces.
France recently agreed to send "military means" to help protect the crucial Yanbu oil terminal on the Red Sea, and announced a separate agreement to help protect other Saudi oil facilities, without offering details.
The U.K. government said Tuesday that it would "fly defensive counter air missions" to protect Saudi cities and critical infrastructure from Houthi attacks, but that the aircraft would not take part in strikes against the group in Yemen.
Egypt announced Sunday that it was prepared to provide military assistance to Saudi Arabia.
Greece has operated a Patriot battery in Yanbu since 2021 and Italy, which has troops in Saudi Arabia and provided the Saudis with radar and anti-missile batteries before the war broke out in February, said in October that it could be willing to bolster the European Union mission protecting Red Sea shipping if other EU nations also step up.
There have also been reports of Saudi Arabia attempting to recruit foreign fighters, and using less reliable Chinese interceptors.
But this many-pronged approach to national defense could be problematic.
"Do you eventually get to a point where that patchwork is too patchy?" asked Minor. "The interoperability of different troops and aircraft and radar and interception systems — does that become too much to manage at some point?"
The key question, she said, is the extent of the Houthis' own weapons stockpiles.
"The Houthis have maintained a very steady pace of attacks over the past few weeks," she said. "It's not clear to me if the Houthis are able to sustain that for the long term — if they're gearing up for another years-long confrontation, or if this is an intense shorter-term salvo to try to get back to the negotiating table on better terms."

Millions in cheese revenue lost as protest hits Italy’s buffalo mozzarella output

A truckers’ protest in southern Italy has halted the production of the famed buffalo mozzarella, causing an estimated loss of €3 million (US$3.37 million) in just 24 hours as the milk cannot reach dairies in the Naples region and the finished cheese cannot reach customers, an official said.

The disruption is particularly damaging to buffalo mozzarella because the production of the protected cheese depends on a tightly timed supply chain.

Our digital lives increasingly depend on data centers. How do we secure them?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:49:58 UTC
02:49:58 KST

When Alexander Olshansky received a call in September telling him that the data center hosting his company's infrastructure in Kyiv had been destroyed by a Russian attack, he made a beeline for the scene.
“As I was driving up to the data center, I saw a column of black smoke, a block cordoned off by the police and fire trucks,” recalls Olshansky, president of the Ukrainian domain registration and Web hosting provider MiroHost. The data center was damaged, but Olshansky’s employees had been sheltering elsewhere when the attack happened.
Despite the facility’s destruction on September 23, just around one in 20 of MiroHost’s customers were affected. The company had reserved enough computing capacity in Poland, the Czech Republic and Slovakia to back up its Ukrainian infrastructure in the event of an attack.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Other data centers haven’t fared as well. In October Ukrainian drones struck three data centers operated by the Russian technology giant Yandex, disrupting services and damaging artificial intelligence infrastructure. Earlier this year Iranian drones damaged Amazon Web Services facilities in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, causing Web outages across the region.
What is inarguable is that, like them or not, data centers are increasingly important parts of our lives, and as such, they’re increasingly seen as fair targets in war. How they are secured is a matter of national—and even international—importance.
“I would say 2026 is going to be the first year of drone strikes taking out data centers being a thing,” says Doug Madory, head of international Internet analysis at the cybersecurity company Infoblox. “I just don’t think that anybody had anticipated this as a risk to interrupt service.”
Because of their vital role in the economy, data centers are designed with multiple layers of security. These include restricted access to the site, constant surveillance and backup power systems. In the event of fire, suppression equipment keeps flames at bay. But those defenses are mostly focused on stopping bad actors from getting inside or on keeping services running when equipment fails—not on withstanding attacks from the air.
“Most data center security standards in the industry focus on physical access restrictions,” says Connor Martin, an international affairs fellow in national security at the Council on Foreign Relations. But protecting facilities against drone or missile strikes is a different challenge—and one the sector must start focusing on. Data centers can seem like sitting ducks from the air because they’re massive, cavernous buildings containing enormously expensive equipment in often remote areas. They “can’t pick up and move,” Martin says.
Still, some protection is possible without going as far as installing missile defenses at key data center locations. Peter Judge, senior research analyst at the Uptime Institute, says operators can build shields around vulnerable equipment such as generators and air-handling units and use overhead netting or screens to hinder aerial surveillance. Yet more sophisticated systems might combine radar, cameras and radio sensors to identify approaching drones or aircraft.
But if a craft is spotted, what can actually be done is trickier. Aviation laws typically prevent jamming drone signals—scrambling their radio signals—or bringing them down without authorization. Some newer drones don’t transmit radio control signals at all.
For his part, Olshansky isn’t convinced physical protection is viable in a war zone anyway. “No fire suppression system is designed for a direct hit by a bomb, missile or drone,” he says.
Truly protecting such a facility could mean burying it deep underground, which isn’t feasible. Instead, the industry’s best approach may be in redundancy—distributing services across multiple facilities so that when one is destroyed, another can take over. It works, as MiroHost showed, but it also costs more: Olshansky says his company effectively doubled its available computing capacity to prepare for an attack.
Madory points out that cloud providers already offer ways to distribute workloads across different geographic regions. The problem is that many customers don’t bother because of the additional cost and technical complexity. “In theory, you could be resilient, but in practice, a lot of stuff is not,” he says.
The recent attacks could change where companies choose to build their data centers, Martin says. The Gulf states have invested heavily in attracting those kinds of instalments, but their proximity to regional conflicts could make future projects harder to justify. Larger countries such as the U.S. and China, meanwhile, have more opportunities to build facilities far from potential conflict zones. But even then, there are no guarantees. As Olshansky says, “It is always better to have two copies of something than just one, even if it is highly protected.”

Vvedensky Monastery in Kyiv damaged in overnight attack: two people injured
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
20:50:16 EEST
02:50:16 KST

The Vvedensky Monastery in Kyiv sustained damage during an overnight attack after drone debris fell onto the monastery grounds, leaving two people with shrapnel wounds, the Union of Orthodox Journalists reports.
"At approximately 3:05 a.m., drone debris fell onto the monastery grounds. The roof and walls were damaged, and windows were blown out. Two people. who were assisting in the monastery kitchen. sustained shrapnel wounds. The brethren were unharmed," the Union stated on its Facebook page on Thursday.
Despite the damage and the injuries sustained, the Divine Liturgy was celebrated at the monastery that morning.
The Holy Vvedensky Monastery in Kyiv was founded in 1878 as a women’s religious community, initiated by Matrona Yegorova, the widow of a Crimean War officer. In 1901, the community was transformed into a monastery. The cloister was closed during the Soviet era. Religious services resumed at the Vvedensky Church in 1992, and in December 1996, the parish was reorganized into a men’s monastery.
