Ukrainian forces have destroyed over 400,000 Russian drones since start of 2026, Defence Ministry reports
Ukrainian forces have destroyed 408,000 Russian drones, including nearly 248,000 fixed-wing drones, since the start of 2026.
Source: Ukraine's Ministry of Defence
Details: The ministry said the downed drones also include nearly 125,000 multirotors and more than 35,000 Shahed-type drones.
For comparison, on 11 August, the ministry reported that more than 260,000 Russian UAVs had been downed since the start of the year, and on 22 September, the figure had risen to more than 350,000. This means the total increased by approximately 58,000 drones over the past month.
"Every hit is recorded on video in the Delta battlefield situational awareness system and verified by the Brave1 defence innovation cluster," the ministry said.
Background: In August, Ukrainian forces destroyed the largest number of Russian multirotor drones since the launch of the e-points E-points are earned by Ukrainian units for confirmed strikes on Russian soldiers and equipment programme.

Three Ukrainian children, their mother and two young people brought back from occupation
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:54:00 EEST
01:54:00 KST

Three Ukrainian children, their mother and two young people brought back from occupation
Another five children and young people have been successfully brought back from temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.
Source: Bring Kids Back UA, a Ukrainian government-led effort to bring Ukrainian children home from temporarily Russian-occupied territories
Details: Under occupation, the children were forced to accept Russian passports and sing the Russian national anthem at school, Bring Kids Back UA reported.
When the full-scale invasion began, brothers Ihor, Andrii and Dmytro (names changed) and their mother were living in their hometown, which was soon occupied by Russian forces. From then on the family lived under constant pressure and restrictions from the occupation authorities.
Andrii attended a kindergarten under occupation, while Dmytro was in the sixth grade at a local school. Their mother said the children were forced to sing the Russian national anthem there, and the curriculum contained Russian propaganda.
The family also faced forced "passportisation", with the occupation authorities demanding that the parents obtain Russian documents.
Experts from the Ukrainian Child Rights Network, working with The Humanity Funds, helped get the family out safely.
The boys and their mother are now in Ukrainian-controlled territory. They will be helped through the adaptation and reintegration processes and will return to the Ukrainian education system.
Two young people, Albina and Viacheslav, were brought back with the assistance of a team from Helping to Leave.
Albina lived in the temporarily occupied part of Zaporizhzhia Oblast and decided to leave for Ukrainian-controlled territory on her own. She planned her route herself and got as far as the Mokrany-Domanove checkpoint between Belarus and Ukraine, but she could not cross the border because she did not have a Ukrainian passport.
It was then that she contacted Helping to Leave. Volunteers advised her on the documents she needed and helped coordinate her onward route.
In Minsk, Albina obtained a certificate enabling her to return to Ukraine and was able to continue her journey. She is now with relatives in Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Viacheslav found out about Helping to Leave from a friend whom the team had previously helped leave the occupation. After he reached out, volunteers helped him plan his route and supported him during his departure.
On the way, Viacheslav also helped a friend by taking two of her cats with him. Upon arrival in Ukraine, Viacheslav was met by a team from Helping to Leave who helped him find temporary accommodation.
He is currently obtaining new documents and planning his future in Ukraine. The cats have been reunited with their owner too.
Background: Previously, we reported on how 23 children and teenagers who had endured constant pressure, threats and fear were brought back from occupation to Ukrainian-controlled territory.

The International Exhibition Centre (IEC) has cancelled its upcoming exhibitions due to the security situation in Kyiv, the press service of the ARS Capital holding company informed Interfax-Ukraine.
Among the cancelled events are three major food industry exhibitions: Agro2Food, showcasing technologies, equipment, and solutions for agricultural processing and the food industry; World Food Ukraine, an international food and beverage exhibition; and inSKLAD, an exhibition focused on technologies, equipment, and solutions for warehouse logistics.
"We understand that visitors, participants, and partners, who invested significant effort into preparing for these events, were looking forward to them. However, under the current circumstances, we are compelled to make difficult decisions and prioritize our responsibility toward people. We thank everyone for their understanding, support, and trust. We look forward to returning to our normal operational rhythm as soon as possible," the holding’s press service stated.
Any further changes to the schedule will be announced on the IEC website.
It was previously reported that the IEC is equipped with a shelter capable of accommodating approximately 2,300 people.
IEC LLC is Kyiv's largest exhibition venue. According to YouControl, its 100% ultimate beneficiary is Maksym Krippa, who gained control of the asset in the summer of 2025. In the first half of 2026, the IEC's net income reached UAH 39.435 million, surpassing the results of the same period last year by 36%, while the net loss decreased to UAH 2.195 million from UAH 16.395 million for January-June 2025.
According to the center's website, the total area of the complex is 73,230 square meters, and the total exhibition hall area is 38,680 square meters. It combines four pavilions with exhibition areas of 10,850 square meters, 10,660 square meters, 10,560 square meters, and 6,600 square meters, along with 18 entrance groups and 20 cargo gates for delivering oversized cargo directly to the exhibition halls.

Türkiye, Canada seal strategic partnership to advance economic, defence ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:36:25 UTC
02:36:25 KST

Türkiye and Canada have launched a strategic partnership aimed at strengthening bilateral cooperation in trade, investment, energy, defence, security, and technological development.
The announcement followed a meeting between Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday at the Presidential Complex in Ankara, where Erdogan welcomed Carney with an official ceremony.
The leaders held bilateral talks, followed by discussions between their delegations and a joint news conference.
'Canada-Türkiye partnership is essential'
In a joint statement on the partnership, the leaders said: "In an increasingly complex global security environment, rising geopolitical uncertainties, and evolving humanitarian challenges, a strong and resilient Canada-Türkiye partnership is essential, providing a foundation to mitigate shared threats and capitalise on new opportunities.”
Building on 83 years of diplomatic relations, the partnership aims to expand political dialogue, boost economic growth and trade, advance technological development, and strengthen shared security objectives, it said.
Both countries are NATO allies and reaffirmed their commitment to human rights, individual liberties, democracy, and the rule of law.
The leaders also launched a three-year action plan built around four pillars: trade, investment, and innovation; energy and climate cooperation; defence and security; and government-to-government dialogue and people-to-people ties.
Trade, investment, and innovation
Under the first pillar, Canada and Türkiye agreed to work toward successfully concluding a bilateral free trade agreement and expanding trade and investment in priority sectors, including energy supply, defence production, aerospace, and artificial intelligence.
They also committed to ratifying the Canada-Türkiye Air Transport Agreement, strengthening cooperation between trade and export agencies, including on projects in third countries, and promoting collaboration between their innovation ecosystems.
Energy and climate cooperation
The two countries pledged to advance cooperation across the energy sector, including liquefied natural gas, civil nuclear energy, renewable energy, clean technologies, and the resilience of critical energy infrastructure.
The plan also calls for encouraging investment, facilitating dialogue among nuclear sector stakeholders, strengthening sustainable mining and critical minerals supply chains, and expanding cooperation on climate resilience and environmental protection.
The leaders welcomed a joint statement on energy cooperation agreed upon by their respective energy and natural resources ministers.
Canada also welcomed Türkiye's role as host and president of next month’s COP31 UN Climate Change Conference in the southern city of Antalya, starting on November 9.
Ottawa expressed its readiness to work closely with Türkiye's presidency to ensure a successful conference.
Defence and security
The leaders pledged to deepen bilateral and multilateral defence cooperation, including through NATO, building on a recently signed statement of intent on defence cooperation.
They agreed to strengthen efforts to support peace and security in the Euro-Atlantic region and beyond, including in Ukraine, the South Caucasus, and the Middle East, particularly Gaza.
The statement also welcomed the conclusion of a memorandum of understanding on defence sector partnerships between Global Affairs Canada and Türkiye’s Defence Industries Secretariat.
The agreement is intended to facilitate expanded defence industry partnerships and advance discussions on further cooperation in areas of mutual interest.
The leaders also emphasised the importance of initiating a dialogue on strengthening mutual legal assistance in criminal matters and extradition.
Political dialogue and people-to-people ties
Under the fourth pillar, the countries agreed to establish an annual Canada-Türkiye Strategic Dialogue while continuing annual meetings of the joint economic and trade committee, as well as political-military and counterterrorism consultations.
They also pledged to strengthen cooperation on consular matters and migration, explore measures to facilitate travel and mobility, and promote cultural exchanges and engagement with their respective diasporas.
The two leaders agreed that their foreign ministers would oversee implementation of a three-year action plan with the goal of deepening bilateral relations, promoting international security, and building prosperous green economies.
Carney expressed appreciation for the Turkish government's warm hospitality during his visit, described in the joint statement as the first visit by a head of government between the two countries.
Türkiye also welcomed an invitation for Erdogan to visit Canada at a mutually agreeable time.

Russia’s Justice Ministry insists every fact in its online history exhibit was checked against archival records. The exhibit included a mangled Putin quote and a Nazi film praising Hitler.

02:44:07 KST

Russia’s Justice Ministry insists every fact in its online history exhibit was checked against archival records. The exhibit included a mangled Putin quote and a Nazi film praising Hitler.
Every fact in the Russian Justice Ministry’s online exhibition was checked, and the “foreign agents” who found errors in it were knowingly spreading false information, Deputy Justice Minister Oleg Sviridenko said in a TASS interview cited by the news outlet Agentstvo.
In late July, the Justice Ministry posted an exhibition on its website titled “Zashchita suvereniteta Rossiyskogo gosudarstva. Istoriya i sovremennost” (“Protecting the Sovereignty of the Russian State: Past and Present”), about attempts to “violate the sovereignty” of Russia. Independent journalists found a propaganda film about Hitler in the section containing photographs and documentaries. Elsewhere in the exhibition, they found numerous errors, including factual ones, and signs that artificial intelligence had been used to write the text.
In the interview, Sviridenko was asked whether he had expected such a strong response from “foreign-agent media outlets.”
Sviridenko called the attention “foreign agents” paid to the project “a predictable reaction.” “Their job is to spread distorted information among Russian citizens, falsify history, and replace facts with interpretations that serve their Western ‘employers,’” he said.
He said all the exhibition materials had been prepared with input from “historians, representatives of Russia’s leading museums, historical institutions, and organizations involved in historical scholarship.” Sviridenko said every fact in the exhibition had been checked against primary sources in archives.
